Evolve is one of those games that, from my point of view, most people hated for the sake of hating. The gameplay was fun, rewarding, and very well done. It's the pricing and business aspect that spawned a mob of anger that spread across the community like wildfire. Alot of folks found themselves hearing: "It's a great game, but don't buy it". Due to this, and overall disdain of the game and the business practices that came with it, the community was left a barren husk with very few new players, and even less older ones.
With Stage 2, the game's developers take a new route, one of the complete F2P model.
I'm extremley excited by the new additions and platform, which will bring in more and more players to a fantastic game, while not falling into the trap alot of f2p games do. The unlocks system isnt tedious, annoying, or one designed to make you spend money. It's a fun system that brings rewards quick enough, but provides alot more if you do decide to invest some cash. All characters are very well balanced in Stage 2, and therefore sticking back and not having everyone unlocked is still a viable and easy way to play.
Turtle Rock has proven to be a devoted and wonderful developer that has taken all the hate and criticisim in the world, and turned it around to make their game brand new and even more of a blast to play than it was when it first realeased.

In Turing Test you take position of Ava who was just woken up from hybernation by T.O.M., an AI controlling a reserch facility built on one of Jupiter's moons. Something in the facility happened and T.O.M. can't find any member of the current research team, so Ava is supposed to find them. After arrival on Europa it seems that ground team barricaded themselves and only way how to get to them is solving Turing tests - tests which can be beaten only by a human. Neither Ava nor T.O.M. knows why, so they need to get to them in order to find out.
✪ Interesting story, not a one to win nobel prize, but still makes you think about things that have been said in this game.
✪ Graphics, visuals and surroundings make nice sci-fi like environment
✪ Puzzlesolving in new interesting ways
✪ Relaxing gameplay, calming music
✪ Lack of explanations. The game is more philosophical than explaining, there are many questions raised, but almost none of them answered. I know its on purpose, but I'd like to know more from The Turing test universum.
✪ This game is beaten in 5-6 hours for completionist. I think its very short time for this kind of game.
✪ Most of the puzzles are way too simple and not much thorough. On the other hand it makes the game flow.
The Turing Test is a first person puzzle game which shows inovation in this field of gaming although The Turing test borrowed a lot from Portal 2, which I think is only a plus. Eventhough the puzzles are more or less simple and quiet repetitive, beating them is still very enjoyable, especially afterwards, when you uncover more information about events that happened on Europa where the story is set.
In spite of the potential the game shows I think the game mechanics was not exploited enough and The Turing test could have been much better with the right care. There could be so much more, I imagine deeper story, better puzzles etc. Nevertheless I personally enjoyed the gameplay as it is now and recommend it to anyone who's looking for something relaxing, not challenging.

Also - I was always impressed with Portals puzzles in how you actually do truly solve them and there is no way to "hack" through a puzzle by blocking a door with a cube or some other mechanic that is "outside" of the possibility of solving the puzzle.  In TT, there are a few puzzles that appear to be unsolveable without doing just that such as tilt the platform just right so the height that your character can jump allows you to go somewhere you really didn't figure out how to get there the normal way, or block a door with a cube.  You could argue "That is solving the puzzle" but it leaves a disappointing feeling that you just tricked out the game and didn't really complete the task.
Regardless - was worth the $$$.  Good graphics and game play. Good things in general:
+Parkour
+Beautiful scenery
Good things compared to the original game
+Investigations are gone. While it's a shame that there are no missions where you can learn additional info about your targets or something that would help you in the assassination, considering how the original game had plenty of repetitive tasks for barely useful info, I guess nothing is better than something bad.
+The storytelling is much better. Instead of the whole story basically spanning only the first and final few scenes, with tons of filler in the middle, most of the main story in the game feels like it actually is the main story. And it was quite interesting.
+The story in this game spans several years, rather than just a few months, with timeskips in appropriate places, thus not making it seem like everything is resolved in a day.
+Addition of customisation and an actual variety of weapons. Though, too bad that it's mostly just an upgrade from a weapon with lower stats to a weapon with higher stats. Would have been nice if multiple weapons were good, but in different areas, thus giving you a choice in gear based on your preferences.
+A money system and a home economic system. A nice incentive for working on side content.
+Ability to hire followers to serve as a distraction or help during battles.
+Guards no longer just randomly attack you for looking at them funny or just riding on a horse. Though, otherwise, the notoriety system seems a bit of a hit or miss to me. Throughout my playthrough, it built up quite slowly, but was awfully easy to get rid of. Could just be me though.
+Certain guards actually have the brains to look in various obvious hiding spots.
+Fast travel is incorporated into the world as caravans that you can hire to transport you to places. An in-story explanation for fast travel is a nice touch.
+The possibility of outrunning guards to lose them, instead of always needing a hiding place or killing all the pursuers just to get them off your back.
+All the collectables actually have some sort of reward.
+You no longer need to pickpocket specific people just to replenish your ammo. You can now either loot consumables from fallen enemies, or just buy the stuff at a store.
+The real world segments are far rarer and less interruptive than in the previous game. Though it's a shame that the real world still basically didn't really matter at all.
Some bad things about the game
-uPlay. A completely unnecessary annoyance.
-Can't replay missions unless you start over, unlike in the original game.
-Still can't skip cutscenes. The cutscenes are nice the first time, but not so much the second time.
-The pistoletta takes too long to aim and it's loud, so it's worse than throwing knives most of the time.
-Fast travel can't be used to travel between districts in the same city.
-No feature to replenish all ammo at once. Replenishing everything manually is a bit annoying.
All in all, Assassin's Creed 2 was a fun game to play, especially compared to the original.

- Just like the original game, gameplay is so tight. Its incredible fun jumping from roof to roof, escaping enemies and assinating them from stealthy positions.
- The storyline is very engaging. The characters are well fleshed out and the dialogue is well written and funny at times.
- Animations are varied and very well done, sound design is great. The game ran perfectly with no major bugs or breaking.
- Altought a few years old the cities are still pretty breathtaking. As you're sitting atop a tall building looking down on a vibrant city, you can't help but be amazed at times.
==============
================
- The game is very easy. I played on normal difficulty initially and it was a walk in the park. They only times you're really going to fail is being discovered during a stealthy mission or falling from a large height (which is sometimes the fault of a bad camera angle)
- I did mention the gameplay is great, and it is, but at times it can be frustrating when Ezio doesn't do what you want him to. Also they added a monetary system which felt like a waste. I always had tonnes of money, so much so that it became redundant. Costs 100 to fast travel somewhere? Cool just take it out of my 1,000,000. This also made purchasing health too easy, in turn making an already easy game, even easier.
- The AI at times felt a little weak. On the roof of a huge building while its occupant is worried about an assasin? The guards will just tell you to get down. That guy will get fired. Escort missions can be a tad frustrating and even one time an enemy half way across the city somehow could still see me when he got stuck. I had to travel all the way to kill him as he walked into a wall.
- Although there is a lot of variation, some of the missions types become quite stale towards the end.

The Cave isn't a hard game to recommend, it has a charming art style, some brilliant voice acting, and a focus on interesting characters that has been somewhat lost in gaming recently. I doubt that you'd be surprised to hear that this game was developed by Double Fine, as the Psychonauts-esque zaniness and humour remains present in this title.
The game is not without its peeves though. Take for example the fact that there are 7 characters with unique stories, yet you cannot adventure with more than 3 of them at the same time. This means playing through the game 3 times, once with 2 characters you've already played with, left as irritating third wheels. What's more, each character has a good ending and a bad ending, which means playing through the game more than once with each character anyway in order to obtain all the endings (Which I wouldn't personally recommend doing, seeing as the endings change very little) There are even several default levels in-between the character driven story levels, which you have to play every time, and playing through these levels becomes tedious very quickly, as you are often forced to backtrack in these stages.
Despite all this, I'd recommend this title. Maybe not full price, but on sale, it's a no-brainer purchase.

Intro:
Ah Evolve. How you shook up Gaming's little big planet (LBP REFERENCE) when you announced your DLC plans before showing us a single clip of gameplay footage. How angry we were when the game's season pass didn't cover all the DLC. How people went bonkers after finding out about the amount of DLC offers and the cost of microtransactions after paying full price for a Triple A videogame.
And there you were.Trampled, hurt, on the verge of kissing Death itself... When a wild Free to Play appears and heals you at the nearest Pokestop. (POKEMON (GO) REFERENCE).
Evolve was a success in commercial terms. The game was fairly well received and initially it sold well, it's just that the outrage and the media caused so much damage to the game's image and the DLC was so expensive that it wasn't enough to sustain its life long enough. People were sick of it. TurtleRock Studios however, seem to believe in the game's concept because they decided to make a move that many wanted and predicted, but didn't expect to actually see. A Free to play Evolve with a generous and rewarding progression system.
TRS seem to have figured out that making this game free to play, and giving players the option of unlocking all the characters (and other content that was previously DLC-only) would give the game a highly successful second lease on life.
-------------------------------------------------
The facts:
So, what's changed? Is it just a transparent pretty picture on a cardboard box? (METAL G- *Shot*) Or is it really that good?
1 - Gameplay
The game's mechanics have changed a great deal. From slow matches that involved calculating Hunters following an elusive hard-to-catch monster across relatively large maps (when compared to the maps we have now), to a game where catching and tracking the monster is the least of your concerns. Hunters are fast and have abilities that can show the location and direction of the monster.
The monster evolves faster than before, making the games last about half as long as it was before. Combined with perks (Think Call of Duty *SHOT* That wasn't a- *SHOT*) that can do anything from making you do more damage/over time, to eating faster, to being able to boost your speed more often, you name it.
For both the monster and the Hunters: The pace of the game has increased to, one could say, Arcade gameplay. To some gamers's discontent.
2 - The Progression system
The progression system now offers you so called "Keys". Which are actually just silver coins with a giant "K" inscribed on both sides, but whatever. They put flamethrowers on dogs.
- Levelling up your account, and characters (Hunters and Monsters) offer variable rewards. One level could give you a free level of a Perk, or you'll get a new badge (profile icon), or maybe some extra Keys. These rewards are not randomized and so increase based on your level.
- A daily reward system. Log in once a day and you'll get a daily reward. Log multiple days (can have pauses in between) and you'll get an extra reward. The extra reward can even be complete, full, characters. Save up the money for the ones you don't get for free!
- Daily Challenges. Every day you'll receive a few challenges to complete. "Win a match". "Win a match as support, assault, or Kraken." "Play 3 matches as an assault, medic, or Goliath". These are just a couple of examples, and these too offer a variable amount of Keys.
3 - Content
Evolve Stage 2, at the time of writing, is in Beta. As I stated, the gameplay is faster. The maps are smaller. Half of the game's maps and some other content, hasn't been re-made in the faster playstyle. This means that not all of the original Evolve content is playable. TRS has said they will be released as time goes by, maps being free, and chars. being unlockable.
4 - A metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of players.
Evolve was dead, Jim. Did I mention that? It ain't now. More than a million new players within two weeks of the game's launch is a good sign. Of course some people will like it more than others. Some will recommend it to their friends, while others won't. At least this time, Evolve won't perish because of its corporate greed, or lack of content. It will probably be far in the future, on Evolve 2's release date. (One can hope).
Did I miss anything? Criticism? Comments? Go ahead. I'll be sure to reply or ignore you depending on which way the wind blows.

Assassins Creed 2 is a massive improvement over the first game in every single way. The first game lacked so many features that make a game enjoyable and was just a barebones, repetitive experience (in my opinion). Assassins Creed 2 has good graphics and great music. The story is interesting with excellent voice acting. There's actually some really awesome parts and intriguing concepts in there, story wise. There's quite a lot to do in this game, there's the main story, side missions, viewpoints, codex pages, glypths and finding chests. There's also actually shops and items now, which is a welcomed addition. The world isn't really "open world" with a huge map, it's more just free roam inside a city with some outskirts, still cool though. The world really feels alive too. After a like an hour you unlock the ability to upgrade the Villa by spending money and collecting things which increase the value and in turn give you income. I LOVED this feature, like seriously. The more you spend on it, the more you get in return (over time), it's such a great concept.
Now some things I didn't like. The climbing and movement still isn't the best, so many times your character jumps off of something when you don't mean to. The combat is average at best. At first it seems really cool with the awesome animations and counter attacks and dodges etc, but it gets old fast, especially against "bosses". You basically just either spam, throw an enemy and stab, or stand there and wait for the counter attack. Also if you've got allies you just keep walking up behind and stabbing, I don't know, it doesn't feel "fun" after awhile, it's just boring. I mentioned bosses, but the thing is, there's no real "boss" battles besides 1 or 2 big bosses but thats it and it's just spam them to death. The game also feels quite repetitive after awhile, and after like 60% of the game you'll have bought everything and money will mean nothing which sucks. Also the game crashed like 5-6 times during my playthrough.
A few things that are personal opinion, some might like it, others (like me), didn't like it at all. There's no real customizable progression system here. I mean like, sure you unlock more stuff as you play, more tools to use and such, but there's no skill tree or way to change the game to suit your playstyle. There's also so many super lengthy jumping puzzles that get extremely tedious and frustrating after awhile. The Glypths..... like 80% of the puzzles seem impossible to solve without just random clicking or 200 IQ. I know many would disagree, but I think the stealth is quite poorly done and can be super frustrating, to me atleast. One small little thing and you fail and have to repeat, and unless you know the perfect way to do every stealth mission it's just trial and error, which gets annoying.
This is quite a small thing, but I don't like playing with subtitles because I feel that I spend too much time looking at/reading them that I'm not really watching the scene and feel less immersed, but the game almost forces you to use subtitles. There's so many times when Ezio and others talks in Italian so unless you got subtitles on you'll miss quite a lot of dialogue. One last thing, the map is really laggy, doesn't really matter too much though.
Overall I think Assassins Creed 2 is a really solid game. I personally found most enjoyment in this game through the story and upgrading the Villa, everything else didn't really impact me that much.

Do you pine for the days when men were men and had to fight tooth and nail to finish a game? Then Waveform is for you.
This game is so simple to learn it's almost criminal. You control a sine wave, modifying only the amplitude and wavelength using the mouse. That is all. XY axis, no mouse buttons, no keypresses.
Simple to learn, yet hard to master. It will test your reflexes, dilligence and patience. It will force you to memorize wacky level patterns. But it always plays fair. No RNGesus to rely on - only you and your wave.
After 100%-ing about 140 titles (some trivial, some very hard) I can say: this is one of the hardest, most satisfying and overall best games I ever played.

Not even on a Steam Sale
First the good stuff: Art and character design
This game has a whimsical art style and can be a fun cross between puzzles and light platforming, with particularly funny narration and character design.
The bad stuff: Poorly executed forcing of replay
The game punishes users for indulging in that whimsy. The game forces painfully slow backtracking as you figure out a puzzle. Funnily enough, what's worse is when you can't backtrack: Because you frequently pass points of no return accidentally and the game autosaves, you can't have fun exploring an area you've completed because you risk losing access to collectibles or missable achievements. If that is a part of gaming you enjoy, it pretty much forces you to play with a guide open to keep you from missing anything, completely devaluing the collectibles and achievements.
However the most aggregious, avoidable design sin is tha for each playthrough you select 3 out of 7 characters (I'll say it again: Three) to take through the campaign, which changes three character specific levels to the game. Did you catch that? The selection of three out of seven? If you are going to obligate replays like this, why not have a number of playable characters that is divisible by three!? This is infuriating and since several puzzles in the cave are permenant fixtures, not character specific, this means you have to play through some puzzles 3 times, and other puzzles (for the two characters you'll play twice) 2 times. Getting all achievements demands a total of 5 playthroughs, but by then you'll have lost all interest.
There are some great indie-like titles on Steam, I encourage you to find them instead of buying this one, regardless of the price.

Too hard and not fun.
First, I should say that I rarely play sidescrollers these days.  I bought Cuphead because there's a ton of hype around it currently and the art style is very unique and attractive.  After spending an hour with this game, it's clear that I am not the intended audience and asked for a refund.  I can only envision someone who already currently plays hard sidescrollers as being who this game is made for.  I say that because it is ridiculously hard from the get-go.  Personally, I need an amount of acclimation to a game before I decide if it's worth it or not to play it in a more challenging way.  Cuphead doesn't really give you that option.  The boss levels have an option for "simple", but the run-n-gun levels do not and it was the very first one (with the flowermen running at you) that showed me that I would need to play it A LOT in order to advance through the game.
There has been an ongoing trend for a little while now of extreme difficulty in some games. It's fine if that's what you're into, but too often I feel like this is synonymous with doing the same thing over and over until you (luckily) succeed.  I would like to be given a chance to master the mechanics without the nagging "game"yness of dying then taking a couple of seconds to respawn while the music resets.  I think many games can go a long way to alleviate frustration by having instantaneous restarts and letting the music continue without interuption.  Hotline Miami does this well.  I can die countless times and not feel a lot of frustration because the music is appealing to me and keeps playing.  On top of which, the instant restarts keep me in the experience of feeling like I have control.
While the art style is exceptional, one problem I have with it is that it can be difficult to see what is going on.  Those flowermen enemies when killed turn into a ball of smoke that can obscure other enemies.  A couple of times I found myself dying by whatever was blocked out by the smoke.
So, the purpose of this review (and all reviews) is too give others an indication as to whether this is for them or not.  If, like me, the challenge of repeatedly doing something over and over again before you're able to advance doesn't sound fun then I would not recommend you get Cuphead.  Cuphead is just too hard, too quickly for my tastes.  It's obvious that a lot of people are into this, so measure my opinion against what sort of experience you are looking for.

Typing of The Dead: Overkill is a game where you kill zombies by typing, it is based on the zombie game House of the Dead: Overkill.
Gameplay is simple and straightforward. Your point of view moves through the game world automatically, all you have to do is type every word that floats into view in order to kill the zombies. About capitalization, spaces, or punctuation you do not have to worry. How fast the zombies in front of you will attack is indicated by the colour surrounding the words.
The words that pop up are randomised, so each player's experience of the game is unique.
The storyline is presented cinematically with film scratches, a psychedelic "intermission" screen when data is being loaded. Each of the 9 chapters arrive with a movie trailer voiceover that perfectly captures the spirit of the cheap golden age of bad movies.
Besides of the normal game mode there is a little arcade mode of mini-games where you can try out a survival mode with forever-spawning waves of zombies. The game also comes with the full version of the House of the Dead: Overkill, so you can play through it with mouse or controller if you want.
The game can also be played cooperatively.
The graphics are bad. The textures and models look pretty miserably when you are playing.
The sound and dialogues can be really annoying after a while.
However, I think criticising it for being ugly is to miss the point. The game is funny with hilarious characters and overall an enjoyable game that I would recommend if you want to improve your typing ability.

This game has everything I could ever ask for: Lovable characters, a creative world, interesting story, multiple endings, and Niko.
Niko is by far the best thing about OneShot, and I highly recommend checking it out just for them.
I do have ONE major issue with this game, but I'll get to that in a moment.
The art in this game is stunning. I absolutly love every bit of it. The music is pretty and also fits the atmosphere nicely.
The NPCs are all interesting, and for the most part they really add to the whole "I need to save this world" feeling. Meanwhile, you have Niko who is the sweetest thing, which instantly made me want to protect them at all costs.
Now, my one issue is that light puzzle towards the end of the game. It's randomized, and it didn't seem to give me proper feedback. What should have taken less than 5 minutes to complete took me 45 due to the lack of information I was given. This single puzzle broke the immersion I had felt and soured the playthrough. Had I not been invested in Niko's character, I probably would have just given up on it.
It's a big flaw to an otherwise perfect game.
Overall, if you love an interesting story filled with lovable characters, you'll adore this game. This has easily won it's place in my Top 3 Favorite Games of All Time, and I hope more people get the chance to play this for themselves.

To many times you will start typing a word for who you think will attack next only to be completly wrong and have a different zombie attack. There should be some kind of numerical or color code as to what will attack you next so you can apply a priority. I also felt a words were often nonsensical. All in all I dont think I can recommend this game. Its a novel idea but is exectued badly. Wait for a sale if it interests you.

To be frank, I don't like RPG Maker. At all. Compared to other developing software like GameMaker you can see its limitations to make a gameplay oriented game . What you CAN do  with it however, is to tell a story. There are no bounds to ones imagination and OneShot is a prime example for that which you see rarely in todays gaming world. With that being said, do yourself a favor and purchase it if you haven't already. The game's journey is just that good.
Beforehand, my verdict for most categories are subjective of course except for gameplay and presentation where I try to be as objective as possible. If you don't agree with me in one category, that's just too bad.
---------------------------------
Story: 9.5/10
Wether the idea is unique or not, doesn't matter. In the least it's something you don't have that often in games. It does sound cool on paper and when you turn on the game and play it for yourself you'll see that it really is just as good as the summary.
Sound: 8.5/10
There's actually not much to say about the soundtrack except that it's great! Along the games I've played during the time I played OneShot it certainly pulled my strings the most. And they pretty much catch the feeling of the situation Niko and the world are in.
My favorite tracks are
,
,
,
and probably the best of the bunch,
Graphics: 7/10
As far as pixel art goes OneShot could easily handle the 16bit era. It's (of course) not on par with Owlboy or Hyper Light Drifter but in the pool of Steam's pixel games it's definitely somewhere in the top. Just take the in game city as a reference, it's beautiful.
Gameplay: 6/10
And this is where we get to the obvious weakest aspect of the game, the gameplay. Despite the limit of the RPG Maker software, OneShot is as minimalistic as possible. You basically collect items, find the right people to talk to and solve little puzzles. Though, there's a twist which saves the gameplay related stuff by quite a lot: For several quests you have to use your computer and look through several folders to find the solution. In regards to the adventure genre, this one is a unique and superb addition. Seriously, nice one.
Presentation: 9/10
A story is just one device of a game's presentation. A good story does not necessarily mean that the presentation will be good and vice versa. In regards to OneShot however you can wipe any doubts away because the game delivers pretty much in every aspect:
- 4th wall breaking done right, in my eyes, is always a plus, no matter if it's a game, a novel or a movie.
- We have a strong (in regards to writing) and likeable protagonist we learn more about as the story goes on.
- The lore and story building is phenomenal. The journey starts in a barren wasteland and continues later on in a, at first sight, big and lively city. But that just might be an illusory world...
- The ending might be a hard choice for the player to make. It was for me at least, which happens not so often. The choices in Bioshock for example feel like a joke against OneShot's.But even after the ending it's not over,yet...
When I have something to criticise about the presentation, then it is the cast. I like them but it is obvious that so much focus was put onto Nico that the rest of the cast drew the short straw. So I couldn't put as much thought into them as I actually wanted. Which is a shame, even the side characters in OneShot are, for the biggest part, great.
Replayability: NORMAL
Without much spoilers, you will need at least two playthroughs. I won't say more.
Otherwise it's definitely nice to guide Niko through the game once in a while.

I bought and played this game when it was first released, and to say I was disappointed would be an understatement. I spent about 30 minutes running around with little sense of purpose before being killed by a giant sandworm.
I wasn't having fun at all, and quickly refunded it. To be fair, when it was released, it was an early access game in the very EARLY part of its access. Still, I find myself returning to the game (after buying it again) and having a
better time, this time around.
I suddenly feel like I have a clear purpose in the world, as well as a clear sense of progression. When I first played, it was like I was dropped in the world and told
. This time I'm being led to thrive. I have skills, a skill tree, and attribute points at my disposal, a stark difference from my first time in the game.
There are more structures, more varied landscapes, and I think even other planets to explore. These all didn't even exist in the game when I played before.
Ignoring their most obvious comparisons, ie: they're both Space survivial games, Osiris has done the same thing No Man's Sky has done. It has improved to the point that it's actually become exciting and rewarding.
Sure, there are people who've been playing Osiris since the beginning, and they'll insist that the game has
been fun, so I am not speaking for them. I can only speak for myself, and I had an absolute blast with the game, last night.
Go figure that two of my favourite games this year, just so happen to be games that I had previously written off as being uninteresting or shallow.
It's nice to see things exceed expectations, and Osiris: New Dawn has done just that.

I have played this game for about 14 hours, built all available structures and made all the vehicles. Some are not working correctly and obviously there are still some bugs to iron out, being early access this is accepted.
I would say that this game *could* be a potential hit for survival/sci-fi fans if they quickly manage some of the more annoying early game life bugs, such as missing inventory and construction glitches whilst adding more content quickly to keep up interest.
If you want a content filled extravaganza, Id suggest you wait a while, expecially if you are a survival veteran who can tear through content quickly and require an end game, there isn't one yet, apart from public server PvP, or just more building of the same handful of structures that aren't very functional.
I would recommend this game if you don't mind jumping in very early, are happy to explore an alien planet with just a few hours of content to play around with and don't mind  being subjected to some bugs and annoyances, and Im not just talking about the local wild life!.
Overall if you want in now, you will have some fun for a while and are likely to hit the content wall after 10 or so hours, if this bothers you and aren't happy to wait for several months of patching don't buy it yet but keep an eye on it.
The future for this game could be amazing, it's all there but lets hope the developers (2 of them) are up to the task of content creation this game deserves.

The Turing Test was a really enjoyable experience, and well worth my money.
Gameplay was smooth and very engaging. It is well polished, and I encountered very few bugs. The puzzles weren't anywhere near as difficult as those in Portal, but were difficult enough to keep me interested. New gameplay mechanics are introduced throughout the entire game, so there is always something new to try.
The story was what really hooked me into this game. It is very conceptual, deep, and interesting. Expect to do a lot of thinking after playing this game. The game was rather short, I took about 5 hours to complete the campaign, including several of the optional missions. I won't say more here so I don't spoil the story.
Graphics quality is amazing. My mid-range laptop could run this game on medium settings at 20-30fps, and it looked brilliant. If you like games to have amazing graphics, this will live up to those expectations.
To summarise:
PROS
- Engaging story
- Amazing graphics
- Great soundtrack
- Polished and fun gameplay
- Can (just) run on low-mid range computers
- Price is decent
CONS
- Puzzles aren't very difficult
- Controls can get confusing and/or awkward during cutscenes, and you can still move around during these.
- Short campaign
Overall, I would give this game a 9/10. I highly recommend you buy.

Hold the Mustard was the last spin-off game to the Spy Fox series and the only one that features a villian who doesn't appear in the main series trilogy. The plot is about a mustard company CEO named King Konglomo(yes he is a parody to King Kong) who is fed up that cosumers are preferring ketchup over mustard. So he crafts a crazy plan to rid of the world's supply of tomatoes so that way consumers will have no choice but to choose mustard for their burgers, hot dogs, pretzels, etc. Word of the scheme is notified to Spy Fox who is aided by Quack & Monkeypenny to stop King Konglomo's insane plan. By piloting a hoverpod called the M.E.S.S., Spy Fox must go on a global quest to destroy all of King Konglomo's robot probes that are stealing all of the tomatoes. Like the Cheese Chase game, it's an arcade style game except instead of it being a rail shooter it's a free roaming style game. In each level you control the M.E.S.S. and must destroy as many robot probes as possible in order to proceed to the next level. Most levels are challenging when the number of robot probes becomes overwhelming. While certain levels are easy when the objective is not to destroy the robots but instead destroy a control center that is controlling them. There are various power up items that can help you out for a limited time. If you played the Cheese Chase game, then you'll know what to expect with this game. The game play is very fun, and highly recommended for anyone who likes Spy fox or the Humongous games in general.

Comfortably the best 'whole of' Second World War grand strategy game yet released.  While the inherent complexities off a game modelling World War Two (WW2) at a division/ship/aircraft level mean that there are still elements of the game that could benefit from further polish, the game in its current state is a lot of fun and a genuine strategic challenge as long as one is either playing multiplayer or not taking advantage of exploits that the AI can't match (and, of course, playing a nation like France or Italy will be more of a challenge than playing one like the US, USSR or Germany - but that should expected (and desired) in a WW2 grand strategy game.
As with all 'core' Paradox Development Studio games, there is a team continually working to both improve the base game and develop DLC, which promises great things for the future.  The game is also well supported by modders, with both active WW1 and Modern Day mods in development, as well as alt-history favourites like KaisserReich.

I typically love Double Fine's games, but this was a great disappointment.  The dialog and art style are the two good qualities this game offers.  The frequent backtracking regarding puzzles, need to repeat the game multiple times for completion, and obtuseness of some puzzles (or ease for some) are only some of the negatives.
The worst part of my experience (having played this one and one half years after release) was the game-breaking bug of one of my characters falling into nothingness and being deleted from my three available slots.  This left me unable to continue in the game.  The only thing left for me to do is to restart from the beginning which I will not be doing any time soon as replaying these puzzles is tedious at best.
As an aside, while the game allows for multiplayer, this may as well be reduced to pass and play with a controller.  This is only a single player game despite what it may be advertised as.
I would have a difficult time even recommending this game if it were free, and I wish this weren't the case.  There is too much wrong to ignore.

I think the most impressive feature of this game can be found in the multiple choice set up.  Choosing from seven characters you pick three and switch between their skills – e.g. teleportation, a brief moment of immortality, Telekinesis, etc. –  to travel through the cave and ultimately "survive" the game.  Characters each have their own backstory which are experienced through areas assigned to their stereotypical being.  As the adventurerer you will find yourself in a pyramid recovering a sarcophagus while, as the Monk, you search for enlightenment in a temple.
All of the above enables you to replay this game without experiencing déjà vu – which is a main reason why many of my games end up on a high shelf – so you can still experience different stories after your first time.
In terms of tone, The Cave is a dour adventure – existing through puzzles – but you can still find yourself grinning by the quirky humour of the cave and the lively gameplay.  The puzzles are never unbearable or difficult.  Given, they aren't difficult at all and constantly having to switch between characters can get weary but, eventually, the game's design and concept makes up for that.  The game will save you some time as you can't leave behind a character due to a lack of switching.  You can either go no further wihout the help of another character or if you are too far ahead they'll eventually follow you to where you are.  The variation in character skills and environments also helps.
Summed up, The Cave is great if you're looking to have some casual fun.  It won't challenge your mind.  You'll find yourself in a world where everything is turned into a joke – sometimes subtle or even cruel – yet the story is well constructed and narrated.  All that through the enjoyable voice of Stephen Stanton. Because after all, you experience the stories through The – speaking – Cave, which on its own is a cheerful concept.
It's a matter of whether you can enjoy a charming, casual game.  Don't expect challenging puzzles and levels that need a large amount of time.  This game can be seen as a piece of art, something to enjoy, rather than something you have to fight through.  8/10

Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones is a worthy seat for a king.
After finishing the game I was left feeling sad,nostalgic and also happy to have experienced what is known as the Sands of Time trilogy.
The third entry and last for the 128 bit consoles is a great end to a great game series.
When I first started I went into the option menu to finally see a support for widescreen resolution, but I also saw yet again the removal of subtitles ( why ? if the second game had it why not this one ? ) and that is one of the issues I feel with the series as a whole.
There is no consistency, not in tone, definetly not in the voice acting, and the prince is on a non stop wardrobe changer with face and tatoo removal galore.
However what IS consistent is the awesome gameplay, fantastic platform which just got better with added elements as well as a fantastic kill speed. The combat is still the same as it was in the second game the combos and weapons all still apply to the same formula which changes once we play as the dark prince.
And playing as the dark prince is just as fun and fast paced as with the normal prince.
The graphics are good with not many enemy variations and some strange fingers and body movements.
Unfortunatly ubisoft decided to revert back from what I thought was great gore and go back to the first game with minimal gore in the US, you see from what I have read there is a patch that was released on the EU version that brings back decapitations, but I never bothered installing it since I didn't feel the need for it.
Story and voice acting as well as the writing are all top notch, The two thrones reverted back to the style of the first one with a more linear path but with a lot more cutscenes and dialogue, all of which are great and kept the game at a fantastic pace never dragging once.
But that also means a blow to the duration of the game which now sits anywhere between 8-10 hours on Hard 100%.
While that is a shame I felt it was the right duration for it and while there still are 3 difficulty levels to choose from there are NO collectibles like in the second game, no weapons,no chest artwork...in its stead we have sand credits which allow us to buy stuff but when I finished the game it was all unlocked so I don't know.
The music went back to the first one and for the better, also we got a lot more awesome bosses which were all a lot of fun to play and figure out.
The final fight and the first I found to be the best especially the final one.
We also get 2 chariot sections which were sweet and short.
SO what did I not like about this game ? well not much really this is the least glitchy game of the bunch and not having subtitles was not a problem since the sound worked perfectly. The riddance of collectibles was a bit jarring and i was kinda saddend by it but since this is a more story driven game I found no issues with.
I don't know why but I felt that I had more issues with the platforming than the other 2 games.
Also speaking of difficulty this is by far the best balanced game of the bunch. Hard is hard but not impossible or exaspereting like it was on the second, there were no moments where I thought it was unfair. The difficulty balance was perfect.
Overall this game is really really good and tides up the trilogy nicely and gives us a prince we care about and love.
Score for Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones will be a 8.5/10
While I appreciate the story and linearity for a better told tale the duration for the game suffered greatly just being a little bit longer than the first one and 2 times shorter than the second one, there really is no replayability and while I could see myself replaying the game for its story I doubt I ever will.
Also if you came from Warrior Within straight into this one the change in tone and characters faces and wardrobe is really jarring as well as the music while better than the last game is not as memorable save from 2-3 tracks
I did love the call backs from previous games like you get the one hit kill sword and have YET AGAIN climb a tower to get to Farah and the amazing final fight which not only looked epic but ended the game on a great high note.
This is a Fantastic end to the Sands of Time trilogy.
PS: I don't know if this is a glitch or it is supposed to be but when you reach the end at the middle tower an ambient music starts to play that is absolutly atrocious to listen to, its horrible it has this god horrid saxofon blazing in my ear and it was all made worse with a glitch where i got stuck in the air and had to replay the whole seciton again and listen to this piece of S H I T.
But good game nontherless.

I got this game from SEGA bundle a long time ago and was reluctant to give it a try since I thought it's some sort of a keyboard trainer in a weird zombie setting. But the game is much more than that as I found out.
First of all, the game is based on SEGA oldschool classics "House of the dead" - an arcade machine rail-shooter. It features two game modes - one, where you should type words in order to shoot your enemies' brains out, and the classic one, where you shoot zombies with your mouse cursor, using a wide range of upgradable weapons. Both modes support co-op, but sadly achievements don't unlock while playing in co-op. There are also several mini-games there as well.
What really makes this game an epic experience is the trash/exploitation/grindhouse atmosphere style of cinematics in between missions. The whole game is presented in a form of 70s-80s low-budget zombie exploitation flick with characters, jokes and dialogues typical to such setting. I completely laughed my♥♥♥♥♥off several times during the playthrough.
I cannot recommend this game to just anyone but if you happen to like and enjoy the abovementioned stuff, this is definitely the game to get your hands on. I recommend getting it when this title goes on sale or has some discount.

Hope you know how to spell and type without looking at your fingers, because otherwise you’re dead. In the Typing of the Dead: Overkill - a typing-themed version of on-rails shooter House of the Dead: Overkill - the light-gun is replaced with a keyboard. Zombies shamble towards you with words or phrases in front of them, which you need to type out quickly and accurately before they eat you and your fumbling digits.
This isn’t the first time a House of the Dead game has been turned into a typing tutor: it’s the same premise as the Dreamcast cult classic Typing of the Dead (1999). It’s a strange mix that works well: the goofy nature of the story and “grindhouse” aesthetic combined with comedic words at inappropriate times. While Overkill by itself was an average lightgun game, this typing iteration comes across better. It’s got a funky soundtrack, multiple difficulty levels, full Steam integration, and two-player cooperative play arrives later as free DLC. Boss encounters have been especially tweaked to better utilize the new input method.
As a bonus, the game contains the full Extended Cut of the PlayStation 3 version of Overkill, playable with a mouse or controller. Extended Cut was a re-release of the original Wii version, with improved visuals, two new levels and a bunch of tiny tweaks.

Typing of the Dead: Overkill is a typing/rail shooter game, where you type phrases as quickly as possible to kill zombies. I've always kind of enjoyed typing games, and while I don't think this game has much merit in teaching you how to type properly, it's a fun game with an interesting sense of humor.
There's not too much to talk about with the gameplay. You type as quickly as possible, using Tab to pick up secrets and power-ups. What's more interesting to discuss with this game is how it's presented: as an old, low-budget horror movie. It tries very hard to be as cheesy as possible. Sometimes the phrases you type relate to the level you're playing, which gets pretty funny in the strip club level. This game is a bit lewd at times, and the swearing is excessive... not saying that's a bad thing, but it's something you should know going in to it.
Typing of the Dead: Overkill also includes House of the Dead: Overkill. The story is the same, but you play a standard rail shooter with normal controls instead of typing. I definitely support buying Osiris: New Dawn in its current state. While it is in Early Access, helping to fund its development could lead to a great end result. I've supported previous survival EA games that tanked, with their developers disappearing or ruining it entirely (h1z1, reign of kings, etc.) - but this one looks very promising!
Quick Points:
+ Devs seem passionate about doing it right, and acknowledge the failed / dishonest survival games out there (No Man's Sky for example)
+ Gorgeous graphics.
+ Mass Effect 1 feel to it.
+ Solid soundtrack.
+ Night time / sandstorms / alien combination is terrifying.
+ The Martian / Dune / Starship Trooper feel.
+ Enjoyable / In depth crafting system as far as an Early Access (EA) game is concerned.
+ Wilson Robot is a great help when playing SOLO or Multiplayer.
+ Multiplayer (private server) experience is fantastic.
+ Fair number of resource types [Sand/Meat/Gases/Metals/Plastic/Rubber].
+ Rather large planet, and we will be able to travel to other planets in the future.
+++ Feels like a legitimate astronaut experience, with a great HUD and movement/breathing system.
- Minor bugs and glitches (stuck in cieling, outside sounds clip through building in areas they shouldn't, etc.
- Aliens are not plentiful enough even on 'infested' setting, and are easy to kill during the day.
- Unavailable buildings (Gas Tanks for storage) for unknown reasons.
- Caves and other landmarks [expedition 1 ruins, you are expedition 2] that have no lore/loot/interaction function.
- Multiplayer servers experiencing issues, so private server is the way to go right now.
+-+ Giant fricken sandworms that burst out of the ground, casting naught but a shadow of death before you look up and scream. Death in this way can't even upset you, it's so awesome lol.

Surprisingly tense and exciting, with elements of horror due to the traps and dangers that can happen and the fear of the unknown. Very much in the vein of the film 'Cube'.
Behind the Tron style aesthetics is a rather simple game. One where you have a semi-random maze presented to you (with the player or host for multiplayer games choosing parameters for that) and your role is to move through room by room in the grid to find the exit. Each room can potentially be safe, the exit you are seeking or trapped. You can use observation, sheer luck and your most precious of tools - your shoes - to try and make it. By throwing a shoe into a room you can try to trigger traps and then react in a timely fashion to whatever happens - move in if nothing seems to be triggered or run away fast if a trap appears. Sometimes traps are more easily avoidable if you are fast enough, leading to Indiana Jones style moments where you rush past an incroaching laser cutter and grab your shoe on the way through the door.
The game is incredibly cheap and so the bar is set lower, of course. Even then this is a game that is very fun if you have strong nerves to handle it in single player and more fun still for a group to join in. The simple mechanics of it will make it easier to get a group together, as will the variable form of the mazes from very small and easy to large and deadly (as well as the option of the maze being different shapes and the layout of the exit and features being in certain patterns or random). Remember, more shoes is always better if you want to survive. As are expendible comrades you can send into a room first once the shoes run out. You can always draw straws for who gets to go first...
The controls are very simple and use standard FPS set ups (barring the shoe throwing key which only has a close comrade in the Stalker games where you throw bolts to try to trigger anomalies, its traps). Keyboard and mouse or a controller is optional.
A no-regret buy for the majority.

The Cave is set up like an old-school 2D side-scroller.  Seven adventurers, each with a dark past, go down into a magical cave in a journey of self discovery.  At the beginning of the game (which is narrated throughout by The Cave itself), you choose three of the seven advernturers and descend.  Each section of The Cave is a puzzle that requires your three characters to work together.  Three of the sections are uniquely designed (by the sentient Cave) for the characters you've chosen.  In this way, The Cave encourages you to play though multiple times.
The drawback is that there's also three generic puzzle sections which you cannot skip.  I'm on my second playthrough, and while it's nice that the game shuffles the order of the puzzles, it can be a drag to re-solve old puzzles to get to new content.  And the achievements require you to play through the game... I don't know how many times, but I imagine The Cave's jokes (while clever) will start to wear thin on the fifth playthrough.  If you really want to get 100% achievements, you might consider reviewing the achievement list online before you play, despite the mild spoilers.

The game is quite fun and offers unique gameplay mechanics utilizing typing to advance the game. It seems like a nice way to teach kids words and spelling (assuming you can ignore the gore and blood involved in the process).
At its base the game consists of two gameplay modes. The first is where you type random words attached to mutant zombies in order to kill them. The second mode is more akin to the old arcade game machines where enemies appear on-screen and you aim the gun to shot (meaning you can't move, you just shot what appears when it appears). Both modes can be adjusted for its difficulty levels (longer-harder words and etc).
The story and mood of the game is set as a 1970's B-movie and while cliched (as expected) is quite entertaining. To add a little spice, you can pick various collectibles scattered throughout the different levels in the form of a comic-book, concept art, posters, audio tracks and 3d character models. Also, in case you have become bored with the choice of words present there are several dictionary-themed DLCs you can buy, ranging from movies and novellas to just plain filth.
Be advised though, at first the game seemed to have bug with Steam overlay. For some reason it got resolved by itself the next day (maybe a restart after installation of game/redist was in order, but it didn't ask for one). There were also mentions of black-screen issues (I think it got fixed) on the game forum so might wanna check that beforehand.
Long story short, get it. Even just as a guilty pleasure for the B-movie story if not for the unique mechanics.

I decided to buy Typing of the Dead: Overkill since it was on sale for nearly nothing. My previous experiences with the series had consisted of me playing the first two games of the series alongside my brother with a really crappy computer years ago using a dual mouse setup. It had already been quite long but i still remembered how we spent hours upon hours shooting the hordes of undead (err, mutants) back to the grave and shouting at each other to cover our backs.
Upon launching the game a wave of nostalgia came crashing down to me, as if it was a warm welcome to a home you had spent your entire childhood running around in. Absolutely nothing has changed in this release, it might have different levels and story but the gameplay is spot-on identical to what the original titles were. It's missing the dual mouse support (And actually, local multiplayer isn't even supported although you can go online with your friends.) but that's something that most likely will not annoy you since the gameplay is so, damn, perfect.
The game consists of you trying to type sentences that are placed on the top of the zombies' heads, and after completing each sentence the creature dies. It's extremely fun and fast paced, and is something someone would even go as far to call a rhythm game. On top of that, it's even educational, yes, killing zombies can be smart! If you're someone who hasn't never really gotten into fast writing, then this game is a very powerful tool to make you learn the quirks. There are even some tutorials online from the older title to help you get on it quickly.
Soundtrack in ToD:O is pretty good, it's mostly your basic "bar rock" stuff that you wont remember after turning the game off, but it gets the job done. Sound assets and graphics in the title are basic to say the least, you'll be hearing the same grunts and sounds a lot, and the zombie models are re-used quite a bit. Maybe even to a level that it might start irritating you. The game also sports a bare minimal options menu, in which you only have the option to change resolution, AA, and gamma settings. It's not a visually stunning experience but a bit more variability would have always been nice.
Content wise the game is extraordinary, after finishing the story/arcade mode you'll unlock the hardcore mode which makes everything harder. You can also play the original House of the Dead: Overkill in this release, in which you can use your mouse or gamepad to shoot the zombies as you would in the arcades. And last but not least, they also decided to add a crap-ton of unlockables and minigames to keep you busy. I havent had the time to test it all, but i'm pretty sure something so mechanically perfect can be nothing less than enjoyable.
But all in all, even though it does have some shortcomings in term of the technical standpoint. It's a really good title that's jam packed to the brim with content that will keep you enjoyed for a long time.

Typing of The Dead Overkill (TOTD) is an HD remake of House of the Dead 2 (HOTD2), an arcade “rail shooter.”  I never played the original (which came out over 15 years ago) so I can’t tell you how closely it follows the original story. I can’t imagine it’s too closely though since Typing of the Dead Overkill is filled with profanity/nudity.
The original HOTD2 was a basic rail shooter where you have no control of movement, you just point and click at any zombies that pop up on the screen. TOTD is similar, except that instead of using the mouse to point and click, a random word will pop up on the screen over an enemy's head and you need to type it into the keyboard as fast as you can (otherwise the zombie will bite you). For example, you’re moving down the hall and two zombies shamble into view from one of the doors. Above each zombie’s head is a word, such as KILL or DEATH. If you type the word in correctly, the zombie gets “shot” and dies. If the zombie runs in from far away you might have to type in a longer word, and if an enemy throws a knife at you, you might just have to hit one key to deflect it. It can get pretty hairy when half a dozen zombies crawl out and you need to pick which word to type first (kill the closest zombie first!) Each level has a boss at the end, often with some special way to kill them.
Storywise, every level has a prologue and epilogue along with a bunch of wisecracks during the missions. You play one of 2 cops who are chasing a madman who released a zombie virus. On alternating levels, you play one of 2 strippers who are also chasing the same bad guy. By the way, like the arcade the game is made for 2 players, though I haven’t tried multi-player. The environments are varied and so are the enemies, but the variety is really just for visuals since you kill everyone the same way (type the word over their head).
In addition to the TOTD campaign, the original HOTD2 game is included with updated graphics. It’s basically the exact same game except you use the mouse to point and shoot enemies. Using the mouse is actually a lot harder since you actually need to aim at some smaller enemies (evil crows!) and shoot bosses in their weak spots.
Pros:
+Learn to type random words fast like your life (points) depend on it!
+An over the top story that would never fly in a movie, unless it was a Grindhouse film. Can be funny at times.
+House of the Dead 2 included. (Point and click version of the game).
+Scary and gruesome at times. We’re talking zombies and monsters after all.
Cons:
-Kind of short, maybe 5-6 hours.
-The point & click version can be VERY hard. You have to aim at the knives that get thrown at you or the mutant babies charging at you. I played through easy mode and couldn’t get through a level without being hit.
You might think that with all the typing you’d be a typing expert by the end of the game, but alas I still have to look at my hands when I type some of the words. This might be because you’re only typing in random words instead of complete sentences.  Overall I’m glad I bought the game (Humble Bundle BTA) and would recommend it to anyone who likes rail shooters or zombie games.

"The Two Thrones" is the final chapter in Ubisoft's Prince of Persia trilogy from the early/mid 2000s. It combines the best parkour/platforming elements with the rich storytelling from the first two games, all while expanding on the rock-solid combat system of "Warrior Within." For 2005, it had good FMVs (remember when those were a thing? ;-) ) and decent graphics. The voice acting is solid, the controls responsive (mostly) and the game itself is as close to a seamless blend between gameplay and storytelling as you can get for an action-based medium. Honestly, what prevented me from scoring it a '10' was the dialogue. The voice acting is pretty on point, but what comes out of the mouths of the characters is often... mediocre. Sometimes, it's just plain disappointing. I was over halfway through the game and thinking to myself, "This is such a great sequel. "The Sands of Time" is one of my favorite games and thus far, "The Two Thrones" is a worthy follow-up to that splendor. The dialogue is atrocious, but this is still a 9/10 experience."
Then I got to the second chariot race and had to dock the game a full point for that travesty. In addition to being unnecessary, it was entirely too long. I understand what the goal was, from a storytelling perspective: create a dynamic element to the the rising tension by adding in another dramatic, action-filled chase sequence. Very cinematic. Unfortunately, no narrative devices were added to, enhanced by or resolved because of this sequence. While the idea of contrasting the Prince's parkour with exciting vehicle chases probably seemed cool, it fell utterly flat in execution. If the Prince had to stunt between vehicles or overtake them, to rescue someone from a chariot, for example; THAT could have been awesome. But the sequences that made it into the game? Patently not awesome. Especially having a boss encounter DIRECTLY after the second chariot event. That was about as 'fun' as having my thumbs Gorilla Glue'd to my palms in a room full of angry wasps, where the only way out is a door that's secured with multiple combination locks.
Something else that was not awesome: losing your secondary weapon during a cut scene. I kind of get why you never have a weapon when you revert to yourself (after a time as the Dark Prince); the Dark Prince has a dedicated secondary weapon in the form of the Daggertail Whip. He's also kind of a♥♥♥♥♥♥ so I can totally see him 'accidentally' dropping, losing or otherwise discarding the weapon his other self was planning on using. From a story standpoint, it makes the regular Prince look weak and soft; he's more dependent on the Dark Prince. It makes the player even more eager for those intervals where you play as the Dark Prince, too. From a technical standpoint, it also works: no need to create memory issues, art clipping or inventory conflicts. But really, guys: if the Prince could keep his sword, axe, mace or whatever during all the jumping around and wall running through fire and collapsing buildings, I'm pretty sure he could keep it through a conversation with Farah. Or chasing down Kaileena. Or a goddamned chariot race.
8/10, two thumbs up. Every entry in the "Prince of Persia" franchise is an incredible mix of parkour-fueled, action-driven adventure: "The Two Thrones" is no exception. It's a fantastic conclusion to the series. Like the first game, the platforming/trap difficulty and number of puzzles ramp up about 75% of the way through.
A note about controllers: I used an Xbox 360 Wireless and encountered no difficulties. I had to reconfigure the default control scheme (not every function was assigned, initially), but my set-up persisted through all play sessions. The only issue I had was if I powered the controller on after the game had launched. In that instance, the fix was simple: exit the client, power cycle the controller, launch the client again.

I can't but not recommend this game. I love puzzling games, Portal 2 is one of my favourite games ever and I have spent dozens of hours playing test chambers from the community. But...
The puzzling is cool, but just because Portal 2's puzzling is so. This game is SO Portal in every single way.
- Short half-playable half-cinematic introduction with nearly no explanations
- Puzzle chambers with dialogues and lore pieces inbetween
- An AI controlling all over the facility
- Lasers
- Light bridges (Yes, exactly the same as Portal's)
- Cubes
- A puzzling gun
And more.
So. The game has some dialogue I actually liked, talking about what it means to be human and conscious... And that's it. It doesn't get to SOMA's level, for example. The only really good dialogues are the one from the robot, the humans are just too dumb and speak so nonsensically. The game tries to make you empathize if the robot, failing completely. You don't feel anything for a so non-charismatic robot, hell, the game doesn't even explain things properly.
There are some secret chambers where you find dialogue between crew members or with the robot, giving absolutely nothing important.
And now, I'm going into spoilers, but don't worry, this game's story is so bad you should thank me for telling it so you don't have to loose your time playing it.
You are a crew member in Europa, Jupiter's moon. At first, they tell you that your job is to find the other crew members who have misteriously disappeared. But in reality, they purposely escaped because they found something that repairs DNA, and thus, achieving inmortality, and they want to take it back to Earth. Your job is now to stop them, but you never really know which side you are on due to the game's nonsensical and poorly developped story telling. The humans NEVER EVER explain why is a good idea to bring inmortality cells to Earth, their whole dialogues can be classified between these:
- "The robot is evil, don't listen to what it says"
- "We are not evil, we just want the best for humanity" (Never giving any arguments to defend their point, I insist)
- "You are human. We are human. We like living living living! Life life life! Hippie hippie hippie!"
And nothing else. I repeat, humans are too dumb for anything and I often found myself talking to the screen asking why in the world would anyone hire that people.
Now. If we forget all the story and stupid dialogues, we have a pretty interesting puzzling game. But it's just too short and the final levels of this game didn't feel as such, in fact, the final 5-7 levels are easier than the previous 20 ones, and the last chamber is not something epic like, damn, I'm in a frozen satellite moving around Jupiter stopping some humans from  taking inmortality cells to Earth with a gun that moves some energy orbs around, I guess something cool can be done for the final chamber.
Hell no. The last chamber is even simpler than the previous 4-6. Doesn't feel as such. It's just one more chamber. And you  have been waiting the whole game for that chamber because the game itself tells you the amount of chambers left before you finish the game in a panel before every single chamber.
Oh, and yes, it took me so few hours to complete the whole game, and you have to subtract 50-70 minutes from my playtime because I forgot it opened once. And yes, it costs four times its length.
This is my verdict. If you like puzzling games, play Portal 1 and 2 again, else, you've got Talos Principle, a very solid and not-stupid-at-all puzzling and chambering game. And both of those games are +9/10 in quality.
The Turing Test: Repetitive, boring, nonsensical and some good (even great) test chambers inbetween.

I didn’t expect much of this game, I don’t even remember buying it to be honest. But when I finally tried it out of curiosity, I was actually quite impressed by what it offered.
So what is Waveform about? You follow a ray of light on its journey through the solar system… that’s pretty much it. The story isn’t impressive and it clearly isn’t the focus of this game. This already shows in the way the story is presented to you: brief screens of text before/after certain levels. It wouldn’t have made much of a difference if the story was left out completely, but whatever, it’s there and offers the bare minimum of storytelling to keep me satisfied, so I can’t really complain.
The controls are quite simple, you tweak the frequency and amplitude of a wave in order to maneuver through levels full of orbs to collect and obstacles to avoid. As easy as that sounds, I can definitely see people struggling with the controls as it takes a lot of time to master them and later levels require incredible precision. I too had problems at first, but after playing through various Deep Space Levels (endless, randomly created levels that exist for each area) I finally got the hang of it. After that I was really able to enjoy this unique and refreshing go at controls and perceived them as very intuitive. But as I said, it takes time to get there, so you better bring some patience or you won’t be able to enjoy this game.
Regarding the overall level design, it’s obvious that the developers put a lot of time and effort into creating each level and giving every area new and creative gimmicks. It’s really fun to ride through accelerators, destroy mirrors and kill space squids. However, some levels can also be really, REALLY frustrating, especially the moons. The reason for this being, that the moon levels all have an additional feature build into them, and some of those (like Distortion, which – you guessed it – distorts your entire screen) are way to annoying. But I still admire the amount of thought that went into every level, and I’m someone who likes a good challenge, so I found myself returning even to the most frustrating levels multiple times in order to perfect them (or at least try to).
Overall, I’d say that this game can become quite addicting, especially if you want to S-Rank everything for the achievements (don’t let the stats fool you, they are messed up, I highly doubt that many players completed Waveform in its entirety). If the core game isn’t enough for you, there also is the already mentioned Deep Space Mode (which I really love) and a Challenge Mode (after completing the game) that adds even more difficulty to the gameplay.
Finally, the graphics and soundtrack are great and fit the game perfectly. I have nothing to complain at this front, so to wrap it all up: This game is not for everyone. If you like being challenged and are patient, the game will provide you hours and hours of enjoyment (for very little money). But if you’re impatient in learning a game or any of the above mentioned aspects seem like they would bother you too much, you better skip on this one.

The Cave, made by Ron Gilbert, best known for Maniac Mansion and the first two Monkey Island games, along with many other fun, creative, enjoyable games.
I wanted to like this game. That's how it's supposed to work, right? A creator who pioneers an era of video-gaming gets shoved aside for a few years, and he comes back, proving he just needed monetary backing to let his creative energies flow and creates a solid game that showcases his unique vision and proves himself worthy of great respect and consideration.
I wanted to experience that... but I did not.
The puzzles are fun the first playthrough, and the concept of "different characters can solve the puzzles different ways," filled me with nostalgic glee for the original Maniac Mansion, but it's not to be. The majority of puzzles are the same no matter who you choose. The characters' individual powers only really matter for their individual maps and some token moments. Moreover, most of the characters just aren't that interesting. The Scientist's story was probably the best. The Twins' was at least amusing. But, the rest...
The game has multiple endings. The ending you get depends entirely on a choice you make at the very end of the game. You must play through the game a second time to see the other ending. No saving and reloading. This is not how you do multiple endings in a satisfying way. This is just wasting our time.
You probably would be better off watching a Let's Play than actually playing the game.

I bought this on sale quite a while ago, out of nostalgia for when I had it for the Nintendo Gamecube many years ago. I have to say, I'm very disappointed with this port. It has the option for using a gamepad, but the option is nonfunctional. The camera controls with mouse and keyboard are poor, at best. I decided to throw in the towel after it glitched twice in a row shortly after the start, since I didn't want to sit through the unskippable cutscene three times in a row. I'd save your money for something else, as I don't see this being patched any time soon to be more playable.

Overall, I enjoyed this game and would recommend it. The combat is changed slightly from the previous installment as the prince transforms into a sand-powered chain-wielding badass for 50% of the game. The fighting mechanics from the previous game are kept for when the prince is his normal self.
The story is a bit less dark then Warrior Within (the previous game), and it kept me interested throughout. There are a few new parkour mechanics like wall springboards which adds to more diverse level design. The artistic style of the game is very nice to look at. There were a few moments in the story where I got really frustrated. Two were from boss fights: once you die and respawn, you either have to wait throughout a 20 second in-game unskippable cutscene before you can get back into the fight, or you have to wait for a similar length of time as you travel to the destination. These were extremely annoying because the broke the flow of the game, and I died a lot during those sections. Other than those parts the game was actually really good in keeping me hooked. I looked forward to coming home and playing after work each day, which is a bit rare for me nowadays. The story is pretty good and the characters are interesting. I really liked the rendered cutscenes, as they have that cool-early-2000-cgi artistic look. So much detail is put into them that you really appreciate the time the developers put in (loads of people and enemies running in different directions, some leaping fluidly with their own unique animations across the obstacles in the terrain).
The game concludes with a satisfying ending, and I felt a great sense of finality to the whole trilogy. Would highly recommend fans of the series to play this, and would recommend newcomers to start a the beginning of the trilogy and play all three.

Really just... phenomenal.  A genuine story and a clever design, I was more emotionally invested in OneShot than I thought I would be given the 6 or so hours I spent playing it, front-to-back.
Forgive the cliche, but it really feels like a contemporary of Undertale.  That said, it stands on it's own without being derivative or a copycat.  OneShot is entirely it's own game, but manages to hit the same highs.
The way the game treats itself, and it's characters, is charming and endearing; even if only for a moment, my disbelief was entirely suspended.  I wanted these characters to exist, I wanted my actions to be meaningful.  When the game told me that I--not Niko, but the person behind the screen--wanted to save the world, I'm not sure I disagreed.
Beyond the emotional impact, the game itself is well thought-out.  The entire gimmick of the game being multiple "Psycho-Mantis" moments, where the game challenges you to play the game while outside of the game itself.  It's a very cool idea, and very meta, and for the most part works entirely as planned, minus a couple of hiccups.
This is where the most obvious comparisons to Undertale flourish, as both games manage to play with the medium of video games in a way that is both unusual and exceptionally effective.  However, OneShot is it's own beast.
Overall, OneShot manages to be a short and conscise, yet touching and heartfelt experience.  One that's definitely worth playing, and one that I will not forget easily.

When I first got this game I expected something like undertale, but not as good. What I got was something completely different.
First off, this game has super fun and not-so-hard puzzles. They kinda force you to explore every square inch of the map in fear that you might miss something necessary to progress. Some puzzles were unclear, forcing me to look up the answer, but those were minor.
Secondly, the characters are interesting and loveable. Some require some getting used to, but definately by your second playthrough you will grow attached to these characters.
Another unique part of this game is how it treats The Player (you) different from the character you are controlling in the game. It actually treats you as completely different entities. You will know what I mean once you play the first 10 minutes. But it made the game feel more realistic, which I liked. No other game I've ever played does this.
Finnally, the endings were great. Without spoiling anything, both endings (regular and solstice) were great in their own right. Both were emotionally touching (similar to Undertale) and left me greatly satisfied.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who liked Undertale or who likes a game with an emotional element to it. Also fans of puzzle games should try it. No regrets. Definately worth the 10 bucks!
