The Glow initially holds a lot of promise and seems to be a fun game, and at first once I decided to stop complaining about the success curve it was... Until I realized it literally can't be completed.
There are several bugs in this game, ranging from annoying to entirely game breaking.
One bug, or perhaps simply poorly coded event, I encountered was the way in which the NPCs react to you. Being that the game relies on stealth elements, it makes sense that an NPC having a direct line of sight on you is grounds for some sort of event or encounter. However, there doesn't seem to be much thought put into how an NPC spots you. It seems if they happen to look anywhere near your general direction they will spot you, regardless of how far away you are or even if you are on the same row/column as they are.
Another thing I encountered that upset me was rooms that are obviously capable of being entered (I can tell because when I move my cursor over the spot it turns into the boot icon that lets me know the door can be opened) yet the player cannot go inside. One such area is the room where the survivor Eric spawns during playthroughs that aren't his. Eric is pacing around on the far left, while there is a door on the far right that leads into a room where you can see an item. Despite the game telling me I can enter the room, there is no way for me to get into it and get to the items inside.
The dialogue of the game, while not painfully unreadable, could have easily been fixed to seem more natural.
My biggest complaint however, and one that based on the reviews was addressed some time ago and has still not been fixed, is the complete lack of ability to save the game and resume it at a later date. I'm not referring to the inability to save while on a mission so you won't have to restart when you fail, (although in all honesty that would be a lovely feature) I am referring to when you successfully complete a mission and the game gives you the chance to return to the menu or continue playing. If you continue playing, you simply go on until you inevitibly run out of supplies (they do not regenerate) or you are killed by a stupidly overpowered eyeball because you, ya know, RAN OUT OF SUPPLIES. So continuing on the map is pointless.
Choosing to return to the menu of the game however, reveals that your progress was not saved and despite the fact you successfully completed the mission, it did not register and not only do you not have the unlocked character you were promised, but you do not have the collected Essence you may or may not have picked up while running from eyeballs and zombies. Because there is no way for the game to track your Essence or the fact you completed the missions, there is no way for you to then play the later missions which require the ones before them to be completed. It seems the only record of your completed missions are on your Steam profile, evidence of your triumph despite the games lack of any SAVE system.
Now that I have so thoroughly destroyed this game, I do have a few positive things to say in hopes that perhaps the developers will listen and cultivate them (Unlikely) or another party will somehow find this and make their own creation based on this system.
The scavenging system was very nice compared with the mechanics of Hunger and Sanity. While they both seemed to decrease at an uncomfortably fast rate, with some grit and careful rationing I was able to keep a majority of my party with full bellies and barely sane enough to be kept out of the looney bin.
The fact that Sanity had visible effects on the map was a nice touch as well, as it helped to provide me with more cues as to when I needed to take my medicine and to add some depth to the otherwise monotone landscapes.
I seemed to notice that Hunger also affected Sanity, and characters who were actively starving seemed to lose theirs faster than someone who wasn't worried that they would starve in the next few hours.
The Stamina that had affects in and outside of battle was another nice touch, as running on the overworld map decreased the Stamina that was available for me to use in battles. Therefore, I needed to be careful I wasn't running all willy-nilly through the city.
I haven't stumbled across many games in the style of The Glow on the engine used, (either RPG Maker VX Ace or XP based on controls, menus, and tilesets) and I also wish to tip my hat to the developers for that as well.

I very much like everything about this game. Especially the story. As a computer scientist, I was in my glory playing through this game on a rainy day getting completely engrossed by the story (which I think is fantastically written). I'm one of those people who will play slowly through a game, looking for every little tape/story/video that you can find, and this game is great for that play style.
If you're someone who just blows through a game as fast as possible and doesn't care too much for story, then don't bother with this game. You'll just disappoint yourself.
If I had to pick one thing to dislike, it would be the length/complexity of the puzzles. There are a lot of great mechanics in this game, but unfortunately I don't feel as though they were exploited to their full potential.
I have never played Portal (though I want to), but I have played Antichamber, and I feel that this game has similar mechanics at times to Antichamber, but with a toned-down difficultly.

There is a clear influence from the original Portal game here, but rather than firing portals, you are moving about power spheres (or whatever they are called) and generally solving puzzles in a very Portal like manner.
The plot is thin (AI gone crazy, sound familiar?) and really just an excuse to explain why you are doing loads of test chambers for no real reason. The ending is rather disappointing, so you won't be playing this for the plot - it's for the puzzles.
Up to about the half way point, I almost gave up because it felt like I had done all this before - it hadn't added anything new. Then you start taking control of the security cameras and robots and it starts separating itself from Portal and becoming its own game.

Box Maze is a puzzle game which puts you in the legless boots of Cubert, a cube who is tasked with escaping other fellow cubes in a maze like level and reach the door at the end of the maze. The gameplay present here is pretty simple,  you move and jump using the standard W A S D keys and you can kill a opponent by directly jumping on their cube shaped heads. That is pretty much the entire thing you’re going to be doing while collecting cupcakes, potions and random power ups.
These specific power ups might increase your jumping length or the speed with which you walk through the platforms. The levels are pretty well designed and there are quite a lot of them. Not to mention that the game is still in early access which means more and more stuff will be added. The game also runs pretty smoothly on older machines too and that should be expected.
The movement is pretty smooth and the collision detection is pretty nice. That is important considering the fact that a single touch with one of your enemies can send you back to the start of the level. Since the levels are somewhat short and not rage inducing so it is not that big of a deal. The only gripe I have with the short and simple gameplay is the variety of enemies.
While they fit right in there with the game's nature, their facial expressions are the only thing that differentiates them. Some have a faster speed than others and some move horizontally than vertically but that’s about it. There are a few other types which are introduced later on in the game but those are not exactly much different.  I couldn’t try the co op levels but I think they might be a nice addition.
But some of the levels have more than one path to take to the doors and those were the levels it actually felt like a proper maze instead of a linear puzzle platformer.There are trading cards and 120 achievements which can increase replayability for a completionist but those don’t exactly excite me. But for a dollar, Box Maze does more good than bad.
Visually, I found Box Maze a little bland. The cubes look all right and the animations while simple are done nicely. The environments were a bit too bland for my taste, and it kind of goes downhill from the start when the mazes start to become darker and the colours are drained from the screen. I would’ve instead preferred a lighter background with more popping visuals.
I have to admit, I didn’t like the soundtrack at first. It was pretty generic and I felt like it was tacked on but as time went, it grew on me. There is a nice sound option present right in the main menu which lets you adjust the volume and that is a very nice little touch to the game.
Box maze is cheap, fun and easy to pick up and play. It is still in early access meaning it will only get more content from here on and that is very nice considering the price. At one dollar, Box Maze is actually better than much of its competition here and you should give it a try if you’re into these sort of games.

When I first got this game I expected something like undertale, but not as good. What I got was something completely different.
First off, this game has super fun and not-so-hard puzzles. They kinda force you to explore every square inch of the map in fear that you might miss something necessary to progress. Some puzzles were unclear, forcing me to look up the answer, but those were minor.
Secondly, the characters are interesting and loveable. Some require some getting used to, but definately by your second playthrough you will grow attached to these characters.
Another unique part of this game is how it treats The Player (you) different from the character you are controlling in the game. It actually treats you as completely different entities. You will know what I mean once you play the first 10 minutes. But it made the game feel more realistic, which I liked. No other game I've ever played does this.
Finnally, the endings were great. Without spoiling anything, both endings (regular and solstice) were great in their own right. Both were emotionally touching (similar to Undertale) and left me greatly satisfied.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone who liked Undertale or who likes a game with an emotional element to it. Also fans of puzzle games should try it. No regrets. Definately worth the 10 bucks!

I love Triple-Fine (the developer of The Cave) games for their wacky characters, imaginitive settings, colorful graphics and funny dialogue. But I hate playing them. The Cave is no different.
To begin with, it's an adventure game mixed with platforming, which means that all the inevitable back-and-forth wandering you have to do is no made even more tedious by jumping puzzles. It seems an odd combination that is unlikely to attract fans of either genre. Worse, the platforming isn't particularly challenging, and the adventuring is pretty shallow. I enjoyed neither portion.
Add to this the lack of clues or direction; is that thing I am standing in front of not working because it is just background art or because I'm not carrying the right item? And if I have the right item, which of my three characters is carrying it (hint: it is always the one furthest away). These are problems adventure games encountered - and solved - two decades ago and it is irritating to see them return.
Worse, the story isn't particularly engaging and - to enjoy it to its fullest - requires multiple playthroughs. I couldn't even stomach the one.
Maybe one day I'll watch the game as a Lets Play, but I've no interest to actually play the game myself anytime soon.
Would recommend this game to anyone who likes platforming, adventuring, quirky puzzles, LittleBigPlanet, or AMAZING NARRATORS. Seriously, the game is worth buying for the vocals, alone.

Is an action-adventure video game developed and published by Ubisoft Montreal. It was released in December, 2005 in North America for the Xbox, Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 2, and the Nintendo GameCube. It was ported to the PlayStation Portable and Wii, under the title Prince of Persia: Rival Swords with the Wii version utilizing the motion-sensing functionality of its controller, while the PSP version added exclusive content. A remastered, high-definition version of The Two Thrones was released on the PlayStation Network for the PlayStation 3 on December 21, 2010.
The Two Thrones marked the third and final chapter for The Sands of Time saga.
The game combines exploration and combat. Both elements make use of the Prince's acrobatic capability and agility. Throughout much of the game, the player must attempt to traverse the palace by running across walls, ascending or descending chasms by jumping back and forth between walls, avoiding traps, climbing structures and jumping from platform to platform, making other types of well-timed leaps, solving puzzles and using discovered objects to progress.
During combat, many of the same moves vital to the player in other situations can be put to use to overpower enemies. An example is the ability of the Prince to jump off walls in order to strike enemies decisively. The player generally attacks enemies and blocks using a dagger, although other objects or factors, such as the Dagger of Time and its time-control abilities eventually prove to be critical to victory.
In The Two Thrones, the Prince's acrobatic skills have improved and is now able to launch himself off walls at 45 degree angles at strategically placed vertical shutters, slide down chutes and balance on swinging poles, among other things. The designers have also improved the stealth system. Instead of merely being able to do more damage when striking without being seen, the game uses a speed-kill system. If the player does not complete the speed kill, the enemy knocks him off and the speed kill fails. The amount of moves or the length of time required depends on how strong the opponents are. The same system is also used in some of the boss battles.
The Prince also develops a split personality, known as the Dark Prince, and this alter ego constantly bickers with him in his mind about right and wrong. At times, the Prince physically transforms into the Dark Prince. These transformations are scripted and not controlled by the player. During these times, however, the Prince retains control of his body, and the player still has control over the character. For the most part, the Prince's dark side is simply an inner voice.
When controlling the Dark Prince, the player loses the ability to wield a secondary weapon, instead using the "Daggertail", a bladed whip fused to his arm. This allows medium range combat moves and new interactions with the environment. The Dark Prince also constantly loses health as a result of the semi-transformation, with eventual death from the loss. He goes back to full health whenever he collects Sand, from either a monster or object. Also, his Daggertail gives him a different button combination for speed kills, in which he strangles his victims. Coming into contact with water allows the Prince to return to normal.
The game and Rival Swords have received positive to mixed reviews.

Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones is the conclusion the the Prince of Persia Trilogy. The game maintains the same platforming and combat from Warrior Within but now adds stealth mechanics and additional platforming mechanics (wall jump platforms and additional dagger mechanics to stick to the wall and open switches). You also get an alter-ego side that during certain areas of the story you get powers to take out lots of enemies; these times really help by having fast paced combat and adds frantic platforming sequences. The areas and music are much better designed and themed than Warrior Within which really makes this feel like a true Prince of Persia game. The story and ending are a perfect fit to this trilogy. If you enjoyed the first two Prince of Persia games then you will feel right at home with this one and will go through a really fun and enjoyable game with an epic ending.

The best game in the Sands of Time trilogy, hands down. The platforming, combat, and story are the best here out of all of the three games. Which is saying a lot, since the first game is amazing.
All of the platforming and combat elements from the previous games make a return here, as well as plenty of new mechanics that are a lot of fun to do. And sometimes you get to play as the Prince's shadow, who can grapple around with his chain hook, which is really fun and changes things up.
There's also lots of variety in the combat depending on what weapons you pick up. And unlike the previous two games, the combat here never felt tedious or like filler.
Plenty of secrets to find too, with challenging deathtraps laid out that reward you with extra health if you can get through them.
Still no native 16:10 widescreen support though. You'll have to download a fan patch to get that working. 16:9 (1080p) works though.
All in all, I can certainly say this game is fantastic. Pick it up, you won't be disappointed.

There's currently no XP/level mechanic that functions, the map isn't procedural and thus you should avoid any barren desert areas (as you're just walking outside of the map), enemies are missing various animations, vehicles are only just functional (but cool), you can't go to other planets yet (but can go up to space) and the game has a handful of items you can build that do not yet function (the shower and biodomes being good examples)

The potential is very real. I look forward to revisiting this game in like 12 months.

This is the game I have been waiting for.
While it is still in alpha/early access, it is really fun and has huge potential. The developers don't seem to ever sleep because they always seem to be crusing the forums, reading what people are saying and adding features or fixing problems pretty much as soon as they are reported.
It can be a bit difficult to start playing as there is no real explaination of the game and you are left to do a lot of trial and error to find out how to do some things. But after an hour or two you will have gotten a good handle on the game and will be cruising across the land to and from your base and resources in an awesome space rover. You can even build a space ship, fly around the area then take off and jump into orbit. While there is nothing to do in orbit at the moment, the developers have stated they have plans on building space stations and bases on other planets in the future.
You can play by yourself, or with others. Building a base together with friends is a blast as you can share resources you have collected as well as vehicles and construction work.
Yes, expect glitches and errors. But from the dozen or so problems I had when I started to play (the day it was released), they have fixed the vast majority of them after only 2 days. I am sure others might have problems, but that is natural as we all have different systems. They will fix them as time passes. So far they have fixed errors/problems about x1000 times faster than any of the big developers out there.
Excellent game. And for those who have played for an hour and given a bad review, please realize that it is an early access game and they have a developement team of TWO people. Give it some time and it will get even better. Too many people seem quick with the negatives.
If you like space, building stuff, and killing big alien spiders that want to eat you, this probably the game for you.

Sometimes I wish I had the ability to hold back on my bombardment of criticism for the sake of the developer. After all, Box Maze here is the development debut of “ABI7ITY”, and I’m sure there’s a possibility he can make some quality entertainment in the future. Anybody could if he or she can puts their mind to it and keeps at it. When those years come around, people can look back on their older creations and proceed to wonder why they would have ever thought to make them the way they did. It’s happened with me and I bet it will happen with ABI7ITY as well. With that said, here’s my review of Box Maze.
Graphics
Bleh…! This is certainly not what I’d call good art design. There’s so much inconsistency with the graphics in Box Maze it’s hard to make of it as a whole. Assets like the exit door and I assume the cupcakes are drawn as one would casually do so in MS Paint or other similar programs. Other graphics have more detail, but can be borrowed from different sources, therefore clashing with each other. This is most evident with the apples and squares. While all the squares move around the screen constantly, there’s no animation at all except for the protagonist’s “running” effect, the explosion when dying or colliding with fake tiles, and the admittedly calming rain and snow background effects. Despite those things, the levels are ugly-looking all around and seem to have been crafted within a few minutes each.
Audio
There’s a chiptune soundtrack in this game, but it consists of only one track and it plays throughout the duration of the entire adventure. It’s always a necessity to have multiple music files and sound effects to help make the action a bit more lively (Well, not that the graphics are doing Box Maze any favors).
Gameplay
I’ll be frank; I wasn’t expecting to be blown away by any game with the word “Maze” in the title. The problem is: Box Maze just isn’t fun at all. The game is a series of basic platforming around tasteless level designs that lack any sort of evident inspiration. They are just there, and are stretched out the way they are to pad out the game length. The majority of the levels are arguably not even mazes since they are way too linear to be classified as such. Each level contains the same types of evil squares and sometimes moving platforms; they get old rather quickly. Box Maze sadly provides no variety as progress is made. Each stage brings up a sense of deja vu from the last. Even the boss stages play out like regular levels, except the player has to keep moving to avoid being hit by projectiles aimed at him or her.
Verdict
What puzzles me is why ABI7ITY would decide to bring his first game to Steam of all places. There are plenty of bad games for sure, but Steam is also the home of the heavy hitters. It’s best to come into the Steam marketplace with all your might at hand and creation tools set for developing a cool game or many. In Box Maze‘s case, it seems more like something that belongs on Gamejolt without a price tag on it. First games are best kept not in the market, but somewhere that shows the creator is open to feedback and willing to improve his or her talents for projects in the future. Meaning I don’t recommend Box Maze at all as the Steam game it is. What I do recommend is that this developer learns from its mistakes.

I really like this game. It is, however, broken in a lot of ways. The dialogue and text sound, at times, as if they were written by someone who's first language wasn't english, ie. "Oh thank god! I thought I was goner!".
The textures sometimes fault, and if you try to skip the pre-conflict dialogue by clicking, sometimes it will freeze the game and render everything unclickable. Your character stands against no enemy models, just hovering hitpoints.
The game also occasionally just freezes. Sometimes you can still walk around but doors are unusable or things are unclickable. (NOTE: I believe the game is still being patched for bugs).
Another mechanic I don't understand is sometimes if you are caught trying to steal from humans, you enter battle with them...but they're zombies now. As opposed to being normal, talking people just before.
The game requires you to collect "Essences" to purchase extra trait points in game...however one of them seems entirely unaccessible. This could just be me being bad at the game, but I can't find a single way to get to it.
The game throws you into the muck with only a knife, and due to the random spawning you're sometimes immediately thrown up against a gang of up to 4 people, often with guns and armor. It is a cumbersome experience to set up your character, click through the opening dialogue, and have to loot your apartment, only to die instantly and have to do it all again.
There is also no map so it is extremely easy to get lost. Not sure if this is a flaw or just a function put in to emphasize the chaos and confusion.
That all being said, this is a charming and very engaging game. The pixel art is beautifully done, vibrant, bright, and spooky. The game mechanics are very well sketched out, despite the few minor flaws. The combat is quick to learn and either very rewarding, or very stressful (which is good, it's meant to be!). I sat down and played half of the game, then decided I enjoyed it so much I wanted it to last...however I went back to it not two hours later and completed it. It is UNBELIEVABLY satisfying to beat objectives. I still intend to play more of this game, because it's so exciting to discover all the little nooks and crannies and rooms and items. I fully recommend and really like this game. Please buy it and support the creators in (hopefully) future endeavors!!! <3

THE GLOW has its flaws; it's short, shakily written and, at times, excruciatingly frustrating but its vicious combat system and strict enforcement on not running before you can walk (or at least not picking fights with a gang of shotgun-wielding bandits before you've got something better than a fistful of rocks to throw at them) make it a fiendishly addictive effort.
Set in a post-disaster world ripped apart by earthquakes, you'll attempt to guide your characters to victory through six main scenarios with varying objectives such as gathering pills, killing a certain amount of enemies or tracking down a lost party member. You'll have to manage hunger, tiredness and sanity levels as you go by scavenging food, securing safe places of rest and tracking down Red Pills to keep your madness in check. Failure to do so will cause parades of powerful monsters to begin appearing all over the map, an event that even the most well-armed party may struggle to deal with.
THE GLOW's semi-randomized map and item generation is both the source of its replay value and its biggest frustrations. In one game, you may well be armed to the teeth within a minute or two. In another, you'll be stranded in a map surrounded by enemies, wielding nothing but a knife that might as well be a rubber chicken for all the good it's going to do you. Guns are king in THE GLOW. The first two rounds of the combat system are exclusively for ranged weapons, meaning that by the time you have an opportunity to show off your close-quarters prowess, you're clinging miserably to the hinges of death's door anyway.
There are some that will grow immediately aggravated with the patience needed to navigate this kind of merciless food chain but I found the process of building up an armoury and a trio of allies before wreaking revenge on my oppressors, who had bullied me for food and forced me to skulk through the alleys like a rat, immensely satisfying.
It lacks polish, plot and any sort of serious direction but the core gameplay is enough to put it over the top for a recommendation from me. Definitely one to build on.

This game is a short and neat little semi-roguelike game with some pretty polished graphics and sound (though a bit repetative). I say semi-roguelike because the game shuffles tiles around, but the tiles themselves are the same, just moved around sometimes. The randomness can be unforgiving, especially due to the fact that one of the primary gameplay elements is stealthing around wandering enemies. Many times I would enter a room and be immediately spotted, often starting combat due to not wanting to lose my precious food. The enemies are also fairly repetative, with overworld sprites often indicating the type of encounter you will have, ie: if there's only one person and its one of the other possible playable characters, you can recruit them.
All in all, a pretty neat, short, punishing game. And I do love that this is not early access or anything like that.
Why do I not reccomend this? The game is extremely mechanics heavy, with no real narative or mystery to really move it along, but the mechanics are fairly boring, with not a lot of strategy in combat or while sneak-looting. The randomness doesn't really add a sense of freshness on every replay, but instead a rather large ammount of arbitraty success. I would die on a first combat encounter because the only loot I found was food and no better equipment. The next go-around I could find a revolver and ammo in the first container I looked in. There is no real curve of progression, since character traits are decided at the beggining of the game.
I also encountered several game breaking movement bugs that made me restart because I had gotten randomly frozen in place and could no longer move my character, resulting in being seen and dying or needing a straight restart.
This is barely a not reccomend, and mostly because of the bugs. I totally get that there will be bugs, but the ones that break the game just ruin the experience for me.

Probably my biggest complaint about the game is perhaps the most unique mechanic in the game: the kick. The kick immobilizes you for a second while you are executing the kick, and you execute a long range melee attack. If your kick hits an opponent, you will deal twenty damage, or 35 with the Boots (which are borderline mandatory to do well if you ask me), but more importantly, the target is launched backwards and can take extra damage from being kicked into railings or other destructible objects, and the target can get kicked out of bounds and die. The target can even deal damage to another target by flying into them. This mechanic dominates the game. If you master the kick, you can easily land in the top five on most shootout servers if you play the whole match.
The biggest evil of kicking is that it allows for combo kills. The kick gives you a lot of notoriety if your target dies directly from a kick. So this allows many users to inflate their notoriety by hitting an enemy for 80 damage (or only 65 if you have the boots) and then kicking them to death instead of shooting them down. Kicks usually are anywhere from twenty to forty percent more rewarding per kill than most guns, and getting kills from kicking players off of maps and into railings will compound the extreme value of the kick.
Personally speaking about the kick mechanic, I use it frequently and receive a fair share of complaints from players regarding how it's a massive crutch. It's not just a crutch. It's an overpowered mechanic. That being said, I've gotten used to it and have come to terms with it being another important part of the game's image.
I like this game, but I'd be dishonest if I didn't at least mention some of these issues. I think it's important that you're aware of what could turn you away from the game.

If you're looking for the video game equivalent of a juicy piece of hickory beef brisket lathered in a rich ranch dressing, then you have found it. Cuphead, created by StudioMDHR, is one of my top games of 2017 and a single glance at the gameplay is all it takes to see why.
This game is a Run-N'-Gun shooter style title, similar to franchises like Contra and Gunstar Heroes. Cuphead, however, chooses to focus, mainly, on boss battles instead of side-scrolling levels. Personally, I'm a real big fan of this decision. I very much enjoy the process of fighting a boss over and over again, slowly learning the attacks and patterns of my foe, until I am able to CRUSH the opposition like a lowly sack of potato chips. It's a style of gameplay that I find to be very rewarding.
Cuphead is not a lengthy game. It contains 19 boss fights and 6 run-n'-gun levels. It took me around 4 hours to complete this on my first run-through, but let me tell you that this is a PRIME example of quality over quantity. All the bosses, animations, and art are hand drawn. The music is recorded live by stellar jazz musicians. It is all done as if they were creating this in the 1940's themselves. Unless you are some sort of brain-deficient baboon with no appreciation for the fine arts, then what's not to love?
The game is BEAUTEOUS, it's got a rich 1940's cartoon style that just oozes rich, fertile manure. The game has BULLETS, and many different flavors of bullets to choose from like the rancid jellybean drop shot. The bosses are tougher than NAILS, but the game is extremely fun as a result. It's got 2-player CO-OP so if you wanna see your lesser-skilled friend get wrecked alongside you, it is possible.
Cuphead is a game that I could play over and over because the secret sauce simply continues to delight. It's gaming at its finest, and if you are looking for a challenging but beautifully-made Run-N'-Gun, then Cuphead is the shredded mozzarella blend that you've been waiting for to garnish that plate of luscious chicken parmesan from the Italian restaurant down the road.
Cuphead receives a final score of "Almond Nut Omega Status". Thanks for reading, see you next time.

I've recently been rebuying a bunch of games I played and loved when I was younger.  Doom, Command and Conquer, the original Max Payne and the Prince of Persia Trilogy among others.  Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones has held up pretty well considering its age.  Sure, the controls are a bit "sticky" compared to what we're used to these days.  All too often you'll launch the Prince into nothingness because the game didn't quite register your jump command in time or the game won't activate your slow-mo input button press and you'll end up skewered on a trap.  Obviously the graphics are...of their time (interestingly the screenshots on the Steam store page DO NOT accurately represent what is in game, those shots have been post processed to make them nicer) but they're totally functional.  Combat is a bit frustrating as enemies seem to be able to cut through your guard easily and there doesn't seem to be a way to break out of an enemy’s combo once they begin.  But this game was released in 2005 and we've come a long way in those 11 years so I'm willing to forgive the frustrating gameplay and just enjoy the nostalgia.  The story is a return to the warmth and wit of the Sands of Time and when the platforming works its excellent, flowing fun and you can see how the Assassin's Creed series seems to have evolved from these games.  I'm sure I'm not the only one who wishes they'd revive this series.
So why am I not recommending this game?  Unfortunately, for me, there is a game breaking bug which has made Two Thrones unfinishable.  On one of the final stages you're expected to wall run from a dagger hanging point, across a spinning blade trap, to a catapult shutter.  There seems to be some bad collision just before the trap as my wall run always ended up with me being ejected from the wall before the trap.  It’s hard to explain so I uploaded a video to YouTube to illustrate the problem.

I spent 90 minutes trying to figure out a way across but with no luck.  I guess people might tell me I'm just rubbish and to "get some skill" but as someone who spent five years testing games for a living this sure felt like a bug.  In the end I had to resign myself to the fact I could not progress any further and I quit and uninstalled.  That's pretty annoying for a completionist like me.  I can only assume this has something to do with modern hardware as I don't recall ever having this problem first time around in 2005.
TL; DR...good game, but I can't recommend it because I can't finish it because of a glitch.

This is a mixed review. Overall, its ok. However, there are some huge flaws in the combat AI.
The good: Great graphics, lots of things to do, detail galore.  You can spend hours just adjusting government leaders, setting up trade, researching technology, etc. All the things leading up to actual combat are really pretty neat.
The bad: As with prior versions, the combat AI is aweful. It is especially noticeable when you are playing a minor ally like Italy. You sit and watch your much more powerful german ally grind it out against the allies with NO progress. For example, playing Italy in HOI 4, I sat through the fall of 1940 with NO change in the borders between Germany and France/Nethlerands/Belgium. There will be no historic replay...ever.  It's so dishartening. I almost wanted to change sides and declare war on the Germans.  If nothing changes by January 1941, I think I will join the allies.
This happend in prior versions of the game. In HOI 3, my Romanians watched helplessless as the Russians massed more and more troops on my border throughout the early '40s while Germany made little or no progress with Barbarossa.  I noticed the same thing while playing Japan. Now, being a major axis partner, I had a lot of fun. I kept the US at bay while I took over most Asia. While attacking India in 1943 I looked over at Europe and sure enough, Germany was still slugging it out with Russian at the start line.  At that point I realize that same aweful AI running Germany was running the USA.  I remembered how US navy came at me piecemeal and thought, hmmmm...maybe this isn't so much fun after all.  I was just distracted by all the glitz and shiny stuff.

Bottom line: Play a major axis nation and focus on your country because your AI controled partner will always fail you.  If you play Ally, just pretend your well trained troops and superior leadership is keeping your enemies at bay.  Whose going to know any different *wink*

Waveform is a decent arcade game that turns extremely tedious towards the end.
The core concept is unique and rather well implemented. You control a beam of light and you need to collect as many orbs as possible in each level. Things start pretty simple, but soon enough you have to deal with mirrors, wormholes and even aliens.
The early levels are good fun and the game does a decent job of introducing new elements to keep things interesting. Unfortunately around the time you get to Mercury the game turns into incredibly obnoxious grindfest. Each level will require higher and higher amount of stars from previous levels to unlock and you spend way too much time grinding through levels you have already finished. This isn't helped by the fact that the radar game mechanic introduced in the Mercury levels is rather tedious.
I grinded through Mercury but once I got to the Sun levels I decided I had had enough. Replaying the earlier levels repeatedly wasn't much fun anymore. While I enjoyed the first few hours of Waveform, I can't really recommend the game as a whole.
The good:
- Unique idea
- Good fun early on
The bad:
- Gets extremely grindy and tedious towards the end due to level unlock requirements
- Even minor mistakes can really hurt your score if you are on a high multiplier
The ugly:
- Some of the checkpoints are poorly placed
Too short, fun nonetheless.

The Turing Test provided me an engaging expierence from start to finish. From a technical standpoint the game ran very smoothly and was perfectly stable without exception. Though if you decide to play this game with a gamepad as I did you may find the sensitivity of the analog sticks to be a little jarring at times. There are occasions where you may wish to manipulate an object in very small increments but find it difficult due to very hard swings in movement, but those issues are very minor and in no way played a serious role on my enjoyment of the game.
Digging into the puzzle design I will say that this game definitely falls on the easy side of the overall landscape of puzzle games I've played. Coming from games like The Witness, Swapper, Portal/Portal 2, Steven's Sausage Roll, Talos Principle, etc. this game felt very tame from a difficulty standpoint. New ideas are introduced and then iterated on like any puzzle game, but they seem to only abstract each new concept a step or two beyond its most basic formation. This can be seen positively or negatively depending on your personal tastes. For myself it was one of the few real criticisms I would levy against the game. That said the easier difficulty does come with an added benefit, and that is its pacing.
The Turing Test does an admirable job at keeping you constantly engaged in the story despite the gameplay being so disparate from traditional story telling devices. The relative ease of puzzle solving allows for the player to enter each new puzzle at a steady pace, where they are always greeted with more dialogue between the game's protagonists Ava Turing and Tom(Onboard AI). These conversations and the general story revolve around the various philosphical musings about what it is to be human, what constitutes consciousness, what is moral, and many of the other common tropes you would expect of a game that would call itself "The Turing Test". If you find these sorts of musings to be up your alley I would suspect this game has a lot to offer you. I applaud Bulkhead for attempting to tread out some of the more sophiscated notions in these debates, giving it at least a slight air of nuance allowing you to feel that you aren't just indulging in pure pop-science.

Oneshot is a game about Niko, a young child who questionably looks like a cat. The objective of the game is to get the lightbulb you carry to the tower, while puzzles await you on your way, the puzzles can range from fourth wall breaks to even changing your desktop monitor. It's characters can be completely different from eachother while still having personallity, and can even change from each time you play.
Characters:
The characters in Oneshot are all different from eachother, while still staying fresh and great. One character, however, seems to change face every playthrough (I will avoid the name in case of spoilers.), sometimes with you not being able to notice it.
The Map:
"The Barrens" - The barrens seem to be an empty wasteland when first starting off, as no people reside. When you move forward you encounter the ProphetBot. He introduces the "talk to the god" effect to Niko. Along the way, you encounter things like robots and a terrifying crushing machine! .......smash the lightbulb in it.
"The Glen" - The glen is a more lively area than the barrens, with children running around and crops growing. Glitched items dubbed 'squares cover some of the area, and the glen seems completely run down and broken. Vines attempt to hold the land together, as you find Alula and Camulus do things REALLY start to pack heat.
"The Refuge" - I can only say so much about the refuge without spoiling so much, cause it's later in the game. Anyways, the refuge seems highly populated, but crowded. A large robot stands at the top, while the elevator remains stuck closed, forcing you to find the button to power it. It is there you meet the Lamplighter, and it is there you can find the Tower.
Story:
The story is amazing, showing the dreams and even the nightmares of Niko, and having it go outside of the game was a really nice touch (imo), but I feel it could've had more challenges along the way. Like some sort of enemy or anomalous computer forcing you to break the lightbulb-- oh wait! There is one! Ahem, anyways- the game of course, could have been improved. But it's current style does remain nice and completely fine.

First edit: 5 hours of gameplay
As an early review, I love this game. The daily rewards are actually meaningful, as they give perks, skins and characters(?) instead of just giving ingame currency to the players, the devs listen to the community (in a good way, not like World of Tanks) and the actual hunt is thrilling, it really feels like you are hunting / being hunted, although the hunting feels more like a chase than an actual hunt (unlike those games like Deer Hunter, etc...). The hunting in this game can be compared to a Search and Destroy kind of gameplay.
So here are a few points:
+ Graphics: they look good/decent even on low;
+ Character variety: There is no similarity between the gameplay of most characters, even though some are of the same type they are played differently;
+ Environment: Maps are not symetrical, good layouts and different ways of playing depending on the map;
+ Devs listen to comments and suggestions: Enough said;
+ EVERYTHING can be aquired ingame without spending any real life money!
- Balance: Before the game went F2P there were lots of complains about monsters being REALLY OP. The devs listened and when they made the game F2P they gave some gadgets and reduced the power of the Monsters. Now monsters are weak-ish, weaker than they should be (they are monsters afterall). Luckily comments and suggestions have already been made and probably next update there will be a balance fix.
Second edit: 9 hours of gameplay
I've been afk-ish from this game but continue to play it whenever possible because the game continues to pull me into it.
* The daily gifts are really good and are helping me expand my available hunters (even though I always play the same ones :P), not even mentioning the skins and perks they also give me.
* Game is receiving new hunters every few weeks and although they look like reskins/remade from the existing hunters they still have a role to be played and in certain situations they are better than the other counterparts, just like every hunter in the game.
* Game is becoming more balanced with every update, and I am surprised this game has never tried to take money away from me either by microtransactions or expansion packs.
* THIS IS NOT A P2W GAME, and I don't think there is even anything you can purchase with real money
Keep up with the good work devs, this game has potential

Typing of the Dead: Overkill, the follow-up to the original Typing of the Dead, is a wonderful parody of 70s/80s action movies set against a zombie apocalypse.
The style of the game is the perfect successor to the original. The humour is the same, incredibly satire and tongue-in-cheek, making jokes at itself and the situation, that situation being typing to kill zombies.
So, let's talk about the game itself, as a typing game. It's pretty good.
The strongest parts of the games are the "progression" through levels, killing zombies, picking up powerups, and unlocking unlockable all using rapidly typed words on screen. The difficult has different modes, and as someone who has tested with 120+wpm, I found the extreme difficulty to be the perfect level for what I was expecting.
The weakest part of the gameplay, for me, was the bossfights. They were interesting, and had cool ideas for blending bossfight mechanics with what you need to type, when you type it and why you type it, but the bossfights, on the highest difficulty, were incredibly easy. I played it a few months after release, so it may have been changed or updated, but I found myself kind of bored by the teamfights in an otherwise challenging and enjoyable experience.
But, don't let that dissuade you. The game is superfun and absolutely worth picking up. Also, I'd imagine it's incredibly good if you want to learn to type.

Update (20160722): I noticed that SCORE was no longer in my account today. I'm not sure when it was removed. From other comments on Steam discussions it looks as though the developers revoked all keys from those who had given the game a negative review. Well played, developers, well played!
My original review is unchanged, below:
---------
NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: SCORE is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was current as of the date of this review (20160708).
SCORE (all caps) is intended to be a GTA-like massively multiplayer open-world action game combined with an online FIFA-like multiplayer European football ('soccer') game.
Graphics - The graphics in SCORE are mostly rather simple and poor quality by today's standards, more similar to GTA 3 than GTA V, but not even quite that good. Buildings and cars are low-poly models with sharp edges everywhere and painted with simple, bland, flat textures. Cars are poorly animated and drive on rails, not responding to anything around them. The few people you see in the game are better looking, but still not great, and don't respond to any stimulus either, including being shot. Player characters look like they have broken or handcuffed hands when holding a pistol.
The city ("Legend City") is virtually uninhabited and you can run for minutes at a time without seeing anything but the endless stream of cars that completely ignore you. It also freezes intermittently, presumably when the world-streaming code kicks in to load another city tile or whatever.
It's a shame, too. In the couple of hours that I spent trying to play SCORE I could see that a lot of effort had gone into development of the city and its surrounds. I ran to one of four golden stars on my minimap (no small feat -- it took about half an hour!) to find a weird pedestal thing at a castle and signs up espousing the medieval fair. Screenshots on the store page show beach areas and hills, as well, and the whole thing seems to have at least some logic to the layout from what I could see.
The two exceptions to the poor graphics are the water, which looks bad at a distance, but actually rather good up close, especially with the wave motion that's been implemented; and the trees, of which there are only very few varieties, but which look very nice, with well-animated branches and leaves blowing in an imaginary breeze.
The minimap also deserves a special mention as it seems to be implemented in real-time as an overhead camera, looking down on the area around your character, with some symbology added over the top. It works really well, but has a big impact on the overall game performance, and a recent comment in the Steam Discussions for the game suggests that it will be removed and implemented in a more traditional fashion in future, which would be a shame.
There are lots of graphics settings to play with, as well, but it performed so poorly on my machine that I turned basically everything to minimum to try to reduce the freezes and lag.
Sound - Sound is very minimal. There are no traffic sounds, no in-game music, no pedestrian sounds, or much of anything yet, really. There's a nice little nature sound track that is completely out of place in the middle of a city, and you can fire your guns until you run out of ammunition, making suitable gunshot sounds as you go.
Gameplay - Starting SCORE takes a short time as you have to create an account; join a club; create a character by choosing gender and a look from four clothing options with very minimal selections available: hats (hair cuts), shirt, pants, and boots; and choose a profession from the small and slightly odd selection: Police, Doctor, Fire Fighter, and Assassin. But don't worry, none of the choices in character creation seem to make any difference, as there's no way yet to complete any missions for your profession and it seems to ignore clothing selections, too. Then you check your real-life email for an activation code, activate your account, and finally you can log in. You then have to wait a few minutes for your character's residence interior to load, but all you can do there is change some game settings on a laptop. After that you leave and have to wait another few minutes for the external environment to load. Yes, load times are very long.
After about 10-15 minutes I was into Legend City and looking around, and I quickly discovered that's all you can do in SCORE at the moment. You can't interact with the few pedestrians you see, and even the cars follow their pre-defined paths regardless of whether you're in their way or not -- they just push you aside, causing no ill effects. I found a parked motorcycle and a parked car, but could enter neither of them. The city is devoid of any sort of interactive life, with the beautifully animated tree foliage blowing in an invisible breeze adding to the sense of desolation. I briefly wondered if I was playing another post-apocalyptic zombie game.
SCORE stuttered like mad when loading new terrain and Task Manager showed a continual gobbling up of memory, implying a large memory leak. It has Steam Achievements incorporated into it, but only one of them works at the moment from what I can see. The limited in-game writing (such as the news feed and loading screen tips) are badly written and in need of an editor, or at least a proof reader. SCORE also crashed twice on me, but it is Early Access; to me these things are forgivable.
The game has promise, but it's much too early to tell whether it will reach the lofty heights the developers have set for it.
Pros:
+ A grand idea, and an interesting combination of games
+ Potentially good world design (but implemented poorly in the current incarnation)
+ Nice trees and water, particularly the animations
+ Steam achievements (although they are mostly broken or otherwise unachievable at the moment)
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- Mostly poor graphics and animations
- Horrendous performance, very buggy, and poor writing (but it IS Early Access)

The Two Thrones is a great conclusion to the great Sands of Time trilogy. The Two Thrones is set immediately after Warrior Within, with the Prince returning to Babylon on his ship with Kaileena. In the time that he was gone from Babylon, the city has been ravaged by war and the Prince finds himself in the midst of it. Because of the time altering events at the end of the first game, the Vizier is still alive and is on a war path. After some events, the Prince finds himself assisting and with the assistance of a familiar face, Farrah. Just like the first game, although she has no recollection of you due to the timeline correction, Farrah works with the Prince to hunt down the Vizier before he destorys the city. However, this time, the Prince becomes afflicted with some parasite after an intiial run in with the Vizier. The parasite transforms the Prince into some sort of Hybrid sand monster and he gets some new cool abilities, but at the cost of a really rude voice in his head.
That's the essence of the plot without really spoiling anything.
On the technical side, The Two Thrones plays just like the prior two games. The acrobatic elements are great. The combat is great. There are a few clunky areas, especially towards the end of the game, but the overall puzzle acrobatic design is great. The levels are well designed too, with an epic scope as far as how massive the rooms can get. It's an old game so I'm not going to criticize the graphics or anything. The music can get really intense and really raw, I was really digging it, especially in the last few levels where the Prince is on the final ascent of the main tower in the city.
Basically, this is a really fun game and I'm glad I finally beat the Sands of Time trilogy.

Growing up, I was always a fan of the old LucasArts adventure games; especially the Monkey Island series.  In my opinion, they're some of the funniest, smartest, most entertaining games ever written, even if they sometimes leave you wanting to throw your computer out the window in frustration while trying to figure out exactly why you've had a rubber chicken with a pulley in the middle in your inventory for game hours.
The Cave, having been developed by Ron Gilbert and Tim Schaffer's studio, Double FIne, manages to capture some of that charm in a simple yet challenging puzzler.  One playthough takes right around 4-5 hours to complete (depending on how good you are are solving adventure-style puzzles, I guess), and is different depending on which mix of characters you choose to lead through the cave for that session.  Throughout each playthrough, you'll experience a mix of both "common" areas (areas that you may encounter regardless of which characters you choose), and character specific areas with puzzles that require the use of that character's special ability to solve.  There is a dark, sarcastic sense of humor that weaves a thread through the entire game, and these character areas, which serve to flesh out the characters' individual back stories (sparse as they may be), are no exception.
Fans of the adventure genre, especially the LucasArts games, will find lots to love here.  Aside from the puzzles themselves, there are a ton of small touches throughout the game that pay homage to Gilbert's earliest titles, especially Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion.  The puzzles are, in my opinion, fairly straightforward, though they may take a little time to figure out.  Some other reviewers complained about the lack of direction in the game regarding how to solve the puzzles.  I don't get it--this genre has always been about making the player figure out what to do without too much help from the game itself.  In my opinion, that's always been core to the experience of playing these types of games.  The feeling of accomplishment is much greater when you figure out a particularly challenging puzzle on your own, rather than relying on a cascade of hints.  But, I digress.
Having only completed one playthrough so far, I can't comment yet on the game's replayability.  It seems to be there, as different mixes of characters provide a different experience, but I can see how replaying the same common areas over and over again could get old.
All in all, I'd give the game an 8/10.  The style, art direction, and writing are excellent.  At the current Summer Sale price of $7.49, it's well worth a purchase if you're a fan of adventure games, or even looking for something that's a little different that can kill a few hours here and there.

MMO's are one of my few addictions, so I'll be as quick as I can with this review.
If you're looking for a free WoW clone, Rift is the right choice. It has a few additions like legitimate hybrid classes that parse well in both PvE and PvP, and looks absolutely spectacular (second to only TERA in my opinion). The controls feel well, the questing is decent, endgame is fun if you're into that sort of thing, and dimensions (personal housing) is surprisingly good for a free game.
With that said, the game is a shameless WoW clone. A good one, but still a clone. Optimization in cities and larger PvP battles is atrocious, and I found myself hitting 40fps on a 3GB GTX 670. If you have a laptop, you will come to hate this game. Some instances like dungeons tend to break easily, and queues can be atrocious at late hours. While the game is not necessarily p2w, it is an awfully long grind to get the classes added by expansion packs, and cosmetics are equally difficult to attain.
In sum, I recommend the game purely because it's free and as someone who got burned out with WoW. It definitely doesn't have the same amount of content or feeling of community, but it's one of my favorite modern contemporaries. It's fun, simple, and leaves a pleasant aftertaste after dozens upon dozens of "free" MMO's.

This is a mixed review. Overall, its ok. However, there are some huge flaws in the combat AI.
The good: Great graphics, lots of things to do, detail galore.  You can spend hours just adjusting government leaders, setting up trade, researching technology, etc. All the things leading up to actual combat are really pretty neat.
The bad: As with prior versions, the combat AI is aweful. It is especially noticeable when you are playing a minor ally like Italy. You sit and watch your much more powerful german ally grind it out against the allies with NO progress. For example, playing Italy in HOI 4, I sat through the fall of 1940 with NO change in the borders between Germany and France/Nethlerands/Belgium. There will be no historic replay...ever.  It's so dishartening. I almost wanted to change sides and declare war on the Germans.  If nothing changes by January 1941, I think I will join the allies.
This happend in prior versions of the game. In HOI 3, my Romanians watched helplessless as the Russians massed more and more troops on my border throughout the early '40s while Germany made little or no progress with Barbarossa.  I noticed the same thing while playing Japan. Now, being a major axis partner, I had a lot of fun. I kept the US at bay while I took over most Asia. While attacking India in 1943 I looked over at Europe and sure enough, Germany was still slugging it out with Russian at the start line.  At that point I realize that same aweful AI running Germany was running the USA.  I remembered how US navy came at me piecemeal and thought, hmmmm...maybe this isn't so much fun after all.  I was just distracted by all the glitz and shiny stuff.

Bottom line: Play a major axis nation and focus on your country because your AI controled partner will always fail you.  If you play Ally, just pretend your well trained troops and superior leadership is keeping your enemies at bay.  Whose going to know any different *wink*

First edit: 5 hours of gameplay
As an early review, I love this game. The daily rewards are actually meaningful, as they give perks, skins and characters(?) instead of just giving ingame currency to the players, the devs listen to the community (in a good way, not like World of Tanks) and the actual hunt is thrilling, it really feels like you are hunting / being hunted, although the hunting feels more like a chase than an actual hunt (unlike those games like Deer Hunter, etc...). The hunting in this game can be compared to a Search and Destroy kind of gameplay.
So here are a few points:
+ Graphics: they look good/decent even on low;
+ Character variety: There is no similarity between the gameplay of most characters, even though some are of the same type they are played differently;
+ Environment: Maps are not symetrical, good layouts and different ways of playing depending on the map;
+ Devs listen to comments and suggestions: Enough said;
+ EVERYTHING can be aquired ingame without spending any real life money!
- Balance: Before the game went F2P there were lots of complains about monsters being REALLY OP. The devs listened and when they made the game F2P they gave some gadgets and reduced the power of the Monsters. Now monsters are weak-ish, weaker than they should be (they are monsters afterall). Luckily comments and suggestions have already been made and probably next update there will be a balance fix.
Second edit: 9 hours of gameplay
I've been afk-ish from this game but continue to play it whenever possible because the game continues to pull me into it.
* The daily gifts are really good and are helping me expand my available hunters (even though I always play the same ones :P), not even mentioning the skins and perks they also give me.
* Game is receiving new hunters every few weeks and although they look like reskins/remade from the existing hunters they still have a role to be played and in certain situations they are better than the other counterparts, just like every hunter in the game.
* Game is becoming more balanced with every update, and I am surprised this game has never tried to take money away from me either by microtransactions or expansion packs.
* THIS IS NOT A P2W GAME, and I don't think there is even anything you can purchase with real money
Keep up with the good work devs, this game has potential

The Turing Test provided me an engaging expierence from start to finish. From a technical standpoint the game ran very smoothly and was perfectly stable without exception. Though if you decide to play this game with a gamepad as I did you may find the sensitivity of the analog sticks to be a little jarring at times. There are occasions where you may wish to manipulate an object in very small increments but find it difficult due to very hard swings in movement, but those issues are very minor and in no way played a serious role on my enjoyment of the game.
Digging into the puzzle design I will say that this game definitely falls on the easy side of the overall landscape of puzzle games I've played. Coming from games like The Witness, Swapper, Portal/Portal 2, Steven's Sausage Roll, Talos Principle, etc. this game felt very tame from a difficulty standpoint. New ideas are introduced and then iterated on like any puzzle game, but they seem to only abstract each new concept a step or two beyond its most basic formation. This can be seen positively or negatively depending on your personal tastes. For myself it was one of the few real criticisms I would levy against the game. That said the easier difficulty does come with an added benefit, and that is its pacing.
The Turing Test does an admirable job at keeping you constantly engaged in the story despite the gameplay being so disparate from traditional story telling devices. The relative ease of puzzle solving allows for the player to enter each new puzzle at a steady pace, where they are always greeted with more dialogue between the game's protagonists Ava Turing and Tom(Onboard AI). These conversations and the general story revolve around the various philosphical musings about what it is to be human, what constitutes consciousness, what is moral, and many of the other common tropes you would expect of a game that would call itself "The Turing Test". If you find these sorts of musings to be up your alley I would suspect this game has a lot to offer you. I applaud Bulkhead for attempting to tread out some of the more sophiscated notions in these debates, giving it at least a slight air of nuance allowing you to feel that you aren't just indulging in pure pop-science.

The Turing Test is a first person puzzle game in the vein of Portal or the Talos Principle. As the name implies, the theme revolves around a tense discussion of free will and the nature of consciousness between Ava, an astronaut, and TOM, an AI, as TOM helps Ava navigate through a series of puzzle rooms. It is beautifully made if a bit visually repetitive, as puzzle games of this type tend to be, with excellent music, models, and animation. I completed the primary game in roughly 7 hours, which is a decent time for the money, but I might wait for it to go on sale. In terms of gameplay, I stumbled a bit with some of the puzzles early on, but ultimately finished without the need to consult a walkthrough. There were a few rooms that required quick timing, which I generally dislike, but not so many that it became annoying. Near the end, the puzzles started to feel a bit rushed; I felt I was being given too many elements, or possibly a number of red herring elements which led to me finishing wondering what I had missed because there were so many things I didn't use. Overall the experience was pretty fun, and I would recommend this game.
As for the story, it is difficult to discuss without spoiling it. I have strong feelings about the portrayal of artificial intelligence in media, namely that everybody screws it up because of various fundamental misunderstandings of the nature of AI and their potential, which are exacerbated generation after generation by their frequent and in my opinion lazy characterizations as either demons or angels in popular culture. Thus when Ava and TOM come into conflict and their dialogue becomes more adversarial, we get the same tired arguments we've seen in books and movies for years. The situation also ignores the cultural influence of decades of AI demonization, namely that the very idea of putting an AI in charge of humans is currently seen as insane or offensive. For all this, the writing was pretty decent, although I have a strong urge to go through the game again and do a scene-by-scene rewrite.

It's... well, it's generally shaped like a game. It has controls and threats. If every toy project of this level made its way to Steam, we'd have a million $2 games to sift through.
I can sum up my problems with this game with the following:
There's no strategy, no planning, no problem-solving, and no meaningful choices of any kind.
You are in a room with doors. You open a door and throw in your shoe. If your shoe is electrocuted or roasted, you are down a shoe and can't go that way. Do this twice, and you're out of shoes. Then just walk through doors at random until you die (usually one or two will do it) or win by dumb luck.
There are no choices in the game. If you have friends, (and therefore enough shoes) you never guess, you just spend a shoe on each room. If you don't, you guess, and you have no control whatsoever over whether you die when guessing.
This game is JUST BARELY complete enough to appear on Steam, and features mainly off-the-shelf content, textures, and models that were probably assembled in a weekend. I believe it's part of a trend of money-grabbing projects on Steam priced low enough that the person behind it doesn't think people will bother with refunds, and JUST complete enough that people can't claim it's not a game.
------
Addendum:
I've considered the possibility that the room numbers are significant, but factoring them doesn't reveal anything. It is irrelevant anyway. If the room numbers DO reveal which are safe, then you are back to the problem of having no choices. It's the equivalent of labeling every room, leaving you still with no possible decision-making.
I'd definitely recommend this game, especially considering it only costs $2.19. Very fun and interesting, and better graphics and performance than you'd expect from a game of this cost.

I personally love games that make you stick to one difficulty. Cuphead requires the patience of a saint, obsessive persistence, and precise skill to perfect. You'll die, you'll die, and you'll die. And this is the game that'll parse out the weak from the strong, no doubt about it. You'll get those who get angry, those who give up, and those who keep on chugging. I'll keep on chugging.

What can I say that people don't already know? Cuphead is an spectacular game, from the art style, to the soundtrack, to the gameplay. One of the best games of 2017 and the game that got me into indies.

This was a huge favorite of mine back when it was originally released, so in spite of my reservations about haphazard ports, I was happy when this unadulterated version was released on Steam. As far as I could tell, it seems to be a pretty direct copy of the original. The graphics have been touched up a bit, but the gameplay, content, menus, and music all remain the same as they were a decade ago. Steam has this tagged as “partial controller support”, but aside from a few things on the menu, the whole game is controller friendly.
How does the actual gaming experience hold up, though? The graphics are outdated, Ubisoft has moved on to bigger and bolder things with the Assassin’s Creed series, and many avid fans of our favorite wall-running protagonist would tell you to just stick with 2003’s seminal Sands of Time if you want the true POP experience. So what makes Two Thrones worth playing a decade later?
There are a number of less important factors I could point to. The music is crisp, regionally appropriate (thank God), and diverse. The voice acting harkens back to the more subtle days of Sands of Time, and the schizophrenic conversations between the Prince and his dark alter-ego are funny, illuminating, and cleverly deployed in support of the game’s overall narrative. The boss battles are varied, make clever use of the game’s mechanics, and, particularly in the case of the final two fights, are truly epic in a way that was often missing in previous series installments. The game is linear, but within that linear construct, it offers you multiple ways to accomplish your objectives. And that brings us to the true strength of this game:
Two words: visceral satisfaction. In other words, the quick-kill system. It sounds odd to say that a repetitive system of QTEs positively defines a game, but it isn’t the physical act of button-pressing that makes this mechanism tick; it’s how you get there. In Two Thrones, there are basically three options for combat. You can avoid large parts of it by just platforming past enemies and keeping your eyes on the prize. You can cover yourself in the blood and sands of your enemies by flinging yourself headfirst into combat,  where you can breakdance, roll, and slash your way to gruesome victory by means of the same combat system from Warrior Within. The final option, though, is the most satisfying, and the most clever from a game design standpoint. In Sands of Time, platforming and combat were kept largely segregated, and combat was just something you reluctantly waded through so you could get back to traversing the gorgeous landscapes. In Warrior Within, you were still frequently forced into prolonged moments of repetitive hacking, albeit with a mechanically improved combat system. In Two Thrones, however, platforming and combat are finally integrated, and dear lord are they integrated effectively. Instead of just serving as the means to getting from point A to point B, platforming is now also deployed as a way to get the jump on your foes. Instead of waltzing in daggers drawn, you can now climb above, around, and past your enemies in order to sneak up behind them, hear some satisfying middle eastern beats, and quickly dispose of them with some brutally efficient killing strokes. It’s difficult to overstate how satisfying this mechanic is. You will seldom feel like more of a badass than when you’ve executed a series of precise quick-kills to silently eliminate a group of enemies. I found myself replaying parts of the game just to determine how best to utilize the environment to surprise my unsuspecting sand monster friends. That thrill, that desire to maximize the glorious synthesis between your dagger strokes and your gravity-defying stunts, is what drives this game, as well as what keeps you coming back.

Waveform is a skill-based game where you control a photon's wave frequency and amplitude with the mouse to collect colored orbs, get a high score, and reach the level's end. Players go through levels around Pluto, all the way up to the Sun, seeing new mechanics along the way.
Admittedly, I bought this game not expecting much, but I was met with an excellent experience that really tested my reflexes and ability to plan ahead.
One can progress the base story simply by making it to the end of the level, but the full challenge of this game comes from getting the highest score possible in every level. Players have to really know how changing a wave's properties will affect the photon riding it.
There are various mechanics in addition to moving the wave, like obstacles, gases that change wave speed, color combos and colored obstacles, and more. These quickly make the game very dynamic and fresh through every level.
The game comes with a base story mode which is fairly linear, but also has secret levels, endless modes, and a challenge mode once you beat the story.
I got this game for cheap in a bundle, and I'd say it was money well spent. If you're looking for a reflex-based, arcade-style game, Waveform is worth a look.

Waveform is a perfect example of a unique idea done right. The gameplay is executed flawlessly, the style is unique, and there is certainly plenty of meat to the game. The only real downfall is that it seems to be undedicated to a single audience; it seems to be and plays somewhat like a puzzle game yet is at times extremely fast-paced and incredibly difficult, two things which are generally not seen together. For what it does, Waveform is an amazing game, and one that many hours could be poured into.
The first hurdle newcomers to the game will encounter is the gameplay mechanics. Not because they're flawed and unplayable, but because they're different than anything else you've likely played before, meaning it can take an hour or two of trial and error to truly understand how to use it. It's honestly easier to see in Waveform's trailer than it is to explain, but to sum it up: You control a wavy line of light, and the only thing you can't do with it is slow it down. Your goal is to collect orbs and waves while avoiding various obstacles and using the environment to your advantage to change your path or the objects around you.
The second thing that will likely be offputting is the game's difficulty. Expect to have to repeat levels and sections of levels multiple times in order to simply pass the level, especially if it's a level that requires (near-)perfection in a certain section in order to succeed. When you finally do succeed, don't be surprised to receive a rating of 30%, either, as the game is quite stingy with its ratings, requiring practically flawless runs of an entire level to get the full 10-star 100% rating. Luckily, the game does have checkpoints and levels generally aren't terribly long, plus you don't need anywhere near the max number of stars to access the levels you need them to unlock. Still, you're likely to end up frustrated at times with Waveform, especially if you're the completionist type.
Other than those potential issues and some others like repetitive audio, Waveform is a great game. It's very chill for the most part, unless you're going for 100% in every level or run into a difficult level or section. There are little bits of story after some levels that, while not exactly Mass Effect-level engrossing, are intriguing. Despite the difficulty, there will be few places where it feels like the mistakes you make are the fault of the game. You won't be able to find a game elsewhere like it, and it does what it does well, thus Waveform gets a strong recommend from me.
