Solid, but expensive for what it delivers.
The AAA+ part is the soundtrack, art design and controls. They're all pretty much as smooth and amazing as you'd expect from WayForward, this is where The Mummy Demastered really rocks. It's got great atmosphere and you can tell there was love put into at least some parts of it. Almost certainly the best licensed, movie tie-in game I've ever played. Though that's not exactly a high bar to cross.
Where The Mummy Demastered(hereonwards shortened to TMD because I can't be bothered to type it out every time), flubs it a bit, is the actual level design, gameplay content and, as a perennial WayForward shortcoming if you've any experience with the Shantae games... boss battles.
The areas themselves aren't badly designed, but certain aspects, like respawning enemies, tend to make some of them pretty tedious to explore, and once you have the HP pool to just tank a few hits and keep going, you'll find yourself running through the enemies to get those areas over with. This is further worsened by the fact that the game enjoys having you loop back through previously explored areas(the fast-travel option only covers, I wanna say, a third of the actual gameplay area, so it's a bit vestigial), to collect stuff you've opened up access to. In some games you could say, "pshaw, you'd only get those things if you wanted to wring more gameplay out of the game, due to enjoying it! Or because of completionism! Because you want those FAT CHEEVOS for collecting everything!"
But in TDM, no, Jesus, you want to collect all of that stuff so you actually have a chance at the boss battles. Most of the bosses(bar one, who is resultingly laughably easy) have varied attack patterns, with no real distinguishable tells and often very little warning once you can see what's coming. So if you're not already in place to dodge it, you're getting hit, which means you're gonna need those health increases. You're also definitely going to want all of the ammo pack increases so you can actually USE your non-basic weapons for more than one room at a time, and to make beating the bosses not take an aeon(also please learn to give your bosses goddamn health bars, having them change colour is not a substitute).
I want to say I'm not bad at platformers. I've played a good few of them, and in a lot of games, I can zero-hit or close-to-zero-hit the bosses, because the attacks have good tells, and you have some form of actually functional dodge move, and more than a pixel of dodging space to use. Genuinely, though, TDM has some boss attack patterns that I have no idea how ANYONE is meant to dodge, so unless you're absolutely a better player than me, like me, you're going to want to collect ALL the powerups. Which means ALL the backtracking. Which means ALL the putting up with the respawning enemies(and I don't just mean "when you leave the screen"-respawning, I mean "keep on pouring in while you're on the screen"-respawning, which is an annoyance during jumping sections until you get the no-knockback-from-enemy-hits upgrade).
You're also a bit boned unless you grab a completed map from the internet, because you're expected to blast open certain areas to access them(don't quite understand this, though, at two points, before getting the first explosives, and before upgrading them to better explosives, it serves as a roadblock. After this, it just serves as a timewaster and an annoyance). Some of the time, I want to say 50% of the time, the game shows you these doors you can blast option. But the other 50% of the time, it's just a featureless edge-of-the-level. And some of them require upgraded grenades to blast open, so you might pass them once, try the basic grenades, not blast them open, then assume there's nothing to explode there, and move on. Then completely miss something close to half of the game's health and ammo capacity upgrades.
Ultimately, I didn't need to force myself to complete this game, so that speaks in favour of it. I'd recommend that people who start shivering if they don't get their regular fix of platformers grab it, and anyone who spots it on sale. It's not worth 20 of your hard-earned [insert currency here].
Also please release the damn soundtrack on Bandcamp, not iTunes or whatever other awful services are available. Let me download my damn music.
Edit: I forgot the most boneheaded game design decision. Of course, the game has save points. And of course, you respawn at them when you die. But! You respawn without all your stuff and upgrades, and you have to kill your undead self to re-access them. This is fine... EXCEPT. You respawn with barely any ammo and none of your upgraded health refilled. For ammo, no problem, there are ammo refill points... but no such thing for health. Have fun grinding randomized health drops for half an hour so you actually have full health for your second shot at the boss battle that killed you.
Where the hell did this game come from?

At first glance buying this game felt like a huge gamble, and here's why, not only is this a licensed game (typically licensed games end up just average at best with most of em being shovelware that tries to take advantage of people who know the brand) but its a licensed game based on a movie that wasn't that well recived compared to the original (I have not seen the original or the reeboot, so I cant judge the game on that, but thats just what I heard)
Let me make a minor point, there's licensed games, which are just the regular junk  that I mentioned beforehand, then there's licensed gems, games that make great use of source material, are given to a proper developer, and translate great to a game
To my excitement and joy, this game overcame all those hurdles and is proudly under the licensed gem category, with a wonderous soundtrack, excellent gameplay reminicisent of Metroid-vania style games, with contra gunplay and just a tad of dark souls recovery (u need to get your stuff back from a zombie of yourself when u die) You  will utterly enjoy every moment as the textual cutscnes (Super Metroid style) make you go deeper and deeper into an intriguing story whilst you search every nook and cranny trying to uncover secrets, and again, just like Metroid-vania games, coming back when you get more upgrades to either find more secrets or to make yourself stronger
Add to all of this invigorating boss fights and very challenging enemies that may seem easy at first, but get harder later on as you need to keep an eye out for ammo/health drops, and you have yourself a wonderous experience
It just goes to show you that in the right hands, even a licensed game can turn out great, and this game goes up there with Ducktales and Battle for Bikini Bottom imo
NOTE-While this is a positive review and I rarely do this in reveiws, I cannot stress that due to how bad the movie did, you never kn ow how long the game will be up or how long the license will last for Wayforward, if you plan to get this game, get it while you can, because it will be "vaporized" so to speak and be delisted before you know it

WayForward generally doesn't disappoint with games and The Mummy Demastered while not one of my favorite of their outings does a solid job of mixing elements from Metroid and Castlevania into an enjoyable, albeit short, game.
The novel mechanic is upon death losing all your weapons and then having to defeat the undead version of yourself to acquire the weapons back. I only died once during my initial playthrough and honestly this mechanic seems more like tedium than something particularly interesting. The fact that there is no health stations means that depending on where your death is you could be facing a particularly difficult challenge to continue. The lack of health stations also creates an annoying feeling of wanting to farm health before a potential boss, even though none of the bosses are particularly challenging. If you are a veteran of Metroidvania games these bosses will not prove to be that formiddable whatsoever.
On the artistic side it is very well done with both a great retro artstyle along with a solid soundtrack. I wish there was a slightly greater amount of location and enemy variety but again this game was relatively short.
Overall I think for fans of Metroidvania style games this is a worthwhile pick-up but the price of $19.99 at the time of my purchase felt a bit steep. It is pretty quick to plow through and even going back to get the 100% item and map achievements don't add a tremenous amount of time to the game.  I do hope that WayForward does take the experiences from a game like this and maybe do an IP of their own as a Metroidvania since I always enjoy playing games of this genre. I leave this game satisfied but wishing for a little more.

This is a surprisngly good 16-bit Metroidvania. If you're a fan of the genre, I highly recommend picking this game up despite one seriously irritating flaw. It follows the plot of the recent Mummy movie but only in the barest sense. As in, you're a soldier who has to defeat the titular mummy. That's about all it has in common with the movie, which is fine since the movie was a cinematic dumpster fire. Explore an open map, collecting various weapons and mobility upgrades, and fighting Egyptian-themed undead enemies and bosses. Anyone who's familiar with games like Super Metroid or Castlevania: Symphony of the Night will be right at home here.
Pros:
- Tight, responsive controls.
- Beautiful 16-bit visuals and music that would be right at home on the SNES or GBA.
- Cool secondary weapons that are powerful as hell. Seriously, the flametrower is awesome.
- Decently sized Metroidvania-style map that opens up more and more as you collect new weapons and upgrades, encouriaging you to return to old areas and explore places that were previously inacessible.
- Interesting boss fights that are difficult but fair.
- Unique death mechanic. When you die, your soldier comes back as a zombie. You return as a new soldier without any of your health or weapon upgrades. You have to find and kill your old zombie self to get your stuff back.
Cons:
- No way to quickly regain health. Recovering your equipment gives you your health containers back but doesn't fill them.  There are rooms that fill up your ammo but none that fill your health. The only way to do so is to kill enemies and destroy objects for health/ammo pickups. This is especially annoying when you die on boss fights because it means that, in addition to killing your old self, you need to spend 10-15 minutes grinding to get back to full health and ammo before taking another crack at the boss. It doesn't make the game more difficult, only more frustrating. It got to the point where I would just quit and reload if I was near death on a boss fight simply to avoid the grind.
- The collectible relics don't really contribute to the game in any way. In a good Metroidvania, every secret you find benefits you in some way (or at least gives you some insight into the game's lore.) The relics in this game are just sort of... there. They feel like a ham-fisted attempt to extend play time for completionists but they're completely optional so you're free to simply ignore them if you want.
- Unskippable cutscenes before boss fights, even if you've already attempted the boss before. A minor annoyance since they're usually only a few seconds long but still... game developers should know better by now.
- Fairly obtrusive tutorial level. Again, a minor problem because it's only a few minutes long but there are better ways to teach the player the controls.
The last 3 cons aren't a big deal at all, the first one is really annoying. Two changes would make the game much better:
- Make it so that recovering your equipment instantly fills your health and ammo.
- Add healing rooms before boss fights.

For this price I can commend it.
There really isn't much to the game. It's a set of rooms layed out in a grid pattern, all rooms look the same when you see them the first time. Rooms can have one of several traps: either a no-escape-trap (the doors get blocked off followed by a fatal trap), or a dodge-trap (you can dodge the trap and continue through the room), or a laser-trap (a laser appears in the door, making it unusable for one cycle; the room may contain other traps as well), or there may be one of several enemy spawns, which are all avoided by standing in the corner. The goal is to find the room with the exit panel. To find out if a room has a trap, you can throw your shoes in which trigger all no-escape-traps (making the thrown shoe unobtainable) and some dodge-traps. Each room has a coordinate, a X and Y if you will. The letter makes for the Y position, while the followed number defines the X coordinate. The coordinates are shown in the room in one of several colors, where each color indicates how many traps are in the rooms surrounding the room the coordinate describes.
Does this sound familiar? Have you seen the Cube-movies? It's exactly that. There are also some random civilians which clearly have some mental disorder, just like the calculator-guy in the movies. But he serves no purpose in the game, other than amusing and misleading you. If a crazy dude is jumping around in the room it must mean there's no trap in there, right? Wrong. You can see him get covered in lava and acid, and he still continues acting like a chicken. This was actually the most unintuitive part of the game.
Once you figure those mechanics out it's a mix of Minesweeper and coin flipping. Once you've lost both your shoes in no-escape-traps, you have to guess which other rooms are no-escape or dodge traps. This part of the game sucks, since it comes down to luck. In the easier difficulties you can mostly win the game by doing the Minesweeper logic, but in the hard difficulty this won't cut it. You can obtain shoes from a random enemy spawn which is some terrorist blowing himself up and dropping a shoe, or when another player who had a shoe dies. That's it for mechanics. After about an hour you start developing a workflow to scan the rooms in a fast manner. I'm sorry to say that at this point the game won't have much more to offer, neither in gameplay nor in content.
The best part about it is the multiplayer. That is because it's fun to coordinate your approaches, even though they're very minimalistic.
I had fun for little over 2 hours with a friend, and I really don't ask more of a 2€ game. If you have nobody to play it with I don't recommend it, but if you've got some friends with some bucks to throw away, this is worth it in my opinion.

After clocking in 30 hours and completing the campagin and more, I believe it's time to review this game.
Straight off the bat, the story is... not well. Many may argue against me, but in my opinion, the story dragged on WAY too much. More than half of the campaign was not important and did not need to be included. Don't get me wrong, in the beginning, the story was incredible. I loved it. But as it went on, it got more and more sidetracked, and just got to the point where I was thinking: "When is this game going to end?!"
Camera angles. Boy where do I start. Absolutely awful. I cannot express how much this destroyed the game. Assassin Tombs and Templar Tombs were more my enemy than the actual bad guy in the game. Immovable camera angles that changed every bar you jumped onto made the tombs a pain in the a** and less of a fun challenge. As perspective changed, so did the way the game interpreted your keyboard input, therefore, if the camera was behind me and I was pressing W, and it changed to be in front of me, I would then proceed to go backwards. Also, combat. DAMN. Wood, buildings, people, anything possible would stand right in front of the camera.
AI. As a person who has played AC2, AC3, and AC4, I can tell you, the AI is buffed in this game more than any other. They are smart, which is not a bad thing, but it just gets stressful when it's you vs 50 men and they all attack at once.
CONTROLS. Boy, was this a problem. Instead of simply displaying the button to press, you had to memorize which button was Legs, Hand, Head, and whatever other random unnecessary things they added. In the cutscenes, it would ask you to press the Hand button quite a lot. It takes me the length of the cutscene to figure out which button is the Hand. By then, I missed it, and now the cutscene is changed.
Callibration. Man this needs work. When someone attacks, and I'm blocking, and I press the counter button, I expect Ezio to counter. Makes sense right? Not to Ubisoft. In Ubisoft's eyes, if you press the counter button, Ezio only counters if he chooses to, and if he doesn't want to, he'll just but his guard down for a few hits.
I could go on, and on, and on about all of the bad things this game has to offer. I do NOT recommend this at all to anyone unless they want to play all AC games and/or they are being forced to play.
On a scale of 1-10, I would give this game a 4/10. Bad story, bad camera angles, bad graphics, bad controls, bad nearly everything. Go play AC3 or 4 instead.

Assassin's Creed II is a historically rich stab to the back.
Featuring a somewhat dual narrative, the game primarily follows the footsteps Ezio Auditore from the day of his birth.  A 15th century child of nobility living in Renaissance Florence, Ezio grows up a well meaning trouble maker just like his older brother as they often engage in brotherly shenanigans across the city.  But after his father and brothers are publicly executed whie he narrowly escapes, Ezio discovers that his family heritage is a part of an ancient Assassin order that pits itself against the conspiring Templar Order in a bid to safeguard humanity's free will from their conquest.  Taking up his father's blade, Ezio sets out to avenge his family and to erase the entire Italian branch of the Templars.  Riding shotgun on this adventure is Desmond Miles, a 21st century Assassin who is training by reliving his ancestor Ezio's life and memories with the help of a special machine called the Animus.  The story of ACII is a meandering mess with zero sense of pacing.  It has plenty of heart and human warmth to its characters, but the narrative surrounding them is just one Templar kill after another.  The primary story thread takes almost the entire game to be made apparent and the majority of the assassinations in the meantime are mostly unrelated filler to pad the game out.  But the worst story offender is the passage of time.  ACII takes place over the course of twenty-three years while showing absolutely zero signs of change in the world.  You wouldn't even know time passed if you weren't paying attention to the time stamps on the chapters.  There's a deeper running story thread as well though; something that predates the world as we know it, and that story is a lot of fun any time its head peaks above the surface.
ACII utilizes a unique movement and freerunning system.  So long as freerun mode is active, Ezio will make the decision to climb, leap, drop, or dive based on the direction the player is pushing him.  For the most part it works incredibly well, but sometimes Ezio will absolutely blunder any and all of the input you try to feed him.  It's not a perfect system but it works well.  Combat is depressinly barebones.  Swords, knives, hammers and more all come into play, but they're all functionally identical.  What's more, they're obsolete from the outset.  Ezio's hidden blade is intended for quiet kills, but can also block attacks and instantly kills anyone you use a counter attack on in combat.  Other tools like throwing knives and poison are even less efficient.  The game suffers from a considerable lack of challenge, a massive amount of filler treasure slathering the open world cities, and constant repitition of simple and relatively unengaging mechanics.  Money can be used to buy obsolete weapons and armor as well as change the color of your outfit, purchase art for your home villa, or invested in the villa itself to fix it up over time.  You can also buy maps showing you where more money is.  Even the vehicle sections meant to break up the monotony are monotonous.
Assassin Creed II's flawed but saving grace; the presentation has just enough kick to really sell it.  The mix of synthetic, string, and vocal (sometiems operatic) music is so perfect as to be described as instant classic.  You'll visit major Italian cities and each one is sprawling, beautiful, and distinct.  People fill the streets, heralds bellow with the sound of news, and shops pine for attention and coin.  Texture and sometimes model quality is on the abhorrently low side, but this is compensated for by incredibly human and detailed animation.  All these combined make for a magical visit to 15th century Italy that just barely manages to help one ignore the significant shortfalls.

This has quickly become my favorite FPS. Whether you will like or hate it comes down to these very simple distinctions it has from other FPSes: The pacing and extremely good gun play.
* Reloads take longer than other games, often taking several seconds.
* Moving quickly sharply reduces accuracy
* Being injured or reloading slows you
* Weapons are semi-automatic, lever action, or reloaded after every shot or two.
Consequently, the game has some intense, suspenseful moments, and accuracy is ever more critical. The game has a unique feel, and the gun play is really what carries the game. The slower pacing does NOT lead to a lack of action, I cannot stress this enough.
Interestingly, some weapons are (deliberately) stronger than others, but the weaker a weapon is, the more points it awards for scoring a kill with it. Environment based kills, like kicking someone into a cactus or igniting an explosive barrel awards more points as well. In objective based game modes, stronger weapons simply cost more points, as one would expect.
PROS:
Extremely good gun play
Very unique pacing
Solid map design
Surprisingly diverse weapons
Well balanced weapons
CONS:
Fairly dated graphics
Some bugs here and there, mostly with the train
Kick stuns are relatively annoying
All in all, it's an extremely good game, and I cannot possibly recommend it enough. If you want a unique experience with some of the best gun play you'll ever experience, give it a go; it's free, there's no excuse not to.

I love Cuphead. I think the different shooters, supers and charms add a nice dynamic to the game where the player needs to decide what would be best to use for each boss or run-n-gun based on how that stage is played out. I love the parrying system and the fact that dashing is in the game. This game has a well balanced base difficulty, in which I think some of the bosses will be hard for some players and easy for others. I love the diversity in the combat styles of the bosses because it makes the first couple of tries on every boss a struggle no matter what. The 1930's aesthetic made this game feel like a jolly good time even though things were being killed every two seconds.
I didn't like how once you got to a certain point in the game it almost didn't make any sense to use a charm that wasn't the plus two hearts. I also found the second and third supers to be greatly inferior to the first super. I only used them when I first unlocked them to see how they would play out in a match before exiting to map and switching back to the first super. Even with these flaws I still highly recommend this game to anyone who wants to play a run-n-gun style game.

This game has so much potential to be one of the best Metroidvania style games to come out in quite a few years, but it falls short in a few places. For starters, nearly all monsters are direct rips from both Metroid and Castlevania series. While this is not necessarily a deal breaker for a game, and could be just a blatant homage to the two games that paved the way, it's just kind of lazy. Many of the characters keeping you from reaching the waypoint each section take a ridiculous amount of ammo to kill.
I'm certainly no stranger to hard games. I grew up playing NES/SNES, Sega and Playstation. I do appreciate the level of difficulty this game is set, but at some points it's just extremely tiresome. There's lots of busy work. If you die, you not only lose all of your power ups (health and weapons cache), but you have to fight yourself in order to get those power ups back. I can admit this is a fairly creative way to respawning. You'll spend a bit more time than expected to defeat yourself, then you'll need to farm all your powerups again. No, defeating yourself doesn't restore your health and ammo to your last save. If you die on a boss, you'll spend a good 5-10 minutes getting back to full health and weapons. It's just small details like this that make this game tiresome.
Visually the game is exceptional, and it really relies on those mid to late 90s graphics to get the job done. Navigation and control are also very high for a game like this. Manipulating your character is quite easy, especially if you have a lot of experience with Metroid and Castlevania games. Overall I'd give this game a 65/100. Jt's good enough to recommend and to keep playing, but there are just enough annoying aspects to keep it from a top score. I suspect the developers set the difficulty at such a high bar to make up for development, such as character design and boss levels (spiders, dinosaurs, etc).

I seriously can't recommend this game any higher than what I can.  It's so crazy that we happen to live in a time where a developer can create a game based on a mediocre/below average movie and make an actual FANTASTIC game.  For those who don't know what you're getting into, The Mummy Demastered is a 2D Metroidvania game that feels a bit like Super Metroid, a bit like Symphony of the Night, and a small touch of Metal Slug.  You play a nameless soldier due to the fact that Tom Cruise's likeness can't be used in games or toys, BUT your good pal Russel Crowe contacts you a few times throughout the game.  Gameplay mechanics go as normal for Metroidvanias: you don't have a specific piece of gear to get passed an area, so you go looking for it and then you're able to backtrack and progress.  You have about 7 to 8 different types of weapson, 3 different types of grenades, health upgrades, and ammo capacity upgrades.  Outside of those extra upgrades, you'll also find maps for each of the areas, 50 relics scattered around the map, and more unique items that you benefit from such as weapon damage or damage reduction.  You gain power ups from certain scrolls that you uncover during your playthrough like a higher jump or being able to breathe underwater.  However, the devs decided to do a unique way of death, almost similar to the death mechanic in Hollow Knight.  Because you're an unnamed soldier, you're not a hero.  You may fail in your mission and perish, but due to Ammanet's powers, that soldier is revived.  You then begin again at the recent save point as a new soldier.  Your priority as that new soldier is to find the previous soldier you were playing and kill him so you can get all your items and upgrades back.  It's a mechanic that is a hit or miss for people, but me personally I enjoyed it because the concept itself is much more different and original than just restarting from a checkpoint as if it never happend, but also the whole nameless super hero trope can be a bit boring.  Now you would think that if you got into an area that you can't get back to without an ability, don't worry.  The soldier will spawn in a room close to that area that you can get to, so the game doesn't lock you out from continuing.  The music, which is done by the amazing Monomer, is a nice array of Retrowave/Darkwave which you wouldn't think fits with the setting, but the music is so good.  The animations are smooth, environments are different enough to where you're not getting bored with copy pasted rooms and the bosses are unique in that some behave just as tank and spank while others are more bullet hell-like.  The one minor issue I had with the game is that there are a few monsters that rise from the ground.  This is completely RNG and can rise from underneath you.  While the early zombies can be dodged, there are a few times when they just immediately pop out with no animation.  The sarcophagus enemies later, however, become a pain because of this.  Overall though, I think because this game impressed me when it had no reason to actually be impressive at all (because most movie based games are normal cash grabs), I literally think this is worthy of being on my top 10 for games this year.  It was just a great experience that like I just can't put down.  I worked on 100% then I started to route for speedrunning.  The devs did an amazing job, so cheers.

The Turing Test is pretty much what it says on the tin--an adventure puzzle game.  But I say 'pretty much' because if they were interested in being fully accurate, they would add a few more words to that sentence.  Because The Turing Test is actually a minimally adventurous and fairly simple puzzle game.
The 'adventure' consists of walking through a series of test-chambers which, by and large, contain an array of quickly solved logic puzzles and an autonomous AI program named TOM that hurls an array of poorly written dialogue at you.  Which is a shame, because The Turing Test has a very ambitious goal from a narrative standpoint--trying to explore the philosophy surrounding Alan Turing's famous thought experiment regarding intelligent machines.
Unfortunately, the writing team on the project simply didn't have the chops to pull off such a delicate task.  Instead, you get a cast of characters flatter than cardboard cut-outs whose motivations are non-existent or nonsensical; a thick, gooey, hamfisted layer of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ half-understood philosophy of the mind; and an antagonist who is, literally, his own worst enemy.  And this is something that I can't stress enough.  TOM spends more than half the game actively and repeatedly working to thwart his own stated goal (which, without dropping any spoilers, makes utterly no sense anyway).  Further, the plot is one long railroad from start to finish--and given the linear nature of the game that would be fine, if the characters had a reason to be on the train.  But if you actually stop to analyze what's happening in the story, you will swiftly realize that the entire plot is simply one long string of non-sequiturs.
It's a classic example of a great idea terribly executed.
From a visual and audio standpoint, the game performs well enough.  It's a journeyman-level utilization of the Unreal 4 engine--though you will get tired of seeing some of the same assets again and again, and the character portraits look like a middle-school photoshop project.  The graphical and audio design are nowhere near the caliber necessary to overcome the hurdle of a woefully clunky narrative, however.
So unless you're desperate for a poorly scripted Portal clone with less interesting characters and less challenging puzzles, The Turing Test is probably best avoided--or best purchased during a sale, and at a sizeable discount.

is an Action-Roleplaying-Game (ARPG) set in a Viking themed world. It has everything the roleplaying fan could expect and then some more:
What you get from the developers (TangrinEntertainment) is a solid ARPG experience in terms of story (nothing too fancy nor too bland – it is more of an appreciative nod in the general direction of ARPGS with a humorous approach), in terms of developing or building your characters (you get a lot of different skills and items to equip your characters with) and in terms of quests (main and side quests) and items (looting, treasure chests, crafting).
What you also get are some features that are non-standard ARPG stuff. You get the slow-time function to issue orders for your different characters in battle. Though it is no infinite slow-motion nor is it a pause. The game can be slowed for about 20 seconds before you need to let the slow-meter fill up again.  There are also puzzles in this game, not too hard, not too easy.
Between quests which take place in different parts of the games world you always return to your hometown to shop, craft, talk, get new quests and more story background, get special assignments and take your time to experiment with new skillsets and equipment.
It is a solid game with some proven mechanics and some experimental ones.
Sadly there is no voice over for the substantial amount of dialogue you get. Visually the game is good-looking. The character and enemy models are done quite well. The models in the character and inventory screen seem a bit clunky, but you can see every equipment change on the character. The places you explore seem alive with plants and animals, different climate. The music is very well done, outstanding really if compared to other titles in the genre.

If you like ARPGs and could enjoy some fresh features in a unique setting, KYN is definitely worth your time.

This game is pretty bold in its mix of traditional point and click adventure aspects and jump and run mechanics. You choose 3 out of 7 characters, who all come with their unique abilities, background story and areas. You move around by climbing ladders and ropes. There are common areas where you need all three characters to solve the puzzles and specific character areas that need the respective character's ability to be solved.
The puzzles are stupidly hard, I played this game with my partner, and we couldn't of finished it without the aid of the walkthrough. You would need some very critical thinking in order to get past the second level without some sort of guide.
As this was my partners first proper PC game she had played, apart from Sims and WoW, I think it did a very good job of introducing different game mechanics for people who haven't even played this sort of game before.
This title is not very linear, which will catch many modern gamers by surprise, who are used to heavy handed scripted playing. The humor is dark and entertaining, so are the individual stories behind the characters. The art and mood is amazing in here too.
The annoying part of the game is that you often at times have to walk back and forth to solve puzzles, which is compounded by the fact that you sometimes need to move three characters to a specific location. A character summon function would have been handy here. But that doesn't ruin an excellent gaming experience for a low price.
I hope the younger gamers will appreciate it despite the lack of heavy scripting from newer games. We both thoroughly enjoyed the game, but like I said, without the aid of a walkthrough, I fear there may of been an argument at times at deciding which way to do the puzzle!

This game is a vry good one It is a puzzle platformer but nonetheless you can have endless fun traversing the halls of The Cave

The Cave speaks, so it introduces it self and presents seven characters that are about to enter it, but you can only choose three of them. They are: The Knight; The Cientist; The Adventurer; The Twins; The Monk; The Time Traveler; and The Hillbilly. You'll be taken on a journey to find what they desire most and what they would do to get it. The cave is divided into seven character themed stages and three unchangable stages that are interconnected. So whenever you play you'll go through three stages based on each of the characters you choose at the start and three that will aways be the same. The Cave is filled with puzzles, interesting stories and a funny narrator. The only problem I have with the game is the fact that to play with three new characters I had to go through the other three unchangable levels and there was still one character left to play with, but this one I watched on Youtube. Overall the puzzles are really good, but some are better than others. I would recommend you to play with the Cientist, the Time Traveler and the Hillbilly, because they have the best stages. Then play with the Adventurer, the Twins and the Monk, which are ok. The Knight has the worst stage, but it is on the start of the cave so you can easily play it as the last character and then watch his endings on Youtube.

Much of what I have to say about the Cave has been said in previous reviews, but I think it bears repeating in addition to some other things I've noticed.
The story is an amusing one of dark humor, the graphics visually appealing, the music subtle and fitting, the controls easy and relatively smooth. The puzzles are simple and fun, but can get frustrating at times because of the lack of direction/clues/whatever you want to call it, which sometimes makes it hard to figure out where to start without referencing a guide. As people have said, there is a lot of repetitiveness, and there is a lot of running back and forth in many of the puzzles which at times can be frustrating if you don't have a lot of patience like myself. I never found myself having a problem working with the three characters per se, but at times it is annoying to only be able to carry one item at a time (which relates back to the running back and forth part). Having seven characters to play through with is certainly annoying by the time you reach the last one, because as people have noted, this means you have to redo all the puzzles for two of the characters you've already finished with. I definitely agree that for the most part the replay value is not very high, however, after playing it today for the first time in about six months, I found myself plesantly surprised at my renewed interest.
The game has great potential and it's a bummer that nothing really gets switched up from runthrough to runthrough. I really enjoy the games that Double Fine puts out because they are simple but entertaining, with a colorful cast of characters and a little bit of snark and wit in the stories. I think despite it's flaws, the Cave still holds true to all of that. (And the scientist, time traveler, and adventurer are all women, which was a fun bonus perk for me because you don't often see women in those roles in games. None of that affects gameplay, but I still thought it was rad.)
Overall, I would recommend the Cave. Maybe a 7 out of 10.

Another masterpiece by Paradox.
Pros:
Much better graphics than HOI3 and a better diplomatic system instead of just declaring wars and either conquering or puppeting other countries.
The national foci provides a large variety of choices, either historical or alternative. France can have its own faction and the US can strike United Kingdom. Also, shifting ruling party's ideology will change the nation's name and flag just like VIC2. Specific countries will even have a unique name and flag when they are puppeted by a particular country. For example, when you are playing as German Reich and puppet Belarus and Ukraine, they will have the same flag as German Reich and will change their names to "Reichsprotektokrat Ostland" and "Reichsprotektokrat Ukriane". This makes the game even more interesting.
The new air combat system makes commanding an Air Force much easier than it is in HOI3.
More complicated in equipment production and division training ( also more realistic since you have to produce the
equipments like guns and tanks via military factories and production lines ).
The battle plan system makes commanding an Army much easier than in HOI3 where battleplans are of no uses.
Cons:
I somehow dislike the simplified Theater-Army-Division structure. Indeed it is much easier to manage but I still like to see a complete structure under a Theater-Army Group-Army-Corps-Division-Brigade system.
Finally, only VPs and provinces have there names while small regions on the map don't. When playing HOI3 I can say "I encircled an army at XXX" but in HOI4 I can only say "I encircled an army at this region in XXX province". Really want the developers to bring these names back.
Lots of playable countries do not have their own focus trees (e.g. ROC and PRC, Sweden, Netherlands and some others ) hope that Paradox can continuously add focus trees for other minor countries.

Full review (including score):
The Mummy Demastered is a movie tie-in game that is actually good! With some fantastic visual design, a great soundtrack, and a diverse pool of enemies, The Mummy Demastered hits several of the marks for metroidvania games right off the bat. Even so, it does not come without some problems.
The overall design of this game is fantastic. All of the sprites (especially the bosses) and backgrounds were really well done. The soundtrack was great as well, featuring a good mix of spooky, more ambient tunes, and adrenaline-pumping ones all of which are done in an electronic-chiptune style. All of these aspects work together to bring out the “retro” feel, one that has become a staple in many metroidvania games today.
There is a wide variety of enemies to be found in the game world, enough so that it never felt like I was seeing the same enemies too many times. For a game that took me 5.5 hours to beat, there was just enough variety to keep me interested. New areas introduced new enemies with new attacks and unique designs, so there was always that to look forward to. The bosses too, each with their own unique attacks and design. It was a lot of fun fighting the different bosses and learning how to manage their different attacks.
Health is not regained at save stations and is only regained when earning a new health upgrade. Unfortunately, this leads to a grind whenever the player needs to regain his/her HP before moving on. I would often find myself moving into a save room, destroying all of the boxes, lanterns, etc. in hopes of a health orb dropping from them, then exiting the save room and repeating. This is not as bad in the early game, when the health only goes up to 99, but later in the game, when the player has health in the hundreds, grinding for little health orbs that only restore 5 HP (sometimes 20 if lucky enough) becomes incredibly repetitive. It was frustrating to die to a boss then have to redo the whole health-regen grind for 5-10 minutes before attempting the boss again. I probably could have shaved an entire hour off of my 5.5 hour playthrough if I did not have to grind for health so much. Either save stations or the helicopter fast travel spots should bring the character back to full health, rather than just when finding new health upgrades.
This is a movie tie-in game, but it did not feel like it at all. In fact, if I did not know the title of this game, I would not even be able to recognize the fact that this game is directly related to Universal’s “The Mummy” movie, which I have not seen. It felt as if the story was an afterthought to the game, like the game was created before it was decided that it would be based on The Mummy and those elements were just added at the end. The movie tie-in elements felt cheap and this game could have easily existed without them.
Overall, The Mummy Demastered is a solid metroidvania game. The game’s visual design and soundtrack are fantastic and the enemy variety is large enough to not make the experience feel repetitive. The game does suffer from a frustrating health regen grind and a rather lackluster story, but it is still a very fun game to play.

Taste is very much subjective, so I'll tell you why I like this piece of entertainment software.
I've played a reasonable quantity of metroidvanias to have an opinion on the genre as a whole. Looking back into my gaming past I can tell you that I've enjoyed Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony Of the Night atmosphere quite a lot, however, Castlevania: Bloodlines is one of my fondest memories gameplay wise. Yes, it is one of the least exploration oriented of the genre, you could even say it's just a platformer and not a proper metroidvania, yet the gameplay is more interesting to me. The stage and enemies seem to be very interestingly placed, and caring about how you move and hit monsters is very important. Also the game is very much brief, which is something I've grown more interested lately. The Mummy has all those things that I liked about Bloodlines, and one more thing: Contra-esque combat. It's not veeeery contra-esque, but you can tell it's there, and it sure feels cool.
I can also tell you that I'm having a blast with Cuphead at the moment, while Hollow Knight bored me to death. Though I would still recommend both games, because they're equally well cafted experiences, the second one has been sitting too long in the shadows of other games, such as Dark Souls and Super Metroid, to interest me.
Now, based on my words, I invite you to ponder if The Mummy Demastered  is worth roughly two burritos with guacamole from Chipotle, or if it's the value of a single Spicy McChicken from your very own McDonalds.
Godspeed.

SUMMARY:
-A really solid little Controidvania (can you combine all three into one word?)
-7.5/10, worth your time if you enjoy the genre at all.
PROS:
-Good pacing
-Fantastic sprite and visual design
-Fun, huge bosses
-Smooth action
-Sweet weapon unlocks
-KICKASS, bumping soundtrack
CONS:
-Overall short playtime (though can be argued it doesn't overstay its welcome and knows when to wrap things up - see what I did there?)
-Grinding is the only way to regain health outside of picking up an energy tank - err, I mean, health kit.
-Many of the powerups, while useful, aren't especially exciting or creative.
-The relics seem to be nothing more than a tacked-on way of extending the game because they don't actually award any benefits.
EXTENDED THOUGHTS:
-When you die, your agent becomes a zombie. You respawn as a new operative with minimal equipment that needs to hunt down your fallen comrade in order to re-obtain all your gear - I see some others complaining about this, but I didn't mind it in the least. In my opinion, it adds a little meaning (both gameplay and story-wise) to player death, but isn't overly punishing or annoying.
-The boss fights were JUST right in my opinion. Calibrated perfectly to be challenging but doable on your first attempt, which really is excellent design in my opinion. Keeps the stakes raised and the tension up. You start off feeling confident, but they have enough attacks/phases to whittle you down. Pretty soon you're down to one health bar and are completely out of ammo aside from your peashooter, fighting for your life, and then you JUST manage to finish them off. SO satisfying.
-I don't mind a lack of full-heal stations, but I wish the health powerups scaled up with your max health so that healing up didn't take so long toward the endgame.
-I hope they release some DLC to extend the game; I would gladly play more of this.

A good first person room-based puzzle game along the lines of Portal or Talos Principle. While not quite up to the lofty expectations those games have provided for the genre, it's definitely worth being in the same discussion. The setting and plot is very interesting, and while it doesn't tread into exceptionally deep psychological ground, it does one thing right: sci fi. This is what I had hoped Europa Report would be. Good sci-fi.
The game's only downfall is simply that its puzzles never quite explore the furthest extent of their premise. In all but maybe 5 of the 70 puzzles, a solution was obvious from the start. I rarely had to wrack my brain and think outside the box the way I did with Portal or Talos Principle. In fact, there were a few puzzles I solved in ways that completely circumvented their design. It felt cheap to be able to do that, as if the designers didn't even test their puzzle designs. Instead, puzzles simply get bigger instead of harder. Adding more rooms to the puzzle doesn't make it harder. It only makes it longer.
But hey, it was still a fun ride, and maybe I expect too much. Perhaps next time these designers can take all that they've learned from making such a good game and in turn follow up with a GREAT one. I could see it.
It's a little better than the first game, but I still wasn't wild about it. The action could definitely be more fun and, for that matter, challenging.

TL;DR : despite many "bad things", I actually had fun playing this game, that's why the thumbs up.
I've started this review when I started the game and I kept updating it while playing. It took me around 55 Steam hours (inside the game they are only 37, I don't know why this difference) to beat the game at 100%, included "The Truth". I didn't go fast, I actually played enjoying it as much as possible.
- the game is actually funny and the gameplay improved a lot compared to the first episode (especially with the ability to swim)
- it's possible to select the italian spoken language, thanks to which all the people within the game are dubbed by real italian speakers. With the english spoken option they mostly talk with foreign-accent italian.
- "It's a-me, Mario!". It deserves a plus only for this.
- Monteriggioni management is nice
- there's Leonardo Da Vinci and you interact with him and use some of his historical devices
- historical locations are quite faithfully reproduced and you can actually learn their history and historical characters' history within the game
- Venice has been reproduced in a nice way and you can even navigate with a Gondola. How cool is that?
- at first it took me an hour just to make it work with a controller: I tried JoyToKey first, but the feeling wasn't so good, then I've found the file that people suggest to install in the forum. And thanks to that, it finally worked. But still, why the game isn't compatible with a controller? Are we supposed to play it with keyboard and mouse?
- the game passes through Uplay, not directly via Steam. Yes, that's a negative thing to me.
- selecting "english spoken", the characters still use some italian word, but with foreign accent. I would have preferred if they spoke only english instead of a broken italian.
- also, selecting "italian spoken", EVERYONE speak italian, even Desmond and other american characters. It would have been better if it was possible to just have the right language for each character. English for the americans and italian for the italians.
- not funny when you try to enter an area and you receive the message "Unlock this map through the Ubisoft Club". Especially if it's necessary for the 100%. Luckily it's easy to get it, but you have to search how it works (I usually avoid Uplay, so I didn't know anything about it) and have to spend Ubisoft Points (which you get also playing the game). I just don't see the reason for this, it could have been better if it was already accessible.
- the audio volume is pretty low even at its maximum
- the game gives you A LOT of money with treasures, quests and stuff, and all this money is quite useless. Especially treasures are completely useless inside the game, they are not needed for 100% and you don't need all that money at all.
- dancing camera: that sometimes becomes nauseating, especially in tombs where you need to be really careful with your jumps. When you fall and die because of that, it's really annoying and a waste of time.
- automatic Camera too is bothering sometimes, and it seems there is no way to deactivate it. It should help you showing you the path where you have to go, but it doesn't understand if you don't want to follow that path
- Monteriggioni management could have been better: you end up finishing everything too quickly and the money later is useless.
- after a while the game started to crash and close it for no reason. Then, after more hours, it stopped and worked fine. Strange.
- I've found the main story to be a little too long. After a while I just wanted to finish it but the story was still going on. Too much is too much.
- there isn't Rome (they later included it in Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood)
- if you lose your weapon in combat and can't find it on the ground anymore, the only way to retrieve it is to go back to the Villa and take it. That's a waste of time.

Waveform tasks you with controlling a wave of light through a galaxy of planets. The goal is reaching the Sun from Pluto, a journey which traverses over 100 levels through 11 different worlds. As further levels are reached, the goal of reaching the Sun expands into stopping a singularity that threatens to darken the entire galaxy. More elements of the story are revealed in later levels.
The concept of controlling a wave of light is executed flawlessly through beautifully rendered levels and a challenging, but addictive gameplay experience. If you are looking for a truly unique and innovative experience you shouldn’t hesitate to add Waveform to your game library.
Overall verdict:
Highly recommended!

Before I start, even though this is labeled as recommended, this is a mixed review. Since there's no opinion for mixed, then I have to say recommended.
I would've loved this game.  It had amazing artstyle, immersive atmosphere and overall nice story. The 4th wall and puzzles felt special and really helped to increase the atmosphere. But they'res three things about it that really cause me to feel apart from the experience.
1. The endings: Throughout the game, the tower was built up as this sacred place where the previous sun was spilling its light across the world. Once you got there with Niko, at first it was this dark place where the only object around was the computer which contained the entity. After some trickery and sleeping later, there was a series of puzzles which involved using an outside application to build a path. This part was honestly pretty boring, but that's not the point. When you finish the last part of the puzzles, you reach an elevator which leads to the top of the tower. Here you're given two choices: return the sun or return home. Despite the steam tag of choices matter, they really don't as you always are given the same choice regardless. (unless you're on the solstice run, which i'll touch on later) When you chose return the sun, a cutscene of Niko placing the sun and the game cutting to credits. This is probably the worst ending i've ever seen in a video game. I mean, sure you get pictures of the game's characters reacting to the sun between the credits, but that part gets missed out by me. If you chose return home, the screen cuts to black with the screen shaking and a glass shattering sound effect. Then you see Niko going home through the game window and it crashes. This ending is certainly better than the other ending but still lacks satifiscation or sometimes sadness that endings are supposed to give.
2. The gameplay:
The gameplay is essentially a third person point & click. Most of the game has you wandering around looking for items to combine with each other. For example, near the beginning of the game Niko has to build a new battery for the generator of the Barrens. This is how the battery is made, just to paint a picture of how repeitive and tedious this mechanic is.
Metal pipe + Press = Crowbar   Crowbar + Box = Broken Battery  Camera + Crowbar = Lens    Broken Battery + Lens = Empty Battery  Lightbulb + Empty Battery = Charged Battery  Generator + Charged Battery.  It gets worse later in the game. This reason probably will get backlash, but it's honestly true in my view. So now let's move on to the final reason.
3. The characters:
Before I start, this will also get backlash, but it's true in every direction, at least for me. The characters feel empty. Almost every character feels a lack of personality, or anything for that matter. (There's one exception but that will be discussed with the solstice part) So let's review each character with a portrait briefly. Prophetbot doesn't feel anything else than glee. He goes on and on about you being the messiah and being able to communicate with the player, even though he was programmed for this and knows it. It's just, wrong. Then we have silver, who is always content and never smiling, despite being tamed. The rowbot is just there. Alula and Calamus are like Silver and are always content. They do smile, but it's a rare occurance. (sorry birblovers)  Magpie is there to trade you the ink for the wool and sometimes the shirt. That's all. Maize is a slight exception as her sadness has a defined reason, that being the sun is out and since she's a plant, Her energy is gone. The Lamplighter or Plight, is just content and sometimes surprised. George is another exception since her personality is different every run, but these different personalities have very few differences from eachother. Dr. Silverpoint is also content and sometimes sad about Silver. Then we have the Entity and the Author. These two are hard to nail down, but let me try. The Entity just wants die because it doesn't want to kill Niko, even though it has the intelligence of a 10 year old child. The author has no personality onceover. (thats a little debatable in my opinion) Niko is the only base game character to have personality, so that's why I didn't say much before. (Niko is only slightly cute, jk)
And the solstice characters will be discussed in the Solstice section. So there have it. Most characters in this game have either no personality or just contentment. So now it's time for the reason I didn't give this game a full not recommended.
The solstice run.
SOLSTICE:
After I had finished the main game, I didn't expect more after the first two endings. I really didn't. But no, there was more.
And I have to say, this the best part. Upon seeing there was more, I thought this would be the same, but I gave it a chance. I'm glad I did. Enough of that, time to tell you my reasoning. The three new characters, Prototype, Cedric and Rue, actually felt real, like they said they were. The story was built upon so much more, to the point where I could deal with the gameplay and felt I needed to know more. And even the base game characters had more personality with Silver sacrificed herself to save Prototype and Niko from the collapsing cave, Maize used the last of her strength to build vine bridges to necessary areas and the Birbs were displaying other emotions. It felt great! Then the big reveal with Rue about the Entity being the World Machine, and the tear-jerking moments with Niko and their lack of purpose. Finally we have the best possible ending that the OneShot Team could have made. All the characters were brought back by the World Machine, all to bring to a sad goodbye to Niko. Atleast they made it home. ;) (I cried a little at this part)
Overall, a pretty great game! 7.5/10 Feel free to comment your opinion.

I've played a lot of Role Playing games over my lifetime from Ultima, Phantasie Series, orginal gold Box Series of Dungeons and Dragons, Pillars of Eternity, Divinity Original Sin, Dungeons Siege 1 and 2 and part of 3, Lords of Xulima and the list goes on and on.
Kyn is not a very good Role Playing game.  I've seen it compared to Dungeon Siege 1 and 2 and to say it's their successor but it isn't even close.  I'm on mission 4 and you only have 2 Characters that are customizable at that stage and not a complete party.  You get Random guys to join you on certain missions but they just leave at the end of the mission.
Some of the problems with this game is you mostly only get crafting materials from Treasure Chests instead of Items so you have to buy all of your equipment.  Number 2 the characters you have already have their own names you can't name your characters and "create" your own party.  Also Characters are not very customizable at all.  The only stats they have
are Control , Body and Mind and you put all of your points that you gain each level into those 3 stats.  There is not a long list of stats to put your ability points into.  There is only overland adventure also, no dungeons, nothing underground to explore, you can't enter into any buildings, open doors , etc.  All of the loot seems to be in treasure chests and you just bash them open.  No lockpicking ability nothing.  Also the game is very very linear.  All of the maps have very narrow corridors that you explore so you can't just explore everywhere on the map to see what is out there.  You can only explore in the very narrow window of the map.  Also talking to villagers is generally worthless.  You can click on talk to them over and over again and they will say the same thing over and over again and most of them just say the same thing the other villagers do.  In Divinity you can get quests from all kinds of villagers not just ones with a question mark over them like this game.  And you can actually communicate with them.  In this one all of the guards and general villagers are generic and don't really do anything for the "Role Playing" aspect of the game.  I totally disagree with the other review that says these are comparable to Dungeon Siege 1 and 2.  They are not at all.  Those are really good games.  I do agree with him that Dungeon Siege 3 is a joke because they totally ruined that game.  Interacting with most villagers in this game changes nothing in the game and you learn very little information as they are so generic.  If the bug I've encountered in Greenport gets fixed then I may finish this game as I have nothing better to do right now but it's not a very good game.  Pick up one of the newer titles if you want a good Role Playing game like Pillars of Eternity, Divinity Original Sin, Lords of Xulima (Which I didn't think was that great at first but it grew on me) or go old school and get Dungeon Siege 1 and 2 or really old school and find a computer that can still play the original Gold Box Series of Dungeon and Dragons Role Playing games.  I would pass on Kyn though.

Kyn is a unique isometric ARPG, which offers linear missions and slow-mo tactical combat. Skills/abilities are limited to two per class plus an additional based off items. Tangrin based in the Netherlands is essentially a two-man operation. These creators definitely show their love for RPG's and game development but lacked the necessary broad stroke. Kyn suffers in a few areas. That isn't to say it's a bad game. It just could've been more.
The Good:
Visuals mixed with an exciting soundtrack.
Inventive re-working of a tactical combat system.
Level design and interactive puzzles.
Challenging gameplay experience.
The Bad:
Camera controls that feel lacking.
UI which feels generic.
Skills/Abilities which are not expansive.
Underdeveloped NPC interactions.
The Ugly:
Storyline, with the dialogue. It's extremely bland and is underwritten.
Extremely underwhelming animations.
AI tracking system for mobs.
Character customization and item customization.
Overall, Kyn is a decent ARPG. You'll have fun with it, if you're into the genre. The character customization could have been better. Yes, you can craft and ingredients drop from everything but it just had a bland approach. The three skill tree have 80 or so skills all together. Certain skills are more powerful than others and it really didn't feel balanced nor synergized. I will give it a recommendation if you're looking for a tactical ARPG. There are much better options for the $19.99 price tag on the market. Giving it a 6.5/10 score.

Hearts of Iron 4 is a rush though. Whether you’re carefully crafting a plan or just throwing your country into turmoil because you believe the United States is better served in invading neighbouring nations rather than interfering with Hitler’s plans, there’s plenty of havoc to be wrecked. World War II enthusiasts will love the historical accuracy even if fans of the franchise don’t quite appreciate some of the changes made to combat and provinces.
There’s so much to unpack here and so much to learn that you’ll spend quite a significant amount of time just getting your bearings. Once you’ve attained a solid base and made your fair share of rookie mistakes, Hearts of Iron 4 will really start to beat information into you till you can take no more of the build orders and menu screens and conflict. And I mean that in the best way possible.
If you’re seeking a grand strategy title that focuses more on war planning and execution, then Hearts of Iron 4 is definitely worth a look. It allows you to experience as little or as much of the war-mongering process as you’d like, giving your all to conquering this world while immersing yourself in it further. The drab interface, lack of tutorial and absence of any real assistance for all the micro-management is disheartening, to say the least, but this only slightly wears on the game’s fun factor. Just remember – war is a cruel, crazy, difficult mistress in Hearts of Iron 4 but it’s oh so worth it.

This game was essentially my major introduction to the Metroidvania genre of games.
The Mummy Demastered took me roughly about 5 hours to beat and was a mostly positive experience.
For a simple Pros and Cons list here is what I liked and despised while playing this game
Pros:
-Progression felt like I was actually getting stronger with the new guns and relics
-Atmosphere was great especially with how fitting the music is for this game
-Great set of enemies in both design and difficulty scaling
-Bosses are fair
-Backtracking felt rewarding with the amount of ammo health and passive upgrades that were missed in previous levels
-No Tom Cruise
Cons:
-Impossible to heal back to full health easily, you will spawn back with almost nothing and after killing your former self you get about half your health back and no ammo. There should be at least someway to refill your health without grinding bats and lamps for 10 minutes
-No free aiming. You are limited to 45 degree angles for firing which isnt awful when getting used to but the amount of bats and bugs that could have been prevented is sad.
-Every boss is a huge damage sponge, the damage relic helps a bit later in the game but you end up unloading way more rounds into the boss than you'd want to.
-The collectible relics are essentially useless, outside the achievement there is no reason to go for them since they give no reward in the slightest
-No Brendan Fraser
Ultimately the game is about a 5 hour adventure if you don't rush through it, it doesn't bring much to the genre that other games appear to do but it is definitely a solid pick. If you are ever looking for a new metroidvania to play, this game is on sale, or you just want to play a game with mummys, this is the perfect game.

WayForward's The Mummy: Demastered is a Metroid-clone licensed for the movie that I have not seen nor do I particularly ever want to see.
It is a Metroid-clone through and through. You don't waste your time with RPG elements, stats, Dual-Card Systems or whatever it is that's cool with the kids these days. Go find the whoever's in charge of this mess and shoot them in their ugly face.
It's fantastic-looking, beginning to end, with pixel art that they've just put their all into. Colours, intricacy, variety, animation, the lot. This is the best-looking WayForward game I've ever played, and easily one of the best looking pixel platformers I've ever seen. Maybe even the best.
With this is a killer soundtrack that's all explorative electronic that still maintains a faster pace to keep you interested. Honestly it's a great package and it holds up.
Gameplay-wise, it's Metroid. Run n Gun, but you can lock yourself in place to shoot in any direction. I heavily recommend using a gamepad for this one, if you don't it'll basically control like you're using an emulator: entirely keyboard/WASD based, you shoot in eight cardinal directions. Playable either way.
Character progression is mainly handled by finding a better gun, more ammo or more health. Your starting peashooter is pathetic, and you work your way up through shotguns, harpoons, flamethrowers to reach some absolutely legendary endgame weapons that I don't want to spoil for you because they're amazing.
Your playstyle changes appropriately. At the start, you're a single mook that's incredibly vulnerable, expendable and incredibly defensive. Every hit takes a chunk out of you and each mook takes effort to take down. And by the end, you're an invincible phase-dashing super-soldier with Rambo levels of ammo for your screen-clearing guns.
But, there's a caveat to this. It's pair of mechanics that slap the game across the face if you're prone to them and are pretty much responsible for every negative review you see.
If you die, you have to hunt down your old corpse and kill it to get your stuff back. Like Killer 7 and Zombi U, you're back to a weak, single mook with a hyper-defensive panicky playstyle until your sock your old buddy.  Honestly, for this one I'd recommend just not dying. It's an inadvisable career path for most people. I comfortably didn't die on the first playthrough, it's not a ridiculously hard game. Get too low on health, quit back to the menu and just start at the checkpoint.
But WayForward doesn't agree with that business: they kinda want you to die. Just once or twice, to show off their mechanics.There is not a single fullheal in this game outside of picking up a health boost, there's not a lot of those. Your main way to heal is to break crates and lanterns for 5 point health pickups. In a game where you can have 1100 points of health. It sucks. No, you can't just restart the game at a checkpoint to get health back, they thought of that. Not sure why they thought of that. Not sure why this is in the game at all. It sucks, WayForward.
Now with how the game handles health drops, once you're at five or so health boosts you can comfortable coast through the game on half health picking up enemy drops, and only need to be full health for the boss fights that tend to have fountain areas of lanterns or crates.
Those are your caveats. That's it. This is a fantastic game that's well worth your time, that I had a lot of fun with and remained amazing to look at and play throughout, and gets thoroughly ridiculous the more you upgrade.
Absolutely recommended to anyone interested in these games.

I've started this review when I started the game and I kept updating it while playing. It took me around 55 Steam hours (inside the game they are only 37, I don't know why this difference) to beat the game at 100%, included "The Truth". I didn't go fast, I actually played enjoying it as much as possible.
- the game is actually funny and the gameplay improved a lot compared to the first episode (especially with the ability to swim)
- it's possible to select the italian spoken language, thanks to which all the people within the game are dubbed by real italian speakers. With the english spoken option they mostly talk with foreign-accent italian.
- "It's a-me, Mario!". It deserves a plus only for this.
- Monteriggioni management is nice
- there's Leonardo Da Vinci and you interact with him and use some of his historical devices
- historical locations are quite faithfully reproduced and you can actually learn their history and historical characters' history within the game
- Venice has been reproduced in a nice way and you can even navigate with a Gondola. How cool is that?
- at first it took me an hour just to make it work with a controller: I tried JoyToKey first, but the feeling wasn't so good, then I've found the file that people suggest to install in the forum. And thanks to that, it finally worked. But still, why the game isn't compatible with a controller? Are we supposed to play it with keyboard and mouse?
- the game passes through Uplay, not directly via Steam. Yes, that's a negative thing to me.
- selecting "english spoken", the characters still use some italian word, but with foreign accent. I would have preferred if they spoke only english instead of a broken italian.
- also, selecting "italian spoken", EVERYONE speak italian, even Desmond and other american characters. It would have been better if it was possible to just have the right language for each character. English for the americans and italian for the italians.
- not funny when you try to enter an area and you receive the message "Unlock this map through the Ubisoft Club". Especially if it's necessary for the 100%. I was alerted to The Turing Test a few days before its release, from some videos that Many A True Nerd put on youtube. As a result, I had seen the first 3/7ths of the game, as well as an Easter Egg from the Prologue. Regardless of this, I found The Turing Test to be a brilliant puzzle game, despite the obvious similarities that could be brought up with Portal and The Talos Principle.
As a first person puzzler, The Turing Test has a nice mechanic involving energy pellets, which over time have different properties along with various tools for you to reach the end door of each 'test chamber'. Where the game shines (mostly) is in its narrative, which explores themes of free will and consciousness, similar to the real life Turing Test that they often refer to.
The majority of the in-game plot is told through small audio logs and emails sent between characters, which you come across after every 10 levels. While a nice form of presentation, as it breaks up each section of puzzle solving, it left me a little irritated when my AI friend would inform me of something I already found out by rifling through somebody's bedroom.
The only real thing I could criticise this game for is the final act, because it solves almost all the mysteries, while leaving what was - to me - the most important one! The test chambers that you go through are apparently made by other humans, so that only a human being could solve them (so basically the reason why you're playing and not just leaving your AI friend to do it all for you). That seems all well and good...until
This issue is never addressed, and it really bugged me. They hint that this whole situation is being engineered, but beyond that I still don't know why the puzzles changed in the way they did except for adding a new and interesting mechanic.
Overall, I still heartily recommend this game, as it lasted me a good 6 hours and I found it consistently engaging. There are some gripes narrative wise, but that aside I think you'll enjoy this if you like similar test chamber style puzzle games.

Even after the rework, the game's basic problems remain.
The monster is on a timer.  The hunters aren't.  They don't even need to chase the monster - even at Stage 3, he is absolutely no threat to a well coordinated and placed hunter team.  It's actually more dangerous to chase the monster - fighting in unfavorable terrain can allow even a Stage 1 monster to wipe the hunters.
Therefore, the wisest course of action is go directly to the Power Relay and wait.  Even at Stage 3, the monster is left with an impossible choice.  Assault the hunters in their preferred terrain overlooking the power relay or do nothing and lose when the timer runs out.
The monster is incapable of dealing more DPS than the Hunters can generate in damage negation through shielding and healing per second from passive health regeneration and medic healing.  If the monster is incapable of splitting of the team up, it is actually impossible to down a hunter in a straight battle.  Even if they burn all of their special abilities at Stage 3 on a single target in a long combo without missing, the a coordinated Hunter team will keep that person above 50% health by the end - and now the monster's abilities are all on cooldown, so they are generally incapable of dealing damage for a few seconds.
This creates a game where only the way one side can win is if the other makes a mistake.  If the Hunters do not, they win by default.  This encourages very boring static defense style gameplay and attempting to win by burning down the timer, while discouraging chasing the monster at all costs.
I want to give this game high praise, because when it's fun, it's fun.  But the asymmetrical design that makes it so attractive also makes it completely impossible to balance, with Hunters losing nearly every single in lower tiers against an even half compentent monster, and Monsters losing nearly every single game in higher tiers because the basic game mechanics make it statistically impossible for him to succeed and rely on the Hunters not utilizing their kit to their absolute maximum capacity.
That said, the flaws still make it absolutely boring to play.  The winner of the match is determined before it's started and easily predicted by the first engagement.

This is a challenging little game... and I do recommend it (specially since you can almost get it for free) ...But it definitely has its pros and cons. It's a great game to play while listening to your own music or a podcast, in that way, it is quite relaxing. The difficulty increases as you progress, but it's a lot of fun to go back to the first levels and realize that even though they are the same levels, the player has improved considerably and gained a lot of skill with no need for any type of ingame mechanics. In a way it's you, the player, the one who's leveled up. And that's something I really appreciate and find interesting.
However, the game gets repetitive soon enough. I had planned to see the end of the game, but right before the final stages, you basically have to go all the way back and get better scores in every level for you to be able to carry on. As I said, that can be fun to do once or twice to see how you have improved, but to do them (almost) all again?
To be honest, the game had already started to get quite tedious at this point and blocking the end behind a score didn't really help. Many casual players will probably see this as a burden, more than anything else. And I don't think Waveform appeals to a lot of hardcore players, as the reviews in steam show (as far as I can see not many have played more than an hour).
So to sum it up:
+ very cheap price
+ interesting and original concept
+ natural progression of player's skills
+ relaxing and slow paced: perfect if you want to listen to podcasts or music while playing
- ending blocked behind score requirements, forcing you to play almost everything again
- quite repetitive
