Since my last review, this game has recieved a handful of updates that have improved fps, clarity, and fun in the gameplay. The controls have been added to the loading screen (absolutely fantastic) and a lot of the sandstorms have been made easier to work with. If there were a direction I would like to take the game in, I would like to to further have "colony" benefits. Everyone has to build their own beacons, and most of the time if they have a mining location they all place it in that location. The map tool itself is still largely ineffective at helping the player navigate.
--
There is HUGE potential for this game. It's getting there, but there's a lot of fixes that need to go through before I'd say "BUY IT". The game is also extremely hard to play--not challenging, like, "oh damn I really gotta try to play this game," but more like, "♥♥♥♥ this game is so ♥♥♥♥ing hard TO play," as in the controls are unclear. there is absolutely zero information on any of the items in game or how to survive; you're not informed of anything other than "find materials to build a forge." The landscape is great, but it's really boring. Think Fallout New Vegas, but with 90% less things. This game might as well be called 50 shades of orange and one shade of black. You also can not play during night because you can no see anything. Also, sandstorms are more annoying than they are atmospheric. They don't add to the fun or the challenge of the game, they just drop fps and make it hard to see where your goddamn equipment is.
Maybe you're the kind of person that wants to spend an hour learning how to turn on your lights, but I'm not.
A lot of clarity needs work. Suddenly, you land on the planet and ... ? That's it. You're given a mining tool, a map that, honestly, shouldn't be an item but something in the 'tab' menu (btw, did I mention nothing informs you that your inventory is on tab?) and a 'multi-tool' object (what is that? I don't even know, and I've been playing this game for two hours), and duct tape (which btw can fix up your suit in a jiffy, no matter whether you were pricked by a bunch of poiny bushes or whether you were fkn smashed by a giant crab monster--use a lil' tape and you're fine). Four things that have no explanation, no real tutorials on how to use.
You can NOT play this game without having the wiki open. That's something to think about. If you want a game that gives you some sense of HOW to play, then this is NOT the game. Not yet. Hopefully, but not yet.
A few bugs:
-Sometimes the aliens can attack you from OUTSIDE your inflatable domes, and can knock you out of it.
-Aliens can also enter your dome somehow.
-You can not change your view distance.
-The force kill button does not kill you irl.
Overall, 6/10 as it is, but can easily become a 8/10 if clarity is added. I understand this is early access, and I look forward to continuing to play this game as it develops.

Rift is a fun MMO, that reminds me (personally) of WoW, in terms of the interface and how it feels to play. Being F2P does not affect users much, though it will prevent you from selling on the auction house.
Classes are pretty standard, though they are very customizable, which is a very nice feature. Gameplay is also fairly standard, though Rifts and Invasions keep things a bit more entertaining during leveling.
Haven't tried PvP yet, though from what I've heard, it's a big draw for many players. Dimensions are interesting, instanced areas that a player can decorate in a variety of ways, and even create mini games for other players that visit it.
Biggest issue is that you cannot (easily) buy the base game anymore, unless you find it online. The base game gives 6 character slots per server and 5 bag slots per character, up from 2 and 3 respectively. You can still buy these individually through the store (with Real Money), but it's far more expensive that way.

This is the very first MMO I have found that did free to play *right*. When I first heard Rift was going free, I was preparing to run away as I've done in the past. Fortunately, Trion has kept their promise. Every single quest and piece of progression in this game is completely free. The microtransactions are mostly boosts, cosmetic and dimension based.
Let's take a moment to talk about dimensions. It's one of the most robust housing systems I have ever seen. In fact, I happily hand Trion a little money some of the time just to make one of my dimensions look better.
Rift has a unique class system. You may pick one of four classes, but once you get into the game a whole new world opens up. Every class is able to heal, tank, do damage and support. It's up to you what role you want and how you want to play it. Even though each class is able to do this, every class is also different.
The only real criticism I can give is that the PVP needs a bit of work. End game PVP is stagnant and very very gear based. The auction house could also use some love and updating. However, the PVE at end game is fantastic.

One of the more polished hot-key MMORPGs out there. As with any MMORPGs the leveling process is a bit of a pain. There's plenty of content after hitting max level primarily raiding and pvp. There are 4 classes in the game which are Cleric, Mage, Rogue, and Warrior. With the recent patch all classes can essentially Heal, Tank, DPS, and Support. Keep in mind that you start off with the basics souls and that you have to purchase the storm legion souls which cost around $35 per bundle. You can change the appearence of your armor which to me is always a plus without the limitation of a class only appearence. There is a cash shop where you can purchase Raid gear(Tiers 1 and 2) however at this point into the game it's more pay to catch up to Tier 3 content. You can buy REX (Credits) with in game currency to buy whatever you want in the cash shop. The subscription is worth it while leveling up otherwise at max level the only real benefit is just cutting time off to getting best in slot items/upgrades.
Max Level Content:
Crafting Rifts
Great Hunt Rifts
Stongholds (Group defense)
World Events
Warfronts(PVP)
Conquest (Large PVP)
Storm Legion Expert Dungeons
Chronicles (Solo/Duo Dungeons)
Dimensions (Player housing)
Tier 1 Raids ((2) 10-Player, (2) 20-Player)
Tier 2 Raids ((1) 10-Player, (2) 20-Player)
Tier 3 Raids (I think there is 4 at the moment)

(Contains spoilers, don't read if you haven't finished Cry Of Fear yet! Seriously the game is free, just go download it.)
(Oh, and I have NOT played Afraid Of Monsters yet, so I won't be comparing the two.)
Here's a little review that I've decided to write for a game that was released ALL the way back in 2013, So...In my
personal opinion how does it hold up today? I'd say it manages to hold itself up pretty well, It provides a pretty solid
campaign with memorable locations, and a somewhat engaging story. The reason I'm saying the story is...somewhat
engaging was due to how, well...The two stories (The one that goes on inside of Simon's book, and what is actually going
on.) I felt like the "Book" story was a bit rushed in a few ways, there were some plotholes that weren't quite filled, Say we...never really learned who Doctor Purnell really is, along with that we never do know what happened to Simon's mother too. Which I feel leave the Book's story feeling...Unfulfilled. But as for the "Real" story, I'd say it was handled pretty well, I loved all of the small hints to what actually happened to Simon, as for the endings, well...I'd say they were enjoyable and wrapped up the "Real" story quite nicely, with an ending count of 4 (Not counting the extra endings with the doctor's story and the multiplayer ending(s?). Plus ending 5 because, well...I wouldn't count it as an ending, It just explains who hit Simon, plus it was a REALLY nice nod to afraid of monsters as well.) Which those endings are rather simple to obtain. Which is a bit of a turn off due to how simple it is to find out how to get whichever ending. That's where I come to the next part of this game, It's replay value which...Oh boy, there's a LOT of replay value. Sure, there are getting the other endings but, ontop of that you have nightmare mode (which I have yet to even attempt.)  And a few more goodies. This is where I'll start talking about the completion bonuses, various different hoodies for Simon for completing certian tasks or just simply finding them laying around (My personal favorite being the half life creations hoodie.) They are only cosmetic but, having Simon walk around in a Hello Kitty hoodie was hularious, and made for one HELL of a second playthrough. But then there's the other completion bonuses, which you can get by say, beating the game under 2 hours or so, Or using a specific code to open a hidden door to basically get the "I win" Button of the game. Which all of these special items can be simply found inside of a bonus room, which really do give the game really good reasons to be replayed.
Now onto the gameplay.
The gameplay for Cry Of Fear is what you'd expect from a FPS, with some nice twists here and there. For example being able to strafe, which in my opinion makes the combat enjoyable with the melee weapons. Seriously, don't tell me taking out a monster with the switchblade due to how you could dodge really well isn't satistfying as hell. But sadly I found the limited inventory space a neat idea but...VERY under implemented. Like, I found it more of an annoyance than anything, take for example how there are plenty of guns in the game but, you'll really only needed the glock, and you'd be set for the entire game! Seriously the glock gets WAY more ammo than it really needs, and the other guns really don't get much ammo so, you'll just end up dropping them due to how they'll just take up inventory space, which is usually always filled with syringes and other items that you'll need to finish the game! Which a bummer, because there is a decent ammount of weapons to find. But what I did like from the inventory was the ability to quick select items and even combine them was VERY useful. So, in short, I'd say the combat was...decent, it has a few glaring flaws here and there. But still manages to be enjoyable.
Now onto the final part of this...The graphics and how the game looks!
Well, due to my PC being...basically a potato, I couldn't run the game at it's full graphics settings but...I can say gladly that the textures for areas and such looked nice. But then we have the modles, which...I'd say I really liked the detail that was put into every little thing that's laying around, most of the stuff that you find that's usually small has a pretty good looking model, plus it's textured REALLY nicely. As for the Character Models though, they...could use some work...Mainley Simon's FACE. Seriously the guy looks dead inside all the time, it's hularious. But...no facial expressions aside, I'd say the character models do look a little rough around the edges, but are still well made. As for the monster designs, I'd say...they have the potential to look creepy but...often look hularious texture wise. Say if you were to kill and then crouch over a dead monster, and get a GOOD look at it's disturbing face...they'll usually have a rather funny looking expression. It's bound to make a few people giggle. But that's when the Animations for the monsters come in and...Oh boy they sure were handled well! Every monster twitches viloently and rushes at you faster than you can even react, most of them usually jump out of coners to give you a good scare! It's pretty spooky at times, but with the...awkward texturing for the face, it can take away from the spook factors a bit.
With all of that being said, should you get the game? Hell yes, It's free for crying out loud. Give it a go if you're interested.

What attracted me about this game is that the screenshots looked really good. Without even consulting the "About" I made the decision to buy this game.
At first glance the game seems well designed with nice art and fairly descent sized maps. Starting the game and getting used to the controls needs some practice. So be certain to look through all the controls before you starting playing.
You start of with two characters which both can control together or seperatly, which is tottaly new to me. Atleast in this kind of game. So this can be of a struggle from time to time.
Environment:
What i've encountered so far the world looks good and well designed but if you look more closely you find some minor flaws ( yes i'm getting very nitpicky here), the ground clutter could use some more variation, at some places in the world you will find areas where the ground clutter is practilly the same all over. At some times this seems very unnatural.
Second, the finishing of some objects for instance, rock staircases, instead of putting edges on them they covered it with rocks and boulders which is a shame, cause the textures of the game seem really good, I rather would've seen some more time spend into designing such stuff.
Further more it seems pretty well designed and even though they've used low poly trees, they made it work really well. And if you don't look the the enviroment to well you wont even notice the points noted above.
Gameplay:
You start of with two character you can both control at the same time or individually. Which may need some practice but  you'll get the hang of it after a while. You control what to make of your characters, either make them a healer, archer or warrior. In the begging you can choose between 9 spells ( 3 for healer, 3 for archer and 3 for warrior). You can pick what kind of spells your character can use. With leveling up you can also choose how to strengthen you character, do you want your character to have more health and attack, choose body, and etc. Points awarded for each skill like body can be reassigned again if you want to, for example, your character to be an archer. You hold the power to do so.  While traveling through the land of Kyn, you will find many enemies to 'hack and slash'. Colors above their body suggests how strong they are. For example grey = weak, red is bit stronger and so on. Whilst roaming you will find UPC who will need help. Here you find your quests, this ofcourse can be various takst to complete. For finishing quest you will be awared loot or gold. Also, before I forget to mention it, mobs will also drop loot. The stronger the mob, the better the loot.
Throughout playing the game you will find puzzles you will have to complete with the help of both characters. Sometimes you have to control your characters seperatly to finish this puzzle and get further into the storyline of the game. Puzzles are well designed and thought. It may need some practice and brain cramps but you'll get there eventually. Some puzzles are ofcourse harder then other, but still understandable for everyone.
Loot:
I probably won't have to tell you this. But i'm still going to do so. Loot can come in many form and shapes. Loot can be gold, crafting items, armor and weapons. Weapons and Armour will get better the further you will get into the game. The game uses colour codes for the item. Grey items being the 'weakest' for instance purple are 'stronger' and get extra bonuses such as, +8 damage. This is the same for crafting items, the further you get in the game, the better the items become. And ofcourse you can craft better items with those.
Crafting:
Havent tried it yet -- so further information will be here soon.
But still the basics, the better crafting items you have, the stronger of items you can craft.
Controls:
In my opinion this could've been designed better. Although you can costumise your own control to make it work a little bit better. With 'A', 'W' and 'E' you control the basic spells of each character. You can switch between them by using the 1 and 2 keys. Haggling between them to keep both character is a little getting used to in the beginning, but you'll get used to it. Or just use 'Tab' to switch between characters. The struggle sometimes is, espescially during a larger fight knowing when you're in control of both characters or not. It's best to know before hand how to properly control both character else you will make it harder for yourself. Where in most games this is second nature, it isnt here.
Moving your characters is doing by clicking the right mouse button, instead of holding it and let the characters move to the point of where your mouse is,  you have to click again and again to get your characters where you want. But this can be a personal preference. Up to you to decide which is nicer.
Movement of character, whether your character of 10 pixels appart of 100 pixels appart. Whern you move both characters at the same time, the distance between them will be kept the same. Which unintentially can cause, that the character you dont want to be in front, will be in the front of the fight. So switching between characters all the time can be a bit frustrating. But maybe is just because im tottaly not used to it, it is new for me.
To add to the part of clicking and hold to move, when youre in town apperently this function excist by using your left mouse button, but when youre out in the field. The function doesn't seem to excist. Bit weird?, but oke.
In conclusion, the game seems really well made and thought of , world can be designed a little bit better ( but this not of a big deal at all). The fighting against mobs seems good, occassionally your character can get stuck between them. But as long you can control your characters well it doesnt seem to be a haggle. The game could need some little bit of polishing but the base seems really firm. Defently worth a try.
PS.
Forgot about talking about the "Slow Time" button which can be used in fight to help you assist in placing your characters in the fight. Which can come in very usefull if your character are in low health and you need some quick healing to be done.

Others have compared this game to the first two dungeon siege games. I would do the same, except i enjoyed those games.
This game is brutally repetitive. There are no tactics since you cant effectively pause the game. The slow motion is less than useful, you have time to assess the situation and issue one or two commands if you're lucky. This goes down if you're actually in a large battle with 6 party members and 15 monsters. The most effective "tactic" ive found is to just bumrush one monster after another and burn them down sequentially with autoattacks...no abilities, nothing else.
The abilities are very poor compared to your characters auto attacks once you get them decent weaponry. Those are the ones you get to choose when to use. The "feed" skills claim to pair 9 gems with abilities. There are only 1/3 of the combinations implied by t he game, as 3 gems work with each of the 3 skill trees, and there is no overlap. I.E. the life gem ONLY works on feed skills in the mind tree. With all this complicated nonsense of charging up an ability, the results should be pretty spectacular right? Nope, they feel just like another ability (underwhelming at best); one that you cant count on in a pinch. As a result i ended up ignoring the feed skills entirely.
Missions are ok i suppose. I didnt finish the game TBH. I stopped on account of my blood pressure on the WORST escort mission of any game i've ever played. Getting 5 civilians through a gauntlet of rotating turrets that will 1shot them is unpleasant to say the least. Coupled with a very clunky reload system when you ♥♥♥♥ up, it makes it downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Gear is completely centered around crafting. Beyond the first mission you'll never equip anything you find. Its vendor trash to fuel buying components to craft your own gear. Chasing down random chests in the wilderness for component loot is fun at least, but I do wish the giant purple boss guy would drop something good enough that i'd consider wearing it.
All in all i cant say i recommend the game. Certainly not at list price. I paid 5 bucks, so i wasnt out too bad. Might be a title worth picking up on super sale, however.

If you love space and puzzles like I do, you will love this game. I find the tags attached to this rather odd as it clearly is not an action game. The game requires a combination of careful planning, timing, reaction and precise mouse control; you must be one with your mouse.
The game's premise is simple but executed in an addictive format that will challenge you. Don't let the videos fool you, this game is difficult.
You control both the frequency and the amplitude of a light wave in an effort to collect objects and map your way through the universe as cleanly as possible. Harder difficulties add obstacles and items, adding to the variety of the game and keeping if fresh in addition  to adding a nice challenge.
The game can become quite addictive as you strive to come close to perfecting each level, a difficult task in itself.
All in all, a beautiful, challenging, and addictive ride through space. You will enjoy this.

Where to start. lets jump the big hurdle first. When you die, you come back as another generic agent, and you must hunt your former agent and kill him for your stuff back, while dealing with whatever else spawns in this room. If you die during that attempt, then youll have to go deal with 2. Yes its hard, but thats the point.
To call this game a Metroidvania is somewhat inaccurate. I would call it a Controid. It has the level design of metroid, and the exploration. The combat and weapons, all Contra. Now the feel of the game, the ambiance, environment, and enemies are remeniscient of Castlevania. but gameplay wise, it borrows more from Metroid/Contra.
Its not a hard game to grasp, simple controls, there is however somewhat of a difficulty curve to it. Which isnt exactly a deal breaker, but it will tick you off. Controller reccomended.
The music matches the ambiance of the area your in fairly well, but lacks that Metroid/Castlevania feel.
The graphics are awesome, some of the best 16 bit gaming Ive done. You can feel the love in the detail, at least for its level of. The animations are nice and smooth.
Overall, if you were a Contra, Metroid, or Castlevania fan, then this game is worth it, Even more so if you catch it on sale.
EDIT: After clearing the game, ive a few side notes to make.
-Need more bosses/minibosses
-a couple more weapons wouldnt have hurt
-difficulty options for repeat plays

The Turing Test is a suitably clever first-person puzzler with an interesting primary device. The energy orb gun is easy to understand and utilized well through its puzzle rooms. Puzzles require diverse solutions and getting through levels is somewhat like deciphering logic gates. Other devices come into play, including magnets and platforms, which are typical of the genre and interwoven logically. A major change at the half-way point gives the gameplay a fresh perspective. Even the story provides adequate breaks although its delivery could be better. Fortunately this puzzler shares the brevity of the Portal series, taking around six hours to complete with nary a misstep. The Turing Test may not hit as hard as Portal, but thanks to all the energy orbs it keeps the lights on, and shining bright.

This game starts out slow and tedious. Your pea shooter does little damage, and movement is very limited. However, with each new weapon or upgrade, the game becomes exponentially more fun, and fighting enemies becomes much easier. Movement gets really fun as well! It's an enjoyable ramp-up.
The level design varies from uninspired to good. Enemy placement is deliberately annoying in some rooms, which can be frustrating, but some other rooms are arranged to be traversed quickly as long as you keep your finger on the trigger. The boss fights are all fun, but they're far from being challenging - though they do have a lot of HP, the bosses have a limited number of patterns, and you'll be more impressed by the spritework of the attacks than by the difficulty of dodging them.
Collecting items isn't difficult until you get around 70% of all items: at that point, finding the remaining relics (and upgrade, if you missed any) becomes much more of a challenge. Fans of the genre should not have any trouble with it though, as the well-hidden items are locked behind familiar tricks.
I haven't died once, as I played pretty conservatively, and health drops are pretty tedious to get in this game. Thankfully there are a few ways to grind for health in select spots, letting you recharge your batteries. It was very rare for me to have full health going through the different parts of the map, and I fought most bosses with missing health.
The game is good-looking, though a little uninspired at times, especially when it comes to basic enemies. The levels look good, but some repetitive backgrounds here and there spoils their otherwise varied looks.
I got a kick out of the music! The chiptunesy synthwave is a great fit for the look and ambiance of the game, and I'll probably purchase the soundtrack at some point. Great job, though I would have loved a different theme for each boss, La Mulana style, fitting each area and boss fight more than the slightly generic theme we got.
There are a few flaws I can find with the game.
First of all, there are no Hard Mode or New Game+ options. That would have added some challenge and longevity to a game that's already on the shorter side.
Secondly, the anonimity of the player character is necessary, considering the setting and the corpse-run nature of the game, but that has the unfortunate effect of putting you in control of a faceless, charisma-less character. The titular Mummy isn't really all that cool either. Her dialogue is stilted and cliché.
Finally, the Tutorial Man is a liiiittle too eager to talk to you! His messages really pulled me out of the world and ambiance of the game, and I was afraid it would remain this way throughout the entire game. Thankfully, after clearing the first area, Tutorial Man only popped up a few more times for story exposition. Thanks to that, I could immerse myself in that messed up London that the devs cooked up for us, Monomer's music blasting in my ears as I juggled between weapons to tear open a path through gross critters and reanimated corpses.
Compared to another recent $20 WayForward game, Shantae: Half-Genie Hero, it's obvious The Mummy Demastered was made on a much smaller budget and schedule, but I think you're getting your money's worth.
Hats off to WayForward, purveyors of quality titles since forever. Time for me to go back and chase the last few relics I'm missing.

I absolutely loved this game. A cross between Portal and 2001: A Space Odyssey.
Graphics:
Absolutely stunning. Very well made game. I didn't come across any issues with graphics other than a black line across the centre of the screen when stood outside the drop pod at the start of the game (only if looking in a specific direction).
Audio:
I think this is one of it's strongest points. The voice acting, sound effects and music are all very well done. Loved that James Faulkner is the voice of the A.I. Very fitting! Sounds a lot like Jeremy Irons which is never a bad thing.
Gameplay:
If you have played Portal or any games similar then you know roughly what to expect. Lots of puzzles using energy intead of portals as well as a few variations using magnets and droids. Was very satisfying figuring out the puzzles which get more challenging the further you go although not to the extent of pulling out your hair.
Plot:
I personally found the plot really interesting. The conversations between the main character and the A.I are entertaining and at times worrying! To get the full story, I believe you need to complete all the optional sections of each chapter (you can walk through the force field type barrier, which I didn't find out until late in the game). There are, I believe, two endings, although not 100% on that as only just finished it and won't be replaying it for a little while yet.
Overall:
If you enjoy games like this, then I would highly recommend it. Definitely worth the money for what you get!

SO, Kyn.
It's a good introduction to the party RPG. Combat is gratifying and easy, Like Diablo but also has more management involved. Characters only have 2 skills and one feed skill, so if you're not brilliant at micromanaging everyone at the same time you don't have too much to wrap youself around.
Item stats in the game are really straightforward with an easy to read UI. The game does involve crafting, but don't let it be too daunting, All of the materials can be purchased in town with the rarer ones costing upwards of 4k - 8k gold. There is a very large variation when it comes to weapon and armour skins, which is always nice, Being able to change the colour of your armour at any point is also really good.
Now the only gripes I have with this game. Most of the skills seem rather worthless, There are alot of skills that achieve the same goal but just in different less efficient ways. Most of the first tier spells are often the best spells, The taunt for Body users is ridiculously good.
I wish there was more customisation to do with your actual characters, I understand that there are characters that are involved with the story and it does bring a better all round storytelling experience, But since the characters don't have any voices (Yet ?) I don't see how conversation couldn't be as simple as just changing names and certain situational quotes. I also feel like you gather your full party at a rather slow speed. At around the halfway point of the game you still only have about 4 - 5 members out of the full 6.
So here's my rundown.
Pros:
-Easy introduction to the Genre
-Nice micromanagement
-Good stats system
-Nice crafting
-Good variation in items
-Nice UI
-Enjoyable story with likeable characters
Cons:
-Skills feel lacking at later tiers
-Feel slightly detached from the characters
-Slow progression which feel monotonous at time
So all in all, the game is very enjoyable and is quite cheap for the content it offers. The development team are also really active and helpful to anyone who has issues adn they are not afraid to add major game changers like the Rotating camera. Enjoyable game. Had fun playing it. 10/10 would buy a sequel.

Assassin's Creed was the first title to not only employ, but invent the Ubisoft formula. It featured sheer infinite content compared to the first game and a lot more to do to break monotony during story progression. Most of the equipment is entirely optional, but there's a lot of versatility in AC2 which AC1 was desperately lacking.
Assassin's Creed 2 might not be a masterpiece, but it is a milestone of gaming history. And it does pick up more and more with Brotherhood and Revelations, which are the second and third entries of the Ezio trilogy.

Assassin's Creed 2 is a well-aged open-world action game with an epic storyline and immersive environment.  The graphics have held up surprisingly well over time; though the cutscenes certainly look dated.  I completed the game (not 100% collection) in around 25 hours.  The free-running aspect of the game feels intuitive after a little practice.  There's a good mix of platforming and combat.  Amazingly, uPlay isn't even that annoying anymore.
I did experience one desktop crash, but the game loaded right back to where I was when it happened.  The keyboard/mouse controls can be a little awkward (WASD vs. joystick) and presenting controls as symbols instead of buttons is frustrating until you get used to them.  Going for 100% completion is very repetetive; there are a lot of unmapped collectibles and generic assassionation/race contracts.
Overall, I highly recommend this game in 2017.  The main quest is enough, though.  There's no real need to seek out a 100% completion.  Search the internet for  the completion cutscenes and save yourself hours of searching for collectibles!

I picked this up from the recent Assassin's Creed sale on Steam. I decided to buy the Ezio collection (2/Brotherhood/Revelations) because I never finished 2 on the console years ago. Hearing people claim this to be the best one has me worried for playing future installments as I would barely rate this a recommendation.
By far the biggest frustration for me was the controls. As a disclaimer, I played using an Xbox 360 controller. I dont know if it is better using KB/Mouse, but I figured since there is no real aiming needed, and its a console port, a controller is a safer bet. Well, I would say about...80% of the time Ezio did what I wanted him to do. The other 20% I was usually screaming at my monitor saying, "WTF are you doing Ezio??!?!" The game has a lot of timed sections, as well as tense moments when your fighting with guards. Having Ezio do something you dont want him to do can be REALLY annoying. To extrapolate on this, I'm fairly certain I took more damage from falling than from fighting over the course of the entire game.
Also the story. There were many times were it was just plain bad. One instance comes to mind is you are met with a problem of you needing a ticket to take a boat. Immediately upon knowing this a woman starts yelling for help: she is stuck on an island. You get a boat, and take her back to land. It turns out she just happens to be the owner of the castle? Like wtf? Why is the baroness of the entire area stranded on an island randomly? The entire middle part of the game is just fluff and errands. I feel like the game could have been told in a portion of the time and have done much better. Also in a reation to the story, Ezio felt really lifeless. Aside from the first few hours when his character is built up, the game does nothing to really make you care about him, hes essentially a lifeless killing machine.
Thats a lot of negative points. What about the positive? Well the parkour and animations are done well (when it works). The game does a good job (when it works) of making you feel like a badass stealthy assassin. Also, it feels like the classic mechanics that invented it all, the type of fighting and movement systems you see in more recent games (Batman and Shadow of Mordor) so its fun to experience the "grandfather" of these type of mechanics.
The graphics are also starting to show their age by modern standards. I was delighted to have the game work and look good (for its age) on my 4k monitor, but the graphics just look bland and foggy. Leftover console port issues I'm assuming.
Overall, I recommend AC2 to experience the origins of Ezio's story, but I will not be doing a second playthrough. It was too frustrating with the controls.

Seeing as I have played this game almost nonstop since I got it I feel like I should write a review.
Osiris: New Dawn is missing the majority of its content, so if you dont want to play it until its content is all there, then wait a little while.
The games area is massive. Youve got a massive planet to start on, rediculously large, however the playable are of that is much much smaller. The actual playable area is only about 5000 meters by 5000 meters, where as the rest of the world is so large that me spring jumping it for an hour in one direction till i died of dehydration didnt reach the poles.
Then you have space (spaaaaaaaace) right now it sucks, theres nothing to do up there, all you can see is a space station you phase through and a few asteroids that aren't at all reachable to crash your ship into.
Half the resources needed are missing from the game, but the devs tell you this.
So as of now the game is very small, Ive built everything you can, and have gone everywhere there is to go, and found all the obtainable resources.
That being said: This game is going to be a fantastic game. It already is for how little content it has. The games scope is immense, it doesnt add any really new mechanics to the survival genre but my god is it beautiful. Everything about this game spells success, it takes everything we all love from ark and puts it in space while throwing out all the stuff we dont love.
So thats really all I have to say, as long as the devs keep building the game up it will be something to talk about.

这款游戏并没有难点，玩家只需要围绕一些简单的操作就可以让动画继续，点击让人物移动，启动打开开关，滑动来让插头插在对应的位置等等。只要找个一些场景的正确按钮，就像点击了播放一样，画面就会继续了。在游戏中，玩家扮演一个着一个插头，刚开始还对爱情充满的希冀，可之后经过了种种挫折后心灰意冷，决定去变性，变性之后的插头对于爱情的看法更加的畸形，从此他的私生活变得很淫乱，开始了“即插即用”的日子。
这里的插头们，没有思想，没有感情，仅仅是把互插当成一种本能或任务。然而我们的主角，还没有被这死寂的世界同化，他感到了互插的特别意义，那何尝不是感情的传递，于是他问他插过的……插头：“do you love me?”插头们自然是对这种异类不愿靠近的。至于主角最后有没有找到他要找的人，我不知道。但是看那两只手，也许是一段凄美的爱情故事吧，最后一只手死了，另一只手把他插入插座，预示着他们终究逃不开这个死寂的世界与他们悲惨的命运，又何尝不是暗示。

Hits about as much as it misses, a solid 6/10. A short, relaxing casual puzzle game. If you want to be challenged look elsewhere.
Pros:
- Great voice acting
- Nice graphics
- Some parts of the plot are interesting
- No timing puzzles
Cons:
- Very easy puzzles, hardly any difficulty curve
- Fairly short due to lack of puzzle difficulty
- Overall the story felt rather generic
In terms of gameplay, this game is much closer to Portal than to The Talos Principle. That is, you're guided through from one puzzle to the next, with no chance of backtracking (though you can load chapters in the menu).
Sadly the creators played it safe and did not include any hard puzzles, even the optional ones are fairly easy. Playing it casual, reading the extra documents etc for backstory, as well as doing the optional puzzles along the way, it took me about 6 hours to reach the 7th (final) chapter.
The story is very hit and miss for me, it starts out well but quickly devolves to a bland mix of well-known sci-fi elements, spoiling almost all twists and turns the story offers.
To sum it up, it's not a bad game, but it's not a shining star like Portal or The Talos Principle. It's like a decent frozen pizza. It tastes alright, gets you filled up, but isn't terribly exciting.

So, it was not really clear to me what kind of game this was. But yes, it is a game where you kill zombies by......TYPING on your keyboard stuff that comes on the screen. If you are familiar with the house of the dead series (ever been to some arcade game center?), this is just as fun, with grindhouse style, funny dialogues etc. On pc is almost impossible to properly have a peripheral that simulates a gun (on PS you have PS move, on wii the wiimote...), so they chose they keyboard as a shooting device. It's LOTS of fun. I have a mechanical keyboard (Razer Blackwidow latest version) and it just looks like you're machine-gun-shooting letters in the face of the enemies. If you are a fast typer you will really enjoy the challenge. If you are a slow typer, you will enjoy it too, just will die more :D
Also reading the words that come on screen is fun because they may make you laugh from time to time. Funny stuff.
On the downside, the normal 'house of the dead' which is required anyway if you want to get all achievements, is boring as hell....shooting stuff with a mouse watching the cursor is not really entertaining......
Only CONS:
- they released different vocabularies (check the DLCs).....but each vocabulary is sold separately and is not very cheap. They should have released all the dictionaries in the normal release of the game, without limiting to one or two dictionnaries.
- the game renders at 720p whatever resolution you choose. Menus will look fine but the game engine output stays at 720p.

I flawed game. Definitely.
My issues with it.
First off the map. I think they went graphics heavy on this to make it a selling point but in all honesty, I did like the map look the last few paradox titles had (Ck2, EU IV). The graphics make the game chopping and it just doesn't look good. It definitely won't age well. It doesn't represent WWII well and I think the overall UI is... I guess tone deaf is the appropriate word. It just doesn't pull me into the era, while I can tell they worked really hard on it.
Second, this game focuses on military strategies and it digs deep in planning as well as utilizing specific units. That's the agenda of the developer but what I feel is that it needs more political intrigue, economic diversification (one nation depends on deals with corpoations while another is authrotarian and the government runs the factories), stuff like that. They need to bring that sense of identity between the countries. One does one thing one way, while hte other does this... I'd like more domestic options on how to handle sitatuions, and how I as a leader can change national unity and political gain. This will add personailty and I've seen it done in their other titles.
Third... Too ♥♥♥♥ing overwhelming with stuff I see little different in. So I research a very specific type of tank. Ok. Cool. Does it make a difference? Not sure, but it'll also take you a while to figure out how to hell to implement it properly. I don't consider this depth, I consider a poor choice in how information is convey, how we can understand, and a bit haphazard into putting all this work into all these variations of research when in reality it's just annoying to click through. It's complicated and not gratiying once you learn it.
It's busy work... This whole game is busy work into things you think won't make a difference, while you want to explore elements in the game that just aren't there.
With that said, it took a while for me to understand the game. I really like certain elements of it, but it's super flawed. I can recommend it, but get it at a discount.

This one is hard as balls for someone like me (who sucks at this genre)
So yes, it's difficult. That's not a bad thing. Also you likely know this already, but this game is utterly stunning with its art/animation and music. If you appreciate hand-drawn, hand-animated, hand-done everything 1930s Fleischer-style animation and jazzy music recorded live as if from the era, you'll love this game.
It all feels so genuine, and you can tell how much effort was put into making it that way. You can see it in every frame of animation and hear it in every second of sweet scratchy tunes. It's a success on every front in terms of presentation. You can really feel the passion that went into crafting this game and its atmosphere.
The focus is on the incredible and varied boss battles, but there are also your basic run 'n gun levels (where you can collect coins to purchase weapons and charms) and a few levels where you do nothing but parry ghosts to earn super moves. This game is worth it even just for the art and animation. That said, the gameplay is definitely underrated. I really enjoyed this game, though I got a bit tired of the game's process of beating bosses towards the end. I can tell how much effort went into this game and I appreciate it for that. 7/10 for me.
+ As I said, amazing animation. I love it and you can see the effort put into the art.
+ Great boss design, and surprisingly fun gameplay.
+ Simple game, doesn't try too hard to be more than what it is.
+ Isn't too short or too long, hits that sweet spot of finishing right as it starts to get repetitive.
- The process can get a bit tedious towards the end. Essentially, this game is a bunch of boss fights, and for each boss, you just have to face them enough times to learn all their moves and subsequently dodge them and beat them.
- A bit frustrating, not because it's hard, but because it's just repetetive. You'll learn the first and second forms of each boss pretty quickly, but you'll make a mistake or two most runs and won't make it to the last forms all the time. However, since you make mistakes, you won't know the last forms as well and the few times you do get to the end, you're even more prone to mistakes then. This is an entertaining process at first, but once you become aware of it, it gets a bit old after a while.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game and I appreciate the effort put into the art and design of the game. Despite the amazing boss design, this game's process of beating bosses does get a bit repetitive towards the end, and I definitely felt myself having less fun towards the end (and rather trying to just finish the game). However, the game is well done, and it's very satisfying to beat the bosses. I'm happy I played this.

Is "The Cave" good?  Well, despite having solved all the main puzzles in the game I bothered to unlock both endings for all the characters, so that says something.
On the bad side, "The Cave" is plagued by various bugs (keyboard suddenly not responding, and the keyboard controls actually being outright broken for one of the Monk's puzzles) that require restarting the game, and there is a woeful lack of ability to skip the cutscenes as far as I know (or the method to skip the cutscenes wasn't included in the meger in-game instruction).
It's an interesting concept with various nice touches.  The puzzles aren't too difficult for veterens of the genre, but most of the character special abilities are of limited use outside their own special sequences.
Storywise -- and in adventure games, this does matter -- it's one of those tales that is layered with room for reflection.  In a change of pace for the genre, the "Good" endings are the alternative endings (which I discovered in a most cinematic way, dawning on me shortly before point of no return, mimicing the whole touching Hollywood moment) and some routes create an equally satsifying story, depending on character.  The presentation of characters like The Twins contrasted by characters like The Adventurer make you wonder if the adventure in The Cave is a warning, a reflection, or a second shot at redemption (or all three).
In closing, The Cave's strengths lie in its concept, puzzles and story where its weaknesses are the graphics, controls and various bugs that while aren't crippling are definitely annoying.

Review updated after 80%+ completion.
TL;DR? Scroll down to pluses and negatives.
Visually Kyn resembles Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons (though less polished), which I'm going to admit I find very pleasing. The music sounds at times like it could have come straight out of Torchlight 2, generally it has a fitting Celtic vibe. The atmosphere of the game is, therefore, highly satisfying.
Gameplay-wise, this puts me in mind of an MMO more than a typical hack&slash. You hit space to slow the game to a crawl, issue commands to your fighters, then hit space again to see the commands executed in real time. You don't need to keep clicking to attack. You cannot pause for long, which gives the game a more intense feel than others with a Real-Time pausable combat system.
There are no classes in the game, though quickly you learn that you'll need to specialise your fighters to get the most out of them (I immediately modified my starting heroes so that one was a ranged healer and a melee fighter). But specialisation is somewhat simple: just pump all your stats into 'Body' for a fighter; 'Control' for an archer; 'Mind' for a mage or healer. This lacks the depth of a Diablo 2, or a PoE.
The game plays as a series of small challenges. You traverse areas fighting mini-combat challenges and solving puzzles. These often involve splitting up your fighters and stepping on switches and are a nice diversion from thwacking goblins and skeletons. The combat, however, is too easy on Normal difficulty and only really becomes a pleasurable challenge on Hard upwards. You literally have to micromanage every action your heroes take to keep them alive - especially when the suicide-bomber skeletons appear. This is why it feels like a series of combat challenges. Enemy types can become repetitive, however, and some are downright irritating (Hydra, I'm talking about you).
Unfortunately the enemies quickly become repetitive. Literally, you fight the same four enemy types throughout. Worst of all, they are imbalanced in diffiulty. You start on Mission 1 fighting skeletons. When they reappear in Mission 15, they are as easy to defeat as they were in Mission 1 - its like they haven't leveled up with your characters.
The game revolves around a central hub 'village' in which you are given missions. You then hit a 'Start Mission' button to get transported to a mission map. Kyn isn't open world and you backtravel backtravel through previous areas. This create problems later when you need increasing amounts of money and loot to upgrade your equipment - and cannot afford it. You basically need to grind, but cannot: you cannot revisit old areas and enemies do not respawn. As a result you need to make a decision: upgrade some equipment, or upgrade all for only some of your team. Shame.
Loot is a real problem. You don't get better loot on quests and from enemy drops than you can make or buy. To get loot you sometimes have to perform interesting (but lengthy puzzles). The most egregious of which is one where you have to rescue a creature from a cage. To do so you have to undertake a time-consuming puzzle involving a series of mine carts. Takes ages. Reward: I got a shield that I immediately sold as it was so much worse than the others I had equipped - or had access to.
The plot is workmanlike. The biggest problem is in team composition. You start with two guys. By the end you have 6. But you have no choice in who you fight with. There are a few NPCs you spend time getting to know (including one, Keira, who you do a load of quests for) but they don't join you. Instead you are joined by a bunch of heroes you don't care for, and cannot substitute them for those you do. A shame and I hope they allow Keira to join you (this would also re-balance the total lack of women in the game). On this note, there is a disturbing amoung of misogynistic language from some of the heroes towards the end of the game (the enemies are continually referred to as '♥♥♥♥♥es' and 'she-♥♥♥♥♥es', for instance).
My main criticism (and probably why some websites seem to think this is still in Early Access) is that the interface is unpolished. To save your game you have to hit escape (opens menu); then select the file you want to save to; hit 'Overwrite' and then 'Cancel'. There's no prompt to say 'Save Successful' and no visual indication you have saved the game. Most frustrating are the shops. Whatever you sell shows up in the display of any shopkeeper, implying they share an inventory. Yet if I go to the Blacksmith to craft an item, he won't have any of the crafting materials. You have to constantly trudge between Blacksmith and Vendor to craft items, with increasingly lengthy shopping lists. (I had to start making actual shopping lists on a pad of paper, you need to buy that much loot).
+ Nice visuals
+ Nice soundtrack
+ Interesting gameworld
+ Puzzle solving
+ Occasionally Complex combat mechanicsc
- User interface could do with some tweaks
- Repetitive enemy types
- Unrewarding loot
- Broken vending and crafting mechanics
- Normal difficulty and below are too easy
- Disturbing lack of female characters and misogynistic dialogue in the later stages.
I won't bother completing it, life is too short. But I will revisit in a few months and I hope that the devs (who are still working on the game) have fixed the vending mechanics, difficulty, added more playable characters and sorted out the lack of enemy variety.

(Reluctant thumbs-up.)
Fans of the metroidvania genre who have already played all the best ones and are just looking for a new game that offers more of the same beloved formula, with little regards to quality, length or originality. It also helps if you prefer 2D sprites rather than 3D models (looking at you, Samus Returns).
Honestly, everyone else. There are too many better games competing for your money and time right now, so this one isn't really worth it unless you're a metroidvania fan who just wants a few hours to kill in a new game.
- - - - -
The main problem with this game is that it doesn't do anything to stand out, so it ends up feeling like a filler game. A good filler game, but a filler game nonetheless.
While the basic metroidvania formula is always fun, a great metroidvania should do more than that. Establish a world with characters in it. Do something new with the gameplay.
Sadly, almost nothing about this game will surprise you. It feels like Wayforward put together a standard Metroid template, then slapped a Mummy skin on it and called it a day.
Yet despite being nearly identical to Metroid, they managed to mess up the health system. The save stations don't restore your health, so the only way get your health back is to farm enemies for a couple of minutes, which isn't really fun and makes death overly punishing in a tedious way. I only died 3 times total (to the same boss) but others may have a tougher time with this game and they'll feel discouraged to continue after dying a bunch.
Also, you don't really get to customize your playstyle much, which is a bit disappointing. You get a few guns to choose from and that's about it.
The bosses are pretty great but there's only a handful of them as the game is fairly short.
Visuals look quite nice and are probably the most consistently good aspect of the game.
Music's pretty groovy but your gun noises are so loud that it can be pretty hard to hear (no option to reduce SFX volume).
The story is just "go kill bad guys" and there is no lore, no interesting secrets, no NPCs, etc.
Overall this game isn't bad, but it does feel pretty lazy and uninspired compared to Hollow Knight.
Wait for a sale if you're interested.

One of the most tedious metroidvanias I've ever played.  So much of the game design is actively designed to encourage you to alt+f4.
Not out of frustration, but because it is actively more efficient to avoid the game saving when you're dead, or if you've lost a lot of health, as there's no efficient way to restore to maximum health other than a health max up, and dying saves you at a minimum health state.
The death loop is:
Lose weapons, reset hp (99, starting HP) EDIT (Forgot the most important: Have game auto save this state)
Hunt down corpse zombie to get weapons and hp back
Get weapons with previous ammo (ie 0 if died in a boss fight), get maximum of ~300 hp (regardless of max health)
Go back to an ammo cache to restore ammo
Grind HP because you're never at max, or just try to ace bosses
Do boss
Run out of ammo during boss because every boss has more HP than you have ammo
Beat boss or loop this flowchart.
The game actively divests you of your time to participate in it.  Even if it was a better game, I cannot abide such a thing.  Souls (which has infested games with this corpse run concept) has never done anything other than lower your max HP and take away your souls.   The death loop is "do it again, but better", so the punishment is just having to play the game more.   This game prevents you from playing it instead of just giving you a game over.

A tough one. If there was a thumbs in the middle option, I'd be using it here. But I'll always lean to a positive in a close call, and hope that the information below makes it clear if the game is for you.
There's nothing “wrong” with the core of the Mummy Demastered: it's an average metroidvania that's a bit on the short side. But the problem is simple: it does nothing to stand out among the crowd, especially in a year where there's a lot of good metroidvanias to your left and right. Despite Wayforward always bringing love to their projects (and it still showing here), there's that X factor missing here: that unique charm that always lies in their other series. The presentation despite being completely different from their normal style still works here, as the details still bring creatures to life. The presentation is the game's strongest element, even if the music is only slightly above average.
The gameplay is average, and it's nothing that you haven't played in the genre before. Which would be fine if it kept a pace and a reasonable flow to the game. The problem is that the game interrupts that pace with a segment that doesn't make a lot of sense, or a platform that causes a tiny bit more frustration then it needs to. There's just oddities here that pop up now and again, like a platform that the player is expected to get to and it really doesn't make it clear how to get to it, or it a bit more difficult then it really needs to be. Or an enemy that's placed in a way that you're going to take damage on a room transition. The main combat, especially half way through the game, just doesn't hold up. You become too powerful against enemies, especially when you can spend ammo like I spend money during a Steam Sale.
The problem in essence is what exactly the game's target audience is. For veterans, you're not going to get enough out of the Mummy Demastered length wise, or challenge wise. For newbies, there's a bit more there but there will be those frustrating moments when the game doesn't tell you what to do. Those who love the mummy (2017) aren't going to be happy with the lack of.....well any significant story, and this just feels like a game that Wayforward was asked to make, but just doesn't have any pull to make it unique. Even Wayforward fans may have some trouble adjusting to this one, as it just doesn't have that colorful bright appeal.
It's a sale title for most, and given the strength of the competition here, I'd suggest games like Hallow Knight and Half-Genie Hero over this one.

We reviewed this. Here's a select quote from the review:
"In all, The Mummy Demastered took me around six and a half hours to complete. Despite a few issues that I had with the design of certain zones, the abundance of endlessly spawning enemies, and the lack of interesting upgrades, I thoroughly enjoyed it. It is a fast-paced, fluid Metroidvania that will provide you with a decent amount of challenge. It uses what few mechanics it has in interesting ways and constantly challenges you to think outside of the box in order to keep moving forward. It’s a far better game than I ever expected from the franchise and one that is well worth picking up."

Overall: 4 / 10, play it for the puzzles and get it on sale.
Trying to be a game in the vein of Portal and The Talos Project, The Turing Test wants to be some mix of interesting story, philosophy, and puzzle platformer gameplay. It certainly succeeds in the puzzle platformer gameplay, with some interesting mechanics and generally good progression of difficulty... but at times it feels like they have needlessly inserted tutorial puzzles for mechanics that are well-understood. Many puzzles are trivially to complete with extra energy balls (door keys, essentially), but completing puzzles optimally gives no benefit. The game contains optional side areas, but these provide little other than a few objects to turn over and audio logs.
So for puzzles: 8 / 10. Should be good for all age groups, but serious logicians may be bored.
But if puzzles were the only thing we were hoping to get out of this, we could just play sudoku or something. No, this is a Video Game and so it needs story and characters and deeper meaning. This is where the game falls flat.
It's pretty obvious that the game wants to be seen as clever and meaningful, but it's so painfully forceful about it that it feels awkward and shallow. The main character's last name is Turing. There is a concept about AI known as the "Turing Test". The antagonist is a robot. Oh, the mind reels with possibilities. At least, it did in middle school when I just heard of these concepts. Imagine if Tolkien named one of his protagonists "Lord O' Rings" or "The Hero's McJourney". It's not even sarcastic.
Okay, so the "deepness" of the story in question (they bring up the Chinese Room thought experiment a few times, and you eventually encounter a literal Chinese Room, complete with examinable pieces of paper with Chinese characters on them; I kid you not).
But at least the banter between the protagonist and antagonist should be interesting, right? Uh, no. TOM (the computer antagonist) is stiff as a board, raising his hackles on occasion but mostly spouting off the same tired gibberish about humans being emotional, that they can't be trusted, morality, ethics, blah blah blah. Your reparteé takes place over small snippets throughout the game, but it feels like the script was written as one big dialogue and then parceled out a little per level. So you start a puzzle, you and TOM say a few lines, and then it's silent until the next room; even when you're literally yelling at him that you don't want to die or be his slave, you politely let him have his word until you're done with the puzzle at hand.
Okay, well, there are other characters, too! We learn their names early on, there's lots of foreshadowing and you get to learn about their personalities and hobbies and listen to audio clips about them. It's laid out like there's some kind of grand mystery you can piece together by checking out all the clues... except it's very repetitive and it's all given to you right away. You learn a little about one character's motiviations, and it seems like he's gone insane at one point... except that he's right all along and the rest of the crew agree with him immediately after, so there's no payoff.
The main conflict is muddled and it's not clear why there is a conflict in the first place, except that nobody seems to understand how medical and scientific experimentation or quarantine works. In the end, you're given a false moral choice that feels hollow whatever you do. I enjoyed becoming TOM and firing space machine gun rounds into our bland protagonist as TOM seemed saddened by her death, but I was laughing and laughing because of how tonally wrong the scene was. Obviously they were expecting me to hesitate or pause before murdering our heroine, which would have given the scene depth, but instead they let you shoot right away without even listening to anybody's dialogue.
The game "rewards" you for "exploration" with a handful of optional puzzles, with the treat at the end usually being an audio log or two or some kind of note or item to be examined. I found myself skipping the audio logs (rare for me, as I am a story completionist) because you couldn't do anything other than stand still in front of them while they played (the audio cuts out if you get too far away) and they went nowhere and had nothing interesting to say about the characters or the story that isn't spoonfed to you by TOM. There's plenty of little objects to look at, but other than a few notes here and there (also pretty dull) they're pointless, useless clutter that wasted my time. They include a globe in one crew member's room that is clearly a Mercator projection mapped onto a sphere (ironic), and so it includes no Antarctica, Greenland looks bigger than Africa, and the equator is somewhere around Washington DC. It's not really a big deal, but it's one more thing that makes the game seem thoughtless and lazy.
In the end, Story: 3 / 10. Boring and cliché.
All in all, a middling affair that might be fun for the puzzles if you get it on sale. Otherwise, don't bother.

I had a couple hours fun playing "Cube: The Game" with friends. I also really liked the movie, and to see it as a game is pretty cool. Playing it as is, it seems functional, though being an early access game it is a little light on the content.
Speaking of as is, the variety of traps seems to be split up like this,
Trap room, Will it lock the player in (Yes/No)
If yes, it is defeated by throwing a boot inside, and having that room locked off from that point forward.
If no, can the player navigate the room with the trap deployed,(Yes/No)
If yes, In which direction and for how long?(Rotating/Side to side)
If no, how long do they have to realize the room is trapped and to exit accordingly?
The speed that the doors open is a little slow, though I suspect the reason for the current speed of the doors is balanced with the speed that the trap deploys. One thing I would like to see in addition to more trap variety, is different
clues for the player to pick up on to realize which trap they have or are going to spring (if any).
These clues can be visual or auditory, but should be if at all possible, as subtle as possible.
An example would be a room that slowly disintigrates them while they stand within it.
Since it is suble and works slowly at first, the player might think they found a safe room, but would lose while they                 are contemplating their next move.
Clues might include very small objects that could be emmiters on the ceiling and/or a slight difference in ambient
light. Additionaly, there could be visible cosmetic damage to the player model, or a gradual building health loss.
Which brings me to a different suggestion, a health system. Encounters with some traps need not be a win/lose situation. If in addition to a player needing to pay attention to the number of shoes they have left, they also have to be aware of their physical condition, then they might chose their next room more carefully.
Whereas, with the current method of "Throw a boot if you got one, if you don't, does the room have a guy in it, if not, flip a coin", I largely found myself blundering into rooms hoping not to die.
Once you run out of boots, it does become a coin toss whether or not the next room will lock you in with death.
Anyway, it seems like a really cool idea for a game, and I look forward to seeing what it becomes in the future.
As for how it is as an early access title, I think it is worh at least a couple hours of fun.

This game is basically the spiritual successor to The Typing of the Dead, which was a modification of the original House of the Dead such that you killed by typing words rather than shooting a laser gun. (How cool is that!)
In this case, the original source material is House of the Dead: Overkill, which received relatively positive reviews years ago, in part due to its stylistic integration of cheesy B-movie film genre and the House of the Dead game franchise.
I don't think anyone plays any House of the Dead games for the plot or characters or anything, but still. The execution couldn't even rate as a neutral factor here, sadly.
I don't think I've ever actually watched a cheesy B-movie film before, and so the style and humor was amusing ... at first. If there were ever an example of beating a dead horse, this game is full of it. Excessive cussing. Lame dialogue. Annoying characters. And voices that make your ears bleed. By the end, all the long cut scenes were a real chore to get through. The cut scenes are skippable, but I generally prefer to watch everything through the first (and in this case final) time.
As each zombie approaches you, an associated word box will pop up onto the screen. If the zombies are close enough to strike you, the word box will flash. Pretty straightforward. To kill the zombies, you must type the shown word or phrase.
My one complaint is that there are times when there are multiple zombies approaching, and it can be difficult to figure out which word box represents the closer zombie, which can result in unnecessary hits.
If you want to switch to another word box or zombie, I think there's a button that will cancel your progress in the present word box that is faster than just backspacing and typing the other phrase, but I can't remember it off the top of my head.
There are special power-ups, health replenishment or collectibles throughout. If you see them on the screen, hit Tab and they will be automatically collected.
I'm not an achievements ♥♥♥♥♥, but collecting things in this game is so easy because of the linear nature of the game that there's no point NOT making the effort. But the layout to view your collectibles is so horrible. There's no grid ... you literally have to cycle through everything, one by one, and then you have to click on it to see what it actually is. Hugely inefficient.
The mini games are a complete waste of time. I can't see anyone enjoying them enough to play them. Only completionists would bother.
This might be more fun to play in multiplayer, but just getting through the single player campaign completely wiped me to the point where I had zero interest in playing this again.
Adding theoretical value is the inclusion of the original House of the Dead: Overkill. However, I didn't play it, so I couldn't tell you whether it's any good.
Overall rating: 5/10. It was fun at first, garnering maybe a 7/10 ... but a few levels in, everything is so repetitive and annoying that the game ends up being quite the unpleasant experience overall.

Were it not for the destinctive art-style; the poor controls, weak writing and dull gameplay would never suggest that this was a Double-Fine game. While co-operative gameplay may be different, playing alone will require you to make the same journey to the next puzzle for each of the three characters you control, meaning a minimum of 3-times for one-way, 6-times if you need to double-back (and you likely will), and any number more if you get stuck. This game offers little more than repetition and traversing the more-or-less linier path, which is rendered a chore by the clunky and innacurate controls. If you're looking for a fun, beautiful, side-scrolling action-puzzler, you're far better off with Trine (which also offers 3-player co-op).
If you're a die-hard fan of Double-Fine, as I am, give it a go. There are nods to your favourite games and glimmers of that humor we all love (not to mention the beautiful drawn-art and character design), yet within an hour I was bored and frustrated, and by two I'm writing this, not expecting the experiance to improve. Do yourself a favour and get a copy of Brutal Legend: a visually stunning and rich world full of action, humor and emotion that this game seems devoid of.

One of the single most moving and atmospheric games I have ever played. The comparisons to Undertale are apt, as are comparisons to OFF, but I'd call them second cousins at most. OneShot stands on its own with some very unique elements and takes on the meta RPG genre.
I will say, some of the fourth wall breaking bits were genuinely unsettling. I do unsettle pretty easily, so maybe that's not a high bar. But I definitely started tensing up whenever I saw a computer in-game.
More than anything, though, I found myself feeling such an easy and effortless connection to Niko. Within an hour of playing, I was willing to die for this child. After four hours of play, I found myself willing to make some choices I would not have thought myself capable of at the start of this game.
OneShot is a game that effortlessly balances charm and existential dread. I really wanted to know more about the world, and I was surprised at just how much the world seemed to know about me. It's a perfectly sized little game, too, so no one element outstays its welcome.
Make sure to try and take some time to explore and try new things! You might get a unique bit of dialogue or stumble onto an achievement by accident. Thank you, Niko, for not letting me take a crowbar to the sun because I forgot you were still holding it.
If I have a critique, I'd say that the sound design for this game never really grabbed me. I struggle to remember any given track even now, and those that I had to let run on for a while would start to grate a little bit. But there are no music puzzles in this game, so you can just mute it if you have the same problem I did.
EDIT: 9/07/2017 - I wrote this earlier review before I finished the Solstice ending. I did that because I didn't think the Solstice ending could impress me any more than the rest of the game already had. I was completely and utterly incorrect, and now I'm sobbing. But it's the good kind of sob. What a damn good game. I'll never forget you, Niko, or this world. That's a promise.

Osiris is a multiplayer (with optional single player) space survival game for PC which was released on September 28th 2016. The game is currently in early access but does not come with the stigma attached to most early access titles. Osiris offers a lot for the £18.99 price tag with a decent crafting system and a vast planet to discover. The atmosphere in this game is extremely eerie and even when playing with friends you very much feel alone and stranded… The ability to leave the planet and explore a number of other planets out in space will be coming to the game very soon. When your journey starts you are given a few starting weapons (Assault rifle & Pistol) and an inflatable dome kit (your home base). From there you’ll follow a decent tutorial to get comfortable with crafting and basically getting your bearings with the game. It’s not all crafting, gathering and fluffy clouds, NO…You are greeted by Aliens, Parasites and GIANT Sand worms (Oh My) waiting to tear you and your friends a new♥♥♥♥♥♥hole!
Overall the game is fantastic for the price and since its release a couple of days ago the developers have already patched a few problems! There are a few issues on the public servers at this moment in time but the devs are aware of the issues, so expect a patch very soon. Private servers on the other hand work just fine, so get some friends, get online and start exploring.
This game should definitely be on your radar!

What I hoped would be a good strategy game quickly turned into something beyond frustrating and unfun.
There seems to be almost no connect to what logically makes sense in a war plan and what the game DEMANDS you do instead.
Numbers are totally irrelevant. Because of the very questionable combad width system, it doesn't matter how many soldiers you really push out into the field, it all comes down a grinding slog.
And the combat really is terrible. In other Paradox games, wars are things you plan ahead and have every maneuver drawn out. Here, it doesn't *matter* what you plan, because your soldiers are just going to ignore your orders or take off in a different direction anyway. For a game about being a WW2 combat, the *actual combat* makes you feel like barely a participant.
The battles operate on moon logic. Defenders have this utterly absurd defensive advantage, and can fight off battalions a hudred times their size for a year. Naval invasion are arranged to be as frustrating to manage as possible. The navy almost feels ignored and with the recent patch, submarines are utterly useless. The resources (various currency in each territory that determine what you can build) doesn't even seem like Paradox put even a tiny amount of research into the resources countries outside the main contributers of WW2 had.
HoI4 is not a good game. About the only thing it really captures is how frustrating and boring real war is.

I loved this game in it's original incarnation, it was a really unique asymmetrical experience that provided great fun either coordinating a well thought out set of abilities with hunters or an exhilarating super stressful experience as the monster.
Now it's F2P and that's great, player base is huge, but the gameplay changes kill this game for me. They basically removed the phase of the hunt where you hunt the monster by making dome so automatic and giving the trapper the new auto find ability. All the great moments this game used to have, like barely trapping the monster in the dome, support stealthing and running when losing to the monster, monster losing the hunters like a boss and backtracking to the other side of the map... they are just gone. The upside is they also eliminated the ability for a single scrub to tank your team and drastically cut down on match times, but what's left is just not compelling.
I guess the hunt was my favorite part of the original evolve.

Gameplay:
Pros: Good game.  The gameplay is a bit like The Talos Principle and Portal (but closer to Talos).  Nice graphics, nice puzzle logic, and a refreshing lack of any annoying zero-tolerance perfect speed timing puzzles (which I really hate in a puzzler game, which should be about smarts not how dexterous you are at the game.)
Cons: I'd say the difficulty was slightly too easy, though.  I mean there were some tough puzzles but they weren't that hard to work out, but I was able to get through in just 2 sittings, where games like Portal 2 and Talos took me a lot longer to figure out some of the puzzles.  It's just barely on the lower edge of how many hours of gameplay I'd expect out of a $19.99 game.  It's just barely long enough to be worth it, but if it was slightly shorter it wouldn't have been.  If you expect a very high ratio of hours of play per money spent, you might have more misgivings about this.
Plot:
Pro: Super neat.  And unfortunately it's impossible to describe without massive spoilers.  I just want to say there's a big twist halfway through that makes it all *click* and helps make the title of the game fit perfectly.
Con: It does present one of those sort of ethical dillemas that feels totally fake (fake in that it pretends there's only two possible choices, both bad, when there actually are more.)

The Turing Test is a puzzle game, with the name in homage to Alan Turing OBE FRS who was the founder of modern computing, and the story based on the idea that an AI would have the ability to be indistinguishable from, that of a human.
Thus leading to our main characters TOM and Ava. TOM is the AI who needs Ava to solve the puzzles using the Energy Manipulation Tool (EMT), a gun that holds various types of energy charges, that are used to power doors, lifts, magnets, platforms etc To help progress you through the story and discover the cause behind the disappearance of the ground crew stationed there.
The game pays great homage to Portal, and is similar to others like QUBE and The Talos Principal (Other great games BTW!) There is a great script and whilst Ava's lines seemed Mediocre and unconvincing, Tom really steals the show, with a nice passive voice (I swore it was Jeremy Irons lol), thats makes you believe hes the wise, senior type. Giving a great story throughout the game, thats very much the mystery scifi experience without Portals comedy element.
Length wise there are 7 chapters with 10 levels and bonus levels earning you achievements for their completion (Sector 6's will drive you nuts!) with Audio logs, and tablets, letters lying around to cover more story.
Visually its stunning, using Nvidias DSR with Ultra settings and getting 60FPS (Well it is first person!) With an ambient score, and scifi sound effects to boot.
One problem I found was the loading times, but this is a good thing as it loads the entire chapter it would seem, as opposed to Portals one level, get in the lift (Hate that thing) which may prove slower on some older systems, but that was my only gripe with the game.
One of the few games ive preordered and whilst ive put in around 8 hours, it could have been completed in shorter time, giving it decent value for money, but we will see what the DLC holds!
