The economics side of the game is really well-modeled; all your equipment and weapons take on a new importance in terms of industrial production, requiring some careful thinking and foresight so as to avoid mid-game issues. Striking balances between military and civilian factories according to your foreseeable needs makes for an interesting meta-game aspect. Early military build-ups may take preference for military factories for instance, but can you afford to let go of those civilian factories for much-needed resources? The player will definitely ask themselves questions like these throughout the game.
Diplomacy is thankfully more fleshed out this time round, with a new option to create factions and non-agression pacts actually becoming usable in single player. A smart 'reasoning' system has been implemented, making NPCs react to the player country in certain ways. It's as entirely viable, for example, to create a faction via threatening force against your neighbours as it is to do so with a charm offensive by improving relations. Trade has been simplified in an interesting way - swapping civilian factories for a set number of resources - so no more painful micro-managing of trade deals to get 100k of all resources.
Combat is also pretty well done, with battles taking a little longer now compared to HoI3 and a raised emphasis on success at the operational level, which can be accomplished a number of ways thanks to doctrinal foci. Commanders intending to build a strong infantry-based army heavily supported by artillery may wish to adopt superior firepower doctrines, while others focusing on a more mobile, tank-led military would prefer doctrinal training for mobile operations. The use of tactics form a major, realistic part of battles now, with better-skilled commanders more likely to use better tactics in order to win battles.
At this stage you might be thinking why am I not giving this a thumbs up? Well, there are a few reasons.
AI issues is a big one. The AI is rather weak in terms of its intelligence. It remains tied by feet and hands to the battleplan system, which is a really ineffective way for it to fight on many occasions, as it will perform rapid strategic re-deployments to areas which are not necessarily the most urgent. Take Italy for instance. Poor, poor Italy, whose navy gets crushed almost every time in the Mediterranean, whose soldiers consistently fail to defend the most important Italian VP locations, allowing the British to stroll right into Rome in 1940. This happens a lot, and brings me to my next point: naval invasions.
Naval invasions are implemented terribly. You need a minimum of 50% air and/or naval superiority in the seas along which you intend to send your invasion fleet. This is too easy, requiring a few destroyer squadrons or fighter wings at best, both of which the AI has a tendency to spam. If you can reach that minimum, you can invade anybody with the bare minimum of effort. The solution to fix it of course is simple: require air and/or naval
, meaning 100% control over those seas.
Historically, when the Western Allies invaded Normandy in 1944, the Luftwaffe could muster only approximately 170 fighters to duel with more than 12,000 of their Allied counterparts, and the Kriegsmarine remained locked up in north German ports, sending only a few
to harrass the invasion fleet. This situation is the very definition of supremacy and there's absoutely no reason why this shouldn't apply in-game.
World tension is something of a very irritating, sandbox-y annoyance. It's a measure of how tense international politics are and various kinds of action will increase or decrease it. Declarations of war, annexations and post-war treaties in the realm of non-Democratic nations tend to increase it, while natural decay, guarantees of independence and declarations of war from Democratic nations tend to decrease it.
The developers seem to have this idea in their heads of providing an additional challenge for the Authoritarian and Democratic players, in that keeping WT low is ideal for the former, while raising it is ideal for the latter. This is obviously very silly, since WT as an element in itself is not bound to ideology; Democratic actions should ordinarily have just as much impact on WT as non-Democratic ones.
It's also heavily advantageous for Democratic nations. By providing them with the guarantee option at 25% WT, they are able to throw out ahistorical guarantees willy-nilly to anyone who is being justified against by a non-Democratic nation. The problem is 25% WT gets reach
quickly, within the first two in-game years, providing little to no room for non-Democratic nations to do ahistorical things, quite in spite of the fact that the guarantee options are ahistorical themselves; in reality of course nobody but Poland got anything like a guarantee of independence prior to 1940. And yet, try justifying against Portugal as Nationalist Spain in 1937 and the Anglo-French will have none of it.
Again, the solutions are very simple: massively increase PP cost for ahistorical guarantees; decrease WT effects for non-Democratic actions; or remove ahistorical guarantees entirely.
My final reason for the thumbs down is a simple, oft re-hashed yet critically important one: the continuation of PDX's DLC release business model. I just can't abide by this. I understand perfectly well that game companies need to remain competitive in the current environment but what we are going to end up paying is about $120/£90/E100 for the finished product. This is unacceptable, especially when the DLCs don't really improve the gameplay experience in a significant way. Unique focus trees? Improve puppet dynamics? This is mod-creatable stuff which should absolutely be in the base game anyway!
Worse yet, there's a dirty little piece of reasoning behind all this: PDX are intent on continuing to release DLC and patches for previous, long-ago released games in their line-up. They won't be named because you know exactly what I'm talking about. But it's a very poor business practice and shows a lack of commitment to current and future games.
TL;DR: Don't buy this for the time being. Go have a look at other titles, put money and effort into them and wait until a 'Panzer-Pusher Final Edition' has been released, then grab it on sale. This review is updated as of Feb 1st '17.

So this game dropped in EA yesterday. In many way it smacks of early Subnautica and Ark as many have already pointed out.
The question is, is it worth supporting?
Yes, it is. However you'd need to be aware before buying that it is literally one day old so far as its release cycle is confirmed. I'm not playing multiplayer so cannot confirm, but it does sound like they've got bugs 'a' plenty to deal with. Hopefully they'll continue to refine the experience as this title definitely does show at times that it was developed by a two man team and not a twenty man team.
For example, its weird to me that you seem to be unable to even pull up a list of controls in the options menu. Additionally the multi tool implementation needs work. It's janky having to switch between the multi tool and pickaxe to swap items between the droid and the repository. Multi tool functionality in base building needs refinement too and tutorials are required as the building mechanics are not as intuitive as Ark or SN.
Enemy AI is interesting but needs to be more fluid. Attacks are super easy to dodge and rarely end up damaging the player. A simple jump + shoot dispatches most enemies.
The survival needs to be more hardcore. Water and hunger drain are trivial and all both resources are available in abundance either way - definitely need to rebalance the stats and put more thought into survival - without having to worry about food, water, damage and ammo the game risks turning into a mining simulator.
Additional content is a must. Ark and SN are successful because there is an abundance of flora and fauna in their worlds and a rich and balanced crafting system to compliment it.
Crafting in Osiris needs work too. That's all I'll say for now.
I know it seems negative, but in spite of all of the above you really should support this game. It has great potential to be one of the best. Unknown Worlds stated that Subnatica was so sucessful because the input from the community helped to shape the state of the game. I hope the same positive influence will be enjoyed by these Fenix Fire and I look forward to updating this review as the updates roll out.

Chaos Souls is a 2.5D action-platformer mixup narrating the story of Eris, an half-act, anime style girl which also is a skilled demon hunter. One day, her sister Petra is abducted by an evil Succubus and so the quest begins. Infiltrated inside the Succubus' castle, Eris has to face many foes and bosses to free her sister.
===
Chaos Souls is a very action oriented side scroller, inspired by the famous Souls series because of certain mechanics inherited from it. The core gameplay consists in our heroine defeating "rooms" filled with a certain number of enemy waves of increasing difficulty, only when all are defeated the Dark Barrier will vanish allowing her to progress. The controls are pretty basic and straightforward, it is much better to play with a Gamepad rather than KB and Mouse. The depth level we talk about here is not high, the environments feature not alternate paths or secrets nor special enemies, there is no loot / equipment system, only form of progression consists in Upgrade Points awarded after defeating bosses. This is where this "souls inspired" game starts showing some lacking: in Dark Souls one of the core mechanics consists in gaining experience from normal enemies to then upgrade your character and overcome difficulties; such mechanic is absent in Chaos Souls sincce the only upgrades are gained from Bosses and NOT regular enemies! You can very well deduct what it means. Apart from this, there is not much else to talk about gameplay in general, the game is all about combat and defeating rows upon rows of foes, so let's discuss about Combat in the next section.
So here we are, the star of the show, Combat System, the spear tip of any even inspired "souls" title SHOULD be this, and in Chaos Souls the only thing to do is fighting, so must be a damn good system right? Wrong.
Combat in Chaos Souls revolves around different moves: we have a 4-hit light attack combo using X, a 3-hit heavy attack combo using Y (of course these combos do not need to be fully executed each time), a Ranged Attack with B, Jump with A, Dash with RT, use a magical barrier to shield from damage with LB while RB is for using one of the three available Potions to heal up.
So what's wrong with it? A lot of things. First of all there is no form of Parrying / Counterattacking, the mechanic has just not been implemented period, so take of one layer of depth already. Next: there are no signature checkpoints in levels, (Bonefires in the Souls series), if you happen to be defeated you just die and have to restart the whole section from the beginning, which also happens for Dark Souls but with not such long intervals, plus Dark Souls has multiple bonfires in the same area, Chaos Souls has not. This united with the fact regular enemies DO NOT GIVE EXP POINTS concoctes a really frustrating and time-wasting combination. The character movement speed is slow and there is absolutely no customization of class or skills, just a barebone upgrade system to enhanche things such as Damage or Defense and a bunch of others. Hitboxes of the main character are inaccurate, you WILL be hit from attacks dodged 1 meter away and so on. Enemies have almost nonexistent animation delay, they just stand in their idle animation then in a very unreasonably low timeframe, act and use skills/attacks in a blink, this is a way of artificially increasing difficulty and is NOT appreciated by most, including myself, because it reflects the Developers lack of will to construct more complexly layered systems in favor of artificial challenge.
The game features a decent variety of enemies, but the lack of an equipment system, no alternate / secret paths in levels, and a barebone upgrade system, put this title in the "low content" tier just because its maximum gameplay depth is likely a puddle of dirt. Talking about play time, i guess the game can last a good amount of time, depending on player skill and willpower. It needs much more complex combat system with articulated mechanics, not this basic thing we have here.
Balance is quite ruined because of the Combat System problems mentioned above, nothing else to say.
You surely will struggle, not to uninstall it because of how rotten the combat is. Try and see.
===
Backgrounds are of surprisingly good quality, really, quite a lot of details and good lighting system give the game a good look. Character and enemy models are of much lower quality and it really stands out, almost as background  and characters were made by two different teams entirely! Drawings in the visual-novel style cutscenes are of good quality, not excellent but not bad either. Particle effects are of mediocre craft and nothing special about them.
Nothing stands out about Chaos Souls' sub-average sound compartment. There also is no voice acting.

Typing of the Dead is the kind of game that tells you exactly what it is just by looking at the title. The game is half Mavis Beacon and half House of the Dead. Cry of Fear
-----------
Cry of Fear is a survival horror shooter where you play as Simon Henriksson, a 19 year old Swedish boy suffering from depression. The concept of the game is very interesting as it has you fighting through the streets of Sweden while warding off monsters that represent different anxieties and insecurities Simon is haunted by.
The soundtrack and sound design is phenominal, although some of the tracks are purely for atmosphere such as "Heart" and "Kill Yourself/F--cked", and sets the mood perfectly with tracks such as "Loney" and "Brandon".  They're available on Spotify if you want to save time rather than digging through the game files or visiting Youtube-MP3.
The combat in the game is decent with a variety of weapons from Simon's switchblade, to a glock, to an M16 assault rifle. Melee combat in the first few chapters can feel wonky but gun play is satifying with weapons like the shotgun that deal deadly blows to your enemies. However, it certainly takes its inspiration from the creator's previous game "Afraid of Monsters", so don't waste your ammo and aim your shots carefully.
The map design is breath taking and looks great visually despite being in the GoldSrc engine. Maps are usually fairly straight forward, but there are times that it allows you to explore in search of ammo or morphine syringes, and be sure you stock up on those if you're playing on a higher difficulty. Although I think the maps themselves are more of a hazard than the monsters you encounter and will sometimes require a bit of trial and error as they can throw things from groping hands reaching through bloodied floor grating, to twitiching insta-kill tentacle headed corpses in strait jackets. Some deaths might be unpredictable, but some planning at the "GAME OVER" screen, using clues given in the form of notes or wall maps, and spamming morphine until Simon starts puking should suffice in overcoming them.
The only major complain I have regarding map design is that there comes a time in the game where you must back track a considerable ammount to collect a fuse to unlock a door. Back tracking in any game is already annoying, but the monsters thrown in the way make it infuriating. I myself took a break from the game before diving back into my Easter Egg Hunt from Hell.
Puzzles in the game, namely the statues in the park, require a bit of critical thinking but no one will blame you for having to look up a guide a time or two. Credit where it's due, the puzzles are often times clever and sometimes embarrassingly obvious after you finally figure them out.
But, if you're looking for a good horror shooter that's more horror than action, I'd suggest giving this game a try. It leaves a lasting impression you'll remember long after closing the game, and the possiblities for alternate endings gives it some replayability. RuMple is a man of many talents, from music to games and I hope to see more from him in the future. I'd also suggest checking out his band "Intig", if guitars and screaming about suicide is your cup of tea.

Hello everyone! My name is DigitalGamer and this will be my first review on a game on Steam. I had to talk about this game because everytime I watched or played this game it always blew my mind, so I decided to dedicate my time talking about it. This is hands down one of the best horror games I ever played from the storytelling, action, jumpscares, and the survival aspect of it. I have played a lot of horror games and seen a lot of horror games on youtube and don't get me wrong there is a lot of great games like Outlast and The Evil Within that were really fun to play, but don't add up quite like Cry of Fear. This game has you hooked from beginning to end. You feel so attached in the game with its huge mystery and unconventional storytelling that really makes you stratch your head until the end of the game is revealed to you. Here are the pros and cons about this game.
Pros:
- THE STORY: This game, like I said, is very unconventional and won't make sense but I promise you it will be worth it just give it a chance. Also the central dark theme of this game is really good and makes the game even scarier and depressing.
- GRAPHICS: You can argue that the graphics are not all that great but for this to be a mod for Half-Life 1 and looks this amazing is pretty impressive. I enjoyed the graphics because to me it always gave me this nostalgic feeling when ever I play it.
- GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is really good in this game it makes things challenging but not difficult and that is what I like about it. I hate when games are so difficult that it ruins that enjoyment of the game. The survival aspect is fun because it makes you think of what weapons to use, which one should I carry, should I save my bullets, etc. This is what I mostly enjoy about the game is the variety of monsters and weapons uses in the game that makes the game more interesting and challenging.
- ACTING: The acting isn't really fantastic but it is not bad either. I forgive the acting in this game because this is a mod for a game and was made for very low budget, so I can forgive the voice acting in it but I can still see the actors/actresses trying their best to make their characters so real in this game.
Cons:
- GUIDANCE: I have had a problem where the game doesn't really give you any guidance of where to go and, to me, I got lost easily in this game if you don't know where you are going. It can make the game difficult at sometimes.
- OP MONSTERS: There are some monsters in this game that can be very difficult to kill and they can kill you easily sometimes or there will be some many monsters that can be overwhelming but the game tries to balance that out with the weapons.
- HEALTH: I've heard a lot people saying that it is difficult to find some health in the game and I never really had this problem but I can see why. If you are jusy playing it for the first time I would recommend you get use to the combat system and exploring a lot in the game. Doing these two task will help you find more health in the game because this game is all about exploring to find items and you wont lose so much health if you understand how the combat system works. Also be conservative with health syringes and don't waste it on you losing a bit of your health.
Overall the Pros tackle over the Cons heavily because these are minor issues I had in the game. I would highly recommend you play this game if you are a huge horror fan. Also I've heard that this game can be glitchy and can crash at times and I never had that problem before so be aware and save alot

It's good but it's just not quite good enough.
The economics side of the game is really well-modeled; all your equipment and weapons take on a new importance in terms of industrial production, requiring some careful thinking and foresight so as to avoid mid-game issues. Striking balances between military and civilian factories according to your foreseeable needs makes for an interesting meta-game aspect. Early military build-ups may take preference for military factories for instance, but can you afford to let go of those civilian factories for much-needed resources? The player will definitely ask themselves questions like these throughout the game.
Diplomacy is thankfully more fleshed out this time round, with a new option to create factions and non-agression pacts actually becoming usable in single player. A smart 'reasoning' system has been implemented, making NPCs react to the player country in certain ways. It's as entirely viable, for example, to create a faction via threatening force against your neighbours as it is to do so with a charm offensive by improving relations. Trade has been simplified in an interesting way - swapping civilian factories for a set number of resources - so no more painful micro-managing of trade deals to get 100k of all resources.
Combat is also pretty well done, with battles taking a little longer now compared to HoI3 and a raised emphasis on success at the operational level, which can be accomplished a number of ways thanks to doctrinal foci. Commanders intending to build a strong infantry-based army heavily supported by artillery may wish to adopt superior firepower doctrines, while others focusing on a more mobile, tank-led military would prefer doctrinal training for mobile operations. The use of tactics form a major, realistic part of battles now, with better-skilled commanders more likely to use better tactics in order to win battles.
At this stage you might be thinking why am I not giving this a thumbs up? Well, there are a few reasons.
AI issues is a big one. The AI is rather weak in terms of its intelligence. It remains tied by feet and hands to the battleplan system, which is a really ineffective way for it to fight on many occasions, as it will perform rapid strategic re-deployments to areas which are not necessarily the most urgent. Take Italy for instance. Poor, poor Italy, whose navy gets crushed almost every time in the Mediterranean, whose soldiers consistently fail to defend the most important Italian VP locations, allowing the British to stroll right into Rome in 1940. This happens a lot, and brings me to my next point: naval invasions.
Naval invasions are implemented terribly. You need a minimum of 50% air and/or naval superiority in the seas along which you intend to send your invasion fleet. This is too easy, requiring a few destroyer squadrons or fighter wings at best, both of which the AI has a tendency to spam. If you can reach that minimum, you can invade anybody with the bare minimum of effort. The solution to fix it of course is simple: require air and/or naval
, meaning 100% control over those seas.
Historically, when the Western Allies invaded Normandy in 1944, the Luftwaffe could muster only approximately 170 fighters to duel with more than 12,000 of their Allied counterparts, and the Kriegsmarine remained locked up in north German ports, sending only a few
to harrass the invasion fleet. This situation is the very definition of supremacy and there's absoutely no reason why this shouldn't apply in-game.
World tension is something of a very irritating, sandbox-y annoyance. It's a measure of how tense international politics are and various kinds of action will increase or decrease it. Declarations of war, annexations and post-war treaties in the realm of non-Democratic nations tend to increase it, while natural decay, guarantees of independence and declarations of war from Democratic nations tend to decrease it.
The developers seem to have this idea in their heads of providing an additional challenge for the Authoritarian and Democratic players, in that keeping WT low is ideal for the former, while raising it is ideal for the latter. This is obviously very silly, since WT as an element in itself is not bound to ideology; Democratic actions should ordinarily have just as much impact on WT as non-Democratic ones.
It's also heavily advantageous for Democratic nations. By providing them with the guarantee option at 25% WT, they are able to throw out ahistorical guarantees willy-nilly to anyone who is being justified against by a non-Democratic nation. The problem is 25% WT gets reach
quickly, within the first two in-game years, providing little to no room for non-Democratic nations to do ahistorical things, quite in spite of the fact that the guarantee options are ahistorical themselves; in reality of course nobody but Poland got anything like a guarantee of independence prior to 1940. And yet, try justifying against Portugal as Nationalist Spain in 1937 and the Anglo-French will have none of it.
Again, the solutions are very simple: massively increase PP cost for ahistorical guarantees; decrease WT effects for non-Democratic actions; or remove ahistorical guarantees entirely.
My final reason for the thumbs down is a simple, oft re-hashed yet critically important one: the continuation of PDX's DLC release business model. I just can't abide by this. I understand perfectly well that game companies need to remain competitive in the current environment but what we are going to end up paying is about $120/£90/E100 for the finished product. This is unacceptable, especially when the DLCs don't really improve the gameplay experience in a significant way. Unique focus trees? Improve puppet dynamics? This is mod-creatable stuff which should absolutely be in the base game anyway!
Worse yet, there's a dirty little piece of reasoning behind all this: PDX are intent on continuing to release DLC and patches for previous, long-ago released games in their line-up. They won't be named because you know exactly what I'm talking about. But it's a very poor business practice and shows a lack of commitment to current and future games.
TL;DR: Don't buy this for the time being. Go have a look at other titles, put money and effort into them and wait until a 'Panzer-Pusher Final Edition' has been released, then grab it on sale. This review is updated as of Feb 1st '17.

When the first Assassin's Creed game released in November of 2007, it brought with it an entirely new genre that has yet to be replicated. Fighting as an Assassin in the era of the Third Crusade, battling the opposing Templar faction while seeking a legendary religious artifact that's known as a Piece of Eden; all the while having a modern story element entwined. It's no surprise that the game exploded into the 12-release franchise that we know today. Although the first installment was deemed unique, yet repetitive, 2009's Assassin's Creed II raised the bar by attempting to change the formula, while still keeping the base aspects of the series intact.
Equipped with a new protagonist and era, players will now find themselves in the robes of Ezio Auditore da Firenze; a young Italian whose home lies within Renaissance Italy. The modern day segments, while limited, still revolve around Desmond Miles; a bartender who was captured by Abstergo, a corporation that created the high-tech piece of equipment known as the Animus that allows its users to relive their ancestor's memories. It's revealed that Abstergo, who are actually the current era Templars, chose Desmond in particular as his Assassin ancestors knew the whereabouts to the Apple; a Piece of Eden that contains legendary power. Early on, Desmond ends up escaping Abstergo with the help of some current era Assassins, and they hold up in an abandoned warehouse as Desmond continues searching for the highly coveted religious artifact.
When you talk to Assassin's Creed fans about their favorite character, you're most likely to hear the answer "Ezio" more often than not. The classy Italian ladies man with a thick accent and lucious locks is undeniably a fan favorite, and it helps that his presence spans the course of three games. Assassin's Creed II takes place from 1459, Ezio's birth, through 1499, landing the beloved protagonist at age 40 by the end of the title. So as to not give much away about the intricate plot, let's just say that Ezio's tale is one of loss, revenge, and acceptance. His father was an Assassin, a fact that was hidden from Ezio until he was about 18 years of age, and from there onward he became part of the historical guild himself.
As this franchise is one that is known for it's historical accuracy, at least to a point, Renaissance Italy works well within the universe. There are a handful of locations to visit, including a large, sprawling Venice and Florence, as well as many well established landmarks. Along the way, Ezio also meets many well known figures from the era; most notably a young Leonardo Da Vinci. As Ezio upgrades his home villa, he can purchase real-to-life Renaissance paintings to adorn its walls, and when examined they come with factual tidbits about the pieces. Needless to say, the game is brimming with historical accuracies and educational material, all the while throwing a unique spin on some of the actual events that occured.
If you've never played an Assassin's Creed game, you're in for a bit of a surprise. The gameplay is unlike any other title on the market, with free-flowing parkour in an open world full of missions and dangers. You will be tasked with climbing to some of the highest points of the game to unlock view points, which subsequently reveal a larger portion of the map; afterward, you can perform a signature Leap of Faith off of the top into a bale of hay. In some areas, you will be required to be stealthy and unseen, avoiding guards at all cost. Other times, it doesn't matter and you can go in blades blazing. Now if you have played a game in this franchise before, specifically one of the newer ones, you're going to be frustrated. Assassin's Creed II's climbing system is primitive at best, frustrating at worst, but still not as raw as the original title.
Regretfully, there are a few more pain points that extend beyond the climbing mechanics. One is the notoriety system, wherein if a guard sees you commit a crime, your wanted level is raised by a fraction; this includes accidentally stumbling into some bumbling idiot carrying a box and making them drop it. To lower your rating, you must remove wanted posters, bribe heralds, or kill officials. If guards see you do any of these things, they will raise your notoriety level back up to where it was, and potentially begin conflict with you. The battle system can also be irritating at times, as it's not fluid in any sense of the word; it's also incredibly dull, leaving it better to avoid conflict at all cost. Despite the array of weapons you can purchase, you will only find yourself using a handful of them throughout the game; a good chunk of them are absolutely useless filler.
Aside from its 13-15 hour campaign, there's a plethora of content to keep gamers busy for dozens of hours if they wish to seek ultimate depth from the title; parkour race missions, beat em' ups, view points, collectible feathers and symbols, chests to plunder, courier missions, Assassin tombs, Templar lairs, and more. Players can even upgrade Ezio's armor, weapons, pouches, and homestead. Full completion never feels like a chore as the beautiful landscapes are enough eyecandy to keep even the most ADD of gamers appeased; although the Assassination Contracts can become a bit repetitive after a while.
As far as the entire franchise goes, Assassin's Creed II is a classic in its own right, and a beloved favorite by many fans of the series. The story is remarkable, the characters are lovable, and the entire experience is extremely memorable. There are a few pain points here and there, such as the outdated and sometimes frustrating climbing system that can take some time to get used to. As well, the amount of idiots carrying boxes that stumble into you, causing you to get in trouble, is ridiculous. Needless to say, there is obvious room for improvement. However, the game runs great on PC, and given its age the graphics aren't terribly outdated. If you own a console, I highly suggest picking up The Ezio Collection; while the mechanics aren't updated, the textures and lighting have been given a breath-taking overhaul, and the game feels brand new once again.

I am writing this review while having played maybe a third of the game.  But my impressions over this first third are such that I recommend this game to any interested in giving Assassin's Creed a chance.
I recently posted a negative review of the original Assassin's Creed, which I found mechanically frustrating beyond any potential for enjoyment.  So for Assassin's Creed II, I want to start by saying that most of those issues were addressed.  The game still doesn't have a Quickload or Quicksave function and still uses checkpoints, but checkpoints are regular while pursuing the story and readily available while simply exploring.  The game's interface and menu systems, while a little difficult, are far more user-friendly.  Character movement is much improved, and camera issues are mostly gone.  You can quit to desktop quickly and easily, and getting back into the game is a fairly standard experience now.
The game isn't without a few flaws.  At random points, it won't be clear what you need to do next.  Helpful hints will flash on the screen only to disappear before they can be read.  Control instructions are often controller-exclusive or contain partial or inaccurate keyboard instructions.  If you are playing this on PC, you will be thankful for Google.  But these instances do not significantly detract from the game experience.
There are plenty of improvements and just enjoyable extra elements in the game.  Taking advantage of the setting, the game adds an economic system -- an extremely welcome improvement.  The game also includes a home base that you can improve.  This is a feature I absolutely love in games, and has elevated games such as Might & Magic 7 and Dragon Age: Inquisition to be among my favorites.  I look forward to seeing what else is in store as I delve farther into the game.

Geometry Dash is a game based on a simple concept, a cube that jumps over spikes. It seems easy, but after you discover the basics of this game, there's so much more to learn... Here are some of the awesome features of Geometry Dash that help define the game.
-Level Editor:
You can create your very own levels so you can show them to your friends. (if you have any...) This ensures that you'll never run out of levels to play.
-Comments:
You can leave comments on levels to tell the creator if they sucked or not.
-Friends:
A feature for those who need more friends. You can add friends and message them. You can even collaborate on levels with them. (soon there will be a feature for that... soon...)
-Achievements:
Completing levels, collecting coins, dying on levels, collecting more coins and following RobTop Games on Twitter are all special achievements that can be unlocked as part of the game. Did I mention you can collect coins...?
-Unlockable Icons:
From achievements come... (*drum roll*)... Icons? You can unlock additional icons to use in-game or just to show off your achievements to others.
-Mechanisms:
You don't even need a GamePad to play, you can just left click on the mouse and you're good to go. There are also new and exciting gameplay modes, so you'll never get bored of the same thing. There are icons for those as well.
-Secrets:
(Shhh...)
-And last but not least, Updates:
This game gets updates every once in a while. (*cough* years *cough*) With updates come more features for the Level Editor, more options for your account / making comments, more achievements, more icons, more gameplay modes and secrets. (
)
Without all of these features Geometry Dash wouldn't the game it is today. It started out simple, and as the updates came, the game grew bigger. It is an honour to have played Geometry Dash for more than 2 years and to be a part of the GD community. I look forward to the next ultimate update, 2.2!
P.S: Yes, I know I did say the word "features" quite a few times.

"Typing of the Dead" is a zombie game where you TYPE different words in order to kill the zombies, pretty interesting concept which was first published in 1999 in the arcades and in 2000 on the Sega Dreamcast, and it can be somewhat challenging at times, especially when there's longer words and complicated spellings along with SEVERAL zombies at one time. "House of the Dead" is also included in the "Overkill" package and is the classic light gun arcade zombie game (wow, that's a mouthful) introduced back in 1996 (three years before "Typing..."). In that game you're just using the mouse to shoot the zombies like you're doing in any regular first person shooter.
Now, that's the only difference between the two modes. They share the same story, same graphics, same enviroments, characters etc., that said... there's none to very little replayability to be found here. The only scenario I can think of where you'd like to play it again is if you've invited some friend (or friends) over and you play together (it is possible, but I don't know how though).
The story revolves around the cops Agent G and Detective Washington, the strippers Varla and Candi and the bad guy Papa Caesar. The years since the Cold War has passed, the military tried to create a new superhuman formula called "Formula X" (dun-dun-DUN!). Well, that project failed and the bunker where it took place was left unaccessed... until now. Guessed who got access to it? Right! Papa Caesar. So you're trying to stop him from using it... and you're failing miserably. I think, I stopped paying attention after the fourth mission, something like that.
Well, the game is decent but it took me about two hours to complete "Typing..." and I only just began playing "House...", I'll leave that part for some rainy day. Worth paying a dollar/euro/pound (whatever your money is called!), not more, not if you ask me. But I'll put a "recommend" marker on it, 'cause it's not a bad game after all.

I really wanted to like the game but right now it has too many breaking flaws and Paradox doesn't look willing or capable of fixing most of it, instead being content with slowly milking the player with subpar DLC.
The most glaring issue is the AI: the game just can't play itself and will make the weirdest strategic decisions like bleeding itself dry on a far away continent while it's being invaded by a couple divisions.
It will pretty much never really use the division designer, so they will have an absolute crazy amount of very small infantry divisions just waiting to be gunned down. You can take over the world as Italy if you just manifacture a dozen medium armor divisions.
A good number of design decisions are also questionable at best. The lack of resource stockpiles has no pretence of realism and this would be fine if it actually made the game smoother, but it's actually even more of an hassle when added to the complete lack of control over convoys, the nonsensical market mechanics and the sad state of the sea part as a whole: Submarines are useless, you don't actually feel in control over anything that happens of sea, you just stack the largest fleets you can and pray for the best. The fact that the AI has no idea what it's doing really doesn't help since you have no real feedback over your actions: again, you can easily curbstomp Great Britain's navy with pretty much no clue on how the system works.
The Air part of the game suffers from lack of clarity and utter lack of balance: I don't even know why Heavy Fighters and Strategic Bombers are in the game right now, they underperform massively and go down like they were made of paper. Again you don't have much of a choice, and you just ammass thousands of planes in the same air region, hoping for the best. At launch you could lose hundreds of planes in a few seconds, now they "fixed" the problem making air fights less lethal...which just means that it's the same mindless thing, just slower. Again the worst problem is that you have no way to correctly judge what went right or what went wrong apart from "you needed more stuff"
At least the way you come to ammass your stuff is strangely satisfying, almost to the point of being the best part of the game for me. The way you churn out a massive army as a strong nation always makes me rub my hands in anticipation. Then the war starts and it's like beating up strawmen.
I also want to briefly mention that the game is very poorly optimized. I should annihilate the recommended requirements, but the game still stutters and slow down to a crawl past a certain point. Again, this is a most prominent problem that a lot of players report since launch and it still hasn't been really fixed.
My verdict of the game would be more lenient had the developers shown the will to fix the game's foundation before starting to build upon it with DLCs. Instead after only two major patches which didn't really address the worst aspects of the game in a satisfying manner, they have started to milk the costumer.
My final advice, to you as to myself, is to
They have a real history of releasing games in a messy state. Sometimes these games grow into something quite remarkable, like EU4, and sometimes they head to a much less promising future.

Beach Bounce is a slice-of-life visual novel developed by AJTGames and published by Dharker Studio. After Tomoyo's grandmother suddenly becomes ill he is immediately put in charge of running her beach resort pleasantly known as "Beach Bounce". Down on his luck and with no other prospects on the horizon he quickly jumps at the chance and embarks on a quirky adventure surrounded by a rather interesting group of women who work at the resort as they all attempt to keep the place afloat while it's matriarch is away. Will Tomoyo suceed in keeping Beach Bounce operating, also will he make some new friends in the process or possibly find love? How the story plays out is entirely up to you?
This visual novel features a multiple choice and directional story with many pathways and endings. There is a chance for good, bad and fun conclusions as well as several different possible romances with various characters depending on the decisions that you make. The narrative in Beach Bounce is fun and light hearted which is what I completely expected it to be. Maybe it's just me being weird but I actually do read visual novels for the stories and not the eye candy which usually consists of scantily clad women with what many consider to have perfect physiques. Don't get me wrong because I do like those things but if that was all I needed from a V.N. then I could easily get my hands on any number of the well known and somewhat lewd "Sakura" titles and not meaning to upset anyone who likes those but after having read just a small portion of one I can honestly tell you that I did not enjoy it at all. Without even a sliver of a story there really is nothing to hold my interest in a V.N. but thankfully Beach Bounce does not suffer from this problem. It may not be the deepest visual novel, story-wise, that I've read but there is enough substance there to keep me entertained and that's all I ask for.
As they are in all Dharker Studio V.N.'s, the visuals in this novel are absolutely gorgeous. The artwork is, of course, heavily manga inspired and is of the upmost quality in color, shading and detail not only on the characters themselves but the environments as well. It's just a really beautifully illustrated V.N. which compliments the story nicely. The audio quality is good as far as the music goes but this visual novel noticeably lacks the small ambient sound effects that really flesh out a V.N. like the sound of doors opening and closing or the background noises that you hear when you're outside or riding in a vehicle. I really enjoy it when a V.N. uses those ambient sounds to really immerse you within the story. Sadly there are none whatsoever in this visual novel. With that said, Beach Bounce still manages to do a fantastic job with the presentation visually but only somewhat aurally.
Despite the blantant innuendo that the title suggests, giggity, Beach Bounce had a thoroughly interesting story with a variety of quirky characters and terrific locations to visit. Also, with the multiple choices and branching narrative there is a high level of replayability so this is a title that you can easily revisit. I got the bad ending on my first playthrough so I definitely plan to replay this V.N. and make different choices. Option-wise, there are the basics for audio, music and text speed, also there is a CG gallery to unlock, a decent original soundtrack, Steam Achievements for the hunters as well as Steam Trading Cards to collect. If you enjoy a fun tongue in cheek story, making decisions that matter and conversing with pretty women then I RECOMMEND Beach Bounce not just to visual novel fans but to anyone looking for a fun read.

WARNING: This game contains mature content. Extremely mature content.
On the other hand, I'm yet to play a better typing help game. Unfortunately the voice acting isn't as awesomely bad as the original Dreamcast version and I do wish there were more penalties for missing letters (on normal), but it's intense, it's fun, you can laugh at it, and it does what it's designed to do.

This game is best experienced with a clickity clackity mechanical keyboard (others are good too) and a decent typing speed
This game is refreshing from what you'd get from a railshooter and a typing game. Although there are many other games that require a lot of typing, this has a lot of variety. The enemies are different, and this would be from typing a letter within milliseconds, or a single a word within a second. They have zom... MUTANTS that will rush at you and explode vomit, small animals like mutant birds or monkeys (they vary which mission you play, but they kinda have the same properties), and a couple more. You just don't type a sentence within a time period, you have to choose which mutant you want to type first, as they will throw things at you, while the others attack you. If you type 57-60 WPM without errors, you will be fine, but there are opportunities for extra damage in boss battles for those who type a couple million words per second. The level design (well doesn't matter since it's a railshooter), is pretty as each level takes you into a completely different place, as the setting fits each level fine (The train level is really cool.) It even contains the full 'House of the Dead: Director's Cut' from the PS3 version, so you can mouse click all you want. The graphics are meh, as animation is sloppy (although the executions are satisfying), the lip-syncing is not good, some textures are blurry, and Washington's bald head doesn't have enough polygons. It's good enough, as the lighting (in my opinion) is very nice. It's optimized, as I get over 60FPS in 1080p (with a GTX550Ti), so you should be able to run it on a crappy computer. The cutscenes has a lot of film grain/texture, a narrator with a cool voice, and the story resembles a movie-like plot. The game is hilarious, ♥♥♥♥ING FILLED WITH PROFANITY (NO JOKE), and the main two characters are likeable (but some are just really flat and don't have much to them). The dialogue is really odd sometimes (not the cursing), but it might be just me. It's has a lot of laughs, has some horror here and there (great maps), and overall a great buy for 20 dollars (although I got it for 6 on the humble bundle, which was a steal.)
GET THIS GAME, IT'S SO FUN AND YOU WILL FEEL LIKE A TYPING GOD.

TL;DR the TL;DR 5/10 - Get it if you want to become good at typing
TL;DR - Awesome to see a re-birth of this style of arcade gaming on the PC. The typing mechanism works well and is well thought out. Too bad the "storyline" and the characters are terrible.
Long version - spoilers ahead:
Gameplay: Typing of the Dead has some really nifty typing mechanics that makes this game fast paced, just like an arcade shooter. You will type single letters, abbreviations, words and sentences in order to kill the mutants (see game screenshots). What I did not expect was that there is a fair element of strategy where you might surrender writing a long sentence to hit a couple of single keys as these tend to have a shorter time span before they hurt you. Some words are long and unusual forcing you to keep your eyes off the keyboard in order to see how they are spelled. The difficulties seem to be designed with progression in mind, and thus you actually become a better typer as you play!
Story: The game is obviously not meant to be serious in any shape or form. Many of the words and sentences tht you write are related to the environment around you and can sometimes be quite clever, making you smile and sometimes lose your pace.
Unfortunatley thats where the positive experiences end. Apart from the above, this story can best be described as trying to cross as many lines as possible, and then claiming that it's ok - because comedy. I disagree, mainly because it's not funny.
The main characters are: A white guy trying to be cool and a black guy cursing. Then there are two side-kicks who are best described as "boobs with guns" - one of them being extraordinaryly stupid. The game makes sure that we see them this way by focusing the camera on their breasts whenever possible. Of course, they don't survive. After finishing the storyline I've seen racism, sexism, incest and disabled people being bullied, and that just ain't comedy unless your idea of fun is "Ha ha, that guy is in a wheelchair".
I know that the story comes from the original and they guys who created the typing-mod deserve a lot of credit for a game well done. However I just couldn't shake the bad story and found myself dreading the next cutscene and this is why I don't recommend this game. Hopefully someday there will be a brand new installment of this game where the characters and story have received some love. That game would be a 10/10 for sure.

Typing of The Dead: Overkill had me crying at points on its hardest difficulty.
Not just from the Grindhouse aesthetic and inane story about Papa Caeser and his Z... er, mutant fixation and love of Chinese takeaways or the dialogue between the Agents, the other characters you play as and that intentionally awful narrator. I was crying with laughter because of the phrases it was demanding you to type in a matter of seconds.
"Down with this." for one. Their comrade fell down to "Careful now." TOTD: Overkill's dictionary is a book of popular culture from Father Ted to Zero Wing.
Practice yoiur... your touch typing to this unabashedly slick and cheesy game. Then go get an Ice Cream Truck.

In this game you play as Mavis Beacon. Only zombies have sprung and you have to adapt your touch typing skills to combat the undead. She also sports double D's and bazookas inorder to kill zombies, using the power of the English language.
In all srsness TotD:O is a sequel to the original Typing of the Dead, only it is based on House of the Dead Overkill. It is a parody of grindhouse movies and regularly makes fun of itself. The main strength of this game is it's humor. Things like the level design, the dialogue, the fact you type out words to kill zombies. It is as ridiculous as the genre it exists in, so take solace in knowing that.
While the game does serve as an effective teaching aid for typing. I wouldn't say it's as good as the original. The nonsensical grindhouse atmosphere doesn't really compare to the gritty PS1 graphics presentation of Totd. It is also less difficult, and for typing veterans it won't exactly be your next Dark Souls. On the flipside the game allows you to switch to a fully functional port of House of the Dead Overkill.
At the very least Typing of the Dead Overkill continues the tradition laid out by it's predecessor by being one of the only educational games that doesn't suck.

the issue with it, is the triggers on xbox controllers. because they are analogue the game wont recognise them or allow you to set them. so unless you use the two files (a dll and another file contained in the zip must be copied into your AC2 folder), the controller cannot be set up in any logical way, and the default controller setup is basically unworkable. for example the triggers spin the view around instead of lock target or high profile. to high profile someone says they have to hold the start button in another thread on discussions! the zip fixes this, BUT it means you are unable to reconfigure the controller - it basically gives it the  xbox 360/ps3 controller config. once you have done that its playable.
other issues are present regardless of control method. the big one i have is that unlike console version, the icons for the thieves, courtesans and mercs do NOT appear on the maps no matter how you try and fiddle with the config. this means you will play this slightly differently since you will not want to spend a lot of time hunting around for a distraction group to set on enemies - you will most likely run out of patience and just resort to combat more. this is a shame in one way but its also an advantage in making this slightly fresher than the console version.
despite the issues its still a good game worth having with a good storyline; and great to play this then go straight into brotherhood and then revelations (if you own those two games also).

I don't usually write reviews.  I'm not the best at expressing my opinion usually.  But this time I had to give it a try.
DO NOT BOTHER WITH THIS GAME!!
Hmm....that was simpler then I thought.  Ok so yes this game is now 'free' and the premise is kind of fun.  But this is just a repackage as a pay to win game now.  Sure you can 'earn' coins and buy all the perks and upgrades just by playing but others don't have to wait.  And match making is done on your level which is based off of the number of games you have played/won/lost.  What matchmaking doesn't take into account is people that spend real money to max out the high level perks.  There is no lvl requirement for using perks you just have to spend coins on them.  So this was my experience:
Day 1:  Joined my first game.  Was a bit lost but learnt the controls quickly.  Teammates were in the same situation so we still manage to complement each other.  Monster gets to stage 2.  We corner it but in a hard fought battle we lose in the end.  Second game I knew more so I was able to stick with my team better.  We managed to harrass the monster at stage 1 and keep it moving and not feeding.  We finally cornered it and managed to kill it...first win!!  End of day it was FUN.
Day 2: Joined my first game where I got put into being the monster...had no idea how to play it so took me awhile.  Ran in circles most of the match and didn't even get to stage 2 before I was cornered.  I fought long and hard but lost.  Second game, got monster AGAIN but this time I knew what I was doing.  Fed better but the hunters were more skilled.  They kept harrassing me and made it hard to feed.   I get cornered in a cave which is blocked at the other end with the dome.  I managed to hit stage 2 at that same moment.  Fought, took 2 of them out, and then just barely got killed but it was satisfying.   Third game I didn't play monster but had to do support which I wasn't good at.  Monster nearly killed us several times but we managed to win in the end.  End of day again I had a great time.
Day 3:  Everything changes...... First game.  I get my choice of class, a decent looking team, and someone that WANTS to play monster.  Yay...right?!  We drop in and immediately start tracking.  We pull a nice move and cut across the map to where we predict the monster will circle...and BAM there he is.  Shield up and guns out.  Boulders and bullets fly and....we barely hurt him.....we get torn to SHREDS in less then a minute.  Everyone dead and I'm confused.  We are all lvl 2-3 players so I think it was just bad luck.  Second game.  Same deal with class and someone picking to be monster.  Drop in....and monster is waiting just ahead.  Doesn't even run.  We throw up shield and attack...adn then I notice...its armor is maxed out and its hits are doing MAJOR damange.  Dead to a stage one monster again....lather rinse repeat for two more games.
End result....@#$& YOU!  Seriously the game went from fun to unplayable in 3 DAYS! Thanks to pay to win perks!  The idea of the game is the stage one monster runs and the hunters try to kill it.  Stage 2 should be a more even fight and should be challenging for both sides.  Stage 3 should be a reverse of Stage 1 with the monster having an advantage.  But NO with pay to win if the monster has the right maxed out perks its just a slaughter at Stage 1.  And to compete?  Well you need all 4 hunters to pay up as well to max out their perks to compete which you don't get at low level match making.  They could have fixed this if they wanted to by simplying increasing peoples levels to match the perks they 'buy' instead of letting lvl 2 monster players have maxed out armor and damage right at stage 1 against a group of hunters basically armed wtih slingshots and spitwads.

This game is not currently worth the asking price in it's current state. After seeing many Early Access titles remain in Early Access for years, and seeing such innovations as Early Access titles offering paid DLC, I no longer believe the label to mean anything about the future. As the Early Access Game banner warns you,
"This Early Access game is not complete and may or may not change further. If you are not excited to play this game in its current state, then you should wait to see if the game progresses further in development."
At this time, Osiris: New Dawn is not worth buying. The game is very buggy. Most of the content is not yet implemented. Building recquires many hours of resource gathering, at which point you will have access to buildings with functions that are not implemented. Food and water concerns are non-existant (I have been alive for multiple in-game days without draining the food or water bar.) Buildings are indestructible, unless you press the no-confirmation 'destroy' key with your multitool out (which is the same as the 'put away multitool' key). Finding specific resources to harvest and hauling the wide variety of recquired resources was how most of my playtime was spent. The payoff for accomplishing these feats was... nothing. None of the advanced buildings (laboratory, large sattelite dish, biodome) are mechanically implemented.
The creatures are imaginitive. The ideas of the game are grand. I look forward to checking back in on this game in three to six months to see if it has progressed to the point where it is worth buying. For now, save your money and keep an eye on it.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
Early Access. We should all know what this means, but apparently many do not. For a game STILL in development, this is showing some promise. There's alot to look forward to in this title, and can still provide a few hours of fun with some friends, but by no means is it feature complete, and people who are bored looking to jump into the next new thing (Me.) should be wary.
As stated, for an early access title still in development, this game so far is great! The textures, the look of the creatures, the world, the lighting, it's all beautiful. Surprisingly it also runs like a hot knife through butter. Gun play is standard fare, kind of reminds me of HALO, but you know, much simpler as there are only two useable guns at the time of me writing this review.
It can genuinely be terrifying at night time with some of the strange aliens attacking your base, giving it an almost 7 Days To Die meets Starship Troopers feel, and again the aesthetics of the creatures are amazing, the giant sandworm (FOR SHAI'HALUD!") scared the crap out of me the first time I saw it flying towards me, its mouth agape.
Mining feels solid, and you don't need too many pieces to construct the various objects currently in the game.
Ah crafting, this is where the current weakness of the game resides. It's lackluster, with only a few recipes. Some buildings are buildable, but not yet functional, but still they look great! Rather than going the route of Minecraft or Empyrion, this time around the structures are prefabricated giving it the look of a space colony instead of allowing you to build a medieval castle love hotel, which I do like. They are customizable in that once you place the frame down, you have different options, like windows, a connecting tunnel, a solid wall, etc.
Vehicles, I imagine will work the same, in that they are prefabricated models instead of building one yourself from scratch, but I can't comment nor review their use due to them not being yet implemented at the time of this review.
For an early access title, this shows alot of potential, but we've seen it all before right? A game shows lots of potential, but then the devs lose sight, give in to too many changes, or simply abandon the project. Only time will tell what Osirs: New Dawn becomes, but so far...it's looking great.

Hearts of Iron IV is a tough strategy game to get into, the first time you will start this game up you will be overwhelmed by the amount of options and menus. But if you pull trough the game will pay off 100%. After having played over 200 hours atm I can tell this is the best WWII strategy game that I have ever played. Being a Total war veteran I thought I would steamroll the French and Russians as the German Reich.....how wrong I could be. After being totally beaten the first few times I started the get the hang of all the options, supply, templates, airpower, naval invasions and general production. The game starts being more enjoyable once you get better at it and once you have blitzed all the european nations you truly feel like a Rommel or Zhukov.
Things HOI IV does right:  Combat system, Map graphics, Tech trees, Multiplayer/Co-op, Historical mode and overall feel of the game.
Things HOI IV can do better: More political options(peace offers), the AI can be kinda irrating(pointless naval invasions) and a more balanced warscore system(less points for bombing and more for general combat).

Hearts Of Iron IV, The game where i create Greater Finland and make Adolf Hitler throw Joseph Stalin into gulag. This game is historically accurate, if you enable historic AI focuses of course and it provides challenge and is fun to play. I have written this review based on my hours spent playing this game.
Pros:
-Brilliantly made strategy game that offers different difficulties to players.
-Installing mods can be done through steam workshop
-excellent equipment and factory/naval dockyard system
logistics, trading and gaining resources is implemented much better, unlike in Hearts Of Iron III
-The visuals, sound and music are overall great, again much better than in HOI 3
Now the things that Paradox should work on aka cons:
-AI, you might ask "what's wrong with the AI", i'll give you an example: you're playing as Japan and you conquer British Raj, suddenly out of nowhere: Germany, Soviet Union and US declare war on you, even though you have warm relations with them and they declare war on you without even justification. tl;dr: AI sometimes tends to do things that it shouldn't be able to do.
-Naval balance: want to win without effort? just spam submarines and naval bombers, everything else is total garbage.
basically if you went to the war with UK, and you have a fleet larger than them with better equipment, you would say "I'll win these chaps easily" well no. I don't know why but it's just that the naval bombers and subs are more efficient than any other naval ships.
-Not supporting CPU multicore: Games in the HOI series tend to only use one core of your cpu, and this can cause lagging, even if you would have the best CPU in the market chances are you might still encounter this problem but there isn't a 100% chance that you're game would start lagging.
Even though the game might have some problems with AI, It still is enjoyable to me. as you are reading this i'm probably trying to kick Stalin out of Europe while playing as Finland. HOI IV is 4/5 in my books.

PROS
- Ezio's journey. I cared about what happened, even if the story wasn't such a revelation to me personally.

- It has tons of fun stuff to do. Very differentiated quests (mostly killing, but fun!).

- Collecting things makes sense, they are relevant to the story.
- Double air assassinations never get old.
CONS
- Towards the end, the story took over and the gameplay was a bit mechanical.
- Too many timed quests (and close shave at that) for my taste. If I wanted to constantly worry about the clock ticking, I would be a track athlete.
- Video- audio was not synchronized in many of the cut scenes.
- Guards can be annoyingly stupid, blind and deaf.
- Ezio has a ladder fetish. No, really, just walk by them and he gets an urge to climb.
- Jumps and reaches have game logic. 2 meters away, if the game needs it? No problem. 40 cm if the developers didn't want it that way? Nope.
This was my first AC game, and now I'm itching to play all of them.

Overview:
Dishonored allows a player to play through the levels however they wish to. Whether that is stealthing their way through an entire level without killing a single person, or going in with sword, crossbow, and gun blazing, there are multiple ways to play and enjoy this game, and multiple endings to go along with each playstyle. Actions have consequences.
Graphics:
While the graphics now are decidely old, the game itself will run on almost any computer. My first playthrough of this game was actually on a notebook with a GT 520m years ago. That, however, did not detract from the fun of each and every level. The DLC extend the game for a lot longer and are worth it if one liked the base game.
Replayability:
First playthrough was guns-blazing. Second playthrough was stealth only, minimizing kills. Oh, and enemies are decently hard to kill without thought on the hardest difficulty. DLC are fun and provide a different perspective on the world.
Dishonored is definitely worth the money, especially on sales!

TITLE OneShot
PUBLISHER Degica
DEVELOPER Little Cat Feet, LLC
GENRE – Adventure/Puzzle/Indie
THE BASICS:
OneShot is a little indie charmer that seeks to break the mold – by messing with your head, not to mention, your computer. Your little on-screen avatar, Niko, is able to talk directly to you, at times, even as the game lets you know that the solutions to certain puzzles can only be found on your actual computer system. Naturally, both she(?) and the game refer to you by name (the one in your Steam profile), even though you never told the game what it was...
Note that the game has this name for a reason. The game auto-saves whenever you turn in for the night, or otherwise close the game; there is no going back. Sometimes, this is even necessary in order to trigger a dream sequence for Niko, who might then ask you if you saw it, too. The game world knows you are there, watching...waiting...learning.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
Niko, a little human/cat/something with huge eyes, has awoken in a strange, new world she's never heard of before. Much of the landscape is cold and dark, having been blasted clean by some past disaster. The husks of deactivated robots lie everywhere, and our little would-be heroine ends up with this world's sun – a huge lightbulb – in her possession, and so, she reluctantly sets out to put it back where it belongs, in hopes of somehow getting home as a result. With your help, of course.
CONTROLS:
“Partial” controller support. Just use a keyboard.
GRAPHICS:
8~16 bit era indie gfx, made for a game creation compo in 2014. Dark and foreboding – you are literally the light in the darkness, here.
SOUND:
Wonderful tracks set the mood, helping you to fall into this unexpectedly engaging game.
OVERALL:
Very clever writing, frequent, wonderfully flagrant abuse of the fourth wall, and an overall sense of paranoia make for a wonderful and engaging experience. The game is about as meta as they come, possibly even moreso than brilliant games such as Undertale.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Basic. Recommended: Don't play in full screen mode; sometimes the game will pop up dialogue boxes via the Windows UI, and you don't wanna miss them.
REVIEW BY: Eric_Kei
STORY: 90
GAMEPLAY: 90
GRAPHICS: 85
SOUND: 80
FUN FACTOR: 80
ATMOSPHERE: 100
Pros:
The paranoia induced by a game that knows your name, messes with files on your computer, and creates more of it own, helps to extend the foreboding atmosphere of the game beyond its window borders, in a very meta fashion.
Creative and clever dialogue
Great tunes that fit the mood
One of those games that you fall in love with very quickly, even against your will
Clever cheevos, for the most part
Cons:
That same paranoia – If you take umbrage at a game accessing your drive without warning, this is not the game for you.
Clues within the game, especially those pointing to solutions placed beyond the fourth wall, are often vague
Some graphics quickly become repetitive
Game doesn't always make it clear when you need to go bed down for the night (in order to force a save/close and, often, trigger a new dream)
When they say you have one shot, one save – they MEAN it!

Just had to get that off my chest.. now the actual game!
They said how they're going back to the roots.. blah, blah, blah.~
It doesn't really feel like DR1 or remind me anything of it, aside from hearing the name "Frank West."

It feels like DR3, but faster. And I do kinda like how it feels to control Frank, I haven't had really an issues so far.
He controls fine, driving is easy as expected, but the hud..
It's nothing like DR1. Where are the dumb cheese blocks? Where is the complicated and somewhat annoying way of selecting items? Exactly, they're dumb and annoying.. but that's how it is in DR1. Why take that away? Let alone the timer!

Now I haven't finished the game 100%, like I'd want to.. but I find it hard to even find the motivation to. It's pretty boring for me, and everything gets old really quickly.. at least for me. I realized far into the story that it wasn't really fun for me, but felt more like a chore.
Pretty much, one it's own.. Dead Rising 4 isn't a terrible game. It's not great either, though. It's just.. decent.
But Dead Rising 4.. trying to be a Dead Rising game.. well, it's a horrible game. It's just not Dead Rising. It doesn't feel like Dead Rising, and I never once got any vibe or feel that it was a Dead Rising game besides key words and names that remind you it's even a Dead Rising game. If you're wondering about the combo weapons and vehicles..? They're just whatever, like the story. They're all pretty fun and interesting for like a few mintues, if even that and then they just die off as another boring item to use.
Now they recently added a huge package for the game.. rightfully named "Frank's Big Package." ... because male genitals.
Now it seemed to improve AI and other things that didn't matter THAT much to me, but it did help the game out.. a bit.
A certain thing they added REALLY boosted the game for me. That certain thing being.. Capcom Heroes mode.

Mavis Beacon, eat your heart out.  The Typing of the Dead: Overkill replaces guns with words and phrases, some of which are completely random.  Be aware that the dictionary is set to UK by default, but you can set it to US.  Otherwise, you'll be typing "honour" and "pyjamas".  Thrown items are deflected with a single letter, and if you're in the middle of a phrase when you see it, hit Backspace to abort the phrase and switch priorities.  However, my typing skills must not be that good for Normal, considering I die at least once on every level.  You can't collect health packs (or any collectibles) either, unless there's a method I'm not aware of, which makes things harder.  Be prepared, there's a twist for the final boss too.
When you're done killing enemies with your words, you can switch over to the original House of the Dead: Overkill, where you can upgrade weapons and collect stuff by shooting at them, but be aware that reloading can open a window for your enemies to attack you.  Completing HotD: O will unlock the Director's Cut mode, which gives longer levels with more enemies that rush at you (also, have fun with the middle of Ballstic Trauma).  The Director's Cut is not available for Typing.  Also worth mentioning that Typing and House both have levels not present in the Wii version.  They both star Varla Guns and Candi Stryper.  Level 2 is Naked Terror (between Papa's Palace of Pain and Ballistic Terror), and Level 5 is The Creeping Flesh (between Carny and The Fetid Waters).
The game does have its issues.  Models do pop in and pop out.  There are sound issues where all the sound effects will stop in order for a character to speak, and during Carny, you can't hear any sounds or voices when beating a Rage mutant with a hammer.  Also, this is a grindhouse/exploitation-style game, so bear in mind this game did get the Guiness World Record for the most uses of the f-word, and there's violence galore (granted, this is a game involving shooting zom-err, mutants), so keep the kids away from this one, lest they start talking like Detective Washington.

No longer does the player have to endlessly micromanage individual divisions on opposite side of the world. Instead you can plot a course for your armies and observe. Also, the new trade system is much easier to manage than in HOI3. Just a few clicks and, assuming you have the factory power, you're good to go. These improvements are just a few of the pros of HOI4.
The main con of the game is the AI. They are utterly incapable of using any form of intelligence; whether it's warmaking, battleplans, diplomacy, or pretty much anything. Even with this negative point, the game is still one of the best of its kind, and I will not stop playing it for a very long time.

Beach Bounce is another adult-themed anime visual novel from Dharker Studio.
In Beach Bounce you play Tomoyo, a young law-school dropout favoured by your sick grandmother, Umi, who owns the Beach Bounce seaside resort. Following your grandmother's wishes, you step in to help run the resort, making friends with the five young women who work there.
Graphics are mostly good, with nice-looking backgrounds and attractive characters. The mature scenes are a bit disappointing, looking much more amateur than the rest of the game.
For a text-based game, the font is also quite hard to read in some scenes, as there's not enough contrast between it and the background layer.
Music is mostly forgettable, but not annoying enough to turn off. Sound effects are minimal. Unfortunately there are no voices; all of the in-game discussions are text only.
Beach Bounce plays like any other anime visual novel. You progress through the story, clicking to advance through each little piece of text, and occasionally make a choice. In Beach Bounce the choices are ultimately all concerned with in which area of the resort you choose to work, and with which of the seven attractive young women you spend your time.
The female characters are mostly stereotypes and include the nerdy girl with glasses, the big-breasted blonde bimbo, and the short-haired grumpy girl. There's also a girl with heterochromia, which makes for an interesting change from the norm.
The story is quite short and straightforward, not offering any plot twists or surprises. The writing won't win any awards, but it's appropriate to the setting, with few errors. In my opinion it's not quite as good as other Dharker Studio games that I've played. Some of the wording in the mature scenes, in particular, made me cringe.
In typical VN fashion, there are multiple endings -- at least one per female character -- and Steam Achievements included for each. The skip text feature is standard for a Dharker game, and as usual it's very well implemented, making replaying the game to see the different endings a breeze. There's also a freely available adult/uncensor patch.
Pros:
+ Attractive female cast who are drawn well
+ Multiple endings with an easy-to-use skip feature
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- The mature scenes seem to be much lower quality than the rest of the game
- A bit too short
Beach Bounce isn't the best VN I've played, or even Dharker Studio's best, but it's a fun distraction for a few hours. Pick it up on special if you're into anime VNs with mature content, just don't expect too much from it.

So, just to get this out of the way, yes I recommend this game. Not at full price perhaps, but I did actually enjoy it.
As far as the story goes, it's adequate.  You get called in by your ailing grandma to help out at her beach resort full of (surprise!) hot 20-something-year-olds.  The story is a little bland, but serviceable.  It's very basic, but that's okay.  This isn't some genre-defining game.  It's eye candy with a little plot.
The girls essentially throw themselves at you like convicts in a women's prison at first sight.  Again, it didn't bother me, as it kept the pace of the story quick.
Now, the eye candy itself.  I guess some people just really don't like the art.  I myself find the girls "cute".  Yes, they're all very stereotypical and relatively shallow, but that didn't really bug me. There are numerous options of girls to pursue, and many of them are at least mildly rewarding. A couple of the girls though
felt like total afterthoughts and their routes are really only good for getting the achievements.  That said, the primary girls were different and interesting enough that I actually read all their text per route and didn't just click click click to finish it.
Oh, and I did in fact get the 18+ patch and a few of the added H scenes seemed to fit well, some others - not so much.  It was sporadic at best and not exactly vital IMO.
The game itself is realtively short.  I completed it at 100% in about 4 hours.  I did use a guide after I finished a couple endings just to make sure I got the rest effeciently. But right at the start, I picked a girl (Aiko <3) and went straight for her.  Most of the choices seemed like common sense, and obviously playing the gentleman gets you the "happier" endings for the long haul.
So, as I stated at the top: yes, I recommend Beach Bounce. Not at $13, but I got it in a Dharker Studios bundle from Indiegala and it was well worth the less-than-a-dollar-per-game I paid. If you're not too hung up on innovative stories and just enjoy it for what it is - a time waster with b00bs - it may be right up your alley. For less than half price anyways.
