The Cave is an ambitious adventure game that has quite a lot going for it: Beautiful cartoonish art design. A twisted yet charming sense of humor. Quality voice work. Fun puzzles and scenarios that are interesting and just the right difficulty. Several playable characters, each one with their own unique themed level. And despite being limited to 30 FPS, the game still feels quite smooth (much less of a problem than I anticipated).
Unfortunately, it's not without flaws. The controls are very floaty which makes platforming imprecise. The story-telling has its moments but feels a bit shallow at times. Worst of all, because you're tasked with controlling three characters at once, you'll find yourself constantly switching between them and moving them one by one. This gets repetitive very quickly and becomes more of a hassle than anything. Why there was no option to control all three at once is beyond me, but it could've gone a long way towards eliminating the annoying backtracking that hampers the game's pacing.
While the game's significant backtracking/pacing issues keep it from being truly great, The Cave still excels at being a fun and humorous adventure game. One that warrants multiple playthroughs if you hope to experience everything it has to offer.

I am quite the fan of Double Fines work, and I’m glad to say this game wasn't a let-down for me. I've heard it didn't get the best reviews, but in all honesty, i think they couldn't be more wrong.
You start your adventure choosing your selection of characters, there is about 7 completely different characters, with different personalities, story lines and lives. All looking to venture through the cave to find something they desire.
You pick three at a time, so it takes about 3 play throughs to see each story. I found the way you navigate the cave quite clever, your characters can only get into the section that’s for one of the three, so you aren’t dragging yourself through stories for people that aren’t even there.
Then you have the same in-between puzzles that are the same on each play through. so you do a general puzzle, a characters story, general, story and go on like that until you have reached the end. Where even at the end you have a choice, to change the path of your characters. A sort of, "choose your ending", kind of thing. I didn't notice it at first. So completing it 3 times to see all the characters, then realising you could change the end, i completed it 3 more times. Even though the second 3 times were repetitive, i still enjoyed it a whole lot and didn't get bored.
The game has a wonderful kind of humour i love seeing in Double Fines games. "The Cave" as you know from the trailer, talks. He’s quite quirky and makes the journey that little more engaging. You can also collect fun little paintings along the way that opens up a little more about the past of your characters; you learn why they are there and what it is they are searching for.
The puzzles aren’t too difficult, and are somewhat easy to figure out, which personally, i liked. I hate getting stuck on a game, it “throws off my grove”. I only got stuck once, but after a break and a think, i had it. It flowed well for me and i even went as far as to collect all the achievements for the game, which one in particular proves this game has replay ability for me.

All in all, I loved this game. And I think it’s worth a try, despite what some reviews have said about it. It has great gameplay, nice music/ambient sounds, interesting characters and story lines, fun puzzles and a quirky sense of humour.
Double Fine, you've done it again.
TL;DR : Fun, several playthroughs worth of replayability, great sense of humour, fun/quite simple puzzles and is worth every penny.

In Pro Game Manager, you’re given the option to play through one of two careers: Gamer and Manager. You are locked into whatever you choose and can’t experience another path unless you start a whole new game.
Choosing either does nothing to change the storyline, as there isn't one, or the core gameplay mechanics, but it does affect the tasks you can undertake in game.
From there, you can choose from one of two games: MOBA and FPS. The former is called ‘Foba’ for whatever reason, though I’m pretty sure the genre isn’t copyrighted. Nomenclature aside, your game type won’t significantly change gameplay: in fact, none decisions you seem to really affect anything, I’ve found.
Upon starting as game, you are thrown into a room which, though nicely illustrated with simple but colorful components offer you no explanation as to how to proceed. Right clicking brings up a menu with possible actions, but it’s a matter of trial and effort to figure out just how each will affect you or, if you’re a manager, your team.
As a gamer, you have the option to…
Managing a team is slightly more involved in terms of matches due to the fact that you can click between three play styles - defensive, balanced, and offensive - but much like everything else, there’s not enough feedback to be able to tell how much this is affecting your chances of winning. I won't list the options available simply because they don't seem to correlate.
That aside, there’s not much else to do in Pro Gamer Manager. Every action boils down to watching a timer tick down and that swiftly becomes tedious.
The art style is simple and clean and works well. It would have been nice if there had been more than static images.
The music consists of one looping track that swiftly becomes maddening when coupled with watching the timer circle fill.
.Pro & Cons.
.Bottom line.
Pro Gamer Manager is a good idea that was poorly executed. It would take one small change to change this negative recommendation: if stats and decisions seemed to make a difference or even if battle outcomes were decided by a dice roll or rock-paper-scissors, this would feel more like a simulation game and less like a waiting game.

Overview:
Dishonored allows a player to play through the levels however they wish to. Whether that is stealthing their way through an entire level without killing a single person, or going in with sword, crossbow, and gun blazing, there are multiple ways to play and enjoy this game, and multiple endings to go along with each playstyle. Actions have consequences.
Graphics:
While the graphics now are decidely old, the game itself will run on almost any computer. My first playthrough of this game was actually on a notebook with a GT 520m years ago. That, however, did not detract from the fun of each and every level. The DLC extend the game for a lot longer and are worth it if one liked the base game.
Replayability:
First playthrough was guns-blazing. Second playthrough was stealth only, minimizing kills. Oh, and enemies are decently hard to kill without thought on the hardest difficulty. DLC are fun and provide a different perspective on the world.
Dishonored is definitely worth the money, especially on sales!

(With ASCII graphics, because when I was a kid we used to walk both directions in the snow, uphill, to play our PC roguelikes).
As an adult (technically, I guess) I have happily bought this game, ADOM, and Caves of QUD - all true to the original spirit of roguelike RPGs, in my opinion.
Specifically for TOME:
Pros:
* Graphically Accessible - for modern day and age...all the old-school roguelike spirit with reasonably pretty sprites.
* Replay Value - perfectly encapsulates the 'one more turn' feeling that a certain class of gamer like myself craves.
* Non-evil Developers - gamers vote with our wallets. Shut up and take my money, you beautiful developers!! :)
Cons:
* Steep Learning Curve - again, I love these but it might be an individual taste thing. I feel like the game gives you enough info to get you going, but 90% of the game's complexities are underwater, waiting to be explored. If you like deep, meaningful games with tons of choices, a bunch of mechanics to explore, exploit, learn, then go for it!
* I'm trying here. I really am. I just can't come up with anything significant that is worth mentioning. It's a niche game, in a niche genre...and so worth playing whether you're a fan of the genre or not.
Notes:
* Many levels are procedural, but quests are static - this is 100% like ADOM used to be, but it does inherently limit replay value, to some lesser degree, when compared with other models (I thought FTL handled this nicely...retaining the story arc but leaving the order of operations highly variable).

Non-combat Arcade Side-scroller
Easy-Medium

You play one of a small fleet of flying creatures: a flying unicorn, a parrot, a bat and a bee.
Your objective is to get through as many "gates" as possible on the procedurally generated map.
A gate is any obstacles on the map.
At first those are totem poles that tries to crush you from top and bottom, but soon arrows are introduced. Other obstacles are meteor showers, blade saws and a lot other obstacles.
Any obstacle will kill you in once touch.
The further you get, the more obstacles gets introduced.
On your way, you are able to collect gold coins. Those gold coins act as a way to continue, should you be killed by any obstacle. At the first death you can continue for 50 coins and the more continues you use the more expensive each continue becomes. Fortunately the price of the continues reset back to 50 once you decide to no longer use any continue.
Luckily for you, you are able to dash left and right to time the collection of gold coins and getting through the gates.
You can also do a power move by pressing left dash and right dash, which will propel you further to the right than a regular dash.
You compete against yourself and the leader boards to see who can get pasts the most gates.
0/10
The game has no narrative.
I would have personally liked to know why those totem poles and arrows are trying to kill us, why we are collecting coins and why we are dashing through those "gates".

Dash Fleet is a casual 2D game that has been ported onto Steam, after spending  nearly one year on Android terminals. Its developer specializes in this hybrid genre of retro-style casuals, has sufficient experience on the PC platform and from what I’ve seen of its previous releases, they seem quite decent and definitely not the low-effort excuses for games that have kept popping up on Steam, in the past couple of years.
No exact storyline per se. There is no formal introduction either, instead once you start the game, you are presented with the static page about the in-game controls. You maneuver flying creatures through obstacle courses. Would you need a plotline to this? My thoughts exactly.
The visuals (courtesy of Unity Engine) are a throwback to far simpler times. 2D, large pixels, colorful backgrounds and assets. I like the incorporation of that arcade cabinet/machine around the edges of the screen. It strengthens the retro feel to Dash Fleet and controlling the characters, actually moves the border “joystick” as well. A nice touch from the devs which clearly cater to a certain group of gamers that are increasingly nostalgic about their hobby’s  humble beginnings. Before marketing ploys such as DLC or expensive fads like Virtual Reality headsets represented the present and uncertain future of the gaming industry.

Repetition is the keyword here. The sounds are few and far in-between. Given the genre though, I wasn’t expecting an award-winning soundtrack. Perhaps the diversity of several tunes, but you can’t have them all for its price tag.

It seems easy enough. Instead of the “patented” Up/Down of Flappy Bird and its clones, you can dash further to the right or left and behind. The endless runner-like backgrounds and deadly traps, ensure that constant need to redress the flight pattern of your creature of choice. We’re talking of parrots, bats, bees and unicorns for now, since the developer promises more. They all fly at the same speed and feature the same maneuverability. Only the sounds they make and the effects trail they leave behind (such as rainbow, for the unicorn), really set them apart from each other.
Besides the more common crushing traps in the form of giant totems, some levels feature ballistas shooting large arrows, swinging hammers or the occasional fireballs. All these obstacles need to be avoided since they spell “Game Over” as soon as they touch you. Your ultimate goal in Dash Fleet, is to attain the highest score you can, by intersecting mid-flight with floating coins. This action does get repetitive eventually and visual diversity will only get you so far. Just play in short sessions and you should be able to reach the game’s Achievements sooner rather than later.
I wouldn’t have agreed to review this title if I would have considered it another useless cash grab on Steam. It’s very true that the Android version of Dash Fleet is free of charge, yet I can’t bring myself to drain my smartphone battery on gaming since I’m always within reach of my desktop or laptop. What you get for those 2 dollars/euros, is fully worth even the initial asking price. Steam Cards and Achievements, not to mention another title to your total games count. Dash Fleet is most certainly gonna get bundled at some point or get discounted even more during a Steam Sale. If you like 2D casuals, you have no reason not to purchase and play it.

Occasionally I got stuck and had to read a walk-through guide to figure out how to continue. At times it was annoying having to control three characters because I had to move them all separately which was pretty boring.

Overall, 7 out of 10.

Possibly one of the worst games available on Steam, this turd is laughably bad, even when you strip away the notion that it "could have been good."
When I first got this game, I thought it was conceptually awesome. I'm a big fan of eSports just as a sport and following the LCS in LoL makes me substantially happier than playing the game. So I was willing to put up with a completely unfinished alpha build of a game.
This game is full of placeholders. Almost every graphic, nearly every menu, every instance and event is clearly a placeholder. There is only one animation on the MOBA side of things, a spinning circle that is meaningless. Everything else is just stills and moving from one still to another. That's fine, Game Dev Tycoon is fairly light on animation, though at least in that game the screen does have movement. Everything in this game may as well just be text based because the images lend nothing to the game.
I would have given a pass on the placeholders when I first got the game because there were updates almost weekly, and you got a sense that somebody was clearly developing it still. There were comical gaps, sections that were just plain empty, enormous bugs, and spelling errors everywhere ("Silly season is over" meant to be "Offseason is over" or the spelling of "Okey"). I assumed this thing was being thrown together by a couple guys in Sweden, and so I'll give them benefit of the doubt, they'll get this eventually I'm sure...
Well here we are. The product on the MOBA side has released zero updates in over 6 months, and the FPS side, which I never played, is apparently a train wreck that I'm terrified to go near. I know a lot of people are complaining that the newest "update," which was supposed to be the patch to finish the game months ago and was so bad it needed to be immediately rolled back, has been announced as a DLC which will eventually cost money. That is certainly a horrendous and despicable decision, but I don't think reviews should even be upset at that; they should be busy losing their minds that the game is out of Early Access and still is nowhere near even a beta-level of release.
Here are some bugs, just on the MOBA side, just off the top of my head:
You have a 50/50 chance of a spelling error in any given message.
Using the "Update free agent" staff member in MOBA Owner mode will cause the menu to no longer be available and erase your B team, not that you have any control over that team or input, and you must quit and reload to fix this.
If you rank up in Career mode and are in the top 100 or so, you will over rank and get a ranking like -74.
You will get notifications in your inbox but the email will be blank.
No matter what league you're in, you won't be able to view the roster of at least one of the teams. It will always show another teams' roster.
Players in owner mode can still skill up after hitting 99 and will show having skill points to spend, even though they can't be spent.
If multiple players choose not to re-sign with your team on the same day, only one of them will show up in free agency.
Let's also remember this: the game is stateless. That's right, a sports simulation game that is stateless, figure that out. There are no divisions above and below you until you move into that division. If you make it to the pro division in MOBA owner mode, you will always see the same teams. If you get relegated then return to the league, you will see those same teams again and players. This is especially fun if you picked up one of the players from one of those teams as now two of them will exist.
If you drop a player into free agency, their age, nationality, rank, face avatar, name, and even role can/will change. Players also never age because the game has no general state. How long is a season? I don't know. All you can do is go to the next day and then if you do you can play a new match. After you play every team twice, the season is considered over, top 2 teams get promoted, and then it starts over again. There's no timeline, no real offseason (sometimes it lasts 2 days, sometimes 3, sometimes 4), and no schedule.
For fun, here's a list of things you cannot do in, I will remind everyone, a game that is supposed to be a sports simulator:
Trade players with other teams.
Negotiate contract salaries with free agents.
Negotiate contract term length with free agents.
Negotiate contract term or salary when re-signing a player.
Have more than the exact number of starting players (5).
See the different leagues you can/will move between while not in them.
Skip simulation of games or simulate an entire season (you must "play" every game).
You only get one-shot with a free agent; if you accept their offer they may still just sign with another team with no chance for you to make a counter offer.
Look at a calendar with all upcoming matches.
Participate in play-offs or a championship.
That's embarassing. There are plenty more I would put on the list but technically can't. They're listed as being in the game but don't actually do anything. For example, you can set up what the team does in their practice time by just clicking one of three options. It doesn't mean they'll improve in those skills because those aren't skills they can even improve in. You can also select a strategy for your "meta" but you can't see them execute the strategy, you don't know your opponent's strategy or style, you have no information on them, and it also has no impact. You can even decide what style each individual player should take up but again, it will not impact the results in any way.
When matches are being played, here's what will happen. The game will give each team an overall score based on the five players skill level (1-99). And before you ask, yes every player can just get to 99, nobody caps out, nobody specializes, they just generically reach 99. It will then "draft" a team comp, which is you watching with no input on what is picked, not that you would know what any champion does or is because there are no descriptions for them. Pause review: there are no descriptions of anything in the game, nor any tutorials. Zero.
After the draft it will tell you some meaingless sentence at the bottom like "GlassCannon Comp" or "HighMobility Comp." Again, these aren't described, you don't see anything play out, they don't mean anything. Your team won't have mastery over certain comps, so it may as well just say nothing. Then you enter a new screen with just the two teams on either side. You have three options: "Defensive, Balanced, Offensive" and guess what, none of them do anything. They aren't related to your comp, or your players' strengths, they don't change anything. All that matters were those numbers at the start. If you get an all 99 team, which you inevitably always will, you will always win every league game, with the odd rare exception to I guess make it look like a random number generator. But that's it.
Except the goddamn international trounaments. I don't know what the ♥♥♥♥ happened with these because they're the part that makes me actually vehemetly angry. The rest of the game I shrug and say "sure it's a piece of crap that doesn't do anything but at least it's numbers sort of make sense, even if arbitrary and meaningless and random. Team of 99s should always win, more or less."
Ha
I welcome you to hell then. Try an international tournament. Put in your team of all 99s. Guess what? It doesn't mean jack crap. I swear to god they are an intentional joke meant to test your patience. It's like the developers knew they were making a♥♥♥♥♥♥game that doesn't do anything, but they also knew people would play it, so they wanted to test how far they could push us idiots who go early access on nothing but a concept by creating this wasteland of a game mode. It's completely random and meaningless even if you win.
So no, I would never recommend this. It's not a completed game and they're not trying to change that.

Free to play was the best change Turtle Rock could have made for this game. I'd always loved Evolve, but the price was never worth it on top of the ridiculous DLC. None of that matters anymore.
Right now, the game is being revamped and is in beta. The grind is a little rough, but there are currently no microtransactions present in the game. The only people who have any sort of advantage are founders, who were given a pile of the ingame currency and the characters and skins they had from the previous version of Evolve.
Gameplay is solid. Both monster and hunters are on fairly even playing field when matched against players of similar skill. However, I will say most pub games are favored toward the monster. This is due to the nature of the Hunter side, which has to communicate and work well as a group of four, as opposed to the monster who only has to rely on themselves. For the game to be balanced at the competative level though, this has to be how it works. If you want to play Hunter, remember to always communicate with your team mates, because you cannot win the game on your own.
There are some bugs that need to be fixed (Behemoth is unplayable), some numbers that need to be tweaked, And the grind could be made less rough, but the game is in a very good spot right now. The devs have also been transparent on their plans and very responsive to player concerns. I highly recommend the game.

: All opinions are solely my own. I do not side, I do not show bias. My purpose is to give a fair and objective review to anyone who is considering getting the game.
Evolve Stage 2 Review:
Since the move to F2P, Evolve has become massively popular again. Asymmetric 4v1 style, tons of variations of both hunters and monsters, massive maps and beautiful design makes this probably one of the best F2P-class games there is out there right now.
I give it a 10 because it is literally possess the best graphics out of all the F2P games out there. Even when it was B2P, the graphics alone were amazing (though a low-mid end PC might have to turn down the settings). Textures, ability SFX,
character models are brilliantly and precisely designed. Each map is pleasing to the eye and boasts all sorts of environments, from damp, dark caves to gushing waterfalls. The monsters and their abilities are likely the uncontested champions in terms of design, detail and effects. If you are someone who likes running people over as a big bad monstrosity while looking pretty, Evolve's monsters are exactly what you're looking for.
This game is a lot of fun to play. In a market filled with arena shooters and MOBAs, its not every day that you see an asymm man versus beast style game. The novelty is what makes this game so refreshing and the gameplay distinct. As a 4v1 game, Evolve is more fun if you have a small group of friends to play with, as with all other multiplayer games, playing with pubs can get frustrating at times.
However, Evolve has a really high skill floor, which is why I reserve an 8 out of 10. I say this because the game is actually quite unforgiving towards new hunter players. The 4v1 aspect makes the monster player undeniably more powerful than the individual hunter and a high degree of understanding of the mechanics, as well as team communication is needed, neither of which is a resource that new players will have amply. The game also lacks a proper tutorial which makes learning the game even harder, but TRS is working on the tutorials as we speak so its a matter of time before they come.
With the wide selection of both characters (hunters and monsters) and the players behind them, each match feels solidly different from the previous. Several maps have been temporarily taken down to be reworked, and we will see them likely added back in the near future. With more content incoming, it is bound to get more interesting.
There are still several annoying bugs present such as party breaking. But keep in mind the game has moved back to a Beta phase. Bugs are always there but as the TRS team has shown, they get down working on them really quickly. That said, the game still lacks a punishment system for leavers. I will refrain from commenting on skill-based matchmaking as I have not tried ranked play. In quickplay, I believe players are matched based on level, which means there still can be a wide discrepancy in skill, but overall, nothing too frustrating. Due to the revived playerbase and influx of new f2p players, search times are very short and a match gets going pretty quickly, which is a big plus for multiplayer games.
If anyone is interested in competitive ranked play, there is somewhat of a ranked system divided into the bronze, silver and gold divisions. As I have not tried ranked, I can't comment too much on this.
The fact that Evolve shifted to F2P makes it an absolute recommend. If you want to play a great game without any cost barriers, Evolve Stage 2 is a game not to be missed.

On paper this game should be right up my alley. My Steam profile details hundreds of hours spent on rogue-like games which doesn’t count the hours I spent before Steam was even invented.
For a few hours, I was in the zone with an archer type build called ‘Robin’ that was most enjoyable. He explored the world, dealing mass destruction to enemy types that got too close. Fantastic loot was found everywhere and Robin’s character sheet was the dictionary definition of potential.
The character building is most enjoyable for people that like overwhelming stats to comprehend and nurture. Different races and classes are available on character build and then others unlocked as you progress. I liked spending more than a few moments staring at the screen comparing the stats of loot trying to decide whether to keep them or not. Your character learns skills as they level up, some which must be activated whilst others are ‘passive’, remaining on all the time.
I liked that my character had a Ray Bradbury, Illustrated Man feel by having the ability to transfer tattoos on my body, tattoos that can be activated in combat for buffs, instant healing, regeneration and even teleport abilities!
Later on in the game I came across a town with a bunch of vendors that had me drooling and even some sort of strange arena for budding heroes.
Before all that fun though, note TOME is a top down, old-school, simple graphics, bare sound, complex game. A very helpful tutorial helps you on your way and then you are thrown into the deep end. The game can be mostly controlled by mouse and it contains the worst in game map I have ever seen since Wasteland 2.
There were some “One More Go” moments that any gamer wishes for like the Holy Grail. But in the end, the game ground me down. Too many elements of the game unexplained. Too many locations described in-game as suitable for low level characters that ended up being devastating. Too many instant deaths where my character was wiped.
Instant Deaths is the bane of computer gaming and players die not due to their own lack of planning or skill. But to some error of the programmer.
If you can get around this with superior patience and knowledge, you will be able to find a lot to enjoy in this game. For me it just misses some basic elements that would please me immensely.
In the end though, the stark reality of some design choices makes me reluctant to recommend this game where on paper I should really love it to bits.

It's roguelike, it's fun, and it's hackable.
ToME is a modern-ish, roguelike, turn-based rpg with incredible modding support. It features procedurally generated content laid on top of decent premade lore. Decent, nothing too amazing, but not too shabby either. In fact, I enjoy following some of the dungeon lore, and hasn't come to find lore notes that are particularly annoying or inconsistently written. Gameplay is fun, but let's talk about it in a series of pros and cons:
Pros
- Relatively balanced race / classes with different play styles
- Enemies don't respawn, meaning you *probably* don't need to grind
- Decent amount of side quest and extra dungeon
- Mode with extra lives for those who suck at roguelike, like me
- Hackable, with a crap ton of addons already out there
Cons
- It's pretty barebones, and might be hard to get into. You may need to get past tier-1 dungeons several times and play with different classes to fully grasp what you're really doing in this game.
- Steep difficulty increase with little to no warning in some areas
It's well-made, and it's worth the price. When in doubt, go get the free version, which is the full game minus several cosmetic feature and the convenience of Steam Workshop support.

I hate my friend for getting me into these, but i do understand now. These games actually do have a pretty decent story line, alot of good, involving dialogue, life choices, etc. Say what you want about the devs, but in Beach Bounce, you can't just go around all hunky-dory, f***ing every girl you think is hot and manage to end the game with a happy ending. You just can't.

You play the role of Tomoyo, a young man who receives an invitation to be of assistance at his grandmother business, a resort named Beach Bounce.
Poor granny is dying, and you as a college dropout can't make a fool out of yourself, so you accept and hope for the best! The resort is full of young women, with smiles as big as their chests, but it's not all fun and games!
Like all Dating Sim, your goal is to date one special girl that will make you happy for the rest of your life. This works very well to any substitute of life expectations though!
You get to meet all the girls, and you can be nice to them, or cold. Like gravity, actions will have their weight on you eventually, that's why this game has a huge replay value. It's around one hour and half each run, and if you add the uncensored patch, its a few more runs (just out of curiosity).
The story line is really good, I don't want to spoil it, but it's really involving around you, your past with the resort and the future that is up to the player.
Each girl has a different personality, but I wish they had more designs for the backgrounds... Don't get me wrong, this gives me a huge "90's JAP" vibe, but having the same images during the day and night feels cheap.
The girls could have more poses too, or at least more facial expressions.
Overall its a nice game, with a really cool story that is worth checking out!

As an example, a friend and I are playing and form our own fascist faction - the United Imperial Nations - he is the United States and I am an angry Argentina. By July of 1940 he's taken Canada and Mexico and is now the Free American Empire, and I have taken all of the South American continent for the glory of the Argentine League. We begin consolidating our power base as a unified American continent - a terrifying military machine, to be sure.
Germany and the traditional AI join the Axis. Norway, Sweden and a few smaller island nations are in the UIN (our faction) and the Allies, the usual lot sans the United States, are basically at war with every other faction in the game at once, even the communist COMINTERN nations.
Fast forward to Sep. 1949. The Free American Empire covers from Canada to the Panama canal, as well as 90% of the African territories and the entirety of the United Kingdom. The Argentine League had conquered New Zealand, Australia, and all of the islands supplying any naval routes in the Pacific ocean. It was, of course, an intense and hard fought war. Covering many fronts and foreign lands, it was a valiant fight that saw more than 500,000 brave Argentine men and women die for their homelands. After the fall of the last bastion of Allied power, the British Raj in India in January 1950, the Allies unconditionally surrender to the multiple factions that have laid waste to their lands. REVIEW IS INCREDIBLY OUT OF DATE AND WILL BE UPDATED WITH THE NEXT EXPANSION
Things to know before you get angry: As I said, this is for the "CURRENT STATE OF THE GAME". As things are fixed, added, etc. I will adjust this review. Should Paradox actually fix a majority of these problems I'll be more than happy to change this to a positive review.
I want this game to succeed, but I'm not going to give Paradox the leeway I would have given them 10 years ago because they're no longer a 'small studio' and they're not trying to do something 'they've never done before' anymore. They are a successful and large studio that produces their own products as well as publishes other developer's titles.
With that said, here's the list both critical and harsh on the game and the developer. I'm not kind but it's also not my job to be their best friend.
: Useless. I'm not even kidding, they're still broken even in Oak.
: Not needed, you will only need one basic navy to invade the United States from Germany.
: Obsessed with mini-naval invasions that accomplish nothing but annoying the player. In addition to that, the "snake invasion" still happens where the AI goes on a roadtrip because the AI wasn't fixed at all. The video below is an accurate depiction of what the AI is like in Russia and Africa.
In addition to that, the AI still manages armies poorly (divisions are a mess), factories poorly (they cram as much as they can into a single line, resources be damned) and will do the weirdest things like Japan sending troops to Africa instead expanding their own areas in Indochina. Ask any person who has played this game, let the game run and then switched to one of the AI countries whether they were impressed with the AI's managerial skills. I can guarantee 9 out of 10 of them will say they weren't impressed and/or facepalmed.
*PATCH ADDITION: Oak 1.4, AI still building ridiculous divisions that can be plowed over by the 7 infantry 2 artillery build. Astro-Hungary can topple the Reich by simply sitting on a fort until Germany's supplies are gone and then rush to Germany.
: Absolutely no control over them so deciding which waters to patrol to protect them is nullified. Don't worry though, the AI is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
: If you loved the resources in HOI3 making the game strategic this game will make you rage. I hate the term "dumbed down" but there is no better explanation for what has happened with it since oil is just a manufacturing resource and has nothing to do with sustaining your army, navy or air force. You could literally have 100+ Yamato-class Battleships floating around the world on active combat missions and it will not harm your overall economy one bit. I'm all for 'gameplay over realism' but this is a war simulator and Hitler sacrificed an entire army to rush Russia's southern oil fields for a reason and it wasn't because he needed oil to increase tank production but to keep the tanks functioning.
: Don't build anything but heavy tank TDs. Win the game.
: The only useful aircraft at the moment are fighter aircraft. I was able to defeat the whole world without having to build anything but fighters and a few token transport planes for paratroopers. All the other aircraft are simply for roleplay purposes. Still the same with Oak.
: Underwhelming. The infrastrucutre damage they do hardly affects the enemy. We're not asking for the nukes to wipe out entire armies here, but at least damage the enemy's manpower and national unity a bit more than it does.
: Possibly the worst part of this title. Takes away player agency and diplomacy to force nations into war. Rather than the AI thinking for itself it relies on national focuses to drive it to a conclusion. The only way to get an ahistorical approach is to do super gamey ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to force the game into a direction.
An example of why this is a problem: Historically Germany declared war on the Soviet Union
the defeat of France but that doesn't always work like that in a video game since variables can change things or the player changes things. Say, for whatever reason, Germany is stuck at a standstill against the French and British. If the national focus for a war with the Soviet Union is up next on the chopping block Germany
take it and
go to war with the Soviet Union when it's done regardless of their ability to fight such a war. This is the same whether you're in historical settings or not, the National Focus is the same regardless and it not being set to historical just randomizes the AI's choices, not their thinking and execution. I hope this explanation drives home why EUIV style diplomacy is FAR preferable to the current state of the game. The AI needs to think and not just follow an order of pre-set casus belli event flags as it does right now.
: See above. If you want a diplomatic game get EUIV, Victoria or even Civ. Peace Conferences at the end of wars are not optimal. Due to my character limit I suggest other reviews for a more in depth analysis of it and trust me, there are many and one of which is the AI declaring wars they cannot win.
: Constant vacations, poor community support, slow patches, broken patches when finally released, the only working patches tend to be done by the community, DLC of paid features that were present on launch in previous titles, abrasive staff that is combative with community criticism (visit their forums) and the list goes on. Paradox from the days of CK2 and EUIV seem to be gone and replaced by spiteful 'LALALALALALALALA' moderators that don't pass along complaints but instead try to make excuses. It has even hit the point where they are now telling us to be thankful that they were ever so generous as to include 3D sprites claiming they are "time consuming and expensive" when the mod community produces them for free all the time without extra cost or hassle.
: It's better than your standard Paradox game.
: As of Patch "Torch" 1.3.3 the performance has been improved a lot. I was able to play into 1944 without the game turning into a slideshow for the first time since launch.
: They've done a lot of work with the sound effects. They get repetitive, but this is a strategy game. Can't judge too harshly on something most of us turn down the volume on anyways.
: Mods disable achievements, which is annoying as ****, but they make the game better. Honestly, I sometimes wish these modders would be hired by Paradox because they do a far superior job to their current staff. They make better 3D models, better music, better tech trees, more imaginative gameplay mechanaics and so much more. Paradox used to be some of the best developers out there but lately their games are only as good as the mod community can make them... holy ****, sounds like Bethesda.
: Save your money right now. Even into the first expansion this game is worse than some early access titles I've played and far more expensive than they are. I also don't recommend buying this game on my praise to the skies of the modding community, this game is incredibly lacking and I don't think many of the big modders will be around when this game is finally finished. If this game improves I'll remove this, but as it stands now I highly recommend waiting and seeing how it turns out in 1-3 years and by then Victoria 3 will be out which, hopefully, Paradox will outsource to another studio.

If you are looking for a solid free-to-play MMORPG, then you need look no further, because RIFT is an amazing game. While some might argue that the combat is more old-school or maybe slower paced than other MMOs (see Neverwinter or DC Universe Online) its method of combat is tried and true (see WoW). And if you can get a group of friends or guildmates together for its many raids, dungeons, random events, and quests it gets even better, however soloing is in many instances a viable option as well.
In regards to the game being free-to-play I did not find any pay walls that hindered my ability to continue making progress in-game. Granted you can buy better equipment with real money, but the only time I feel like this would be very necessary is if you were going to do PvP (which the game offers as well). After 20 hours of playing time I did invest 5 dollars towards getting a mount for my character, and was able to get many other things beneficial to my playtime in that investment (equipment, inventory slots, etc.) in regards to F2P probably the most efficient 5 bucks I've ever spent.
Overall I have found the game to be incredibly enjoyable, and if you are looking for a decent MMORPG to get into, I suggest that at the very least you give this one a shot.

The best WoW-style MMO out there.
WoW fans looking for something familiar yet refreshing needn't look any further than RIFT.
The Instances are challenging, ranging from 1/2-man Chronicles, 5-man Dungeons, and up to 20-man raids, which can get butt-clenchingly difficult for the hardcore crowd at endgame. PvP is great fun, although it could do with more maps and modes to spice things up. Open-world questing is fairly standard, but dynamic zone events like Invasions and the titular Rifts keep you on your toes. For those who want it, there's Crafting and Dimensions (player housing) as well as a well-structured cash shop, with some purchases for freeloaders that want to get serious being well-worth the money.
The 'Soul Tree' character builder is the big selling point here. You choose one of 4 Classes (Warrior, Cleric, Rogue or Mage). Inside that Class, you can combine any 3 of the 9 (soon to be 10) availible Souls to create a completely new play style. Mix up the Beastmaster Soul with the Paladin Soul to tank with a pet! Dual spec a Mage to have Elementalist and Necromancer Souls to wield all the elements as well as the power of death! The possibilities are endless. With the forthcoming update, every Class will be able to fulfil any Role in the game (the Roles being tank, dps, healer and support). A Warrior healer? Why not. A Mage tank? Go ahead.
Even players new to the genre needn't fear - there are now many audio/visual tutorials added to the starting zones that should be really helpful for easing you into the world of Telara. It could do with more PvP love and some more fantasy elements to heighten the immersion, but Rift is definitely worth your money. Oh, wait - it's free! :)

TL;DR: A beautifully animated, themed and orchestrated "game over" screen simulator with a progress bar.
It's just ludicriously difficult for no better reason than it's simply designed to be ludicrously difficult. I didn't find it to be nearly as fun as it looks and sounds. It's not BAD, I just didn't like it, can't get into it, and don't care enough to try. I feel bad, because all of the talent and effort put into the animation and music seems... wasted.
Some areas are fun; the run-and-gun ones are pretty fun! Some of the "simpler" bosses are fun!
The overall experience is like playing Dark Souls 1 with NO idea what you're doing or where to go: mostly frustrating.
Most of the "levels" are 100% condensed, compressed and concentrated frustration. They are totally lacking that "just one more try" panache we've all come to expect from difficult games. Instead of wanting to work to defeat a boss, I found myself saying "F*** this; I'm gonna go play a better game, like Hyperlight Drifter or Dead Cells."
My #1 gripe: There's NO consistency between battle difficulties. One battle can be beaten without a scratch, where the next battle kills you a hundred (literally) times, and then you just "get lucky" and blow through it without trying, too.
For me, I like a game to have a bit of a "if you play long enough, you CAN (most likely or randomly) become overpowered" mechanic, of some sort.
Examples:
Think about a game with a random/large item system. It drives the game. (Diablo, Castlevania: SoTN, etc...)
Think about a game with bosses that have a certain method to defeat them, consistent with the difficulty curve. It drives the game. (Shadow of the Colossus, Hyperlight Drifter, Dead Cells)
Think about a game with an upgradable protagonist. It drives the game. (most all RPGs)
Think about a game with a rich story. It drives the game. (whatever story-rich game does it for you)
This game has none of that. A one-trick-pony trained to look sweet and break your knees.
If you LIKE getting your a$$ handed to you repeatedly, for solely THAT exact reason, then pick this game up.

Tales of Maj'Eyal (ToME) is an Open Source rogue-like with two alternate campaign storylines and lots of classes and races to choose from. You start the game with a very limited selection of races and classes, and then must unlock the others as you play.
That prelude said, the game is relatively linear in that you pick a race and class and start at Level 1. You move through tiered dungeons that never change. The content within them is relatively random except for the dungeon bosses, however the dungeons themselves and the order in which you move through them tends to always stay the same no matter how many times you have been through them or which character you play. The only thing that really does change is the race/class and the points you spend in them as you level up. This is constrained by the fact that certain class/race builds tend to always be more successful than others. In addition, one race in particular - Shalore - is very overpowered making some of the classes you play as Shalore basically an automatic game winner.
The main developer Dark God is very responsive to the community and he works as a volunteer, as is customary in most Open Source projects. You can donate to the game if you like it to help support his efforts. The game is user friendly for Linux and MAC as well.
The games cons are its inflexiblity and redundant nature. The pros are its fantastic lead developer and the community.

At first I wasn't a fan of this game. It seemed complicated and strange. Wow, I am glad I kept at it. I have found an incredibly fun rogue-like dungeon crawler. There is an overworld with things to find and explore, tons of quests, and tons of things to unlock. There is quality lore here that I am enjoying, as well. Many classes have their own mechanics and skill trees, giving each one a unqiue feel. Those at first seemingly complicated systems were actually pretty easy to understand. What helps is there are plenty of tooltips for everything. Just mouse over it and you can see what something does.
The control scheme can take a little to get used to, but it isn't that bad. P is used for skill trees, I for inventory, M for mapping a skill to your hotbar (just drag it down), and Page up/down for different hotbars. Those are the most important and everything can be reassigned to a different key. Pretty much everything else can be done with a right click. The context menu when you right click offers a lot of options and the ability to inspect your enemies, which can be very useful.
I highly recommend this game. Since I gave it a fair shot, I haven't been able to put it down. I'm glad I bought both volumes to support this developer. I hope there is more to come, as I will grab up each and every expansion released!

The mechanics for that, however, are odd considering that you do not have a motion controller and must point and click to shoot. It's definitely a decent buy for fans of the series, and is definitely worth buying, but if you'd rather have a gun in hand and shoot your CRT television set with lasers, I would recommend playing the original few games. This old style rpg from MOCBJ Software has much more going for it than I thought I would see, especially considering the price. So, not expecting a lot, I decided to give this one a go.
As with any rpg, the story is hugely important. Without a decent and captivating story to tell the game can lose your interest, but this one tells a tale that keeps you interested and involved from the beginning.
An earhquake has tossed the main hero, Fred, on a beach needing to make his way home in a now shattered world. Along the way he meets the rest of the party, discovers what is behind the upheaval, deals with various side quests (16), battles thieves and assorted monsters, and collects more loot than you can imagine.
Loot comes in the form of "scrap material", "mystery meat", coins, and many other collectibles which are all used in the crafting system featured in the game.
And although the crafting system is not seen in these old style games that often, it is easy to learn so that you can have the items, weapons, armor, etc. that you need to have success in the game.
In a lot of ways this game reminds me of the original Final Fantasy, or even the old Phantasy Star seies. In addition to the crafting, the graphics really take you back ---- for those who remember playing those classics when they came out.
And there are aspects that give it a thoroughly modern feel as well. The characters are fun with lots of personality (Alan), the humor is current, nothing forced with a few LOL moments. And the music is great and adds greatly to the game's enjoyment.
I was impressed with the ease of working the menu with just the keyboard, and the game flowed quickly and smoothly with no glitching at all.
Save the game often as you never know what's coming next (even in the towns). Also, if after a recent save you are not  happy with the loot you pick up when there are a bunch of boxes, chests, bookcases, etc. ---- just go back to the last save and try again because the loot will be different.
Clocking in at around 15-20 hours, it's a can't miss addition to the rpg library.

First things first, this is an odd game. That is not meant as a negative as the light-hearted and irreverent nature of the storytelling helps elevate a well-worn RPG story (a group of diverse warriors have to save the world from annihilation) beyond the trappings of the genre. Combine this with some interesting ideas related to grinding in dungeons and crafting new gear and you have a fun and fresh take on old school RPGs.
The game is not reinventing the wheel as much as t is refining some of the characteristics that have defined this style of RPG for years. One of the best ideas, in my opinion, is the ability to skip random encounters in dungeons once a minimum number of battles have occurred. While this might not sound like much, as someone who likes to wander around to see what all I can find in a given area, it makes backtracking and investigating the rest of the world for loot much easier.
If you hate this style of game, Macabre is probably not going to change your mind. If you are like me, however, and used to love this style of game but have moved on to more modern RPGs, this game deserves a look.

Macabre is a nice and simple JRPG in the style of the old 16-bit classics.  Does this game hold a light to those games?  Sort of.
Story:
-Despite the game taking place in a medieval setting, the story isn't 100% typical of your usual save the princess, stop the evil guy plotline.  The story takes a couple of interesting turns and the settings are varied enough to keep you interested throughout your short journey.  Also, the main character looks like Guile from Street Fighter with red hair, which is pretty rad.
Gameplay:
-The battle system is quite typical.  You have the option to attack, cast spells, and use items.  The only real unique aspect is that characters can only gain new spells by using spells, similar to how Saga Frontier handles it.  Outside of combat, you can equip your characters with various weapons and armor.  There is an additional "augury" equip slot that allows your characters to get various stat bonuses at level-up but the mechanic seemed a bit underwhelming.
-Exploration is rewarded with loot and various side-quests.  I found that grabbing as much loot as I could left me with a stockpile of gold and supplies by the end of the game.  There are a limited number of random encounters in each area.  Once the limit has been reached, the player is given the option to turn off the encounters to allow from uninterupted explortation.  I found this to be a nice touch.
-Crafting is a bit tedious.  In order to craft the best weapons and armor you have to craft A LOT of items.  Crafting items that you already have feels mindless and is really only a waste of time.  I had well over 100 crafting materials by the end of the game because I didn't want to craft the same sword over and over in order to get my crafting level high enough.  The equipment you get from shops is good enough that I didn't see much of a reason to craft any more.
Graphics:
-The quality of graphics wouldn't have been acceptable in 1995, let alone 2015.  On the bright side, the graphics are consistently bad so the game has a certain style and charm to it.  If the developer were to make another game I'd recommend either hiring extra help with the pixel art or giving your artist more time to work on the sprites.

Music:
-I'm not sure if the soundtrack is original but it fits the game rather nicely.  Each area seems to have its appropriate song matched with it.

Replayability:

Dishonored rarely challenges you unless you're playing on a higher difficulty and/or are going for a run'n'gun playthrough, but that isn't really the point. With its vast levels, openness, and its plethora of different ways to play, Dishonored's difficulty comes from what you are trying to achieve, whether that is going for a full no-kill ghost run, or trying to kill everyone in the most creative/skilled way. The compulsively replayability feel that Dishonored has will have you wanting to go back and find a new rout, elimination method or combination of abilities, and will require multiple replays to fully learn and utilize game mechanics and environments. The bold stylized artistic design and colorful characters give a dark, stirring, yet beautiful pastel look to a divided world that will change somewhat depending on how many people you kill throughout. This approach to putting narrative and gameplay together works great, because if you make the choice to go through killing many people, later levels will have more enemies to fight, however if you choose to do the opposite than there will be less and it will be easier to sneak around. Although by this time the second installment is already out, I would highly recommend playing this great game if you haven’t already.

This is the sort of game that has the potential to become an obsession if it really ticks your boxes.  ToME is my first rogue-like, and what attracted me to it was the fact that it looks like the love child of a SRPG and an ARPG.  If that sounds good to you, let me tell you that it really delivers on that promise.  This is essentially a single character game of Final Fantasy Tactics staged across a series of Diablo dungeons.  I love it.
I have hundreds of hours logged so far, and even though I've won a few times, I still feel like I have lots to do if only because of the sheer number of classes and achievements, not to mention that I've yet to move beyond the Normal difficulty level or try any of the numerous community developed add-ons.  Even so, I'm well aware of just how flexible the add-ons make the game.  If you like unlocking everything yourself as I do, there's a fair number of unlocks to chase, but if you want all the classes immediately, you can get the add-on that does that.  Play how you want to!
Speaking on which, if you are turned off by by the idea of a rogue-like but otherwise think this looks interesting, it's worth knowing that the default mode is the more forgiving "Adventure" mode, which is more akin to the limited continues of an old-school NES game.  The game remains hard, but with some practice, a few extra lifes prove to be a pretty good cushion.  There's even an "Exploration" mode with unlimited lives if you'd really rather be sure you can finish.
The game still gets updates as well, and that looks likely to continue for the foreseeable future.  There are two additional DLCs in the works at the moment, as well as occasional updates to the core game for balancing or even the occasional new class.  Good stuff.

Again, I wish Steam had review options other than just positive or negative.. this one falls somewhere between. I rank it a "Not yet" rating. There is a really good frame here for them to build on, but there just isn't much content. Normally in early access I wouldn't ding a game for this, but the EA status description lead me to believe there would be much more.
Quote:
What is the current state of the Early Access version?
“Traditionally, publishers we've worked with define Alpha as “content complete” and Beta as “feature complete,” with Gold referring to a full release candidate. We'd currently place ourselves between Alpha and Beta: call it "early Beta" if you will.
/quote
In their words an Alpha is content complete, and they state the game is beyond Alpha. If this is truly the majority of the content they intend to place in the game, this is a definite Not Buy. There is a small number of things you can build, and many of them are not working properly. Buildings beyond the main dome do not pressurize for example.
State of the game: a lot of small bugs, some annoying and some near game breaking. There are problems such as items disappearing from containers, structures disappearing or duplicating when exiting and reloading a game, holes in the world, creatures and resources spawning on cave ceilings, and game status resetting upon re-entering an existing game.
Currently the E button puts away whatever tool you are holding in your hand. You need to do this to move at full speed. When you have the multi-tool in your hand, which is used to build walls for example, and you press E when aiming at a structure it will delete that structure. No confirmation or warning, and no resources returned, just POOF it's gone. That's a frustrating situation, and having that on the same key that is used to put your tool away makes it easy to do.
Performance is really good in single player mode. In official multiplayer servers the frame rates are reduced severly, even when no one else in on screen. I am guessing this is server side lag, and it makes multiplayer nearly unplayable.
The atmosphere is excellent, if not brutal at times. The dust storms will make you seek shelter and wait it out. Night time is tense as you can't see very well and aliens will sneak up on you. The fog is very nicely done, even though it again makes it next to impossible to accomplish anything. I am tempted to suggest that they tame the environment down a bit because there are many times when you can't do anything, but then that is part of the charm in a way.
The pacing of the game is slow. Really slow. Incredibly slow. To quote Joe Dirt, "I saw a snail over there. He said, that thing's slow, it ain't moving fast. It's boring, dull. I'm yawning". I believe the slow pace is to cover the lack of content, because it will take you hours to gather enough resources to place a single structure. There needs to be a better system of mining. Doing it yourself is too slow because you can't carry much without your movement speed getting reduced to a crawl, and the resources will be spread all over the world. You do have a droid that can mine, but it's hit or miss. To sum it up: I think and hope this will be a really amazing game one day. If you purchase, do so knowing that there is little content, and only if you want to be a part of the development. Your two hour refund window will be up long before you see enough of the game to know if you like it, again because of the slow pacing. In two hours you will probably have placed the temporary inflatable dome and collected a fraction of the resources needed to place the dome of a real base. How to uncensor it: Open your Beach bounce folder (OS>Program Files x86>Steam>steamapps>common>Beach Bounce). In your Beach Bounce folder, there should be a folder named 'game'. Open it. In the 'game' folder, there should be some files. Open the 'patch.rpy' file. Chances are you will not be able to open it by double clicking it, and that's ok. Just simply open the RPY file with notepad. Change "$ persistent.censored = True" to "$ persistent.censored = False" The game should be uncensored. To make sure it worked, when you open the game, it will say "uncensored version" in the top right corner of the start menu. Happy Fapping!

With as much fun as the game has the potential to be, I cannot recommend this due to issues with how it runs.
There is no sound control, meaning the game is always playing at 100% volume. The only workaround to this is adjusting your PC's volume. Port or not, it's a very simple thing that should be mandatory in all PC games.
The game crashes whenever you try to close it, causing an short obnoxious loop of the title screen's music, forcing you to use task manager to successfully close the game.
That this game has been on Steam as long as it has and neither of these have been fixed is unacceptable.
Another aspect that I found obnoxious was the unskippable credits at the end. You have to finish the credits in order to save the game and continue and to do so, must sit through a credits roll while nothing interesting happens. We're talking at least 8-10 minutes of credits that must be allowed to run in order to advance the story. There's no excuse that you cannot at the very least speed this process up.
If these kinds of things are not gamebreakers for you, give it a try. It's a fun game when you actually get into it, and the story isn't too bad. I'd be interested in playing the sequel if it ever came to steam IF they can fix these issues.

Ruin is a great NES / SNES style RPG.  There is loot all over!  The crafting is well done & makes treasure hunting exciting.  There is more mystery meat to be found here than a school cafeteria.  Luckily it can be synthesized into steak.
A quick & responsive menu system makes playing a breeze.  The simple controls were easy enough to program to my controller.  It makes sense & doesn't hinder the game at all.  I especially like how fast one can navigate through it all.
There is a wonderful score with flowing transitions.  The music is mastered well & sounds terrific on surround sound.  It truly is beautiful, adding lots of atmosphere to the pixel world, the way Nobuo Uematsu did in the Final Fantasies.  The sound effects are good with nothing abrasive.
Remember to save!  This game is no walk in the park and has a challenge more similar to early 90's RPGs.  The option to toggle random encounters in areas already explored is quite nice.  Even better is the other option to turn on the XP modifier so that the encounters are more worth while for obsessive grinders, like myself.  I would suggest leveling up respectively, as advancing too fast will kill your party outright.  I found myself on the edge of my seat many times whilest fighting.
Magic / Abilities are handled similarly to the orgional Final Fantasy, MP being called Mastery in this case.  The nice twist is that they are learned in a fashion more akin to Final Fantasy II.  Practicing abilities in battle advances the characters knowledge, which makes more sense than buying them in shops.
The characters are charming and enjoyable to read.  Alan's semi Scottish / Nova Scotian sort of accent is especially well done.  They are all definitely unique, and that is difficult to do these days.  Without spoiling too much, the plot thickens well with vendetta and heroic questing.  One feels compelled to help this ruined world.

I think the direction they took for this game was a poor choice. This game sells itself on bringing back Frank West (the protagonist from the first game), so I figure it wants to attract people who loved the first game. Sadly, they also took out a lot of the charm that made the first game such a great title. Namely, psychopaths. while there are "maniacs", the fun oftentimes hilarious boss battles with what happens when regular people snap in a zombie apocalypse are nowhere to be found. Instead "maniacs" are just people in a vaguely themed costumes that attempt to kill you because they are crazy. No cut scene of awesome characterizations, just human grunts that take a few more hits to kill than zombies. Also, the time limit is gone. Now that may sound like a good thing as a time limit until game over sounds stressful, but the original games give you more than enough time to beat the game and allow you to explore the open world. In the first game it was three days until your helicopter came back to pick you up, and the second was three days until the military comes to save everyone. In this fourth installment there is no time limit and it cuts down on the tension dramatically. that is not to say every game would benefit from a time mechanic, but rather it was a staple of the series and was not necessary to remove. As clunky as the first games were the quality of life improvements made in this fourth installment do not make up for the disappointment a fan of the original will feel. Also I had various game freezes on my play through, might not be the games fault although I do meet the recommended hardware specs but buyer beware and all. Would recommend to try the original Dead Rising available here on Steam.

Cuphead is a brilliant game.
I'm not going to go into much detail about the art style and music because there's not much that I could say that hasn't already been said by others. I enjoyed both of these aspects of the game, but what sells it on top of everything is the gameplay.
Cuphead is a challenging game, but what fascinates me the most is that eventhough it stays consistantly challenging, the game never felt frustrating or aggravating! I never felt like "rage-quitting" the game, because eventhough there were bosses that I had to retry 20-30 times before I could properly nail them down, I still had fun. With every time I retried a boss, I felt like I was learning something new, figuring out new ways on how I could beat a certain stage even faster than before. This constant feeling of re-evaluation and improvement is what kept me afloat. And at the end it truly felt like I deserved to beat the game.
A lot of games now a days are too eager to just hand you your victory. This one makes you work for it and it pays off in the end. I just felt satisfied playing through the game.
I've played through it on Regular difficulty in ~9-10 hours. After that, there's still more challenges for you, like beating the game on Expert or playing through each stage without killing an enemy. For such a cheap game, there's a lot of content to be had.
I can't recommend this game enough, especially for people that like this sort of bullet hell/run and gun gameplay.

A big step up from the first game, Assassin's Creed II succeeds in improving many aspects of the franchise.
Pros:
+ Many side quests and puzzles were added and helped a lot in making the game less repetitive and boring in its missions, as it happened with its predecessor. Namely, this time you get your own house (villa) and have various accessories to collect in order to improve it, as well as your character
+ Very interesting conspiracy story, with many real facts mixed with fictional ones, which made for a good history lesson in Renaissance Italy as well
+ Many interesting characters, both allies and enemies, based on real historical persons, with the best one being the main character, Ezio Auditore da Firenze. Getting to interact with Leonardo Da Vinci was also great and the way he was portrayed was very good too
+ Many weapons and ways of assassination were added, giving the game a bigger variety in gameplay
+ Huge and detailed map, which included Florence, Venice and a small part of Rome, as well as some smaller cities, each containing a big variety of secret places too
+ Hearing the characters speak in English, but with an Italian accent was funny
+ Mind-blowing ending, this was probably my favorite part, since I didn't expect it to include a twist of these proportions and I found took the game to a whole different level
Cons:
- Despite the many added side quests to keep you busy and the improved weapon and assassination system, the main gameplay's structure remained the same as the first title. You follow someone until a certain point or you fight or you run, that pretty much summarizes what you do for the whole game, failing to avoid repetitiveness to a certain point, although not as much as the first game (an aspect that the Arkham games managed to handle better, in my opinion)
- The fights and assassinations, though stylish and cool to watch, felt a bit too easy and not much challenging (with some exceptions)
- The soundtrack was just OK, in fact it might be the only field that I found weaker than its predecessor, since the first game had a very good theme when you were being chased, absent here. The tracks were good generally, but mostly forgettable
These minor flaws aside, Assassin's Creed II is a great game and I definitely recommend it, be it for the various added improvements or to get a detailed taste of Renaissance Italy, mixed with conspiracy schemes.
That said, I still consider the franchise's ancestors, the Prince of Persia games, to be overall better in structure and more fun, so it's a pity Ubisoft discontinued them to make way for this series, but since things turned out this way, be sure to step into Ezio's footsteps and learn the ways of the assassin!

Sitting down after investing 5 hours into the game(Single Player), I like it. (Do note that this game is still in Early Access and as such will change in future.)
Stuck on a planet with your floating robot companion who functions as a sentry, a mobile storage and also a guard, you get to set yourself up on a seemly resource filled planet.
Build up your base, but be prepared to fend off the local fauna as they can be rather aggressive and will not hesitate to take a potshot at you.
Mining can be fun but the hunt for them will make you run several hundreds of meters away from your home base. Carrying too much will make you encumberred and slow you down, any more than that will make you unable to run or use any of your tools.
The maps are huge from the initial start and there are resources lying around for you to start.
The ingame tools can be rather confusing, such as the map tool which does not indicate your base however acts more like a compass instead. Others are self explainatory such as the assault rifle or shovel which needs to be crafted.
The crafting system is fun to experiment with however it could be improved.
Do note that there will be bugs to content with and the devs will definitely need to patch them to ensure a better overall gameplay.
I will continue supporting the devs and hope that they are able to make the necessary improvements before they release the full game.

Best roguelike in recent years with modern quality-of-life improvements that many roguelikes sadly neglect (i.e rebindable hotkeys, customisable UI or even just having sprites at all!)
There are tons of classes with different skills that allows different playstyle though it does go with my one complaint - too many of these classes rely on just a differently named resource bar (i.e. renamed mana) though some do have unique ways of generation/replenishment.
Damage of certain magic/ranged enemies can also be reduced as they can 1 or 2-shot you and newbies are advised to avoid "vaults". This does somewhat restrict builds to require some sort of "ohshit" button or certain damage migitation skills. Melee classes are naturally harder to play/weaker because of this. Randomness on drops (but what's a roguelike without this?) and escort quests can also be annoying but that can be worked around because..

I don’t know if I am the only one who played the original The Typing Of The Dead that was released on 2000 but it shames me not to state that as hilarious as that game’s voice acting was it was still a very effective teaching tool for me. Prior to that game I was a “search and peck” (looked and the keyboard looking for the key to press, press it then search for the next letter in the work I wished to type) but just after a few days I found myself typing without looking down.
The original game began with step #1 like any typing game/program does and that is with the basic “A S D F” on your left hand and “J K L ;” on your right hand. The game will then show you what keys you hit with great accuracy and what keys you have trouble with. (Not everyone knows this or have even noticed the small raised line or dot on the “F” and “J” keys on the keyboards) You could only imagine my confusion as to why would any typing game never mind a sequel to the typing of the dead would overlook this very basic of basis!  At the very least the first mission on its lowest difficulty could have been used to learn the ASDF and JKL; keys before the player is expected to type “Jasper V2”
…But what if this is not supposed to be something to help your typing skills?
Although the original was hilarious due to its poor voice acting, this game not funny because of the excessive searing. Every single cut scene from this game (including the very first one) has someone saying Mother F*cker, Sh*t, F*ck and so on. You could swear it was written by a 12 year old.
At the very least the mode where you use your mouse to shoot a gun is fun, this should have been the original basis for the game since they face planted with the typing version.
PS: I am proud to say I am now a very efficient typist, I am just very disappointed in how far my tutor's series has fallen.

Azure Striker Gunvolt. Right off the bat, I'll say if you loved the old Megaman and Megaman X games, this game is perfect for you. For those still wondering if this is good, well the short answer is yes. I will note that this version of the game is literally a 3DS emulation program to run this. Many features that you think would be 3DS exclusive still exist in this PC port. In terms if you should get this version of the game, that would be up to you. Personally I would say the Nintendo Switch version is the best one available, for it also come with the sequal. However, in terms of pure looks this is the best version.
The controls for this port are very hit and miss. From what I've done you can't easily get a  control scheme you like, without constantly restarting the game. But once you get controls all set and ready, this game controls very nicely. I would also recommend to have a good D-pad for this game. One that has a connected + shape (Like most Nintendo controllers) will give you the best experience.
The music choice for this game is also top notch. Using a very fitting high tempo electric soundtrack for almost every piece of music. Same thing goes for character design. Everything fits and nothing seems to far out of place for this si-fi city.
All and all I would recommend this game, and especialy the sequal if you can get your hands on it. In terms on platformers, I'd give this game a solid 9/10. But if you can play the Switch version I highly recommend that version. It's easy to just start playing and finish this game in about 4 hours. Plus speedruns and highscores are very encouraged, and very easy to do.

[This is a brand new review for the games relaunch from a new studio. I previouly did not recommend the game, but had high hopes it could be fixed]
Well, that was a bummer. I don't know how they could have made it worse, but they did.
It mostly has to do with them launching the game with only about 20% of the actual game in it. You make ~10 decisions at the begining, then your only input is when to eat, drink, sleep, and make the decision to play the CSGO clone. You make no decisions in game, there are lots of upgrades to buy that aren't in the current build, and the graphics are, in the kindest words I can manage, fugly.
At least the last game let me choose how I would play a particular round and what character and role I wanted to play, even if that♥♥♥♥♥♥was totally random, and gave me options besides just play the game and sleep. Not only that, but on top of several needs you need to manage (guys, your game is A sim, not THE Sims. I want to play games, not shove food in my face); the time which had previously gone down with every action now ticks down continuously.
There was a great game in here before, now there's at best a good one, but in this current build it's neither. It was dropped too early and at this stage I think it would be generous to even call it a beta. Proof of concept for the core mechanic maybe?
Immediate update: The dev's know they messed up this launch and had the courage to admit it up front and apologize, which gets huge amounts of respect from me.
I'm sorry 501, I can't change the recommend to a "Yes", but I still belive in you all and your ability to make a really solid game. The vision you had wasn't terrible, I may have personally disagreed with choices made, but that doesn't mean they're inherently bad. Do ya thang and make the game we know you can.

Reasons why it's bad now:
1. The new FPS career takes SO LONG to get through a single game. In the old version with MOBA, the games took a little bit to pick your hero, playstyle, etc. Now it's just sit there for 5 minutes and stare at the screen as a bunch of guys shoot other guys with boolets (not really, it just sometimes says you dead and you fall over), and the announcer has THE EXACT SAME TWO LINES.
