Enjoyable VN game. I recommend it to newtime VN players and to veterans who want something shorter before they play their next 40 hr one.
I'll say this first; this game is relatively short. After completing 100%, my steam time says I've played 120 minutes, though I did use the skip feature to miss previously read text. The game also doesn't have voice, being made in Ren'py.
However, the game is very well made, and the art is really nice, although all static images.
There are plenty of branch options leading to the different endings, which help to make you feel like you're Tomo (the protaganist) aiding in your immersion. The choices generally feel like they are doing something worthwhile; only a couple feel like they're there for the sake of it.
There are seven girls to choose from. Each of the characters is interesting, and their personalities are fun, although Nymph could have been fleshed out a little better, though arguably she is only a side character, and a little more history for Minami wouldn't have hurt.
I really recommend this game; it was enjoyable, made me chuckle a few times, and despite the girls having Japanese names, the game doesn't have a tonne of Japanisms, so is accessible to those who aren't as familiar with Japanese culture; this means I can recommend it to all VN players, old and new to the scene alike.
If you are of age, I highly recommend the uncensor patch available at the developer's website; although the game is fine without the adult scenes, its more enjoyable with them. Apart from a little bit of "messiness", they're quite tastefully done, and help to make the characters feel more rounded.
Pros:
-Nice story.
-Fun characters. (Seven girls to choose from)
-Good art, the CGs are nice to look at.
-Nice range of branch options.

(Originally posted 11/25/2009; contains spoilers for Assassin's Creed 1!)
Back in 2007, the software company Ubisoft, which had previously done more realistically-themed stealth-heavy action games such as Splinter Cell, Rainbow Six and their sequels, came out with a cross-time tale of genetic memories and conspiracy, Assassin's Creed. You took on the role of Desmond Miles, a modern era bartender with a somewhat shadowy past, but seemingly more interesting ancestors.
A callous, uncaring scientist, Dr. Vidic, at a research firm called Abstergo forces his prisoner, Desmond, under the supervision of his subordinate Lucy Stillman, to use a machine called the Animus, which is able to retrieve Desmond's genetic memories and visualize them. One of Desmond's most important ancestors, at least to Abstergo, was known as Altair, a Middle Eastern man living in the 12th century Holy Land. Altair was one of the Assassins, whose sworn enemies were the Knights Templar.
While the details of the epic story are best experienced for yourself, suffice to say, Altair is able to safeguard the Holy Land against the Templars, but Abstergo has a hidden, sinister agenda for the information the Animus reveals...
Assassin's Creed II continues the story just seconds from where the first game left off; Lucy and Desmond, revealed to be modern-day Assassins, realize that Abstergo has become a very dangerous place and that they must leave quickly; Lucy escapes with Desmond to a secret hideout, where a new Animus is set up.
Together with Lucy and a new support team of a historian and technician for the Animus 2.0, Desmond explores the life and times of Ezio Auditore da Firenze, a young man in late-15th century Renaissance Italy, and experiences his trials and tribulations first hand. Ezio, who discovers his Assassin heritage fairly early, gets many opportunities to test out, among others, that most important weapon of the Assassins, the wrist-mounted Hidden Blade, which can kill a man before he knows he's in danger. Over the years, Ezio has many experiences, good and bad, and assassinates many behind the conspiracy against his family, who were killed or traumatized in the opening hours of the game, and attempts to subvert a plot that could threaten the entire world.
Ezio makes a home base at his family's villa, and is able to repair and renovate many aspects of it using the money he finds or earns in his journeys, and is even able to make more from the visitors to the shops and amenities of the surrounding town. Ezio, and through him Desmond and the player, adventures through many regions of Italy including Ezio's home city of Florence, Venice, and the Tuscan countryside. With his uncle Mario and several other Assassins, Ezio begins to piece together the mysteries surrounding several ancient, extremely powerful artifacts and strive to keep them from the Templars.
The graphics in this game are simply beautiful; review sites have said this is the best-looking free-roaming game ever, but I believe it's about tied with Grand Theft Auto IV. The animations, just like in that game, are pretty spectacular; you'll rarely if ever see Ezio miss a nook or chink in the wall while climbing unless you cause it to happen. Each one of his movements is accounted for in the architecture.
Free-running, sometimes called Parkour, makes its return in this sequel. Letting nothing stop you from going forward, always finding a way over or under obstacles, the several locales that Ezio finds himself in are very fun to navigate. With methods created in the first game, you as Desmond control Ezio's movement, fighting, climbing and jumping with the greatest of ease. It can be very dangerous when you run out of rooftop during exploration or a chase, and should you fall, you don't automatically heal in this installment; you must use pain-numbing smelling salts.
This is definitely one of the best games I've ever played; from beginning to end, I was greatly entertained, from the great combat to wonderful exploration to shocking denouement, and I was pleasantly surprised at the portrayal of the real historical figures I met. If I could give this six stars on my established scale, I would, but I give this five stars.

One of the best Rogue-likes out there, with a default difficulty between "casual" and "instagib me now please" (though every option in between is available)
A variety of interesting classes and races, and a deep mechanical system that leaves plenty to learn. (through many, many many avoidable deaths.)

Imagine creating a character, going through quests and being really happy with his awesome super lucky dropped sword and the perfect quest rewards to fit your play style. He dies miserably to the first mishap.
Now imagine the opposite, a pretty meh character you don't care for never getting the right stuff you want. He somehow survives twice as long as previous character.
Even though they both die, you probably managed to unlock a new class, or race or skill tree on top of all the already existing choices, allowing you to try for a fresh start with a character that can play completely different than the previous one, which combined with random elements make it surprisingly replayable.
Nightmare difficulty is my recommended difficulty, it helps speed the starter levels up which is great when you are constantly remaking characters on permadeath (which I recommend over the lives system personally), as well as adding more rare encounters.
Its worth the 7$, otherwise you can get the base game for free as well from the game's website. I played it for years, and purchased the game on steam later to support the development. Plays well on both linux and windows.

As a big fan of both normal history and fictional "alternate histories" like the TV-series "The Man in the High Castle" this is one of my favourite games. A game that allows me to conquer the world as a facist version of Russia is a game that deserves every bit of praise it gets. But it's still a Paradox game so we should expect it to improve and improve in a bunch of following DLCs.

I won't be touching bugs and glitches, because, while numerous at the moment, it's likely that they'll be fixed in coming days (and so there's no practical reason to bash on it).
However, I would like to describe the amount of content currently available in the game. Which can be divided into three parts:
1) You walk/run/jump around the playable area to find resources and bring them back to your base. Gameplay time-wise, this is the main filler - you will be doing it at least 90% of your play time in SP (60-70% in MP due to cooperation);
2) You place prefab buildings in the world. There's a not particularly large "building tech tree" at the moment, where you have to place certain "crafting benches" to be able to create more complex items and build further.
3) You shoot/whack mildly aggressive respawning mobs. Unless you're completely terrible with first-person shooters, this part is entirely trivial and doesn't really affect your survival (your pistol has endless ammo and with a little bit of time you can shoot anything to death while dodging its attacks).
There's also PvP in multiplayer, but it's entirely pointless at the moment - you can kill people and wreck their buildings (both of which is incredibly easy), but you're not going to get anything at all out of it. There's also "survival", but I can't even write anything meaningful about it, as currently it's nothing more than a placeholder - you can skip most of it by things like endless "berry trees" (free food), or simply don't care about it at all, as dying is only a very minor setback - all that happens is that you're back at the spawn point and your current inventory is lost (but you can pick it back at your body).
For the given amount of content available, I can't give the game "thumbs up" in good faith. There's way too little available right now to justify buying it at any price point above the "trash" (~$1) level. Now, if you're willing to invest in the game in hopes that your money will fund further development - sure, you can do so.
Some assorted facts that seems to be poorly understood quite often:
1) This is a small-scale MP game with public and private servers. Not an MMO, no matter how you stretch the definition.
2) The world is not "procedurally-generated" - the landscape is the same every game and resources are always in the same spots. An absolutely empty desert surrounds the hand-crafted playable area.
3) There's only 1 planet available and there's no space travel (though it's in development roadmap). If you watched the trailer - it is misleading in this regard and it shows you stuff that is not yet implemented in the game.
4) Building is prefab-based. Meaning, you're not "building" things out of simple blocks, you place structures and objects premade by developers.

Dark Commands: Prepare to crash edition
Well, here we go. Police Quest Collection comes with Police Quest I, II, III and IV. Most of my playtime is on Police Quest I and a bit on the other three, just to try them out. As I think a lot of people will like to try the first one, I feel like I want to review at least the pain I got with it, even if its just one game of the collection. Maybe I'll update on the other three when I have the urge to play them. But I don't know, the first one felt so tedious, that it just took all my energy and curiosity left on the series, which doesn't mean any of them are bad, maybe it's not my type of genre.
INTRO
Police Quest I: In pursuit of The Death Angel is an adventure/police simulation game based on the real life tasks of a police officer. All of its rutine, from the beginning of its day until the time he goes off-duty. Your character is Sonny Bonds, obviously an officer on Lytton's Police Department, who will have a rollercoaster of a time doing his job on his following days. Chasing wrong doers and investigating crimes that he'll have to resolve with some help of his mates.
IN-GAME
The intro and theme music were pretty cool, it got me really excited to play it. When I finally pressed enter because the intro looped, I just spawned in the hall of a police department. No information, no "Hey, you have to go here", I was just there. Alone.
I said, "Well, I should go check the place". When I realized I had to attend some briefing, I got in it and a "Game over" window poped up. I was late for it. Restarted the game. Went straight into the briefing. 1 minute and nothing, went out. I didn't know what to do. I was searching for a clock or something because in the briefing room there's a blackboard with an hour written on it. Then I said, lets just stay here for a while. 2 minutes, 2 minutes and a half, the briefing started! There were 4 tables, I picked one and stayed still. The seargent told me like 3 times to get in my assigned possition, which I didn't knew I had one. Game over music. Restart. Walked in and I've finally got it right, finding my possition by passing through the 4 tables. The briefing ended and then I didn't knew what to do. I just took the police vehicle key, that was the only thing I recognized (I tried to take the radio extenders with the command "take" but it said I didn't needed it, but it wasn't that I didn't need it, I've put the command wrong, because I had to put what I wanted to take. "Take radio extender" was the correct command) and went to the parking lot. I drove just a little bit and a game over popped up again. Why? Because I got a flat tire. Restart. All over again. Then I understood because of the manual, I had to abide a vehicle safety procedure before taking my car out. I discovered I could save my progress also too. I got some calls on my car radio, attended them. Until I got in a point in which I had to stop a woman for a traffic infraction, passing a red light. I got her, parked. I've talked with her, wanted to fine her and couldn't get the command right. There was no way to fine her. Although there was one. "Write ticket" was the answer. I finally typed that and the game said to me. "You need the ticket book". Then, I realized, the bathroom that I visited on the department had lockers which contain all the objects a police MUST have, which I overlooked. NICE. Neat, isn't it? The woman leaved, saying that cops are lame. That was just some of the things that happened in my playtime. There was a lot of "I really don't know what else can I do here to progress/complete my task/do something" and "What command do I need here, what should I do, where should I go?", many, many "what".
Oh, and so many "game over" boxes. So many sweet "game over" boxes.
CONTROLS
They're pretty straight forward. Arrow keys to move Sonny, although he walks painfully slow. Too slow. I don't know if it's this dos-box version or if the standard game was like this, too. For the car, oh, the handling. It's terrible. Your car is a rectangle that won't let you turn easily on the streets, because horizontally, your car goes faster. Controls are arrow keys too, but, you have to use functions keys to change speeds. "F6": Normal speed. "F8": Faster speed. "F10": Persecution speed.
This adventure game uses the "type your desired command" thing. So it's very precise. Maybe synonyms won't work, just the words the game knows. And maybe there's only 2 commands that can work for one action if you're lucky.
"ESC" lets you learn some of the functions, like "F3" to repeat command, if you select Help.
IMPORTANT TIPS
READ THE MANUAL. I REPEAT. READ THE MANUAL. You can google it. There's a sierra site that holds it. It will help you start playing it and because you MUST abide all of the standards, codes and procedures if you want to progress, it's the best thing you can do. Failing these will punish you with a game over, every time, because this game is very, very tedious in the aspect that if you miss something, the game won't tell you, nobody will tell you about that. When the time comes, you'll be speechless finding that you lost because you didn't obey all the procedures. The game will keep going until you crash into your inevitable demise or just simple, but fatal mistake.
Save only when you know you have all that a police officer should have on its inventory and that you've done something correctly or face the sad truth that you saved on a point in which you cannot go take the gun you left on the jail locker.
MY PLAYTIME
When I progressed in the game, I was having fun and felt a bit rewarded. Even with the few times that the game tries to make you smile a little. But yeah, this game felt like a job, I felt like a cop just doing his job, and that bored me a ton, although it was very interesting to know what goes through the minds of cops and all they do to protect their citizens. Also, this game thought me about checking all the things I can on a room and to be less forgetful.
But, as I got stuck in the stage of "I don't know where to go now/I don't know what to do to fix this", I got really frustrated and just looked a walkthrough of the rest of the game. I'm persistent, but there's a point in all of us that calls it quits.
PROS
+ Realistic situations
+ Complex Puzzles
+ A little funny sometimes
CONS
- No help in-game
- Can get stale overtime
- Figuring out the commands
VERDICT
This is a very complex game. When you get the hang of it in the first few "missions" it's okay. But when you progress further it gets tough. Or at least it did for me. Maybe you have a better run than mine in this game. But, I'll still recommend it, it's interesting and an ol' good gem for its time.

Just ended the Dear Rising 4 story mode. Still, I have not touched the multiplayer segment of the game. So, here goes my take on DR4's story.
>PROS:
01. Story is brilliant: The story build-up is great. Even the ending is also great.
02: The map is huge.
03: Lots of customizable costumes, ranged weapons, melee weapons, combo weapons and throwables. Rinse and repeat the zombie killing never got boring for me.
04: Frank is hilarious AF! His story narration is incredible after every case ending. It will just put you into mood after a hectic series of long episodes in a case.
05: Easy controls and character movements
>CONS:
01: The game is not challenging at all, too much arsenal of weapons, a wide array of melee weapons and throwables just makes the game less challenging. Worse, all of these are acquired easily.
02: DR4 removes timer counter on side missions, which proved a really bad omen for the game. Even the side missions are just blah!
03: No melee combat moves, all you get is a simple punch, an easy counter hit and jump kick. The 52 years Frank West has literally grown old and lost his charm in melee combat after DeadRising 1.
04: DeadRising series have been known for multiple endings, but Capcom has changed the trend. To see alternate endings you will need to buy DLC. That is a big time bummer for FW and DR fans.

Evolve is back with a major revamp, biggest of all being that it's 100% free to play.
The game has been changed to focus on having multiple, small and fast fights against the monster instead of playing constant hide and seek. The dome has been changed so that all hunters can use it, making the hunters not so heavily dependant on a good trapper. Overall the matches feel much better than previously. The only downside is that the stealthier monster players can't rely on sneaking as much as previously.
Unlocking stuff is done by spending silver keys which you earn by playing, leveling up, completing daily challenges, or reaching various milestones. The amount you get varies heavily on match to match basis, depending on if you leveled up, completed a challenge, etc. Unlocking a new hunter or monster takes anywhere from 5 to maybe 15 games. With the game length being anything from instant 2 minute deathmatches to 20 minute struggle, it feels very fair imo.
The hunters and the monsters have a wide variety of perks to slightly alter their gameplay, these are unlocked by leveling up specific characters, or by spending silver keys.
Overall, the game is very fun, the hunter gameplay is much more action heavy than it used to be.
Especially hunting with friends (or hunting your friends, why not) is a blast.
Happy hunting!
-If you are a founder, meaning you bought the game before free to play change, you keep all your owned characters, get some perks and skins, and a massive stack of 30 000 silver keys to unlock things with.-

You dynamically control the frequency & amplitude of an ocillating sine wave as you ride its peaks and troughs, guiding your 'ship' to collect stars and powerups whilst avoiding obstacles.
On paper Waveform's extremely addictive gameplay is simple, in reality though, it's a fiendish game to master. It's one of those games that is infuriatingly difficult to get 100% completion on a level, but luckily the fun-factor is high and you always find yourself having 'just one more go'.
The catchy electronic soundtrack provides very pleasant accompaniment - never irritating, and its blippy tunes have a charming retro feel to them.
As a way to wile away an hour or two, Waveform is hard to fault - and harder to put down once started.

fast paced levels with a boss at the end
skippable mid level check points so you can get back into the action quickly if you die or challenge yourself by skipping them.
A variety of modes to change things up including easy and hard difficulties and some other modes.
Extra challenges for each level.
Additional special stages unlocked after completing the true ending.
Prevasion which allows players having difficulty to lose energy instead of health(when they are not attacking) particularly useful if you are having trouble with a boss
Cons:
stage music is generally lacluster unless you can get 1,000 kudos in a level or die and are then revived, then it switches to an up-beat J-pop track.
A basic leveling system that increases your max health and unlocks a few special skills not really useful for much accept a quick heal during a level or boss fight or a finishing blow to a weakened boss.
port could have been done better
requires gamepad to properly experience.
Other:
A crafting system to create accessories only really used for getting the true ending, or you can use the stuff to get better scores times and help beat challenges.

I want to start off by saying I am a die hard Megaman fan and seeing something that Inti Creates made after Megaman Zero, was exciting.  WARNING, THIS IS NOTHING LIKE MEGAMAN, This was just a disappointment, I have so many issues with this game.  The enemies are uninspired, the level design is just silly with the half way loading points, the clearly ignored movement mechanics that you are handed but never given the chance to use AND THE BOSSES, OH MY GOD THE INFURIATING BOSSES.
Now when you play a good platformer with bosses like this, most of their moves are telegraphed, or they start doing certain movements or patterns before they use a specific ability.  Don't even trust that here, because these bosses will ♥♥♥♥ you up.  Yeah they have different phases where they start using new abilities or their previous ones a little different but when they do this UNAVOIDABLE damage crap, it is maddening!  Between the fire boss doing a "Bullet Hell" type ability, to the "LAZY LASER" going off instantly, or even the midway boss slowly walking towards you shooting bullets that while HALF the time you can destroy, eventually you just can't so you try to jump over her, but it always ends in failure and her hitting you harder because of it.
Let's talk about abilities, oh my god boss acquired abilities don't even feel worth it to use, I don't want to use them they're so useless.  When you think back to every Megaman game ever, you sometimes get excited to use that boss ability, whether because its powerful or because it's new and you haven't seen it, just yknow it FEELS GOOD.  Not here in this game, again just like the enemies, they are uninspired.  I feel no reason to ever use them because they're so bad.  Between a SINGLE bullet I can redirect once for only one stack of that stupid electricity thing, or the splitting "bullet hell" double shot.  Leveling up even feels like a joke, you can barely control those abilities.
The crafting system unlike Megaman Zero is completely based on luck if you can even get the parts you need, I didn't play far enough to even care about crafting upgrades but i'm sure they suck too.
Even the dialogue is to be desired, they tried too hard to be funny with their double entendres and adult jokes, it was funny the first few times until it felt forced.  If you've played this game I think you know where I drew the line on comedy.  Literally there is one specific moment I just stopped caring.
Listen if you want a damn good game like Megaman, get a 3ds and try Megaman ZX and ZX Advent, those are lesser known titles that are surprisingly good.  Hell even replay Megaman Zero or the entire series of classic or X again.  This game I am sure has it's own audience that somehow finds it entertaining, but if you're looking for Megaman, he's not here.  He died with Capcom...

This review will be split in 2 parts as there are 2 different ways to play:
The Typing of the Dead: Overkill.
The whole point of the game is to type the words as fast as you can, while prioritizing whatever is coming at you first ( projectiles, mutants, etc. ) It's pretty basic in that aspect but nonetheless, very fun. Also you have to keep your eyes open for bonuses and collectibles! I'm sure this game would greatly improve your typing speed if you play it alot. Mixing typing and a video game together makes it surprisingly addictive if you like those 2 things.
I do type 120 words+ a minute and ''medium'' and ''hard'' difficulties are both just right for me. I can tell that there is not that much difference between the 2, but it is not as easy as I thought it would be, I didin't complete a level perfectly yet and i'm currently trying to do that. The ''easy'' mode is probably fine for almost everybody who can type without looking at a keyboard. I only played it once to test it and it was alot easier than the other modes.
In the end, the story mode took me 2 hours 30 minutes to finish, which is pretty short, but there's other stuff to do in the game anyways! Such as Mini-games, House of the Dead, Hardcore-mode... Etc.
-------
The House of the Dead: Overkill.
I was really surprised by this. The game actually has the whole story mode, playable with the mouse, just like the good old House of the Dead! Even the mini-games, challenges and more are playable with the mouse!
You even have a gun shop, you gain gold while playing and you can upgrade your guns ( 5 upgrades per gun with 2 levels each ) and there is 6+ weapons.
I found the accuracy to be pretty harsh with the automatic guns... Guess I should have sticked to pistol, but oh well. The story is really different with a mouse, the bosses are not played the same way and if you are better at FPS games than you are at typing on a keyboard, this mode will be easier for you.
-------
Overall, I recommend this game, the few bugs I have found so far weres not being able to shoot 2 mutants, after I used a grenade on them in the House of the Dead, sound clips missing during slow-mos and Rage mutant finishing blows, game closing and re-opening itself after typing a word, the rest of the levels played just fine.

The Police Quest series is an extremely underrated part of the classic Sierra canon of adventure games and many modern games such as "LA Noir" owe a lot to these titles. The games center on the character of Sonny Bonds, a police officer in the fictional city of Lytton. Created by former police officer Jim Walls, these titles require the player to strictly follow police protocol in order to complete the game.
The first game was built on the text input-based AGI game engine developed for King's Quest and told the story of Sonny's rise in from beat cop to narcotics detective as he takes down the infamous "Death Angel". The game follows a linear plot but is built around a top-down open world map which allows you to drive between game locations. However, the version included in this collection is the point and click remake built on top of the SCI1 engine.
Police Quest II was built on the SCI engine which was also text input based but did feature some point and click functionality. This entry replaced the top-down driving simulation with an over-the-shoulder view which to some degree made the world feel more restrictive. Still, the game benefits from a variety of realistic locations and the same attention to real-world detail as its predecessor.
Police Quest III was built on the SCI1 engine which eliminated the need for text entry. This title returned to the top-down driving view but the point-and-click interface proved frustratingly non-intuitive for navigating around Lytton. Still, Police Quest III features a remarkably emotionally-driven storyline centering on Bonds' relationship with his wife Marie (a character from the original two games).
Open Season is the first game not to be developed by Jim Walls, with former LAPD Chief Daryl F. Gates taking the helm of the project. Although graphically impressive for its time (it was build on the SC2 game engine which relied on photographic scans for its visuals) the game lost the realistic procedural element of its predecessors, instead relying on graphic violence and sensationalism to move the story forward. The game also ditches the character of Sonny Bonds in favor a new protagonist which squanders the emotional resonance built up over the first three entries. I therefore consider this to be a sequel in name only.
The forth is a depature from the rest but still a fun addition to the series. The graphics a pixilated and the controls are old but the plot makes up for it.

A Collection of 4 Police Quest titles released from 1987-1993. It's Another great Inventory Adventure series that Sierra On-Line created back when MS-DOS & Windows 3.1/95/98 was still by popular demand. The first three games were produced by former police officer Jim Walls and follow the adventures of Sonny Bonds, a character whose name and appearance was loosely based off his own son, Sonny Walls while the remainder Police Quest games were produced by former L.A. Chief Daryl Gates, in a different style in both atmosphere, and later even in genre.
All 4 Police Quest games are recorded on Location by the Men & Women of the Laytton Police Department.
All suspects are Innocent until proven Guilty in a Court of Law.
In Police Quest 1 EGA/VGA - In Pursuit of the Death Angel:
Assigned to traffic duty, Sonny Bonds investigates what appears to be a simple car crash but turns out to be a homicide. Relieved by his supervisor, Sergeant Dooley, Sonny goes on a short coffee break with a fellow officer and returns to duty. He gives a traffic violation citation to a driver, single-handedly faces a tough gang of drunken bikers, and makes a DUI arrest. As the game progresses, he advances from patrol officer to temporary narcotics detective to undercover agent in hope of tracking down a murderous drug dealer named Jessie Bains, "The Death Angel". In order to find Jessie Bains, Sonny enlists the help of his former high school sweetheart, "Sweet Cheeks" Marie, who is now working as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
In Police Quest 2 - The Vengence:
After arresting Jessie Bains, Bonds is promoted to the homicide division. He begins dating Marie Wilkans, who helped him in his undercover work in exchange for the dismissal of prostitution charges against her as "Sweet Cheeks" Marie. A dark shadow is cast over Sonny's happy life, however, when Bains escapes from prison and seeks revenge. With the help of his partner Keith, Bonds must protect his girlfriend's life as well as his own while pursuing "The Death Angel" once again. Despite Sonny's efforts, Bains kills several people who were involved in his arrest and abducts Marie. Sonny pursues Bains to Steelton, the current home of Donald Colby, a reformed drug pusher from the original Police Quest.
In Police Quest 3 - The Kindred:
Sonny and Marie are married following Bains' death. Promoted once more, Sonny now has to deal with rampant crime as a drug cartel begins operating in Lytton and evidence of a satanic cult starts to appear. When Marie is stabbed in a mall parking lot, Sonny's police work becomes personal. Sonny must deal with a partner with questionable ethics as well as find patterns in crime to find his next lead. The Bains family also plays a role in this game.
In Police Quest 4 - Open Season:
You take the role as John Carey in Los Angeles, California. Carey, an LAPD homicide detective whose best friend was killed in the line of duty, must track down a serial murderer in L.A. where numerous mature themes are depicted in the game, including hate crimes, Neo-Nazism, and youth involved in crime. Graphic imagery within the game also includes the body of a child murdered by gang violence and a severed head in a refrigerator.

I must honestly say that I never liked Police Quest. Unlike contemporary series such as Larry, Kings Quest and Quest for Glory they always seemed to do everything wrong. The player is typically left to his own devices without any clues as what to do next, forced to perform boring police procedures and lured into dead ends which forces you to restart the game over and over.
They have not aged very well either, the "realistic" graphics are dated, no voiceover and a clunky interface plague the series. You also have the "integrated" copy protection scheme which requires you to get information from a manual on how to do certain tasks (Such as opening your locker in PQ1), but they did not even bother to include the necessary information to play the games in this collection.
Normally I would recommend this for fans and give a (small) thumb up, but seriously: If you have good childhood memories from these games you ough to just leave them alone.

Coming from a person that has played not all too much MMo's, but has played a fair few, this game was and still is relatively enjoyable, and very easy to get into. It has the old style feel of how MMo's used to be, and overall the game feels really well. The map design is flawless, and they way they handled their AI made it so that it wasn't too terribly difficult, but still a challenge. Rifts are near impossible to solo if the rift is relatively close to your level, which is good, as rifts are supposed to be group based events. The bosses are incredibly huge and flashy, which for me is a big thumbs up, but for others maybe not so much. World events are interesting and can keep you hooked for a good amount of time.
Combat mechanics are easy to get used to, and there's not a lot of learning curve besides building your skill trees correctly.
Although a lot about this game is good, there are some downsides. The game does get repetitive after a good bit, and in the later 30s-40s, it becomes more and more grindy and the quests are not as nail-bitingly addictive. The mounts in the game could definitely use some reworking, as it's incredibly hard to get decent transportation at lower levels, and the amount of time and resources it takes to get a good mount are quite steep. On top of these things, lower end computers, laptops mainly, will have trouble handling this game unless you have relatively good graphics.
Overall a 7/10 game, which is good! I'd recommend this game to people who are new to MMo's and to experienced MMo players alike, this game is quite enjoyable for all.

This is basically Psychonauts, but without the protagonists, aside from the obvious sidescroller vs third person difference.
In this game you follow 7 characters as they fall prey to their inner "dark spaces" and fall into madness. Because there are no protagonists, there is no chance for redemption, and so you replay, for the want of a better word, their mistakes.
The events leading up to and leading from these mistakes are gathered in memory snapshots exactly like the piggy-banks in Pyschonauts.
Without the protagonists, the game loses a lot of its charm, as their is no banter between the afflicted and the observer. There is narration to fill in some of this void, but there can be no back and forth between characters and a narrator. There are also no enemies, per se, as the characters cannot die whilst exploring themselves. Instead, only the puzzles remain.
There is also a distinct lack of a tutorial. Q or middle mouse activates the characters' special abilities, which you can see easily enough in the menu if you look (which I didn't).
In all, Psychonauts is far superior, in terms of humour, challenge and story. But if you still want more pysche-delving matter, then seeing how these 7 characters come to grief will tide you over somewhat until Double Fine makes a true sequel to Psychonauts.
So a reasonable game, but nothing special.
Edit:
Later on I discovered that there is redemption for these characters, but to get to it you have to trapse all the way through the caves a second time and make a decision that you didn't even know you had right at the end. It's a pretty poor excuse for showing a lighter side to the characters, and it's tedious to unlock. But if you want to see the whole story, then you'll have to double your playtime or otherwise manipulate the autosaves.
This is a small thing, but does not really take away from the message in this review, as it may as well not exist in the first place.

Cuphead is a run and gun Indie game that mimics the animation style cartoons used in the 1930’s. In the game we follow Cuphead and Mugman, who find themselves at the casino one night and in a predicament with the devil. Cuphead, on a winning streak, makes a deal with the Devil himself, and loses the bet. Begging for mercy, the two cups have to repay the debt to the Devil by defeating several bosses, and upgrading their abilities throughout the game by collecting coins found within the run and gun stages. There are 4 main worlds, Inkwell Isle 1, Inkwell Isle 2, Inkwell Isle 3, and Inkwell Hell, each with their own distinct themes. I would definitely encourage someone to buy this game because the soundtrack is simply amazing, and because the art style is absolutely fantastic. However, the game is mostly criticized for its tough difficulty, which has definitely caused me rage several times. In spite of this, the satisfaction of finally beating a run and gun stage or boss feels amazing. The game has won several awards, such as being nominated for ‘Best Soundtrack’ and ‘Better Than I Expected’ in regards to the Steam Awards. You should definitely buy this game!

Cuphead is a challenging shoot em' up game where you essentially play as Cuphead trying to defeat bosses and run and gun through stages. Some bosses can be more difficult than others and most likely would have you get angry at that one boss you have been trying to beat for the last hour. For me, this game is not as hard as I had initially thought once I get the mechanics of each boss, as each boss has a certain mechanic that you need to learn in order to get higher scores and get faster victories. Some bosses can be very bull at times (Honeycomb Herald and Junkyard Jive, if you get farther in the game you will know what I am talking about here), and some bosses can be so simple in their mechanics that you can beat them on your first few tries. The games charm is presented in it's graphics, and the animation style is staggering to say the least, MDHR did a fantastic job at replicating the visuals of cartoons from the 1930's and with it's animation being completely hand drawn, it makes it even more true to the animation of the era.
Overall, it's a challenging game that I recommend everyone check out. It may have some faults but nothing game breaking and the difficulty and graphics make up for it as it took a long time for this game to be made, and it was certainly worth the wait for it and it is a fantastic game.

Is Dead Rising 4 (DR4) worth your money or time? If you enjoy killing zombies then the simple answer is yes. If you're a fan of the Dead Rising series like me, then the answer is of course yes regardless of actual game quality. Regardless, is DR4 a good game?
Dead Rising 4 is indeed a good game if not a great game. It's definitely nothing revolutionary or innovative for the franchise despite the radical change of removing the timer on story mode; giving players the freedome to explore, collect, kill and have fun at their leisure. I'm not naive to the importance of the timer to prevoius installments in the series, its purpose being to serve the game's difficulty&challenge, as well as providing a greater sense of immersion through a sense of literal&technical urgency. However, being that this installment -- similar to DR3, is set in a city rather than an enclosed mall or metropolitan area like DR1/DR2/DR2: Off the Record -- having no timer at all makes sense for allowing players to enjoy killing zombies & exploring the game's large world of some town in Colorado, without worry of losing story progress & having to replay through everything over again. Die hard Dead Rising (DR) fans enjoy pointing to DR4 as the "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child" of the franchise for its lack of a timer & handling of Frank West's character.
Frank West is important to discuss since the voice actor is not the same as Frank from Dead Rising, and his personality is more fleshed out in my opinion instead of simply being completely altered from the first game. His crude and forced humour is purposeful and entertaing to someone willing to give this game a chance on its own & without nostalgia goggles on wishing for a cool & composed Frank just hunting the next big story for journalisitc praise as in the first DR. He's an old man, and if you know any old people in their mid 50's onward they don't really give a ♥♥♥♥, especially old men like Frank who had an overtly selfish nature as a young man as displayed through his character in the first DR. In DR Frank helped survivors because he either had to do it for safety or more importantly journalisitc purposes ("I'v covered wars you know".), and due to an odd emotional attachement here and there.
The story of DR4 itself is fun and simple, making it a joy rather than an over the top hodge podge of randomness that's meant to be appreciated based on the merit of quirkiness *ahem DR3*. Frank is old & wants to play mini-golf (Lul), his university student tricks him into going after an investigation of good ol' Willamette, the destiantion of the first game's outbreak. The events of the story that follow are just as simple and light-hearted, thus maintaining a consistent tone of frivilous fun & humour that matches up with the core of this game: KILLING LOTS AND LOTS OF ZOMBIES FOR THE SAKE OF KILLING.
Gameplay wise this game controls far better than all prevoius entries with a totally revamped control scheme. In this regard DR4 is actually innovative contrary to my introduction to this review. Switching between melee, ranged, and throwable weaponse feels totally natural since using each is not relegated to switching through the D-pad, but rather through simply using the items right away, alternating between all on the fly, through clever mapping of the left and right triggers & bumpers on a controller. Thus, killing zombies has never been more fun and organic in a Dead Rising game.
Graphically this is my favorite DR game, the blood splatter effects are a treat to look at, and them alone are incentive enough for me to hack, slash, shoot, explode, electocute, burn, etc. zombies without a care for any story or franchise integrity. The varied environments are detailed and heavily littered with easter eggs, and a joy to explore, especially since Capcom Vancouver have taken full advantage of Capcom's cache of wonderful franchises (Street Fighter, Mega Man, Bionic Commando just to name a few). The mech suit after beating the game is Megam Man X for God's sake (ILY Cacpcom Vancouver <3)
Since this review is already far too long and I feel as if I still have so much to say about this game, I'll try to sum it up here. Dead Rising 4 is a great & fun game for someone who doesn't take themselves or the Dead Rising franchise so seriously to the point of aristocratic nobility (Lul). This self-aware, comedy driven zombie game is a great deal of fun to the average/casual zombie killing fan. If you're a hard core survival horror fan go play Resident Evil and stop whining about this game not being as serious since it's not meant to be, in fact it's meant to be the opposite. All in all if I had to rate this game I would give it a 7.5/10. It's sligtly above average thanks to its voice acting, entertaining story, lack of timer, enjoyably explorable world, innovative gameplay & graphics in the context of this franchise, and crude humour.
People may say "ohhh but the first DR is serious like Resident Evil so DR 4 & 3 both stray away from what the frachise is about at its core" and my response to this is: no, no it very much isn't. However I am mentioning this in regards to the STORY as in the outbreak of Willamette mall in DR 1 starts after an old lady busts through the barricade holding the zombies back to chase after her poodle....... so the games have always had a wacky story with a somewhat philisophical but not very deep commentary on consumerism.....IN REGARDS TO GAMEPLAY ACROSS THE FRANCHISE It is important to consider that DR 1 & 2's gameplay was more difficult based on the presence of a timer, more punishing zombies, and well designed boss battles (Psychos). DR 4 can be made extremely difficult on "Black Friday" difficulty but it is not gratifying in the same manner or to the same degree of enjoyability as in the original DR because it relies on simply making you take a ton of damage super fast, and making food items give you less health.......it is a challenge ill give em that...... an absolutely terrible one that I went through with for some achievements....... which was not gratifying in a fun way, but rather in a more a annoying & frustrating way..... nuff said? Good day sirs.

More and more aspects build the game from level to level, keeping it interesting and totally immersive.
The game is loooooooong. About 100 levels.
Even after you finish (I haven't yet) all the levels (or before), you can enter a "deep space" mode -
a random mode of the game and compete for the leaderboards, a feature missed in so many other good games.
So, let's recap how your life will be organized if you dare install:
1. Get better and better on your mouse instincts.
2. Progress through the levels (you can also try to get 100% levels if you're hardcore).
3. Find out there are a lot of levels and even more instincts involved.
4. Continue up the levels (collecting "stars").
5. Realize you're addicted and get help.
6. Return from getting help and play indefinitely. FTW.

To any other developers currently working on space survival games, I'm sorry but... it's over.
Osiris is brand new, and this early access release is light years ahead of any other space-based survival game in this genre. It's very rare for me to have an overwhelmingly positive initial reaction to a game, but at the moment I started this game up in single player I could tell this was IT, from the depth of field which made an entire alien planet seem to stretch out before more for miles to the atmospheric effects on my suit's bubble visor, I felt like I had been instantly transported to a seemingly Martian landscape. The realism is absolutely superb. Ark, while a very similar game, doesn't even compare.
There's nothing particularly new in terms of the gameplay, it's the same elements you'd recognize from other games, mine rocks, pick fruit, collect materials, build forges, housing, etc. What's going to set this game apart is the ability to craft mechs, space ships, capital ships and then go out exploring space. It's very much like Empyrion without the building blocks, graphically though there's really no comparison. I only just started, so I haven't had the opportunity to get very far in this regard, but I get the feeling this is going to be a pretty incredible game when it comes to multiplayer PvP.
If I had to compare Osiris to a movie experience it would definitely be "The Martian". It's around the same time period, same technology level, and the setting is obviously very similar. Of course Osiris isn't just about surviving the harsh conditions of an Alien planet, it's also about surviving the hostile attacks of indigenous life forms and the way this has been handled in Osiris is nothing short of breathtaking. There's definitely a cinematic feel to an alien attack, and while Aliens are not common, they can sneak up on you in the dead of night, especially if you're moving around. I like the fact that alien life is sparse and special and that each time you encounter some it's a memorable event.
I highly recommend picking up this game in Early Access. It will likely follow a similar development style as Ark with content updates, new additions and improvements. The game runs great on my Pentium i5 with GTX 970 and 16 gigs of ram with all settings set to max. I recommend playing with your headphones on and your lights off and where possible, with friends.
After you play the game, it feels like an experience rather than a game. Also haunts your dreams.

Surreal and unusual, Plug & Play is a prime example of an art game.

Cryptic as my review might sound, if you end up finding any of these descriptions intriguing in any way, the game is worth your mere 3$ (less on sale). But it's not something you play for enjoyment or fun. It's not something you play for a challenge or to get high scores. And it doesn't really have a story, not in the conventional sense. It's an experience, a sort of Coleridge poem of video games.
If all of this sounds like absolute nonsense and crap. Don't buy it. It's not worth a cent of your money.
If it doesn't. Buy it. The experience is highly potent.

Cuphead is a punishingly hard 2D platformer run and gun/shmup styled after cartoons from the early 1930s. Lovingly hand-drawn, this game is extremely stylish; the whole thing recalls cartoons of the 1930s, from the audio to the visuals to the fonts to the characters in the game. Every bit of this game is bursting with 1930s style; unlike “retro” video games, this is genuinely a game intended to look as if it was made in the 1930s.
At its core, Cuphead is a boss rush game. Most of the levels in the game take the form of some sort of multi-stage boss, which transforms itself into new forms as you fight your way through. There are no hit point indicators in this during the course of a match; you simply have to beat on the boss until it transforms into its next stage, with your hits only registering as brief flashes on the boss to indicate that your attack had indeed scored.
This gives the game a rather intimidating aesthetic, as the bosses are not easy; the game starts off with a couple of fairly simple bosses, but rapidly ramps up to much more difficult fare. By the end of the first world, you’ll be fighting bosses harder than what you see in most 2D platformer games; by the end of the second world, things are even harder.
But you will persevere; the game, while very difficult, also is designed to help you predict the enemy movements, which, while somewhat randomized, are telegraphed (albeit without much time to react in some cases) and can all be dodged. Every level can be beaten without taking a hit – and you’d better get good at dodging, as you only have three hit points.
The bosses operate on 1930s cartoon logic as well, and often involve both pun names and visual puns. The enemies change their attack patterns and often undergo physical transformations – often wild ones – as you fight your way through them. Unlike modern children’s cartoons, at times these could be fairly dark, and the bosses become increasingly intimidating in many cases as the game goes on, while simultaneously often maintaining their comedic air and recalling ideas from the early 20th century like mysticism, hypnotism, and old school circuses and amusement parks.
The game’s core gameplay is pretty simple – you can move around, angle the cursor to shoot at angles (including downwards), crouch and shoot, do an aerial dash, and “parry” pink objects, which absorbs them, bounces your character upwards, and charges your super meter. There are five stages to the super meter, and you have both a basic “super” attack which deals some extra damage and goes through enemies, and a more powerful one that consumes all five super meter stages and gives you a devastating super attack that can chew off about half of a boss stage’s hit points, makes you invincible, or boosts your attack power.
In addition to the boss stages, there are a relatively small number (about 2 per world) of levels that consist of running through a stage beating a series of enemies in a more standard side-scrolling type game. These levels themselves can be fairly challenging (though they’re generally breathers compared to the bosses) and they help mix up the gameplay by incorporating more standard 2D platformer elements.
There are also five or six shmup bosses in the game in the game, where Cuphead is in an airplane fighting against a flying boss. These levels tend to be by far the hardest in the game; you cannot customize the plane’s weapons, which are a preset pair, and the bosses themselves veer into bullet hell territory, as projectiles often fill the screen save for a relatively narrow path. While some of the 2D platformer levels occaisionally have a lot of projectiles, it is the norm for many of the bosses, and oftentimes, these projectiles are a mixture of multiple kinds of projectile, each with their own path, which makes dodging them significantly more challenging – especially given that there are sometimes four different ways in which they can be combined in a single stage of a boss, and which one comes up is the luck of the draw. It is here that the game can feel the most unfair, and the very last of these – a medusa mermaid – is likely the hardest boss in the game, and her attack patterns can feel almost unavoidable at times.
Between the stages, you walk around in a “world map” type thing, where you can interact with a small number of NPCs, who will sometimes challenge you to do things and reward you with a coin, or going to the shop, where you can spend coins to buy new options for your characters. Some are new attack options – such as tracking shots that deal less damage, or the ability to charge up shots like Megaman at the cost of not being able to hold down the button to fire continuously – while others enhance your character in other ways, such as making you invincible during a dash, giving you an extra hit point at the cost of dealing less damage, or automatically parrying when you jump.
This game is fun, but not in the same way that something like Portal 2 is fun. Rather, this is a game which is fun because of its challenge and because the aesthetic pairs nicely with the gameplay. You are going to die if you play Cuphead. You are, in fact, going to die many hundreds of times before you get to the end and win your soul back from the Devil (gambling is bad, kids!). If you don’t like hard games – if you don’t like failing many times while learning the bosses patterns, so that you can finally succeed – you won’t like this game, as repeated deaths while learning the boss patterns is all but inevitable on all but the very easiest stages.
If you like the idea of working hard to overcome a series of difficult mechanical challenges, this game is likely right up your alley. And while the game is hard, it is ultimately fair in its difficulty. The charm of the game helps to make the challenge feel less miserable, and the fact that there is a constant goal hovering ahead of you, pulling you forward, makes it feel like you are, in fact, making progress, no matter how many times you fail. Overcoming the bosses feels really good, and after you beat them, it is remarkable how much easier they are to beat again for a better score. It is remarkable how much better you get at this game simply by playing it, and while it is quite the gauntlet, when you’re done with it, you’ll feel like you’ve earned your victory.

"The Cave" is made by that guy at Double Fine that everybody loves, and has you traverse The Cave attraction, an interactive Cave which has you explore the inner desires of the adventurers (3) that you take control of.
The Cave is brimming with personality and humour, and for the first playthrough (4 hours) if an absolute treat. However, afterwards is where it falls flat.
The game provides you with 7 heroes, each with a different story. Your first playthrough, you can complete 3. Your second you can do another 3, and then you have 1 left over.
Now, a second playthrough has you play 3 more heroes in several identical zones, with no change of Act 1 or 3, just Act 2, meaning the majority of the game is the same as the first run. The last run is even worse, as you need to perform only 1 scenario different with 1 new hero.
This math problem, and poor level/game design, leads you to completing it once with absolutely no desire to do it again, which is a huge shame!
The game is fun and bright and whimsical, and I'd love to complete it again, but I refuse to force myself through recycled content for the sake of completion. I look forward to patches/new DLC (hopefully?) which might improve/resolve this.

This game is as funny and imaginative as you would expect a Double Fine game to be.  It's a adventure game disguised as a platformer.  The game requires replays and that's where things fall apart.  With the exception of the character-specific levels, the game repeats itself.  Despite how clever and funny the dialogue, it can't cover up the fact you're doing a lot of tedious jumping and item placement all the while switching between three characters you have to navigate individually.  And you'll have to play through the game at least three times (six if you don't save before getting the bad endings) just to unlock all the character's cave paintings and see both endings.
Good for an entry-level point-and-click adventure game newbie, straightforward puzzles and a great storyline. Decent replayability too.

In Summary: Don't buy this, even if you are a Double Fine or LucasArts adventure game fan.
I love me some adventure games. The Ron Gilbert name--man behind legendary games Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion-- followed by the Double Fine logo and promotional material (mainly the character trailers) got me to invest in this hybrid game of platforming and item collecting and witty antics that are a staple of adventure games. The Cave fails to capitalize on any strengths of its genres.
Platforming is not fun. The game never tries to make jumping fun or innovative. Most envoirments are just elaborate corridors with road blocks disguised as puzzles at best and "match with the best character's 'get out of jail free power'" at its worst. It never comes close to mimick a traditional platformer. Platforming here is padding to get to the next vender for keys and their doors. The game never challenges your relfex skills, but that's okay because movement is terrible; floaty physics and hit detection, followed by falling death, and it's too simple to die from fall damage. It doesn't take much distance to make vertical space deadly, and you will die because you want to go through areas as fast a possible. Dying makes you respawn, but that can either net closer t your destination or back to redo your mistake again.
Many puzzles revolve around fetching things and making Player Characters (PCs) stand around. You must move each inividual character by controling him or her; there is no way to make the other two characters follow your selected spelunker. The games tries to mediate by having them warp to your controled person on selected events, but it's annoying when a certain puzzle requires two PCs and your nearest comrade is meters away. Multiplyer makes you share the screen. That's bad.
The biggest problem is the characters, or lack thereof. The game already hints at a "dark, terrible secret" in each persona. While it's not a requirement for characters in a story to be likable, they have to be interesting. They are not interesting. None of the PCs talk, only the Cave and minor charactors do. PCs do not attempt to express themselves in other ways. They do not react in in-fame cut-scenes or express any emotion besides waiting, pushing things, and dying. Wall paintings barely flesh out their backstories, but not enough to characterize.
The humor is good. The Cave's monologues are the highlight, and one-liners from other characters are clever, but it's not enough to trench through the along mediocre gameplay and level design.

The game focuses primarily on using more than one character to solve a puzzle, and how you solve a puzzle may depend on what three characters you select at the beginning.  There is a story to each character and every character comes with an extra level of their own to find a solution to.   I've played through once and I'll definitey be playing through again with the other characters.
So it's got a few tricks that were in Maniac Mansion, a similarly grim sense of humour and the obligatory references (keep an eye open for Chuck the Plant!), but it's a lot more linear than Maniac Mansion (definite level progression, not so much exploring one large setting) and characters can only hold one item at a time (no amassing large quantities of stuff and trying to work out things to do with them).   As said, it's not Maniac Masnion reincarnated but it is fun in it's own right. :)

From an idea that builded up for almost 20 years, "The Cave" has finally been released. IMO, this isn't a good game...OR a bad game either. Sure, it burrows its concepts from "Maniac Mansion" (another Ron Gilbert game) and the humor is not that bad BUT the puzzles are sometimes too simple, there's a lot of unessecary backtracking (especially if you're playing by yourself) and with 3 characters to control, it bogs down the game's length and the gameplay. The only time when all 3 characters come together is if you come across a new area in the cave. If only I have 3 other people...
What I DO like about this game is that the level design changes depending on what character you choose (somehow reminiscent of "LIMBO" in how the background changes because of the protaganist's state of mind), and I do love the creativity behind the main idea of choosing a character to enter the cave to explore their darkest traits. For example, on my first playthrough, I picked the Adventurer, the Knight and the Time Traveler and in each area you encounter is suitable for a particular character in a party you decided to choose (for the Knight, a "Princess in a Castle" scenario), which gives you room for replay value to try different characters and venture through the entire game again. Also, the time traveller is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to control. There were a couple of glitches and bugs that I discovered while playing the game. One of them was...THIS:
This game does have secrets and unlockables though but they're very easy to find. You find cave paintings in particular areas of  the cave and you get to unlock artwork. That's just it on what I can say on the unlockables. Not really interesting unlockables either, IMO.
So, to sum up this game in a nutshell, it has a creative idea and story behind it, good replay value and interesting level design based on character support but the game is very easy to traverse through as there is no rule of dying (which deducts the challenge) and its main gameplay bogs the game down as you have to multitask by choosing a character one-by-one and moving them along...like chess pieces. Give this game a try if you want to but I was expecting a bit more.

Alright, let's look at the checklist here...
1) Do you like Grindhouse?
2) Do you like games/movies that don't take themselves seriously?
3) Do you like rail shooters?
4) Do you like shooting zombies?
If you answered no to two of the four, get out of my face.
If you answered yes to three of the four, WELCOME MY BROTHER! Typing of the Dead: Overkill is the game for you! This is a game so cheesy, so badly acted, so violent, so sex filled, and so much damn fun. Even better, it's two games in one!
Typing of the Dead is the simple "type-'em-up" highlight of this title in which you quickly type words to kill zomb- I mean, mutants. The faster you type, the deader the dead. As such it's ironically more adrenaline filled than the original this game was based off of since you'll have to pay close attention to which zombies are closer to you and if any are throwing any projectiles since you'll have to backspace out of the word you're working on to smack that fool. Plus there are three difficulty modes to work with so it's fun for all skill levels!
So let's say you're not very quick on the type, well that's okay! Because Typing of the Dead: Overkill also comes with House of the Dead: Overkill, originally for the Wii, then updated for the PS4, now here in its final perfect twenty-episode long fight form. Surprisingly enough, shooting with your mouse is actually very easy AND fun. While it isn't as rapid fire as the original HotD games have been (minus the boss fights, aka DAKADAKADAKADAKADAKA) there's still a fair bit of precision and skill required if you're aiming for high scores (otherwise, just don't stop shooting). Even better, there's online multiplayer for both modes so coupled with adjustable difficulty levels, relatively well-sized levels, lots of unlockables, additional free and paid DLC word packs, and just good old fashioned rail shooting, you really can't go wrong with this game. If you're really on the edge for this game, just wait for a sale, but seriously, it's cheap enough already for a lot of fun.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is the game that finally got me addicted to roguelikes.
There a several reasons for that. The acessible graphics and interface helped, but what truly sets ToME apart is how it blends the roguelike formula with more traditional RPG elements AND an amazing tactical turn-based combat.
First, it's a roguelike, but you unlock new classses and races as you play, so there's a sense a progression things even if you die. And if you don't enjoy losing your character you can disable permadeth - or give youself some extra lives.
The world is fixed, but races/classes have different starting points and many quests have multiple solutions, so there's always something new to see or try in each playthrough. In one your Psionic Dwarf might become a mage hunter that vows to never use magic items, in the other your Elven Necromancer might join an evil warlock and raid the mage hunters.
Finally, the classes, races and items are all designed to offer you plenty of choices in combat. ToME will throw crazy challenges at you, but it also offers crazy powers - travel back in time, turn into a demon, redirect damage, teleport, raise walls, summon tsunamis, become a lich, etc. It's never about level or DPS - what's important is using your skills wisely.
So if you always wanted to try a roguelike but ADOM, NetHack and other classics never got you hooked, try ToME. :)

Just as a preface, so people don't think I'm some unappreciative punk. Back in the 80s and 90s I adored Sierra On-Line and all their games. The Space Quest and especially the Quest for Glory series are still some of my favorite adventure games of all time. But the Police Quest series just can't hang with any of their other games.
So far, I've only played VGA version of Police Quest I. But it's pretty awful. The VGA era for Sierra On-Line was like an awkward stage in puberty. Gone were the colorful graphics of the first two generations of EGA, and in their place was an absolutely hideous attempt at "realism" rather than stylization and attractive appearance. Additionally, the first generation of point-and-click interface is clunky and difficult to use, mainly because this is a remake of the EGA version, and they've attempted to shoehorn in a lot of the original parser actions into the very limited set of icon actions. So in some places, you can click with the hand icon to use things, like a door, but in others, you have to use the walking icon to use things, like the shower. Because, you see, in the original, you couldn't type "use shower", you had to walk to it. Dur. And the modified driving interface for the VGA version is an utter pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to use.
Outside of that, the actual content of PQ1 for both the EGA and VGA versions is essentially identical, and is embarrassingly 80s in terms of its utter simplemindedness with regard to drugs and the drug war. This was the era of "Just Say No", and some of the hackneyed nonsense that I just absorbed as a child sounds clueless and hopelessly dated today. "I think my daughter is on drugs! Her grades are slipping and she's stealing money from us. Oh and she has nosebleeds." Cringe.
My memories of the second game, which was of the second generation EGA parser style, are all I have to go on so far, but I seem to remember it was pretty decent, although I don't think I quite completed it. The third game was done in the VGA era, and I remember hating the controls and graphics in that one too. There was also an utterly abitrary and impossible to know about part of the game where you had to do something in the middle of the game that affected the ending. But you wouldn't know you'd missed it until the end of the game and it said oh btw sorry you're screwed. Spoiler:
Of course I never bothered to go back halfway in the game and replay it all. I never played the fourth game, so I'm holding out some hope for that one.
And as others have mentioned, the manuals and such that come in this Steam version are woefully incomplete. You'll have to look elsewhere on the Internet to find everything you need to get through even the early parts of the game. Hint: The code for the locker in PQ1 is
.

puts you in the shoes of Corvo Attano, a wronged royal protector, and pushes you onto a quest for bloody revenge -- or for non-lethal justice, depending on your playstyle. And that choice of playstyle is where the greatness of Dishonored comes from.
Face enemies straight on or ghost every map with extreme care. Slay all wrong-doers without mercy or find alternative solutions. Or anything in between. Your tools of the trade include a handful of different weapons, items, and supernatural powers. For instance, the game's signature skill, Blink, allows you to quickly jump around the well-designed levels and makes the gameplay often quite vertical.
Combat is fast and dynamic, especially with speed and jump upgrades that bring in additional fluidity. There is a certain sense of familiarity for those who have played
previous title,
.
Performance-wise Dishonored is well set, running stable on the Unreal Engine 3. The game's textures could definitely be sharper but the art style more than makes up for it. It is by no means an ugly game. The place, Dunwall, looks very authentic for a fictional city that's inspired by Victorian Era London.
One thing I'm not particularly fond of in the game is its chaos mechanic. The world is either in a state of low or high chaos, which is mainly determined by the number of kills you've made. The chaos level affects how NPCs talk and how certain events play out.
Using your lethal gadgets and powers without constraint -- basically having more fun than favoring the non-lethal route that has fewer tricks -- leads to the world's tone becoming darker and more depressing. NPCs get angrier and more agitated. It's an odd dissonance to have in a game -- to take advantage of its full potential and feel bad or severely limit yourself for a happier playthrough.
Apart from that, however, Dishonored is easily one of the best games I have ever played.

As a TL;DR for this review, I absolutely reccomend this game for anyone looking for an alternate art style game that delivers compelling stories with perfectly crafted combat and movement systems.
Dishonored, a game created by Arkane Studios, delves into the world of Corvo Attano, a highly respected assassin who must take back Emily Kaldwin, the kidnapped daughter of Jessamine Kaldwin. Using stealth or outright combat, along with a powers tree that is determined by the player, Corvo must make his way through multiple levels to silence those who oppose him, or to find out information of Emily's whereabouts.
The powers allow the player to choose how they play, they can even play without them. But they supply a whole range of attacks and advantages to Corvo that will shape the game world. For example, killing multiple people will riddle the game world with rats that can attack the player, and harsher enemies. A pacifist style player will see less rats, and a calmer world to deal with. These choices of powers come at a cost.
Throughout the world, players can find runes and bonecharms, the runes will supply the player with powers that they want to use, and the bonecharms offer bonuses such as a certain skill lasting longer, or sneaking quieter. These are just few examples. There is also a currency in the game, to buy equipment and upgrade them. Stealing fancy painting or wallets off of guards without their knowledge is just one way a player can expect to make money.
Dishonored is a game that can be played in so many different ways, and can reward you for doing so. Such as achievements and equipment in the game that tailors itself to a specific playstyle. Anyone new or veteran to a stealthy game like this is easily going to fit in, with just a bit of training with the blade and powers, you'll be the next Corvo Attano.
For my summary, the game is rewarding to a player that likes good play or good story, as the game supplies both at a beautifully high standard. Whilst it may no longer be the best, most cutting edge game or engine out there, it is sure to blow the likes of gamers away with its sheer immersion.

Please capitalize the first letter of the word 'dead' in the title. It bothers me so much.
Half Dead is a game similar to the 1997 film Cube, about a group of survivors navigating their way through a dangerous set of trap rooms. You and your friends are trapped in the maze of rooms, trying to reach the room with the exit, but if you are caught in a room with a trap, you most likely die. However, each player is aided with two shoes, which you can throw into rooms, testing if there is a trap present.
At this point, Half Dead hardly counts as a game. Most games follow the same formula: Throw shoe into room, wait for something to happen. If nothing happens, go into room. If something happens, don't go into room and wait until it is same to retrieve your shoe.
There's no strategy at all. You throw your shoe into a room and hope it doesn't blow up. From what I can tell, there's no pattern as to which rooms have traps versus which rooms don't. in the film Cube, there was a pattern to which rooms had traps. The graphics are fine, but it gets so laggy on public servers that you can barely get above 10 FPS. Not to mention the lack of traps.
Half Dead feels like a really good game that needs to have more variety and be much less random. At this point, I can't recommend it.

Introduction
Assassin's Creed II, takes place during the height of the Renaissance in Italy.
You play as Ezio Auditore da Firenze, the Assassin on a quest for vengeance against those responsible for betraying his family.
The second title in the franchise, adds many features to the game. This includes the Hidden Gun, the ability to swim, a graphics overhaul, some flying mechanics and many refines to combat.
Gameplay
Assassin's Creed II favors stealth over full-on combat.
You can run, ride horses, swim, or use paddle boats to get to your destination.
Parkour has been improved from the first game, which allows for smoother and faster movement and many different animations have been added from the first.
Combat
The combat in this edition of Assassin's Creed, has been improved from it's predecessor, becoming more fluent with appreciated changes, however there is still a sense of button mashing in there and does not require skill which i prefer.
Being able to use the Hidden Gun, will bring a whole new advancement to the game's combat.
You can now purchase armor and weapons, which will increase health and change Ezio's appearance.
Story
As stated above, you play as Ezio Auditore da Firenze.
He starts off the game young and reckless, until his family is hung because of templars wanting to take control. Before his father dies, he learns that his father was an Assassin. Ezio goes to collect his fathers gear and flees the city with his mother and sister to the safety of his uncle Mario's villa in the countryside. As he assassinates his targets, he identifies the mastermind of the plot: the Spaniard Rodrigo Borgia. In modern day you play as Desmond Miles ,who is the ancester of Ezio Auditore, and you are on the run from the modern day templars. Unlike the first game there are more things to do in modern day suc as some missions and a little free roam.
Graphics
Considering the game was released in 2009, it doesn't have the best graphics.
Colors are quite bland, shadows are horrible, and render distance is short.
With a SweetFX patch, and with 4k DSR 60fps, the game doesn't look that bad.
Optimization
Optimization is quite poor in this game.
Frame rate will jump around a lot, no matter the settings you use.
Bugs
Enemies will attack you even when you block them.
Bad performance.
Personal Experience
Beginning of the game is rather boring, and didn't interest me all that much.
Once I got to the middle of the game, I really liked it and was really interested.
Performance wise, I was playing on a RX 480 with everything maxed out at 2560x1080p. I could easily manage 60fps+.
The game was a great improvement from the first game.
Pros
Interesting story.
Loveable main character.
Great landmarks.
Cons
Poor performance.
Micro-stutters.
Bland coloring.
Conclusion
Great improvement over the first game, and gets interesting once you're through half of the game.

The Cave is a fun, enjoyable adventure, but it has a few flaws.
Let us begin with the good things it has to offer. It has a good sense of humor, even though some of it is hit-and-miss. It also does a decent job at managing the multiple stories. You'll be playing with 3 (out of 7) characters at the same time, all with their own story. As a result there's also a bit of replay value there for those who absolutely enjoyed it all the way through.
And while I liked it there were still a few things that bothered me. The first and most obvious are the blurry graphics. Yes, it uses a certain style, but it was still below my expectations. It's nothing groundbreaking, not as a game or an engine, so I expected better here. The characters are well animated though. It reminded me of something... I can't quite put my finger on it. But I do know is that I've seen this animation style before.
The puzzles are actually pretty decent and require some thinking. I had to use a walkthrough more than once. You see, I'm not that bright ;) And except for The Walking Dead (which isn't really a traditional adventure anyway), (point-and-click) adventures usually aren't my cup of tea.
So forgive me if I say that I won't be playing it again with any of the other characters. One playthrough was more than enough for me. Like I said, it's a good game, but nothing extraordinary.
But, you might have an other opinion if you're a die hard adventure player, of course. I myself expected better from a studio that brought us the brilliant Brutal Legend, Psychonauts, Stacking and Costume Quest. You're better off playing any one of those.
