Believe the hype.
Cuphead isn't just a pretty face. I mean it is pretty,
pretty. The 1940s cartoon aesthetic is so spot on there is no room to criticize. The muted contrast colors are remniscient of the old technicolor style. It even has a film grim overlaying each scene, even the loading screen. The number of sprites they drew for this work of art is astounding. And it is a work of art; every boss, miniboss, and trash mob is beautiful to behold with absolutely no palette swapping to speak of. Entering each new level is a like a new present to open and gawk at the wonders inside.
Even sound design is perfect. The sound track is custom made for the game, and the Big Band and jazzy themes are just perfect for the era they are invoking. Explosions, gun play, even the limited voice acting all complements the look & feel they are going for. You can even hear the record player surface noise in between music clips.
But this is still a game. You can't just look and listen to it, you will have to eventually sit down and
. And they nail this too. You've probably heard that this game is difficult, and it is, at least relative to most games. You are highly unlikely to beat any level on your first try. On average expect a dozen attempts per level. But each time you play a level, you will make more and more improvements. You'll recognize patterns, learn how to dodge certain attacks, maybe switch up your weapons to fit the enemies. This is a game where experience is key, and by 'experience' I don't mean some number you are trying to increase to level up, but your experience of learning how to tackle each encounter. When you finally tackle that tough boss you've been plugging at for the last 20 minutes you get that gratifying experience that's like a drug for games like this.
I can best compare it to the Dark Souls series. I don't mean the aesthetic or even game style, but in the sense that the game is hard, and defeat is punishing. Both of them send you back if you fail, with nothing to show for it but a black eye. But once you've learned what your enemies can do, you will start dodging their attacks like it's second nature. And after hitting your head against that wall a few times it'll start to chip.
Cuphead is a Run & Gun game in the vein of Contra. But unlike most games where levels are terminated by boss battles, standard running levels are separated from Boss levels, where you strictly only fight a boss with no preamble. And it's a good thing, too. Having to go through an entire level with 3 hits, only to die during the first phase of the boss would be too punishing, even for Cuphead (well, spoiler alert,
too punishing for Cuphead). There are about 3 times as many Boss levels as running levels, and they are much more enjoyable.
Your move set is basic: Run, jump, shoot, dash/dodge, parry, and a super attack that builds up as your play. There are 6 different types of weapons but rather than being straight upgrades they have their pros and cons. Picking which weapon to use for a particular fight is itself its own puzzle. A handful levels are a bullet-hell style Lifeforce shooter, and are a nice change of pace. Even though the controls are simple, they are tight, responsive, and rarely are you dying through anyone's fault but your own.
I have only small quibbles about the game. The co-op mode is disappointing. Adding a second player increases the health of the bosses, meaning if you wanted to play with someone new or just bad at the game they are going to make it more frustrating for you. Since you both have to dodge the same projectiles, buffing the bosses doesn't make much sense. Lastly, some of the foreground is intentionally placed to obscure your vision of the character. One could consider this part of the challenge, but I found it cheap. Think of someone randomly jumping in front of your computer screen and you'll get an idea of what it feels like.
Cuphead is astounding. It's the most satisfying game I've played all year and is a joy to play. Worth it at full price.

OneShot has everything you'd look for in a game like it - plentiful characters with varying personalities, many immersive environments, and a soundtrack to get you in the mood for playing. The world around Niko - the main protagonist that adventures alongside you - feels super alive and there's plenty to explore and see.
The game also puts off many moods - at times it can be warm & cuddly or comedic. Other times, things take a sort of dark and depressing turns. Not every game can pull this off correctly, but OneShot definitely did.
The puzzles are clever, and even challenging/confusing at times. I've found myself completely stumped a lot of the time, and the only hint I can give you in regards to that is sometimes you'll need to "look outside the box" - literally.
All in all, OneShot is an experience that I have enjoyed myself, and for that I definitely recommend it to others who are looking for a puzzle game with a nice story, characters, and world.

I really like this game and it had a lot of potential, but I do not recommend it to anyone unless they want to play single player or you genuinely want to support the developers of the game. I have a decent setup (gtx 1070 with an i5 6500 and 16gb ddr4 ram) and on multiplayer i was averaging 15fps which was just terrible. Apparently even though the servers only carry up to a max of 12 players, It was impossible to build anything because apparently there was a structure limit on the planet.This literally stops you from progressing through missions because you HAVE to build a base and some utilities along with a habitat. I feel like all the features are dumbed down a bit. For example, I was killing some enemies and I know for a fact that my pistol would not take out half the alien's hp but it's like the ai just "quits" and dies. In my personal opinion, I like to build bases block by block if possible or component by  component so having pre built structures to place is kind of a turn off. I don't think i ever used anything from the survival kit which was a shame because I thought I had to keep an eye out on my hunger/hydration levels. There's also some kind of frame rate cap in the game (you cannot go into the config files to change this)  which you can't turn off so in sp mode, you're stuck at a certain framerate (depends on your build). The UI, in my opinion, is not very well polished. You can't really transfer items except by clicking and dragging them between inventory spaces. Forges for example, don't recognize their own inventory. so here's a tl;dr pros and cons
+ sp plays at a solid framerate with minimal issues
+ unique flora and fauna really makes them feel "alien"
+ games looks really good
+ potentially an amazing game in the future
- Servers have 12 player limits.
- Servers have a structural limit.
- Game breaking bug which cannot let you alt tab out of the game.
- Fps cap that can't be removed.
- Multiplayer fps makes game almost unplayable online.
- UI needs a lot of work.
- You will always have at least one resource that is almost impossible to find.
- Features are dumbed down.
- Some enemies just "quit" fighting you and die half way into battle.
- Does not make me feel like I'm working towards my survival since running out of resources isn't really a concern.
If you want to support the devs and knowing that you won't see a well done multiplayer set up for a while, the by all means buy the game. You can still have fun in single player and there's a lot to for a game that just came out into EA. If you just want to play a multiplayer game that has to do with survival and expect to have a well made multiplayer system, then you will not find it here yet and this is why I can't recommend this game to anyone right now.

Don't get me wrong. I LOVE me some TotD, and giving this title a thumbs-down was not an easy decision for me to make.
TotD: Overkill, based on the extended version of House of the Dead: Overkill, features 4 main characters: Agent G, Detective Washington, Varla Guns, and Candi Stryper. With bullets and F-bombs, they fight their way through hordes of zombies (er, mutants) to take down the man behind the infestation.
There are 9 chapters in the campaign and 2 game modes: Typing of the Dead and House of the Dead. In Typing of the Dead, each enemy has a word or phrase attached to them, and you need to type the word/phrase in order to kill that enemy. There are 3 difficulty levels and a Hardcore Mode which requires you to type the spacebar in phrases containing more than one word (normally, you can ignore spaces). In House of the Dead you use the mouse or a controller to move a cursor around the screen and shoot. You can also buy different guns and upgrades using money found in the levels. I've beaten the whole story in TotD but not HotD, so most of my points below are directed toward TotD.
What I like:
+ The tiered combo system is a nice improvement from the old combo bar in the first TotD.
+ Throughout each level, you can find different unlockables which include 3D character models, posters, and pieces of music that are accessible through the game's main menu.
+ Some of the words that you type are unique to each level, like carnival-related phrases in the carnival level or law-related phrases in the prison level, which I think is a nice touch.
What I don't like:
- The story and presentation is clearly a tongue-in-cheek parody on cheesy action movies (deep-voiced narrator with corny puns, characters dropping the F-bomb every 10 seconds, lots of explosions, etc.), but the humor in that falls off pretty fast as the game goes on.
- Even on "Motherf*cker" difficulty, it's pretty easy. The later levels only feel slightly harder than the earlier levels, and (light SPOILERS) the final boss battle is creative but very anticlimatic.
- The House of the Dead game mode is a nice feature to have, but I don't think the mouse cursor has the same precision and accuracy as a light gun, making the experience a bit frustrating.
- There are numerous graphical and audio glitches.
- All civilian encounters have mini-cutscenes, making them feel more scripted and less spontaneous, which (in my opinion) defeats the purpose of having civilians.
Overall, I'd be lying if I said that it's not fun. However, I think it's worth closer to $10-$15 rather than its current $20 pricetag.

Please capitalize the first letter of the word 'dead' in the title. It bothers me so much.
Half Dead is a game similar to the 1997 film Cube, about a group of survivors navigating their way through a dangerous set of trap rooms. You and your friends are trapped in the maze of rooms, trying to reach the room with the exit, but if you are caught in a room with a trap, you most likely die. However, each player is aided with two shoes, which you can throw into rooms, testing if there is a trap present.
At this point, Half Dead hardly counts as a game. Most games follow the same formula: Throw shoe into room, wait for something to happen. If nothing happens, go into room. If something happens, don't go into room and wait until it is same to retrieve your shoe.
There's no strategy at all. You throw your shoe into a room and hope it doesn't blow up. From what I can tell, there's no pattern as to which rooms have traps versus which rooms don't. in the film Cube, there was a pattern to which rooms had traps. The graphics are fine, but it gets so laggy on public servers that you can barely get above 10 FPS. Not to mention the lack of traps.
Half Dead feels like a really good game that needs to have more variety and be much less random. At this point, I can't recommend it.

What an absolute joy of a game. And this really is as pure of a game as I've played in a long time.
You have a small ball of light trying to traverse the cosmos (various maps set against a back drop of space) by way of a sine wave. You control its travel by altering the sine wave...move the mouse up / down and the amplitude (height) grows / diminshes...move the mouse left / right and the frequency increases / decreases (how steep it goes up / down). Hit power ups, multipliers, and various other typical point scoring devices to get a high score and progress from map to map. Dodge black matter and various other space based hazards otherwise you lose points / fail the map.
The basic gameplay structure (points based map completion) is old hat, but the mechanic of controlling  something via manipulation of a sine wave is unique and utterly appropriate for the simple premise of the game. Combined with a an excellent soundtrack (which somehow manages to combine a light hearted sound with something suitable to wandering through the depths of space) you'll find yourself smiling as you play this wonderful game.

Purchasing Waveform when it's on sale is a no-brainer. The game runs fantastic on linux, and offers a huge amount of content for those who become enamored with its simplistic formula: hidden levels, endless mode, challenge levels, chase sequences, and mechanics exclusive to levels are used to great effect.
The initial campaign has a solid pace (for the beginning), with new aspects being spinkled in frequently and gradually becoming more difficult, and should last around 8 hours. However, towards the late game, you will be required to grind to gain access to the game's later levels if you score below a certain threshold consistently, as I did. Fortunately it's not too much of a chore to do so, since your skill at the game will allow you to easily ace the earlier levels.
All in all, Waveform is stellar if you can afford the pricey 19 cent pricetag. It'll lure you in with its bargain, and pleasantly surprise you with its quality.

Short Review: You're just a jump from finishing the level, at 1HP, and a FREAKING BOSS shows up MID JUMP.
10/10 Would jump towards a surprise beating again.
Long Review: I still haven't got through the first Isle, but damn! This game is something else!
I came from Super Mario Odyssey feeling the game was too easy, and therefore short. Me and my uncle got through it in pretty much a single day.
Cuphead, on the other hand... OH OH OH... BOY! You're in for a beating! A very cruel and repetitive one indead, but oddly satisfying because it is actually challenging, and absolutely thrilling when you get through the GOD DAMN LEVEL!
The visuals are surpreme. The music... (I bought the game mostly for the DLC Album). And the gameplay... makes me feel like a child "gitin gud" again... except that I'm pretty much through a third of my lifespan already. And this game might be making me physically old, but mentally younger!
The sense of improvement is easy to notice after a while. You'll be speeding through the first half of the level almost automatically after a while, and repeating levels may surprise you to how easy they feel compared to the very first try.
Timing is everything. Once you memorize the spawn rates, platform movements and enemy attacks you'll start going through those "sweet spots". If you get killed the first time you reach a certain point in the level. Don't get frustrated. You probably didn't know what was going to happen, nor how you should react. JUST TRY AGAIN, WHINER!
Also, it is worth pointing out that, for those who've never played Run and Gun platformers, you should forget about some of the traditional tropes from Sonic, Mario and other similar titles. It's basically like Soviet Russia: Jumping on enemies doesn't kill them. IT KILLS YOU!
And, finally, don't play this game when you're full of♥♥♥♥♥♥to do. Leave it for holidays or something. Unless you have time to dedicate for this game, you won't be able to get through it anytime soon. Also, ask someone to play with you as well. BF/GF, friends or family, get along! Play this game! Have fun! And try to get through it casualy... please... don't start beating up each other/breaking up because of the game... -.-
A phsycological tip: Practice a lot, but also sleep well. During your sleep you'll unconsciously get through the day, and improve some of the skills you've been practicing during the day. When you pick up Cuphead the next day, you'll be surprised how well you seem to do the same exact stuff. This applies to pretty much everything. A good night sleep will help you A LOT. A bad sleeping habit WILL make everything WORSE.

Have you ever wanted to start your buy and sell gun business? Gun-Running War Dogs lets you do that. I saw this game on sale for like 0.69 USD and decided to pick it up because it looked interesting. I instantly loved the art style, mechanics and the background music that plays ingame.
You start by signing deals and buying the guns from the black market in order to make profit. You start with deals that earn you 100-500 USD profits and as you progress, you start getting 20000+ USD deals after earning more rating stars, which is basically your reputation in the market.
Managing your office is really cool and I love the variety of items and rewards each level of it offers. You move offices and get new items (hookers and bodyguards/thugs on couches, big as$ 70" TVs, bongs, tables, file cabins and so on) to throw your money on and decorate your office. You also earn weapon and self protection upgrades for your character and bodyguards as you level up your office.
The firefights are fun and balanced imho. It can be either you or the dealer you're buying from who starts it. But sometimes they can be really annoying because you could lose a lot of money if the dealer has no guns and decides to open fire on you in an attempt to rob you.
Overall, the game is really cool, fun and addicting! Even though I got it on sale, it is more than worth its full price. Get it and start your gun dealing empire!

1) The pace of this game has been accelerated and the dynamic is in a very good place, not just compared to its original state but for a game of this type in general. It is a genuine 4v1 at all stages of the game now where all players have a role, contributing and interaction with each other in meaningful ways. The main problem with the games previous version was that either the monster got caught and killed early with no counter play or the monster evaded the hunters for eight minutes straight and at the end of the turkey chase there was a stage 3 monster, which again had no counter play. This has been smoothed out so that interactions between hunters and monsters are frequent and meaningful, but counter play is still available to both teams.
TL:DR The game is in a good state for both sides, unlike the previous version.
***FOUNDERS NOTE***
If you previously purchased the game you get a significant amount of free content and 30,000 keys PLUS additional content in the future. I am a founder and the exclusive content in actually quite unique.
2) The amount of variety from match to match is actually surprisingly high. Most characters play so vastly different that changing one of them from game to game is enough to make both sides drastically alter their strategy. The skill cap for the both teams is in the knowledge of how the hunters work together and how to employ a players abilities to best compliment the team, or crush it in the monsters case. The progression for unlocking content is fairly well paced and players are awarded unlocks for completing tutorials in addition to a free week rotation for both hunters and monsters.
TD:DR You won't get bored after the first couple dozen matches.
3) The game is very well optimized and performs almost flawlessly, with no noticeable lag, tearing, graphical shuddering, or anything of the sort. Matchmaking, on the other hand, is currently quite buggy especially when trying to play with a party.
TL:DR 8/10 for under the hood dev work.
4) I will say this is my one complaint: the cat and mouse dynamic of the game is completely gone. Stealth is completely removed from the monster's side and with the global tracker, evasion is almost impossible to achieve at any stage to the game. The functionality changes to the dome make interaction mandatory which, while this does lead to much more satisfying game play for all hunters who aren't the trapper, it does feel like a lost game play option when playing the monster. I would like to see some alternate way for the monster to evade hunters rather than being forced to sit in the dome and brawl it out until one side or the other is obviously losing. A small loss for us old-timers, but new players will be blissfully unaware of anything they never had.
TL:DR Veteran players get salty when anything about a game they play changes. Nothing new.
***Final Thoughts***
I would recommend anyone looking for a competitive and unique game pick this up, I mean it IS free. The characters are well developed and the story line that you learn about as you play is actually quite interesting. There really is a chance this game has a Diablo III level revival with these changes. Happy hunting!

Don't give me that BS about using the scanner to my advantage, as a new player I barely know how to FIGHT as a monster, let alone manipulating the terrain when hiding is impossible and so is growth.

All in all, Turtle Rock needs to nerf hunters before I'm going to try to play this game again. Make the cooldown on the global scanner higher, take away the baby-cage from everyone but the trapper, anything to make the game playable!
Thus, I will say that I do NOT recommend this game. At least, until there is some balancing.

So I finally got this and completed it.
It's definitely showing its age not only graphically but also gameplay wise. The freerunning was still at its infancy here and it requires pressing 2 keys to do it ( which, naturally, brought a lot of problems until they figured a way to make it work with just one key) - so expect a lot of frustration. Plus, there's the keyboard and mouse aspect... These games were developed for consoles and controllers, not KB&M - and it definitely shows. Still, you can mostly get around this except for a few areas where the lack of a joystick shows.
Story wise, it's fairly good: Enzo's a likeable guy and you get to meet a lot of characters from the history books. They did overdo it a bit when putting Machiavelli as an assassin - but it's something you can overlook. There's also a "vibe" that you just haven't seen since AC3 - which mainly comes from Desmond's story arch and his encounters with the precursors.
Soundtrack is classic Jesper Kyd...nuff said.
Overall, 8/10. Recommended to fans of the series and even casual players, like myself, who may be looking for a good game to immerse themselves in when they want to kick back a bit and relax.

This game is drastically better than the first in the series but still lacks something needed to make it fun for me. I can't quite put my finger on it but I found myself frustrated and angry the majority of the time while playing this title.
Much like its predecessor, the controls are wonky and annoying when you use a keyboard which leads to some frustrating moments when you are up against the clock or trying to chase after someone that you can't fall too far behind.
Also like its predecessor, the combat is fun to watch but extremely slow paced and makes the game feel like it is dragging on longer than it needs to.
The story is fun though and the voice acting is pretty good. The map and environment looks a lot better than the first game in the series but to make it run smooth I had to enable 'Max Pre-rendered frames - 4' in my control panel. RIFT is a classic style fantasy MMO that went the rout of doing everything you are used to very well rather than striking out into uncharted territory.  The leveling is well paced and moderate in speed, the class customization is excellent, balanced and diverse, the end game content is rich and satisfying and the graphics are shockingly good.  For those of you who have played the Warhammer MMO, you will recognize some of the PvP but it has been polished and some of the early simple games never get old because of balance and fun.
The game is really solid for both players that love to group and those who like to go it alone.  There are several types of events that require groups to complete that have a simple join feature allowing you to participate without having to create premade parties.  There is also more than enough content for those who like to collect things and there is a very rich reward system for doing so.
I cannot recommend this game enough for classic MMO fans.  The only drawbacks are the character animations are still and unrealistic and the game really is nothing you have never done before.  However, once you try it I think you will find it to have plenty of unique takes on some of the best aspects of this genre.

I gave it my first full playtrhough on the PC version after playing through a small part of it on 3DS. It took about 6 hours, which is more or less what I expected of a fast-pace action-platformer. Good amount of content, especially for the money.
The graphics are great, but with the PC version being a near-direct port of the 3DS version, the graphics are identical, with possibly some exceptions here and there- just scaled up to fit a larger screen. I definitely give the PC version slightly lower praise in regards to that. The double-screens being optional for the most part was nice. It made the in-game experience more enjoyable, especially for myself, since I have trouble reading the 3DS's smaller screens (including the New 3DS XL's much-larger-in-comparison's screens). However, some cutscenes were placed into dual-screen mode for what seemed like no discernable reason, which felt odd.
The soundtrack, sound effects, and voice acting* were great. (*Since I played with Japanese Voice Mode on, I heard the entire game in Japanese with the original Japanese text translated into English, as opposed to the English localization.) All of Lumen's songs had nearly the same vibe, likely to keep the gameplay hype going, but the lack of variety in AZURE PHOSPHORESCENCE (as a result) caused me to lower my opinion just a little bit. Other oddities include the "Boss Defeated" jingle, which feels strangely lackluster compared to the rest of the soundtrack.
The story was great! I really like all of the characters in the game, and I'm honestly a little disappointed there isn't much more of (most) of them to see. However, a particular set of character arcs became wildly uncomfortable in my experience due to the way it was written and portrayed as the story wrapped up, and the True Ending leaves too much to the imagination and does little to actually close the story besides leaving it there. Speaking of, there is a Bad / True ending system in the game, where even if you meet all the necessary requirements otherwise, you can't access the True ending until you've seen the Bad one- and have been subjected to the game credits once already. (Almost the exact same credits reel repeats when you complete the true ending, and all though you can make the text scroll faster, you can not skip it.)
The in-stage gameplay feels fantastic at almost all times. Everything controls tightly and even though your fingers will become a little tired after a few hours, I have very few complaints about the in-stage gameplay. Some checkpoint placement is weird. The seven jewels- which you need to access the True ending- are almost always nearly in plain sight or completely overlookable. (One that is easy to miss, upon looking it up online, suggests speed-run-like strategies to acquire it before explaining that it is, in fact, a puzzle.) Dying is sometimes your best weapon, as Lumen (also known as Joule) will occassionally revive you and boost your abilities ten-fold.
The out-of-stage gameplay is often a blend of visual-novel like interactions with Joule, reading mission briefings, accepting "challenges" for when you replay stages, and trying to figure out what materials you need in order to synthesize new gear, which can be equipped to Gunvolt to add a variety of additional, generally useful effects. This creates a "material farming" grind, which unfortunately is not my cup of tea, but the optional challenges give each stage more replay value and make the grind feel less grindy.
Since I've mentioned the True ending requirements a few times, I feel like I felt it was a tad odd that in order to access the True ending, you have to sacrifice your access to one of the game's staple mechanics (or, if the player has already ditched it, an item that provides some other boost in capabilities), in order to equip essentially nothing in its place. I understand that the developers might have felt the need to have the player "earn" the True ending- and maybe story-wise it makes some lick of sense- but it felt poor, considering accessing the True ending means you get the mechanic back before the credits roll again anyways.
I've watched players speedrun the game using the speedrun mode. Seems like a great addition, and I'd love to try it out for myself at some point soon.
I definitely recommend this game to those looking for a good action-platforming experience, desiring good plot or otherwise. There are several sections of the game that feel completely great, but there are a slight few that, depending on your mindset, you will either feel neutral towards them or discomforted / discontented by them.

I came to this game looking for something that would appeal to my nostalgia for Mega Man Zero. To me, that means retro anime-ish visuals, a fast-paced mix of platform and run-and-gun gameplay, exciting and challenging bossfights, and a colorful cast of characters in a plot that at the very least explains why everyone is fighting. That's all I wanted, and that's exactly what Azure Strike Gunvolt delivered.
I hope the sequel comes to Steam too.

OneShot is hands down my favorite game I have ever played. The artwork, story, everything is beautiful and instantly hooks you in. My favorite ending is the solstice one which completely changed the story and had wonderful characters, custscenes, and dialogue. As soon as possible, I will be getting my friends to play this as well. It's quite an experience. Protip: Read all of the dialogue, look at all the things, and read every book/sign/paper for the best experience.

In an age of soulless cash grabbing game titles and the absolute absence of innovation, of any feeling of "love" put into the work, OneShot is about as refresing as a cold sweet tea in 100 degree heat.
If you're looking for "gameplay" in its typically understood sense, that being action or other sense-stimulating activities, you're not going to find too much here. But OneShot isn't about chewing through baddies or dodging projectiles. If it was, that's not where it would shine. No, play this game for its narrative, its context, and its interaction with YOU. Read, explore, get to know these characters. Get immersed. Get engrossed. Trust me, the game makes it easy for you. Sink your teeth into it and don't let go until the journey is done.
I don't praise modern games lightly, there's a lot to criticize these days. Indie games in particular get the magnifying glass from me. This passed all tests. Whatever it lacks in one department, it makes up in the delivery of much more than you could possibly ask for in others.
I was recommended this game by the YouTuber and ameteur critic, MisterCaption. A quick perusal of his channel will reveal his extremely critical, almost brutally cynical, opinions on video games and their flaws. Not this one. He told us to go play it straight away. I was not let down.
I was shocked. At the end I was nearly in tears. You will be too.

The Typing of The Dead: Overkill is the game I wish I had back in grade school. It's crass, vulgar, and at times cringeworthy. I loved every second I've spent with it.
There is a point-to-shoot version of the game packaged along, but Typing is what really makes this game shine. Between the different DLCs and the standard set of words I was giggling the entire way from start to finish. Don't worry about your typing being slow or not up to par, there's a difficulty mode for everyone. If you're looking to improve your typing skills and words per minute then I can think of no better way then a few afternoons with The Typing of The Dead: Overkill.
That all out of the way, it does fall flat during cooperative play. There is a noticable amount of lag that combined with my partner's finger-pecking typing style led to some very annoying situations. Despite that I maintain that as both an educational tool and as a novelty game Typing of The Dead: Overkill stands proudly above the crowd.
Edit: They added custom dictionaries, which translates to player-made banks of words for the game to choose from. The community has created everything from multi-language translated packs to a complete dictionary. ...And yes, Internet Memes and Porn jokes. The only downside is that these DLC and Workshop dictionaries don't work with the cooperative multiplayer element.

Did you like the original Typing of the Dead? Are you a luddite who needs help learning to type? Did you feel that Planet Terror needed a video game adaptation? Then you might like Typing of the Dead: Overkill!
You know the deal already, you type words to kill zombies and other monsters. I would say that the word selections surprised and delighted me, though I am unhappy that they released extra dictionary files as paid dlc and not, you know, free because they're just word lists.
If you have a light gun or get bored by the whole "type to kill zombies" they also include a regular "shoot to kill zombies" mode, which is not nearly as fun.
There's dialogue in this game. It's dumb and sexist and stereotypical. They actually make ingame reference to how dumb and awful it is, but this does not stop it, being kind of a staple of the exploitation films it's aping.
I recommend that you BUY THIS if it's a steam sale and this game is $5 or under.

A simple game that starts to get more involved as you progress. It's a neat game that does well to pass time and it's satisfying to find the perfect "track" to collect all the light.
The game is a bit tedious in the sense that it's not incredibly hard to run into moving obstacles while on an awkward wavelength and having to subtly adjust constantly to avoid getting hit, which may have you miss a lot of light in the process of not following a certain path. I don't know if I would've paid the full $5 for this game but I would say it's worth the current $0.19. If you don't mind those things, or a game that starts to slowly become more challenging while keeping its mainly casual feel, I'd recommend this game.

So to go about 1km it will take you about 5-10 minutes (one way) of walking to HOPEFULLY find the plutonium and titanium (resources do not render into view unless you are about 100 m from them so good luck trying to actually plan where to go before you know where they spawn) you need to build the forge and then try to manage the weight of it to bring it all back. THis is literally how the game goes. grinding in a survivaly game in some areas is a necessity.... but usually has some interesting points to it... this game... the grind is literally walking around bored stupid trying to find basic resources which all involve being hit with a hammer so you can bring it back to the base.

Without spoiling the plot, short story short you end up working at the resort after you arrive. Everyone there is female of course and they want you big time. . In the two currently present chapters your decisions make no difference apart from a few changed sentences. 5 out of the 7 women in the game's banner art will offer themselves to you no matter what you do, the rest doubtless to follow in later chapters. The actual plot is brought up only occasionally and you just spend your time chatting up the ladies so far.
The game's artwork on the whole is fine, but it's scarce. There's one girl you actually do a fair number of non-bed activities with, but all you get are some sentences over the area's background CG and character portrait instead of art to capture the moment. It's no secret that this is an X-rated game and a big selling point for the Steam version is that there's an official uncensor patch. Without the patch you end up getting a pink screen transition to the next scene with lipstick marks just before nudity would occur. What do you get with the patch? The image that normally transitions away has layers of clothing disappear as you get dialogue with oohs and ahhs. The image is always just the girl splayed out so don't expect much variety.

Very interesting game in general, in its current form, I personally think it is 60-75% complete in terms of core mechanics and gameplay, but only 50-60% complete in terms of the full experience.
Playing this game reminds me of Star Citizen, how it promised many things and indeed, those promises are being fulfilled one by one, but also the abysmal amount of bugs and frame rate drops in the game.
Some Pros and Cons then!
Pros:
-Fairly completed game, even in its early release stage, many things to craft and advance with.
-Healthy amount of buildable and craftable objects, mechs, vehicles, and expanding the colony all seemed diverse.
-Impressive graphics, guns mechanic is good, terrain and mines have very impressive textures, creatures are very well done.
Cons:
-Bugs and glitches, if the developers can see this review I would like to report cases where if you are in a cave and you look up, you can see and shoot at structures, creatures, and mines above ground, please fix this! Also: in a game sometimes some creatures move without animation, i.e. they just shift around, please fix this too! It kills the experience so much!
-Frame rate fluctuation, most of the time frame rate is fine, but you don't always feel so comfortable about it as you play it.
-Way too expensive objects for startup: 1 steel plate requires 2 iron ore, 1 magnesium (very hard to find), and 1 aluminum (moderately hard to find), it is just exhausting work to roam the terrain to find these things.
-RPG system is DEFINITELY far from completion, I played for hours and crafted a habitat (a lot of work to build) with NO level advance.
-Water, a necessary supply to replenish thirst, is non-existent in its natural form on (at least) the planet I played on.
-I don't know how the "temperature" system of this game works, but indicators show that environmental temperature can drop down to -300 degrees celsius sometimes. Now I know absolute zero is -273.15 degrees celsius, so...developers planning to fix this??
-Official servers have rediculous frame rate drops, I only have 3-5 fps on official servers while I can maintain 30-45 fps on private universe.
Despite all that con, I don't think the game would disappoint players when the developers complete it, my friend and I opened up a private universe and we had a lot of fun even at its current condition. Right now I don't see very lethal disappointments that would make me not recommend this game, so I would, at its current stage, maintain a recommendation for this game.

If you were looking for any kind of successor to Mega Man, then this game is by far the closest to it. Azure Strike Gunvolt manages to be both the Mega Man X AND Mega Man Zero spiritual sequel I always wanted. The action is fast, the platforming is precise, and the boss battles are tricky but satisfying.
The battle system, and overall gameplay as a result, is less about highly lethal enemies with tough patterns; it’s more about figuring out their simple ticks and defeating multiple enemies at once using your electric chain attacks. The bullets from your weapons do damage, sure, but the electricity you use to shock multiple enemies is what hits hardest, and it’s what keeps the action flowing. You mark multiple enemies, then you shock them with your powers. You’ve also got a devastating arsenal of super moves, complete with a flashy intro sequence for each one. The bosses also do the same thing! Honestly, this is one of the few truly ‘innovative’ games I’ve played in recent memory, and while it likely won’t appeal to all, due to the repetitive nature of the mark-and-shock gameplay, it’s still a refreshing adventure.
The story is some very typical anime nonsense (in a good way), and the characters are the usual assortment of anime tropes (once again, in a good way). The character designs are cool enough though, and you can clearly see the inspiration for a lot of the bosses, as well as Gunvolt himself (obviously, with the blue outfit and gun). The anime aesthetic is strong throughout, extending to the JPOP songs you hear in the game every so often. The music itself is awesome; frantic, subtle, tense. Each track fits the relevant stage, encounter and scenario you find yourself in. Gunvolt’s personality and motivations are hit or miss, depending on what you’re looking for in a sci-fi action hero, and your mileage of interest will vary just as much for the rest of the cast as well.
One of the major appeals of AZG is the reward for replaying. After completing a stage for the first time, you can instantly jump right back in to shoot for a higher score, a faster completion time, finding hidden secrets, or just levelling up. The game allows many different approaches, and none are particularly penalized. You can customize Gunvolt to equip new weapons, gear, skills, and improve your current skills using better materials. Each skill and ability could potentially lead to a unique run of a level each time!
The challenge of the experience isn’t all that punishing, in fact, due to having infinite continues and checkpoints. However, you can easily choose to make the game as hard as you want it to be, by not equipping useful skills/gear, attempting to mark the maximum amount of enemies at one time, or aiming for no-damage speedruns. Like many modern 2D platformers, it manages to appeal to an easy-going casual audience, whilst also allowing enough room for the hardcore crowd to find something to test themselves with. This is accentuated by in-game challenge missions which require special, difficult completion parameters, and they net you decent rewards. The bosses are of varying difficulties, and a special recurring boss tends to be somewhat tougher than the rest. The final boss does provide a slightly jarring difficulty spike, but once you figure out the trick to it, it’ll be much easier overall.
AZG is a very cool idea, and it’s awesome to see IntiCreates, the team responsible for the Mega Man Zero series that I adored in my teenage years, at the helm of this new exciting IP. AZG 2 is currently out for 3DS, and there doesn’t seem to be any announcement of a Steam version just yet, but I can hope so! I’m really glad I finally got to play this game, and I’m definitely a fan of the Gunvolt franchise.

OneShot
What: OneShot is a puzzle adventure game that plays similar to older point and click adventure games, but does so from a top-down perspective. This means you'll travel around collecting items and using them in combination with other items or the environment to solve a puzzle the game has put in your path. OneShot also makes use of the 4th wall as a central mechanic for both telling the story and solving some of the game's puzzles. This constant breaking of the 4th wall is the central mechanic to the game.
Pros:
The use of the 4th wall for narrative delivery. OneShot liberally breaks the 4th wall, not only acknowledging the existence of the player, but it also has the main character of the game, Niko, speak directly with the player throughout. This gave me an increased feeling of agency in the story as Niko was directly interacting with me, which made me feel a lot more invested in what was happening than I would have otherwise. Normally with these kinds of games I feel like the game is playing itself and I'm simply observing things unfold, but this direct channel of communication between the main character and myself helped to keep me invested and interested in the story.
The use of the 4th wall for puzzles. Along with using the 4th wall to deliver OneShot's story, Oneshot also uses it as a way to create puzzles.
These kinds of puzzles had me thinking about how to solve puzzles in different ways than what I have seen in other games and I really liked that about them.
The game is short. OneShot is about a 4 to 6 hour experience. It is a nice compact experience that doesn't outstay its welcome and keeps a relatively brisk pace throughout. I found this aided the game greatly because it was finished before I became tired with the 4th wall breaking mechanic that OneShot has at its core and also wrapped up the story with there being only short segments of downtime.
Cons:
There wasn't any overarching problem that stood out to me while playing the game. I'll acknowledge that some, or all, of the factors I found enjoyable about the game wouldn't be fun for everyone, but I found OneShot both fun and refreshing for the reasons stated above.
Rating: I enjoyed it. Would recommend to fans of puzzle games or fans of games that utilize the 4th wall.

I've considered a lot before writing this review; Is this game a cash grab or is thiis game just flat; is this game worth the price of admission or is it overpriced; is Frank West just being used to make money? From what I understand from the plot, Frank West is on a new expedition rather than surviving a zombie Outbreak. The element of time wouldn't matter so much in these circumstances but time elements could have definitely played a role in this game. When I think about The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask and how it used random events over a timed 3 day period, I wonder why this game didn't do the same with saving survivors or somewhat important events to the story. I guess the popular assesment that this game was simply a cashgrab is more conducive to the flat feel of this game.
I myself have fun with every horror game, good or bad. There really isn't a bad Horror in my opinion, since it is all about the imagination. This game falls more in line with a "Zombie Killer' which is a sub genre of horror that I like to call games like this. The Zombies are the horror but then again they're more like padding than a part of gameplay. Unlike previous games, I'm not afraid to run through a pack of zombies. The Zombies are way too weak, In comparison to the aformentioned zombie threat, Dead Rising Case Zero is a true Zombie Experience. Case Zero has greatly timed elements as well as a Zombie threat that makes running through a pack of them more on the line of fatal endeavor. Zombies in Dead Rising 4 are more or less easy kills because of the huge health bar and ridiculous weapons. After awhile the Zombies of Dead Rising 4 just seem to melt into the background as an annoying gameplay feature.
The threat that makes this game a Horror is so weak that it isn't a Horror. When I imagine myself in Frank West's shoes with super strong weapons and a gigantic grip on life, I don't see why this game is something I could recommend people. There are some wonderfully awful Horror games out there like BadMojo, Resident Evil Survivor, and Obscure but Dead Rising 4 can't be considered among them because Dead Rising 4 is utterly flat. It's a bottle of Coke that has set out in the sun for 6 minutes and is now half warm and cold. Vomit inducing and good only at the beginning because you haven't tasted the samey flatness to come.

Very enjoyable and fun addition to the dead rising series. Personally I did not have any technical issues with the game. It is easier than the previous Dead Rising games and a lot more forgiving in almost every way than the previous entries. There no longer is a timer or a clock that forces you to run around like the wind. Personally, I found it good decision to get rid of the clock, as you can explore the world at your own leisure and pace, but your opinion may vary on the issue. The other notable change is the behaviour of the survivors. In previous Dead Rising games you had to escort them back to the safehouse, but in Dead Rising 4 all that is required is for you to kill the zombies in the survivor's immediate vicinity, and they will find their own way to the safehouse. Again, I found this a welcome change, but your opinion may vary. It seems  a lot of the negative reviews and complaints with the game revolve around the changes they made to the clock/timer and survivor's behaviour, and if you have no issue with those changes it's definitely worth a try and a very fun game all around.

Spend the time to crack down on some of those achivements such as maintain a goregasm for 2 minutes in The Typing of The Dead, and complete a level without taking damage.

TL:DR The game is in a good state for both sides, unlike the previous version.
***FOUNDERS NOTE***
If you previously purchased the game you get a significant amount of free content and 30,000 keys PLUS additional content in the future. I am a founder and the exclusive content in actually quite unique.
2) The amount of variety from match to match is actually surprisingly high. Most characters play so vastly different that changing one of them from game to game is enough to make both sides drastically alter their strategy. The skill cap for the both teams is in the knowledge of how the hunters work together and how to employ a players abilities to best compliment the team, or crush it in the monsters case. The progression for unlocking content is fairly well paced and players are awarded unlocks for completing tutorials in addition to a free week rotation for both hunters and monsters.
TD:DR You won't get bored after the first couple dozen matches.
3) The game is very well optimized and performs almost flawlessly, with no noticeable lag, tearing, graphical shuddering, or anything of the sort. Matchmaking, on the other hand, is currently quite buggy especially when trying to play with a party.
TL:DR 8/10 for under the hood dev work.
4) I will say this is my one complaint: the cat and mouse dynamic of the game is completely gone. Stealth is completely removed from the monster's side and with the global tracker, evasion is almost impossible to achieve at any stage to the game. The functionality changes to the dome make interaction mandatory which, while this does lead to much more satisfying game play for all hunters who aren't the trapper, it does feel like a lost game play option when playing the monster. I would like to see some alternate way for the monster to evade hunters rather than being forced to sit in the dome and brawl it out until one side or the other is obviously losing. A small loss for us old-timers, but new players will be blissfully unaware of anything they never had.
TL:DR Veteran players get salty when anything about a game they play changes. Nothing new.
***Final Thoughts***
I would recommend anyone looking for a competitive and unique game pick this up, I mean it IS free. The characters are well developed and the story line that you learn about as you play is actually quite interesting. There really is a chance this game has a Diablo III level revival with these changes. Happy hunting!

This is a great game, you should definitely check it out if you get the chance. I'm not saying you should go out and buy this right now, because it does have its fair share of problems.
The artstyle and music are phenominal. The platforming itself is great but could use a little work, especially when compared to how well games like Mario control.
Each of the seven characters are unique and interesting, as are their specific challenges. You will want to play through this game more than once just so you can experience all of the characters and collect their cave paintings and endings.
This leads into where the game comes up short. It was meant to be replayed but has little replay value. For each character there is one specific dungeon, along with each of those three unique dungeons there are four mandatory dungeons that must be completed in every playthrough regardless of the characters you are using. The four mandatory dungeons are the gift shop [extremely tedious], the mines [extremely tedious], the zoo [a little tedious (can be skipped by bringing a hotdog from the gift shop)], and the island [pretty tedious].
The mandatory dungeons are tedious enough the first time, the prospect of having to go through them again may be enough to dissuade you from replaying the game.
Here is how you complete the gift shop (tutorial) dungeon so you know what I'm talking about: Walk all the way to the end, grab a crank, walk all the way back, use crank on well, grab bucket, walk all the way to the end, place bucket, grab fuse, walk all the way back, place fuse, grab hotdog, walk all the way to the end, place hotdog, with a second character grab fuse, walk all the way to the end, replace fuse.
Then there is the fact that the "sultry and mysterious" intro along with all character interactions are unskippable. You will spend a bit of time listening to speeches you have already heard before you can move on if you choose to replay this.
This next part isn't so much a con, it's what makes what I said above so bad though. Each of the seven characters has two endings; a good and a bad. You can only see one per playthrough so if you want to experience all fourteen endings you will have to play through the game at least five times.
It may seem like I'm really ragging on this game, but it is very enjoyable and you will probably have a ton of fun with it, even if you choose to replay it (a couple times).
However, if you have a short attention span or dislike doing the same thing two or more times this might not be the game for you.

So if you're gonna beat every stages for SS Ranks achievement, you're about to play the Retry/Restart Simulator if you got hit at least ONCE.. But hey, practice makes perfect, right?
Cons;

• Completing the game and especially getting a perfect game carries a high prestige along with it which is great to see in comparison with other games that cater to an audience of weak players

• This game has failed to leave me in awe or bring anything new in terms of gameplay since at the core it is just a very well polished, brutally difficult version of a flash game
• Levels exclusively consist of the same two things, dodging and shooting which isn't that bad expect it never will feel fresh since every level is inherently the same
• The fact that you cannot regenerate health by any manner means that you are often forced to retry every time you loose a life so that you can save your lives for the difficult part, this wastes my time even on the smallest things like in the beginning of a stage you aren't focused since you've mastered it
• Stages and obstacles in each boss fight will become monotonous and stale after five minutes of figuring it out
• Hitboxes are not at all representative of their model, at times you are able to go into an object or enemy's model but not get hit and other times you get hit from objects you aren't even that close to
• In some bosses, earlier stages are either so petty you begin to daydream while playing or are so brutally difficult you will get lucky enough to see the later stages
• Achievements are brutal and unforgiving so I do not recommend this game for any completionist
• Attempting perfect scores ruin the enjoyment for any completionist
• Does not offer any level of creativity and wastes the time of players who try to find innovative ways to beat bosses
• Punishes players who cannot achieve anything short of perfection
• Controller compatibility issues
• A strange bug where you are able to parry upwards of five times on the same object by spamming jump
• Begins to have frame rate issues and lag after an hour play session
• Often you are able to parry but also get hit somehow by an object which is odd because a rule is that parrying an object nullifies it
• Some bosses and characters are irritating by their sound effects which is amplified by the repetitive nature of the game
• After countless times of retrying for a perfect score, I can't even feel accomplished apon beating a boss since I feel more disappointed wasting so much time playing
• Aesthetic objects in the background will obstruct the field of play and can ruin the game for you

• Some objects don't stand out that well and will blend with the background
• During most boss battles, some obstacles are randomized leading to some runs being far easier than others depending on which obstacle you are faced with
• Absolutely no detail is given on boss health or weapon damage outside of vague descriptions
• Some various enemies, such as the fish on "Perilous Piers", serve no purpose other than to draw your attention and act so erratically that they become nothing more than an infuriating waste of time
• This game finds a way to rub salt into your wounds time after time even after being used to the frustration it always finds a new way to give you that negative emotion

Before I begin I would like to state that this game is phenomenal. It is a masterpiece of creativity and is nothing short of art in comparison with today's games. Combined with the beautiful art style and the love and care the developers put in by drawing every frame by hand is mind blowing. The characters are based off 1930s cartoons feels unique and has many references and bit of irony sprinkled in. Cuphead is a boss fight 2-D platform game oriented towards high difficulty. This high difficulty is a double edged sword for the gameplay of Cuphead. The game will spark immense joy apon completing a difficult level if all the blood, sweat and tears are worth it. With the exception that this game fails to give you any sense of accomplishment. From level to level, you don't gain anything new, it is just a quest to finish the story. Not only is there a lack of incentive to keep moving forward but towards the end but I was beginning to not have any excitement after completing a level I would be more ashamed I wasted yet another chunk of time to get absolutely nothing in return. What I mean by this is that other games will reward you with a engrossing story, a life lesson, or great memories you had with friends but after playing Cuphead, all I have is wasted time and increased blood pressure. For anyone who strives to get all the achievements and are a completionist, this game is hell. Levels can draw on for hours and you're often able to get caught in the spider web of a monotony. To get perfect runs, it is more efficient to restart the level when you loose health since there is no way to get health back and you know the rest of the level will be near impossible without full health. This fact alone makes Cuphead absolutely unbearable because if you make a slight error in the beginning of the level, you have no reason to continue. This can be easily fixed by adding a way to gain health back so at least if you make a small error and loose health, at least you still have a chance of completion. Coupled with the fact that there still major flaws that need to be addressed such as hitbox problems, glitches when parrying, lack of any detail or statistics on weapons or boss health, controller detection issues, unavoidable damage, just to name a few. One of my biggest complaints is that the levels get boring since the bosses do the same thing time after time. For the same reason Pac-Man cannot hold your interest, that there is nothing new each time. Despite raving reviews of this game, I can genuinely say this game will feel like a massive waste of your time and at end of the day you do not feel satisfied.

Dead Rising 4 is an open-world zombie-slaying sandbox, and it's awesome. The world is rendered in loving detail. Honestly this may be the most detailed open-world I've played to date, other than RPGs like Fallout 4. Almost every building and store is enterable and fully detailed. Lots of objects are interactable and can be used to bludgeon zombies and hostile survivors. It's just grade-A pure fun♥♥♥♥♥♥and a blast to play. The centerpiece of the setting is the Willamette Parkview Mall, a surburban megamall. Presumably it's the rebuilt mall from Dead Rising 1. It's an amazing and hilarious place to explore, complete with themed sections and employee tunnels. If you've ever just wanted to blow things up and have fun in a shopping mall, this game has that.
Having said that, Dead Rising 4 has a couple of problems.
First, compared to the earlier games, some gameplay elements are gone. Dead Rising 3 has a more robust hand-to-hand melee system and you can throw weapons. That's absent here. But I don't really see any problems. My biggest complaint is that they took out the weapons locker from Dead Rising 3 so now you have to manually re-collect any weapons from their original locations. If I want the halberd I gotta go all the way back to Medieval Town in the mall.
Much more serious is that they took out psychos and the psycho cutscenes. Having just started playing Dead Rising 3 also, I'd say that's a big step backward because that game had some ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious psychos. Dead Rising 4 still has maniacs, but these guys lack all of the satirical humor of the earlier psychos. And no cutscenes of course.
These cutbacks notwithstanding, the gameplay component itself is much improved from the earlier games. Combat is more visceral. The blood is more plentiful. There are dynamic blood arcs and splatters. Zombies number in the thousands on-screen, and performance remains great. This game actually has better performance than the PC port of Dead Rising 3 despite the vast improvement in visuals.
The second problem is the playable character Frank West. A lot of people have a problem with his voice actor and appearance changing compared to Dead Rising 1 and 2. I never played those games. I don't have a mental image of how the "real" Frank West should be like, but I love Dead Rising 4's Frank West. The man is ♥♥♥♥ing badass and hilarious.
The game does have a small problem with inconsistent tone. But I never found it as jarring as a lot of other players and reviewers. People make it seem like you're watching Schindler's List punctuated by Jerry Seinfeld segments, and that's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Does this game have a tone problem? Yeah. Like in one instance towards the beginning one character accidentally has an Anthony Weiner phone moment, and that spoiled the seriousness of the scene. But really egregious stuff like that is rare.
Overally, try it. It's hella fun.

At it's core, Oneshot is a cute, dreamlike puzzle adventure game. You progress by exploring your surroundings, talking to NPCs, picking up objects and interacting with your environment to progress. At least that's what it seems at first.
Oneshot interacts with you, the player and Niko in many surreal ways. Through its plot and mechanics, it makes you question what is real and what is fake in both the game and real world. It employs some creative and clever use of game mechanics which I won't spoil here but it's simple yet impressive at the same time. The characters are very endearing, especially Niko, and I'm amazed how short it took for me to care for them.  Graphics look simple but are totally on point, with charming illustrated cutscenes coupled with the subtle but beautiful soundtrack which makes for a dreamlike atmosphere.
Oneshot is not a very long game. But the memories will stay with you long after you close the game window. I put this game in the same league as Undertale and To the Moon.

Let me start by saying that Paradox has a special place in my heart. All of the titles that drop out of whatever cave that these people call home are well designed, fresh, and original. So my review of this game is already in their favor before I hit launch. Hearts of Iron IV is not a game for people that don't have the power to play a game that is more than point and click mindless fun. That being said this game is a blast, and well worth the money. The UI is deep but well designed. If you have a basic understanding of political science, history, military strategy, and can embrace those things in product involving all of those factors, then you will lose a whole pile of time to this product. My first campaign as the United States had me devoting most of my efforts before entering the war turning the people of Italy and the Soviet Union towards democracy. There are a ton of variables involved playing into the courses this game takes. My first hours of gameplay saw the war against Germany almost over by 1941 with me not firing a single shot in Europe with Italy a democracy in control of half of France and most of Germany. My choice to devote my time to trying to forward the progress of Chaing Kai-Shek to fight Soviet influence and the defeat of communism in China resulted in in the communists getting their teeth booted in while the empire of Japan engulfed even more of Asia meaning the defeat of the Axis was not certain and less of a problem for anybody not the United States and the Soviets. My involvement in foreign politics, and straying from isolationism meant that even with the fall of the Nazis the world wasn't a more peaceful place. BOOM! My brain matter covering the walls. How could this happen? I looked at the clock. It was 4 in the morning after a double digit hours long shift in front of my monitor, I realized that nerdbola was deep in my blood. It was only a matter of minutes before my eyes started to bleed. I left my computer covered in shame from all the time I had played. I climbed into bed next to my wife, who loves me so much she didn't even make me go shower the shame off. The ability to rewrite the history of the 30's and 40's makes this game have a lot of replay value. If you enjoy the previous Hearts of Iron games then you will enjoy this game. If you enjoy a game that shows the impact of your choices, involves a ton of strategy, are single; or have an understanding spouse/significant other, then this game should be on your radar.

After barely finding patience for finishing this game, I'm honestly shocked by how many people seem to praise it. It's painfully slow (both in animations and pacing) even by adventure games standards, badly voiced, and full to the brim with virtually all the big mistakes one could make in this genre.
You'll be walking around a lot and talking slowly to boring people about boring subjects with very little important details. You will have to guess that right-clicking an object SOMETIMES does something "special" (like making your character actually examine something in detail after he's already looked at it a couple times and told you there's nothing important about it). Most of the time, though, left-clicking is enough (sometimes multiple times). Unless, of course, the game doesn't want you to take / use / examine something until it decides it's time - which happens constantly, so you'll also have to do a lot of pointless backtracking.
Think talking to character A, then going a few screens back to character B, then back to A, back to B, back to A - all of this just to make A move elsewhere and let you progress a little bit further. Or maybe you try to move something, it turns out too heavy, and then you have to go back a few screens and suddenly find a helpful item in a place where there weren't even any hotspots to click a minute ago. And these are just a few examples of an overall pattern: the whole game is built like that.
I can't even begin to imagine what its designer's problem was, but it is clear as day that he deliberately designed Black Mirror to frustrate the hell out of the players and waste as much of their time as humanly (and inhumanly) possible. If you are still not convinced by the previous examples - you must also know that there is a "waiting mechanic". Yes - waiting! There are times when you ask someone to help you with something and he tells you to come back later, since he needs time to do it. Do you think that means that you should go elsewhere and solve some more puzzles, like it would in any sane game? Nope, wrong. When that happens, you are probably fresh out of other useful things to do - so you can only wait as you are told. Which means, you should go back and forth between random available locations, then come back to that person and hope he's done by now. Or maybe he's not, because you've only "waited" by flipping 10 random screens instead of 20 (or whichever other number the game expects - who knows). Go back and "wait" some more. "Patience, my son!" (c)
Oh, and there are also a few death traps. You won't find any until late chapter 2, so by then you might decide that this game does follow the modern unwritten rule of no deaths in the genre. Be assured - it doesn't. It just breaks it rarely and, usually, unexpectedly. No "last warnings" here - you simply click something you shouldn't have clicked, then you die... There are also a couple timed death episodes where you have to do something quickly. The first of these might even be unsolvable if you don't do everything "just right" on the previous screens (because your character is a dumbass who can't do a simple task from first attempt without extremely careful preparations). So, if you still want to play this for some reason, do save often.
There's even a maze near the end... Oh well, It's not really a maze where you can get lost, so it's not THAT bad. It's still bad, though. And it can also kill you in a few ways, of course - what else would you expect by now?
To be fair, there is one nice twist in the story (even though I did guess it shortly before it was finally revealed). But then comes the confusing and utterly meaningless ending...
So, can this game possibly be worth the time necessary to finish it?
I can only hope the sequels are better, since I've already made the mistake of buying them all in a bundle...

This was... amazing. It is truly a masterpiece. A flawed masterpiece, perhaps, but when compared to other games of its genre, the difference is like night and day. I don't know where to even begin, so I'll just sum it up over pluses and minuses:
The good:
+ Excellent story, characters, pacing, atmosphere, and overall great use of writing techniques. Writers, take note, THIS is how you pull off plot twists and foreshadowing especially without it coming off as a cheap gimmick.
+ Incredible attention to detail in the graphics and sounds. Perhaps more modern games with full 3D engines may be more realistic, but this takes statically rendered graphics about as far as they can possibly go.
+ Flawless gothic atmosphere featuring all elements you would expect: architecture, weather, spiritual themes, even actions. What could be more gothic than digging a grave in the dead of night?
The quirky:
? You might find this anywhere from charming to irritating, or both at the same time. Everything, from the action to the voice acting, is extremely formal and deliberate. Though the action takes place in the modern age, most characters, and the main character especially, speak like characters from a book as opposed to real people. Think Dostoevsky's noble characters and you will get the idea. Personally I find that this somehow perfectly fits the setting, but I admit others might hate it.
The bad:
- You will have problems running Black Mirror I on a Retina computer. Beware! I had to resort to an older PC I had lying around.
- Most of the puzzles in the game are fair and well balanced, but occasionally the game will make use of a criminally badly designed "wait mechanic", whereby a character will tell you that they need time to complete and action and that you should return later.  If you are used to other adventure games, you will take this as a sign that you still need to do something for the plot to progress. But no, you just have to run around aimlessly flipping screens until a certain number of transitions (not minutes!) have passed. This was a critical error on part of the designers and is bound to confuse most people.
- As mentioned before, the action is quite slow, especially in the first chapter. This is not a game for the easily bored.
Finally, a funny/strange occurence. Before playing this game, I had just complained that I've never seen a game where the protagonist relates seriously and positively with any sort of mainstream (esp. Christian) religion. Well, this game is indeed an exception. Without giving too much away, though God does not seem to overtly intervene in his adventure, Samuel is indeed religious, explicitly so, treats his religion with respect, and does ask for help and guidance in his time of need. I was genuinely impressed.

1) The pace of this game has been accelerated and the dynamic is in a very good place, not just compared to its original state but for a game of this type in general. It is a genuine 4v1 at all stages of the game now where all players have a role, contributing and interaction with each other in meaningful ways. The main problem with the games previous version was that either the monster got caught and killed early with no counter play or the monster evaded the hunters for eight minutes straight and at the end of the turkey chase there was a stage 3 monster, which again had no counter play. This has been smoothed out so that interactions between hunters and monsters are frequent and meaningful, but counter play is still available to both teams.
TL:DR The game is in a good state for both sides, unlike the previous version.
***FOUNDERS NOTE***
If you previously purchased the game you get a significant amount of free content and 30,000 keys PLUS additional content in the future. I am a founder and the exclusive content in actually quite unique.
2) The amount of variety from match to match is actually surprisingly high. Most characters play so vastly different that changing one of them from game to game is enough to make both sides drastically alter their strategy. The skill cap for the both teams is in the knowledge of how the hunters work together and how to employ a players abilities to best compliment the team, or crush it in the monsters case. The progression for unlocking content is fairly well paced and players are awarded unlocks for completing tutorials in addition to a free week rotation for both hunters and monsters.
TD:DR You won't get bored after the first couple dozen matches.
3) The game is very well optimized and performs almost flawlessly, with no noticeable lag, tearing, graphical shuddering, or anything of the sort. Matchmaking, on the other hand, is currently quite buggy especially when trying to play with a party.
TL:DR 8/10 for under the hood dev work.
4) I will say this is my one complaint: the cat and mouse dynamic of the game is completely gone. Stealth is completely removed from the monster's side and with the global tracker, evasion is almost impossible to achieve at any stage to the game. The functionality changes to the dome make interaction mandatory which, while this does lead to much more satisfying game play for all hunters who aren't the trapper, it does feel like a lost game play option when playing the monster. I would like to see some alternate way for the monster to evade hunters rather than being forced to sit in the dome and brawl it out until one side or the other is obviously losing. A small loss for us old-timers, but new players will be blissfully unaware of anything they never had.
TL:DR Veteran players get salty when anything about a game they play changes. Nothing new.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is an extremely deep Roguelike dungeon-crawler in the same vein as Nethack or Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup. With that in mind, I would recommend ToME to anyone who enjoys RPGs of any kind. Unlike most dungeon crawlers ToME also has an intuitive and beautifully designed interface which makes the hotkeys easy to get the hang of. The class roles are deeper than any other roguelike I've played with Diablo-style leveling trees for every class and several opportunities to learn secondary trees from quests. ToME also has a well written and extremely lore-intensive story, setting it apart from more barebones games like DCSS. Try it out, it's free. Or buy it! I have definitely gotten my money's worth out of the expansions.

In Tales of Maj'Eyal, you will do the following:
-Spend the first 200 hours learning how to not die.
-Open treasure chests
-Die
-Get one-shotted by the boss class monster that spawned out of the treasure chest
-Open more treasure chests
-Die
-Slay dragons
-Die
-Rescue Damsels
-Unlock new classes for no apparent reason
-Travel the world
And much, much more!
