This game has been in my wishlist for quite long time, and I always hesitated to buy it, due to my fear of the 3Ds port. Then the summer sale came...
...and I regret deeply waiting so long to buy this game.
In brief, the game takes inspiration in Mega-Man, but it manages to have it's own identity.
This was a great surprise,  I thought the game's story would revolve only around a concept to justify what happens, but it managed to develop a story, the world around it, some key characters, and the twist in the ending was absolutely awesome.  There are some CGs even. Speaking of story, pay very attention to the ending...there may be more than you think...
The soundtrack is really nice if you like J-POP, and all of the few voice actings are in japanese, which is a plus. The OST can be bought here on Steam if you like.
The controls respond very well, and the movements are very well placed. You can shoot with the gun (7 different types throughout the game, with different shoot patterns) and one concept well thought was the Tag. Basically, when you shoot someone, you Tag him, and then, you can use your electric powers to attack him. Fortunately, this mechanic is not only used during combat, and you will have to use it many times to interact with the scenario.
Other highlight is how they managed to make each mission unique. In one mission, you are in a horror-like underground facility and almost everything is pitch black, while in other, you must run against time to escape from drowning in a underwater complex. Every mission has some unique mechanic to them, and they are a blast.
When the mission ends, you get a score based upon your performance on the mission. They are based on damage taken, kill streak, how fast and how you killed enemies and so on. There's only one mission that I achieved the S+ rank, but it's nice how the game rewards for playing well. Not just with getting a good rank, but with random items pickups when the mission ends.
You get items either by finishing missions, or buying them on store, but why do you use them? To craft equipment. Yes, the game has an equip system, with different categories and effects. Not only that, but it has a Skill system, with up to 4 skills equipped at a time,  and you get more as you kill enemies and level up, increasing your HP in the process. These RPG  features are taken off in the Hard Mode, but it isn't a letdown, since it's supposed to be hard, but I think the Normal Mode is fine as it is.
Another highlight. The bosses are really fun to fight, with moderate difficulty, encouraging you to learn their patterns and defeat them as best and fast as you can.
The final bosses, however, honor their "final bosses" title. They are very hard, with 1-hit kill skills at the end of the battle, and one mistake will force you to start the battle again.  Even though I got frustrated some times, I don't think they are extremely overpowered. You're reaching the end game, and the game really gives you the feeling that the villain is a real threat.
If you like platform games, like Mega-man, do yourself a favor and buy this, it's a really good title, It has only minor flaws that don't compromise in any way the experience. The story and characters are great, the gameplay is awesome and there's an awesome twist in the ending. After you beat the game the first time, don't stop...
You haven't reached the true ending yet...

Azure Striker Gunvolt is a game that was developed and published by the Japanese game development company Inti Creates, the people responsible for the development of the Mega Man Zero series (including Zero Collection), the Mega Man ZX series, the Gal*Gun series, Mega Man 9 and 10, and were part of the development Shantae and the Pirate's Curse. To put it simply, Inti Creates is well known for 2D Action-Platformer games.
The game first launched as a Nintendo 3DS exclusive title along with Mighty Gunvolt, a spin-off to Azure Striker Gunvolt featuring Beck from Mighty No. 9,  from the Gal*Gun series, and Gunvolt from..this game I'm reviewing. This game managed to please the crowd and Inti Creates has created a port for Steam with extra content and used to have monthly updates (the copy I'm reviewing). The sequel, Azure Striker Gunvolt 2, is currently out on the Nintendo 3DS (and soon the Nintendo Switch) digitally and via the Azure Striker Gunvolt: Striker Pack, which is a bundle of the first and second game. It is unknown if the sequel will have a port for Steam or not. And Mighty Gunvolt Burst, a sequel of Mighty Gunvolt, will be releasing soon on the Nintendo Switch.
With that out of the way, let's get started reviewing shall we?
Go ahead and get yourself a cup of coffee or whatever you drink, as this might take a while.
And I won't talk about the story, as I rather let players experience it.
The gameplay is very similar to the Mega Man franchise: you jump, you shoot, and you move around like a platformer. However, there are some key differences from this and Mega Man. For starters, Gunvolt wields his "Azure Striker" septima. Flashfield is an ability with multible purposes, such as boosting your air time by gliding instead of falling. Or if you tag some enemies with your pistol, you can use the flashfield and deal damage to enemies with varying damage output depending on how many times you tagged them (which is even more damage than spamming your tags or not using tags at all and getting upclose with your flashfield). You can tag up to three times, starting with blue, to yellow, to red as last. There are many parts you can collect to alter your pistol, most of which can be gathered via game progression.
Medals can be collected during the level for the purpose of gaining extra chances at the bonus game, which is simply pick a tile and obtain a prize. There is a leveling system for the game as well, as you defeat and damage enemies, you gain
. Leveling up is key in order to unlock new
, which allow you to preform powerful attacks, boost certain stats, or even heal! There is also a crafting system, which allows you to craft gear for Gunvolt out of materials you gather in stages. It will cost money,
.
The crafting system, while is a good idea, didn't feel nessesary. I might have been better off just buying the items and upgrading them with even more money as I continue the game. There are also challenges which can reward you with money and/or specific materials if cleared. They are only unlocked after specific stages or other challenges are cleared beforehand. You can only have 3 challenges enabled at a time, so beware.
There are many enemies to encounter, such as Sumeragi soldiers, robots, and..erm..hm. Not much to say actually. The bosses and mini-bosses however are pretty varied. From tanks, to spider and plant combat robots, to even other Adepts; this game does keep some varity. While the adepts don't wield the "Azure Striker" septima (or special abilities, rather), they are still a threat as they have their own septima.
Music wise, I feel in love with every tune that played, so much in fact I bought both the official soundtracks released on Steam.
The game, while it doesn't have 60 FPS, does have a 30 FPS lock, and I found it hard to notice. The game runs very smoothly, but there is one thing that must be noticed. Security software tend to mark the game's .exe file as a virus, and Inti Creates has reached out and given everyone an explaination.
Gameplay time wise, I can't be sure. The game has so much to offer, including speedrun modes, special season-exclusive gamemodes, extra missions for the main campaign, and even difficulty settings for newbies only in for the story and professionals who are extremely familiar with the game genre. I can estimate that it could score around 10 hours for an average player, 35+ for all acheivements (mainly the S+ rank acheivements), and..I am not sure what to estimate for playing every speedrun at least once along with getting every achivement. Either way, the PC version gives more bank for your buck than the 3DS version does. If you can, try and get it during a sale (especially the Summer and Winter sales) along with the soundtracks if you so wish.
Overall, I had a lotta fun with Azure Striker Gunvolt and I do recommend giving it a shot.

Pros:
This game is amazing. Don't think that just because it has an old feel and a 50/60s art style with music that it is a bad game or that it won't be fun. It is fun. So I highly recommend this game and it is worth the price (and it's even better when it's on sale). Every kill feels rewarding and every death feels like you could have dome semthing better, think the game is unfair and too hard (don't worry, the best of us feel that way). The game has an old-esc feel to it, with very well animated character, attacks, and maps. Every detail is emphasized in this game. The objects that you can interact with on the map are more vivid, have a small outline, and move just enough to tell you that you can interact with it. The levels are well thought out, and the game has so much play time. (So far) I only have 8 hours, and I haven't passed the first two levels (but I have been fighting bosses on the first world) because of how difficult they are and how much practice the game requires.
Cons:
The controls on computer are flat out bad. They use the arrow keys and z, x, and other bottons that are useable, but aren't typical and are hard to get used to. If you have a controller for a console, USE IT. Also, I recommend that you change your controls before you start to play too much so the new controls don't feel weird. The game is very difficult. This is good and bad for a lot of different reasons. The bad is because it might detract you from the game and make you mad, probably making you play less and less until it was just a waste of money. So don't get mad.
Overall, the pros outwiegh the cons, and if you still don't believe me, read some more of the reviews. The game definietly has 100s of hours of play time and so many grades to earn, hard to reach hidden coins in every level, and tons of secrets hidden in the map where you select level. If i were to compare this to any game, I would compare it to Super Mario (the new one for the wii). It is a sidescroller with different powerups, a store, and even have a somewhat similar level selection map. The game can have you in an airplane, on clouds, land, and maybe underwater (but I don't know for sure). So in conclusion, I highly recommend this game to anyone. It is a relaxed game that you can play to pass time when you have nothing to do, or when you just want to have fun and play some video games. I hope you like my essay about a game that I only (so far) have 8 hours in.

Alright, I've just finished a first time full playthrough of this game in around 15-20 hours - that I managed to  finish it should be testament to the fact that this isn't the worst game in existence. However, it is far, far, from the best and there are some things you should know before buying this game.
This game shows its age - it was made in 2003, and you can tell. The graphics aren't so awful as to hinder game play, but I did find they took away from the mood of the game - a grisly death just isn't as grisly when it's depicted in 30 pixels. If you're a graphical afficiando, you're gonna have a problem with this game.
The music is great, as is the ambient audio - but as others have said, the voice acting is terrible and I played through the entire game with it disabled for that reason.
This is where the game shows its age even moreso. The animations are tediously slow (want to talk to someone? Gotta wait 5 seconds for them to turn around to begin the conversation!), progressing through the game is oftentimes incredibly unintuitive and repetetive, and there are multiple occasions where you are literally expected to sit around doiing NOTHING for 10,15,20+ minutes of out of game time for npcs to retrieve things for you. I found this extremely frustrating and tedious.
This is where the game shines. I loved the story and it was oftentimes the only thing that kept me going - the mystery and intrigue are very well written, and while there are some inconsistencies in the plot and unanswered questions at the end, these are minor complaints and I really enjoyed unraveling the mysteries of Black Mirror.
Would I recommend this game to others? It depends. Have you played this game a decade ago and want a nostalgia rush replaying it? Go for it, you'll love it just as much as the last time. Are you a video game historian, delving the depths of ancient gaming archives to see how video games have progressed over time? This game is a classic example of early 2000s point&clicks, get stuck in. Are you someone who's never played a point and click before, who's only played games made past 2010, or saw this game discounted on a sale and wanted give it a go? In my opinion you're better off giving this one a miss.
1) Disable voiceovers. The voice acting is terrible and detracts from the game.
2) SAVE OFTEN. This game predates quicksaves, and you CAN and WILL die multiple times with no respawn other than a save file.
3) Be aware that every so often you will need to not only left click objects, but right click them as well to progress in the game. If the cursor remains red on an object after left clicking, try right clicking.
4) I'd highly reccommend searching up a walkthrough and having it handy unless you have a deathwish. This is NOT an easy game, and there will be many times where you will get stuck and the answer will make no sense whatsoever.

Not only do you still have the same hilariously fun light-gun game from the PS3 but you also the typing mode is incredibly fun and challenging, now before you walk into it there is a few things to keep in mind, this is NOT a serious game and this is NOT a game that's trying to 'wow' it's audience with phenomenal visuals, in fact it's going the opposite direction on purpose.
The visuals and sound the game doesn't have much to write home about, the soundtrack and dialogues are fantastic in a cheesy way and they don't skimp on the cheese. The entire game has a gridnhouse, Z movie, vibe to it with a story that's intentionally stupid, chockfull of F-bombs with exagerated gore and hilariously ridiculous plot twists.
There is a good ammount of replay value as well, playing the Typing mode on the Agent(normal) difficulty already proves a challenge and gradually stepping it up to the Motherf**ker (Hard) difficulty with hardcore mode turned on is a whole other challenge altogether. I haven't tried the DLC dictionaries but they should also add a new layer of difficulty to an already challenging game.
If there are a comple of downsides. One, is that the bosses often have a very unforgiving timing to counter their attacks or that the final boss just didn't feel very well polished. Two, is that the leaderboards are often hacked, so even if you'd like to try to make it to the top-scores the hackers just ruin it for everyone.
To sum it up, like it's predecessor, it's still an unique game, I've yet to see any other games to take this aproach to on-rails shooters and it still is a very fun experience, no mention that playing enough of this game might even improve your 'motherf**king' typing skills.

10/10 - Best Roguelike I've ever played.
1. DEPTH - This game is the holy grail of roguelikes, a hidden diamond in the rough -- if you like the roguelike genre at all and don't have this game, buy it immediately. The depth is insane and best of all it manages to break out of the "fantasy" cliché of classes while still maintaining core principles of a turn based roguelike. Some of the concepts are so foreign that you won't initially understand the mechanics and you're like "what the actual #$%& does this do", but once you learn the mechanics they add a whole new layer of fun to the game that's all but lost in games today.
2. MECHANICS - It's like nothing you've ever seen. Each class and race is eerily unique in several ways and is filled with all kinds of new and interesting ideas. “Wait, I can melee with mind abilities?”
3. ITEMIZATION - Lots of gear, lots of stats, lots of resist types, lots of damage types, lots of status effects, lots of "hmmm I wonder if this piece is better" or "I really should put these points into health, but I can't say no to more damage and if I kill them fast, they can’t hurt me! Right?"  Changing gear usually requires a compromise of offense, defense and knowledge of what your character can handle.
4. CHALLENGE - Took me ~85 gameplay hours to beat the game on Normal, I probably lost 20-30 characters before successfully winning. It's possible that I'm just really bad, but I like to think the game is just really challenging. Also, the beginning of the game is not easy, it's quite difficult; I remember thinking "Wow I just died 3 times in the first starting zone."
5. SKILLS - A huge variety of skills, trees, opportunities and playstyles. This makes for fun and inventive combos, skill synergy and interesting deaths. "Hellll yeah I got a skill that lets me move through walls, oh #$%! I just suffocated in the wall."
6. MONSTERS - A massive monster variety, each time you play you'll start to notice the different monster types, their skills, strengths and weaknesses. On higher difficulties, it's extremely important to know what you're going up against to get that next level advantage. “OHHHH #$%* another necromancer.”
7. ACTIVE DEV & COMMUNITY - Active development on the game, balance patches, new classes, races, and content (DLC). The community is great, can be very helpful and from my experience non-toxic (I guess we're not call of duty scrubs). As a bonus, every now and then you'll see messages from the DarkGod (DEV) who bestows you with some random buff for "absolutely no reason."
8. DEATH - You will die a lot. You will rage. You will learn from your mistakes. You will make the same mistakes again, die, and rage more. You will lose multiple lives to the same monster because you’re too stubborn to choose the “safe” option when talking to the ghost lady after you die. You will switch to another class because the one you were playing before felt 'weak' and this other class has GOT to be better, but then later go back to the first class because you now understand that it's really strong and you were just bad. You will die to the first boss in the first zone ON NORMAL and come to some inevitable realizations about how the game is meant to be played. You’ll say to yourself -- "WELP that guy just 1 shot me for 1565 blight damage, when I only had 923 heath good to know I stood a chance; probably should have more than 11% blight resist."
9. JUST BUY THE GAME - If you've read up to here you could have already lost 2 characters in the addicting, adrenaline fueled, unforgiving journey to save Maj’Eyal.

The Typing of the Dead Overkill is far-and-away the weirdest game I've had the privilege to review. It's a typing tutor by way of a Robert Rodriguez movie, relying on your mad (you hope) typing skillz to destroy a horde of "don't use the 'z' word" mutants coming at you from every angle. The game is  cheesy and hilarious and a hell of a lot of fun.
I picked up the original House of the Dead Overkill PS3 port a few years ago but I didn't get past the third level because, well, mostly because I'm terrible at console shooters, even using the Move as a lightgun-substitute (which, in theory, is easier). The original House of the Dead series of games were light-gun rail shooters and while I enjoyed the story I couldn't get very far in the game due to the mechanics (or my lack of ability, depending on how you choose to look at it). Modern Dream modified the input scheme to rely on accurately-typed words, phrases, and single letters in lieu of wielding firearms to put down this undead uprising. It's not really a typing tutor in any real sense, but if you're pretty good at typing with celerity and accuracy then you will do well.
The PC release includes the original game as well, if you're terrible at typing or if you prefer FPS mechanics. The House of the Dead levels include a gun shop that allows you to spend money you earn by completing levels (and shooting stacks of cash that you see) on upgrades to your weapons and new boomsticks. While the HotD version of the game is essentially identical to the PS3/Wii version, it's much easier to aim with a mouse-and-keyboard.
As I said earlier, the story is presented with a grindhouse aesthetic, including cutscenes with film grain, gratuitous nudity, gore, and intense violence. Detective Washington and Agent G are out to stop crime lord and part-time mutant maker Papa Caesar, aided by the angry and vindictive Varla Guns and the dumb-as-a-post but sweet Candi Stryper. The dialogue is ridiculous, the characters are over-the-top, and the setting is somewhere in "Bayou County" (i.e., south Louisiana). The tale unfolds over nine chapters where the two agents or their stripper colleagues battle mutants in settings that range from a swamp to a prison to a circus. As you play, you can shoot (or hit TAB) to collect memorabilia, including pages from the Prelude to an Overkill comic, concept art, 3D models, and audio tracks from the soundtrack.
Oh, the soundtrack. I'm listening to it now as I type this review. It's hilarious, toe-tapping, and occasionally a bit disgusting; in other words, it is the perfect aural companion to this game. The tracks are a mix of rockabilly, funk, and metal, interspersed with game dialogue. Sadly it was never officially released by Pitstop Productions or SEGA, but it is available on Grooveshark. An intrepid soul might find a way to download it .
The game isn't without its issues. Graphically speaking, it's nothing to write home about, although you're basically looking at a 3-year-old console game, so that shouldn't really surprise anyone. It also only runs in a selection of widescreen resolutions so it may or may not run fullscreen on your monitor. Also, the aforementioned memorabilia can be tough to collect a complete set of. Apart from the items available in the standard TotD mode, there is another set of unique collectibles in the House of the Dead mode as well as yet another set in the HotD Director's Cut mode; those require some fast reflexes and/or several playthroughs to get because of the brevity of their onscreen appearances.
Those minor quibbles aside, this is a great, albeit short (probably 6-8 hours to run through the story mode once) experience that is perfect for fans of typing, zombies, and/or faux-grindhouse action. It's not a game-of-the-year contender by any stretch of the imagination, but it is a lot of fun.

Azure Stiker Gunvolt is a very good port from a 3DS game. It's a 2D action platformer with interesting mechanics.
Asure Stirker Gunvolt have a pretty interesting battle mechanic : You do have a gun but it does almost no damage, instead, you can lock your opponents by shooting them. Now that you have locked them, you can do heavy damage by releasing thunder on them (you have an energy bar that show you how much thunder you can release, but it reload itself quite quickly). Also you have a skill system : on the top right of your screen, one can see 4 slot for different skill which can be very usefull in boss battle (it does heavy damage or can heal yourself or reload your energy bar faster). The game itself isn't that hard (besides the final level that gave me a hard time) but it's still chalenging so you can enjoy yourself. There is also a shopping/crafting system for your gear but exept the double jump gear, it's not usefull at all and your money will be useless because you can't buy anything, only crafting (which cost money but your always have money but you always miss the parts that you loot at the end of each level)
It's a pretty well done port, the keymapping to compense all the touch screen bontons of the 3DS is well done, there is no problem to control your character. Still, I notice that during some "cinematics" (when they show some full screen CG) my frame rate goes down but it's only during those and not while playing.
It's very pretty : the chara designs are well done and the design as well. That really looks like a near future universe. Also the animation is almost flowless, maybe a little too flashy sometimes.
The musics are really catching and pretty cool, it really fits to each level. The sound effect isn't too repetitive and we even have some good voice acting.
So it's in a cool universe but does it have a good story ? I have to say no, everything is very predictable and the characters have good chara design but they are plain, as plain as the story. It's not that bad, but it's not good either, if you skip the talking you wont miss anything significant. And to get the true ending (and fight the final boss) you have to collect all the jewel, it's not really a spoil but
Pros :
- Interesting combat mechanics
- Very good art and musics
- Challenging difficulty
- Good port
Cons :
- Shopping, crafting and equipement system that could have been improved
- Story
- A little short (7H) but with speedrun potential and (I think) a good replay value
80/100 With a more than correct price, I highly recommand you the game and also the soundtrack even without discount.

There are aspects of this game I do really like.  But overall I cannot recommend it.  The point and click adventure part of the game, which should be the meat and bones here, is too flawed.  I've only played partway through chapter 3, and I've had to consult a walkthrough too many times to figure out what to do next.  There are no objectives explicitly given so often I'm left loading up area after area talking to everyone hoping to advance the game.  When that doesn't work I'm left to pixel hunting scene after scene again and again wondering if I've missed something.  Most of the game so far has wandering around wondering how I'm to accomplish what at least I can figure out what I'm supposed to do.
And usually I have problems because it's so easy to miss something.  Once it was a right click.  Right click is used sporadically in this game; sometimes it does something, but most often it does nothing.  One missed right click on an inventory object or hotspot will get you stuck.  Several times it's been one tiny hotspot overshadowed by another much larger hotspot right next to it.  If you buy this game, don't assume all hotspots are separated from each other.  If/When you get stuck look for slivers of a 2nd hotspot along side ones you've already found.  There's also some degree of misdirection in the game.  I was told to leave the main house once to procure an object.  However the game wouldn't let me leave.  After talking to everyone and not getting anywhere I had to resort to a walkthrough only to discover I wasn't supposed to leave at all, but I was supposed to procure a substitute object another way.  That's kind of cheaty IMO.  If the main character I'm playing wants to do that then the game should inform me that's the objective.  There was another event where I died repeatedly; I couldn't figure out how to survive with the objects in the character's inventory.  Again, back to a walthrough to discover that prior events had to be completed in a very precise way in order to survive the dangerous encounter.  I guess I should revise my earlier statement:  one missed right click on a hotspot can get you killed later, so save often.  (Disclaimer:  I don't find point and click mechanics like this much fun.)
The graphics are fine for a game over a decade old.  The character models were rather pixelated, but forcing Nvidia antiailasing fixed that.  Characters move slowly, and there's a lot of waiting to converse with NPCs, to load up the next scene, to enter and leave animations, etc.  The Black Mirror is a slow paced game, which was unexpected but not a problem after I got used to it.  The voice acting is awkward, but I thought it was entertaining at least.  The story seems fairly good so far.  Then environments do an excellent job of evoking the right atmosphere for the game.  Family relationships are not well spelled out.  You play Samual Gordon and run into various other Gordons without really knowing how you know them, who your parents are, or how these other Gordons are related to you.  I got some of that online (don't use wikipedia, there's a major spoiler there) just so I better understand the situation.
However, it's the point and click mechanics that bring the game down for me.  I find them more exasperating than challenging, more tedious than fun.  And occasionally the point and click puzzle solutions are nonsensical in ways I thought were only common in hidden object games.  I will push through to the end of the game, just to see it through.  If the point and click mechanics get better in the 2nd half of the game I'll update my review.  Otherwise, I think The Black Mirror is only for point and click adventure die-hards, those who don't mind pixel hunting, or those who don't think twice about looking up a walkthrough when you get tried of being stuck for so long.
edit:  I finished the game, took me a little over 19 hrs.  That would have been considerably longer had I not consulted a walk through so much.  I didn't care for the pixel hunting aspects which continued to plague the 2nd half of the game.  Several puzzle solutions were totally illogical IMO.  I should have stopped trying to figure out answers and just systematically tried every inventory object on every hotspot.  But that's no fun and you never really know whether you've found every hotspot.
Plus, the game has a certain mechanic where you have to wait for other characters to do something for you before you can continue.  There's nothing else to do except leave the screen, reenter, and try talking to them again and again.  I couldn't tell if waiting was time based or just based on the number of attempts to talk to the character (as a guide suggests).  I didn't think this particular game mechanic worked well.  It was more annoying than anything else and really slowed down the story.
Anyways, the 2nd half of the game was much like the first half except there were more puzzles and less conversation required to advance the story.  The ending was unsatisfying.  It didn't really convey what the protagonist accomplished, although if you think about it you can sort of assume what the critical cut scene was supposed to explain.  With a few exceptions I pretty much knew what I was supposed to trying to solve, unlike the first half of the game where I was clueless of what to do a lot more often.  I also didn't think the ending adequately explained the central crux of the plot.
Conclusion:  I liked the story for the most part and the atmosphere and environments were very well done.  But that was slightly overcome by too much pixel hunting and illogical puzzles.  Overall, I'm pretty "meh" on this game, just over the "not recommended" threshold unless you are a big fan of point and click adventure games.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Overall this is a very good game with a lot of depth and some very fun well designed classes that said its not without its problems,
Partially I take issue with the perma death mechanic. I tend to like games with permadeath as far as rougelike games go. Nethack is amazing a gritty survival game and every playthrough is unique and you feel fragile and human through out it. ToMEs playthroughs all start roughly the same and get better 10/15 levels in. Those first 10 levels are a slog after you have done it a couple of time. Pouring 10 hours into a character then getting a clumsy death when you are on you last life is pretty painful because you have to restart with the same plot, with the same dungeons, and often with the same unique item drops. It becomes uninviting.
Exploration mode you say then.. but that has no penalty taking away the tension completely. You need a middle mode between exploration and adventure, perhaps losing all your items (bar the three stocked in your box) for a continue? Or at least gaining a life after a major boss. If you pour 10,15,20 hours before dying its a huge time investment and its very punishing. Particularity because the early game is relatively dull. More choice and divergent paths in the early game might help.
After a death you pretty much have to play with a different class (which are all brilliantly designed and play fluidly with so many build styles changing gameplay/strategy considerably) and it can take awhile to get to grips with how that class functions often this can result in silly deaths. Which is the bizarre thing that you have to play a class to have a good idea of how you want to build it, but due to the time commitment you would rather restart with a different class then master one.
Basically if you have a lot of time to try the different classes and get good go for it! The amount of depth in the character builds is staggering with some really awesome stuff. (I love the time manipulation ones which you can really mess around with placements and divide and pool enemies together) but all of them offer valid play styles, from adaptable to min-maxing synergies. The depth of build is the real core strength of this game and trying a new class is what makes you play again after a bad beat. There are very little games with this much content and its a lot of value for money.
Pros:
Intelligent strategic gameplay
Huge choice of classes and viable builds within classes offering dozens of different play-styles
Challenging game play and while your character improves to godly levels it remains challanging
Enormous amount of content and most of it at a surprisingly high quality
Interesting and engaging mechanics which meaningfully change the game with different classes.
Cons:
Same starting areas get samey
Punishing consecutive mistakes. 5 bad minutes can destroy a 15 hour playthrough
Weak overwritten lore has potential but is wordy and unengaging with hard to believe motivations between groups
Some bugs that need ironing out
Some mechanics are poorly explained and pretty unclear.
Not really a game that is forgiving to people with a job/relationship/other interests huge time sink with very little value outside of its mechanics
Would I recommend? Absolutely. Very few games this good at this price range play a few times get some decent playthroughs going then put it down and maybe pick it up again later.

ARK: Survival Evolved - Space Edition.
I was fortunate enough to receive a review copy of this game from the developers and have played approximately 7 hours over the past day and a half (Update - I have now played over 30 hours, and my initial thoughts on Osiris: New Dawn remain unchanged). Whilst there's undoubtedly tons more that I need to discover and learn, I think my hands on time with the game has given me enough insight to formulate a fair and informed opinion and a well-rounded review.
For anyone familiar with ARK, you'll immediately draw the connection between how similar Osiris and ARK actually are. The similarities however, aren't just cosmetic (there are MANY costmetic similarities). The gameplay mechanics, combat, leveling system and base building components also VERY similarly resemble those of ARK. Of course, similarities between survival games is to be expected, but I honestly feel like Osiris: New Dawn "IS" ARK: Survival Evolved - in space.  For me, this is actually a good thing as I love the sci-fi genre significantly more than the prehistoric one of ARK, but from what I have seen in the 7 hours I have played, there isn't anything particularly "new" or "novel" that Osiris brings to the table. If you're a fan of ARK or someone that looks for more than novel ideas in a game, then Osiris: New Dawn will be right up your alley. I want to really emphasize however, that the points I just raised are by no means meant to be a negative thing. I can have an absolute blast with a game regardless of whether it's throwing new ideas in my face every couple of seconds, provided that the gameplay mechanics work well and are engaging - and in Osiris: New Dawn, they are. The graphics are also beautiful, which is another huge thumbs up.
Perhaps the biggest draw for me is the prospect of building space craft and travelling to other planets. I'm still not sure how that is going to work, but I'm extremely excited by the thought. The base building components are also a lot of fun and now that the launch day patch has been implemented, various resources that were missing as of yesterday have now been put into the game. There are still a few utilities that are uncraftable due to an apparent unkown bug, but I have notified the developer and he/she is working on a fix.
As for server latency, they have been VERY unstable over the past day or two with only a maximum of 20 people playing at the time. I can see the devs having problems with this when the game launches and thousands of people start bombarding the servers. I'm sure they'll find a way to make it work, but I encourage those of you that may have issues NOT to jump the gun and write a negative review because the server load was too great on launch day. Be fair and understand that these sorts of things are sometimes unavoidable. Fortunately the game can be played offline in single player mode, or you can make a private world for you and 5 of your friends, which runs like absolute butter. This is what I am doing and it's super smooth.
It's worth noting that the game IS still an early access title, and as such, has a long way to go before it's properly optimized. The amount of heat generated by my GPU and CPU is higher in Osiris than any other game that I have played in the last couple of years - including GTAV with everything maxed out. My PC has suddenly shut off several times due to overheating issues, so that's something to be aware of. You'll need proper cooling and your fans on high to keep things manageable at 2k on Ultra settings. I imagine that this will get better when the game is further optimized after its proper release.
I've bumbled on long enough here but think I've included most of the main points that I wanted to and have addressed the issues that I think most review readers are going to be looking for. So far, I'm having a wonderful time with Osiris: New Dawn and wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to any fan of the survival genre. It's a solid game that runs amazingly well for an early access title and has an immense amount of potential for things to come in the future.

Waveform is an imaginary line representing all parts of a wave where particles are vibrating in the same phase and have the same distance from the source.
Waveform is related to speed, wavelength and frequency .
- Wave speed (v) = Distance traveled by a wave per unit of time.
- Wavelength (λ) = The distance between two consecutive points which are in phase.
- Frequency (ƒ) = The number of complete oscillations made in one second.
Where:-
Speed = Frequency (ƒ) x Wavelength (λ)
v= ƒλ
The higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength. At constant speed, when the frequency increase, the wavelength will decrease.
In this game, you have to modify the wavelength and amplitude and guide the particle to collect light orbs in order to score points. Thus, you're playing a Displacement-Distance (s-d) graph game. Where amplitude (a) and wavelength (λ) will be playing as the main role of the game.
The bigger the amplitude, the shorter the wavelength, the faster the particle will travel throughout the wave.
Vice versa, the larger the wavelength, the smaller the amplitude, the slower the particle will travel throughout the wave.
Basically this concept is easy to understand with this Waveform Simulator, however to modify the wavelength while the particle is traveling at super speed will be tough and challenging for some players to master this game.

OneShot made me curious, made me smile, and made me think throughout its entire duration. OneShot also made me dive through my computer's hard-drive in a scramble to progress. OneShot finally held my moral compass hostage up until the very end, where I was actually so afraid to finish its journey from the consequences hovering over my back.
The genius of OneShot is how deliberately it tries to makes you -not- care about the world. Yet the quaint interactions you share with its denizens, how intricately you witness the environment operating, living and collapsing as you explore it, and the attachment you grow with the wide-eyed, innocent (and so adorable!!) main character as you guide him, constantly unsure of yourself if you're leading him down the right path-- all tie into an incredible bond between reality and the world intended for you to save.
OneShot's gameplay is really just a series of scattered puzzles and conversations, and yet both aspects have moments that can suddenly be so unorthodox, so spontaneously clever when they spring out of nothing, that the impacts left upon you drop like a hammer when it's your choice to decide whether every experience was worth it.
I could go on about this game's magical, transformative power, but like with Undertale, its emotionally-manipulative cousin that I can draw so many parallels between - and even suggest some ways that OneShot surpasses it - I should leave this review short and say that the positives I told you about are waiting there for you and more.

In The Typing of the Dead: Overkill you play as a special agent who partners up with a potty-mouthed detective to track down the villain Papa Ceasar and save the county from a mutant outbreak.  The story unfolds over nine episodes and combines horror with potentially disturbing, over-the-top comedy.
The game is a reworked version of the first-person rail shooter The House of the Dead: Overkill - Extended Cut, in which the shooting mechanics of combat have been replaced by quickly and accurately typing words and phrases that appear on screen.  Words are randomly chosen, so they are different every time you play, and multiple difficulty levels are available to provide a challenge for typists of varying skill levels.
A port of the Playstation 3 version of House of the Dead: Overkill - Extended Cut is also included so, if you type exclusively with your index fingers or simply don’t enjoy the activity, you can always take out zombies the old-fashioned way.  In this mode, you must aim and shoot traditionally and may buy and upgrade guns after each episode with the cash you were quick enough to grab.
Movement and camera are on pre-determined paths so the experience feels like taking a ride through a haunted house at the fair, allowing you to focus on destroying zombies, picking up collectibles, rescuing civilians and racking up your high score.  Boss fights at the end of each episode are well-designed and two-player co-op is a lot of fun, but it is possible to frequently encounter bugs in multiplayer that require you to restart the episode, such as words not appearing properly or the game desyncing and freezing.
Since the game involves dialogue littered with profanity (F bombs), plenty of gore, and touches on themes like incest and making fun of the handicapped, it’s not for the squeamish or those who may be offended by such things.  If you don’t take your entertainment too seriously and can handle the outrageous content, it’s very much worth the quick, three-to-four-hour playthrough, but no one would blame you if you couldn’t.

Listen to me very carefully before you think all im going to do is praise this game just because i give it a thumb up. This game has a lot of faults, yet at the same time it does a lot of things correctly as well. Not specific enough? Well lets get specific.
The good things? It is fun, the grind isn't bad at all - you can literally get to level 50 in 1-2 weeks without even noticing it - and still get good gear provided you know what you're doing. (If you pvp, do warfronts, and you'll get plenty of pvp gear.) PVP is very accessible - it doesn't require you get the best gear on the right away. PvE is very fun as well, and is diverse provided you're progressing at a good rate.
Now comes the bad stuff. For me this game got old really fast at level 49. I didnt bother to do quests because, well, i was already outleveling them because i was pvping. (Although you could de-level by mentoring and do them to get a 'challenge.')  Additionally, this game is not rewarding. The loot is terrible most of the time - and if you're pvping you'll never ever use it simply because you'll probably have enough 'favor' (ingame currency) to buy better rift store gear, and as another addition, the auction house is locked down until you've managed to either shell out five bucks, or get a rift-exchange in order to get 1500 credits.
Now the AH and pvp doesnt make the game. There's a lot i didn't see, and a lot i didn't get to do. Among more pros, the classes are diverse, and you can play more than one role, making switching 'easy-as-pie' if you want to try something else. But for me, the game got repetetive, and in the end, despite the innovations, still reeked of the deriviative mmo-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t most mmo games tend to smell of nowadays anyway. Not much new. However, still gets a 'recommended' simply because its enjoyable.
To sum it up.
PROS
Good and diverse classes. Easy to play multiple roles.
Diverse PvE content.
PvP can be fun, and is easy to get into.
Something i did not mention - Professions are enjoyable.
The grind is barely noticable. (Until 50-60)
CONS
Loot is a joke, and the rift store reflects on this, making this game absolutely unsatsifying in some instances.
Gets repeteive.
AH is locked for selling (You can still buy.) down unless you shell out 5 bucks, or save a bunch of ingame currency to buy a rift exchange. (rex)
Overall, good mmo, but has its fallbacks.

Overall this is a very good game with a lot of depth and some very fun well designed classes that said its not without its problems,
Partially I take issue with the perma death mechanic. I tend to like games with permadeath as far as rougelike games go. Nethack is amazing a gritty survival game and every playthrough is unique and you feel fragile and human through out it. ToMEs playthroughs all start roughly the same and get better 10/15 levels in. Those first 10 levels are a slog after you have done it a couple of time. Pouring 10 hours into a character then getting a clumsy death when you are on you last life is pretty painful because you have to restart with the same plot, with the same dungeons, and often with the same unique item drops. It becomes uninviting.
Exploration mode you say then.. but that has no penalty taking away the tension completely. You need a middle mode between exploration and adventure, perhaps losing all your items (bar the three stocked in your box) for a continue? Or at least gaining a life after a major boss. If you pour 10,15,20 hours before dying its a huge time investment and its very punishing. Particularity because the early game is relatively dull. More choice and divergent paths in the early game might help.
After a death you pretty much have to play with a different class (which are all brilliantly designed and play fluidly with so many build styles changing gameplay/strategy considerably) and it can take awhile to get to grips with how that class functions often this can result in silly deaths. Which is the bizarre thing that you have to play a class to have a good idea of how you want to build it, but due to the time commitment you would rather restart with a different class then master one.
Basically if you have a lot of time to try the different classes and get good go for it! The amount of depth in the character builds is staggering with some really awesome stuff. (I love the time manipulation ones which you can really mess around with placements and divide and pool enemies together) but all of them offer valid play styles, from adaptable to min-maxing synergies. The depth of build is the real core strength of this game and trying a new class is what makes you play again after a bad beat. There are very little games with this much content and its a lot of value for money.
Pros:
Intelligent strategic gameplay
Huge choice of classes and viable builds within classes offering dozens of different play-styles
Challenging game play and while your character improves to godly levels it remains challanging
Enormous amount of content and most of it at a surprisingly high quality
Interesting and engaging mechanics which meaningfully change the game with different classes.
Cons:
Same starting areas get samey
Punishing consecutive mistakes. 5 bad minutes can destroy a 15 hour playthrough
Weak overwritten lore has potential but is wordy and unengaging with hard to believe motivations between groups
Some bugs that need ironing out
Some mechanics are poorly explained and pretty unclear.
Not really a game that is forgiving to people with a job/relationship/other interests huge time sink with very little value outside of its mechanics
Would I recommend? Absolutely. Very few games this good at this price range play a few times get some decent playthroughs going then put it down and maybe pick it up again later.

Dead Rising 4 loses a lot of what made the previous Dead Rising game so entertaining.  The open world loses a lot of personality compared to the casinos in DR2 or even the city in DR3.  Each section of the world seems only superficially detailed, it's either mall, stores, or houses with very little personality.  It feels as if the content is stretched out to make the game area larger without making it more interesting.
The crafting system is probably the largest downgrade from previous Dead Rising games.  While there are a number of weapons to create, virtually all of them require very specific components that are only found in a small number of places.  Want to use a boxing glove weapon again?  You have to find a tree topper or a holiday bell to make them compared to just needing a bladed weapon in DR2.  Weapons that were in previous Dead Rising games are missing and there are many items which cannot be used in crafting at all.
The game would have been much improved if they had let you use categories of weapons to craft rather than needing specific items so much, as it is now, you're essentially limited to a handful of weapons that have easy to find components while the other fifty or so weapons are unused.  Vehicle crafting is similarly limited with only a couple of vehicles readily available.
The game does address the lack of available crafting items by letting you buy combo weapons and vehicles from survivors in shelters.  But this takes away a lot of the charm of Dead Rising which is feeling like you're surviving on your own with whatever tools you have at hand.  Instead it feels like a standard open world game where you look for collectibles, grind for money, and go back to base to resupply before doing it all over again.
I purchased the game on sale for half off, but I would not recommend DR4 if you still haven't played any of the other Dead Rising games.  This is aside from the loss of features such as a time limit and large amounts of replayability that have slowly been stripped out of the games.

This is my favorite game this generation.
Just a word of warning to game hoarders; it's a game that only shows it's true value if you invest time in it. If you play it as you'd play any light platformer ("I just want to finish this thing"), you'd be missing everything that makes it so great.
This game is made for people who like to get the most of their platformer action games, not just finish them and toss them aside (not that there's too many of them worth a try nowdays). It's for all of us who were having a blast with Mega Man 9 and 10's challenges, time attack and endless modes, or were aiming for no-death runs on Hard Corps: Uprising. It expects you to take your time... learn from it, get good at it, and try all of its difficult challenges.
And by my experience, it's the modern action platformer that best achieves this feeling. After all, its a gameplay concept that's been evolving for a long time by the hand of its developers.
Inti Creates' Mega Man Zero series introduced the next step of what I felt was the natural evolution of the Mega Man X series (more so than Capcom's own in-house later entries, X7 and X8). It continued refining the ranking system and performance-based powerup prizes first experimented with in Mega Man X5, and as soon as they reached the first sequel, Mega Man Zero 2, they changed the way you play these games altogether. Now the game rewarded you with missable powerups based on your performance. In a way, it taught you how to play it well rather than just play it by "surviving through it", so by the time you got the unlockable Hard Mode, you'd be up to it. They were somewhat short games, but thanks to these mechanics, they gained a lot of replayability.
They kept rewarding skill with Zero 3 (good times), but later softened a bit with Zero 4. Maybe they started to hears some criticism? That would explain why later, with the Mega Man ZX series, they tried something different. They kept most of Zero's core mechanics, but lost some of its pace and feel due to the introduction of interconnected maps you had to traverse "by foot" instead of a select stage screen. It was a weird mix of slow-paced exploration feel ("thing you only want to go through once") that didn't mix well with the well achieved learn-and-repeat replayability the game was based on.
After the abandonment of the Mega Man franchise by Capcom, and Keiji Inafune's collaboration with Inti Creates as an independant game creator (he's credited as the 'action director' of this game), we finally got the next step of Inti Creates signature gameplay's evolution with Azure Striker Gunvolt in 2014.
If you've tried any of the games I just mentioned, you know what kind of tight controls and challenging-yet-totally-fair stage design and combat you can expect. There's shots, there's dash, there's wall-kicking climbing... all the best action platformers standards. Although this time your attacks are not your gunshots primarly, but a combination of shots that "tag" your enemies, and a forcefield that'll hit tagged enemies as long as they're on screen. It's hard to explain before trying it, but it has a good feel to it, and it's a mechanic that makes this stand out among the usual run-and-shoot deal.
Even if the forcefield does the killing, you'll still get different guns as you go on, which change the way you tag your enemies. So now, instead of arbitrary "rock beats scissor" damage charts, you get actual visible mechanics as to why one weapon is better than other depending on the situation (ex: for shielded enemies, you'll want a weapon that tags through obscables; for multiple enemies onscreen, you'll pick the weapon that tags as much enemies at once as possible; for enemies clogged together, the one that spreads behind after its first contact)
Besides the action itself, what makes this game stand out as a performance-based action game is the Kudo system. A plain score system, and the basis of how your performance is measured. The catch is:
i) they multiply exponentially (the more you accumulate in one shot, the better);
ii) you lose all of them if you get hurt;
iii) you don't automatically get them, you have to "cash them in". For that, you need to either use an (optional) special offensive skill, or touch one of the (optional) checkpoints throughout the stage. Or, of course, reach the end of the stage without losing them.
What this produces is a constant gamble where the bets are your own skills. A constant wondering of "am I good enough to skip this checkpoint, so I can keep adding Kudos until the next one"? Then there's another layer of decision: extra score multipliers on top of the total depending on how fast you finish the stage. "Should I rush through, risking taking a hit, or take my time to build up Kudos safely?"
Which makes this work so well, is how the "retries" system is handled: there's no extra lives. No penalties for retrying, or damage taken. All that matters is your Kudos. So if you decided to take a checkpoint, you can retry the next section of the stage as many times as you want. However, for the absolute best ranking, S+ (which is the goal of the most rewarding in-game challenges and Steam achivements), you'll need to multiply your Kudos as much as possibly... that is, no-damage (or almost no-damage) runs.
But it manages to make it less tasking than it sounds, because you have plenty of less demanding challenges to practice and learn the stages from. Besides, you'll get betters skills and equipment over time; yet another incentive to keep practicing. You'll be grinding money and equipment components on each stage run: the better your performance, more generous the prizes.
With all that, the feared no-damage runs become very achievable to anyone who goes through everything the game has to offer.
This is not one of those games you'll finish once, then find a youtube video of someone doing a speedrun and think "that's just crazy"... The game is designed for you to reach that point gradually. And it feels awesome.
Overall, that's the point. This is a game designed to make you feel awesome while playing it. Besides guiding your way up to the more difficult challenges, there's a lot of tiny details that enforce this. The sound effects are satisfying, the animations are beautiful, the UI is sexy (just seeing that huge Kudos score grow ends up being addicting), etc. The cherry on top of all: the regular BGM changes to some very pumped up, DDR-style, J-POP tunes when you're above a certain point of Kudos. The feeling of "you're awesome, just keep at it" is enforced, not only by the score system, but every aspect of the game.
Even though the enemy variety is slim, I think it's better for it. Having a limited amout of hazards reinforces the fact that these are obstacles you're supposed to learn from easily. It works great as it is.
As for the Steam version:
I played this game first on 3DS when it launched two years ago, and now I'm having a blast doing all the challenges all over again. The port is not perfect, it has some flaws (locked on 30fps; you have PC-specific setting on the launcher and others on in-game menus; the controller customization is limited, I had to take Xpadder to assign the special skills to actual buttons because they're locked to either F keys or the controller's analogue)... but it feels really good to be able to play such a powerful action game as it should: with a proper controller in my hand, with a proper screen in front of me... instead of on a crummy handheld.
(Theres new game mode too! And a more faithful retranslation with restored dialogues cut from the 3DS ver.)
So I IMPLORE Inti Creates that they port to Steam the upcoming sequel as well. After having my favorite action platformers locked in small handheld screens for so long (since the Game Boy Advance days, that it), having Azure Striker Gunvolt on PC is a godsend.

While it's not the best port in the world, it's certainly not the worst either since it is functional, with a 30 fps lock, somewhat obscure keyboard controls, and the fact that the menu layout will make the game look like it's on an emulator. I have accidentally came across a way to adjust the size of the windows so if you find the windows too small, hold down left Alt and drag the size of the window until it fits your needs.
Here's a list for the keyboard controls so it saves you some time trying to find them if you refuse to play with a controler like me:
Z=jump
X=shoot
C=electric field
V=dash (double tapping left/right works as well)
Left/Right Arrow Keys=move left/right
F1-F4=unlockable skills
Dodgey ports aside, Azure Striker Gunvolt is a pretty fun side-scrolling platformer that is relatively easy to traverse, but the boss fights will most likely have you tearing your hair out the first time you encounter them (especially for certain bosses that have ultimates that will result in instant death). Why do I say the game is easy? Well, there is a little trinket you start off with by default that makes you ignore damage entirely so long as you're not using your powers and you have energy to use up, but if you want a bit more challenge, there's a hard mode that disables it or if you don't want to change the difficulty, feel free to take it off on your own accord. Assuming you don't suck as much as I do, the main game is relatively short spanning about 3 to 5 hours (maybe a bit longer if you're trying to get the true ending) depending on how much you're struggling on the final boss. I personally think the length is pretty good for a game like this. All killer, no filler.
The combat system is pretty simple as you're armed with one gun with a number of unlockable firing modes with different attributes tied to them and your powers of manipulating lightning. It's really just a case where you tag the target with your gun up to 3 tags for one target and depending on the current function of your gun a total of the listed number of tags at a time while using you're lightning powers as your main source of damage. Just be careful not to completely drain your energy or you might find yourself in a bit of trouble since the cooldown takes way too long to ignore, but you can manualy recharge your energy by double tapping the down arrow key (or the joystick if your using a controller) so long as you still have energy left over. There is a grading system for every level and how you are graded will be determined by speed, efficiency, and how much damage you took. At first, I wasn't very sure what triggered my revival when I died, but I found out that it triggered by chance depending on how often you were talking to Joule back at base before undertaking a mission, although I'm not sure if those chances reset after attempting a mission because there doesn't seem to be a way to gauge that and ultimately feels like the whole relationship system is pointless to have since there really isn't all that much to it anyway.
For $15, I think it's worth having a look depending on how tolerant you are to 30 fps. It's even got extra missions and additional rule sets that is not included in the 3DS version increasing the game's overall value. Too bad the sequal's going to be held hostage by Nintendo.

Before I begin this review, if you don't own any kind of PC compatible controller, don't bother with this game, unless you don't mind  developing Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.
When I first heard about this game, being developed by Inti Creates, and being a "spiritual succesor" of the Megaman Zero series of sorts, "hyped" wasn't enough to describe how I felt, seeing the trailers and such was amazing and i really expected the game to BE amazing.
Sadly, at the time of its release, I didn't own a 3DS, so I had to skip it, until it came to steam, and got is as soon as i could but all i got was disappointment...
Booting the game, everything fine, resolution, audio, etc, all fine, except for the small bottom right window (that I assume originally was the 3DS touch screen) is really small even on 1920x1080, game runs at 30fps but it's not quite terrible unless you're one of those 60fps or bust kind of people.
Problems started when i loaded the game and i started playing, this "port" still has the console controls setup, A, B, X, Y, RB, LB, etc, no mention of keyboard keys at all, so i had to play the guessing game at first to see what button did what, after a few minutes i got it down, but playing with keyboard was borderline impossible, you just have to press too many buttons at the same time and it felt terrible, thankfully i own PC controller that I currently use and works decently, so unless you own a controller, you're going to have a terrible time playing this.
The story is mediocre at best, anti-hero saving the damsel in distress, plot is explained further through loading screens (which go too fast to read unless you own a prehistoric PC), and in-game conversations between characters, there's not much to it really though, gotta save the special snowflake woman from the bad guys that want to use her powers for evil, until a plot twist later which changes the tone of the game, but it's essentially the same deal even then.
Graphics are ok, can't really improve much from a 3DS port, but it looks nice, a few problems are that enemies are big and the screen feels compact, and too much stuff can go on at the same time on screen thanks to you shooting, avoiding bullets, using flashield and the lightnings is shoots, enemies moving around, etc making it hard to maneveur or see anything at some times.
Music is nice, also if you manage to score enough "Kudos" (Game's equivalent to a combo counter) during a stage, you get rewarded with J-Pop for some reason, which is not bad unless you dislike that kind of stuff.
Now, gameplay:
As I said, if you don't own a controller, don't bother with this game, you have to press too many buttons at the same time to actually do anything, you have: jumping, dashing, shooting, flashfield (your special lightning skill), special skills and general movement, and sometimes you have to use a mix of them at the same time.
Stages aren't really hard unless you rush them (which you want to do if you want a good rank at the end), they're your typical megaman platforming stages, sometimes bland and a bit uninspired, go from point A to B, fight a midboss if the stage has one, and reach the boss room at the end, which a healthy amount of spikes and pitfalls in between (thankfully spikes don't kill you instantly this time).
Bosses are your typical megaman boss fights here, they have set movement patterns and attacks, the difference is that each boss has its HP is separated in 3 parts, and depleting one bar gives the boss more movements to use during the fight, kinda nifty, until you deplete the 2nd bar, and the boss does its special move, which will kill you unless you do "something", and that "something" varies from boss to boss, so expect trial and error on each boss since their skills are not really intuitive, and OHKO's can be cheap...
Speaking of dying, the game has an integrated "You suck" mode that sometimes happens when you die (not sure exactly what triggers it, maybe the crappier you do in the stage or something? not sure), which starts playing another J-Pop song and makes you practically invincible, you have infinite flashfield charge, you can fly, but you can't rack in combo counter which could potentially kill your scoring, which ill explain in a bit, by the way you can't disable this, so if you feel like it's a total slap to the face and totally kills the challenge, your only option is restarting the stage or checkpoint and... not dying...
The game has a similar ranking system as the Megaman Zero series but harder to work with. Scoring in this game works like this: You have a combo counter called Kudos, which increases by shooting enemies and bosses with both your gun and flashfield, this counter adds to your score multiplier and remains as long as you keep killing enemies and don't get hit (didn't time how much it takes for the counter to roll down for not killing enemies for too long though, but it's enough time if you keep moving on), along that, you also get extra points at the end of the stage based on how fast you finished the stage.
With better scores you're rewarded with more items at the end of the stage, but given how much stuff happens at once on the stages, unless you memorize everything and are ready for every bullet, missile, laser, etc coming at your way, odds are you're going to get hit, lose your combo counter, and have to repeat the stage/checkpoint again if you plan to get anything past A rank, otherwise it's inconsequential and totally meaningless for the average player since you can keep repeating stages to farm items.
The items you get at the end of the stages can be used with the game's crafting system, which is "Collect X, Y and Z, plus some currency, and craft items", items which range from getting more HP from HP items, double/triple jumps, flashfield recharging faster/lasting longer, weapon upgrades, etc, not a bad system, but if you want them all you'll find yourself repeating stages a lot to farm certain items.
Overall the game is not terrible
you can get past the god awful default keyboard control setup, the insanely hard requirements to get anything past A rank, the cheap OHKO's the bosses can do unless you know exactly what to do, and the amount of crap going at once on the really small looking screen, the game is not bad, just don't expect the same level of gameplay as the Megaman Zero series if you came to this game expecting that level of story or gameplay.
You can play the game as it is just fine, but everything past the ranking, speedrun mode, challenges, etc are clearly aimed towards experts players, so expect an exercise in frustration if you decide to get past A rank and do everything this game as to offer.

When I first started my other YouTube series, Crushing My Backlog, I expected this gaming journey to be an open and shut case of just completing a game, crossing it off my list, and forever forgetting about it. But that’s not the case with Azure Striker Gunvolt, the 2014 Inti Creates 2D action platformer that absolutely captured my heart and added a unique spin one of my favorite genres. Hey, I’ll go ahead and spoil the ending of this review for you – I highly recommend this game. But don’t leave yet, let me tell you why my love for this runs deep.
The game focuses on our hero, Gunvolt, who is one of many people who’ve developed septimal powers known as adepts. You can look at adepts in the same vein as superheroes – people with superhuman abilities, such as, flight, teleportation, or those who can control various elements, like fire, water, or in Gunvolt’s case, electricity. The world is currently a peaceful place, thanks to the Sumeragi Group – although, behind the scenes, the group is actually going to great lengths to attempt to experiment and control the world’s adepts.However, Gunvolt’s employer, QUILL, isn’t going to allow that to happen. You see, the QUILL organization is an anti-Sumeragi group that is directed by its founding member Asimov, who like Gunvolt, is an electricity based adept. Gunvolt owes his life to this man, all because Asimov rescued him from a Sumeragi facility where they were performing horrific experiments on him. Now that he’s free, he has dedicated his life to QUILL and taking down the Sumeragi group. Which brings us to the current events where the game opens with our hero held captive by one of Sumeragi’s henchmen. Gunvolt is tasked with locating and assassinating a unique adept named Lumen who’s housed within a young girl named Joule.
Now it’s no surprise that Azure Striker Gunvolt embodies a Mega Man vibe since the Inti Creates team has worked with the series in the past. Mega Man dealt with Doctor Wily’s robot master antics, while Gunvolt has to hunt down seven crazed adepts who’re associated with Nova and the Sumeragi group. You’ll jump, shoot, and dash your way through stages, just like Mega Man, but in the case of Gunvolt, it’s completely different. His weapon alone does very minimum damage and it’s used to tag his enemies. You see, destroying enemies efficiently is a two step process where you must first tag the enemy with your weapon and then finish them off with Gunvolt’s flash field. Enemies can be tagged up to three times and the flash field damage is amplified with each increased level. As you progress through the game and defeat bosses you’ll acquire new weapons that make tagging multiple enemies much easier for higher scores and bonuses, which is where this game starts to shine.
Okay, so at the end of each stage, the player is given a letter grade based off of how well they performed during the stage and between stages. Then afterward, in Gunvolt’s apartment, they can synthesize different gear to aid them in battle. Some of the more rare gear requires you to complete challenges issued by QUILL to obtain hard to find materials. For instance, there’s a pendant that you can equip that makes spikes lethal and removes Gunvolt’s ability to neutralize damage in exchange for some of his electricity meter, otherwise known as EP. But this accessory adds ten percent to the kudos gained – which is an absolute godsend when you’re shooting for S+ ranks. Kudos matter because they are essential for achieving higher scores. As you traverse through a stage you’ll gain kudos for inflicting damage on enemies, but your kudos will reset back to zero if you receive damage – so a solid performance is ideal. The idea behind kudos is to build up as many as you can, then convert them into bonus points by using an attack skill, passing through a checkpoint, destroying an enemy with a special skill, or completing a mission. You can also acquire bonus kudos by destroying targets with a level three tag, eliminating multiple targets simultaneously, or even killing them while in midair.
At its core, Azure Striker Gunvolt is a high-speed action platformer with plenty to keep you busy and many options that allow the player to customize their experience. My initial opinion of this game was lukewarm. During my first play-through, I kept thinking to myself that the difficulty was way too easy. Health replenishment came from almost every enemy, bosses only took a couple of tries to defeat, zero controllers were thrown, and I never saw a game over screen – something that I am all too familiar with from Mega Man games. But looking at Gunvolt as if it were a Mega Man game is completely wrong because at the end of the day Azure Striker Gunvolt is a completely different experience. An experience that focuses on the player’s skill, speed, and scoring. Sure, I’ve been gushing about how amazing this is, but it does suffer from bland level design where exploration is scarce and enemy variation that is rather lacking, but the mechanics and challenges make up for it. You can pick it up on the Nintendo 3DS eShop for $14.99 and there’s also a demo available if you’d like to try it before you buy it. However, I used the Steam version for this review, which I think is identical and also $14.99; but there is no demo available. So if you stumble upon an extra $14 or you catch it on sale, I’d definitely recommend picking it up. I never thought it would capture my heart, but it did and I hope this review helped persuade you to give it a go, too.

A quick disclaimer: when checking reviews of a game on Steam, the most important thing I look for is not whether a reviewer gave it a  thumb up or down, but the number of hours he has spent actually playing the game. Never trust a positive review from a guy saying "this is the best game ever" but has only 5h playing it. So many games look great at first, only to be forgotten in a week or two.
Now, take a look at some of the reviews for this game. There are people with over a 1,000 hours of ToME behind them. This says a lot about the game's depth, replayability and just sheer fun factor.
I've been a fan of roguelikes for a long time now (maybe for over 15 years? who knows?), and this is hands down the best one I've ever played. The designer knew what to focus on instead of flooding the game with half-implemented features that end up taking away from the fun of the game. There is no hunger, consumables etc. Heck, even crafting was only added in a recent DLC, and even then it's only a small detail.
So what is there that it has? The best and most creative class-system ever seen in an RPG game, together with a great tactical combat system, with enemies potentially having access to the same skills as the player. I mean, in this game you can be a chronomancer and one of your skills called "See the threads" allow you to play the same X turns three times and then choose the best thread to make it "reality". Another class literally possesses mobs and uses their own powers. Every class is very unique and plays very differently. The unique items that can drop are also very cleverly designed, giving you unique and fun powers and not just being a pumped-up version of a normal item with the name in a different color.
Other than that, the game is very hard, which can be frustrating for some, but there are many permadeath options for the less hardcore players out there. The lore is also very rich, even though lore is not really something I care about in these games.
The only downside I can think of are the graphics, which are just bad. No one expects AAA graphics from a roguelike, but ToME just looks kitsch.
