What was once Tales of Middle Earth, a great Angband offshoot, got turned into this game - a good rogue, hidden under layers and layers of terrible menu and interface design, hotbars with ridiculous icons and no way to properly play in ASCII mode.

Playing this game is like reading a 19th century novel; know it's going to take quite a long time and some parts will be very slow but the rich story line and character progression make for a very rewarding experience.
Black Mirror is a very straight-forward, adventure, point and click game where most problems can be solved by repeatedly talking to different characters and finding inventory items. There are very few mini games, but all that are there were really fun.
As always, I must comment on my own personal pet peeve, slow walking protagonists, but in this game it's not just the protagonist that's slow. Every time you click on someone to talk to, there will be an approximately 5 second, animated delay while they stop what they're doing and turn to you. It can get a bit grating but clearly, this is no manic game and is designed for a relaxed game play experience. One small upside is that while Samuel doesn't run and definitely doesn't jump, ha, if you can click on a scene exit, the game will jump to the next screen (though again, after a few second delay).
I also have to warn you about the absolutely most annoying thing in the game, there are two or three scenarios where you have to wait for another character to get back to you about something before you can continue along with the story line. They say things like "Come back later" and well, they really do mean later. There's nothing you can do to speed this along. You can go to every location possible, look and talk to everything or everyone you've already clicked on, or just sit and wait.
Clearly, this does make sense from a story perspective, but having gameplay where the character does nothing but just has to move around or wait is absolutely ridiculous and should never ever be included.
Now regardless of my above complaints, I still really liked this game and I can't wait to continue in the sequel.

I don't know how I missed this game the first time around.  And the $9.99 asking price for a game that's 12+ years old is a little ambitious, but I feel it is well worth the price.
Overall, it's a pretty straight-forward point-and-click adventure.  You're the prodigal relative who has returned to the manor after many years of self-imposed ostracism.  William (your uncle or brother or dad, something like that) has died under mysterious circumstances and you take it upon yourslef to find out what has happened.
It's kind of a modern analog for "The Witness" or "Deadline" or "Suspect", except that it's a touch more linear.  If you remember those games then you like a good mystery.  There are some interesting puzzlers here, nothing too tough.  But truly the plot here is interesting and compelling.  You interact with a lot of characters and you have an opportunity to ask them a ton of questions.  And the characters are written as though they are real people -- that is, they don't see their function in the game as forwarding the plot.  They have personalities, they lie, they have their own interests that they pursue.  They don't just sit there and give you information.
Part thriller, part horror, part mystery, this game makes the hours go quickly.  I haven't even finished it yet at 6.3 hours.
As I wrote before, there are some tedious moments that haunt all point-and-click adventures.  You really have to be careful whisking the mouse around the screen or you'll miss something.  And sometimes you'll like at something fifty times by left clicking on it and then, for snicks, right click and there comes the solution.
Truly, $9.99 was asking a lot for this game.  I got it at a heavily discounted price.  But overall I wouldn't be disappointed if I had paid full price for it.  I can't say the same for its sequels.  But spend some time with this little gem.  Well worth it and you will feel satisfied.
A shame all modern games can't pay more attention to this story and plot that this game has and spend less time on the flash and dazzle of graphics.

Aesthetically, Cuphead is a beautiful game, taking full advantage of its 1930s cartoon-inspired art style. Each and every character, background and prop is drawn and animated beautifully, and the fact that StudioMDHR went the extra mile and utilised cel animation instead of generic computer-generated graphics just shows how dedicated they were to the creation of this game, and it definitely paid off.
The gameplay constantly keeps you on your toes and it never feels as though there's any sort of curve in difficulty - while it's practically unavoidable that you will die a lot and you won't beat any stage on your first couple tries, you never feel as though it's unfairly difficult compared to any other previous experience. The mechanics and controls are easy to pick up and use, even on a keyboard, which is what I used.
As someone who is particularly interested in music and the soundtrack of something, whether it be a game or any other piece of media, I can safely say that Cuphead's soundtrack is magnificent. It truly fits and embraces the aesthetic of the game, and at the same time sounds great on its own. Really that's all there is to say.
To conclude, the seven years that this game took to complete definitely paid off, and I'm glad Cuphead is becoming as well-recieved as it is, because in my opinion it deserves the praise. Not perfect, as is with any other game, but nevertheless definitely one of my favourite games of the 2017. Solid 9.5/10.

Best game I've played in years, plus tons of replay value; I've gone through on all 3 saves and S-Ranked all the bosses multiple times. The difficulty is very refreshing (games hold our hands way, WAY too much these days), and teaches you the core game mechanics early on. That's just the gameplay.
The music is ♥♥♥♥ing incredible. As someone who loves/plays jazz and big band, the soundtrack for this game is beyond amazing. Every boss theme is performed by a real band (no computer-generated, bit-crushed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t) and every tempo is well above 200 BPM, making for very well fitting frantic music while you fight the bosses.
I won't gush about the art too much; don't get me wrong, the animation and art is great, but I feel it overshadows the actual gameplay. Lots of inexperienced 'gamers' buy this game for its' unique 1930's art style and complain about it being too hard.
Segwaying from the last part, here's where the controversey lies. The game is not that hard, and is certainly not unfair. Although this is coming from someone who has S-Ranked all the bosses, I will admit that the bosses gave me some trouble my first time through; it's not exactly a game you pick up and master in half an hour, you have to put time into it. You'll die a few hundred times getting through the game the first time, but by the time you BEAT a boss you know all of their attack patterns and what weapons and charm you should use, making the replay factor much greater. The early bosses do a great job of teaching you the core gameplay mechanics, as I mentioned earlier, so if you just practice, you WILL succeed. There's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, just fair difficulty.
Overall, Cuphead easily earns a 10/10. There's nothing is this game that is impossible to overcome, you just have to work at it. Great art, amazing gameplay and music, and one of, if not the single best replay value of any game I've played to date.
Thank you for reading, and I hope you decide to buy this wonderful game.

Hearts of Iron IV has a lot of good ideas that should work in a Hearts of Iron game, but don't work in the modern iteration of paradox grand strategy games.
Splitting Industrial capacity from HOI3 into two seperate factory types is a good idea and works for larger nations. Smaller nations can barely produce the most basic of equipment with the pitiful industrial base they have. It adds some "gameplay" I suppose. I can click on a slot next to Rifle model BIV and suddenly produce more! But now I have a shortage of iron, better cut back on that tank production! F U N
Equipment is a great idea and should add some sense of depth to the game. The reality is that it creates tedium in having to manage your factories and allows for min-maxing absent in the rest of the game. On top of that, once again smaller nations can barely produce their needs. It's a real cool addition for the first five minutes, then you stop caring about what class of tank or what variation of a rifle you are producing, and default to producing the best model or the model you can build the most of.
The resource system is baffling. I can produce 9 iron a day for consumption. However, if I use only 8, the other 1 disappears into the vacuum of space. It can't be stored. It doesn't make sense that equipment can be stored by the resources to build said equipment cant be. Ever heard of oil barrels paradox? You must have left them in HOI3. Maybe it'll be added in some DLC.
The division designer makes no sense. HOI3 worked just fine and allowed you to work with a lot of unique divisions even with a small template. Why is it necessary to have experience in order to adjust the composition of a division? I suppose we needed more mana bars like EU4. It's just another hurdle of "gameplay" to jump through.
The real meat of a world war 2 strategy game should be the warfare. The problem with that is the simple ease at which the game can be played and beaten. I was unaware that Hitler just needed to draw a line across Russia to conquer it. And I am aware that you can control units idividually. It's pointless. It was better in HOI3. This might not matter if the AI was competent. I have a feeling that the inadequacy is caused by the frontline system as opposed to a theatre system in HOI3. If a paratrooper landed in some province in a theatre that was AI controlled, units would move to retake the province. This only happens in HOI4 if that enemy troop lands in a region that is being activly garrisoned. The AI just isn't fluid. It doesn't react.
I guess this is what we have to settle for now. Youtube bait. Making continuous DLC packs just to get your marketers to entince their audience to one more lets play! Congratulations on reaching a larger audience Paradox. You only sold what made your games great to do so.

Most negative reviews rightfully call out severe problems such as a paid DLC implementing items that should already be in the game and the AWFUL AI, but for just gameplay I think this game is defintely worth it even with all of it's current problems. A good buy in my opinion.

The game is phenomenal. If you like Megaman X or Megaman Zero, this is right up your alley. Be warned however: Some of the boss patterns will feel confusing and unfair on your first try. They're not hard to memorize, as the patterns do not have that much variation, but you'll definitely need to play them at least once before you start getting good.
Music is just what you'd expect from a game of its kind (and it really is top notch). The visuals are what you'd expect from a 2D game on the 3DS (think GBA, except somewhat higher resolution and some flashier effects), and the sprite work is just fantastic. Controls are fast and fluid, the action flows and just feels good... A game designed with a mindset sadly forgotten in the mainstream AAA industry of today: To challenge the player and, above all, to make the gameplay FEEL good. Just controlling Gunvolt is satisfying.
The port could be a little better, but it's good enough. Performance is perfect, you can select resolutions up to 1080p (not like anything over that is needed given the 2D pixel art nature of the game) and you can toggle Vsync. Some parts of the game (like the main menu) require showing two screens at once (as this game was made for the Nintendo 3DS), which makes it extremely obvious that this was a pretty quick console port. The game also used to refuse to detect the Xbox One controller. I'm not sure if it was because of game updates or the updates Microsoft did to the Xbox One controller driver, but as of the date of this review the controller works and remaps flawlessly.
I hear there's a sequel being developed. If it makes its way onto Steam, hopefully it can get a proper redesign to support a single screen and X-Input support as the game currently relies on DirectInput which may cause issues with some controllers, and requires mapping the controls, whereas X-Input would just work out of the box properly mapped for any controller that supports it.
As it is, however, I think this game is well worth it if you're willing to overlook the minor porting flaws. Once you're up and running, you'll be having a ton of fun. Very reminiscent of Megaman X and Zero in every way.

Even after 36 hours played, I feel like I'm scarcely competent at this game. Most of that has to do with the lack of any in-game tutorial or guide; there is a very brief tutorial, but it only covers basic movement and keybinds, not any in-depth breakdown of gameplay mechanics or character-specific strategy. To compound that problem, most of the Youtube guides are for the original game, and don't account for the numerous balance and metagame changes that came with "Stage 2" (the free-to-play update), and so taking their advice verbatim and/or without having enough in-game experience to recognize what's outdated and what's not might make you play even *worse*.
I like this game in concept, and mostly in execution as well, although there do seem to be a myriad of balance issues currently plaguing it. Namely, according to most people who played the original, most monsters were buffed heavily in this update, and this combines with the massive influx of total noobs (myself included) to create a perfect sh*tstorm of awful stage 1 wipes, especially against even halfway capable monster players.

This game is a combat-only spinoff of Age of Decadence (a wonderful rpg that you really should play if you like the genre).
Basically, it's the Fallout:Tactics of the world of Age of Decadence.
All the "civic" skills are gone, with the exception of alchemy and crafting (who can be very strong).
Charisma is still useful because it allows you to have a larger party (up to 4 guys) and also to recruit some stronger npcs and avoid/soften a couple fights.
You should specialize early in a single weapon skill and a single defensive skill (dodge OR block) if you want to succeed: if you know the combat system from Age of Decadence, you will be fine. Otherwise, your first run can be a little punishing, and you may have to restart.
If you run into a seemingly "impossible" fight, you can probably win it by using consumables (poison, sharpening stones, neurostimolants, alchemic fire, bombs, net, bolas...) and/or different positioning and attack types.
Don't blame the RNG if you lose: unless you get a VERY unlucky (and unlikely) streak on a dodge character, you can control fights with good positioning, tools and tactics. Lots of ironman playthroughs can prove it.
Get this game, but please also get Age of Decadence.
Recommend!

Dungeon Rats (DR) is a prequel/spinoff to Age of Decadence (AoD), and if you liked the latter game, you may enjoy DR. You can also read my review of AoD if you like. Be warned, however, that DR is even more brutal and punishing than AoD, and it's not a roleplaying game. It is a squad-based tactical skirmisher with little dialog. If that's something that you enjoy, go for it. If not, you should probably stay away.
To expand on what I stated earlier, I'm a fairly competent AoD player, having gone through the game several times and written a guide about it, and even I found DR to be fairly challenging at the highest, what I consider the default, difficulty setting. According to the developer, DR didn't sell really well, and I can understand why. It's not an easy game to get into, and developing appropriate strategies requires a lot of personal research and experimentation.
Resources are scarce, combat is punishing, and enemies are unrelenting. If you plan ahead properly, I don't think the game is impossible by any means, and the final encounter can be a breeze, but jumping into DR without playing AoD first may be an uncomfortable experience. As a fan of AoD and strategic skirmishers, I'd recommend DR, but I don't think it's a game that everyone will like. Just be aware of what you're getting into.

And combat itself is greatly enhanced with ability to have followers and control them in battle directly. The problem with too much reliance on randomness in fights is still there though, difference between critical hit and miss with counter crit is enormous.
Overall, Dungeon Rats is good game, especially for Age of Decadence fans.

Repetative, Boring, Unrewarding.
What this game is truly missing is some kind of player feedback. Here's the main problem with Cuphead: Bosses and enemies don't feel reactive, they feel like they'd continue on regardless of wether or not he player was there. This becomes especially apparent during sections of boss fights where nothing is happening. When you're standing a few inches from a boss shooting them in the face with a finger shotgun for 10 seconds and there's no consequence, no visible damage, and no indication they are being hurt (other than flashing white for half a second) combat gets incredibly boring. Even a health bar would have made all the difference. As a result, combat feels completely unrewarding and there's no overarching goal other than to unlock more boss battles.
Edit: The worst part is that a simple health bar on the enemies would have made this a better game. With a health bar, you would see the damage, have some kind of player feedback, and it might actually make the game harder. If you know the boss is almost dead, you would make riskier moves knowing the boss might die before getting that next super attack off. As it stands, you just have to play it safe all the time because you have no idea how much health each boss has, you just keep shooting until the level ends. That's really boring.

The game is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥ about explaining how to play it, so two essential hints.

Likes
Thrilling (believable) atmosphere throughout the whole game.
Sophisticated & refined graphic environment (e.g. exquisitely furnished rooms).
Different locations (e.g. mansion, morgue, sanatorium, pub, etc., ... ) + different spaces (e.g. bedroom, hallway, yard, etc., ... ).
Interactive map (gets you from one place to another in the blink of an eye).
Simple, easy-to use interface (e.g. inventory & game settings).
Dislikes:
"Stiff" execution of the script (i.e. conversation).
Lack of flow in regard to character movement.
No auto-save (you may find yourself replaying certain parts or even chapters, if you forget saving!)
Having to go back-and-forth too many times at some point.
************************************************
The game has a beautiful "old-world" feel to it, and looks very enticing (especially the first setting where the story begins: at "Black Mirror" castle); the main character's (rich!) family estate.
I seriously wanted the character to keep going back there for more :). Unfortunately, there's only a small amount of rooms to explore, but the process is still satisfying nonetheless!
The puzzles are manageable. They take enough time to keep the player entertained, without ending up overly frustrated or braindead.
Some of the conclusions drawn by the main character feel a bit "off" (not exactly illogical, but rather insufficiently developed you could say).
This game somehow gets away with it, because the beauty & emotional complexity of the main plot makes up for it.
However, the game progress tends to be tricky at times, in that it will have you running around (in spots you've been before, to get certain items that aren't visible at first, but become accessible only after executing a set of tasks in a particular order).
So you will want to pay attention to that!
All in all, it's a really enjoyable game, if you can get past the initial "stiff" impression, and save your progress frequently.
Regardless of this fact, I most definitely recommend it to lovers of the point&click/puzzle/adventure genre.
It contains a good balance of thrill, mischief & secrecy :).
If you give it a try, you might be pleasantly surprised as I was! ♥

If you are reading this and you enjoy any kind of strategy game then buy this game. This may be the best strategy game I have played since the origanal Starcraft or Age of Empires 2, both of which come nowhere close to how expansive this game is. In a nutshell, this game is a "What if" machine for the era of World War II with each country during the time having many ways of playing. You can play as Fascist America or Britian, Democratic Japan, or even Communist Germany. The resource and trading aspect is very balanced despite the unrealistic nature of some trades and the fact that you're trading production power for said resources instead of other resources or supplies. Army design is probably the most complicated thing in the game (excluding production which is fine but still takes a bit to master) but following the rule of 20 is the fastest way to ensure victory by land; production will decide the air and sea campaigns and balancing these three fronts in the core challenge for small and weak countries. All in all, I could write about all the things I dislike or don't agree with but I can honestly say this game may of been the best game released in 2016 for all genres and I highly recommend it.

Honestly I feel like this is the "Dark Souls" of 2d platformers.
Salt & Sanctuary is a 2d platformer (left, right, up and down) RPG slasher. Basically you are thrown into this world with the purpose of finding some princess. On your way you run into wolves, skeletons, zombies and huge scary beasts and monster bosses. In the beginning of the game you end up establishing your "sanctuary", which you can upgrade kind of like Starbound, with different NPC characters. Those can then help you craft weapons and armor, upgrade them and much more. You can also access you skill tree and update various skills.
The graphics are beautiful, the story is captivating, the RPG aspects are fun and not repetetive, however the game is UNFORGIVING! You need salt to level up and you lose salt when you die... You die a lot, so for me its very hard to actually put any salt into upgrading skills.
The game has amazing controller support, as well as cooperative controller gameplay with one more person. I play this game with my daughter, as the main player will follow the mission, but the second player is basically a support role. It is kind of weird because you need to make a second separate character, by starting a new game, which the second player can then summon/control in your actual game.
So far I give this game a 9/10.

My main advice before playing this game (also stated by some other people) is that you should set the language to English-Japanese Voice Mode. Not because I'm a dirty weeb but because it enables mid-stage dialogue (which reveals more information about the characters), a LOT more dialogue from certain deuteragonist and different end-mission dialogue (rather than your typical "mission complete", it's something minor but a nice touch regardless). Playing the game in any other language not only disables the voices: it also takes out everything mentioned above, which makes the game... almost "souless" imo. I played the original English version without the Japanese Voices and—while the characters are fun and hilarious at times—the game feels incredibly empty in terms of history. The missing dialogue just makes it even worse. I have no idea why the developers did this, but if you really want to grow attached to the characters and the game as I did, you should really play it in English-Japanese Voice Mode.
Also, the 3DS version doesn't have this feature at the moment for EU players as far as I know, even though there's word from the developer that it's going to be added "soon". It's also missing like seven extra modes that you can only play in the Steam version (and by the looks of it, seems like they're going to be exclusives). You should buy it, as it's the definitive version because of everything stated above.
The sequel is also even better, I definitely recommend it if you liked this game. You're gonna need a 3DS for it though.
tl;dr: English-Japanese Voice mode is the way to truly enjoy this game.

Played the game for about four hours and beat it, minus all the extra goodies it has to offer. Wanted to get through it so I could give my bit on what it was, if it was fun, so on and so forth. So know I've played it, and will be going back later to get the achievements (if possible).
So, Azure Striker Gunvolt. If you've seen snapshots and gameplay of this, it's Megaman ZX with a bit of a twist. Instead of just charging up your buster and firing off either little shots or big shots, it's a much more complex system of tagging enemies with your rounds, then electrifying them. I really don't feel like going into much detail as to how the game works, cause the dash works different, the movements different, there's weapons, upgrades, and gear (oh my!), but the core of this game feels like a Megaman ZX. Honestly, I like that about this game, cause I love the Megaman X series. Part if the reason why I bought it in the first place.
Down to the more sectioned off parts of the game, since I've already spoken of the overall gameplay, lets go to the graphics, sound, story, etc.
Visually, the game is not great, but not normal, either. It's got a flare to it that, again, feels like Megaman ZX. I say this because the game's villans are all transforming people with special powers, a lot like the Megamen in the ZX series. The very world itself feels similar, minus the desert stages that always seem to pop up. Now, while I was more focused on the game itself, the visuals were good. Like, 3.7 out of five good. There are only a few scenes where there's a full blown picture instead of just the sprites doing their thing, which is normal, and there's all sorts of neat places that are shown. Cities, jungles, underwater places. Take note, your character can, and will, drown. Fast. So, nothing to really exemplefy in the art/graphics department. What you see is what you get. If you are an in depth guy about this, I dunno. Message me. Maybe I'll get more in detail, but to me, visuals are a game's accompanyment. Sound was fun. It was an electronic feel, each stage had it's own little theme. I didn't pay much attention to it, either. If anything, I have the main menu's theme in my head. But the sound was just as decent as the visuals, where it wasn't amazing, but it was fun to have around. Normally, I never really listen to the music and just have podcasts and what have you in the background, but I'm glad I did mine this way. Also, the game's voices are (of course) in Japanese. No voice acting, though. Not really. Just little quips here and there. Lastly, the story. Now, I ran through this game extremely fast. I did was, again, focused on the gameplay itself. The characters were fun, and I liked them. For a game where there wasn't a ton of dialogue and everything seemed to be more put into the stage creation and the gameplay, I enjoyed the story to an extent. But it's a lackluster story about super powered people, a guy who finds a girl and goes lone wolf on his organization, but still works for them because he needs the money. After doing the rebel organization's dirty work, his waifu is kidnapped, and he goes to save her. Nothing new or original here, really. If anything, the ending is interesting (though I saw it from a mile away). What the story REALLY did for me was want to come back and play the sequel. I hope it's out, cause I want to play it and finish the game. So, while there was little character development and a lackluster story that's been reused more than fifteen times, I want to play the next game, which I guess is what really matters. I just wanted to see some more character development in general, with both Gunvolt and Joule (his waifu, basically. It's more of just a joke for me). I hope that when I go back to get the rest of the achievements, I'll be able to see some more of that, but I don't think I will. Honestly, this game visually, audibly, and story wise feels like a very well done Indie game. But nothing more, nothing less.
Now, the gameplay itself was fun. While I did fly through the game, I did feel like every stage was it's own place. Every stage had its own couple enemies specific to it, as well as the usual enemies that came along with every stage. The stages themselves had puzzles that didn't feel like it was a difficult task to complete, but a screw up would result in some serious punishment. 99.9% of the time, using your electricity will solve whatever puzzle you're having difficulty with. It's just how you use it that matters. Not only that, but the most interesting thing about it all is the risk and reward of using your ability. In most games, your abilities consquences are null. They don't either exist or matter. In Megaman, if you use your abilities, the most that happens is you deplete your ability gauge. So, there's management, but it's simple. In this game, while you do have to manage your ability gauge, that gauge is also what allows you to reduce damage, but only if you're not using it. It can help you float a bit, it helps with puzzles, etc. and so on. There are enemies that will come after you if you use you ability, and using it can get you hurt, but will damage the enemy as well. This risk/reward does no really exist as prominently in most other Megaman games, and it's what I find interesting about Azure Striker. Now, I understand it's not groundbreaking, but I admit they did it well, and I found it more complex than Megaman, which is just hold down the fire button, fire at enemy while dodging attacks, and repeat. With bosses, there's weaknesses, which don't exist in Azure Striker, just your skill with your ability and whatever gear you so happen to hold. If anything, the gameplay was fun and interesting, and is definitly worth a play through, if only because the game's on sale.
Regardless, I'm probably going to come back to this game and complete everything. Not necessarily replay, since I want to be done with this game, but it was still fun. Give it a shot.

The game has a very ambiguous and vague way of telling its story. At first glance it is a slightly vulgar game that has much apparent sexual innuendo, phallic and yonic symbols are also ever-present in the game and play an underlying, much more profound role than what they may represent at first sight.
A ‘plugman’ connects and disconnects with other ‘plugmen’. They run, hit, get hit, touch, pull, push and converse with one another. You will laugh throughout all of this, since it’s an unexpectedly hilarious experience.
There’s not much to the gameplay, you click and drag objects and ‘plugmen’, and hit switches which turn lights on and off.
Design-wise it expects you to get out of your comfort zone. Yes, it’s a fairly linear game, but there are parts of it that require you to try different things out, and the game doesn’t necessarily spell those things out for you.
It’s a significantly minimalist game. All there is are drawn characters, hands, and objects such as light switches, electrical plugs, cables that plug in, and cables that get plugged into.
The ‘plugmen’ are actually very well animated, it’s one of the first things I noticed and appreciated about the game. Animations are very comical and don’t take themselves too seriously, but are very fluid.
Most of the game is silent, unless you’re interacting with something or watching a sequence happen, and those sounds have a fairly high quality.
The beginning of the game has a choir singing, and it was actually a very pleasant choir, it gave the game a sense of duality. What I mean by duality is that the game seems so casual, not serious at all at first glance, and the choir gives it a kind of dramatic alien atmosphere that does feel very serious. I believe this is because the undisclosed themes that you have to read into -such as heartbreak, insecurity, and generally connecting with people- are actually very serious and very relatable to people as human beings.
When I first saw the game on my activity feed, I surely didn’t think I’d end up writing a review for it; I was simply intrigued by its
. The first time I played it I laughed harder than I have in a while, and the second time I played it I almost teared up. I
to play the game twice to really understand the themes that it experiments with. Once I did understand I related to the game on an emotional level. I enjoyed it and found it almost cathartic by the end of my second playthrough, which led me to write this review.
If you think you might like the short yet enlightening experience of playing this game but are doubtful, watch my playthrough and decide. Either way, I do believe experiencing it first-hand is much more special than watching someone else go through it.

Dungeon Rats is the second game in the same setting using the same engine from developer Iron Tower Studio, the first being Age of Decadence. Unlike the first game, Dungeon Rats is focused solely on combat - while there are skill checks in dialogues and scripted events, you cannot progress without violent solutions. Also a huge change is the addition of party members, who you control directly (ergo, no worries about Vic shooting Sulik in the back with a shotgun or Virgil investing all his skill points in fagoting).
You could perhaps say that Dungeon Rats is to Age of Decadence, what Icewind Dale is to Baldur's Gate.
The music in Dungeon Rats is superb, and draws inspiration from Mark Morgan's soundtracks to Fallout and Planescape: Torment. It is a huge step up from Age of Decadence, which soundtrack was already mostly good, and it is a very pleasant surprise to see such an improvement in what could be compared to an expansion pack. This soundtrack would have been a widely acclaimed part of any AAA title - no low production values showing there.
Similar to Age of Decadence, Dungeon Rats' story is mostly told indirectly through exploration where the player is an anonymous cog in a grand machinery and not "The Chosen One", although this time the lack of dialogue makes the story component a very minimalist one. In spite of this, it is possibly the most well-executed minimalist story I can think of. It draws heavy parallels to Age of Decadence, so don't expect any new ideas. If Age of Decadence left you wanting more of the exact same to explore, this is just the fix for you.
If you didn't yet play Age of Decadence, it should be said that the setting is a bit of an acquired taste. Although the superficial components of the setting imitate the late Roman era closely, the mood is very unique and gloomy reminding you of Fallout 1 sans the wacky parts. This is a very deliberate thematic component, just like the ever-impending doom is a part of the Warhammer universe.
Replayability is high because of the many different choices during character creation and party assembly. In those areas, choices truly matter and force you to play the game differently, in other areas (such as dialogue) not so much. Expect one playthrough to take roughly 10-15 hours.
All in all, this is a game to recommend for those who like Age of Decadence, which you should absolutely play first before trying your hand at Dungeon Rats.

If you're sick of WoW-esque MMOs, Rift isn't going to blow your mind. It's heavily based on what has become the standard MMO-template, harkening back to game releases over a decade prior to its own. But the developers of Rift have done enough to really make it shine among the crowded MMO-marketplace.
Mechanics and systems are streamlined to provide the player with the best experience I've had in any MMO. Missed out on some lower-level content or want to play with a lower-level friend? Just lower your level, temporarily, and receive rewards comparable to your original level. Instead of quest items taking up valuable inventory space, they'll be placed in their own cache viewable from your quest log. While they can't wholly take credit for these ideas, the developers at Trion put thought into improving upon most of the issues that are commonly found throughout the genre.
Of the countless titles that follow the fetch/kill quest trope, Rift stands out as far as solo-play goes. For starters, you can expect every mob you kill to drop the quest item you need. But more to the point, the side-activities are varied and surprisingly fun to participate in. While questing you might help a few other players close one of the game's namesake rifts, discover artifacts strewn throughout the world, or participate in zone-wide events that end in a large-scale fight to take down what is ostensibly a world-boss. All of these things come together to create a satisfying pseudo-solo experience.
Rift's visuals are, overall, servicable. Some of the zones are particularly stand out, but for the most part it's nothing you haven't seen before. Opting for a semi-realistic fantasy style, it was just interesting enough to keep me satisfied. In particular, the spell effects are somewhat lackluster. They just don't have enough kick to make you feel as poweful as you supposedly are.
Overall, Rift is the most enjoyable MMO I've played to date, and I expect to put many, many more hours into it. It's just a solid title, all around.

It is nice to finally have a successor to the original Typing of the Dead, although I would have much prefered to see the original Typing of the Dead come to steam instead, and for good reasons!
This version is based off the PS3 updated version of the Nintendo Wii game: The House of the Dead: Overkill.  While the Wii version was great, the PS3 version may turn off some people who really enjoyed the way the game and cut-scenes played out in the Wii version.  Not to say it's bad, if you really want to play Overkill but don't own a Wii, the PS3 is the way to go.  Now it's on PC and... it's bittersweet to say the least.
I say that because there is almost no changes between playing with guns to playing with keyboards.  In Typing of the Dead, which spoofed the House of the Dead 2, your characters had back-mounted dreamcast systems with keyboards hanging in front of them, and it makes fun of the original game, especially in the endings.  This game doesn't do any of that.  It's just simply the same game with the gameplay tweaked to use a keyboard.  You do have the option to use a controller and mouse for the actual rail shooter experience if you prefer, and the online co-op does work well enough.
It is fun to play, although feeling lacking.  If you want to play Overkill, I recommend the Wii game.  Otherwise, this game is worth checking out.

The main game mechanic -- typing in words correctly to shoot zombies -- is this game's saving grace. "The Typing of The Dead: Overkill" isn't a good game, so much as a showcase for how much fun the type to kill mechanic is. If someone picked up the idea and managed to make a less idiotic story with less horrible dialogue and less repetitive, crappy boss fights/mutant encounters, a truly good game could be made off the concept. The rest of it's complete horsepucky, honestly.
The general idea is that your character will move on his own through a level, and you'll type in different words to "fire" your guns, killing the mutants you encounter. There's a scoreboard system which sometimes makes sense, and you get more points for correctly typing a bunch in a row, or killing a lot of enemies without dying. The level design itself doesn't stick out, but the mechanic holds up throughout the game as fun. If you haven't played this type of game before, you should give it a shot.
The reason I give this the thumbs up is the fact that it's the only game on steam where typing in "dost thou bite thy thumb at me, sir?" equals a zombie dying. Wait for a sale, though, because really...I get that the devs were going for an old school "House of the Dead" type thing, but the story is such crap, the characters are such idiots, the enemies so predictable, that it wears on you after awhile. The writing, particularly in the scene with the Warden, is so bad that it that I've alt-tabbed multiple times to regain sanity by listening to leekspin.
In short play this game because the typing mechanic is a blast. That's it, though. Virtually nothing else about this is even average work. You're basically choking down the rest of the disgusting experience so that you can get to the delicious dessert.

I really am a sucker for these sorts of management games, so when I saw this game I thought "Hey, I loved GameDev Tycoon, maybe this will be similar." I was wrong. This game is plagued with unnecessary wait times to get anything done, a lack of any kind of explaination for game mechanics (Let alone nomanclature used for the actual games), and horrible translation and grammar issues.
I played this game both from the solo career side and the management side, and neither of the two options are any fun. In an attempt to stretch out the length of gameplay an arbitrary unskippable timer was included with phrases such as "Your team won the teamfight!" and then a random amount of gold would be added to your team's total. This was entertaining or at least tolerable the first few times, but when you get to realize that this is the game, it's like I'd rather sit and watch a loading screen than play this game even a little bit.
This game could be so great! If the devs added some options to increase the speed of the gameplay, or to skip the arbitrary timer all together I would be much more inclined to play. The addition of mouse over tool-tips or any kind of explaination of the game's mechanics would also greatly improve the user experience for those players not familiar with the general concept of these sorts of games.
In conclusion, both core aspects of the game are flawed for different reasons. The solo career has no explaination at all for what you're doing, and the management portion is more waiting than it is playing. Don't buy the game. Or at least wait until it gets better.

An interesting take on the dark souls style of game, by moving everything to 2D. Overall I enjoyed the game, but I have a few complaints. Most of them are related to things that Salt and Sanctuary does the same as dark souls, but shouldn't have.
1. No pause feature. This made a little sense in Dark Souls due to the online functionality, but this game has limited online interaction and did not need to limit the player in this manner. A pause menu that is different from the inventory would not be out of place.
2. No map. Dark Souls is a 3D world with interesting landmarks and features to help the player recognize where they are. In Salt and Sanctuary, the 2D view doesn't allow for as many of these features. An in-game map would have been helpful, even if it only showed the location in a general way.
3. Bosses with one-hit KO attacks. Almost every instance of this is a multi-hit magic spell that if you get hit early on, it will kill you from full health. Even Dark Souls is rarely this punishing at times, usually requiring at least 2-3 mistakes in a row to get wiped out.
4. Death mechanics. Dark Souls is actually a little less punishing in this regard when you die. In Dark Souls you lose all of your souls and can reclaim them from the ground. If you don't have any souls, the cost of death is minor (just time). In this game there is a second currency, gold, that builds up slower but is lost at a percentage rate each time you die. While I didn't find much that I wanted to buy on my first playthrough, I was still annoyed at how learning a difficult boss (including the one hit KO ones) would lose a huge chunk of my gold.
I have so many complaints about this game because it is overall a really good experience and I would like it to be even better. I just hope that if there is a Salt and Sanctuary 2, it addresses a few of these issues.

Even after 36 hours played, I feel like I'm scarcely competent at this game. Most of that has to do with the lack of any in-game tutorial or guide; there is a very brief tutorial, but it only covers basic movement and keybinds, not any in-depth breakdown of gameplay mechanics or character-specific strategy. To compound that problem, most of the Youtube guides are for the original game, and don't account for the numerous balance and metagame changes that came with "Stage 2" (the free-to-play update), and so taking their advice verbatim and/or without having enough in-game experience to recognize what's outdated and what's not might make you play even *worse*.
I like this game in concept, and mostly in execution as well, although there do seem to be a myriad of balance issues currently plaguing it. Namely, according to most people who played the original, most monsters were buffed heavily in this update, and this combines with the massive influx of total noobs (myself included) to create a perfect sh*tstorm of awful stage 1 wipes, especially against even halfway capable monster players.
The matchmaking is also kinda spotty. It mostly functions fine, but there are a few bugs that I'm surprised to see. Sometimes full lobbies wont launch. Sometimes you get stuck in the post-match screens and have to alt-F4. Sometimes your party will randomly split apart due to some nondescript error and you'll have to re-form the group.
Still, I feel like for the price of *completely god-damn free*, you should at least give it a shot. And that's actual "free" free; the game currently has no monetization/micro-transactions implemented, though that's confirmed to only be temporary.

This game is well worth the single digit price tag and offers a very unique RPG experience. What I thought was the best part about Dungeon Rats was how it forces you to go through trial and error and learn from your mistakes in each fight. It took me quite a while to finally beat the game but it's very realistic in terms of how combat works. You can't just rush in with swords and crossbows blazing and expect to roll over your foes. You have to map out a detailed plan before each battle and make sure the variables are set up and stuff. It's also an unique RPG where there aren't the traditional EXP points and level ups. Instead you get skill points after each victory which you can apply to improving certain combat, defense or utility skills for your character. There aren't special abilities nor classes in this game which is another unique aspect.
tl;dr If you enjoy a classic turn-based and party-based RPG which has an engaging storyline and will grow on you, go ahead and slap a few bucks and change on the table and get it!

Pros:

Cons:

An excellent turn-based RPG with heavy combat focus. Recommended if you like a challenging, tactical game.

- great combat system with different play styles, weapon kinds, many types of attacks that have their specific uses, additional gear like nets, poisons or grenades, positioning that matters a lot.
- well thought-out armor system. You can't just wear the heaviest armor and dodge and move as fast as if you wore nothing. It's a trade-off and a strategic decision which armor and/or shield to use.
- very nice crafting system
- resource scarcity that forces long-term planning. You better think twice before using that rare metal to forge an item or throw all your grenades on a low level enemy. Same applies to healing items. Most devs would be too scared to do it but here you can just spend all your resources and be stuck in a basically unwinnable position. It's not just about winning fights but also winning them without using all your grenades and healing items. By the final fight (playing on murderous psychopath) I've used up ALL my healing items and food, so if the game went on even a little longer I would've been screwed. You can't just go back and "grind" low level enemies for loot and XP, there's a limited amount of resources in the game and you have to make the best use of them you can.
- interesting lore tidbits and optional paths. The game is linear but accessing some things depend on your stats and skills or fighting (hard) optional fights.
- inventory UI... it's alright but could be a lot better (reminds me of Fallout 1/2). Eventually it gets too cluttered and there's no way to sort other than filter armor/weapons/other so searching for a specific item is a pain. It gets especially bad if you have multiple types of throwing weapons and ammo made from different kinds of metal.
- the thing about difficulty and resource scarcity and management. You'll be much more efficient the second time around because you'll know when to craft healing items and which companions are worth keeping. The companions are nice but again the ones you start with are mostly bad even if you level them up there are strictly better replacements later on, so you're essentially "wasting" XP and healing items on them.
- the game is generally not very random in the "random-critical-hit-you're-dead" sense with one exception: enemies using explosives. They don't miss, crit very often and do splash damage. 1-2 hits and you're dead. Basically you have to take them out first or try to abuse their ai so they waste their turn. They only appear in a couple of fights though.

Dungeon Rats is a neat game. It's a very linear, straight-forward game where you move from battle to battle. At 16-hours played, I got more than enough entertainment to justify my purchase. The formula is pretty straight forward; fight your way up, get better equipment, and continue fighting.
My primary complaint with Dungeon Rats is the meta. While the game is advertised as a party-based tactical RPG, the meta of the game is that it is a puzzle game revolving around resource management playing dress-up as a party-based tactical RPG.
I will preface this portion of my review by saying that at a certain point, I resorted to cheating like a madman in order to continue playing the game. Between battles you are given no opportunity to rest and you do not regenerate hitpoints naturally. You can only heal with 1 of 2 items. There are healing salves which are crafted from (rare) herbs, which requires investing precious skill points to make the most of. And there are also rations which are also hard to come by and heal by exactly 1 hit point per. When your character with 40 MAX HP barely survives a fight, he eats a lot of them.
There is no trading system, and once you run out of supplies you will have to make do. While I'm at it, all forms of resources are hard to come by, which means that if you use them early, prior to developing your craft skills, they are low-quality, and therefore wasted. You are
forced to have a high-level smith and alchemist in order to create equipment that gives you
a fighting chance in combat.
The point that I decided to cheat was at the first boss. He had 5 guys, and I had 3; all were heavily wounded from slogging through his army to reach him. At first I only wanted to be at full health to make the fight more "fair." Then I decided that I didn't want to slog through a puzzle-game masquerading as a party-based RPG. I dumped rations and alchemy ingredients into my inventory, I loaded up my skills to the level I thought the enemy was. And at that point, even though combat was still challenging, I started having a lot of fun with it. I still died. A lot. But at least I was able to play the game the way I thought it should be played.
I enjoy a good challenge, but rolling the dice has never been challenging and it's where Dungeon Rats is the weakest in my opinion. Combat is fun and gives you a lot of tactical options to pull ahead which is sadly lacking in most RPGs.

Only Iron Tower could make a game so ideally balanced, that you can drastically change it's difficulty by modifying only one parameter (To-Hit chance). Overall it's best combat-only RPG, and the best game i ever played in my life.
And, like in Age of Decadence, the thing which really amuses me is the fact, how easily can you break this ideal balance and make game a piece of cake.

I've gone as far as level 10 so far, and "Rift" has satisfied every need I have of an MMO. I can turn graphics so high, my computer so high, that i get 10 FPS, or so low that I get 90 FPS, and still experience the same game. Highly customizable character looks, skill trees, and job roles.
So far, I've encountered collections, farming and crafting, as well as dimensional, space, and time travel. not to mention magitec armor. :O)
I was able to break down a "Type" of build, rogue, and using the skill tree, make it exactly the type of rogue I wish to play. not just one of three types provided by most other MMO's, but specialized to my play style.
There ARE microtransaction elements that i don't care for, such as having to buy extra bag slots, but they seem to be one time purchases, so I can live with that.
I also enjoyed the fact that the game was not linear from the get go. before i even reached level 10, I saw a mountain in the distance, off path of where my next quest was sending me, and the game had no issue with me wandering off and exploring it to it's peak. no oddly grouped higher levels down a corridor of your lvl mobs like most MMO's,
Public group events are seemless. I had walked into one without knowing it, and was prompted if i wanted to join the group by the UI. no one even had to put any effort into starting or coordinating the group. it went remarkably smooth.
I'm also impressed with the story so far. if you're actually willing to read it, it's immersive. If you aren't, it's easily skippable so you can move on with your race to the top level. :OP
I enjoyed the PVP elements, as a ranged rogue, I started with a bow, expecting to be using one for the rest of the game. a bow being quiet, dependable, but a bit slow. I was presented with a rifle as a quest reward, and was excited to see I could use it. The tradeoff, of course being that it's faster, but loud. when I engaged in PVP, i was more easily discoverable with it as compared to using my bow. It's the details. this game has them.
I'll be enjoying this game for quite some time now i think, and I'd reccomend it to anyone tired of the "pushed out in a hurry" FTP MMO's out lately that lack any real substance.

Basically, depending on the mode, it can be described like this: Multiplayer Mirror's edge where you have to avoid one guy who wants to murder you, Multiplayer Mirror's edge where you're playing basketball/soccer, or multiplayer Mirror's edge while you're playing tag.
Now it's not perfect. The movement needs tuning since it feels sloppy in a lot of cases, and takes a while getting used to. Additionally the game doesn't really take balance into account. This isn't a problem in the free for all modes, but in the "bitball" mode (the one that's like soccer/basketball), there are two teams and it's up to the host to balance it manually. This can lead to wildly unbalanced bitball games.
The last downside to the game is it currently has a very low playerbase. However, the developers run streams of the game several days a week, with a bunch of people joining in. I recommend people join the discord and watch for alerts on the stream announcement channel.
Now the last question, is it worth $20? Well, probably not. Don't get me wrong, it's an amazing game, but the amount of variety it has right now isn't worth it. However if the devs succeed in fulfilling their promises of new modes, it will likely be worth $20 easily. From what I've seen so far, the devs look like they'll be able to do that, but you'll have to judge for yourself whether it's worth the risk.

I debated long and hard about weather or not to recommend this game. In the end I decided to recommend it based upon what it currently is as of writing this. This is a game with a really fun concept, with lots of possible potential, however at this time I feel the games execution is abysmal. You can select between LoL or CSGO, I picked CSGO because I don't like MOBAs. However it seems the CSGO options are bare minimum and much more attention has been given to the LoL portion of the game. That is not, however, why I do not recommend this game. That comes from the almost 8 hours I've put into this product and realized that your choices, your skill upgrades, your Hero/Weapon selections, everything you do is basically entirely random. Your rankings and stats as a player are totally meaningless, every match outcome is randomly determined with dice rolls, from what I can tell. Even if it isn't you would never know because the game refuses to tell you ANYTHING. There are no Tutorials, there are no Tips or Hints that are provided to let you know which choices you made incorrectly, no way of actually knowing weather or not you are making the right selections. I can make the exact same selections and get wildly different outcomes every single time a match occurs.
The game is also imbalanced in other areas. For example Streaming is by far the most lucrative way to make money, I make enough money from 1 streaming session that it equals like 7 weeks Salary from my Team contract. You can't really interact with anything within the game, it's just "Play Ranked, make random selections, get random outcome, rinse and repeat". You can watch Top Ranked players streams to "learn" how they play the game and get tips from this. However once again the game does nothing to imply what you've actually learned from watching them, from a gameplay standpoint all that literally does is grant you some Knowledge XP to invest into the Knowledge Tree. Which as I've mentioned has no real function and does not seem to factor into anything.
The game also has a problem with assuming the player (you) should already know everything, includeing terminologies such as AWLper or ADC, etc. I've no idea what these terms mean and the game does not care to explain, because obviously you should know already. The game is also littered with Spelling and Grammer errors. You are able to hire an Agent to represent you, and get better contract offers for you, however you are unable to do this unless you already have a team and have a contract already, which imo makes this rather irrelevent for obvious reasons.
TL;DR- This is a game that has the potential to be something great in the future, but currently is an uninformative rock paper sicssors game where your stats and rankings dont seem to matter at all, and the game does not explain anything or make any attempts to help you.

In the management part, it is basically the same. This is my first "roguelike" although I have played a lot of RPGs before. Basically what that means is it's turn-based, levels are procedurally generated, it's fairly challenging, and there is permadeath. (The last can be tweaked a bit in different modes but there are no save slots in any mode.)
The graphics are obviously not the Witcher 3, but are good enough, in a nice semi-realistic "classic fantasy" style. (I personlly don't like cartoony graphics like say Torchlight.)
The music is surprisingly good, some of it is available here if you're curious-
The gameplay is very deep. There are dozens of different classes, including rather exotic ones like "Oozemancer" and one that dual wields shields. Some of these are initially locked (one of the few questionable design decisions IMO), but that can be changed with a mod. There are the usual stats like INT and STR, plus a lot of different resistances and abilities. One nice thing is that bosses are generally not immune to things like stun and slow. Some games (Final Fantasy for example) have trash mobs that are too easy to bother using debuffs on, but then the bosses are immune, so a lot of the spells are pointless. Here you find yourself using all of your abilities fairly frequently.
One of the areas it really shines is in eliminating anything that is tedious. For example, most RPGs have consumables, and you can cheese things by stocking up on them, which requires grinding. Instead of consumables you have "infusions" that are basically swappable skills with cooldowns. This means you have to time your cooldowns well, and be humble enough to run away sometimes, instead of just buying a stack of potions. Another is you can automatically explore a zone. This doesn't make the game easier exactly, since these type of things aren't challenging, just boring. It is really good at streamlining things without dumbing them down.
Given that it's procedurally generated, the story is I would say above average but not amazing, although the writing is quite good and there is a lot of lore. Instead it focuses on replayability and different game modes. There are about 1,300 achievements, however many of these are duplicates based on the three different permadeath modes (permadeath one life, permadeath multiple lives and no permadeath) and difficulty levels. I think there are 9 combinations so 1,300 / 9 = ~140 achievements roughly. Still a decent number. And with so many classes you can definitely have a lot of different playthroughs.
For the price I wasn't expecting much, but was very pleasantly surprised. This is not one of those trendy, shallow gimmicky indie games that you play for a few hours then get bored. It's deep, engaging and very well designed and thought out.

Normally, Waveform would be the kind of game where I say "That looks pretty cool, but it really isn't my kind of game, so I'll pass."
However, I noticed it purely because of the 95% discount on it. The price was taken down to a mere 24 cents. I decided to buy it.
I'm quite pleased. Waveform is has a high level of good design for an indie game, and is more than worth the purchase -- even at its normal, non-discounted price.
The game looks quite complicated in the trailer, and to some extent, it is. Still, it's not as complex as it looks, for whatever that's worth.
Controls are actually quite simple. "You", or the little orb on the left which is moving right, travel in the shape of a sine wave. This is because you play the role of a photon, which behaves as a wave. (And a particle, but lets not get too sciencey) You increase/decrease your frequency by moving the mouse left/right, and you increase/decrease your amplitude by moving the mouse up/down. That's the full extent of the game controls, besides pause, of course.
In layman's terms, you follow a wibbly-wobbly line. Mouse left or right to make your wibble-wobble do a full wibble and wobble in less or more time, and mouse up or down to make the top of the wibble higher or lower.
This is a difficult mechanic to toy with, but the game has a gentle difficulty curve. The first level contains only light orbs -- doodads you collect to score points. The next few contain dark matter -- doodads you don't want to touch. Regardless, the game does a very good job of telegraphing what you need to do, and often, your goal of collecting light orbs coincides with a path that avoids all dark matter.
Over the course of the game, you are introduced to more and more objects that you can interact with. Mirrors can be used to reflect your wave, orbiters can be used to collect light orbs in a wider radius, and wormholes can be used to warp past deadly clusters of bad stuff. These are just a few examples; the list goes on.
The game is also designed to appeal well to both the casual and hardcore audience. Casual players can find suitable challenge in simply completing the core levels. Hardcore players can find suitable challenging in gaining a 100% score in every level. The game doesn't end there either; it also includes "deep space modes", which are randomly-generated endless levels that challenge you to survive against harder scenarioes while collecting points and speeding up ever-so-slightly.

Not every classic game ages well, and old adventure games tend to have shorter shelf lives than most. You still hear plenty about the standouts, your Monkey Islands and your King's Quests, the ones that were either designed well or were entertaining enough to overlook their design flaws. The others fell into obscurity as the genre grew quiet for a time, and that's where you'll find Black Mirror. Whether you want to revisit this dark gem depends on how much patience you have for some very old-fashioned designs.
Black Mirror places you in the role of Samuel Gordon, estranged son of British aristocracy. A tragedy has occurred at the ancestral castle of Black Mirror, and Samuel does the prodigal son thing to prove his hunch that foul play is afoot. The game is presented with pre-rendered backgrounds and basic 3D character models that hearken back to the PlayStation 1 era, leaving you shuffling stiffly around and spending a good twenty seconds pulling a photograph from your jacket. I don't know if it's a modern system issue or not, but some of the animations in the game are absolutely laborious, particularly during dialog. Still, the game retains a retro charm that will take you back to games like Baldur's Gate or Sanitarium in terms of appearance.
The charm extends to the voice acting in a big way, and I have to stress that you need a high tolerance for cheese if you want to make it through this thing. Frankly, I'm not convinced a single British person lent their voice to this game about British people. What you get is a bunch of unconvincing doofs doing silly accents and EMOTING the strangest PARTS of THEIR sentences. If it doesn't drive you crazy, you might find it as loveable as I did... the further in I got, the less dialog I would skip (but yes, you can click straight through dialog).
As far as the gameplay goes, you better have a walkthrough handy. Black Mirror never descends to cat moustache levels, but it has a needlessly complex interaction system that is sure to trip you up. As near as I can tell (no tutorial, of course), left-click is observe/interact, and right-click is... different interact. Every time you left-click on an object, you get a different response. Sometimes you only have to click once. Sometimes twice. Sometimes you have to left-click and then right-click. Sometimes you have to left-click three times and then right-click a different thing. There's so little consistency in interacting with the world, you're guaranteed to encounter at least one situation where you know exactly what to do, just not the sequence of clicks to accomplish it.
There's pixel-hunting, forced waiting, unexpected deaths, and even ways to doom yourself (though the consequence comes minutes, not hours, later) too. Pretty much any sin an adventure game can commit can be found here, but I must admit none are particularly damning in Black Mirror. The scenes tend to be clear and easy to navigate, without too many NPCs, which makes it easy to run through all your options when you get stumped. A map in the first few chapters provides some very welcome fast travel, and in a bit of genius design, double-clicking on the transition to another scene moves you instantly. Honestly, there were enough quality-of-life features to keep me from getting really frustrated at any of the flaws.
It's a long game, at least 15 hours all told, and while the story is a slow burn, it digs deep into its own mysteries. There's not enough energy or action to keep you engaged for long periods, but I found it a good substitute for hidden object or casual games as my go-to chillout activity. If you can look past the artifacts of its age and its admittedly rough design edges, you'll get a charming, meaty adventure to keep you occupied for hours on end.

Hilariously wooden voice acting (seriously: check youtube), and it's unfortunately starting to show its age in terms of interface design -- the options screen has two volume sliders and a gamma control and nothing else, and the game tends to freeze if I alt tab out.  That said, its sequels are amazingly good, and have a different protagonist entirely.  Play Black Mirror 2 and 3 first, get invested in all the characters, and only then decide if you want to play this rusty prequel about Samuel Gordon.
Access the menu by hovering over the top right corner of the screen, inventory by hovering over the bottom.  Tab to highlight things you can interact with in the room.  You're welcome, I lost my first 20 minutes of play by alt-tabbing to search the forums for where the save button was...

Black Mirror
Rating 6.5/10
Overview: Traditional Point and Click Adventure Game
The Good:
+ Although the game starts off slowly it does introduce an element of mystery that begins to unravel the more you play. The story and characters are good and the game slowly begins to suck you in as you become more immersed in the world solving the mystery of your family.
+ The locations are varied and despite the games' age the pre rendered backgrounds still look good even at a low resolution

The Average:
Unlike other adventure games you cannot simply pick up any object not nailed down. In this game their needs to be a reason for you to take an object so things need to be completed in a certain order for you to proceed. On the one hand this makes things more realistic...on the other hand it become much easier to miss important information/objects when trying to complete a puzzle.
The Bad:
- "Pixel Hunting" - The term used when you have to roll your mouse cursor over every little object in the game in the hopes you didn't miss something because the vast majority of the time the reason you can't solve a puzzle is because you didn't see the little object you were suppose to pick up in the very back corner of the dimly lit room. Its infuriating and frustrating and this game has a lot of it.
- Certain puzzles are almost impossible to solve without a walkthrough because the game gives very little if any clues in how to complete them.
- You cannot proceed in the game until you 'trigger' certain events, some of these events make no sense with your current task. I.e. You have to complete one puzzle in one section of the game before you can move on in the story in another section of the game even if both events are completely unrelated to one another.
-Near the end of the game you have to wait for a character to give you information before you can trigger the next events in the story. The problem however is the character sometimes refuses to tell you what you need to hear. Looking online, some people only had to wait a few minutes while others had to wait a few hours...... Nobody seems to know what the trigger is to get him to talk. Very poor design.
- Weak ending
Conclusion
I would love to give this game a positive rating but the more I played the worse the problems started to become to the point where I was more frustrated than having fun. The game does have a lot going for it and if you love the genre you should at least check the game out, just make sure to consult a walkthrough when you get stuck because it may not be your fault that you can't solve any puzzles.

Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2 is a pretty good game! The campaign is short, but that's OK. I like that it doesn't overstay its welcome, plus there's only so much stuff you can do in a sniping game. I very much like the clean design of the whole game, especially the menus. Nothing cluttered with too many options and stuff. It's clean and straight forward, and that's a good thing. Same goes for the gameplay itself. While it is overall a linear game with a lot of handholding, I can overlook that, because the campaign has a nice pace to it. The devs concentrated on the core elements of what they wanted the game to be, and didn't include half-baked mechanics or any other nonsense. Thumbs up for that! Also, there are almost no unfair or frustrating situations, everything seems well balanced. Although checkpoints can be a pain sometimes.
One thing that annoys me though: in the first game, a lot of people complained about the bad recoil on the automatic weapons. That is gone here. Cool, you might say. But instead of working on that recoil thing, the devs just stripped automatic weapons completely out of the game. Enemies can use and even drop them, but you cannot pick them up. You can only pick up sniper rifles that some enemies also drop. That's lazy, devs. It's also totally nonsensical, when I'm out of ammo and there are guns laying around, but I cannot use them. What sense does that make?
Anyways, I like Sniper: Ghost Warrior 2. Good game for one afternoon, better than the first game. Haven't touched the multiplayer, but it is likely dead anyways. If you get the game when it's on sale, I'd say it's totally worth it.

RIFT has some very useful features that makes your game experience a bit more relaxed and enjoyable than the usual MMORPG.
Even if at first it might seem... confusing. Or maybe it's just me getting old and needing some time to adapt to things, in the end you have a product where you are actually incredibly DRAMA FREE.
You can customize your interface, you can decide what do you want to be and create different builds you can easily swap between the same class, so you can actually be A LOT of things in just one character. You won't need to start over 34939 times then regret your first configuration. Everything is adjustable as you play.
There is the very useful NEED/GREED roll dice method, and a public group system that lets you join whatever group of people you encounter in your travels without too much drama and with a very large limit of partecipants.
This makes doing quest that generally require some companions a lot less annoying. Guilds are generally very large and not demanding towards players, due to the fact you actually DON'T really need a guild in this game.
Another peculiar and very wise feature is the fact you actually gain a portion of experience for everything you touch, in the same exact moment you touched it.
Say goodbye to the good old moments where actually farming away something some other player was fighting against was rude and would have made him mad and without exp or without his quest advancements. You can help whoever you want, even if they don't know you, freely.
Also, there are two factions for a good PVP, like in many other games. The same old two factions omg what a surprise, there are the GUARDIANS and the DEFIANTS. But, in PVE servers, you can actually help the other faction's members and freely roam in their territory unless you actually attack them. The only things that would take it bad would be guard NPCs.
But I'm PEACEFUL!!! - Who cares, stay out of the city. - Fine...
I can't say how are things in PVP servers tho, I don't have the mindset for these places.
If following the story and a simple, linear quest line is too BORING for you and you want some senseless, mindless and neverending fight, you will also be able to join some adventures and be added to a huge swarm of people with some common goals to achieve, in a random location, washing away whatever you see.
Being too many levels ahead of your companions will be no longer a problem for none of you two. In RIFT, you can actually decide to lower your lever to whatever level you need. You'll have the same skills and same equipment, but you'll be way less powerful, matching a well equiped character of the level you chose. You will also gain experience according to your actual level, and you will no longer disturb your companion with your skill gaps. Wich is actually great if you have that kind of annoying friends who LIVE on the game, and then spam you because you "keep them behind", when you, yeah, dare to sleep or to eat.
Another drama reason cleared.
This game is MMORPG's peace and love.
And if you want to be an HERO.... - Well things constantly invade your region, so you just have to wait for the next invasion to join the huge battle defending your little villages and defeating the big badass who is trying to conquer everything. Nice rewards for you!
There is a reputation system, everytime you fight a good number of mobs somebody want DEAD, you gain some reputation with that faction, wich will allow you to buy good consumables and other things.
Of course the game is called RIFT for a reason. There are RIFTS, everywhere. And you'd better close them all, run towards them like crazy pokèmon masters when they see a wild pokèmon. Closing them will give you prizes and a materia called Planarite you can actually use to buy very nice items.
If you fear there aren't Dungeons or instanced stuff like that, oh don't worry, you have your dungeons too. Gathering and crafting skills are also avaiable, you can build quite a few nice things without TOO MUCH effort.
You have a personal dimension too, like a "home", you can decorate with "dimension objects" you can craft, find, FISH for, (yeah fishing sometimes gives you some nice not-a-fish catch.) etc., and an artifact collection thing that allows you to find a lot of objects from different collections. Once you complete a collection, you win some prizes.
If you don't care about that, you can also be a "dreamweaver" as you progress in the game, and just convert artifacts into dimension items building materials.
Well I'd say, try this if you like MMORPGs, but you're tired of the many annoying things MMORPGs generally throw at you. I must specify tho this isn't one of these... WOW new super-graphic-ultra-popular games so yeah don't run it with your expectations set to whatever really recent you can find around now.
