I've played over 450 hours of ToME thus far.  I'm not a great player - I tend to get overconfident and get in way over my head.  But ToME is fun.
So what makes Tales of Maj'Eyal special?  Why do I keep going back to it year after year, giving it more of my time than almost every other game in my not insubstantial collection?
There's a grand diversity in the characters you can play, and their play styles are very different.  You have multiple campaigns, as well as the recently improved Infinite Dungeon.
The skill selection is great.  Lots of skills to choose from, each with multiple levels.  Races usually have their own skill progression tree, as well.  There are passive skills, sustained skills (that opponents can turn off sometimes), and active skills.  Each of the active skills has a cooldown.  Some items will give you access to active skills as well, or reduce a cooldown on a skill, or make a whole skill tree a little more effective.
Any active skill can be auto-triggered, if you like.  Most of the races have an instant skill to start off with that gives them some benefit, and you can just say "Yeah, when someone closes in on me, fire off that skill" and you don't have to worry about it anymore.
Which brings us to auto-explore.  Like DCSS, ToME has a great auto-explore, so when you're not min-maxing your character or finding awesome artifacts, you're making meaningful decisions.
In the end, those meaningful decisions almost always end in your demise.  As someone once said: "Playing a roguelike is like being a kamikazi pilot: you start off knowing you're going to die."  Rare is the explorer who does not meet some untimely end.  And that too is part of the charm of roguelikes: it's so very often quickly over, but every so often you luck out and live longer than you have any right to.  And you feel like such a bad♥♥♥♥♥  And then you die.  Again.

This is mostly an old-fashioned turn-based roguelike (by opposition to rogue-lites like Spelunky and Binding of Isaac, which are usually real-time), though it lacks the item identification and the potion and scroll consumables we've come to love from its ancestor Angband, or better titles like NetHack and Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup. It also really likes cooldown-based abilities, so at times you'll feel like you're doing MMO combat.
I found the game too easy initially on Normal, starting the game as a Cornac Berserker regular enemies were no challenge at all, only bosses took some work to kill. The game also drops you in a forest which is quite boring to explore, and the graphics don't make very clear which tiles are traversable and which are not. I recommend using the auto-explore function ('Z' key, rebindable) in levels where you're mostly meeting trash mobs.
With time the game ups the challenge (and you can run into very dangerous areas if you're not careful, the game gives you a message which alludes to the difficulty when changing zones), and with level-ups you start discovering the deep RPG and item system. No complaints here, developing and equipping your character is very interesting, even though the game drowns you a in a sea of magic items with prefixes and suffixes, like Diablo and its ilk. (And unlike diablo, it has a lot of very small modifications to 10+ damage types. Yawning when you find yet another super-rare/legendary is never a good sign.) You unlock new characters and features through quests in the game, which I found cool.
Combat is quite compelling whenever there's a sense of danger. As in most roguelikes, not getting surrounded and paying attention to everything before making a move is key. Between equipment, infusions/runes and skills, you have a lot of abilities with cooldowns, so most turns will be spent picking the right one or positioning yourself to use one rather than simply running into an enemy to auto-attack. What I was most impressed with is when facing boss-type characters, they use pretty much the same ability system as you, and they sometimes have a lot of skills. While it makes identifying a dangerous enemy at a glance pretty hard, it does make for rather epic fights as they cast spells, heal and trigger cooldown abilities just like you. Trust me, the first time you meet an enemy with knockback and spells is really scary when playing a melee character.
The interface, however, is
(despite ridiculous frontpage claims of "modern graphical and customisable interface, intuitive mouse control"), especially the inventory. It's not really comfortable to use with the mouse: instead of displaying a tooltip for what you're hovering your cursor over, it insists on always having some object selected, obscuring your view with the information display. Movement with the mouse is also not very intuitive, as your character will move to where you point... until it finds something "interesting" or an enemy, and then you have to revert to moving a square at a time if you want any semblance of control.
There's also a problem of information overload when looking at map tiles (and other stuff): do I really need to know that I need a "special breathing method" to traverse walls everytime I'm looking at one? The game cruelly needs to display only crucial information at a glance, and then offer to say, press shift to show detailed info like now in the tooltip (see Civilization IV and V and its most complex mods for good examples).
The game has a fixed overworld, story elements and quite a bit of lore, which set it apart from NetHack and Crawl which only offer a giant dungeon. I found this refreshing, but I it comes with suggested level indications for dungeons and minimum levels to use some items, very jarring and immersion-breaking compared to the natural increase in difficulty as you go down in levels in other titles. It's gonna have a massive impact on replayability, too, the world map feels pretty small. There are towns and shops to return to and sell your loot: I think I slightly prefer the approach of Crawl where you can't sell stuff or transfer it to other characters, so you just dump stuff you don't need without hesitation. But if you like sorting through tons of loot Diablo or Borderlands-style, you'll be happy with this game.
There's no downside to resting ('R' key) in this game. In fact I recommend resting as soon as you finish beating a group of enemies, to recharge your health and stamina and bring all your abilities off cooldown. (Annoyingly, some charge bars like "equilibrium" which is need for some powers are ignore by the rest function, leading you to spam the skip turn button or use a mod if you want to get back into an optimal state.) Having to spam rest like this doesn't feel too great, it feels like the game had a hunger mechanic like other roguelikes to urge you on and prevent abusing rest, but dropped it along the way leaving Rest feeling orphaned.
There are a few other weird leftovers in the game, like a "Scrying Orb" which auto-identifies objects... and is completely pointless since objects always auto-identify in this game. Somehow the author hacked that in with a magical item at some point and left it as-is. Also, most annoyingly the game drowns you in loot but unlike, say, Crawl, anything you leave on the floor will disappear after a while. EXCEPT in "vaults", small enclosed areas with treasure guarded by monsters. Good luck identifying what was a vault when coming back to an area you've cleared, though, there are no indications except the room shape. This is an annoying non-feature you'll feel compelled to use, if only to stash stuff until you find the player home (which is also the in-game location of your
, microtransaction-fueled online item Vault), or to make sets of element-resistant armor for various situations.
Overall I quite like the game, but it has a lot of room for improvements in the UI and graphics clarity department. Some of the gameplay choices made that set it apart from other roguelikes give a different, but not necessarily better experience. And as mentioned there are small but nasty oversights in the game design, which ends up feeling like a work in progress based on other roguelikes rather than its own thought-out entity. The community also seems to be blind to most of these flaws, and over-protective of any choice the author makes.
Try it out to experience the sheer amount of content a true roguelike can offer, but do expect a flawed gem. It might be the best game in the Angband family of roguelikes, having gotten rid of annoying stuff like non-persistent levels while still offering mechanics pretty unique to the family like multiplying creatures.

This game is awesome.  I can understand why people were skeptical of it when it first came out due to the microtransactions, but now that the game is free to play, there is no reason to not play it.  Playing as the Monster is one of the most fun things I've ever done in a video game.  It's extremely tense when you are a Stage 1 Monster trying to run away and get stronger as the Hunters track you down.  You are pretty weak early on (although some Monsters can hold their own at Stage 1) so you have to play really steathily and be clever with your maneuvers.  Once you hit Stage 3 though, you can wreak havoc upon the Hunters and it is so satisfying.  Playing as the Hunters can be hit or miss, mostly depending on your team.  With a good team, it's a lot of fun.  Tracking down the Monster is fun and once you start fighting it, things can get really hectic and exhilirating.  Plus, Turtle Rock Studios made playing as the Hunters more simple.  Now that everyone can Dome, the Trapper dying doesn't mean disaster for your team.  Everyone has a lot more survivability too so you can withstand a fight even with a Stage 3 Monster.  TRS made the game much more focused on consistent fighting throughout the match rather than the Monster just hiding until Stage 3 and winning the game, making matches feel much more interactive and making your actions feels influential, no matter how small they might be.
The progression system is fairly simplistic, but it works.  The Perks system is neat.  You earn Perks by leveling up, or you can buy them with the in-game currency (which you cannot buy with real money at the time of this review).  In fact, there is nothing you can buy with real money.  Everything is earned through the in-game currency, which you will be earning a lot of early on.  As you level up, you earn Silver Keys, which are used to unlock characters, skins, and perks.  There are challenges to complete that reset daily that earn you keys and you also earn keys just through leveling up.  As you level up more characters though, you will see a massive drop in the keys you earn, which I think could be adjusted slightly.  A normal win with no level ups or challenge completions only earns you about 50 keys.  One character can cost between 3500 and 9500 keys.  This isn't an issue in the early levels since you'll be earning keys rapidly, but as you progress, you'll earn less keys which makes buying characters take a long time, which is an issue when there are 20+ characters to buy.
The game is insanely fun though.  Part of me wishes the game would have been successful at launch, since I bought it on PS4 around launch and the community died down rather quickly making it difficult to find matches, but now that the game is free, I think more people are realizing that the game is a lot of fun and hopefully the community lasts longer.

TL;DR:
Dungeon Rats is an excellent, low-magic, tactical RPG. Strategy and Character builds are important, and every fight is difficult but winnable. Its a mostly linear experience, and this allows each encounter to be finely tuned and balanced. All told, I think the playthrough I actually beat the game on took about 8 hours, but I had done the beggining a few times by then trying different builds. This is a game I have trouble putting down. If I pick it up to try a new character build idea, I often find that 6 hours have passed before I even notice.
Honestly, I'd feel bad NOT writing a review for this game at this point. This is, by far, one of the best tactical RPG's I've ever played. It should be noted that this game does not mess around with you. For veterans of tactics games, I'd reccommend starting on the medium difficult ("tough ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥"), and for tactics newbies or more casual players, play on the easy difficulty ("nice guy").
Cohesion:
Everything in this game just comes together so nicely. Every fight feels difficult, and the system of rations and healing items gives you incnetive even in the easier fights to try to avoid taking too much damage (although healing items are plentiful). I never felt as though any fight was unwinnable on normal difficulty. You have limited resources as you progress through the mines, so every piece of equipment you scavenge from fallen foes feels like a victory, as you can smelt them down and craft new equipment for yourself at various camps and forges. Yet the resource management fits perfectly with the combat and the atmosphere of the game; you're fighting against the odds, and start the game with extremely limited resources, wielding primitive stone hammers and crude bronze shivs, while by the end, you'll be swimming in the steel armor of your fallen foes. Everything is useful but limited: alchemy ingredients provide a boost for a tough fight, new armors and weapons keep you on a level field with your new foes, and ammunition for bows and throwing weapons needs to be rationed properly, especially early on. Theres no magic to help you with fights, but you can decide where to aim your strikes (legs, arms, torso, head, etc) or use area attacks (whirlwind with you weapon or swing in an arc in front of you) to effect multiple targets.
Difficulty and RNG:
There are some complaints about the game being RNG heavy. I firmly disagree. There are times when you'll be quitely cursing as you miss your third crossbow shot in a row with a 70% chance to hit, but thats what makes games like Dungeon Rats and XCOM fun: being able to adapt to a poor roll or an unexpected miss, and to be able to salvage your battle plan.  There were times when my party got destroyed on my first attempt, and then I thought "huh, maybe I'll try a different formation this time, send one of my men to rush the archers and focus down the target with a net". What was before a brutal loss, became a solid victory after a change of tactics. Using the proper aimed strikes to cripple targets and reduce their accuracy is vital to ensuring your victory.
The Devs:
The devs seem awesome. I think the studio is pretty small, but they have already updated the game twice since inception, including some much needed balancing, and are very active on the forums.
Random Thoughts:
The last fight was amazing, and I really had an adrenaline rush due to the whole scenario and the fight against impossible odds. It was a perfect ending to the dungeon crawl.
As much as I love this game, I do have a couple complaints. Bomb-chucking enemies can destroy your party if you don't have a quick melee fighter to tie them up, and they just feel about 50 times more dangerous than your average opponent, since a critical bomb strike can nearly one shot some of your squisher fighters, and they rarely miss. There were a couple bugs in the earlier version which annoyed me and prevented me from backtracking to do an optional fight, but I think those have been fixed in the most recent patch.
All in all: Dungeon Rats gets a solid 9.25/10 from me. Highly reccommended to anyone who enjoys a challenge, and it is an aboslute steal at $9, to me, this is easily worth 20-30$.

Pros:
* Fun, addicting gameplay (at least while the game is fresh)
* Rich tactical combat options
* Crafting & Alchemy and limited resources that you have to use very wisely
* Unique RNG passive effects for every offensive and defensive skill
* Unique combat actions for every offensive skill (weapon)
* Balanced and challenging (at least on 'normal' difficulty)
Cons:
* Extremely linear storyline and gameplay. All battles are exactly the same, you get the same resources every game, etc.
* Lack of replay value (mainly due to the above). Unless you want to push the game to the max and play with fewer party members or a save scum solo build, I don't see myself picking this up again anytime soon.
* You pretty much have to go a high charisma semi or full support build as your main until you get really familiar with the game mechanics.
* Not enough good gear drops naturally and there is too much reliance on crafting / alchemy. You basically have to get perfect crafting and alchemy and there are only two ways to do it: develop two followers that have naturally high crafting / alchemy skills or get them yourself. Developing the followers takes precious skill points away from more useful followers. Getting one or both of the skills yourself forces your main character into the full support role.
* Periodic crashes (but they at least allow you to fill out a bug report)

Streamline is fast-paced game with 2 (technically 3, but two of them are similar) game modes. In the first one a player tries to hit all the other players with a stop sign, while everyone else collects points by doing parkour across various terrains. The second game mode is similar to quidditch in that players try to score goals with a golden ball, but they still do parkour rather than fly on brooms.
Players move very fast and rounds are full of additional effects that influence each game (chosen either randomly or by viewers' vote if the game is being streamed on twitch). Things such as the floor turning into lava, players exploding if they touch each other and the camera view rotating at disturbing angles make the gameplay diverse during each game.
Moreover, you customize your character with items gained from packs which you open out of play similarly to Hearthstone. From making your character run around in their underpants to having them wear antlers, a gas mask or a hoodie. You can even change your race and gender at any time. Also you have a taunt action which makes your charater do a little performance such as doing the chicken walk or dabbing. It's perfect for when you want want to show off while winning the game.
I got Streamline during a free weekend that was held a few months ago and I've been hooked ever since. I already reached the maximum currently available character level but don't plan on stopping. I just find it that much fun.
P.S. As mentioned above all in-game items are cosmetic, so they don't influence the player's perfomance in the game, i.e. the game is not pay2win. So only play if you've got da skillz :P

My problem with
is that it's a Nintendo 3DS port that was lazily converted to PC. Simply getting a full-screen display took an eternity, but capping a side-scrolling platformer with high skill requirements at 30FPS makes for an exercise in frustration. From hidden endings to achievements to extra stage challenges to speed-run modes... everything seems to be designed for the expert player, except for the game itself. This is not
. You will feel the dropped frames and you will go through loading time (why are there still loading times in PC games?) when you want to restart a level.
Of course, you don't have to play for S ranks. In which case, the game is rather frugal in terms of giving you new toys. Or to put it in another way: you don't get the Robot Master's weapon after defeating them. Some gun sidegrades are given, but shooting isn't how you defeat your enemies. "Tag with my gun, follow with my flashfield. That's how my world turns." Yeah, but it gets old after a while because that's all that you ever do. Air dashes and double jumps are what you want, and such upgrades are only given through a somewhat out-of-place crafting system. Better scores offer more parts, making for a recursive loop preventing you from gaining the tools to get ahead.
As a platformer, there's not much platforming challenges. As an action-shooter, you don't really encounter any hordes of enemies to quickly and creatively dispatch. A better description of the ASG experience would be more as a stop-and-go side-scroller wherein all the gimmicks of the main character are used to better your score. Methodically advancing and destroying every foe that creeps to your right is a serviceable way of clearing a stage, and your reward for such a strategy will be a C score and very little parts for you to craft potentially fun upgrades. Playing to win is boring. Playing to excel is frustration.

Azure Striker Gunvolt or Armed Blue Gunvolt in japan, is a 2D Action Platformer side-scrolling , you control the main character named Gunvolt who helds electric power. Your main attack power comes from electric attack and to maximum its power, Gunvolt uses his gun with special ammo to shoot on any enemy in order to "tag" them then he will uses electric power to homing on them and finish them off, but doing the electric attack costs power which is called "EP" or Energy Power, using electric attack and/or any action related to EP too long or too many times will cause his EP to overheat, which pervert Gunvolt to use any more of electric attack and/or any action related to his EP.
Gunvolt also has ability to dash, jump and climbing wall and he will get more additional ability through gears/items in later game such as double jump, air dash and etc. However, most of additional ability will also cost EP while using same to Electric Attack.
Gunvolt also has ability to neutralize harm, one of his most powerful ability, as long as you have enough EP or not using Electric Attack, he will not get hurt like at all in exchange of losing some EP. This particular makes a game easy enough for casual gamer, who doesn't want to dodge some impossible looking attack from enemy. This ability is called Prevasion. Gunvolt gains access to this Prevasion through most of Pendant eventhough they're not written in the Pendant's explanation. If you remove Pendant, he will not use Prevasion.
Furthermore, Gunvolt also has special skill such as offensive skills that allow him to damage one or more enemy in an instant with heavy damage or support skill that help recover his lost HP, restore his overheated EP or increase his overall attack power, in all of these actions cost SP or Skill Point which player will be given with 3 of them at the start of each stage and if used, the SP will automatically be restored overtime.
Gameplay focuese heavily on player's skill, and then your reflex and memory will be put in to use. Each stage has unique challenge which require different technique. While each stage is easy for a  2D Action Platformer side-scrolling game,  the game provides a ranking system as well as several optional challenges which will put your gaming skill into test. Getting the highest in rank is basically a no damage run and do all the bonus on killing as many as possible, and while doing all of these the player must be very fast to complete each stage in time for highest possible bonus multiplier.
I have mentioned before, there're gear/item in game, each time you completed a stage, you will be rewarded with materials which can be used to craft gear/item which will benefit Gunvolt ever more, making him more versatile. There're no doudt you can complete a full game without any use of gear/item because all the stages are designed for gearless Gunvolt to be able to complete them peacefully but like most game, in later stages, they will get harder and more deadly, having a gear will help you deal with them easier, gears are optional as they're not necessary but they're so helpful that you don't want to avoid unless you want a real challenge.
Visual design in this game is unique, Art style that looks modern, cool dude and cute girl, that stuff. Most characters are well designed and have their own theme, Like Gunvolt is a lighting type super human for example, there're several characters in this game, most of them presented as a boss and Gunvolt will need to face them off and win battle. Each boss represent their own theme, most of their attacks are influenced by such theme. Fire is Fire, Light is Light for example.
One of the most greatest thing is music, the regular music in each stage seems fine enough but if you manage to kill so many enemy and do not take any damage like at all until some point, music will be changed into something else! This ability is belongs to second main character of game Lumen or Morpho in Japan, she will sings a song for Gunvolt if he somehow, has done a fair among of good actions during stage, in order to encourage Gunvolt or the player! There're several songs in game and can be unlocked or heard through out different stage in game. Lumen also has one of the most powerful ability, to revive Gunvolt when he's killed in action. Whenever Gunvolt dies in battle, there's small chance that Lumen will help him get up with song, this ability is called Anthem or Song of Diva, this ability returns Gunvolt into battlefield with full HP and ever more powerful than ever, he will have infinite EP and unlimited Jumps and Air Dashes until the end of stage. Also trust me, you will look into original soundtrack like crazy after you have played this game for a while.
Story is this game has some depth in it despite appearing to be generic kind of story, I don't know where to talk about it because If I say anything about it, it will be nothing but spoiler, I can say it's quite interesting but you have to find that for yourself. Then again this game is all about action and score the highest possible kind of game, the story itself is fairly good when look it in that way.
It's truly a hidden gem in steam. I would recommend anyone to get this game. 8/10 for me.

This is a roguelike done right.  And a free-to-play done right as well.
The world in which the game takes place is deep and immersive, with a rich history you'll rarely see in any game, roguelike or otherwise.  Character creation is incredibly complex... but in a good way.  Same with the implementation of the different classes' talents / skills.  The game somehow manages all this depth and complexity while still being approachable to the less hardcore roguelike fans.  The interface is fairly intuitive, and there's a solid tutorial to help players new to the genre to get a general idea how to play.
There are difficulty levels, which is already pretty unusual for a roguelike, but even better than that, three different game modes.  The masochists (myself included) can have permadeath while casual players can get into the game with Exploration mode, letting them die any number of times without any harsh penalties.  There's even an Adventure setting which gives players up to 7 lives (gained when reaching certain levels) allowing in-between players a chance to experience the intense thrill that only a permadeath-style game can offer, without over-punishing a small mistake.
The game is even more amazing in that it is 100% free.  You can download it for free.  You can even play with the source code if you are so inclined.  The game engine powering ToME is a separate package you can use to build your own games.  And yet it isn't supported by in-game ads (unless you count the very minimal starting-screen ads strictly for ToME DLC) or pay-to-win mechanics.  The entire game's revenue is based on players either buying DLC (which is absolutely not required to thoroughly enjoy the game) and donations (which is effectively what you're doing if you buy on steam).  Donators get access to some special content, and it's good stuff to be sure, but it's not required to have a ton of fun.
I feel like I need to buy this an extra time or two just to support the amazing product and the one (ones?) responsible for it.
I can't go into depth about game specifics; that would take me weeks to write.  Just trust me: it's an exceptional game with some really amazing features, and you can try it yourself for free if you aren't convinced.
(The free version is probably not on Steam, so go to the game's website if you're too broke to pony up the $7 for it)
If you like in-depth roguelike games, buy it. Don't even read anymore rewievs it will just be a waste of your precious time which this game will devour from you anyway.

Oh wow, where to begin?
This game is great. What it lacks in visuals is more than made up for in content. It's one of those games that you'll die a lot in, but each time you'll learn something new and think "Alright, one more playthrough, I've got this figured out now". Later, you realize that you've been playing for the past 12 hours, your eyes hurt, and you still have a lot more learning to do.
ToME can be kind of intimidating at first glance. There's a million different spells, skills, and traits that you can pick through, and it's up to you to learn which ones to use and when. I suggest starting simple, find a skill or two to use that kills stuff, and slowly try to branch out from there so you don't get overwhelmed and quit. If you give this game a chance, you'll more than likely fall in love with it.
There's a variety of different classes, many of which require you to complete a certain quest or objective with a starter class before they are unlocked. The game's difficulty scales fairly well, you're (probably) not going to die immediately upon starting a new campaign, and the first few quest chains aren't too difficult, which provides new players with some time to learn the basic mechanics of the game. In order to truly succeed in the game, however, significant attention will need to be put into resistances and learning which enemies do what kind of damage. Preparation and strategy are required, sprinting into battles is a good way to die, trust me, I know.
The game is difficult, so be prepared. I have nearly 100 hours into the game and - sadly - still have not beaten the campaign. Despite this, I highly recommend the game. It's rewarding, fun, and has high replayability (look at the hours played of 95% of the reviewers). Do yourself a favor and buy ToME.
One last thing, this game goes on sale a LOT. Typically for 50-75% off. If you still run a paper route and $6.99 is too steep for your blood, wait for one of these sales and say "Goodbye" to your free time.

I have been playing ToME for a while now, and I am still enjoying it.
The game is turn based roguelike about creating a character from a race/class combination, and slowly growing stronger by killing monsters and finding random items while trying to not die.
The world, the general theme of the dungeons and the main quests are always the same, but each dungeon floor is unique for the playthrough.
The game is not always fair, but at some level I really enjoy randomly ending up in bad situations, like what to do when you're all of a sudden being cut off from the stairs to the previous level, poisoned, low on hp, and surrounded by monsters; with practise and a bit of thought and soime luck a lot of bad situations are possible to come out of alive, and I find it hugely rewarding when I manage to pull off an unlikely escape to come back and clean up after recovering.
The game contains a large number of secrets that allow more character creation options when they are discovered, which I feel adds a lot of depth to the game; I'm still trying to find them all.
Leveling up allows some skill points to be allocated to any group of skills you know (Some groups may be added to the basic set of skilkls from your race / class combination), and stat points to be distributed among a fairly standardized set of stats. I feel that it is a bit unfortunate that the skills typically scale off a particular stat, for example berserkers have skills that scale off of strength and vitality, so investing in other stats is hard to justify.
The game is still under active development, and patches to address balance issues or add content or fix bugs are released regularly.
This can be a bit of a mixed blessing, as sometimes monsters that used to be easy yesterday all of a sudden can get you killed because they were buffed in a patch.
The game seems to have some minor annoying bugs that still haven't been fixexd, and a few major ones seem to bite people occationally. As of the latest patch the game seems to have trouble saving when playing online at times, but I am sure this will be fixed soon. As I understand it the entire game was created by a single developer, and given how many things there are that interact I think that he has done a very good job.
The graphics could be prettier, and the engine could probably be optimized a lot, but if you can stand dying a lot in the beginning while learning how everything works the game is really fun and rewarding with a high skill ceiling for players who enjoy exploring and creating powerful characters who survive against all odds, and if you haven't picked up this (slightly unpolished) gem already I strongly suggest you do.

OneShot is a very charming game with some pretty good music and quirky characters. It also has a bit of a meta narrative that can probably be compared to the likes of The Stanley Parable, Undertale or Pony Island. And while it does get compared to Undertale a lot, personally, I believe it has more in common with Pony Island instead. It certainly has that unique charm and exploration along with a world with several weird but fun characters but unlike Undertale it doesn't have any combat at all and instead relies on puzzle solving with a few of them akin to how Pony Island does it.
The puzzles are pretty simple as you'd see in any point and click adventure game, selecting an object, using it with something or combining two other objects. The story starts out pretty simple and certainly takes a much more complex turn later on. It's not very easy to get into without spoiling it. The fourth wall breaking moments are extremely well executed and they end up making a good example of gameplay and story integration, in one way or another.
The music is also top notch, it's often calm and serene to often reflect some of the areas in the game and it gets tense and ominous when needed. All in all I'd highly recommend it if you enjoy games that break the fourth wall, have great stories that you can invest yourself in and have great music.

This is, the single most touching and amazing adventure game that I have ever played. I almost never rate or review games on Steam, but for this game, I had to make an exception.

This review is spoiler-free
(I do however, mention my adoration of a character by name.  Said character is in the trailer for a brief moment and there is no mention of game-play related to said character)
Short, Professional Sounding Review:
Simply put- I have a new favorite game.
This game pulls you in in ways that no other game has before.  If you liked Undertale, this is definitely a game to check out.
The soundtrack is excellent, and the art is as well.
Very plot-driven.  If you prefer narrative over game-play (I feel like that is bad phrasing but I think it gets my point across), then this game is a must.
I don't play games all that often, admittedly, but I am skeptical that I will find one that tops this one anytime soon.  It is definitely worth the $10.  Or however much it will be at the next Steam Sale.
Longer, Less Professional Sounding Review:
HOOOOLY WHERE DO I BEGIN??
FIRST OFF: ALULA IS MY CHILD AND I LOVE HER.
SECONDLY: TEARS.  LOTS OF TEARS.
*Ahem* Anyways, this game is amazing.  It goes beyond the boundaries of what a normal game does.  I wish I could tell more but I'm trying to keep this review spoiler-free.  So many things were unexpected.  The puzzles were different from games that I had done before, yet there were several that were reminiscent of previous games.  A good balance of the old and the new, if you will.  Many of the games forced you to think outside the box and come up with solutions that are unusual, but certainly get the job done.
The soundtrack is amazing; I actually listened to it before downloading the game *cough*YouTubeismyfriend*cough* and found it just by itself to be quite enjoyable.  The composer, NightMargin, does a wonderful job of setting the mood for areas and events.  At no point was I removed from the narrative by the thought of "This music doesn't fit," or whatnot.
There are jokes related to programming throughout.  This is always a plus.
I love the art-style used.  Both cute, yet also is very good at setting dark moods and putting the user on edge as points.  The characters aren't overly complicated in design, which is a plus if you draw fan-art (like I do.  I might start a piece right after I finish this review lol)
Admittedly, gameplay isnt that long.  Albeit there were some things that I feel I have missed.  (6/11 achievements??? I finished the game, what more do you want from me???)  It is very linear, but I am personally a fan of more narrative-driven games so this worked out wonderfully for me.
Long story short, I HIGHLY HIGHLY HIGHLY recommend this game.  Definitely worth the $10 for the game.

This is a difficult game to review, because yes, I would certainly highly recommend it as a superb point 'n' click game; in fact I consider it one of - if not the best - I have ever played.  The problem is, it's a very different game to both sequels, which I believe are better introductions to the overall story, rather than playing chronologically.  They have a different protagonist, and are more consistent with each other than their predecessor.
I would, in all honesty recommend playing Black Mirror II & III BEFORE Black Mirror I, as they are, in my opinion superior games.
I think that if you were to play BM I first and you didn't like it, you would be making a mistake not playing the sequels assuming they are more of the same.  If you were to play II & III first however you would enjoy the first game far more.
I have played these games prior to purchasing on Steam, and have been a fan for many years.  I have played them all through a number of times now, and would hold them equal to the holy grail of point 'n' click games, the Broken Sword trilogy. They are very different in terms of tone but... in fact, I would go so far to say the Black Mirror trilogy has the edge.
PROS
+ The environments are beautifully drawn.  Some of the best I have ever seen.
+ The music is wonderfully atmospheric; superior even to my former personal favourite score, from the Broken Sword games.
+ The story is intriguing, gory and sinister.
+ It is not an easy game, and challenges you.
+ The world and setting feel authentic
+ The in game ambient sounds are excellent
+ It is a big game, which will take you a long time to get through.
CONS
- Fairly heavy on the dialogue.
- Character animations can be slow
- Some puzzles are difficult, and I needed to refer to a guide more than once.
- The accents are - on occasion - erm... interesting.
- Higher resolutions are not supported.  I run my PC via a 50" Sony and had to enable image scaling to fill the screen.
I cannot recommend the Black Mirror games highly enough if you want something with a really professional, well crafted feel to it.  Something about the atmosphere and feel of the game is very unique; reviews are mixed, but take it from someone who loves this type of game, it's one of the best.  I would start with the sequels, but this is a good introduction to the story and both Black Mirror Castle and Willow Creek are well worth your time.

Ok ok, remember when you were a kid and you went to the arcade and decided to pick up one of those guns and play one of those game? "Get the ball into the goal" is too simple a premise for you to call it an orginal game. There's plenty of games that do that, but there are usually complexities that make the game interesting and fun otherwise; adding new elements, tight mechanics, or complex rules. This game fails in all of those regards. It lacks anything that makes a game interesting.
It's art style is colorful in a way that seems almost sterile, like a test pattern. None of the pick-ups seem to do anything, they have numbers on them so I assume they're money, but what for? Your characters appearance? There aren't any skill trees or anything, so I really can't see what collecting these little tokens is even good for.
The animations are clunky and the controls seem unresponsive because of it, making you feel like you need to wait for an animation to be done to give your character a command. The goal of the game seems to be just to run around. I'm being literal there, and not overly reductive; there doesn't seem to be any incentive to get the ball into the goal so most players just seem to run around and parkour the tiny levels.
I want to separate this paragraph, and note that my feelings on the SJW-ness of this game did not influence my feelings on the quality of the game itself too greatly. It's a crappy game despite that. That said, the world built in this game (what little world was built) is so overtly preachy in it's left-ness that it almost seems like the only reason the developers made it in the first place.
The blurb that the creators came up with on the Steam page reads like an seventh grade girl trying to make up a sport that will still let her eat cake and daydream about horses. That's a bit of a stretch maybe, but it just reeks of  immature "no Boys allowed" type garbage.
Then there's the fact that the character that everyone starts out with is a black woman, in a sassy pose, and a wide smirk on her face. The only thing that doesn't bother me is the fact that it's a black woman. What does bother me is the smirk and defiant pose. It's like the developers are saying "Yeah, this black woman is the default and there's nothing you can do about it, you racist!" when there wasn't anyone saying otherwise in the first place. To me, staunch defiance in the face of zero opposition is just as cowardly as fleeing or shrinking from opposition.
Then instead of "gender" there's just a "body type" option, which changes you from looking feminine to looking masculine. Again, nothing inherently wrong with a gender neutral game, but making it seem like you've done everyone a favor is obnoxious.
My main problem with all stuff like this is how cheap it all is when you look at it as a whole. When I was a kid my parents were SUPER CHRISTIAN, and they would only buy Christian music and watch Christian movies and buy Christian postage stamps or whatever. At around the age of eleven or so I began to notice that if you didn't look so hard at the message the thing was trying to shove down your throat, you were left with a production so sub-par that really kind of insulted the audience with how bad it was. Stuff that caters to SJWs is the same thing to me. It's preachy and annoying, and when you look more closely you realize that it's cheap and crappy too.

As of 2/4/16, I have beaten the game and probably have some sort of plausable opinion considering that I play MOBAs on a regular basis to say this game is playable yet boring and doesn't simulate pro/casual player.
I want to preface this with a message to the developers:
STOP TRYING TO ADD NEW THINGS TO DIVERSIFY THE GAME AND START ADDING CORE MECHANICS TO WHAT YOU ALREADY HAVE. THE GAME IS BROKEN AND AN UNENJOYABLE FIRST EXPERIENCE.
Onto the review.
Your champion/character picks don't mean anything since their role means nothing, their position in the meta or OP Chart means nothing since it doesn't impact matches, and you can't dictate anything in the middle of the game.
The Pick/Ban phase is useless, since you chose your character prior to the actual select (which nobody would do), and you can't improvise mid game to change playstyle. You do nothing for your character, you can't see what's going on, you can't post-analyze the match, and you can't give your person/character an area to work on.
Champion mastery is also irrelevant. When I select a character who I have never touched before I have a higher winrate than a champion I have spent most of 4 hours working on.
The FPS category is irrelevant since there's literally nothing there. Just some icons.
Managing a team was fun until your players started underperforming for no reason, with no statistical proof of lack of ability to play the game, and you can't negotiate or haggle using contracts with players so you're often stuck with a level 2 mid laner in a team where everyone is level 80+. (I know they don't have levels, it's just easier to explain using such lingo).
My biggest pet peeve is that the character mean nothing. Literally nothing, they're just icons with smaller icons in the top left corner. They don't have pros, cons, weaknesses early, weakness late, magic or physical damage reference, and in general mean nothing. This means that you can't really help your "team" when they ask you for a single target burster. What? Does this fairy thing do burst damage, aoe damage, or does this dragon heal? There is no explanation to characters.
TL;DR This game is a shell and technically shouldn't be an early access game since this isn't a game right now. But I very much like the concept and it would be awesome to manage a character that you love and want to improve and win the FOBA (whatever that stands for) world championships.

After two horrendous modern titles; one that was a ''cinematic experience'' and the other being a pretentious corridor shooter, this game restored my faith in modern gaming.
A stealth based title with an emphasis on not getting caught by guards and sentrys; each level is a large map that presents you with a waypoint to get to and lets you have at it. You aren't given directions, rather the map has  multiple ways of reaching the waypoint and its up to you to decide how to get there. Each map also has a few optional objectives that are attained through exploration, at the beginning of the map, or through eavesdropping on discussions. The main missions themselves have options in the lethal and non-lethal varieties which affect the ending you receive.
The maps are large in that there are many corridors and crevices you can reach. Many doorways to enter and go through; rather than a large field where you can see for miles, you get a tight, compact city with a lot of alleys and vertical movement. The developers succeeded in creating a city that feels as a city should; tight and winding with a lot of places to scatter about and travel through.
The only downside is that stealth isn't so much an option as much as the better overall choice. Combat with the knife feels somewhat clunky and awkward, and the guns have incredibly low range. The crossbows are fine, but the guns themselves are horrible, which makes sense given the historical period, but trash is still trash.
The books you find are also pretty mediocre. The manner in which they're written is meant to be from an informative perspective (not first-hand accounts as is the case with the Bioshock series), but some of the books you find are so long-winded that you start tuning it out. I'm sure that some of the books ar emeant to add to the game world, but something as mundane as whaling shouldn't have a three part short story associated with it. Then there's the literal fanfiction erotica in some of the books. Looks like the Bioware writers invaded the Dishonored offices for a short period.
Lastly there's unanswered questions at the end. Mainly: The Outsider. It's like they wrote a key character with a pivotal role in your character's development then completely forgot him and forgot to mention just WHAT THE HELL IS HE. I mean, I know you have deadlines but come ON. The guy is just...completely done away with. Nothing else is said. WTF. Then there's the plague and what exactly caused it. We know it was ''brought'' over but there's a few things left unsaid.
But those are just slight blemishes on an otherwise versatile and enjoyable experience. The game still holds up plot-wise as a game of political intrigue and backstabbings. Overall I'd strongly recommend it.

Oh wow, where to begin?
This game is great. What it lacks in visuals is more than made up for in content. It's one of those games that you'll die a lot in, but each time you'll learn something new and think "Alright, one more playthrough, I've got this figured out now". Later, you realize that you've been playing for the past 12 hours, your eyes hurt, and you still have a lot more learning to do.
ToME can be kind of intimidating at first glance. There's a million different spells, skills, and traits that you can pick through, and it's up to you to learn which ones to use and when. I suggest starting simple, find a skill or two to use that kills stuff, and slowly try to branch out from there so you don't get overwhelmed and quit. If you give this game a chance, you'll more than likely fall in love with it.
There's a variety of different classes, many of which require you to complete a certain quest or objective with a starter class before they are unlocked. The game's difficulty scales fairly well, you're (probably) not going to die immediately upon starting a new campaign, and the first few quest chains aren't too difficult, which provides new players with some time to learn the basic mechanics of the game. In order to truly succeed in the game, however, significant attention will need to be put into resistances and learning which enemies do what kind of damage. Preparation and strategy are required, sprinting into battles is a good way to die, trust me, I know.
The game is difficult, so be prepared. I have nearly 100 hours into the game and - sadly - still have not beaten the campaign. Despite this, I highly recommend the game. It's rewarding, fun, and has high replayability (look at the hours played of 95% of the reviewers). Do yourself a favor and buy ToME.
One last thing, this game goes on sale a LOT. Typically for 50-75% off. If you still run a paper route and $6.99 is too steep for your blood, wait for one of these sales and say "Goodbye" to your free time.

I have been playing ToME for a while now, and I am still enjoying it.
The game is turn based roguelike about creating a character from a race/class combination, and slowly growing stronger by killing monsters and finding random items while trying to not die.
The world, the general theme of the dungeons and the main quests are always the same, but each dungeon floor is unique for the playthrough.
The game is not always fair, but at some level I really enjoy randomly ending up in bad situations, like what to do when you're all of a sudden being cut off from the stairs to the previous level, poisoned, low on hp, and surrounded by monsters; with practise and a bit of thought and soime luck a lot of bad situations are possible to come out of alive, and I find it hugely rewarding when I manage to pull off an unlikely escape to come back and clean up after recovering.
The game contains a large number of secrets that allow more character creation options when they are discovered, which I feel adds a lot of depth to the game; I'm still trying to find them all.
Leveling up allows some skill points to be allocated to any group of skills you know (Some groups may be added to the basic set of skilkls from your race / class combination), and stat points to be distributed among a fairly standardized set of stats. I feel that it is a bit unfortunate that the skills typically scale off a particular stat, for example berserkers have skills that scale off of strength and vitality, so investing in other stats is hard to justify.
The game is still under active development, and patches to address balance issues or add content or fix bugs are released regularly.
This can be a bit of a mixed blessing, as sometimes monsters that used to be easy yesterday all of a sudden can get you killed because they were buffed in a patch.
The game seems to have some minor annoying bugs that still haven't been fixexd, and a few major ones seem to bite people occationally. As of the latest patch the game seems to have trouble saving when playing online at times, but I am sure this will be fixed soon. As I understand it the entire game was created by a single developer, and given how many things there are that interact I think that he has done a very good job.
The graphics could be prettier, and the engine could probably be optimized a lot, but if you can stand dying a lot in the beginning while learning how everything works the game is really fun and rewarding with a high skill ceiling for players who enjoy exploring and creating powerful characters who survive against all odds, and if you haven't picked up this (slightly unpolished) gem already I strongly suggest you do.

When I first started the game I had no expectations at all. I had no idea yet that it was going to keep my attention for three days straight.
Clunky interface and dated visuals do not impress your mind as you probably get used to. Don’t let yourself get distracted so easily, let it in and you’ll be amazed on how much it has to offer. It invites you to have a very unique, engaging, mature and rewarding RPG experience. The game mechanic and the balance is where the game really shines. It makes you appreciate that every single detail and decision does matter and you will painfully learn about it. Through the each detail it can be tracked how much their developers loves and cares about their product. It is easy to see how they do everything it takes to make it a finished and unique RPG as they envision it to the point that it strikes you personally.
There is no sense in blaming the graphics or the way the story develops which is rather straightforward. This product looks very self-contained and polished as it is. Just make sure to play it with the default «high» difficulty settings, it is really the best way the game meant to be played. If you ever liked turn-based combat games, get this game and check it out, the experience is well worth your time and money.

This review is spoiler-free
(I do however, mention my adoration of a character by name.  Said character is in the trailer for a brief moment and there is no mention of game-play related to said character)
Short, Professional Sounding Review:
Simply put- I have a new favorite game.
This game pulls you in in ways that no other game has before.  If you liked Undertale, this is definitely a game to check out.
The soundtrack is excellent, and the art is as well.
Very plot-driven.  If you prefer narrative over game-play (I feel like that is bad phrasing but I think it gets my point across), then this game is a must.
I don't play games all that often, admittedly, but I am skeptical that I will find one that tops this one anytime soon.  It is definitely worth the $10.  Or however much it will be at the next Steam Sale.
Longer, Less Professional Sounding Review:
HOOOOLY WHERE DO I BEGIN??
FIRST OFF: ALULA IS MY CHILD AND I LOVE HER.
SECONDLY: TEARS.  LOTS OF TEARS.
*Ahem* Anyways, this game is amazing.  It goes beyond the boundaries of what a normal game does.  I wish I could tell more but I'm trying to keep this review spoiler-free.  So many things were unexpected.  The puzzles were different from games that I had done before, yet there were several that were reminiscent of previous games.  A good balance of the old and the new, if you will.  Many of the games forced you to think outside the box and come up with solutions that are unusual, but certainly get the job done.
The soundtrack is amazing; I actually listened to it before downloading the game *cough*YouTubeismyfriend*cough* and found it just by itself to be quite enjoyable.  The composer, NightMargin, does a wonderful job of setting the mood for areas and events.  At no point was I removed from the narrative by the thought of "This music doesn't fit," or whatnot.
There are jokes related to programming throughout.  This is always a plus.
I love the art-style used.  Both cute, yet also is very good at setting dark moods and putting the user on edge as points.  The characters aren't overly complicated in design, which is a plus if you draw fan-art (like I do.  I might start a piece right after I finish this review lol)
Admittedly, gameplay isnt that long.  Albeit there were some things that I feel I have missed.  (6/11 achievements??? I finished the game, what more do you want from me???)  It is very linear, but I am personally a fan of more narrative-driven games so this worked out wonderfully for me.
Long story short, I HIGHLY HIGHLY HIGHLY recommend this game.  Definitely worth the $10 for the game.

First, I'll talk about the positives:
+ Great looking backgrounds even by today's standards. Very smooth and good looking pre-rendered backgrounds fill every frame of this game. It's a very beautifully imagined game and the environments truly look detailed.
+ Very intruiging story. It starts out slow but really picks up from chapter 2 and makes you come back for more to see what will happen next. As I will mention later, despite lots of plotholes and bad dialogue, the interesting story is what resulted in me not giving this game a marginal thumbs down.
+ Great sound effects which are creepy when they need to be and that's almost always in this mystery/horror game.
+ Puzzles are usually very logical. There's a challenging slider puzzle and a few more but most of the game is about using objects in your inventory rather than puzzle-box situations.
And now the negatives that almost made me lose it every time I played the game:
- HORRIBLE main character that acts like a selfish, blue-blooded lord while borderline insulting NPCs who are even helping him with his quest. Sometimes I just wanted to smash in Samuel's head in to prematurely end his own and other's misery.
- RIDICULOUSLY bad voice acting. Once again, the main character takes the cake for being the worst of the bunch. I can't imagine even if a person TRIED to voice as bland and uninterested as the voice actors in this game they couldn't do it this bad. It's a chore to listen to most of the game's dialogues because you feel like they're not interested in the mystery so why should I be?
- Technical issues with the game's FPS. it would drop drastically whenever I was in an outside scene when it was raining. Everything would slow down to a crawl and a simple 5 second task would take 30 seconds to act out. Although I found a temporary solution to it. You can Alt+Tab out of the game and go back to it and everything would speed up but only for 4-5 seconds and it would slow down again. I had no problem with the indoor scenes.
- Character animations and graphics look very bad. It didn't really bother me though I play lots of adventure games and there are but a few 3d ones that have very good character animations.
- There is some pixel hunting to be done. The environments are really detailed so it's easy to miss an important item. But the main problem comes from the fact that you can only pick up objects that Samuel recognizes as useful for the task currently at hand. So there are several instances when you can't pick something up at some point only to come back to it later and pick it up when it needs to be used in an almost immediate environment puzzle solution.
- The last point leads to LOTS of backtracking and not ever being entirely sure that you currently have everything you need to do something and you have to go back to places you've been to try and pick up stuff you left behind because Samuel thought they weren't necessary at first.
- Most of the investigation and interactions are done with the left mouse button but somehow, with SOME items, the only way to investigate further is right clicking on the item/area. This is very confusing and sometimes leads to dead ends where you think you've looked at everything but what you need to do is right click on everything to double check.
- The story has major plot holes and doesn't entirely explain what happened on in the end but it remained interesting enough for me to finish it so maybe it won't disappoint you either.
- It doesn't run in full screen you'll have a black border around your game all the time. I use a widescreen monitor so maybe that was the problem.
- The cinematics look really dated.

Assassin's Creed II is a perfect example of how to make a sequel. There's definitely a good reason why this one is a fan favorite. The basic story is that Ezio Auditore is seeking vengeance and is trying to rid Italy of the Templars. He soon uncovers a bigger plot that will affect more than just Italy. Now, just like with every other Assassin's Creed game, this one takes place in a historic location and time period. This time, we dive into Italy during the period of rebirth, The Renaissance. Before I talk a little more about Italy, let's go talk about the combat.
Now, if you've played Assassin's Creed, you'll know that the combat system in that one was pretty good, but they've definitely made improvements. Weapons, for starters, have definitely been given an upgrade. There's a multitude of weapons, like maces, hammers, swords, daggers, throwing knives, and even a wrist pistol! There are different tiers of certain weapons (Mainly swords) that have different stats. Some add more damage, while some are quicker. In my opinion, the sword is the way to go. It's kind of like Mario in Mario Kart, generally good all around at all of the stats. One very noticable difference from the first game is you know have TWO hidden blades.
Two hidden blades allow you to stealthly take down enemies easier and faster! Now you can kill two guys with one go. The hidden blade mechanics have also been improved. You can jump off legdes to take down enemies, you can effectivally use them in fights (unlike in AC 1), and you can also ledge-shank guards. This simple change is one of the great improvements from the first game. Now, general combat has also changed. It's more brutal, gives you more freedom, and works really well. Also, more death animations have been added, to satisfy your bloodlust.
If you remember just a little bit ago, I mentioned a 'wrist pistol'. What exactly does it do, you might be wondering. Well, it definitely kills people. The wrist pistol is a ranged weapon that you get later on in the game and is definitely not something you saw in AC 1. In terms of usefulness, it's pretty nice. It's definitely not something you'd use for being steathy, because it's loud as heck! It's great for clearing out those annoying rooftop archers though. Still on the subject of weapons, throwing knives are still in the game and they really haven't changed from AC 1. Some more weapons that have been added include a poison blade and a smoke bomb (Which is kind of a weapon, but it can't really hurt anyone xD).
Alright, so what's the enemy AI like? Well, honestly, the combat is really easy in this game. There are a couple of difficult sections, but they're not that hard. The combat is still fun so, there's that. The AI isn't the brightest AI, but they're definitely not the stupidest. There are a few different enemy times, such as archers, your standard guard, armored dudes, and heavily armored dudes (Which can be a pain).
Okay, so we've got all of the combat stuff out of the way, now let's move on to some more stuff. So, the game has a system known as 'notoriety', which is just the level of ablitiy the guards have for recognizing you. If you have high notoriety and a guard sees you, they'll go after you. If you have a lower level of it and stay around for too long, they'll probably go after you. In order to get rid of this, you have to remove wanted posters, bribe people spreading the word about, and sometimes even kill a fool. The system overall is pretty cool and works well. It can also make you more careful as what you do.
Another great thing about this game is its level variety. It never really feels like you're doing the same thing! Sure, there are assassination missions where you're given a target and you've got to assassinate them but hey, you don't have to go around and collect intell like in AC 1. There are a couple of things you do a couple of times, but the levels are unique. Without spoiling anything, there's a level that takes place in a carnival, as well as a level where you fly a glider!
Yet another great thing about this installment is the characters. The characters are very well-written and well voiced! You'll notice a few famous faces in your journey. The characters are very fun and you build a connection to them over time. Also, the main character, Ezio, is a really great character. He's not dull (*cough* Connor *cough*) and he, like the story, is very well-written. Also something to note is the music. The music is absolutely amazing and is probably my favorite soundtrack from any AC game (followed by Black Flags).
We've basically covered everything here except for one thing...the map. Just like in real life, Italy is beautiful in the game. The graphics are pretty great for its time and the maps look great as well. The maps you'll travel through are pretty large and very diverse. You can travel through them by boat (Yes, you can actually swim in this one) or by horse. You can also fast travel back to each of the locations. I've personally never been to Italy, but I've seen pictures and it definitely looks accurate!
Overall, this is probably the best game in the series! The characters are amazing, the music is great, the story is incredible, and the combat is so good!  If you haven't played this game, I HIGHLY recommend checking it out. I definitely recommend starting for the first game, but you'd probably be fine starting from this one too.
(Also, just note that this game does use UPlay)

The game is now out of Early Access. Prematurely, as you'll find out.
Many of the points below - written for an early version of the game - still stand.
There is little to no feedback, not even to mention explanation. If you are not aware of the terminology in League of Legends or Counter-Strike, you will have a hard time understanding without researching it yourself.
The game is a big grind for stats which ultimatively do not seem to matter. The results (winning, losing, stats) seem incredibly random, even if your team is half of the world top 10 players.
I had a lot of hope for the game when it was in Early Access. I do think this was released way too early and the premature release hurt the game in the end.
If you find this review unhelpful, I invite you to tell me why in the comments. Will do my best to explain my verdict and would happily take feedback.
##################################################
##################################################
I was thinking about giving this the thumbs up or not. I decided that I should go by what the game is right now, not what it can be, promised to be nor I hope it turns out to be. The game shows a lot of promise but what's in there right now has too little long time motivation for me to recommend it. (the ammount of hours played is a bit skewed in my case as I left the game open for a night and work day).
The game assumes you know a lot of terminology of League of Legends (since that is what the game is mainly taylored towards right now) and doesn't explain any of it.
I've played a bit of MOBAs but never heard of an ADC in my life, because I haven't played LoL. Friends with multiple hundres (sometimes thousands) of hours of playtime in DOTA 2 and Heroes of the Storm didn't know either.
The game generally doesn't explain itself too well right now. There is no tutorial yet and your performance in the game is not explained.
You select a role (Top Lane, Mid Lane, Jungler, Support, ADC) and a chamption according to your role. There are types for champions (e.g. Sustain, Healer, Chaser, Utility, Tank, etc) but they are not explained.
There are mutliple champions for each type but you are not told what differs Healer 1 from Healer 2, except for the "Tier" it is listed in, ranging from "SS" as overpowered champions to "C" as competetively non-viable champions - though it is not explained why. This tier list changes with patches to the ingame game which is a really nice mechanic in itself.
Selecting a hero oddly enough also takes place before champions are banned (in MOBAs you often have the chance to ban a champion for a game so the other team can not use it), so you can take whatever champion you want.
A Win or Loss also does not seem to take your stats into account. Of course, a single player seldomly carries a whole team to the win but my almost maxed out stats didn't seem to have any impact on the outcome of the game. You are simply not told what you've done wrong nor right.
In order to increase your stats you can watch top players streaming the game, though Pro Gamer Manager doesn't tell you what you're learning. It doesn't tell you what stats increased, if you've learned something about playing a certain champion, etc.
Different compositions of a team make up different strategies that range from a "Glasscannon", "FullAD", "NoInitiation", and "Balanced" to "NoDisengage", "Early Game" and others. None of them are explained so the player is expected to know about them, when they are not self-explanatory.
After the banning phase (you take no participation in because you already have your hero selected) you chose a focus for Lanephase and Teamfights as well as a general Mentality. No explanation on what does what, as it is expected of the player to know. Your selected champion also has no impact on this, so you'll have the same strats availablle for a Healer as for a Sustainer.
Game done, you're rated with a GameScore between 1 (worst) and 10 (best) and can see your Kills, Deaths, and Assists stats. Besides that and telling you if you've won or lost, there is no explanation. You can't watch your own demos in order to examine what went wrong either.
The next game you might win, you will still not know what changed the outcome.
I'm a fan of "eSports" so I've sunken quite some hours into the game and still enjoyed myself. Ultimately, it was just grinding and looking at a circle fill up and percentages increasing, since there is very little going on visually.
There are a lots of areas that need a redesign and lots of bugs that need to be squashed. Having your own team doesn't seem to work too well and cuts you off from areas of the game (improving certain heroes, researching, streaming) for some reason. You also will not know what you're getting yourself into before starting a team on your own (which can happen way too early at the moment). Earning money seems a bit imbalanced, since streaming is way too lucrative right now (in fact, more lucrative than being a Pro Gamer).
All this is to be expected of a game in Early Access and I do imagine a lot of this (if not all) will see itself being adressed later in development but I can only rate the game for what it is now. The current meta of the game is way too impetuous, as very little is explained.
I can't comment on the frequency of updates just yet. However, the lack of feedback is a common theme inside and around the game, since the developers of Pro Gamer Manager could communicate with their current fanbase a lot more.
As a player you are pretty much left in the dark about the progress of the game. So far, patches were posted (the last one was around two months ago at the time of writing this) in the News section but you get no progress reports.
Updates in the form of blog-like posts would be nice, maybe bi-weekly in order to actually know what they are working on as well as confirming they actually are working on the game. This will give players confidence and increase the amount of recommendations.
A beta-branch might even help with bugtesting and getting feedback.
The Store page reads:
The participation on the forums is fairly one-sided. I haven't seen a comment from a developer yet, outside of Twitter.
In the end, I enjoyed playing the game but I wouldn't blindly recommend it to others
. Hopefully I will be able to in the future but right now, the lack of feedback inside the game as well as the lack of feedback from developers is worrying me, personally.
DO BUY the game if you can spare the cash and want to invest in a promising game without any guarantee that it will turn into whatever you imagine. With Early Access, the risk is yours to take. Also buy it if you want to test it, there is no demo and if you play less than two hours, you can get a refund via Steam Support. Make use of this option! Maybe you'll like the game and want to support and fund the game along with the developers.
I'll keep this game on my mind and will certainly change this review if I see improvements or feel my (our) feedback has been heard and acted upon.

After two horrendous modern titles; one that was a ''cinematic experience'' and the other being a pretentious corridor shooter, this game restored my faith in modern gaming.
A stealth based title with an emphasis on not getting caught by guards and sentrys; each level is a large map that presents you with a waypoint to get to and lets you have at it. You aren't given directions, rather the map has  multiple ways of reaching the waypoint and its up to you to decide how to get there. Each map also has a few optional objectives that are attained through exploration, at the beginning of the map, or through eavesdropping on discussions. The main missions themselves have options in the lethal and non-lethal varieties which affect the ending you receive.
The maps are large in that there are many corridors and crevices you can reach. Many doorways to enter and go through; rather than a large field where you can see for miles, you get a tight, compact city with a lot of alleys and vertical movement. The developers succeeded in creating a city that feels as a city should; tight and winding with a lot of places to scatter about and travel through.
The only downside is that stealth isn't so much an option as much as the better overall choice. Combat with the knife feels somewhat clunky and awkward, and the guns have incredibly low range. The crossbows are fine, but the guns themselves are horrible, which makes sense given the historical period, but trash is still trash.
The books you find are also pretty mediocre. The manner in which they're written is meant to be from an informative perspective (not first-hand accounts as is the case with the Bioshock series), but some of the books you find are so long-winded that you start tuning it out. I'm sure that some of the books ar emeant to add to the game world, but something as mundane as whaling shouldn't have a three part short story associated with it. Then there's the literal fanfiction erotica in some of the books. Looks like the Bioware writers invaded the Dishonored offices for a short period.
Lastly there's unanswered questions at the end. Mainly: The Outsider. It's like they wrote a key character with a pivotal role in your character's development then completely forgot him and forgot to mention just WHAT THE HELL IS HE. I mean, I know you have deadlines but come ON. The guy is just...completely done away with. Nothing else is said. WTF. Then there's the plague and what exactly caused it. We know it was ''brought'' over but there's a few things left unsaid.
But those are just slight blemishes on an otherwise versatile and enjoyable experience. The game still holds up plot-wise as a game of political intrigue and backstabbings. Overall I'd strongly recommend it.

This is a pretty damn fun puzzle game with a very simple concept that scales appropriately in difficulty over time. Admittedly some of the features introduced can be quite obnoxious (particularly wormholes) but it's a genuinely enjoyable challenge of skill and timing.
Then you get to the last set of planets and are immediately gated by obnoxious requirements. You see, at each level you are scored a percentage, which awards you a number of stars rounded down to the lowest ten e.g. 79% = 7 stars! Can you see where this is going? Waveform ultimately turns into an obnoxiously grind-fest wherein you're playing the same level over and over to scrap an extra few points out to potentially have enough stars to unlock another level or two. This star requirement is present throughout the game but it really ramps up towards the end.
Honestly it's quite a fun game, but I can't imagine actually finishing it. Probably the perfect tablet game for killing time as you gather those last few stars at a glacial pace over the course of a few weeks. Not worth buying on Steam unfortunately.

In this game you let a circle ride along a waveform that you control. You can make the waveform taller or shorter, but you can also widen or compress it. And while you do so you have to make sure that the waveform follows the line of the stars that you collect. Sounds simple? Maybe the first few levels, but it gets gradually harder. Transporters, distortion, black holes and more make your journey more exciting as you try to get as many lights as you can!

Waveform seems simple enough, but this game is tough. You control the amplitude and wavelength of an orb to run through a gauntlet of space objects. The control aspect is quite intuitive with a mouse, but getting the waveform to follow just the right path is more than tricky--it's downright difficult.
What I didn't realize after completing Pluto is that there are many other planets to be completed. The interface didn't exactly make it obvious (to me at least) that you can scroll through these other planets. With the amount of content this game has to offer, it really is an excellent value for puzzle gamers--just be prepared for frustration.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is a must play for anyone who has any kind of interest in the roguelike genre. It's a proper turn-based, grid-based tactical game with perma-death (although you can play it without it if you're a puss :D).
Set in the fantasy world of Eyal, a land which is filled with deep lore and interesting stories and characters. The number of races and classes available is huge and the varying combinations of these make the game immensely replayable.. And you'll want to replay it because it's incredibly addictive but also very difficult. (you will die. A lot) The difficulty (something which should be expected from any true roguelike) is not unfair however, and there is always a way in which you could have gotten out of the situation which killed you, you just might not know it untill a few playthroughs later. The more you play TOME, the more options for skills and gear and combinations of these you become aware of and this, in turn will increase your chances of surviving a little bit longer.
The game has a huge number of things to unlock by carrying out various actions in the game world, from new races and classes, birth options which affect every character you make thereafter and new skill trees for existing classes.
