I wish I could write a review that isn't riddled with spoilers, but this game is one of those that you need to play 100% blind for the best experience.  So, unfortunately, this review will contain spoilers, but I will hide anything that gives vital plot points away.  Just to be safe, however, do not read this until you have played it, or watched someone play it (Why would you watch someone play it? This game is too good to watch)
OneShot is a puzzle RPG made in RPG Maker.  Sounds simple enough, right? Well, nothing could be farther from the truth.  OneShot is a game that has one of the most immersive, and inclusive stories that I have ever, and possibly will ever play.  It is a game I will never forget.
Your objective is to guide a child (Niko) through this world distraught by the loss of their sun.  Throughout your adventure, you will solve puzzles to achieve this goal, and create a bond with Niko as the story progresses.
It isn't a very long game, but it is 100% worth the price, and then some.
To me, OneShot is more than a game.  It is a masterpiece.
It also taps into depths few games before it have.
I had never felt such care for a video game character.  Niko is so adorable! If I could have one thing on the planet, it would be a little plushie of Niko, because I want to give them so many hugs. *insert cute aggression here* But I'm getting sidetracked.
Unfortunately, as a result of creating such caring emotions, there must come a price.
In short, it has an immersive story, cool characters, incredible puzzles, a great soundtrack, and a special place in my heart.  It's a really thought provoking game that made me question my morals, honestly.  Games that create these emotions are ones I want to see more of in the future.
If you've read this far, go tell your friends, your parents, your colleagues, or even just random people on the street to check out, and play this game.  The critical acclaim is well deserved.
(Also, a lot of people compare this game to Undertale... I don't think that is fair at all, to be frank with you...)

The premise of this game is that you, the player, are a seperate entity from the character you control. You're not so much playing the game AS Niko as playing the game WITH Niko. This unique approach makes the world of this game far more immersive and believable than anything you're probably used to.
The game has an extremely similar style to Undertale in how it challenges and subverts traditional game tropes in unexpected and humanizing ways, though the gameplay is quite different. There is absolutely no combat or fighting in OneShot; instead, you'll be travelling the world in search of items, information, and people with which to solve puzzles and problems. If you liked Undertale's style of making you, the player, feel uniquely responsible for your actions and behaviors - actions that as a gamer you wouldn't have even thought about - buy this game yesterday. Heck, even if you didn't play Undertale, buy this game yesterday.
Also: Keep an eye out for the secret Solstice ending for the full picture.

Just over four years after its release, Dishonored remains one of my favorite games of all time. As someone who was raised playing fast-paced first-person shooters like Call of Duty and the Battlefield trilogy, this game allowed me to take a deep breath and take my time and explore landscapes and try all the different options and branches that the game has. I have beaten this game on Low & High chaos about five or six times each (I also owned Dishonored on my Xbox 360 & Playstation 4) and I would estimate my hours to ~100.
I highly recommend this game to ANYBODY.

Despite the fact I wasn't initially wowed by Dishonored, I'm now playing the entire thing through for the third time (which is a very rare accolade from me). Each time I've played a mission I've heard something I missed previously from the many characters which populate the world, or found a new way to get through, over, under, or around a tricky section, or discovered a good use for one of the magical powers bestowed by an impressively ethereal being called The Outsider. If you want to go at this all guns blazing you'll find a lot to keep you amused. If you want to sneak through the entire game totally undetected then you'll find even more to enjoy. And, as I'm finding, it's entirely satisfying to play the whole game over again, using a different approach each time.

This was a gorgeous game. I saw an Early Access type of demo video for this game about a year ago and that's the first thing that drew me in; The graphics, the geometric and colorful landscapes, the fact that you're playing as a fox with such simple movesets. I love simple, beautiful games like these. One thing I will say is I was expecting a bit more from it. The basic move controls were lacking (you slide around a lot when you use wasd, it's easier to just hold down W and rotate with the camera) and apart from collecting stars and digging up dirt plots throughout the world, there's not a whole lot to do. I understand why that is, but after the second or third area I found myself getting a little bored. The narrative of the story was brilliant, with wonderful voice acting and a touching storyline. While I came for the gameplay (playing as a fox was wildly appealing to me, as I love foxes), I stayed for the story.
It's a game about loss and moving on. Can't say much more other than it made me cry 7 times in 2 hours.

Do yourself a favor and buy Dead Rising 2 and 3 instead.  Dead Rising 4 is barely a shadow of those.  If you already own them then just reinstall and play those.  Avoid this game and the absurb price tag.  Only get this if you desire some real game design headaches and a lacking zombie story.
This is what was not in Dead Rising 4; content that defined the franchise from other great games:
No timer which means no sense of urgency and no time management
No manual bathroom saving
No iconic psycho boss fights
No iconic boss fight music
No preparing for boss fights
No mixing drinks or item buffs
No queen bee
No healing item managment
No power attacks
No main weapon throwing
No variation in healing items restoring health
No icon blocks for a health bar
No survivor escort missions
No limited spawns for survivors
Game design mistakes:
- Saving is only auto and the player has no concept of a save location or time of last save
- Healing level at safe zones does not increase (stays at lv. 1) even though other areas level up
- Vender sells healing items all at the same price however they can be found for free, even in the rooms next over
- Restrooms serve no purpose other than wasted deadends
- A cup of coffee heals the same as a giant medkit
- Buying any combo weapon undermines the purpose of searching and crafting them
- Exo-suit denies the player access to the inventory
- Exo-suit can pick up any item but can not drop them manually
- Exo-suit locks at infinite power throughout story events
- Entering a vehicle causes Exo-suit to be destroyed
- Guns are extremely common and undermine utilizing random melee objects
- Several combo weapons are reskins with different element damage
- Trials produce less scrap and points than killing over 500 zombies
- Clothes vender is a scrap sink and provides no purpose when searching for clothes is free
- Green insect virus is not explained in the storyline but is present
- Day and night atmospheres only happen by story progression
- Player is not given the option to continue playing their original game file after beating the game and is instead forced to do New Game+ in order to play
- Can not skip the entire intro level on New Game+

If I was asked to explain why I play TOME so much, I wouldn't be able to use any of my reasons to convince someone to purchase it.
This game is one of the best RPGs out there, period. This is offset, of course, by the fact that it's about as forgiving and accessible as a brick wall. With spikes on it. And it's somehow firing a steam gun at you.
This is a game that almost kneecaps itself at every turn, in my opinion, only just barely getting good quality out of an idea that could have easily left this game yet another greyed out title on my library.
It's a massive game, sporting over a thousand bloody achievements, but you'll be suffering from roughly twelve types of PTSD by the time you get through the first batch of dungeons and actually start the story.
There's a massive amount of variety between god knows how many classes that are available, but they'll all probably die the same way.
There's a never ending slew of new sights to see and enemies to fight, but every one of them will probably either lead you to or be followed by a gruesome death.
This all being because, as the game so proudly states, it's a roguelike. And as a roguelike it's just about the worst made game I've ever played. Don't take that the wrong way, the game is great, but it's roguelike elements sell it short in places. To justify this, before I am impaled by a billion pitch forks, I'll remind you of FTL, faster than light. By all accounts, a great game. But FTLs biggest shortcoming was its final boss, which required near perfect planning and exceptional luck to beat, and when you lost, as it was whenever you lost, you were sent back to the start of this fairly long game.
FTLs permanent death did no poor job of making you value your ship, and the game was just short enough to make it tolerable. This mentality has been taken in TOME and turned up to seven billion. You could complete a run of FTL in the time it takes you to get through the first batch of dungeons in this game, and the threat of losing it all doesn't get any smaller as you go on.
Well, that's not entirely true. The default difficulty for TOME gives you a handful of lives to play around with, you can of course turn it up to true roguelike, but I'm fairly sure that was meant as a joke. However, the lives system does not take away from the fact that you, unless you're amazing at this game, are going to die from something out of your control at least once. And by "at least" I mean if you have the blood of a leprechaun in your veins and are blessed with uncanny luck. The rest of us are going to be suffering a lot more than that
That brings me neatly onto the most glaring turn off from this game. It's villain. You see, this villain, is not a character that you meet, nor is it a magical force, nor a force of nature. It is a concept, and it is always with you, breathing down your neck, plotting its next attack, ready to steal yet another life away from you without warning, nor mercy.
This villain, is the RNG.
For you will spend your time in this game preparing for when next the RNG will strike. You will hesitate as you assign level up points to consider "Will this help me survive when the RNG strikes?", you will creep around each and every corner, terrified that around it, the RNG will be lying in wait, ready to put all your talents on cooldown, poison you, and chop off half your health all in a single turn. The RNG is your worst, and only enemy, for the enemies that are not affected by it, you shall slaughter in the thousands, you will be prepared for each and every boss that you encounter, through hours of rigorous training, but you can never be fully ready for the minions of the RNG.
In all seriousness, I cannot remember the last time I died in this game to a boss that I fought poorly, or a talent that I used carelessly. I have, however, lost count of how many times I have died to elite wolves with steamguns, to gelatanious cubes with lightning magic, to the boss of the level spawning literally a square away from the level entrance. The game is difficult, but when the RNG bears its teeth in the worst possible way, there isn't much you can do except backpedal to the level entrance and go level some more in a different dungeon, and that's if the poison doesn't get you, because it is always poison.
In short, purchase this game, that's an order. But expect to be a different man/woman/other by the time you've completed it, mainly because your hair will have gone white and you may have aged a few years. It's not impossible, and I'm slowly learning the ways of this horrifyingly difficult world, but I expect to be doing so for a while.

Currently this is my most played game on Steam, and for a good reason - the number of options for character building, equipment combinations and unlockables in ToME is enough to warrant hundreds upon hundreds of playthroughs. Granted, many of them are going to be short - this IS a roguelike, after all - but the game has enough to offer for both experienced veterans of the genre and explorers who are just in for the sights. ToME features a huge main campaign with a pre-determined world map and randomly placed quest dungeons, several dozens of class/race combos with unique skill trees and expansive battle mechanics to liven up the experience.
Unlike many other modern roguelikes, ToME's one and only focus is combat. Even though there's an overworld and a bunch of peaceful cities, don't look at them as more than just trade hubs. What you're gonna do 99% of the time is look for a way out of yet another impossible situation that you recklessly rushed into, be it an unexpected boss or a group of trash mobs that you foolishly underestimated. Luckily, the player is always equipped with numerous tools to deal with trouble or escape to safety - there are runes, infusions, magic artifacts, proccing gear, abilities, status effects designed to keep you alive and your enemies either dead or, at least, a safe distance away. Learning how to use all of these is a different beast entirely, and you'll quickly find that even the normal difficulty playthrough might take you more than a hundred hours to master (even though the total time spent for an actual normal playthrough run without deaths might not exceed 10 hours in total). Once you've done it, higher difficulties unlock, and there's a good chance you also discovered some new classes/races to play along the way, so that your next game is completely different from the previous attempt.
1.5k achievements (currently the record-holder on Steam), insane replayability, a quest progression to keep you motivated, and brutally difficult yet fair fights in the classic turn-based Rogue fashion - there really isn't much else to say. ToME deserves all the praise it gets, and the regular updates only make it that much better.

I like the concept of this game, a tactical real-time naval simulator dealing with the fascinating hybrid warships of this period. There aren't that many tactical naval simulators around unfortunately, and the few that do exist tend to leave a lot to be desired. I'm sorry to say that this one is no exception.
The biggest let down for me was the graphics, which could have been this game's redeeming feature. Had they been really good, or at least on par with Empire Total War Naval Battles, with similar camera controls, this could have been a neat, immersive tactical simulation. Unfortunately, its graphics look like they are based on the video card technology of 2003, and the camera controls are clunky.
On a more positive note, I found the physics simulation of the ships and ballistics to be spot on, but I do wonder if the realistically slow-paced nature of the game has been a problem for some players. Without immersive graphics to look at, it can become tiresome. I mean, these ships were beautiful!
This is definitely an improvement on the earlier series, and I hope the developer continues to improve the game. In particular I'd like to see much better camera controls in the next iteration. I'd also like to see some progress towards better graphics, and the addition of weather effects and crew morale to the game.

"I will show you fear in a handful of dust."
Bottom line up front:  One of the best platformers ever made; buy this and play it with a friend.
Salt & Sanctuary is a sidescrolling, 2D platformer where you wash up on a mysterious island after your ship is boarded by pirates and then sunk by a Chthonic nightmare.  You will progress over many hours through different locations on this lost island, fighting monsters and beating bosses to gain items and experience, while gradually learning more and more about this bizarre world, eventually escaping (or not) from this twilight realm. You increase in level by gathering "salt" (a proxy for life essence), and you rest and save your game at temples called "sanctuaries," hence the name.
Why is this game worth your time?  Obviously, I found it worth over a hundred hours of my life, and count it time well spent.
Art style:  The graphics are simple, but distinctive and beautiful.  Towns, forests and beaches are rendered in shades of grey and muted colors, feeling ancient and foreboding.  Enemies and friends are distinctive, yet clearly all part of the same tapestry of ennui and loss.  And of course the music is excellent, whether simple guitar accompanying exploration, or discordant, angry notes in combat.  Outstanding.
Gameplay:  Character creation takes only a minute or two, but sets up widely varying paths to follow.  The skill tree is enormous, and allows you to mix and match between wizards, clerics, hard-hitting warriors, archers, etc.  I was eighty hours into the game and still discovering new weapon combinations and moves...yes, you can (more or less) pound your way through the enemies, but you'll feel much more elegant once you've learned block and riposte, or how to properly balance the types of magic to maximize the impact.
Enemies:  All of the monsters in the game fit with the overall theme...they are lost souls, twisted by the island, and oddly sympathetic despite their deformed appearance.  Each (and there are dozens) has a short back story which adds a surprising amount of depth.  (One example is "The Hanged," floating corpses who catch you in their nooses and drop you to the ground.  Their story is that they are condemned criminals, but in their homeland, anyone may be spared from the noose if another takes his place.)  This is particularly true of the bosses, which are quite distinctive from each other and require vastly different tactics to defeat.  Again, each is somehow sympathetic, seemly filled with despair, or symbolic of the sins of overreach and vanity.
Replayability:  The maps are exactly the same on each playthrough.  However, there are enough side paths and optional areas to be worth returning to the game.  More importantly, however, your characters can be completely different on new playthroughs, which changes your tactics, goals, and choice of allegiance.  I played it three times completely and enjoyed each.
Difficulty:  This game is really, really hard...at first.  You will die over and over, finding bosses who can annihilate you just when you think you're invincible.  Even some of the minor monsters can be lethal (there's a group of pretty unicorns in one forest who spear you like a kebab).  But death is mainly just an inconvenience, so you can revive to fight again, and eventually you'll figure out how to beat all the bad guys.  Immensely satisfying.  The platforming is usually not too difficult, although there are definitely places (particularly in the optional areas) that can be supremely frustrating (lookin' at you, Fire and Sky).
Co-op:  Very unusual co-op mechanism...the main player can summon a partner to help as a "mercenary."  Generally, this works well, but your friend can't join until you've met certain conditions, and that can be irritating if you just want to jump into some couch co-op.  Overall, I like it, although I wish there was an online option, and the co-op partner can miss out on certain valuable rewards permanently by playing as a mercenary.
Summary:  A wonderful game, deep and story-rich.  Clearly a labor of love by a very small team (I think just two folks did it all).  Money well spent!

Terrible game. Capcom Vancouver completely lost touch on what made Dead Rising a special franchise. DR1 and 2 have never been zombie mass murdering simulator, it's true survival to the core, managing items, using everything to defend yourself, stacking up foods and drinks and trying to run every time you're cornered. Instead, in this game, you have seperate slots for melee weapons, throwable items, guns and healing items. You can't throw away a baguette, you can't mix drinks, you can't use a propane tank to smash a zombie in its head. Guns are abundant, lethal items are abundant, there's no food turning rotten over time. You're angel of death, you have the ability to mow down a hundred enemies with a swift cut, you're ♥♥♥♥ing untouchable. This would have been a great concept if it didn't bear the name of Dead Rising.
DR4's interactivity is horrible. So many clutter background items that you can't simply pick up, because apparently according to Capcom Vancouver, only things that can decapitate zombies are considered to be weapons. NO, THAT'S NOT THE POINT, THE POINT OF DEAD RISING HAS ALWAYS BEEN USING WHATEVER YOU CAN REACH TO DEFEND YOURSELF. DO I NEED TO REPEAT THAT♥♥♥♥♥♥TWICE? The world is lifeless, NPC automatically disappear when you clear zombies surrounding them instead of having you escort them back to a safe house like before. Maniacs are crap, too easy to defeat. No fun minigames like Terror In Reality, minigolf or any casino game. Willamette is terribly designed, it's virtually a long hallway and most of the time, you just spend time in the boring town instead.
Less combo weapons than DR2 and 3. DR2's weapons feel like a really clever guy stitch different components to create a neat weapon, for example spiked baseball bat, teddy bear with LMG or a guitar that can burst electricity from an amplifier. They're useful but never felt to OP. In DR4, weapons are dumb as ♥♥♥♥: hydro nitrogen + a knife = Ice sword??? They're straight up power fantasy crap and make the concept of makeshift weapons obsolete. It has become Saints Row-tier ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but at least Saints Row is self-aware of how ridiculous it is. Dead Rising 4 is just pure dumb, stupid and ignorant with how inconsistent the tone is.
Heck, the protagonist ain't even Frank West. This is an even more grumpy version of Michael de Santa that's trying too hard to roll with cool kids, for example: "too cool for school" - really? Is the writer serious? This is how they made Frank "mature"?
Do me a favor, spend 20 bucks on either DR1 or 2 or even both if you want to understand how the franchise gained its cult status. They're not just shitball themepark playground for kids that concentrate on murdering as many zombie as possible, they delivered quite a remarkable experience that no other game in the genre has ever achieved the same with its magnificent level of interactivity, detail and smart design even though they're not always in player's favor. I won't blame you if you get this game or DR3 just because you want to mow down zombies, there's a reason why I hate this game: The developer said this game is supposed to go "back to its root", and it's a terrible attempt in recapturing Dead Rising's spirit.

Before this review begins I just want to say this is coming from a guy who LOVES the Dead Rising franchise. I played tons of Dead Rising 1 on the Xbox and got it on pc the release date and consider it my favorite game of all time. I also played over 200 hours of Dead Rising 2:OTR without modding it.
I think I have played this game thoroughly enough to write a review for this product (Beating the game once and grinding to level up and collect everything such as blueprints, mysteries etc. etc.) and boy where to begin. Dead Rising 4 is really a unique game. Reaching a ridiculous amount of controversy and complaints. I'll be the one to say it was a pretty fun game to play...But not in the way it should of. Dead Rising 4 had the potential to be absolutely PHENOMENAL, but Capcom Vancouver shunned out the fans of Dead Rising and handed us a product that was such a disgrace to the series, which led to the result of Dead Rising 4. Every complaint you'll see about this game is almost completely agreeable, but a lot of it is also a bit too excessive and heated that it just makes CV look like they murdered your dog. So I will make this this review completely fair and civil listing the Pros and Cons of this game.
Pros:
Fun gameplay: Say what you will about this game. but I did find roaming around and slaughtering zombies a blast and i did like the variety of ways to kill them, but there is always something bad about a good thing but I will list that in the cons later.
Great map: In Dead Rising 3, I was pretty skeptical about how it wouldn't be taking place in a mall of some sort and instead a whole city to explore, but when i started playing it, it became something refreshing and i loved it. Dead RIsing 4 takes place in both the city of Willamette Colorado and in the Willamette Megaplex. It's really nice to be able to explore the mall and the city all the time instead of just being in one or the other.
Huge variety of weapons at your disposal :As cartoony and ridiculous the combo weapons in Dead Rising 4 were to use, they were still very fun to mess with for a while, and there are plenty to go through with many great special skill moves.
Visually stunning graphics:The graphics in Dead Rising games have always been nice and this game was no different. Nothing much to say here except the graphics are just fantastic.
Very well optimization:Dead Rising 3's port was honestly a failure. having to search up fixes before I could even play the game was very tedious, and even then it was still choppy and would crash time to time with my build and it's a pretty good one. But kudos to Capcom for this port of Dead Rising 4, I have had no crashes nor horrible framerate in my 50 hours of playing. I would maintain 50-60 framerate for anything I would do.
Now to move on to the ugly. **FAIR WARNING, LAST CON WILL CONTAIN SPOILERS, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.**
The Developers:I'm just gonna put it out there. The Developers were a disease in making this game as everything the fans wanted for this game to be great, they turned away and did what they think was better. Every question the devs had handed to them they responded with answers that just didn't add up.
Survivors:The survivors you would find scattered around the world of dead rising were always in a desperate need for help, and you would be at their aid and take them to some sort of shelter so they would find solace during sudden and scary times. but in Dead Rising 3 they changed that where instead of fighting your way to get them to safety, you sort of just kill a couple of zombies around them and they just go on there way. In Dead Rising 4, Survivors are now able to drop you loot once you save them, and it's always a combo weapon, but what really bothers me is that while you are helping them out they seem to use the most generic weapon like a baseball bat and don't use it, but as soon as the coast is clear for them they drop you a godamn sledgehammer attached to a cement saw and just go on their way like nothing is going on. Survivors also tend to be glitchy where they won't even give you anything even though it says they will as a reward, they'll also start running into walls after you rescue them and start repeating something like "Someone, help!" and it gets very irritating.
Zombies: in this installment of the dead rising games, zombies are for some reason fast as ♥♥♥♥ and i'm not talking about the ridiculous "Fresh Zombies". Regular ordinary zombies are supposed to be stupid and slow, but for some reason in this game they just start running as soon as they see you instead of just slowly dragging themselves towards you. Also not to mention Fresh zombies and Evolved zombies are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥as Fresh zombies screams are very annoying, and Evolved zombies just jump around with more than enough health. It was annoying enough doing this stuff on hard difficulty so i'm really dreading about doing this on the Blackest Friday difficulty.
Poor character development: With the exception of Frank (not talking about his new VA and look, just his new "I only care about the money" attitude) and Vick being the voice of reason, Every character just seemed placed in the game as a filler and nothing more. It's a shame really because characters like Isaac and Tom could of had more potential. Instead you only talk to Isaac once and you only speak with Tom in one cutscene before later on in the story. I'm not being specific with the characters here i'm just giving examples. and later on you talk to someone named "Jordan", And I had no idea who they were because they were never shown in the game until frank goes like "Oh hey Jordan". This games character development was absolutely terrible.
Frank no more:Frank West has a completely new look and voice actor in Dead Rising 4, and while the new VA seems to enjoy the role he was put in, he is simply not meant for the role of Frank West. The only man fit enough to do that is the Original, T.J Rotolo. CV's♥♥♥♥♥♥poor response really didn't help this situation either. "Everyone loves what Frank has become!" But yet there was an entire petition to have T.J do the voice acting instead and even T.J HIMSELF signed it. T.J wasn't even called about the role from what I heard. Franks new humor and sarcasm really didn't blend with his "I don't care I just want the money" role, and I always like to think about how it would be so much better if T.J was the man doing this.
Maniacs replace the Psychopaths:Psychopaths were honestly my favorite thing about the Dead Rising games. seeing unique cutscenes for these delusional and chaotic antagonists was such a blast and the fights were no different, and then seeing their death scene after you finally beat them was so satisfying. On the other hand, this game introduced the Maniacs, which replace the Psychos and sounds far less intimidating and just really poorly thought of. These fights do not have ANY cutscenes and all the fights are, are just fighting a couple of the main maniacs minions at first, and then fighting the maniac themself. That's all. CV's response to this was "we wanted the boss fights to feel like they belong in the world and not just because they're in it because it's a video game" as you fight a guy dressed as santa claus with an electric axe spawning elfs that attack you. Great response guys.
The Ending:In the end of Dead Rising 4 you fight and defeat Calder, a former human that turned zombie while in a Exo Suit, still able to talk like a normal human, he was responsible for killing over 200 hundred of his former soldier friends that tried to capture him. Frank beats him and later on just dies in an anti climatic way by getting caught by a group of zombies. The REAL ending is blocked by a pay wall instead of the classic multiple endings like the old games. and you play as Zombie Frank. Garbage.
TL;DR. I'd only advise getting this one a sale only if you REALLY want to mess around, Not to enjoy a story.

Plug and Play is pretty much my favourite game. It last only about 15 minutes, but you can replay it over and over again or force your friends to play it (you'll want to share the experience, promise). I don't remember how I came across it, but I'm so glad I did.
Plug and Play is a game about playing with plugs. And cables. And switches. It's all black and white and really simple, but it's also really complex if you think about it. As you progress, you begin to realize, this is not about plugs and cables and switches doing odd things - it's about humans. Plug and Play teaches you a lot. It deals with love, sex, rejection, friendship, loneliness, empathy. It's all about desires, feelings and emotions. It's a weird discovery to make, but at some point, you see yourself in those little plugs. Plug and Play is so close to everyday life, and yet so far away thanks to its brilliant abstraction.
But it laves you feeling not-so-bad about yourself. It's actually quite uplifting to play, especially when you feel heartbroken, or lonely, or both. I recommend playing it by yourself, in a dark room, with no music or anything playing. Take the time, it's really short. Until you start playing it again and again. Because that's what you'll do, and you'll love yourself for it.
Its maybe good enough for a browser game, but maybe not worth paying any amount of money for. Its barely 15min long... Entertaining enough for those 15min, but 15 min, come on.

I have nearly 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews.
One Hour Reviews - Game 4
Age of Wonders - Shadow Magic
Purchase Date: 5/22/2014
I got this game, along with the original Age of Wonders in a Humble Bundle.  I didn't warm up very well to the original, so my hopes were not very high for this one.  So I was pleasantly surprised to find that none of the things that annoyed me about the original game are present here.
I jumped right into the tutorial.  Compared to the original, the tutorial in this game is vastly improved.  The tutorial, like the original, starts by covering the basics of movement around the map and claiming resources, but then proceeds into a lot more detail.  I felt like I had a much better sense of what my options were and what I needed to be doing.
When I played the first Age of Wonders, I actually had to restart the tutorial because I died.  What I appreciated about Shadow Magic is, it gave me a good sense of the difficulty right off the bat, but I didn't have to start the entire tutorial over.  The very first fight I got in, a giant beetle ended up stomping my entire party.  But the tutorial was written to expect this, so rather than having to start over, the tutorial used this experience as a teaching lesson on what to expect.  I really appreicated that.
The graphics in Shadow Magic are better, but that is to be expected given the length of time between the games.  I didn't care for the animations in the original, but here the units move more naturally.  Also the game provided all the resolution choices I'd expect to see.  I played at 1920x1080, and didn't have any problems with menus or reading text.
The actual gameplay itself seemed much like the same turn-based strategy from the original Age of Wonders, which itself brought back memories from the old Heroes of Might and Magic games.  I have a feeling that I'd probably enjoy the original more now that I've played this tutorial and have a better grasp of the game.
The only thing that really annoyed me about Shadow Magic happend when I was trying to back out of a command that I was issuing to my party by hitting the escape key.  This brought me out to the main menu.  I then hit the Continue button, except this command will actually load your last saved game.  I didn't have any save games yet so it ended up not doing anything.  I wanted to resume my game, so I hit escape again thinking it would close the menu and take me back into the game, but instead it dumped me out to the desktop.  And thus, my review ended about 8 minutes early.
I really didn't expect to like this game given my impression with the original.  So in this case I am glad to be wrong.  I'm looking forward to coming back and spending more time in the campaign.
Overall Recommendation:  Keep

I really like the UI improvements and the way you can issue orders to Armies. Solves a lot of the micromanagement issues from previous entries.

Bravo! A truly great strategic-level game, with enough operational-level play to keep it interesting. I tried HoI III but found it too cumbersome and clunky: I was drowning in detail most of the time and the game seemed to churn forever on each turn.
HoI IV deals with all the same theme areas as its predecessor, and all the relevant details, but does it in a far more intutive and streamlined manner. The game also cycles quite quickly on my fairly basic PC. While there is still lots to learn (and I don't recommend HoI as your first stategic  game), I found the learning process much easier and more user friendly than previous HoI.
The political system is much slicker than before, while still allowing you to mess about with interesting "what-ifs". The "National Focus" system is a flash of game design brilliance, bringing together domestic and international politics, research, economics and the arms race under one fateful click. Well done.
The military production is much easier to use than in HoI III, particularly with the helpful Logistics screen that lets you understand the impact of your arms production decisions on equipping your force
Combat, while still somewhat abstract, is quite realistic and detailed enough for a strategic level game. The battle orders system is very good, and is an improvement over what exisetd before, although still requiring a few training games to really master.
On the negative side, I found that there is a real need for in-game access to a detailed manual (not just acces to the Wiki, which is nice but is repetitive in spots and often lacks detail). HoI has lots of excellent detail, but finding out what it all means can be a challenge. It's just as glorious, as trashy and as bad as it's predecessor. I love it! It combines the trashyness of a Sergey Titov title with the most stereotypical mainstream story in a perfect linear CoD fashion! Because, what could ever be better than a story containing a super-assassin-sniper-dude waddling through the swamps of unnamed south-east-asian islands, to find and take out some bad-guy with some ties into some bad-guy-group because he's got some bad-guy-superweapon and a private army of russians? And don't forget, this has got the updated engine, it no longer runs on Chrome (not the Google one), it runs on CryEngine 3, the latest and bestest of which!
So, yeah. If you read the above monkey-marketing-junk, and think "oh, this is for me, gotta grab some Bud Lite's, pack away the shotgun and play one of those darn videogames", well, I can't help but say: By all means buy it!
But if you think "what the actual ♥♥♥♥, I know this story!", then let me give you a little bit more. This is a copy-pasta of the first title. You'll see that in the story, you'll see that in a lot of the models and assets than are just reused from the first title, you'll see that in the gameplay (did I just say gameplay? This is more like an interactive DVD!). This feels completly the same as the first title, with slightly better textures and animations.
Having CryEngine 3 doesn't do it any favors - the engine doesn't make a game look good, it makes a game that already looks good run well. These devs didn't do much in that direction, it's just below B-title quality. Nothing in terms of looks that is standout'ish, but not unplayable bad either. The sound is pretty much the same. It's your typical "blockbuster"-soundtrack, nothing more than that. The guns? Oh, they sound just plain boring.
So, for the gameplay then. It's still the strict "we mark this guy, you shoot, we mark next guy, you shoot"-style of game. It's just never getting any further than that, doesn't get your heartrate up at all. The whole game is a "follow the path and you'll win, don't and you'll instantly loose". The game doesn't react to you trying a different way, it just follows it's own storytelling.
And then there's the flaws, oh, the logic flaws. A 50cal should make a somewhat audible noise, right? It doesn't. No, you can gun as much as you like, enemy's won't hear you. Except for if you shoot a guy that turned just behind a corner - every enemy around him, no matter if they could see him, will be alerted and will instantly fire at you with their $2 toy-Kalashnikovs.
It's just that. A copy-pasta of the first title, with a bit more of the same content. If you didn't like the first one, you won't like this one either and vice-versa. It's the sad reality, but it's not evolved. Buy it, if you think you're up for mediocre, don't, if you expect surprises and excitement.

Deliberate, and brilliantly done.
While you may need a FAQ handy to help you if you're totally stuck, I can't recommend highly enough that you go into this game as blind as a bat. To quote Markiplier, "I'm emotionally devastated. I have to go lay down." And having played through the entire game, there is no exaggeration for how this will make you feel.

It feels bad not being able to recommend this since I love the series (Excluding 3 and this sorta), but I cant recommend this at all if you are a hardcore fan of the series, and if you're a newcomer or regardless of whether or not you loved Dead Rising 3 I persionally wouldn't recommend it now until the Frank Rising DLC comes out. But thats getting ahead of myself, so lets talk about why DR4 is good before we talk about why its a let down.
The color is back, which is nice after how greybrown Dead Rising 3 was
They brought back the mall, bringing back the relaxing mix of killing zombies while elevator music plays in the background really missing in 3.
One of the few games I can think of outside of Parasite Eve, and Yakuza 1/2/5 which takes place around Christmas.
Devs are FINALLY listening to feedback instead of terrible Valve-tier playtesters and have added in multiple difficulty settings and I recommend playing on hard if you want a challenge.
No more weapon lockers which stripped away some challenge in 3
Killing zombies is as enjoyable as it has always been in the series, and DR is still my favorite personal zombie action series
Story at least interested me more than DR3 to see it through to the end even though its still not great as the original or the entire DR2 saga
Runs only slightly better than Dead Rising 3
Character models can look ugly
Camera doesn't really have much purpose outside of investigation missions, unless you complete some faux-achievements it doesnt level up your character making the score system feel redundant.
The controls have been changed, apparently to make things more convenient because they were apparently bad before (?). I thought they worked great, they still work fine here but there is a pointless "stealth" button which you will never ever need to use.
Killing zombies is still treated as a focus rather than a side activity or something that stands in your way.
Characters are either forgettable or completely obnoxious
Mall itself doesnt feel large compared to DR1 or DR2's strip and you dont visit it much storywise in favor of a bland town

Claims that they're going back to their roots though nowhere near as misleading as other franchises "RESIDENT EVIL 6 WILL BRING THE FRANCHISE BACK TO ITS ROOTS", still feels like marketer speak as the game feels less similar to the original than ever.

Absolutely awesome. It really tests your typing skills while delivering a hilarious story. This is one of the most entertaining games I've played in a long time. It's a short game, broken down into chapters, each chapter with a B horror movie spoof cut scene. The characters are ridiculous and completely over-the-top. It's almost deliberately awful, full of profanity, sexual innuendo, gore, and crazy love affairs. Isaac Washington swears nearly every other word, sometimes multiple words in a row, and while some may be turned off by this, it's one of the comedic highlights of the story and is actually relevant to the relationship building between Washington and Agent G. There are some great quotable lines, but nothing appropriate to display (in case kids are reading).
The gameplay is very simple. Words pop up. You type. There are three difficulty settings. They are introducing new dictionaries as DLC to expand the words that you need to type. Each level has collectibles. A co-op mode is included, but I haven't tried that yet.
You can also play the game with shooting instead of typing, though I found this a little difficult to do with a mouse. The typing mode is more fun anyways. There's a variety of mini-games. They are okay, but I only played each once.
Obviously the graphics are dated since this was a Dreamcast game. I think it still looks fine. The soundtrack is good and fits the game well.
If you're looking for a game you can play in 20 minute increments when you need to pass some time, this is a great choice. That's about how long each level lasts.
Very good game indeed. Strongy recommended.

If you're interested in this game, definitely get it. When I first saw it, I jokingly called it Game of the Year. Even if it's not, it's a heck of a lot of fun. I've played the original one and I have just as much fun on this game as the original.
This game is a parody on all those terrible horror movies, with crappy special effects, voice acting, lots of swearing, and so on. So you'll get a good laugh at just how absurd it all is. Gameplay is simple but fun: Type to kill. I don't know if it's because I can type really fast or if it's something else, but I found it pretty easy compared to the original game. I can pretty much breeze through all of the levels and never have to continue, whereas the original got pretty challenging as you got farther (natually). There's also not as many gimmicks as the original. In the original, you had to do various different things: type long sentences while being chased by a chainsaw-wielding zombi-MUTANT (they're mutants!), type the correct answer to a question to attack a 3-headed monster, type a quick word or phrase just before an attack happens, etc. Most of the bosses in this game is basically type whatever is on screen. There's some slow-mo stuff at parts but that's not much. Besides that, there IS one boss where you have to distinguish the real one between the fakes. Type one of the copies and you get hurt.
And now there's co-op, so now you can try to compete for scores or help each other out! It's loads of fun. There's also minigames to play if you want to kill a few minutes. Or if you're not down for typing, you can also switch on over to House of the Dead and shoot zombi-MUTANTS with your mouse or controller. Earn money to upgrade your guns or buy new guns.
I highly recommend you get this game.

By far the best Roguelike I've ever played, Tales of Maj'Eyal still has an active developer and an active community, so it just keeps getting better, both the vanilla game and the mods. There's nothing quite like wiping out 80% of the orcish race as some kind of dragon-person and then being killed by a random halfling unique that happened to get an overpowered class combination.

I got a lot more than I bargained for with Tales of Maj'Eyal. I wasn't expecting much because of the low price point and odd graphics, but I've spent hundreds of hours in the game since I bought it (and all of that was before I installed my Steam copy).
Every character class has widely varied and interesting abilities, which makes them feel unique and fun. Warriors and rogues don't have quite as much to do as mages, but they aren't just "easy mode" like with some games, and the way their abilities behave makes the tactical battles as dramatic and fascinating as if they had magical powers.
Practically every enemy has interesting abilities of its own, and even small ones can be dangerous if you aren't careful. The AI is simple, but effective. You can't just kite your way through fights. Small mistakes can escalate danger quickly, and death is rough (if you're playing on Adventure or Roguelike difficulties, at least), but when I die, it's usually my fault, and I can do better next time.
Loot is plentiful, but easily managed, since you have an inventory item that stores new pick-ups, and sells off junk at the end of each area (at no loss, even). It takes a little while to figure out what items are good for your character, but once you know, inventory management is a breeze.
The story is mainly told through notes you pick up, and the lore is pretty deep and interesting. I'm there for the combat, though, so I'm glad subsequent playthroughs aren't bogged down by having to wait through dialogue and story scenes.
The game is very thoughtfully crafted, and I greatly appreciate the effort that was clearly put into it. I can see myself playing this game for thousands of hours and still enjoying the heck out of it.

This is a surprisingly good roguelike. There are loads of things (classes, races, skills, cosmetic options etc.) to unlock simply by playing the game, loads of very different classes which al have different ways of playing. The game is difficult, but you can choose whether it's classic roguelike (permadeath), if you start with multiple lives, or if you can continue as often as you'd like. Additionally, you get a warning if you enter an area which is way too difficult or easy for your current level. However, there's always the chance of a nasty surprise if you decide to open a sealed off door.. There is a lot of really strong loot to find and secrets to discover. Not everything happens in every run, so you have to keep your eyes open.
Ultimately, I'd highly recommend Tales of Maj'Eyal as well as its DLC. It's a hidden gem which you can spend loads of time on without running out of stuff to do.

Even then players that are bad/new at roguelikes can just change the difficulty level/the amount of lives they get to enjoy the game without fear of losing progress.
With or without the difficulty, you will still get the gripping gameplay of a roguelike (although it is of course better if you have a chance of dying). Additionally, there are many unique classes in the game so that you can find a playstyle that suits you.
Overall, I believe it is the best roguelike of all time, because it keeps the good things about roguelikes and avoids most of the annoying things about them.

Hearts Of Iron is a game that I have poured countless hours into and I love. I understand why many people are annoyed, but I believe that the pros out way the cons. Here is my list of pros and cons:
Pros:
-It has great in depth strategy mechanics.
-It is well researched and has great refrences to real history.
-It has a good multiplayer, though at times slow.
-It is easy to mod, with tutorials made by the very creators of the game and many great mods.
-It has a reasonable amount of replay value, as you can play as any country on the map, and become democratic, communist, or fascist, plus you can be neutral (kinda boring) or actively seek war (the fun way).
-The music, artwork and general game is quite beautiful.
Cons:
-The game is buggy.
-Whilst the developers are making extra content, it's all bullsheit DLC.
-As stated before, the multiplayer is slow and often straight up doesn't work.
-Games drag out forever. I have a facsist America game where I have tried to end the war. Every time I kill someone, some other, hard to reach country joins.
-Often times the game makes no sense. In one game, Britain somehow got 500 devisions, and 20,000 planes, and came to the rescue of who else, the Axis.
-Many mechanics are unbalanced or don't make sense.
-The game often feels half done.
-The AI are fuqin' reptards.
So, time for my opinion. I think these are mostly very valid complaints, my main issue is the expensive DLC. I can't 'ford dat. But I think that the answer to most of the games issue is piratingggg I mean Mods. If you think the game feels a bit repetitive, get a mod that adds some mechanics, or make one yourself. It's not as hard as you'd think. There are mods that fix the AI, make the game run smoother, add different scinarios you can play, like the Great War mod. I assume there are ones that add tech trees for all the countries, if not, tech trees are easy to mod, so I'll probs start working on that. The point is, the community has fixed many of the issues the developers left, which has created a great game, definitely worth the money.
Ps: Maybe wait till all the DLC's out, it will probs be the same price with all the DLC included, so you can save a bit.

On Salt and Sanctuary's presumably fan-run Wiki, its description page calls it a great way for Dark Souls fans to tide themselves over while they wait for Dark Souls 3 (it has not been updated since the release of that game.) That comes off as damning with faint praise, especially since Salt and Sanctuary is an excellent game.
But it is a lot like Dark Souls. You could go as far as to call it a fangame. It's a sucessful translation of Dark Souls' essential concept into 2D, which as it turns out resembles games like Symphony of the Night.
What this means in practical terms is that there's more of a platforming focus. The world has to be laid out on tiers of platforms, or else it would be reduced to a long straight line. In the later levels, it's easy to fall to your death, which can be kind of frustrating when combined with the high punishment for death. Perhaps to reduce that annoyance, the platforming itself is generally easy. It has some appeal as a way to add a degree of skill to the essential movement of the player character, but it's not the core mechanic.
That would be the combat. The enemies hit hard and all attacks inflict hit-stun, so that the player has to avoid attacks and counter while the enemy is winded. Attacking costs stamina and you have to rely heavily on a dodge roll to fight sucessfully. You have the option to parry attacks, which takes precise timing but allows a powerful counterattack when done sucessfully, and the bosses are intended to be difficult, with the expectation that they will take multiple attempts to beat. This all probably sound familar, once again, if you've played Dark Souls, and it's as good a combat system as ever.
There's just one problem: it's too easy. On my first playthrough, I beat a lot of the mid to late bosses on the first try, and many of the rest on the second. Exploring the map and fighting off the standard enemies was generally no more difficult, either. It's still not as easy as most modern games, but the low difficulty was a bit of a let-down for me, personally.
So what makes this game so much easier than Dark Souls. For one thing, with the switch to 2D, rolling behind bosses is too powerful - there are even some bosses whose every attack can be dodged by waiting for the windup, then rolling behind them. It's a bit sad when you figure that out. Most of the bosses - especially the later ones, for some reason - only have a small pool of attacks, so it's easier to memorize them all, and they don't become stronger, or not by enough, as they lose health. The multi-target bosses are especially weak. When one boss dies, the other never becomes stronger, so the fights actually become less difficult as they go on, and targeting down a particular enemy is a too-powerful, simple tactic.
In Dark Souls, health is tied to the Vitality stat. It's not related to any one stat in Salt and Sanctuary - I believe it scales with level. While this prevents tank builds apart from building willpower and wearing heavier armour, it also leaves the player free to invest heavily into damage stats while still gaining some durability. You can also gain more uses of your regenerating healing item through the skill tree, which makes it easy to gain too many of them early on, so that it's near impossible to run out, and you can get even more uses yet by increasing your devotion to your creed, something that can often be done with no real effort from the player - the necessary items will drop as you go through the game.
There are a few areas where the design feels slightly off. Certain areas or bosses are a lot more dangerous than others that appear at about the same time (if you've played the game, I bet you thought of the unicorns as you read that.) And the heavy knockback some enemies inflict can send you flying off a ledge and to your death, which is kind of cheap. Multi-hit magic attacks are universally overpowered and tend to lock you into multiple hits, always killing you from full health, and so bosses that use them are always more difficult, and the difficulty mainly comes from those particular attacks.
Now, since the continued comparisons to Dark Souls are hard to avoid, it should be mentioned that this game just doesn't match the openess or scale of that game. There aren't as many different weapons and fighting styles to use, the progression is a bit more linear, and it doesn't have the same depth to its lore - Dark Souls created an entire world and history, which it used to help define its theme of entropy.
Salt and Sanctuary has a much smaller, more contained story, about the island where it takes place with only very vague ill-defined hints of the world outside. To be fair, there's something to be said for the smaller-scale approach, especially for an indie project.
What I've said so far might make it seem odd that I called the game excellent, but by this point I've already brought up nearly every complaint I can think of. It does a lot of things well: the combat and exploration are a lot of fun, the art style is appealing (although perhaps a bit cute for the tone,) the atmosphere is effective and the monster designs are great - they have a real intimidation factor to them. The story does a good job creating a sense of mystery and of despair, and the eventual payoff and two endings are satisfying. I found it to be quite an absorbing game - I would play for hours longer than intended, because it had a constant sense of discovery and advancement. The branching, short-cut filled map really helps with that. Returning to low-level areas and annihilating the enemies creates the sense that you've grown throughout your adventure, and your character's increasing mobility adds to that too.
Another comparison that comes to mind is Axiom Verge. Both games are essentially derivitive, but they're so engaging and well made that I played them almost non-stop from beginning to end. That's not something that comes easy.

At the time when the series premiered in 2006, it would've been hard to believe that that Dead Rising would still be going strong over a decade later with its fourth installment. While the franchise gained a kickstart with witty photographer/journalist Frank West during the initial zombie outbreak in Willamette, Colorado, the second and third games made way for protagonists Chuck Greene and Nick Ramos respectively. Now, with Capcom heavily pushing the idea of going back to the series' roots, Frank West has made his return, and so has the town and infamous mall of Willamette.
The game takes place 16 years after the events of the first Dead Rising, and a mere year after the outbreak in Dead Rising 3; the year is now 2022, during early December, and Frank is now a 52 year old college professor. After being tricked into revisiting Willamette by one of his students, Vick, the duo soon discover that the town is being used by the military as a massive zombie research facility. The pair escape, only for Frank to be approached by a ZDC agent known as Brad Park, who then convinces Frank to return once more to Willamette to investigate a new zombie outbreak that began on Black Friday. Frank's incentive? To have his name cleared and also to gain exclusive rights to the entire story.
Dead Rising 4 is a game that you're either going to love or hate due to a plethora of contributing factors. Many purists are upset at the fact that Frank's voice actor has been changed, and many are unhappy about his new Bill Murray meets Michael De Santa character model. The dialogue is just as cheesy as it has ever been, and the seven chapter story isn't overly captivating, but it all gets the job done for a game that centers around mindless zombie slaughter. Another huge change is the removal of the 72 hour timer, which gets rid of unnecessary in-game stress and allows for an abundance of exploration leisure time. Capcom have also done away with all post-completion modes, as well as the highly favored co-op mode that was present in the last two titles.
Instead of campaign co-op, this title features a multiplayer mode that can be done either solo or with 3 other people. It has four distinct episodes, wherein you and your buddies must kill X amount of zombies and complete various, menial tasks. In order to unlock combo weapons you need to complete trials, and you also gain PP to level up and distribute skill points as you do in the main game. Honestly, it's a very mundane addition to the series, and most players would've rather had co-op once again. In the future, Capcom should note to sticking with their campaign for this series and not venture into the unneeded multiplayer world.
Along with the aforementioned changes, Capcom decided to nuke the well known Psychos from all of the previous titles. Long gone are the crazy, unique Psychos that we have even come to know and love by name, instead replaced with generic Maniacs that have no personality of their own. Even many of the bosses that are faced in Dead Rising 4 feel commonplace and they are without the eccentric personalities that made the series what it is today. Instead, we've been given "mutated" zombies, such as the fresh zombies which are faster than the normal ones, and evolved zombies that are even faster than the fresh ones. Around the town, you will also find various military personnel who have it out for you, with two special types being the EXO Suit military dudes and the flamethrower guys.
Returning with the new release are combo weapons and vehicles and their respective blueprints. While some old favorites, such as the sledgesaw, return, most of these craftables are new, including the introduction of element-based items such as the flame sword, ice sword, and various weapons and vehicles that shoot snowballs. Many of the new items are based on holiday festivity, such as a wreathe that shocks zombies, a grenade launcher that jingles bells while shooting ornaments, and my personal favorite... a nutcracker helmet that shoots bullets while playing the nutcracker theme. Needless to say, the weapons are both fun and inspired, although the vehicles are rather lackluster; save for the go carts and their combinations.
One of the innovations that Capcom has pushed with Dead Rising for is the new EXO Suit, which is basically mechanized armor that allows you to pick up heavier weapons like a giant axe, Gatling gun, and road signs, as well as find power-ups to transform the suit into an unstoppable zombie killing machine. The suit is just okay, and it's nothing to rave about, the biggest downside is that it just doesn't last long enough; in most non-story scenarios, the EXO Suit lasts for a couple of minutes at best after equipping it, and once its power depletes you also lose the upgrade that you found for it. Just like any other weapon in the game, it simply breaks and then ceases to exist at all until you find the next.
Willamette is no longer just limited to the mall, and now you have free reign of the entire town which is split up into four sections. There's plenty to do so long as you are interested in completing trials, collecting blueprints, and gathering collectibles like newspapers, iPods, and cellphones. There are also random events that occur, but there are only four types; save the survivor from the zombies, save the survivor from the military, loot the military cache, and destroy the military equipment. While these events give you a good amount of PP that will help you level up fast, to the cap of 100, the only ones that are really worth doing are the ones with survivors... so long as you haven't completely upgraded your four safe-houses yet. Yes, each section of Willamette has its own safe-house where you can purchase weapons, vehicles, clothing, and collectible location maps, and each are leveled up by saving a certain amount of survivors.
As far as optimization goes, this game has been running like a dream on my i7 6700k + GTX 1080 + 16GB DDR4 3000 RAM (full specs in my profile). With everything on ultra at 1080p, I found myself topping out at around 124 FPS, and seeing a low of 62 FPS, but having an overall average of 85-95 FPS at any given time. However, Capcom have still not ironed out the glitches in this title; more often than not, I found that Frank had lost his voice overs and I would need to exit to the main menu and then load my save to get his voice working again. Also, zombies love to get stuck in the walls and in other objects quite often, making them very hard to kill if they're required to die to say, save a survivor. It doesn't look like Capcom are going to be fixing these minor issues any time soon.
While it's hard to recommend Dead Rising 4, it's also just as difficult to not recommend it. On one hand the game does have a vast amount of content that one can easily sink 20-30 hours into and still not completely finish everything, but on the other hand it's missing some core elements that made the franchise in to what it is today. The removal of the timer is a wonderful change for those who like to do things at their own pace, but Capcom have shot themselves in the foot by getting rid of campaign co-op, as well as not taking the time to create noteworthy enemies. If you're still on the fence as to whether or not to purchase this game, take into account all of the changes that the developer has made and go from there, otherwise I highly recommend waiting for at least a 50% off sale. If you haven't played Dead Rising 3 yet, grab that instead.

Rift did quite well when it launched. It sold 2 million units and held a pay to play model of $15/month, competed well with WoW, kept updating content without releasing new games, and went free to play with microtransactions. I purchased into this games early launch beta and played for the first 3 months of it's launch.
Rift is a great MMO, encourages exploration and has many puzzle mini games that are quite fun and refreshing after you have been questing and/or closing rifts. The raiding/group system is much like wow with support roles having a magnified and essential role within the group. There are 20 man raids which consist of 4 groups of 5. The 5 man dungeons in Rift consist of a tank, healer, support which heals and does damage at the same time, and two dps classes. The talent trees are fun and innovative, there are 4 classes (mage, rogue, cleric, warrior) and each has 8 talent trees of which you can have 3 active at a time to build your character and dictate what spells and abilities it will have. You can buy many extra talent specs, I know of at least 5 specs being possible.
I play a rogue class and it has 1 tank spec, 1 support/heal spec, and 6 dps specs. There is an aoe spec, stealth assasin spec, ranged marksman spec, ranged hunter with animal pet spec, elemental dps spec, and a pvp spec that has high evasion. I can't speak much for the other classes but I know that the mage has 1 support/heal spec and 7 dps specs, summoner, spellcaster builds, etc. The Cleric has a couple tank specs, many heal specs, and pvp dps tank specs. The warrior has 3 tank specs and 5 dps specs. I don't know much about the other classes but that should be a good enough overview, pardon me if there are discrepencies
There is an intricate player housing system. You can work towards filling your 'dimension' as they are called with tons and tons of items. Items such as beds, chairs, bookshelves, etc. There are More than 200 from what I have seen. Some are purchased through reputation which you have to grind like WoW, some are bought through the microtransactions store, you can trade for things other players have bought, and you can find things in the open world as well as from Group and Raid rifts.
The warfront system is the PvP system in Rift and it is quite fun, there are multiple modes, capture the flag, control points for an amount of time, etc. Much like WoW again. I don't PvP much if at all, it's not what I like about MMOs.
This game had a lot going for it and still does, it has aged very well, still has an active community, and will run on most rigs. It was a strong competitor of WoW and still continues to provide content updates and a fresh take on the MMO genre. 10/10 would recommend.

Gameplay-  While it dosen't re-invent the genre, RIFT's tried and tested formula holds up amongst the ocean of MMO's out there. What you get that is different, is a streamlined, polished experience thoughout all its offerings, with extensive options in general PvE and leveling (with a fanstastic instant adventure feature), Standard MMO fare pvp, and enjoyable crafting and Hobbies ( RIFT has a suprisingly addictive fishing aspect to it)
9/10
UI's/Menus - RIFT has a sleek UI, But once again dosen't break the mould. Standard MMO fare here.
8/10
Content - There's plenty to see and do on your way to the level cap, with the Storm Legion expansion adding twice the content of the original game, just for journey from level 50 to 60.
You also have an absurd amount of collectables to obtain on your journey, with a lot of artifacts that you simply find in your travels worth a fortune on the AH.
When wanting a break from leveling you have PvP, Closing the games signature RIFT's,  Crafting , Artifact Hunting, Achivement hunting and Exploring, and maybe RIFT's best feature, the incredible Dimensions (RIFT's Housing).
Dimensions add this amazing element not generally seen in mmo's since SWG. I could write for pages, jump in and experience them for yourself, and the amazing community built dimensions with waterslides, puzzles and bars!.
10/10

Personally, This game is beyond worth the subscription. The developers deserve the sub fee, and the Benifits you get from it are worth it. You get the equivelant of 8 hours a day of 200% XP, Currency , and Noriety Gain (if you want) as well as a daily and weekly Gift, which often include hard to gain Artifacts, Potions, and vaulable Currency.
On the F2P side the game does feature a robust in game money shop, with decent prices for unlocks. I've never been a massive F2Player and I honestly dont understand why people complain when they don't wanna pay a sub fee but expect the whole game free.

On Salt and Sanctuary's presumably fan-run Wiki, its description page calls it a great way for Dark Souls fans to tide themselves over while they wait for Dark Souls 3 (it has not been updated since the release of that game.) That comes off as damning with faint praise, especially since Salt and Sanctuary is an excellent game.
But it is a lot like Dark Souls. You could go as far as to call it a fangame. It's a sucessful translation of Dark Souls' essential concept into 2D, which as it turns out resembles games like Symphony of the Night.
What this means in practical terms is that there's more of a platforming focus. The world has to be laid out on tiers of platforms, or else it would be reduced to a long straight line. In the later levels, it's easy to fall to your death, which can be kind of frustrating when combined with the high punishment for death. Perhaps to reduce that annoyance, the platforming itself is generally easy. It has some appeal as a way to add a degree of skill to the essential movement of the player character, but it's not the core mechanic.
That would be the combat. The enemies hit hard and all attacks inflict hit-stun, so that the player has to avoid attacks and counter while the enemy is winded. Attacking costs stamina and you have to rely heavily on a dodge roll to fight sucessfully. You have the option to parry attacks, which takes precise timing but allows a powerful counterattack when done sucessfully, and the bosses are intended to be difficult, with the expectation that they will take multiple attempts to beat. This all probably sound familar, once again, if you've played Dark Souls, and it's as good a combat system as ever.
There's just one problem: it's too easy. On my first playthrough, I beat a lot of the mid to late bosses on the first try, and many of the rest on the second. Exploring the map and fighting off the standard enemies was generally no more difficult, either. It's still not as easy as most modern games, but the low difficulty was a bit of a let-down for me, personally.
So what makes this game so much easier than Dark Souls. For one thing, with the switch to 2D, rolling behind bosses is too powerful - there are even some bosses whose every attack can be dodged by waiting for the windup, then rolling behind them. It's a bit sad when you figure that out. Most of the bosses - especially the later ones, for some reason - only have a small pool of attacks, so it's easier to memorize them all, and they don't become stronger, or not by enough, as they lose health. The multi-target bosses are especially weak. When one boss dies, the other never becomes stronger, so the fights actually become less difficult as they go on, and targeting down a particular enemy is a too-powerful, simple tactic.
In Dark Souls, health is tied to the Vitality stat. It's not related to any one stat in Salt and Sanctuary - I believe it scales with level. While this prevents tank builds apart from building willpower and wearing heavier armour, it also leaves the player free to invest heavily into damage stats while still gaining some durability. You can also gain more uses of your regenerating healing item through the skill tree, which makes it easy to gain too many of them early on, so that it's near impossible to run out, and you can get even more uses yet by increasing your devotion to your creed, something that can often be done with no real effort from the player - the necessary items will drop as you go through the game.
There are a few areas where the design feels slightly off. Certain areas or bosses are a lot more dangerous than others that appear at about the same time (if you've played the game, I bet you thought of the unicorns as you read that.) And the heavy knockback some enemies inflict can send you flying off a ledge and to your death, which is kind of cheap. Multi-hit magic attacks are universally overpowered and tend to lock you into multiple hits, always killing you from full health, and so bosses that use them are always more difficult, and the difficulty mainly comes from those particular attacks.
Now, since the continued comparisons to Dark Souls are hard to avoid, it should be mentioned that this game just doesn't match the openess or scale of that game. There aren't as many different weapons and fighting styles to use, the progression is a bit more linear, and it doesn't have the same depth to its lore - Dark Souls created an entire world and history, which it used to help define its theme of entropy.
Salt and Sanctuary has a much smaller, more contained story, about the island where it takes place with only very vague ill-defined hints of the world outside. To be fair, there's something to be said for the smaller-scale approach, especially for an indie project.
What I've said so far might make it seem odd that I called the game excellent, but by this point I've already brought up nearly every complaint I can think of. It does a lot of things well: the combat and exploration are a lot of fun, the art style is appealing (although perhaps a bit cute for the tone,) the atmosphere is effective and the monster designs are great - they have a real intimidation factor to them. The story does a good job creating a sense of mystery and of despair, and the eventual payoff and two endings are satisfying. I found it to be quite an absorbing game - I would play for hours longer than intended, because it had a constant sense of discovery and advancement. The branching, short-cut filled map really helps with that. Returning to low-level areas and annihilating the enemies creates the sense that you've grown throughout your adventure, and your character's increasing mobility adds to that too.

An impressive entry in the first person stealth genre.  A detailed combat system, combined with stealth mechanics, in immersive and well-designed areas, in a gaslamp tech setting.  The game is enjoyable from start to finish and has enough in it to amuse you for whatever playing style you decide to adopt or change to.
The gameplay is a first person stealth game along the lines of thief mixed with a bit of system shock and deus ex.  The stealth gameplay is augmented with a first person melee combat system which is in turn augmented with bombs, guns, crossbows, traps, and magic powers.  It takes a note from bioshock and deus ex for the ability to improve your gear and magic abilities.  The gameplay flushes together smoothly especially in the areas designed to sneak, stealth, and do hit and run attacks in.  Or, you can just say screw it and stab everyone.  The only complaint I have is the amount of abilities you have can leave you confused because there are so many different ways to handle any situation, but it does make for interesting replays.
The areas are tightly designed, and well thought out.  They are immersive with the setting and make you believe people have lived in these places at some point.  There are lots of bolt holes to hide in, places to hide corpses, areas to sneak around, and shadows to jump out of to stab people in the throat.  Understanding the terrain and where you can go becomes as important to the encounters as your abilities and skill at playing.  More than that the areas are designed to expand the story and express the setting in ways words can not describe.  Many people when they talk about how much the love Dunwall, comes from walking around it's streets, alleys, sewers, and run-down apartments listening to ambient dialogue and watching their prey.
The story and setting is unique and I haven't found it anywhere else in books or television.  It's a gaslamp setting on some islands modeled after US-New England/UK-Doverish? where technology is powered by whale oil.  Whales contain some manner of mystical power in their bodies sought after by witches and those following this transendient being called the outsider.  The protagonist becomes one of the outsider's chosen and goes on a quest of revenge which may be as bloody as you decide.
The only story complaint I have is with the chaos/order system they have in it - killing people and leaving corpses causes more guards, weepers, and rats in later levels of the game.  They created an amazing combat system and punish the player for using it too much by denying them the "good" ending.  Incidentally, if you stealth and go for order you can still leave bodies behind and kill some people as long as you don't go too crazy - that may be something some players don't realize.
In all this was a surprising entry and a very good game which can be enjoyed by a very wide audience.

The sound design is good, the visuals are great with it's cel-shaded graphics and overall colorful world.
