An excellent game with progressive pacing, hunkered down somewhat from the Always Online DRM that will often refuse you access to it.
Certainly, a blissful experience and overall improvement from the original. Ezio is a more charismatic character than any other in the series, and if you were ever curious as to what glory Ubisoft seeks to return to in the series, this is it.
The game has excellent orchestration and electronic compositions from Jesper Kyd, who left the series right when it was going downhill (a la Hitman).
Replayability of the main missions are limited, since they are presented in the order they are recieved and cannot be re-done once completed. However, the game sends enough variety your way that you are glad it's not a game of kill-this, steal that.
A few misgivings of the game are its muffled pedestrian dialogue (just like the first game, only less compressed) and the occasional stiff parameters the game sends your way, challenging your skill as you attempt to complete them or risk failure (desynchronization).
It is no Brotherhood, but if this game is cheaper on a Steam sale or you just want to play them all, choose this one first. You will find the narrative bridging the two games incredibly rewarding.

It's been a great many years since I've played this game. Much like Pajama Sam and Star Wars, I was very much obsessed with the Assassin's Creed franchise. Don't worry. I haven't turned into a murderous psychopath. Not yet at least.
I played most of the Assassin's Creed games multiple times, but I haven't touched II since I first played it. I remember hating it purely for the graphics back in the day, but I'm happy to report that my taste in games has matured. Now let's REALLY find out what I didn't like about this game!
To be honest, not a whole lot. Assassin's Creed II is well-justified in being called the best game in the franchise by fans and critics alike. And I mean that as sincerely as I can. It's a pretty enjoyable game.
The story continues right off of the first Assassin's Creed (which I might go back and play a third time for sh**s and giggles soon), wherein you play as Desmond Miles as he accesses memories now of Italian ancestor from Renaissance: Ezio Auditore da Firenze. Desmond's story is nearly inexistent, but where the real juice of the the story comes from is found in Ezio.
See, Ezio isn't a stone-faced brooding Batman-wannabe like Altair and Connor Kenway were. He was presented like an young man who was thrown into unfortunate circumstances and had to dawn the cowl of the Assassin in order to fulfill his quest for revenge. Ezio is very charismatic and likeable, and you genuinely want to see him follow through with his revenge and become a Master Assassin. A lot of the other characters are pretty forgettable, but the game has so much charm and enough little jokes here and there that I felt entertained throughout the whole experience.
Besides the other characters, I did get a little irritated with how one-dimensional the villains were. The only one that really got my interest was the bodyguard, Dante, and he's barely used in the whole game! I felt a bit of rivalry between Ezio and Uberto as well as Vieri, but a lot of the other targest you hunt down are pretty bland. And, of course, the ending with the final target is a bit anti-climactic. But the big reveal afterwards was enough to grab my interest like it had years ago. It's pretty well-implemented, unexpected, and effective in shocking the player at the end of the game.
You play as Ezio throughout five sandboxes across Italy: Florence, Tuscany, Forli, Monteriggioni, and Venice. I like that there's a lot of variety in the locations you visit, so the game doesn't become monotonous. When you travel across the country, it really feels like your traveling to brand new locations each completely different from the other places you've visited. However, there are plenty of loading screens whenever you want to travel and animations that mainly pestered me whenever I wanted to take care of some mundane, but it wasn't enough to completely frustrate me.
The worlds, while well-designed, are a bit under-utilized. There's A LOT of stuff you can do, but I never felt that motivated to run around and collect little useless sh** thrown randomly across the city or complete mundane taks that are pretty much identical to all the other ones you've completed.
In line with the theme of repetition, is the combat. I'm not a fan. You can't break an enemy's defese very easily but you can do the best damage through a counter... which means you have to wait for your opponent to attack you first... which means you'll be doing a lot of waiting in fights. And it's not like fighting is that difficult. Just tap the counter button. That's it.
You know? That's probably the biggest flaw with Assassin's Creed II. It's too damn easy. This game was like scraping my knees on pavement when I first played it, but I think I've become a better gamer since then. At least, I'd like to think I have. And so many missions were so simple to figure out and finish in one try that I rushed through the majority of the game in about 15 hours (the other 5 hours was from all the running around in the cities I did).
BUT since you're thinking about buying this copy of Assassin's Creed II, you're getting the Deluxe Edition! Woo! Mysterious! What does it mean?
You get a couple hour-long memory sequences. Have fun.
Okay, they're not that bad honestly. Originally, the game clipped them out as the penultimate chapters of the story and sold them as DLC, but since I played the Deluxe Edition it just skipped right to the DLC missions. I'm not a fan of removing story content for the purpose of making money but if you don't play these DLC packs you're not missing much. I'll give you a summary of both of them: Ezio loses the Apple. Then he gets the Apple back. It's not that inspired, obviously.
While the Battle of Forli finally utilized Forli which you only were in for one f***ing mssion in the base game, you have a whole storyline behind Caterina Sforza (who, again, was only in that one out-of-place mission in the original game). A couple twin brothers kidnap her kids, and you have the save them to win the Battle of Forli. It just gives some excuse to pad out the story and add some open combat, which isn't the worst thing ever. I liked Caterina as a character, but the story itself wasn't that compelling.
The Bonfire of the Vanities was my favorite chapter of the two. You need to get the Apple back from Savonarola, and to do so you have to assassinate his nine lieutenants across Florence, each with a different twist in how you go about assassinating them. I think Savonarola was a very compelling villain, who was prodded to do what he did because he honestly believe he was doing the right thing by spreading his faith in God to the masses. That and the missions are short enough to justify running around Florence one last time. It was pretty good.
Assassin's Creed II isn't the best thing ever. It certainly hasn't aged well in its presentation. Cutscenes look pretty wonky. The characters, when up close, look like the characters from GTA IV. They look all shiny and fake, but their body and facial animations are actually really well-done. If you want this game to look better, either buy the Ezio Collection like the dirty console peasant you are, or just download some graphical mods. It's not terrible. The game hasn't aged that well.
That being said, the atmosphere of the cities you explore are wonderful. Even though the graphics aren't that great up-close, they look marvelous when you're running around 1400's Italy, and listening to the chatter of passing pedestrians, hearing the howls of the local herald, and listening to the gorgeous soundtrack by Jesper Kyd. It's not the best soundtrack ever, but the main theme of this game and the ambient songs in Venice are some fantastic songs he wrote. This game still looks decent, but it sounds even better.
Like I said, Assassin's Creed II is pretty damn good upon my second playthrough. I don't think if I ever reinstall this game, that I'll go around and do all asinine side-mission B.S. but I'm certainly inclined to play through the story again. It's a decent game, despite its flaws and one of the best games in the Assassin's Creed franchise. I'm giving Assassin's Creed II a 7/10.

This is by far one of my favorite Assassin's Creed games. I've followed the series from the beginning... playing as Altair was fun, but Ezio just has so much more depth to his charecter, not to mention style. That moment you get the second hidden blade is just satisfying. Then ezio gains a hidden pistol, which was also fun. I've played through this game several times... IDK, maybe I am partial due to my nostalgia and overall love for the Ezio games.
The game is not perfect though. As with most AC games, thee main charecter, Ezio in this case, does not always do what you want him to. Trying to climb boxes in front of you sometimes leads to running up the adjacent wall, or just jumping over boxes atogether. Most of the time this problem is negligable, except during the most frustrating aspect of this game: timed puzzles. Specifically, a good number of Assassin's Tombs. Many of the tombs have timed areas and if Ezio jumps in the water or at the wall instead of jumping to that beam... welll, you have to start over. If you don't care about getting 100% or getting Altair's armor, then skip these puzzles. Honestly, you can beat the game easily without upgrading your health much. The only reason I fully upgrade Ezio's heath is so that if Ezio decides to jump off a tall building without my permission, he will live.

Alright. OneShot is one of those games that's very, very heavily story-driven, so do yourself and don't be spoiled. Seriously. Going in blind is a magical experience.
Now. With that disclaimer out of the way. OneShot is one of those games that makes you care dearly for the main character- not because of what they're trying to do, necessarily, or even because they're your avatar in the world.  Ultimately, you end up wanting Niko to succeed because of their innocence and kindness. The game doesn't hit you over the head with moral judgement, instead gently laying choices in front of the player so that they can try to make the right decisions.
The soundtrack is as haunting and melancholy as the art and story, a hopeless premise shrouded in dark blues, greens, and reds.
OneShot's gameplay revolves around puzzle-solving and exploration, with Maniac Mansion-style item searches being integral to the game's progression (though by no means is it the only thing the player will have to do). Its puzzles are novel in the extreme, with many hints coming from within the computer's file structure rather than within the game itself.
I can't really say much more in favor of the game without spoiling some part of the storyline, so I'll just say this: it's good. Very good. One of the very few games to ever make me cry.

I've read a ton of reviews for this game, and the themes that keep popping up are that this is a Metroidvaniasouls game, and that it represents what it truly means to be a Souls-like.  Both of these things are one hundred percent accurate.  This game has some bugs, and some really crappy features, and it is in no way perfect.  Just like Dark Souls wasn't perfect.  It has flaws, and some of them are frustrating, but at the end of the day it hits all the right checks in all the right places, and it's just a great game that will challenge you, bash your casual little skull in, make you quit and run crying back to your mommy, then (after a calming glass of milk and homebaked cookies), come back harder and more determined. Just like the Soulsborne series, it will this until you finally overcome whatever obstacle you were struggling with, and leave you with a fantastic sense of accomplishment.
In short, if you like Dark Souls, and grew up on Super Metroid or Castlevania Symphony of the Night, this game is worth more than the $17.99 they're asking.  It's better than 90% of AAA $60 games that release.

It's the real deal. Like Dark Souls though, it can be frustrating for awhile until you "get it". But eventually you start to figure out all the systems within the game, level up a bit, figure out what kind of weapons you like, upgrades (+transmute), get better at and appreciate the combat (some enemies you have to block, some roll through, some parry, some swap in elemental protection for, etc.), useful consumables and so on. Cool bosses, varied and interesting areas, art, etc. All around great.

Hitboxes are often different size than the actual characters in game, this can be really frustrating sometimes.
The weapons aren't balanced at all, i still regret my choice for my first run of the game.
Combat using a shield is waste of time, it is easy to obtain a shield that negates 100% of the damage as long as you hold the shield up, making it a toggleable godmode, there is even a shield later in the game that reflects physical damage, making it possible to win some bossfights just by standing still and holding the shield up.
I'd recommend to not use shields, as "hold a button to win" is not fun gameplay mechanic.
I'd also recommend to avoid whips, they don't have any different attacks, just the standard whip strike, making them a boring weapon. if you want to use whips, i'd recommend getting a sword-whip, since they combine the moves of swords and the whip.
While the game has "New Game+", there isn't any real effort put to it, the stats of all enemies have just been buffed.
It feels like the developers didn't playtest the new game+, since the stat scaling is bad. some bosses get insanely hard in ng+ modes, and some don't feel any harder than they did in the first run.
Multiplayer is not well designed. The Player 2 has penalties, such as being unable to level up your creed, and having no access to some important items. I don't know why they decided to put such penalties for Player 2, but i think this was a horrible idea. Still, the game is really fun in split screen, just remember to have the better player be the number 2.

I described this game to a friend as Advanced Hide & Seek combined with Hardmode Dungeons in an MMO (except, of course, the boss is not AI, but a real human bean). I think that was a pretty good comparison, but I'm not one to toot my own horn.
As a team of 4, hunt down and kill The Monster before he becomes too powerful. As The Monster, avoid the Hunters, devour local wildlife, Evolve into a more powerful form. Evolve is a meticulously crafted Asymmetrical competitive multiplayer experience.
There are a lot of characters to unlock, both as Hunter and as a Monster, all with their own purpose in battle. Silver is earned at a good click, and so far there's no monetization options, but since you unlock characters and there's quite a bit of characters... well, I can hazard a guess.
Along with characters, you also unlock Perks for Hunter and Monsters. You can have up to three Perks equipped at once and they all boost your stats in different ways. Health, Damage, or Mobility. The perk system is a good idea, but I feel that at least in the early stages of the game balance can be nonexistent due to people not having all perk slots full, thus not being at their full potential even if they're great players. That kinda sucks. Overall, however, more customization can only be good.
Its unlock system could use a bit more work, it's not very well explained how perks are unlocked (I ain't buying them but they're unlocking anyhow) and pricing seems somewhat inconsistent.
The game did disappoint me at first. It's fun, but it's not at all a horror experience. It's not scary. It's stressful, it's exciting, but it's not scary. And, well, I'm fighting (or playing as) an enemy labeled by the game and its player characters as "THE MONSTER". It should scare me, at least as far as my reasoning goes. It's especially disappointing because the game sets up this in-depth world with lore and great visuals and a creepy atmosphere, but it all seems wasted on a game that's more about being a good raid leader than a good hunter. Because, save for players using Wraith, you will find the monster, and it's more about the fight against bullet sponges with telegraped mechanics than a hunt for the mythical beasts.
Despite all that, I still greatly enjoy the game, and damnit it's free and has a playerbase again so I can't really complain about either of those things. Just don't go in expecting an atmospheric experience. It's a competitive game through and through, and if you like those, you'll like this.

Don't be daunted.
Those were three words I used to two friends who were considering playing Hearts of Iron 4.
It looks like a bunch of reading and dull mathematics, but once you open the game, and pick your country to play as (which I must mention can be any in the world) - that country is yours. And there's work to do.
Do you play as Nazi Germany, and fulfill Hitler's quest for world domination, or do you play as Nazi Germany and turn it Communist? Or Democratic? It's all possible in this game. The ultimate "What if" scenario creator, and it's at your fingertips on a global scale.
I won't pretend that this game doesn't need some serious time, but damn is it worth it. Even the stock game, you can easily waste hours ensuring your economy is perfect, researching teschnology of the time, and "national focuses" - which can either be historically accurate or a new direction you want to go with your little piece of land in the world.
Hearts of Iron can be as complicated or as simple as you want it to be. The HUGE community for modding the game transform the game in ways you can't imagine, so regardless of whether or not you're the "strategy" type of gamer, Hearts of Iron has something to offer; and it may actually drag you into the bottomless pit of "What if?"

A very linear and narrow corridor shooter that tries to be a CoD with a sniper theme.
The environments look fairly oldschool and low polygon in places with not all that much detail. You will see the limited amount of assets and props being reused a lot on the maps. Overall the environment looks immersive enough, but it's not quite AAA.
As for the gameplay, it is faily entrtaining, but in a very shallow and arcade way. The game is unchallenging and to easy (hand holding). The only difficulty is the unbalanced mission design at some places.
The game consists of a lot of walking over triggers that activates some action/event, if you stop 1 meter before the trigger spot nothing will happen. So replay value of the campaign is zero, it will be exactly the same the 2nd playthrough with the same triggered events.
'Sniper Elite' has done the whole sniper immersion a lot better without the narrow claustrophobic gameplay.
The low FOV is also a bit of an eye sore, but that can be edited in a game file.
All in all , the game is good and entertaining enough for a playthrough, but overall it's mediocre at best.

For a game that aims to be a sniper simulator it really doesn't place much emphasis on the importance of patience and hitting every shot. While having to consider bullet drop and wind direction/speed does make the experience more "realistic", the assists make it so that you do not truly have to consider these things. While you can turn off the assist and play on a harder difficulty, figuring out where you to aim with heavy winds or across a long distance is not explained to you, so you'll have to figure it out through trial and error.
Furthermore, the AI in this game is terrible. They have extremely limited lines of sight, they tend to not react if you miss a shot, and somehow fail to hear the sound of a 50. calibre sniper dropping their friends stood yards away. Of course, I accept that 100% realism in a game like this would be no fun and would consist of sitting in a bush for hours on ends avoiding rather than dropping targets. But this game cleary sets out to be a somewhat realistic sniper game, and it fails to deliver this.
In addition, for a game released in 2013 the graphics are poor. While the guns look good, the environment and characters look very dated. However, I will admit that this game can be somewhat fun. If you're bored and looking for a cheap, arcade like sniper game. Then I would say to pick this up. But if you want something a little more realistic, with more varied gameplay (something other than a sniper) that's visually pleasing, you'll want to look elsewhere.

Wow wow wow. Dishonored has been sitting in my queue for the longest and I totally regret that happened. This game was unbelievable. You play a former bodyguard turned assassin who is attempting to clear his name. I won't go into too much more detail but you will be crossed, double crossed and fed red herrings along the way. The story and the way it's presented is a lot of fun. Also unique is there are different endings depending on your play style. Keep the killing to a minimum and you'll get the "happy" ending. Kill a lot of people and you'll get the not so happy ending. I went with low kills but it was a lot of fun sneaking up on guys and choking them out. In many ways, this a spiritual sucessor to Thief 2. The sneaking & the looting remind me of that game moreso than Thief 3 did (and Thief 4 from what I understand). Level design is excellent with a myriad of ways to get through them. But SAVE YOUR GAME OFTEN. I can't stress this enough because there are times you'll get past a situation and you'll mis click or the blink runs just short of where you want to go and you're surrounded. Another piece of advice. The two story DLCs are completely worth it. I'd argue "The Brigmore Witches" DLC has the best level design in this game period and is one of the best story DLCs I've ever played. Dishonored gets an easy 10/10 from me and I'll be interested to see how Dishonored 2 compares.

CAUTION:: Mild Spoilers for Original Bioshock game (It makes sense ok)
This game is definitely in my top 10 favourite games of all time, possibly top 3.
Bioshock is my ultimate favourite, BUT Dishonored does a  lot of things better.
When Bioshock came out, everyone was raving (in a good way) about the elements of choice present in the game-- which basically boiled down to "harvest or save the little sisters" -- which only affected a few small elements of the game plus the final ending cutscene. I didn't think that kind of "choice" was anything to write home about, especially when there were clear advantages to one method over the other.
Dishonored does NOT do that. Now, if you decide to go around killing everyone, it doesn't pull punches and all your friends will tell you how much of a terrible person you are in the end-- but you do have that option, and it is a satisfying option, and it does change elements of the game as the story progresses. BUT-- you can also go through the whole game and kill NOBODY. NOT A SOUL. There's an achievement for it, actually. It's difficult-- but rewarding also.
THIS game is the epitome of a game with choice elements, but linear story IMO.
Also, I like stealth games the best when I have cool magic powers.
A lot of the things that place games in my top favourite lists are well-constructed, immersive worlds and settings. Dishonored has this in spades with Dunwall. So many interesting cultural things and I go through the game and I'm just astounded at the detail the developers put into this-- and also how cohesive it is! The Bioshock series does the same thing-- as does the Elder Scrolls series. And Fallout series. and The Witcher series. All really solid. lol. and IMO this game ranks right up there with them. And the DLC is really solid, too. (Especially the Daud DLCs)
If you preorder Dishonored 2 (releases pretty soon), you should get a free copy of Dishonored GOTY edition. But yeah, like I said, it's coming out REALLY soon. But if you do snag it, you will NOT be disappointed.

I bought this game at full price for the ps4. I loved the game, but due to a lack of friends on the ps4 and a dwindling player base, I eventually stopped playing. Now that the game is f2p on steam, I can finally play with all of my friends and rip monsters apart. Sure, I didn't get all of the unlocks from when I was on ps4, but to complain about a dead game becoming f2p is like complaining about lazarus reviving a dead support; both are ultimately for a better experience, but not everyone can be pleased. It's a lot like that doomed trapper 75 meters opposite of the downed support (who is being revivified) or the founders who felt they got robbed after the f2p update.
*The monsters probably need a few changes to balance things out, but they aren't gods. Teamwork is key to kill good monsters right now (something a ton of players lack).
*premade groups can be disconnected from each other while looking for a match due to a bug.
*you can't buy perks outside of the hero selection screen.
*It can take some time before players start to understand the necessary intricacies of the characters, maps, and perks, so don't feel bad if your win/loss ratio doesn't look great for your first 5-10 hours. I myself just got to around 50/50 on my win/loss ratio after 9 hours.
*Hunters play as a team so defeats feel far worse than when one's a monster. The hunter's payoff is a very euphoric victory.
*There are currently, as of July 11th, 2016, only 4 maps. This is because they had to rework their maps for the gameplay changes they've made.
*"story" mode is no longer implemented. I assume it's for the sames reasons as the note above.
*due to it's many changes in gameplay, many matches are exhilarating and can be perceived as fun. (It's about the journey and not the outcome)

One of the greatest games I have played; it's so meta that a fourth wall doesn't even exist - and this is made very clear early on, as the game extends its influence far beyond the game itself. It influences your computer, it influences your mind, it influences the essence of the soul.
OneShot is also incredibly atmospheric. The visuals and the soundtrack (which are both amazing by themselves) blend together amazingly, to create an amazing atmosphere of pure serenity.
The characters are designed creatively and are pretty likeable, especially Niko.
Oh, and by the way, without spoiling anything, when you think the game is over - let me just tell you that it isn't.

The sequel to the original Typing of the Dead, TotD: Overkill is a batshit crazy typing tutor wrapped in deliberately terrible voice acting and grindhouse cinema tropes. Words pop up on screen, you type them out, and completing sentences kills zombies. Things are mixed up a bit with boss fights, minigames, flying cutlery, and an internal dictionary that is beyond deranged. Add to that they throw in regular House of the Dead: Overkill for free (essentially the same game, swapping typing for clicking and shooting) and a host of difficulty settings and modes makes it well worth the £14.99 price tag.

Let's shoot the elephant in the room first, guys.  In terms of language, premise, and treatment of female characters - this game is a full 31 different flavors of wrong.  It puts the over the top grindhouse aesthetic into an Indy Jones minecart and sends it careening down the tracks at breakneck speed to burst through a wall already starting to explode with 5 tons of C4. That's how flat out wrong it is.   Consider yourself duly warned if you're unfamiliar with Overkill from the real world setting.
That said : I'm a fan of the Typing of the Dead treatments of the House of the Dead games.  I bought this largely on the strength of the first 'Typing of the Dead' experience, which was good silly zombie killing fun.  I'm a fairly accurate typist, so it was fun diversion and I was glad to see more of the same available on Steam.
So do we have zombies to kill? Check.
Do we have absurd and fun things to type to kill the zombies? Check.
Are there lots of them? Check. There are indeed. Several container ship's worth of zombies to kill.  All kinds of check.
Entertaining boss battles?    Semi-check.  So-so. The original "Typing of the Dead''s boss fights took the absurdist typing up a few notches, giving you full sentences to type to inflict damage.  Overkill's boss battles are largely more standard zombie kill words with a fancy setpiece. So that was a little disappointing.  I will say this, though - the boss mechanic does get changed up entertainingly for the final conflict. That one I enjoyed.
Do we see our protagonists running around with comedy keyboards to type on hanging from their necks?  Sadly - no, we do not.
Do we have the option to use the mouse as a targeting reticule?  Well, yes. But I have fully no clue why you'd want to when the word 'Typing' is in the title...
At the end of the day, your enjoyment of Overkill will likely hinge on two things : Can you enjoy a game where typing accuracy is a game feature, and can you get past the content issues noted above?
Ultimately I found the game was enjoyable enough.  I rolled my eyes at more than a few things, though, and this isn't a game I'd break out for a mixed company party. I even laughed at some of it.
I just wasn't always very proud of that.

To be honest, I wouldn't even know HOW to describe my thoughts about the game. At first, all you could think about when playing for the first time is 'it's just a game, nothing special'. But after I played the solstice-chapter, I...I-I...
How do I say this? I found like... Like I would take the courage to imagine this to be something that really happened! Like this story is real and I'm the person Niko's talking to. But, when you finish playing, you come back to reality and find that it's just a game made by an ordinary person. Just... Fake... No, not fake, Simulated.
The aspect of that you have to go and actually search through the files of your own, REAL computer to be able to play is amazing! You have to restart the game everytime Niko goes to sleep and so you can continue to play. I even thought about sleeping myself during this pause 'cause, when you start the game back up, you'll start right at the moment she experiences a dream!
I even dreamt about Niko once... That I was travelling through an empty void to find a strange, nice world and... That it's Niko's world! That she was actually real! That it was all real! But then... I woke up and found myself with bloodshot eyes from crying... I actually cried in my SLEEP because I knew it couldn't be real... That I couldn't see her again...
This game is something to only play once. To only play to see the ending and then keep it there as a reminder. I sometimes think about restarting and actually allowing the World Machine to create the 'copy' of Niko, but then I realise... That's not the same. It'll never be the same again. I'll... I-I'll never see... Her again.... #sniff#
To be honest, this review is writen whilst I'm emotional. Who wouldn't? Who wouldn't cry about this? If someone who's reading says he/she didn't then pall, you've got no soul! 'Cause I've cried about this and I don't cry that quickly! I've gone through funerals, through bullying, though the worst days anyone can have and I've only cried once! ONCE!! So if a game can get me crying, then... You know what I mean, don't you all? Please don't hate me through this. I've just finished exams and I've had a though time and this game was something I wanted to try out. It adds new dimensions to the gameplay and is just something you should try yourself. It makes a lot of sense why they call this game a 2D Dark Souls. That's almost exactly what it is. Despite this, it does have quite a few unique elements to it to make it original. I have seen many people complain that there is no proper map in this game, but after playing through it, I do not really understand why you would need one. There is a fast travel system in the game and that pretty much eliminates the need for a map. The game also isn't really a platformer, although it has many platforming elements. The art design is very cool and varied. The leveling system follows a sort of branching path, which allows you to use higher tier weapons and armor. There are tons of shortcuts in the game, but just like in Dark Souls 2, there never felt any need for them, due to the ability to fast travel. At least it gave you a sense of real interconnectedness in the game. If you like Dark Souls, or action RPG's in general, you will almost surely like this game.

I wanted so badly to LOVE this game...but I barely LIKE it. You see, in the transition to 2D, a souls-esque clone must get a lot of things right but it's hard to do so. The movement must feel snappy and responsive to counter-balance the limited space one has in two dimensions; every death must feel like it was your fault (yours alone); and platforming must be solid. Now, I get it - this game is going for a "metroidvania" style and while I typically love those types of games, a lot here feels cheap. It borrows heavily from Dark Souls 1 in the essence that there is no hub, no teleportation...just shortcuts. I feel like this works much better in a 3D space whereby it is a lot easier to navigate due to your brain orienting itself a bit better - in this game, I constantly felt lost. I died so many times to some unfair mechanics (need to reach an enemy archer that's firing one arrow a second whilst platforming on tiny ledges which, if you fall, you die? Well that little arrow knocks you back midair and you're dead). i gues it's just the platforming that got to me - which I found the most unfair. I have been playing Dead Cells recently and it feels like a tighter, much better dive into the genre in the 2D space.

Dungetris is a rather interesting take on the roguelite rpg games. Dungetris insures that the game is different everytime you play it as YOU are the one who builds the levels based on random tetris pieces.
These pieces form the level, include monsters, chests, crates, buffs, cards, stores, and more. You have to becareful how you create the level as you can box yourself in, surround yourself in horrifying monsters, and seal off the good parts of the levels loot with a few misplaced blocks.
Initially Dungetris looks like a cheap mobile game but once you spend a bit of time with it the game really grows on you and the complexity and depth shines.
For a more in depth review check out my first impressions video below.

Great concept, executed fairly well (in early access).  The controls are a little wonky, but with an xbox360 gamepad & Controller Companion and a few tweaks (left-stick = WSAD, right-stick = mouse, RT = right-mouse, X=space, RB=c) I was able to play reasonably well and had fun.  The dev said in discussions he plans full controller support, but it is more than serviceable for now (with Controller Companion anyway).
The game itself is quite fun.  Create the dungeon as you go, fight enemies (just click on them when next to them), and die if your health runs out.  But you keep a lot of power ups between deaths & levels, so you don't lose everything to start over from scratch.
This is a game that lives up to expectations somewhat, and with better controls will probably get a lot better. (3/5 stars as-is at first, 4/5 stars if forgiving controls in early access).
UPDATE: Now I am used to playing with the gamepad (mapped via Controller Companion), and I really love the game.  I like that it isn't overly difficult, and you can take your time, and it matters how you build the dungeon and when to trigger enemies.  I keep looking forward to playing again :).

Dead Rising 1 was a game with a lot of fairly simple appeals. The core concept was essentially building a game out of the shopping spree scene from the 1978 Dawn of the Dead, giving you the feeling of being in a store after-hours and messing with things you aren't supposed to, turning ordinary objects into fun toys in a way that anyone who's been in a 24 hour department store toy section at night with friends knows with the inherent humor of grabbing a giant teddy bear and bashing someone with it. The time limit added a sense of urgency that other games lacked while also giving you enough time to play around if you managed your time wisely, and psychopath bosses were a frequent threat that added flavor to the carnage. Frank West was a protagonist that almost everyone loved, and his quotes are still memes years later. But as the series moved into the hands of Blue Castle Games (now Capcom Vancouver) the series shifted focus to mass appeal, and so the time limits and psychos slowly faded from existance while the core concept turned to "hilarious" weapon combinations, ensuring that you would never, ever find a pair of boxing gloves that you would've once upon a time used to playfully smack zombies with without also finding a pair of kitchen knives immediately beside them, no matter the reason.
So now, for the 4th game, they've decided to try to go back to their roots with Frank in a mall, except they missed their roots so hard that they're not even in the same garden anymore.
Frank is "back", but in name only. He doesn't look like Frank, he doesn't sound like Frank (they changed the VA), he doesn't talk like Frank, or even act like Frank. I assume the new writers think the new Frank is a wise cracking genius, but in reality he comes off as a comic relief idiot character and most of the time his sense of humor rests at middle school level. The game turns the meme dial up to 11 from the moment you start it, pummeling you with a volley of classic Frank quotes delivered by the new and unimproved voice actor instead as if they're desperately trying to prove that a single person on the team actually played Dead Rising 1 and that this person is really Frank West and not some imposter they renamed at the last minute. The time limit isn't even available as a hard mode option like it was in 3, and survivors just stand in protected areas (even if a zombie manages to glitch up to where they are, they don't attack them) until you kill all the zombies around them and then vanish to a safe house. Psychos have been removed entirely, replaced by "maniacs" which are basically just a human enemies with a bigger healthbar and little to no story attached to them. The inventory has been changed into different categories for food, melee weapons, ranged weapons, and throwables, meaning you can't throw melee weapons and you're constantly more limited on what you want to carry around since you're always forced to dedicate a certain amount of inventory space to guns or throwables. The combo melee weapons are at their absolute stupidest, and any shred of groundedness that the original game had has been completely trashed at this point, culminating in them completely jumping the shark by leaving exosuits all over Williamette for Frank to use. The port is good for the most part but it has a tendency to freeze so far, and if it does then you'd better hope you did a story mission recently because even though the game constantly saves your skills, clothing, and collectibles it only saves your actual weapon inventory and overall progression at certain points. And for those of you who enjoyed playing the campaign with friends in the post-DR1 games, they went and made the co-op in DR4 a separate side game, with the campaign being purely singleplayer. The extremely mediocre story that continually introduces new plot elements and then immediately forgets about them culminates in an ending that's insultingly terrible (there's only one, for now), and if you want to get the true ending you're going to have to shell out more money for the season pass because the true ending is DLC this time.
The co-op mode, which was made separate from the main campaign "to focus on providing the best possible experience", is pretty terrible. It's a small 4-episode survival mode where you can pick from various annoying hipsters and do missions in a small section of the mall like "kill 50 zombies" or "photograph dragon heads in medieval plaza", with no story involved. Each episode is short, and barely any of the things that made co-op fun are present; you can't dress up, and even if you're in a vehicle with more than one seat you can't drive around as a group. It feels very half-baked and tacked on, probably solely so that they could say that the game still had some form of online play.
There's really very little that I can say about DR4 that isn't bad. The Christmas jingles that play in the pause menus are cute, and that's pretty much it. I'd say I hope this is the last Dead Rising game but I don't know if the series can even get any more mediocre than this. If all you care about is hitting zombies with different things then go for it since apparently that's all Capcom Vancouver thinks the fanbase cares about, but if you're looking for anything that made the older games special then don't bother, because this isn't Dead Rising, it's just its undead corpse.

I loved DR1 and DR2. I had the Megaman Cannon unlocked for DR1 and was Max Level. I loved DR2 and the setting of Fortune City, and i=I adored Snowflake the tiger.
I could stomach DR3's poor story because I enjoyed arming my survivors to the teeth and mowing down legions of the dead. When Capcom said they were 'returning Dead Rising to it's roots' and that 'Frank is back!', I got excited for the fourth installment.
========================================================================================================================================================================

DR4. DR4. I think if the main character was called anything other than 'Frank', there wouldn't be a problem regarding the protagonist. He's funny, witty, dry. I enjoy his humour and his cynnical disposition, BUT, he is not Frank West. In an attempt to pander to the older fans of the series - such as myself - they've shot themselves in the foot by not creating a new character and having optional audio files  from TJ Rotolo (Frank's voice actor in DR1).
========================================================================================================================================================================
Dead Rising 4. The survivor-escort missions from DR1 and DR2 were 'streamlined' in DR3; you simply killed a horde of zombies around a character and they ran off and appeared in the various safehouses, where they could be recruited into the party and armed for combat. DR4 goes full retard and streamlines this proccess futher, as the survivors can no longer be taken on missions and armed. If anything, I was expecting a revamp to the system and make it much more interesting; maybe adding levels 1 - 5 to survivors so you had incentive to rescue them. Shame.
========================================================================================================================================================================
The timer in DR1 was enjoyable. Coupled with the escorting of potentially wounded survivors, the timer added a much-needed risk/reward style gameplay. I thoroughly enjoyed trying to get perfect runs where id save the majority of survivors and kill the majority of Psychopaths. Without it the game feels....without direction. The first two games' timers meant you could only spend a minute or two killing zombies at a time and so it wasnt worn out. Here (and in DR3) the lack of time constraints mean you're encouraged to kill hordes of the dead (as there's F all else to do). This makes fighting the zombies boring after a few minutes.
========================================================================================================================================================================

The replacement of the 'Health Chunks' from DR1 and DR2 means that instead of losing 1 chunk of health per time zombies bite you, you now have a numerical health value that slowly degrades as you walk past zombies and they flail their arms around. Couple this with an abundance of healing items placed at every turn and it's difficult to die.
========================================================================================================================================================================
When I saw the devs say Dead Rising was 'going back to it's roots', I thought less ridiculous combo weapons and more emphasis would be placed on finding weapons like in DR1 and DR2. Having knowledge of the katana and UZI whereabouts in Paradise Plaza in DR1 or the LMG in the Yucatan Casino in DR2 made you feel rewarded for learning the various weapon placements. Also, these weapons where extremely deadly to zombies and Psychopaths alike.

Combo weapons were introduced in DR2, but instead of them being the main focus, they were more of a novelty. Here in DR4, the combo weapons are your main source of damage dealing and this really doesnt sit well with me. I dont mind having an electrical axe, but I would much prefer it if it was a novelty item placed in one location that you would pick up everytime you drove through said location; not your Go To weapon once you learn the combo for it.
========================================================================================================================================================================
The Psychopaths in DR1 and DR2 were more fun than the actual story missions. Finally killing Cletus or Adam the Clown was a great feeling the first time around as they usually killed me several times before I learned how to best them. In DR4 there are no Psychopaths, instead they are replaced by 'Maniacs'. Maniacs are a group of enemies - usually dressed in a particular theme - that attack in waves and once a few waves have been defeated you can battle their boss - which looks identical to the other Maniacs - and then you're done. No interesting cutscenes showing how warped they've become by the apocolypse. No character depth. Just a mob of baddies and you're done, completely forgettable.
========================================================================================================================================================================
Other than various nitpicks and peresonal preference, the game runs at 60fps the majority of the time, and dips down into the low 40s randomly for no apparant reason, however I'm sure a patch will fix this in a week or two.
I despise how lazy the story writing is. Sneak into a military base? The gate is wide open and the guards are nowhere in site. Locked keypad? Use a hacking filter on the camera to bypass it.
Whether or not you like this game will come down to whether you enjoyed DR3 primarily over DR1 and DR2... There is definitley fun to be had here. The humour is hitting all the right notes. There is real weight and impact to each melee attack now thanks to a small vibration on the xbox controller.
For me personally, I wish they had focused more on survivors and a new protagonist. Hank East for christ sake. I would've prefered the combo weapons to be toned down compared to DR3, not ramped up. I would've really enjoyed seeing multiple factions fight over different areas on the map, and being able to join in on these fights depending on who I personally believed was right. I feel the game is too easy. A 10-year-old could easily play and complete this.
As Rick would put it; "
". Get Swhifty Capcom.

Good god this game is dead.
I know allot of people, out of that fascination for a good asymetrical game come here often, and read the reviews to convince themselves that they need to reinstall it and have a good time. But you've forgotten that their are reasons you haven't played this game in so long, reasons why you uninstalled it too, you've just forgotten the reasons like I did.
There's a reason nobody is playing this game, and their's a reason most the people reading this review stopped too, this game has some serious flaws with its own indentity. I was a hard monster main and have a cruel 91% win rate with the Gorgon, and despite that even I quit this game.
The game is supposed to work like this: The monsters should feel like the prey at first, and if the monster is good enough then that player can turn things around on the hunters and become the predator. But this isn't how it happens, its a mad map wide race, stealth and other options have been removed since Evolve went F2P, the worst offender is the constant map wide indicator that straight up tells the hunters where you are, you won't be hiding or sneaking up on my blind and deaf grandmother in this game; so straight up you aren't out-smarting or out-playing any hunters, only out-running.
This makes me feel like Turtle Rock are having an identity crisis with this game, they designed a pretty simple asymetrical game which works on a simple hunted becomes the hunter premise, but then they add some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that straight up tells hunters where the ♥♥♥♥ you are 24/7; so there goes any intellegent decision making on the part of the Monster because no matter how well you sneak around or trick the hunters it'll be a worthless effort because 3 seconds later they'll know you juked them. But this is a double edged sword, what in gods earth is the purpose of trackers if the game straight up tells you where to go? Its a role that was made redundant, if you wanna be useful you better be a good trapper or medic because their the only roles left that even require brain-cells anymore.
I'm not saying I think the game is bad, the premise is awesome but poorly executed,
, and if you do get a couple matches you will be very quickly reminded of why you uninstalled in the first place.

Evolve Stage 2. Recently made free to play because nobody had played it, so that means that it's a terrible game right? WRONG. This is a great game. Honestly, I can't see why the player count was so low. Lets start with the good things about this game:  (BEFORE TAKING MY OPINIONS FOR GRANTED, KNOW THAT THIS IS THE FIRST EVER EVOLVE GAME THAT I'VE EVER PLAYED. I ALSO GOT IT ABOUT A WEEK AFTER IT WAS MADE FREE TO PLAY. THIS GAME MIGHT MAKE ADVANCES IN WHAT I BELIEVE ARE THE PROS AND CONS OF THIS GAME) [And pardon my typos]
*This game has some pretty amazing graphic quality. This game also has some gameplay like no other; a four versus one match, every time. To me, the combat is fairly balanced (even though I absolutely hate being the "Monster"), as long as the "Hunters," or the team of 4, work together. *The Assault has to damage the monster with no other objective.
*The Medic has to keep track of her teammates' healths and make sure they're up.
*The Support has to guard his teammates indirectly through giving them armour, he has to focus on the one currently being attacked.
*And the Trapper has to track down the monster and ensure that said monster doesn't get out of the grasp of the Hunters. If they do not understand what they're supposed to do, or somebody left and your team is down a man, than you can consider yourself defeated. This is a great game that can teach you to realise that your teammates are more than meat shields (unless they're the Assault). There's also an amazing mechanic in which you can show your most preferred to least preferred to play as. It increases your chance at getting what you want, and decreases the chances at you being what you despise (in my case, the Monster). Lastly, there's no in-game purchases with real money
.
Let's move onto what I believe this game is missing

*First of all, this game has barely any storyline behind it. A few things are hinted at the randomly-generated dialogue at the beginning, but nothing significant.
*This kind of goes along with my previous statement, but it needs to be said: It has no campaign. I always love games when they have a campaign because I can get involved with the characters and mechanics. I can definitely see how a campaign could be implemented into a game like this, but the creators were a tad lazy.
*This game is repetitive. After awhile you'll feel like you're constantly being put into the same exact scenario, with the same exact things. I find it fun, but I also find myself bored after about an hour or two of playing it.
Overall, this is a really fun game with intersting ways and strategies. I love it so far and will continue enjoying it.

I am writing this review due to the release of Dishonored 2 in five days.  I am writing this solely off of the main game, considering that I do not have the DLC packs.  Dishonored is a first person stealth and action based game set in a steampunk universe.  You play the role of Corvo Attano, a man who was in the wrong place at the wrong time and mistakingly accused of murdering the Empress.  You will encounter many types of levels, all ripe with a wide variety of ways to accomplish the mission.  Each level is filled with interesting characters that have unique dialogue options ("Shall we gather for whiskey and cigars tonight?").  Corvo has a large arsenal of weapons that range from his trusty sword to a pistol, all of which can be upgraded to your liking.
On top of the standard weapons, there are also supernatural abilities.  These powers add a new level of creativity to an already stellar game.  Just like the weapons, they can be upgraded in whichever way the player chooses.  The story takes place in the city of Dunwall, an environment that is battling the rat plague.  The environment that you explore will reveal the past of Dunwall and give you insight into individual's lives and how they endure the plague.  The one thing that many people worry about on the PC is graphics and optimization.  I am happy to say that this game passes with flying colors in both sections.  The graphics are absolutely stellar considering it being released in 2012.  You will also have no trouble running this game because the requirements are not demanding.
With all of this in mind, Dishonored is an amazing game.  It is absolutely worth the $10 that the game is set at right now.  Dishonored 2 comes out November 11th, 2016 and I would highly recommend buying Dishonored and playing it.  If you want to save money, you can Dishonored 2 before it comes out and obtain access to Dishonored Definitive Edition which has all available DLC.  Dishonored easily earns a 10/10.

Tales of Maj'Eyal is a roguelike in its best possible form. Assuming you're familiar with roguelikes, ToME's main draw is its combat. Whereas games like Angband, Nethack and the like have a lot of focus on navigating the dungeons and managing your items, ToME sets itself apart from other RLs through its tactical approach to combat.
In ToME, every class is absolutely loaded with skills and abilities. Passive perks, active spells, buffs and the like. There's a class for everyone and a lot of fun to be had with them, and combined with the races you've got a lot of potential for characters. You could play a Berserker and cut people down through your bloodlust, an Alchemist who crafts potions and bombs on the fly to tear apart a crowd, or a Paradox Mage and change the perspective through the manipulation of spacetime itself. Each class has tons of abilities and skill trees, and you can invest into specific types of abilities (say I wanted to focus on grappling instead of one-handed skills) to suit your tastes or your needs for that situation. Combat is a matter of knowing when to use your abilities and resource management. Using an ability puts it on a cooldown and uses up a certain percentage of a turn. Some abilities don't take any time at all, some may use up your entire turn. Each one has a different range, a different effect and a different cost. Summoning skeletons, controlling minds, throwing enemies across the room, and stopping time are among the many abilities you can learn within the game.
Ability costs are an important element. Early classes such as Mages and Warriors may use mana, which is about as straightforward as it gets. The more advanced professions may use alternative resources such as Hate, which is built by attacking and being attacked - or Paradox, which can be used freely, but the more it's used, the higher the chance for you to be affected by random effects such as teleporting and spell backfire. Learning how to effectively manage these resources is half of the challenge, and as you get stronger and fight tougher enemies you'll need every bit of your wits and patience if you want to make it out alive. As with other roguelikes, there's of course plenty of equipment and items to find, and it ranges from armor and weapons with random stats to powerful, unique items that may have a little more behind them.
While it's not central to the game in any way, there actually is quite a bit of information on the world you're in. You'll find little lore pages scattered around the world which tell you just a little bit more about Maj'Eyal. For anyone who doesn't care, the game doesn't force this on you in any way, but for those who want a little extra, it's there.
The game actually has a wonderful presentation given the genre. The little tiles for the characters and maps look quite nice and I can totally tell what I'm looking at, so there's that. The music is nothing to write home about but it's all good stuff and fits the environments well, making my dungeon crawls quite the enjoyable romp. The HUD and info are all pretty clear and easy to understand, and as you get more skills the hotbar expands so you've got everything in one place. You can play the entire thing with mouse, keyboard, or with both, which is nice. It's always nice to keep your options open and luckily there's a lot of em.
Interestingly, there's also online servers. You can store your characters online and keep items in a cloud vault to transfer them between characters. If you access your profile online it'll show all your characters and everything, which is a neat touch. There's a global chat too and the community is very friendly, which is great! If you die, your death is also broadcasted to the entire server, so you have extra pressure. It's a needless feature, but a great one nonetheless.
+ Roguelike combat is indeed challenging and tactical
+ Solid music that really helps with the atmosphere
+ Classes are all fun to play and interesting
+ Optional lore pages do great in providing players extra incentive and fleshing out the world
+ Comprehensible and easy to use UI
+ Serverside saves!

- Smashing goblins with energy blasts you rewound through time and blasting foes with your blood sounds like your cup of tea

I gave it a shot, I really gave it a shot.  I figured that a game with such a high rating must have something going for it that I wasn't seeing and that I needed to keep giving it "just a bit more time".
I think I got about 3-4 hours in before I realized that no amount of "more time" would ever reveal to me what others are seeing in this game.
For me I found it boring, frustrating and mostly luck-based. I really never felt challenged as a player or felt that I was required to truly evaluate what my next move was going to be.  It seemed to be: Either face-roll whatever was in front of me OR kite enemies to a choke-point and then do the obvious attack/skill/whatever.  Continue until you die from circumstances beyond your control.
It presents as a deep strategy game but I can honestly say I felt no strategy beyond absolute basics was ever required for the time I played.
There appears to be a lot of customization in the characters/classes/skills/etc but when it all comes out in terms of gameplay it felt quite shallow.  How can a game feel so shallow when there is so much apparent "depth" to the character customization?  I have no idea, but this game found the formula IMO.
My other big complaint is the UI (user interface) which I found using to be a greater challenge than playing the actual game.
Why won't my character move every 2nd click?  How do I close this window?  Why does this window close when I click OFF it, and this other window requires me to click ON it to close?  Why is there rollover text that needs scrolling, yet when I move the mouse over to scroll it different rollover replaces it before I get there?  Thank goodness I quit drinking because I would have gone rage city while I was still living in the bottle.
The UI- and I want to make it clear I am not talking about the graphics which are a different story - is very bad, very difficult to use, and feels dashed together haphazardly with little regard to how users need and expect information to be presented.  I praise the dev for ATTEMPTING to include font/UI scaling options which more games need. However, adjusting any of the setting made the visual presentation quite atrocious and broke the UI in non-trivial ways.  Resolution settings turned out to be a joke too... anything other than full-screen native resolution made the layout of the UI go berserk.
I don't care that much about graphics, I don't care that much for story, I don't care too much about deep customization.  What I care about is good gameplay, solid craftsmanship, and clean & intuitive interface - I did not find any of those here.

If you're in the market for a dark and complex action game with incredibly bad hit detection, you could definitely do a lot worse than Salt and Sanctuary. I hear they're calling those "Dark Souls-like" nowadays. To be entirely fair, a game shouldn't just be judged based solely on what other games it resembles, and deserves a chance to prove itself on its own merits.
Judged on gameplay alone, Salt and Sanctuary is absolutely worth the relatively modest price tag. The game world boasts a wide array of weapons and armor, many of which lend themselves to specific tactics and strategies for overcoming the varied and dangerous enemies that populate the treacherous world. Boss fights are fairly creative and varied, challenging in mostly the right ways and only annoying in a few minor ones. Characters do have oversized hit boxes, leading to a lot of incidental damage taken from attacks that appear to have missed, but after an initial adjustment period it becomes only a minor annoyance. While there are a few enemies which could have been better programmed or designed (the teleporting skeletons and foes who can launch homing attacks from off screen in particular), on the whole it's really pretty good. It even includes local multiplayer, which is a great and oft-neglected feature.
All right. Time to make the comparison.
Unlike Dark Souls (and Bloodborne, another major influence), Salt and Sanctuary is probably only going to be entertaining for maybe two playthroughs. What makes Dark Souls addictive to me isn't the need to overcome the steep difficulty, gradually adding more and more insane and arbitrary handicaps until I'm finally trying to kill the hidden superboss armed with a tube sock and a bar of soap. That's just something incidental to the real appeal; what I notice in the details of the world that I hadn't seen previous. Catching subtle hints at the greater puzzle unraveling around me as I tread the now worn paths.
This is where Salt and Sanctuary kind of falls short; the story and the world that are presented are interesting and well crafted, but the delivery is incredibly linear. It tries to draw visually and thematically from real-world religions (again, much like Bloodborne), but doesn't really move past the superficial "guts and gore" sort of grotesquerie typical of a cheap horror comic. All of Salt and Sanctuary's best mysteries are eventually explained in perfectly clear english, usually in one or two sentences, and all of the other lore and storytelling concerning the world and the player's place therein are so much padding.
So definitely play it for the gameplay experience, the explorative adventure design, and if possible bring a friend with you! But understand going in that as much as it has to offer in and of itself, Salt and Sanctuary just doesn't tell as deep or compelling a story as the games it seems to be in tribute to.
Seriously, though, still pretty good.

I tried this game out when it was first released. I've since then waited for the day it would get released on Steam (as I would rather wait for the Steam version instead of buying it from the Windows store) and I have to say Dead Rising 4 has been a nice suprise coming from a fan ever since Dead Rising 1.
I was a bit skeptical when I heard that they changed the voice actor of Frank from TJ Rotolo to Ty Olsson, but Ty has done a really good job portraying an "older" Frank West.
The humor of Dead Rising 4 is what really amazed me as a first impression of the game, both the dialog and cutscenes offer some great comedy even though it may be a bit sitcom-ish. They didn't fail to capture the fun side of past installments which I'm very happy about, and even if you're new to the franchise it's not hard for Frank and his humor to grow on you.
Further more the map is larger this time around, taking you back to the beloved mall from Dead Rising 1, aswell as other locations.
One big feature they have removed from previous games are psychopaths, instead we got "maniacs" which technically is the same thing but this time around you need to gather clues before you can fight them.
When it comes to weapons and combining they haven't added much, but it's still as a fun as ever to combine a sledgehammer with some frag grenades and run around swinging at zombies as they explode.
Overall Dead Rising 4 is a solid package, both for older fans (in my opinion atleast) aswell as new ones.
A nice interesting story, a larger map, tons of weapons and combination options, vehicles aswell as the options to combine them for some crazy deadly rides, the humor, voice acting is good, and some different types of zombies, some more dangerous than others this time around. Also kudos to Capcom for taking their zombie franchises back to their roots (sorta).
Runs flawless, looks great, plays awesome and the map is absolutely huge.

Good god this game is dead.
I know allot of people, out of that fascination for a good asymetrical game come here often, and read the reviews to convince themselves that they need to reinstall it and have a good time. But you've forgotten that their are reasons you haven't played this game in so long, reasons why you uninstalled it too, you've just forgotten the reasons like I did.
There's a reason nobody is playing this game, and their's a reason most the people reading this review stopped too, this game has some serious flaws with its own indentity. I was a hard monster main and have a cruel 91% win rate with the Gorgon, and despite that even I quit this game.
The game is supposed to work like this: The monsters should feel like the prey at first, and if the monster is good enough then that player can turn things around on the hunters and become the predator. But this isn't how it happens, its a mad map wide race, stealth and other options have been removed since Evolve went F2P, the worst offender is the constant map wide indicator that straight up tells the hunters where you are, you won't be hiding or sneaking up on my blind and deaf grandmother in this game; so straight up you aren't out-smarting or out-playing any hunters, only out-running.
This makes me feel like Turtle Rock are having an identity crisis with this game, they designed a pretty simple asymetrical game which works on a simple hunted becomes the hunter premise, but then they add some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that straight up tells hunters where the ♥♥♥♥ you are 24/7; so there goes any intellegent decision making on the part of the Monster because no matter how well you sneak around or trick the hunters it'll be a worthless effort because 3 seconds later they'll know you juked them. But this is a double edged sword, what in gods earth is the purpose of trackers if the game straight up tells you where to go? Its a role that was made redundant, if you wanna be useful you better be a good trapper or medic because their the only roles left that even require brain-cells anymore.
I'm not saying I think the game is bad, the premise is awesome but poorly executed,
, and if you do get a couple matches you will be very quickly reminded of why you uninstalled in the first place.

Evolve Stage 2. Recently made free to play because nobody had played it, so that means that it's a terrible game right? WRONG. This is a great game. Honestly, I can't see why the player count was so low. Lets start with the good things about this game:  (BEFORE TAKING MY OPINIONS FOR GRANTED, KNOW THAT THIS IS THE FIRST EVER EVOLVE GAME THAT I'VE EVER PLAYED. I ALSO GOT IT ABOUT A WEEK AFTER IT WAS MADE FREE TO PLAY. THIS GAME MIGHT MAKE ADVANCES IN WHAT I BELIEVE ARE THE PROS AND CONS OF THIS GAME) [And pardon my typos]
*This game has some pretty amazing graphic quality. This game also has some gameplay like no other; a four versus one match, every time. To me, the combat is fairly balanced (even though I absolutely hate being the "Monster"), as long as the "Hunters," or the team of 4, work together. *The Assault has to damage the monster with no other objective.
*The Medic has to keep track of her teammates' healths and make sure they're up.
*The Support has to guard his teammates indirectly through giving them armour, he has to focus on the one currently being attacked.
*And the Trapper has to track down the monster and ensure that said monster doesn't get out of the grasp of the Hunters. If they do not understand what they're supposed to do, or somebody left and your team is down a man, than you can consider yourself defeated. This is a great game that can teach you to realise that your teammates are more than meat shields (unless they're the Assault). There's also an amazing mechanic in which you can show your most preferred to least preferred to play as. It increases your chance at getting what you want, and decreases the chances at you being what you despise (in my case, the Monster). Lastly, there's no in-game purchases with real money
.
Let's move onto what I believe this game is missing

*First of all, this game has barely any storyline behind it. A few things are hinted at the randomly-generated dialogue at the beginning, but nothing significant.
*This kind of goes along with my previous statement, but it needs to be said: It has no campaign. I always love games when they have a campaign because I can get involved with the characters and mechanics. I can definitely see how a campaign could be implemented into a game like this, but the creators were a tad lazy.
*This game is repetitive. After awhile you'll feel like you're constantly being put into the same exact scenario, with the same exact things. I find it fun, but I also find myself bored after about an hour or two of playing it.
Overall, this is a really fun game with intersting ways and strategies. I love it so far and will continue enjoying it.

Bottom Line: If you're looking for a challenging platformer/shooter to hone your skills on, buy it.
Beautiful aesthetic, tons of bosses, challenging in a skillfull way (the majority of the time) great soundtrack, hidden goodies, multiple difficulties. So much of this game is done just right, and then there's plenty of game-y extras too, like shortcuts to find, hidden gold coins, and extra unlockables. The run and gun levels are even designed in a way that you can beat them all without shooting a single shot, and are rewarded for doing so.
No colorblindness support, so for red/green colorblind people like myself, it can be very difficult to tell what items you can parry, and which you cannot. Throughout the entire game, I could never get parry to work consistently multiple times in the same jump, which lead to me believing that you couldn't do it for a stint. This issue made the King Dice fight a nightmare. Two particular of the stages (the dragon and the bee) have a terrible use of randomization- in both of them this encompasses the randomly appearing platforms, but in the dragon fight, the second phase with the fireballs that launch randomly, with a random trajectory (not always directly at you) and a random speed, while you're jumping between randomly apeparing platforms... there's too much luck in that section. Sometimes you get a run where none jump at you, sometimes you get every other one jumping at you, and there's no way to know for sure dodging which way will get you out of its trajectory.
Also, some fights are designed to be easier with different weapon loadouts, yet you can't access your inventory on stage, meaning once figure that out, you'll have to jump through two loading screens back out to the map and back into the fight, Also, the co-op makes the game harder instead of easier, where projectiles that would ordinarily only take one or two hits to kill, suddenly take 4 and completely throw off their function in the fight. And I'm also left to wonder if they tried having a "lock firing direction" button and it just made the game too easy so they cut it out, but it feels a lot like this game could use that.
I know here it looks like the list of cons outweighs the pros, but trust me. The good VASTLY outweighs the bad for this game. If you're up for a challenge, buy it.
Still hoping for DLC!

OK, so I am 37 hours in and here is how I see it right now:
At first, I was overwhelmed by the amount of planning, interfaces, and scale of the game (never got the hang of EU4). By playing the Italy tutorial for 5 hours and accepting the fact that I was going to mess up from the beginning, I managed to get a hang of all the major mechanics.
I was always a fan of the Civilization franchise, but I just can't see myself going back to Civilization with all the depth this game has shown me. Hearts of Iron 4 definitely has some issues even someone as new as me has noticed (allies bottlenecking supply lines, lack of individual negotiating with nations, unable to mass recruit from conquered regions, questionable resource map, ect.), but the satisfaction from plans going well from years of in-game planning is amazing.
There is also a lot of replayablility in this game as well. You can play as any nation and I'm sure DLCs will had more uniquness to this already diverse roster. 37 hours in and I have only really experienced 3 nations so far. I recognize I might still be in the "honey-moon phase" of this game before some issues become really prominent, but as it stands now, this game was worth every penny ($34).

Sniper Ghost Warrior 2 is a decent game, better than the first one. The story is improved, but it is very linear. You cannot choose where to go or where to take out your target from. The gameplay is the same throughout the entire game with stealth that play a bigger part in this game than the previous. The animation for the AI does not seem like it could be from a game that was released in 2013. It feels like this game was made in the mid 2000s with the animation, but the quality is fine for this game.
The music is not very repetetive or way to boring, it fit very well with the situations you where put in throughout the game. And the sound is majorly improved, where as you do not hear the npc's talk like they are right next to you when they are over 500 meters away. But when zoomed in, it sometimes sounds like you are right next to them.
The game's plot was very predictable, but there was 2 times I was surprised because I did not see those coming.
There is still a small issue with the npc's just teleporting in front of you, but this time I had a chance to react accordingly. There where a few times when I was lining up a shot and a friendly npc was getting up right in front of me, so I got teleported a few meters back and up a ledge screwing over the shot.
Other than that, the game is pretty good compared to Sniper: Ghost Warrior. It is a major improvement to the game, but it is very short on just 4 hours and 3 act's. Voice acting could use some work along with mouth movement when npc's are talking in-game or in cutscenes.
I enjoyed the game more than I would like to aknowledge, it still has some big flaws that might be fixed in Sniper Ghost Warrior 3. The game is recommended, but only on a sale.
