If you're in the market for a dark and complex action game with incredibly bad hit detection, you could definitely do a lot worse than Salt and Sanctuary. I hear they're calling those "Dark Souls-like" nowadays. To be entirely fair, a game shouldn't just be judged based solely on what other games it resembles, and deserves a chance to prove itself on its own merits.
Judged on gameplay alone, Salt and Sanctuary is absolutely worth the relatively modest price tag. The game world boasts a wide array of weapons and armor, many of which lend themselves to specific tactics and strategies for overcoming the varied and dangerous enemies that populate the treacherous world. Boss fights are fairly creative and varied, challenging in mostly the right ways and only annoying in a few minor ones. Characters do have oversized hit boxes, leading to a lot of incidental damage taken from attacks that appear to have missed, but after an initial adjustment period it becomes only a minor annoyance. While there are a few enemies which could have been better programmed or designed (the teleporting skeletons and foes who can launch homing attacks from off screen in particular), on the whole it's really pretty good. It even includes local multiplayer, which is a great and oft-neglected feature.
All right. Time to make the comparison.
Unlike Dark Souls (and Bloodborne, another major influence), Salt and Sanctuary is probably only going to be entertaining for maybe two playthroughs. What makes Dark Souls addictive to me isn't the need to overcome the steep difficulty, gradually adding more and more insane and arbitrary handicaps until I'm finally trying to kill the hidden superboss armed with a tube sock and a bar of soap. That's just something incidental to the real appeal; what I notice in the details of the world that I hadn't seen previous. Catching subtle hints at the greater puzzle unraveling around me as I tread the now worn paths.
This is where Salt and Sanctuary kind of falls short; the story and the world that are presented are interesting and well crafted, but the delivery is incredibly linear. It tries to draw visually and thematically from real-world religions (again, much like Bloodborne), but doesn't really move past the superficial "guts and gore" sort of grotesquerie typical of a cheap horror comic. All of Salt and Sanctuary's best mysteries are eventually explained in perfectly clear english, usually in one or two sentences, and all of the other lore and storytelling concerning the world and the player's place therein are so much padding.
So definitely play it for the gameplay experience, the explorative adventure design, and if possible bring a friend with you! But understand going in that as much as it has to offer in and of itself, Salt and Sanctuary just doesn't tell as deep or compelling a story as the games it seems to be in tribute to.
Seriously, though, still pretty good.

Overall, I would give this game a 6 out of 10.
On the positive side, this game is quite fun, and has lots of replayability. Classes are very unique, and there is a large variety of skills. I also appreciate the unlocking system for new classes/races.
However, one of the major downfalls, in my opinion, is that I often run into enemies that can one-hit-kill me. Most reciently there was an instance of a "normal" (not elite, rare, or boss) enemy, lower than my level, that killed me, from full health, from 4 blocks away, and through my summon. So, the only way to not die and lose 20+ hours of gameplay is to... never get within 6 blocks of anyone for even a second? Also, it *kind of* deleted my character, even though I had used an item to get an extra life. The character won't show up anywhere, but when I try to create a new character with the same name, it says one exists.
I believe the creators need to spend some time reworking enemy skills/powers and fix some major bugs before this game is considered complete.

Amazing-if-often-frustrating dungeon crawler:
You will die.  A lot.  You'll quit.  And find yourself crawling back for more punishment.  You'll learn...  evolve...  progress...  Unkillable boss becomes hard to kill tyrant becomes minor road block along a path you know.  There is repetition, but with sufficient randomness to feel nostalgic rather than tedious.
You'll unlock new styles, races, and classes.  You'll find aspects you enjoy, figure out how to master them, and learn coping and survival mechanisms for the diverse critters and situations.  You'll develop that spidey-sense that tells you "hey, I'd better get out of here before I get in trouble, and regroup around a choke point".
I loved this.  I hated this.  I loved it.  I hated it.  I learned that I loved that I loved and hated it.  It's challenging but fair, with a helpful community and deep content.  If you don't require massive 3d immersive graphics, are patient enough to avoid throwing your keyboard, and are willing to devote hours to learning truly "how to play", this is a great, evolving product you won't regret your time spent on.

There are two things in Tales of Maj'Eyal, that made me stop playing this game, and not invest money in more expansions:
1) Permanent socketing. Items can be imbued with gems, which add to the item's stats. Gems can be found and bought, and you can also find more powerful artifact gems. However, all item imbuing is permanent. The result was never using the good gems for imbuing good items, while anxiously wondering whether and when I should. Instead of a bonus, every found artifact became a reminder about potentially shooting myself in the foot. "Wanna imbue me? You know, it's permanent if you do. A better gem might be just around the corner. Better wait...but is it? You're constantly gimping yourself, you know..."
2) Extremely limited item transfer space. AFAIU, you'll get transfer space for one item for every 2 euros you've paid for the game. With the base game at 7 euros, that'd result in a massive quantity of 3 items you can transfer. However, you can find tens - or even hundreds of artifacts in one playthrough. Also, the transfer space can be reached in later game only, never allowing you the possibility of starting fresh characters with good quality equipment. The permanent socketing -issue raises its head in here as well, since different character classes require different items. "Used that nice artifact gem in the sword of your now-overleveled fighter? So bad, you can't transfer it to your new mage's staff now."
To conclude, if these issues were fixed, I'd gladly put more money in this game.

So, once again writing a review here.  This is sort of another "first impressions" review.  I only write one of these when I find a game where I can see the potential of it right away, and where I'm already impressed by it and have an idea as to where the gameplay is going to lead me.  This is one of those games.
However, first impressions can be a little weird with this one.  A couple of things I ran into are things that might put some players off from playing this any further... yet they arent ACTUALLY problems.  But they might really seem like it when you first see them, due to how incredibly different this game is.
Dungetris is a fairly typical roguelike in terms of it's high emphasis on RNG, brutal difficulty, and simple-yet-strategic combat mechanics.  Where this game strays from the norm is it's fantastic "dungeon tetris" mechanic.  At any time, you can hold the right mouse button down to bring up the next dungeon piece; you can see it exactly as it will be, and also see exactly what's in it, before you place it.  These pieces cannot be rotated, and will drop straight down when you click, landing on the first thing they hit, which means you cant do things like place a new piece UNDER an old one.  These pieces can have all sorts of things in them.  Monsters, treasure chests, shops, crates, shrines... all sorts of things.  And of course each also has walls in all sorts of configuration.  And they're different sizes too; sometimes you'll get a piece that's just a single block in size... by far the easiest type to place... but other times you might get one that's three blocks in a horizontal line... not so easy to place.
In effect, this gives the RNG of dungeon layout as in other roguelikes, but here, you control where the RNG goes.  There's ALOT of strategy here.  Monster types, for example, are all different in behavior and tendancies.  I learned really fast that the big rat guys are stupidly powerful... at least early on, I sure dont want those jerks running around. 500 HP with 8 attack power?  When I've got 15 HP and a toothpick?  Yeah.  Too strong!  But the RNG cant just shove them at me by itself... I get to place the piece wherever I want, and it DOESNT have to connect to another piece (meaning I can drop it on the ground a few blocks from the current boundary of my dungeon). Further strategic piece placement can "connect" that horrible rat-piece to my dungeon, yet with walls completely locking him in there, so I can continue building around him without having to deal with him.  But of course, it's just as easy to wall off treasure or whatever, or just make it so that it's going to take a good while to get at that treasure chest you just placed.  You cant skip or choose your pieces, so you *must* place whatever it gives you next, but the great part is you can do this at absolutly any time, and it doesnt use up your turn.  If I want to place 10 dungeon bits before my next turn, I can do that.  This may sound like it could make for OP situations, but.... no.  It's dangerous if you go too far at once, because one way or another, you're going to have to deal with monster pieces, and you cant just keep blocking them off as it'll restrict you way too much.
Really, there's so very much strategic potential just in that mechanic of this game.  Just have a look at the screenshots on the store page to see some examples.  Lots of strategic potential indeed, and the sort that'll have you making very difficult decisions much of the time (which is a good thing).  You'll have plenty of moments where you suddenly realize that you made a seriously stupid move, and it's absolutely your own fault... the RNG didnt FORCE you to put that specific piece there that's screwing you over.  You had other options with it.  You just didnt do those things.  This is much, much less frustrating than some roguelikes where it's like "Here's this potion.  You dont know what it does.  OOPS you're on fire now and there's laser bees everywhere, sorry, you're dead".   None of that.  But you have to think about your placements, and plan ahead.
The game also uses a funky card system instead of normal items.  You hold cards that you can play at any time, which do all sorts of things.  Many of these things are temporary; some stick around but may break.  But none of them do a thing until you play the card, and of course, you cant just hold a kersquillion cards at once.  You're not always going to HAVE cards with you... you dont just draw these from a deck.  You have to find them, which is done in a variety of ways (or buy them).  The system takes a bit of getting used to, but in the end, just adds to the strategy of the game further.
One issue though is that the game might seem unbalanced as all heck when you start.  For example, you see those rat guys, or a particularly strong slime, and go "How in the world am I supposed to deal with that?  That's impossible to beat!  What could I possibly do? It's so broken!" due to old habits gained from other roguelikes.  This game really forces you to put aside your old habits and think differently, as solutions to problems are often very different here.  It's all in the pieces and the cards, and what you do with them, and it's so very different from other roguelikes that it can be hard to wrap your mind around.
The only problem I've run into is that some things can be pretty darned unclear as to just what they do... the game doesnt explain itself all that well.  So that can be an issue for some players.
Other than that though... like I said, this is pretty great already, and has the potential to be amazing as time goes on.  I definitely recommend it, and I cant wait to see where they take it from here.

Okay, Dungetris... where to begin. The graphics are simple and well drawn and work surprisingly well with this type of game. The combination of building the dungeon as you progress through each level makes it both unique and challenging and the card system works pretty well. The music is repetitive, but not hard to listen to. I would assuming at the 30 to 40 hour mark, I'm sure I'd choose something new to listen to.
A few things that are odd to me, however. First, you can collect coins, which I would assume you can use to purchase in-game items, but I couldn't find a place to use them after the first 3 levels... an item shop can usually be found at the main menu. Also, progess in each level in individual of other levels and resets at death. Say you reach level 2 in a level and die, you start back at level 1. This adds to the challenge, but can be very frustrating as the monsters are EXTREMELY overpowered at this point in the game.
I will update this review as time goes on, but this is certainly a solid purchase at $2.99 or $2.59... be warned about the overpowered monsters, however and please don't rage on your keyboard!

This game...... it's good. Very good at times. But.... it's not great. It had every piece and every ounce of potential to be. And there you can see the lack of another 20 million dollars in its budget. Let's tackle the game bit by bit. This is expreiment is a marriage between old school and new school shooters. It succeds most of the times.
The visuals -
There are so many games that boast of being realistic. This game boasts of being beautiful. The lighting and post processing  are done beautifully. No, they aren't made with every piece of technology that you can find. Unlike PBR that boasts realistic results, the textures and lighmaps are entirely baked. My gripe is with some low res textures here and there, and perhaps an improved environment lighting reading system?
The game runs like butter on my HP shitbox.
The gameplay -
The gameplay is pretty awesome. But it is awesome only when dealing with mutants, car combat and weaker human enemies. WIth human enemies with guns, it becomes another cover shooter (unless using the pop rockets with the shotgun). Later towards the game, the enemies just become bullet sponges. The mutant AI is spectacular. They run, they dodge, they flank. Making them rather formidable enemies. But the humans....(no wonder I hate humans). Some may say that the game lacks enemy variety. But it's the same as any Far Cry game. There are the mutants. Special mutants. Boss mutants. Then there are melee human enemies, human enemies with guns, human enemies with guns and beefed up armour. There are also a few races, but they are more of a check list, than something interesting that the surface.
I love how unpushy the game is. It lets you take your time with everything.
The gameworld -
The game world is of 3 types. The overworld, settlements and safezones, and dungeons.
The overworld is the place connecting the settlements and dungeons. It is made for driving and car combat, but every route is filled with enemies, which makes travelling a chore. I wish at some point or some mission, the routes will be cleared.
The settlements and safezones arec places with people who interact with you and provide you with quests.
The dungeons are linear levels with minor exploration (kind of like Skyrim).
As you traverse the world, you get the idea of the world being larger, but that is never explored, but only referenced at times, which is kind of... disappointing.
The NPCs -
There are mutants, bandits, settlers and the autority.
The behaviours of the mutants are explored a bit, but their origins doesn't have that much of a relevation.
The bandits and their behaviours are also denoted pretty well, but the interaction between them isn't developed at all.
The settlers are the deepest. But they could have been deeper with branching dialogue trees or varying dialogues like Dishonored.
The authority.... you get their basic workings but Capitol Prime isn't much explored.
The story -
The story is pretty basic. You are an arc survibour and after getting good with the locals you help in turning the tides of a rebellion with the resistance against the autority. But like I said, the game needed another 20 million dollars to meet its full expectation.
Verdict -
The negatives of this game are rather minor. But the biggest negative is that the game's content is incomplete. The balancing is a bit of at times, and so is the level design. But it's mostly good. The guns feel like... actual guns and not watered down peashooters? If you want to, then play it. I promise you that you will have a good time.
What it could have been?
A sprawling open world adventure without RPG mechanics holding you back (with an additional 20 million dollars).
Or
A hub based game like Dishonored where the main missions are attempted via NPCs. Side missions through a map where you can get via a guide, and the vehicles for escape and chace sequence and races.
I hope they make a sequel or a DLC (naah) that deals with the ending. But if I ever get the chance to make this game, I would. Perhaps someday, when I am a millionaire and buy the IP rights to this game.
Score - 8/10

This is a very strange choice for Carmack's final game.  The idTech engine is impressive as usual, this time showing off some large open bright maps.  But the game?  It's a complete rip-off of Borderlands!  The setting, the look, the vehicles.  Except without the humour.  And the point of Borderlands was leveling up the guns... here there are only 9 guns, and no levels.  But lots and lots of getting quests at point A and driving to point B and then back to point A again.

6.5/10- Final Verdict: Just an OKAY game
Completed on Hard mode in about 15 hours (Okay Length), not too much replay value as there is no choice or decision making mechanism in game.  Graphics are unfortunately not too good, with the texture quality frequently dropping at random.  If you are looking for a post-apocalyptic role playing game, go play fallout since you will not get an interesting story here.  All in all, this game is worth a playthrough, but just one playthrough.  The combat system is phenomenal and the game is jammed packed with great ideas, the problem is many of these ideas just were not really implemented as well as they could have been.  The default controls for playing keyboard/mouse are god awful, and I spent nearly 10 minutes adjusting the controls to better play the game.
Like I said, the combat is good with 9 different weapons, the majority of them being able to use three different kinds of ammo, creating an interesting and experimental combat system.  The enemies actually communicate well with one another and the state of the fire fight can be determined by the conversations between enemies (they will decide whether to push forward or fall back, or even use certain items).  Enemies also have to see you directly and announce your presence to each other before entering an alarmed state.  The enemies largely consist of bandits, mutants, and the big bad government corporation.  There are also a handful of boss fights that spice the game up, however there is no final boss or real major single villain.
There is a vehicle system similar to the Mad Max road rage movies in game, however it is severely watered down and underdeveloped.  When you think that you will get massive races with 15+ cars with varying sizes, models, and factions (not to mention all the various weapon systems like flamethrowers, spikes, chains, and other gnarly stuff) you instead get mild races with just 3 NPC’s all using the same car as you.  In almost half of the racing events you don’t even get weapons.  In the races where you do get weapons, when you annihilate your opponents with either rockets or machine gun fire they will respawn with full health in less than 3 seconds.  What is the point of having a lawless, brutal, weaponized post-apocalyptic race system when your opponents just immediately respawn upon death?  You’re better off just focusing on the finish line and ignoring your opponents since killing them does absolutely nothing.  There are also only 3 playable vehicles in game, with only 2 being race-able.  This is honestly one of the most limited racing systems I’ve ever seen in a video game.  The reward for racing is special credits which can be used to upgrade your vehicles.  This system is somewhat pointless though, because outside of racing, there is no real reason to use a vehicle other than to get to wherever the next mission is.  You will randomly get attacked by bandit cars in the open world map, but since you get nothing from killing them (aside from quest rewards) it is not worth doing.  Especially when the price of fixing your vehicle and restocking ammo afterwards will far exceed anything you’ll earn.
The best part of the game for me was fighting the mutants.  They are fast, agile, unpredictable, and excellent at ambushing the player at various parts in the game.  The game does well in building up suspense and even creating a fear factor with the mutants.  The player is often forced to enter dark, ominous areas in the game that are completely absent of noise with only brief flickering of movement occurring in the corner of one’s eye, announcing the unfortunate presence of a mutant ambush that you will inevitably fall prey into.  The game can be somewhat frightening at times as mutants can rapidly appear and surround a player, trapping them in a situation that is difficult to get out of.  The mutants are excellent at using the environment to their advantage, doing all sorts of flips, tumbles, and jumps to doge your gunfire and close the distance between you.  That being said, actually hitting the mutants can be somewhat frustrating from time to time because of this.  There are 5 types of mutants, the normal grunts, a gladiator-like one, a tough-skinned spitting one, a giant with a flamethrower, and one boss.  This is somewhat diverse, but more could have been added.
The biggest problem of the game for me was sadly the story.  It is beyond me how a game made partly by Bethesda, creator of recent fallout and elder scroll games, could create a game with such a copy and paste story line.  It seems like there is so much to learn and plenty of mysteries to be solved, but for whatever the reason you get nothing.  The game events are slammed together with very little logic involved regarding the transition of events.  You go from earning the trust of a kingpin midgame to immediately (singlehandedly) sieging the stronghold of the generic evil government organization whose sole purpose is to be oppressive and evil for no reason.  The game itself starts out as a steam punk fallout-like theme and ends with a Halo-like theme, making for a rather dis-jumbled game.  The game abruptly forces the player to form an alliance with the “resistance” (AKA an entire 6 people) and become enemies with the generic evil government corporation.  You have no real reason for trusting the resistance or disliking the evil government.  There are no spoilers in game, no characters die, no real bonds are formed, no nemesis is made, no revenge taken, no betrayal, just a predictable and embarrassing mess of a story from start to finish.  You character mindlessly accepts missions for no reason whatsoever and never questions their actions or allegiance in the game.  Throw in an anti-climatic ending with just pushing buttons on a computer terminal and you have overall just a disappointing and majorly flawed story.
So those are my thoughts on the game.  I do not regret purchasing it, but I do recommend getting it on sale.  Like I said, it is worth a playthrough and I hope that a sequel gets made as like I said, the game really is filled with good ideas, they just need to be implemented properly.

And this game was 100% worth it.
The game itself felt a little slow, but goodness, did it make up the minutes wandering around in the beauty and story. I absolutely loved playing through it.
The game follows a mother fox who finds one of her dear children dead, and slowly introduces concepts (That are incredibly, beautifully made) that makes the game feel like it isn't just a story, but an adventure you go through as well. Not to mention the sentimental value and meaning it carries to everyone who was once a teenager with a little angst. An incredibly sad, yet valuable story, that I would recommend everyone to take a look at.
It made me grateful for what I have, and realize how much I've taken for granted.

When jumping onto an object if you don't get it exactly right you'll end up on the side of a rock or some such object, no longer able to move your fox and having to wait until it has slid down the side of the rock. The jump is also difficult to control in general and it seems that you can't really time it properly - I felt like I was lining myself up correctly and should reach the snowflake I was trying to collect but then the fox would plummet to the ground just short. The voice acting was the kicker for me though with some of the sentences sounding forced and the acting not praticularly convincing. It felt kind of like drama class back when I was at school when two people were super trying hard, but just not pulling it off.
With all that said, it is a very beautiful game and the music is pretty, but it just wasn't enough for me to like this.

3on3 Freestyle attempts to fill the void by beloved series like NBA Street. 3on3 Freestyle can be coop game with outstanding graphics and music, also the art of each character of the game. Aside from exhibition mode, you also practice to make your play style more unique and dominate your opponents. You have to play 3 minutes for the 1st half and another 3 minutes for the second half which you can obtain points and experience to level up or upgrade your character.
3on3 is quick and fun, a lot of the game’s offense and defense comes down to timing and ability of your reaction to pass the one who’s guarding you. Once you get to the timing and knowing when you’ll release a shot and the best time when you try for a steal, the game will be more fun and interesting. But lacking of one of your teammate can disrupt that rhythm. A player who’s selfish on the court will not react even though you talk to him and because of that, the team may lose or may forfeit the game.
Despite the fact that your partner is often unreliable, the moments when your other teammate behaves according to plan or making good decision which is making you scores, it can lead to an impressive display of teamwork. Buying skills to make your character more agile and more dominating on the court is the other factor of the game. There’s definite feeling of accomplishment in the process of getting better at 3on3 freestyle. Finding a break to make a three pointer, disregarding traditional rules to shove your opponent away from the ball when they’re most vulnerable, or capitalizing on a fleeting opportunity for a flashy dunk all feel great, and smart plays are often rewarded with expressive, hype-inducing ceremonies or animations.

On the good side, it's pretty fun.  3v3 half court basketball with a colorful cast of cartoony guys and varied playstyles, with something for pretty much any kind of ball you want to play.  The graphics look nice, and it plays pretty well.
The actual gameplay is a lot of fun with a team that works together, and when you don't run into people who've invested money into it.
Which brings me to the bad side - it's pretty Pay to Win.  You can buy the in-game credits with real money, and credits are used for pretty much every aspect of powering up your guys.  You buy gatorade to level up, then you buy books to reset their level and get a new skill, also meaning you need to buy more levelup gatorade.  You buy tokens to level up your skills, making them objectively much better than their unlevelled counterparts, and the rate you earn credits at is a trickle compared to the all the combined costs.  You can definitely grind it out and earn your way up, but it's going to take a
time investment, and if you come up against someone who's sunk some cash into their guy to shortcut the grind, they're going to block, steal, and dunk on you like you're not even pushing buttons.
If it weren't monetized the way it is, I'd sing it's praises.  As it stands, blech.

There are two things in Tales of Maj'Eyal, that made me stop playing this game, and not invest money in more expansions:
1) Permanent socketing. Items can be imbued with gems, which add to the item's stats. Gems can be found and bought, and you can also find more powerful artifact gems. However, all item imbuing is permanent. The result was never using the good gems for imbuing good items, while anxiously wondering whether and when I should. Instead of a bonus, every found artifact became a reminder about potentially shooting myself in the foot. "Wanna imbue me? You know, it's permanent if you do. A better gem might be just around the corner. Better wait...but is it? You're constantly gimping yourself, you know..."
2) Extremely limited item transfer space. AFAIU, you'll get transfer space for one item for every 2 euros you've paid for the game. With the base game at 7 euros, that'd result in a massive quantity of 3 items you can transfer. However, you can find tens - or even hundreds of artifacts in one playthrough. Also, the transfer space can be reached in later game only, never allowing you the possibility of starting fresh characters with good quality equipment. The permanent socketing -issue raises its head in here as well, since different character classes require different items. "Used that nice artifact gem in the sword of your now-overleveled fighter? So bad, you can't transfer it to your new mage's staff now."
To conclude, if these issues were fixed, I'd gladly put more money in this game.

The concept is new and exciting, but the implementation is nothing short of awful.
- clunky, slow and ugly interface. Not evolving for the best either: the four scrolling arrows are a terrible idea, they clutter the screen even further.
- file saving time has gone from prohibitively slow to merely annoying
- contracts mechanics is either broken or insufficiently explained. Some ships that pass validation with flying colors won't be buildable from the spaceport screen for no apparent reason.
- some parts of ship construction are simply annoying chores, especially setting up the various wires and pipes or placing hatches.
What use is it to force the player to add the exact same vent to each cooling unit or weapon, really? Shouldn't they simply be part of the room to begin with?
As for the corridors, they could simply be "painted" instead of forcing the player to add dozens of little bits, each modification requiring yet another rewiring.
All these clunky little bits make the designs terribly painful to modify while the added fun value of picking the exact location of a water pipe or wiring the doors of every single hatch is highly debatable.
- still annoying bugs ins the ship editor: sometimes the parts won't display during placement until you switch decks, the "undo" feature never worked and seems to have been dropped in recent updates, the "wiring" system sometimes fails to work, ruining hours of design during the final chore of fixing the plumbing
- the validation missions suffer from the same annoting interface problems.
Selecting crew members is a pain, the visual indications are unreadable (where are the aliens? What happens during combat?)
The green thingie that obsures the screen each time you change game speed is a complete killjoy. Why not just put some speed indicator in the corner like a thousand other RTS games do?
Establishing the same routes for technicians and pilots in every single mission is very poor game design too. This should be part of the ship design process.
Actually, the interactive part of the game (testing ships) is such a no-brainer (see a malfunction / fire / alien / pirate, send some guys to deal with it) that I'd rather have an AI play it, and limit player input to defining operational procedures (technician routes, soldier placement...) so that the game remains about designing ships and the way they operate instead of turning into a clumsy clickfest.
Again the initial idea is great, but in its current state the game is just an exercise in frustration.

The Strategic layer is (Currently) interesting, Unfortunately while there are tutorials they gloss over a lot of what you need to know, and make completing many of the missions much harder then they need to be. The  interface needs the least work of the three “layers”. But it could be clearer on the types of contracts, some are missions which you need to assign one of your ships too, and the second is a “delivery” type mission where you deliver a single ship for a specific contract. Another issue with contracts is they disappear over time. Great, if they were being replaced with new missions, but not so much when they aren't. It would be great if there was a mission timer for contracts that time out and repeatable missions should indicate that they are. The travel range, sensor range, radio range, and the speed of the ships owned by your corporation could be better displayed on the map. Currently you right click to set both destination and mission (Type? Profile?) and it could be handled clearer, by simply have a drop down menu some where in the ship information at the bottom of the screen (although the current method does work). Mechanics wise, I think it needs the most work, and I hope to see much more in the future, But then the game is about designing and building ships and in that it does quite well.
I'm including the research in this layer, and my opinion is “Could be better”. The Actual  mechanic of research is realistic to a point. The Implementation is fair, but the Interface needs work, there is no summery screen where you can see where you are spending your money, to add or remove money you have to go to each category and manual add or remove money from each section. Which means if you are over spending on R&D there is no quick or easy way of removing or reducing the money spent.
The Tactical Layer, or the ship testing layer if you prefer, needs the least work mechanically, other then better time control it close to perfect at least for what it needs to be. Yes your characters have no AI, and no they shouldn't have any initiative, that is the point of doing the missions your self. Interface wise it needs a little work, Adding short cut keys (their might already be keys but if so I haven't found them) to correctly select your crew members, by type and by deck, and switching between them both by deck and type. Other then that the missions are clear in what you are trying to accomplish, and how you can go about doing so.
The last and most important layer to this game is the Design layer.
It comes in two screens, first is the contract selection screen, where it lists all the contracts available currently available in the game, from here you chose a contract and a hull and then move to the actual design screen. The Main issues here lie in that you can't easily tell the difference from the Mission type contracts and the Delivery type contracts, you have to guess from the value of the missions, (delivery being easier by far to accomplish then the Missions). My second concern is the lack of organization or at will sorting for missions and more importantly the Hulls. The Hulls seem to be listed in the order they were unlocked in, and you can't change their order or sort for a particular Hull at all, not that there is a large number of them (around 20 I think) but it is annoying. Ideally this could be eliminated by just temporally only listing Hulls that are required.
The second part of Design and probably the second most time consuming thing after running the missions yourself. Is the actual layout of the space craft. Here I think the interface is... fine. Its not spectacular, but other then one thing I don't know how it could be improved all that much. The one issue I have is it doesn't list the modules you need to meet the design “Objectives” it lists every thing else, and does have a drop down screen that says in each possible category its either OK, or Missing, but say the Objectives require 3 small shield generators, it doesn't say how many you have left to build or how many you have, which on the smaller ships is easy to find and count but on the larger ships..... I have yet to test if having say a medium radio instead of a small radio, meets the contract out side of the design area. I also want to point out that when you select No contract instead of modifying one how much Energy and Cooling you need do not show up.

I haven't played before Evolve went F2P, so I cannot comment on that transition, but WOW! This game is amazing.  The 4v1 aspect is pretty well balanced with a few notable exceptions (I'm looking at you, Wraith).  Everything in game can be earned for free--even the custom skins--although there is currently no option for monetizing the game at all.
Essentially, the game revolves around four Hunters battling a single Monster.  There's an array of Hunters to choose from, each of which fits one of four classes: Trapper, Assault, Support, and Medic.  Anyone familiar with TF2/Overwatch/any class-based shooter will immediately know what to expect from the later 3 classes (dmg, utility, and healing), while the Trapper focuses upon finding the monster and restricting the monsters abilities in combat, typically through some form of slow.  There's also a number of large Monsters to choose from, each with their own abilities and playstyle.
When the game starts, the hunters are significantly stronger than the monster.  As a result, the monster spends the first few minutes running and hiding and eating everything in sight in order to evolve into a bigger, badder, monster.  Evolving takes a short time, during which the monster is vulnerable to attacks from the hunters, so after eating enough the monster runs off and finds somewhere to hide.  After evolving, the Monster is now Stage 2--approximately equal in power with the 4 hunters.  If the Monster manages to eat even more, it can evolve to Stage 3--at which point it is significantly stronger than the hunters.  The hunters win by (you guessed it) killing the monster, while the monster wins by killing all four hunters simultaneously (there is an increasing respawn timer as the game progresses--so if some of the hunters manage to escape they can regroup and continue causing trouble for the monster) or by evolving to Stage 3 and destroying the Power Relay Building.  From my experience, nobody ever destroys the building however--it's either kill or be killed.
Victory as the hunters requires teamwork--coordinating with your fellow hunters on attack strategy and monster sightings is not only advised, but required for victory.  VOIP, while not technically required, is an enormous help--especially against the more skilled monsters.  Each class has a specific role to fill-though the roles sometimes overlap.  Some Medics can deal significant damage in addition to healing, while some Trappers might have weaponry to rival an Assault.
Monster victory requires a lot of thought against a skilled team of hunters--you need to keep moving so the hunters can't find you immediately, but if you can find an opening amidst the hunters you need to take it.  Plus there's fun  like shoving hunters off a cliff so that they land in a man-eating plant.  Heh heh heh.
With it's innovative gameplay, Evolve does have its share of balance problems.  While most of the Hunters feel relatively well-balanced, there is one monster who is currently unbalanced in pubs--Wraith.  Wraith has a decoy ability which creates a seemingly-invulnerable (it's not) double which attacks any nearby hunters.  It needs a nerf bad--something like making the decoy only run straight until attacked and lengthing cooldown while in combat--this would preserve the deceptive/mind games feel of the decoy while solving the current OP-ness of Wraith.  However, since the dev team has promised weekly updates (especially since the game just went F2P) you can expect a lot of balance changes in the upcoming weeks.
Pros:
-Innovating, thought-provoking gameplay
-Teamwork required to succeed
-Friendly community (I was a little surprised by this, but most people were rather helpful.  Nothing like many popular shooters like CS:GO or TF2)
-Frequent patches promised, so balance concerns should be addressed
Cons:
-Impossible to carry bad team mate(s) against a good/great monster
-Some balance issues
-People who already payed for the game will be disappointed because there are no more pay-walls and limited game modes while they address balance
-I wrote a long review that very few people will probably read completely.
Although the game is technically in beta (again), the gameplay is enough to get me to look past  its shortcomings--especially as they should be addressed in the near future.  If you haven't played Evolve yet, you need to give it a shot now.

Hot Damn!  I had this game in my library for some time and had never played it.  I was searching for a new military or sniper game to try and more or less picked this at random.
Wow!
It feels like Battlefield 2 and Sniper Elite 2 had a baby, but being made in Cryengine amped up the graphics.  The character and movement animations look and feel like DICE from the same era.   Facial and cutscene animation feels dated, but fits with the games producrion date. However, where Cryengine games really shine is the environment.  Instead of worrying about photorealism (foliage in particular) they made shape and interaction top notch.  With an "background" element like cover foliage, it is the right choice.  The overall environments feel realistic and have great depth and lighting. Jungle cover and Tibetan hills are atmospheric and believable.  Sarajevo feels like a city blighted by war.
AI is average (at normal didficulty, it may be tougher at higher levels), when alerted to your presence, the enemies attack and do not forget your presence if you hide.
The shooting feels great.  At normal difficulty a dot appears on the scope to give you ballistic guidance, at high difficulty it does not.  The timing is all you at both settings.  It feels very much like Sniper Elite in my opinion, in regard to the gun play.  Not a bad thing.  On the final kill of any area sweep the game display is a bullet time animation, no x-ray shots, but it is a nice way to mark area completion for the player.  As far as I can see you're not scored on where the bullet strikes the target, but the game does note the distance of your shots.
Like any good Call of Duty or Battlefield campaign, the story feels like it passes too quickly and like those titles, I will revisit it again.  One thing that strikes me as interesting, is that City Interactive was thoughtful enough to included refined controller support, when many major dev's omit it from their PC ports.  I am playing it with a Steam controller, so it doesn't really matter, but it is the thought that counts.
Definitely recommended if you see it on sale.  I actually pruchased it as party of a bundle, along with it's predecessor.  I will have to look into the next game in the series.

I grew up in the days right as the Playstation and N64 were released, so I have absolutely no nostalgia for the 2-D days. I'd played some and while I did indeed play on a Genesis and SNES I was far too young for the experience to leave much impact on me.
That being said, Salt and Sanctuary is slowly becoming one of my favorite games. Mechanically, it's a mix of Metroidvania and Soulsborne games. Aesthetically, it has a very dark, muted color palette with gorgeous and grotesque monster and backgrounds. Each area both looks unique and feels unique, with their own quirks and methods to get around. The story is minimal, but the over-arching story is less important than the backstories of the various locations in the game and in the world itself. These form the true narrative of the game. I found the music fairly nondescript in the places where it plays. I get that they were going for a minimalist, empty atmosphere, but I feel like they could have made the music stronger and it wouldn't have taken away from the atmosphere.
The only real strong negative I can put forward for the game is that there is no in-game world map. I don't necessarily need a 1:1 perfect replica of the world, just a reference for how the levels relate to one another and roughly where in the area they meet up. This game is massively underrated, and deserves so much more attention than it's seen.
The Souls games took off in a crazy way - this is 2D Dark Souls, and in fact it's better than that makes it sound.
The graphics are gorgeous, the gameplay is pure Dark Souls, but 2D and with much better platforming. The lore is really interesting, well written, this game has few faults.
Is it perfect? No, of course not. The skill tree is lacking, though that's only obvious after your first playthrough, and it's only annoying after your 5th or so. There's plenty of play styles to investigate. The platforming, while good, can be annoying. There's a few places in the game that really want to mess with you - disappearing platforms and forced fall damage.
The game is also really easy to cheese once you know how. Most games are, but for this kind of thing, where the challenge is half the fun, the cheese can be a little extreme.
The connectivity of the world is awesome, much better than anything Dark Souls did in that regard but I never hear anyone praising this game for it. All the mechanics are pure souls - parrying, collecting 'salt' after death, leveling up, covenants, bloodstains, etc. Not a complaining, I love all those things, and there is enough S&S character to the game so it doesn't seem like a 2D clone.
Still, fantastic game, just finished all the achievements, and wish there was a sequel.
If you like anything Soulsborne, Metroidvania, etc - get this game.

The First Tree isn't going to win awards based on its game play, game mechanics, level of polish, options menu, or anything else that normally defines a AAA game. There were many many frustrating (but not game breaking) quirks/bugs I found, including collision, obvious LoD pop in, same-y grass textures, running animation, and others that I can go on about. But yet, despite all that, it's a beautiful game. I spent a little bit under three hours playing it, but I was exploring and got lost once, so you can probably speedrun it in under an hour and a half, but please don't. Take your time and explore the world.
(Entire review is spoiler free)
The First Tree is a first person experience/walking simulator except you control the character in third person. The same sort of mechanics apply here: Walk/Run to a glowey spot and press E to interact with it, and you get a few sentences of dialogue/story, and you move onto the next one. There is no expressed or implied failure state, no game over, and no real reason to play it again. The basis of the story, is that the narrater woke up in the middle of the night and had a dream about this fox that is looking for her cubs. Each "level" (there's like four or five), is a big "bowl" of space, with invisible walls (that sometimes make no sense as to why you can't go past), with various obvious "go here for story" spots, and one exit point. Also in the levels, are little glowing star things, which tbh, I don't know why they're in there, other than to help guide the player to undiscovered locations yet (since the glow can be seen from far away and even through shrubbery). But, if you look closely and explore around, you can see discarded human stuff all around, things from a mattress to a police car to a fishing pole to an actual tank (actually, there's a few rendering bugs that I found: I found a fridge on its side, and if I looked through the bottom toward one of the sides, I could see through it, like the culling wasn't working properly. And same thing with the spoiler board on the last level: if I look at the front, it looks like it should, but if I look through it behind it, I can see through it). All the things laying around either give reference to, or give hints to expand on the story told by the narrater and his wife. Along the way, the fox does her plotline stuff, and the narrater comments on it saying "The fox saw this" "The fox did that".
There is some very very light platforming in here, but it's basically "see this wall with 8 strategically placed boulders jutting out, climb up to the top." And, since there is no fall damage, there is no penality for failing it. But, that brings me to a complaint that I have: The double jumping just isn't satisfying. And I think it has to do with the arc that the fox goes in when she jumps, and that you can only get a second jump within the first fraction of a second after you leave the ground, and even if you only jump once, you can't jump again past a certain point. This also makes climbing mountains really difficult and frustrating. The whole interaction of the fox's hitbox with the slope of the mountain makes it so you can't jump at all, but you can still move along the mountain, or slide downward and lose all progress. Now, to be fair, I don't remember the game forcing you to climb a cliff like this, I just did it to get a view of the world and because I was bored.
That's a problem with these sort of games, it keeps me engaged as long as I see a destination or am listening to audio logs, and once that's over, you're on your own to get to the next spot. The music is actually pretty good, a solid soundtrack, but it doesn't repeat at all. The song plays once at the begninning of the level and then stops after like fives minutes, so you're left with the rest of the 15+ mins in silence, with only the atmosphere of the sound effects to make my ears not bored. On the plus side, the fox runs sufficiently fast enough to cover the large levels in a reasonable amount of time.
Yeah, this game doesn't really have an options menu. One catchall graphic quality Low through Ultra, Resolution (does support 4K, which is a plus), AA 0x through 8x, Image effects, Fullscreen on/off, and Subtitles. That's it. It really needs some Level of Detail options for the user (or to make more of them), because the pop in was really obvious. Not distracting, but if you were looking down and moving toward a valley, you will be directly looking at many many trees popping in and being fuller as you grew closer.
I didn't really have any issue running this at a locked 60fps at 4K (monitor native res is 1440p), with my two GTX 980s. There were only one or two times when turning the camera, did I notice a small hiccup, for no apparent reason. Though, it's not really that much of a looker, so it's not that surprising, but it should be reported.
Somehow, despite all its flaws and things I've complained about, I still recommend it. It's a sad game that made me a little teary which was unexpected but not unwelcomed. It's an entertaining game that I don't regret playing at all. It's totally worth the $7-ish I spent for a one time, 2 and a half hour playthrough, and if you'll excuse me, I'm going to go call my parents. <3

Despite the lack of an avatar and all those fancy icons, I have many years of experience with various Paradox games, so I have some idea of what I'm talking about. This game sees some excellent improvements from HOI3, but they've changed a few things that did not need fixing:
1.) Naval Invasions are just far too easy and the AI goes completely mental with it the moment war is declared. Playing as Germany, in what world would the Brits ever invade via the Baltic in 1939?! It's illogical and almost impossible to defend as it takes massive amounts of micromanagement. Having a powerful fleet also doesn't seem to help much. PLEASE Paradox, bring back the basing & supply distance rules for fleets from HOI3 as well as the need to physically build transports and landing craft! This problem needs to be fixed NOW as it makes the game completely unenjoyable.
2.) Army Organisation is now over-simplified. It might have been time consuming for some, but organising your armies into corpses, armies and army groups made historical sense. With the much improved army AI, it would make absolute sense to reintroduce corpses as some tasks do not require an entire army. It should also be possible to issue seperate orders to various elements of an army / army group. (E.g. The Italian Army Group in East Africa should be able to guard the Southern and Western borders while smaller elements launch an offensive into French and British Somaliland respectively.) There also aren't enough commanders to go around should you wish to form large numbers of smaller "armies" to take on the multitude of tasks.

The playthrough of Sniper: Gh-... Wait...
The playthrough of Gunman: Testosterone Warrior took me 7 hours. It was a journey full of shooting at every corner (where the game didn't strictly forbid me to with harsh scripting), and of so much testosterone that that it'd make a MMA tournament look like the girl scouts.
If one looks for a game that has to do with actual sniping, look no further: This is absolutely not it, and the only game which is that is the ArmA series (with the right mods and missions and/or people to play with).
This game has about as much to do with being a sniper as Carmageddon has to do with being an everyday commuter by car. Unfortunately not only the gameplay - which pretty much forces you to shoot your way through most of it - has nothing to do with sniping, but neither does anything else the devs have put into this game.
It supposedly is about a "ghost" warrior. I presume that they mean a creator of ghosts, because there'll be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of them around after he's done murdering half of the country he's in. The things that one would think that "ghost" actually refers to are about as silly as the All Ghillied Up mission in COD4, although that game actually did it kind'a good.
The "ghostyness" of this game includes:
- Your spotter/buddy approaching a gate saying "We've got to be careful.", and when you as the player open the door he'll run through it (and the next 100 meters of who knows what) like it was the start signal for olympic 110m hurdles. Running around seems to be an important theme in sneaking, according to this game.
- Leaving a trail of bodies so rich and dense that a blind-deaf old man could track you down by the smell of blood and gunpowder alone.
- Careful sneaking to stay hidden (with the scripted AI), in places where the sun will show your shadows like huge silhouette figures against the wall beside you, rather than sneaking 2-3 meters away where there is room to sneak. Also shouting and arguing within earshot of the enemy is also fantastic stealth-behaviour.
- Having a 'sniper perch' inside of a building where the character leans through the window, instead of sitting well inside of the room to hide himself, seems to be preferable. No sport in being a sniper if the enemy can't see you, right?
- Firing with an unsuppressed Barrett rifle from just a few hundred meters so that everyone within at least a mile's radius ought to be able to locate you by the sound alone, not to mention all the dust-kickup from that muzzle brake.
- Having such a ghosty sight so that on the highest difficulty where you get no aim assist there is no scientific way to determine where to aim. The mils-scale on the sight is completely useless, so you just have to wing it and hope you hit.
Despite all the above the game is almost okay though, as long as one expects an on-rails shooter. Although the game is heavily scripted and basically breaks if you don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥in the order you are supposed to, it plays quite fine if you stick to the script. It is testosterone-pumped to the point of stupidity; the characters are so full of it that they almost explode, but main grips of the story are still good enough to feel plausible and game-progressing. The game can be pretty tricky on the hardest difficulty too because almost all your UI-help from the easier modes is gone, so finding that particular object or guy to shoot that your buddies are asking you to pop can be very hard sometimes.
The game is flawed. Pretty darn flawed actually. But for the €2 I paid for it on this summer sale I don't feel like I was tricked. I definitely got my money's worth of fun, but it would be senseless to buy this game for its full €10.

DISCLAIMER: I have only played single player up to Act 3
Sniper Ghost Warrior 2 contains the largest amount of annoying mechanics and design choices that I have ever encountered in a video game.
First let's look at positives:
- The only series with the modern setting that is focused on sniping
- Good lighting, interesting environents although textures are subpar
Here is a short list of what's wrong:
- Enemy detection is rather random, sometimes they will notice the kill sometimes they will not.
- Game is linear to the fault
- VERY SCRIPTED, enemies pop in when objectives change, if you take out the wrong solider then you can't kill the rest "quietly"
- Storywriting is rather poor, I didn't expect much when going into this game but come on.
- Camera during the .50 cal moments forces you to look at one area.
- Shots sometimes don't connect even though you can see a bullet hole right where the enemy head was.
- Checkpoints... this became VERY annoying combined with all above, heard this unskipable dialouge once? Well listen again. Beat this annoying section once? Well I heard you like to play those 15 minutes again.
Here are some things that I found stupid/inconvinent
- Helmeted enemies survive a sniper shot from 300 meters, I somehow disbelieve that this range with this caliber is survivable.
- .50 Caliber UNSUPRESSED shots are not heard in a compound 400 meters away from you.
- Expert mode difficulty aiming is rather arbitiary, getting one shots from beyond 300 meters is very difficult but that may just be me sucking at the game.
- You cannot pick up an assault rifle, you are stuck with a sniper rifle/pistol combo (At least as long as Act 3 not sure what happens after/during it)
Play this game if you desperatly need to play a modern sniper game with call of duty style storytelling and atmosphere.

UPDATE for STAGE 2
I'm still really enjoying this game. In retrospect, the DLC decisions 2K made really shot them in the foot. However, it's still a fun game and definitely worth your time. It maintains an interesting dynamic in a playing field filled w/ such games.
I'm not really put-out by the loss of badges and whatnot from my previous playtime as a Founder b/c I don't care about my epeen, but I do really hope they bring the maps they chose to delete back. Those are a real loss to the game.
Original Review Dated Feb 12, 2015 Below:
Putting the DLC decisions of the publisher aside, I am really enjoying this game. I paid $40 for it during a sale and I feel like I'm getting my money's worth.
I may be enjoying it simply b/c of a lucky confluence of events. I typically only play single-player games, but I've been wanting to bust into the MP realm. Evolve came around just when I needed a MP title whose art and gameplay appealed to me.
I have found Evolve to be a great starting place b/c it allows me to choose whether I'm playing "SP" or MP. If I feel like playing alone and not worrying about my team, I play a few rounds as the monster, which I'm enjoying immensely. All of the monsters are very satisfying to play and playing a game as an asymetrical character is a novel experience, at least for me. I have found it to be a really fun combination of offensive and defensive play. If I feel like playing w/ others, I play as the hunters. I've found this style of play to be less enjoyable, but I believe that's simply my preference for playing alone. Regardless, if you manage to have some friends or get a competent team, the hunters can be incredibly fun to play too. I've played 3 of the 4 classes enough to say that I've found each to be unique and that each requires tailoring my play-style to the class; no blanket strategy works for all classes, which is as it should be.
I haven't noticed any bugs or glitches beyond an intermittent inability to connect to 2K's profile services, but this is always resolved through retrying the connection. I have experienced DCs and lag in just a few games, but it was enough so that everyone in the game reported experiencing it and, when DCs occurred, the whole team was dumped to the lobby. This really hasn't impeded my playing b/c it is so infrequent.
The maps and game modes available in-game are diverse enough to make me feel like I'm not cycling the same maps and play-style over and over again. I like Evacuation mode in particular in which the players engage in a 5 map competition to see who can win best out of 5 using various game modes. However, it seems like everyone else is just playing Skirmish, which is the game's 1-off match-up. I do find some of the maps to be on the small side, particularly when I play the monster; however, I understand that this is probably intentional to spur a more heated exchange b/w monster and hunters.
A great deal of the discussion in the game's forums is in regards to balancing in the game. I don't think I'm expert enough at any character or game mode to say any one is definitely OP in a given situation or a game mode is impossible as a particular character. I win some, I lose some and no one character or game mode seems to poke its head above the crowd as OP enough to break the game, in my opinion.
The publishers have a ton of DLC planned and already implemented, regarding which you can find exhaustive discussion elsewhere. I don't care for cosmetic DLC in any game and I just choose not to purchase it and it's too early to make judgments regarding content DLC. Personally, I would like to see larger maps, possibly w/ additional mechanics to off-set any advantage the monster gains from increased maneuvering room.
I'm eager to see what this game will show us in the future, particularly in the way of new monsters and new maps.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

A really inferior port of what looks to have been an excellent game otherwise. There are an incredible amount of graphical and audio glitches, such as music cutting out and not repeating; characters' lines cutting out mid-sentence or just not saying them altogether; preset animations clipping through the environment or through characters; etc.
Plus, a lot of depth from the original game has been stripped; there are no different weapons, and bosses no longer really require skill other than typing speed. I was left feeling like I had missed a lot of interesting gameplay elements from the original game.
Plus, as to be expected, playing the actual House of the Dead game rather than the Typing of the Dead version is completely worthless. It has all the depth that was stripped out of Typing of the Dead, but since it's controlled with your mouse rather than a light gun, it becomes sluggish and unfun to play.
A good game in concept, especially considering the popularity of the original Typing of the Dead, but the poor optimization and lazy stripping of depth really kills what could have made this game a worthy sequel.

A modified version of The House of the Dead: Overkill in which you kill zombies (Sorry, I mean mutants) by typing words, how can it get any more awesome than that? It's based on the Extended Cut version of the game, which means it has redone graphics and two extra levels when compared to the original Wii release. If you get bored of typing, you can also play the entire shooting version of the game, which works pretty differently, meaning you basically get two games for the price of one.
It must be said that the typing side of the game isn't nearly as interesting or unique as the original Typing of the Dead, boss fights don't have fun gimmicks like answering questions correctly or being forced not to make any errors, and the difficulty remains pretty low through the whole game, even on the hardest difficulty, while in the original it was adjusted depending on how well you were doing. Still heavily recommended, just try to play the original as well somehow, because it's definitely better.

If for some reason you do not want to use your keyboard, you also get a full port of HOUSE of the Dead: Overkill, the original shooting version. Actually, it's the updated Extended Cut with 2 extra levels not in the original Wii version.
Both versions of the game have a very grindhouse feel, and are not for the squemish or easily offended in terms of both gore and langauge. Yes, unlike the original Typing of the Dead, this version has not been made kid-friendly, nor have the guns been replaced by Dreamcast powered keyboards.
Another minor negative is the visuals; there are few graphical options and the game is 720p only. On the flip side, this does mean the game should run well on less powerful hardware.
Aside from these niggling issues, I would definitely recommend giving this a shot. Even if you aren't interested in the typing gimmick, you get the original shooting version anyway, so everyone wins!

If you've played Undertale, you'll love this game. It's like that but on crack.
If you haven't played Undertale (which you should regardless of how bad the fanbase is), then this game is one of those games that uses fourth wall breaking as a main game mechanic. If you're into that, you'll be into this.
I don't want to say too much about this, because it's best experienced with as little information as possible.
But anyways, money well spent on this one.

If you want to play a game that's not only for your desktop, this is it.

So, to get it out of the way; yes, I only played 3 hours, yes, this game is very short !BUT! it's also so worth its money.
Granted, I bought it at 5,99€, which is still not that cheap for a game that's only 4 hours long and, here's the catch, meant to only be played ONCE!
So why is this game great? Usually I'm a bit sceptical when it comes to RPG/Game Maker type games, mainly, because there's a lot of reading too much written dialouge and basically just strolling around until the story is over, much like a visual novel. Not my cup of tea.
But with OneShot, you'll not only get an interesting and enticing story, but also very well crafted characters, and such a strange and unfamiliar world, that it will make you want to explore everything on your own terms and soak as much of it in as you can.
The artwork is not only super cute, but also so well drawn, that I couldn't help to hit the screenshot button every other moment.
Let's talk about the gameplay; The game plays like your typical RPG Maker style game, with a top down perspective, a run button and an interaction button, so nothing special there.
Let's rather talk about the aspect, which impressed me the most, besides the story; The puzzles. Now, the puzzles itself aren't really challenging, but let me tell you, they got REALLY creative with some of those.
To put it mildly; you'll have to not only interact withing the game world, but rather WITH THE GAME ITSELF!
I don't wanna spoil it, but it just made me really excited and kinda feel like a real detective/puzzle solver. Maybe I'm the only one who got that feeling out of it, but oh well, I just got so carried away...
And so yeah, this is my review of OneShot, coming straight from the heart. I don't often write reviews, but I felt this game deserved it, and it touched me in a spot, where only a few games managed to do so before (i.e. Journey or Child of Light).
So yeah, I would definitely buy this game, even more so now, that it's 40% off (all hail Lord Gaben!). I will always remember those few hours I got to spend with this little piece of software, where you really could feel the commitment and love put into every byte of it.
And here's a little spoiler for all the people who are afraid, because it's only meant to be played this once:
Thank you for reading thorugh this whole thing. I really hope I convinced you to try the game, and I really hope you're having a great day!
Have fun!

It's no Undertale, but it is in the style of Undertale and has a very different theme to it that differentiates the two. There are puzzles, but no combat whatsoever; this isn't a problem. I felt like the puzzles weren't terribly difficult, but a good number of them had an... external... mechanic that I just loved and wish I saw more of.
Where Undertale is very comedy based with dark undertones/overtones and tells its story in a way that leaves you feeling upset with yourself, OneShot is very lighthearted but dark in an entirely different way; with the comedy taking a backseat and disappearing entirely with time. You're left feeling upset, but now you're upset with the cards you were dealt and the options you couldn't take (not a bad thing, I mean this in a good way).
I didn't find Niko very relatable to myself, but he/she(she) reminded me a lot of someone I know, and I feel like most people would make this same connection. Niko is very young, but definitely has an understanding of someone just a bit older. I don't know if I'd say I bonded with Niko, but I did feel like I understood his/her(her) character a lot better by the end of the game.
Like undertale, the game isn't for everyone. I would only recommend it to someone looking for a good story. Anyone who isn't interested in story will get tired of the game almost immediately. I think the #1 question to ask is "do you like undertale?" and if the answer is anything but "yes" or "yeah, but not the combat" - I unfortunately can't recommend it.
To the devs: thank you so much for making such a touching story. I hope you make even more, I won't have any doubts about getting the next one if/when it comes out.

Do you want to play as a raging turtle berserker, or perhaps a skeleton who has mastered the art of life absorption? Do you like games with hundreds of mods? Do you enjoy replaying a game hundreds of times, yet it feels completely fresh each time? Do you want to get hundreds of hours of content out of a game that goes on sale for a couple dollars? Then Tales of Maj'Eyal is the game for you.

If you're looking at this game and its reviews, you probably have certain curiosity and interest in the "old style" or "true" Roguelike games. You might've tried some but have been put off by their sheer complexity and extremely steep learning curve, so you've come looking for something a bit less complex, something that offers a good entry to the genre.
So the question is whether this game can be considered as such?
In my personal opinion, yes it can.
It combines many elements from roguelikes (such as random generation, permanent death, statistical minmaxing, variety)
and elements from modern (RPG) games (such as UI&actionbar, character&story progression)
For a new player the system will feel familiar and accessible enough to not put off by it while still offering deeply strategic and intricate systems for more advanced players.

I would just sit, sip my coffee, and watch the beams of light make stars in the shadows from the trees. The music selection is perfect. There are a lot of negative reviews for this game, but as someone who's been on a Navy ship and done some engineering, I find it entertaining.
The main complaint I see is people can't put a ship together. Play the tutorials. It's pretty easy, and once you put your ship through its paces in the trials all those design decisions actually matter, which is immensely satisfying (and puts you in a position where you think really hard about redesigning the whole ship to be more functional).
If you enjoy setting up processes and thinking about how things work together, and a little business simulation, give it a whirl, particularly on sale. If you're looking for something fast and furious, this is probably not for you.

The good:
* Runs well on a low-end system.
* Once you've run the tutorial the game has a pretty simple and intuative interface.
* Reminds me a bit of when I designed spaceships with GURPS Space back in the 1990s.
The bad:
* I didn't have stability issues, but the game takes a long time to load and save on a reasonably high-end desktop. Like the load-save stack in the program is horribly ineffecient. Maybe it's doing something like parsing compressed XML files, which I've had slow other programs to a crawl before.
* I managed to make a ship, which was pretty fun to do honestly, but I couldn't figure out how to actually play the ship in the simulator. That might have been because I was trying to go beyond the tutorial's limitations.
* The tutorial needs better visuals for navigation. It has a handful of generic symbols that overlap the info it's trying to show you or simply doesn't point to what it's supposed to point to.
* While it can run on a low end system, I was playing on a Surface Pro 3, which all but requires you to use scaling, and the game recogized the scaling was active but scaled poorly.
The Ugly:
* Overall has a rough, unfinished feel even for a beta. I wish game companies would get games into a more playable state before putting them onto Early Access. Having major, and sometimes fatal, problems for sometimes dumb reasons hurts not only the game's reputation but also the reputation of Early Access in general.

Taking the formula of the original Typing of the Dead and putting it into the Typing Of The Dead Overkill game is not a bad thing. It's a nice game to practice typing skills with, or just relax while blasting away some zombies while making your keyboard sound like a machinegun.
There are, however, downsides to this iteration of the series. There are no mid-level missions like "Kill X zombies in Y seconds" or branching paths. Also sadly missing is the breakdown of how you did compared to previous runs. Gone also are the rank per kill depending on typing speed. And compared to House of the Dead 2 (Typing of the dead), there are more cutscenes which go on for longer. Not that any of these points are downright bad things, but they're different enough that you may want to consider if this is the entry for you.
Instead of per-kill ranking which will give you different scores depending on the speed of your typing, instead you're expected to get a "goregasm" running. Basically a long combo without getting hit or making mistakes.
Also it's now possible to do headshots in the regular mode. With each zombie to kill you may make one mistake. While it will not count as a headshot and will thus give you less points, it will still allow you to carry on your score multiplier.
There is a Hardcore mode you can enable though which turns the difficulty up. When enabled any mistake will not only reset your multiplier immediately, it'll also give the zombie you were shooting a whole new word, forcing you to start over. And just to further up the difficulty: While normal mode doesn't care about punctuation, spaces and caps, Hardcode requires you to not only type perfectly, but also use shift, space and various punctuation. A step up in difficulty from the original House of the Dead.
The House of the Dead series has never been a particularly well told series, relying on plenty of cheese to go through the cutscenes. This entry however seems to ditch the downright silly plotline in favour of a grindhouse style story with an ever swearing bada** cop and A mysterious secret agent, oh and of course the tough as nails chick making an appearance a few times. If you can enjoy the swearing and general parody on this kind of movie you might find yourself enjoying the plotline of the game. If not you'll be cringing often, or feeling downright bored and hitting the key to skip the cutscenes as soon as possible.
Also included is the original House Of The Dead Overkill game, though controlled with mouse instead of light gun. And this mode still has the Director's Cut mode which extends the levels considerably. This mode is sadly missing from the typing part of the game.
In all, The Typing of the Dead: Overkill is a fun distraction if you like typing games. It's not as boring as many other typing tutors. The sentences typed aren't as unintentionally hillarious as the original game. In my opinion, it's a step to the side rather than a significant step forward or backwards in the series.
I can recommend it to those who want a bit more variety than the original Typing of the Dead, and to anyone who wants to try the series and can't find the original. However it is by no means a game you must own, merely a fun dictraction if you like to type.

Okay. I played this game exactly once (and that was too many times).
Strike One: I tried to play with two other guys. The matchmaking kicked both of my party members (or a portion of them) every single time we tried to queue for a match. I could not play with my own friends.
Strike Two: I was unable to pick my class/role. I was able to tell the game which of the roles I was most interested in. First and only game I played in? It picked my 4th desired role. Are you effing kidding me?
Strike Three: I was able to get matchmaked into a game where this guy had a monster that wiped us out in 15 seconds (wraith I think?). How is this even possible? My first match lasted exactly 35 seconds.
So in summary. If you are looking for a game that matches you up as a class you didn't want to play in, with a group of players you didn't want to play with.... Evolve is absolutely the game for you (if you like wasting 15 minutes of configuration time just to get into 35 second matches).
Best of Luck and I hope anyone involved in the making of this game gets sent to North Korea to design family friendly themeparks.

The game is actually alright. Im the first one to write a review for this game, and I might be the first or second person to actually buy the game. It was 69 cents ($1 without sale) so I decided to buy it.
The concept is interesting and is really fun for a casual game and its price. I can tell that it's mostly just a test game for the devs. This might just be a prototype or something, but it's still good. There are, however, a few flaws. There is no save option that I am aware of. If you mess up, you die. You have to start from the very beginning. At the time of writing this I think I've only made it to level 8. But how many levels ARE there? I would be really♥♥♥♥♥♥if I found out that the one level that I messed up on was the LAST one, and I had to do the game all over again. Now maybe make an OPTION for this, but as far as Im concerned, if you mess up, you have to restart the game.
Overall, the game is fun, addictive and very hard. It's worth buying if you like a challenge. If you're looking for a game where you can run through levels and relax, just find a different game.
I still recommend it, because as I've said, it's still fun and addictive.
